JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Imam Nakhmatullaev; Svjatoslav Jakovlev; Eric Juergens; Jaan Juergens; Ilja Karunas; Juri Karunas; Jason Onoufrienko; Renek Tiku; Vladislav Turaskin; Kevin Valdhans; Vjatseslav Zogolev (members of a Russia-based transnational criminal organization controlling nominee-owned DME companies); Hong Yuen Mak a/k/a 'Joe Mak' (pharmacy owner); Boris Manaev (owner, BB Medical Equipment Inc.); Mujjahid Huq (licensed pharmacist and pharmacy owner); Joseph Tony Brown-Arkah (owner, American Medical Centers Suboxone clinic)
State_County: New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Queens County; New York - Erie County (Buffalo); New York - Nassau County (Lynbrook); New York - Suffolk County (Halesite); Florida - Broward County (Plantation)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicare Supplemental Insurers (private health insurance companies); Medicaid
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Device, DME; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Drug_Prescriptions; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: In the lead 'Operation Gold Rush' case, a Russia-based organization bought dozens of existing DME companies through paid foreign-national nominee owners and fabricated corporate records to hide true control, then used stolen identities and personal information of more than one million Americans to rapidly submit over $10.6 billion in false DME claims to Medicare and Medicare Supplemental Insurers, collecting about $900 million from supplemental insurers and $41 million from Medicare before laundering the proceeds through U.S. bank accounts, shell companies, overseas banks and cryptocurrency; approximately $27.7 million has been seized. Four other separately charged EDNY defendants in the same takedown allegedly paid gift-card kickbacks for fake OTC-card transactions (over $1 million, guilty plea), billed $8.2 million for medically unnecessary DME, billed Medicare/Medicaid $2.1 million for drugs never dispensed while concealing pharmacy ownership, and billed $85 million for Suboxone-clinic services provided by unlicensed or excluded providers with prescriptions written sight-unseen plus associated lab testing.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the ownership-change filings (CMS-855S change of information) for dozens of previously dormant DME suppliers show foreign-national nominee owners, shared addresses/phones/bank accounts, notary and corporate-record reuse, and IP/device overlap in the billing portal — all visible before any claim pays. Post-enrolment, each acquired supplier shows an abrupt jump from near-zero to very high claim volume within weeks, beneficiaries scattered nationwide with no geographic relation to the supplier, beneficiaries whose identities appear simultaneously at many unrelated suppliers, and no matching ordering-physician encounter history. Supplemental-insurer exposure is detectable by cross-plan matching of the same beneficiary/HICN-item combinations paying under crossover logic.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment graph keyed on supplier TIN/NPI linking owners, authorized officials, addresses, phones, bank routing/account, EFT forms, notaries, portal IP and device fingerprints; fire a pre-payment payment-suspension and site-visit review when a control-change event coincides with graph clustering across multiple suppliers or foreign-nominee indicators. Add a new-owner velocity edit: for any supplier within a defined window of an ownership change, hold claims for prepay review when weekly billed dollars or unique-beneficiary count exceed the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers, when beneficiary residence is outside the supplier's normal service radius, or when no corresponding ordering-provider encounter exists in claims history. Feed crossover files to supplemental insurers so the same suspension propagates, and run an identity-abuse detector flagging beneficiaries billed by an unusual number of unrelated DME suppliers in a short period.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
SchemeSummary: Annual summary press release, not a single case: the office reports charging dozens of defendants for health care fraud causing billions in intended losses to Medicare and other federal programs, involving fraudulent billing, kickbacks, and diverted or adulterated pharmaceuticals, with unspecified criminal forfeiture and restitution ordered. No individual defendant, amount, or conduct period is identified.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual round-up press release, not a single case: no defendant, amount, service line or conduct period is identified, so no case-specific pre-payment signal can be reconstructed. The nearest payer-side route is the generic portfolio surveillance that the underlying cases would each have triggered (billing-volume outliers, kickback-linked referral concentration, and drug-diversion/pedigree gaps).
FeaturesToCreate: Maintain a standing provider-level outlier engine (billed dollars, service mix, beneficiary sharing, referral concentration versus same-specialty peers) with auto-escalation to prepay review, plus a pharmaceutical pedigree/supply-chain check that compares dispensed NDC volume against wholesaler acquisition records. No case-specific control can be designed from this release.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Jerome Sydney Heyward (North Charleston City Councilmember); Sandino Savalas Moses (North Charleston City Councilmember); Mike A. Brown (North Charleston City Council Member); Donavan Laval Moten (founder of Core4Success Foundation); Aaron Charles-Lee Hicks; Hason Tatorian "Tory" Fields; Rose Emily Lorenzo; Michelle Stent-Hilton (non-profit affiliate and personal assistant to Heyward)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Three North Charleston city councilmen and five associates were charged in bribery, extortion, kickback and money laundering schemes: a councilman extorted a businessman for payments in exchange for official action; councilmen Heyward, Brown and Moses solicited/accepted bribes from Hicks and Fields (acting for a company) in exchange for supporting rezoning of the Baker Hospital site; and Heyward conspired with nonprofit operators Moten and Stent-Hilton to kick back to him a portion of City violence-reduction grant funds awarded to their nonprofits, laundering the kickbacks through intermediary Rose Lorenzo. Four defendants agreed to plead guilty; four were indicted, with no dollar amounts stated.
WaysToIdentify: This is public-corruption, extortion and grant-embezzlement conduct against a municipality and its violence-reduction grant program; there is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, so no prepay claims control applies. The detectable route is grant-side: nonprofit subrecipients whose expense reports include payments to intermediaries or entities tied to the awarding officials, and vendor/official relationship conflicts disclosed (or not) at award.
FeaturesToCreate: For grant and contract programs, build an award-time conflict screen matching subrecipient officers, addresses and bank accounts against elected officials, their relatives and their affiliated entities, and hold disbursement pending review on a match. Add a drawdown analytic flagging subrecipient payments to pass-through individuals or newly formed intermediaries with no service deliverable; no payer claims edit applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Michael Procopio (leader of South Philadelphia's '10th and O Crew')
SchemeSummary: Procopio obtained prescription oxycodone pills from area doctors' offices and unlawfully distributed them on Philadelphia streets through a network of intermediaries; he admitted distributing approximately 14,925 milligrams of oxycodone, and a search of his home found oxycodone and Adderall hidden in a safe concealed in a hollowed-out dictionary.
WaysToIdentify: This is street-level diversion and distribution of oxycodone obtained from physician offices, prosecuted criminally; there is no billed claim by the defendant, so it is not catchable at adjudication of his claims. The payer-adjacent signal sits with the source practices: controlled-substance inventory/dispensing records that do not reconcile with acquisition, and PDMP patterns showing individuals collecting oxycodone across multiple prescribers with cash payment and early refills.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a PDMP/pharmacy analytic at the beneficiary level computing distinct prescribers and pharmacies for schedule II opioids, cash-pay share and days-supply overlap, firing a review referral and prior-authorization lock-in above the calibrated percentile. For practices, reconcile DEA-222/wholesaler acquisition against documented administrations and dispensings and open an inventory audit on unexplained shortfall; no prepay claim edit reaches the street sales themselves.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Community Options, Inc. (New Jersey not-for-profit providing oversight and centralized billing); Community Options New York, Inc. (New York not-for-profit provider of Day Habilitation services)
State_County: New York - New York County (Manhattan); New York (statewide); New Jersey
SchemeSummary: Defendants billed the New York Medicaid Program for Day Habilitation services for adults with developmental disabilities that were not delivered or documented in compliance with OPWDD requirements (inadequate policies and employee training led to deficient documentation), and after non-routine internal reviews identified Medicaid overpayments, they failed to report and return them. Resolved by a $5,016,626.11 total FCA settlement ($2,148,540.37 federal, $2,868,085.74 to New York State) plus an HHS-OIG Corporate Integrity Agreement, arising from a sealed qui tam suit the government joined.
WaysToIdentify: Day Habilitation billing is unit-based against OPWDD-required service documentation and staffing ratios, so the payer can compare billed units per participant per day against the provider's staff schedules, attendance records and habilitation-plan-authorized units before paying. The failure-to-return element is visible when the provider's own internal review findings, self-disclosure log and 60-day-report activity show no corresponding adjustment or voided claims after an identified overpayment. Retention is otherwise a post-payment finding reachable via credit-balance/self-audit review.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit at the participant-day level: deny or pend Day Hab units exceeding plan-authorized units, exceeding attendance-record days, or implying staff-to-participant ratios inconsistent with submitted staffing rosters, with a documentation request for service notes on pend. Add a provider-level reconciliation job that compares certified self-audit/internal-review findings and CIA reportable-event submissions to actual voided/adjusted claims and refunds, firing an overpayment-recovery and enrolment-condition flag when identified dollars are not returned within the statutory window.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Sanjeev Kumar (gynecologist)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a Memphis gynecologist performed medically unnecessary gynecologic procedures on patients using reused 'single use' or improperly reprocessed devices held in insanitary conditions, then billed Medicare and Medicaid as if the procedures were medically necessary and as if a new or properly reprocessed device had been used for each procedure.
WaysToIdentify: Single-use device reuse shows up as a mismatch between procedure volume and the practice's purchase records for the disposable device — the payer can require and audit invoice/serial-number support against the number of procedures billed. Medical necessity is testable at adjudication from diagnosis support, prior-visit indication documentation and abnormally high per-patient procedure frequency for the same gynecologic procedure versus same-specialty peers. Infection-control and reprocessing violations typically surface post-payment via survey/complaint data, which should trigger retrospective claim review.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a supply-reconciliation check: for procedures dependent on a billed or bundled single-use device, compare procedure counts per NPI per period against distributor purchase volume obtained via documentation request, and pend claims when procedures exceed devices purchased. Add a prepay frequency/necessity edit at the patient level for repeat gynecologic procedures without qualifying diagnosis or interval documentation, and an automatic prepay-review flag when licensure, survey or infection-control adverse findings post to the provider record.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
FraudEntity: Mi Ok Song Bruining (clinical social worker and supervisor at Recovery Connections Centers of America, Inc.); Recovery Connections Centers of America, Inc. (RCCA)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; other private health insurers
SchemeSummary: As a supervisor at an addiction treatment center, Bruining billed Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for 45-minute psychotherapy/counseling sessions when patients were actually seen for only 5-10 minutes (sometimes a one-question conversation), and directed staff to record 45-minute intervals without AM/PM designations and to copy-and-paste prior visit notes so the volume of impossible same-hour sessions would not be apparent, yielding more than $3.5 million in fraudulent claims.
WaysToIdentify: Time-based psychotherapy codes let the payer reconstruct each rendering clinician's day: summing billed session minutes per NPI per date produces impossible workdays, and the missing AM/PM convention leaves multiple 45-minute sessions colliding in the same hour. Copy-forward notes are detectable by textual near-duplication across a patient's sequential visits once records are requested, and appointment/EHR timestamps or facility sign-in logs contradict the billed durations.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit computing, per rendering NPI per service date, total billed time-based units and detecting overlapping session time windows; deny or pend claims when summed minutes exceed a plausible workday or when time windows overlap. Add a documentation-request trigger and note-similarity analytic (hashing/near-duplicate scoring of progress notes across a patient's visits and across patients on the same date) with downcoding to the shorter-duration code or payment suspension where duplication and duration collisions co-occur.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Sola, Inc. (operator of adult residential group homes)
PayerName: Medicaid (Virginia Department of Medical Assistance Services)
SchemeSummary: Sola, Inc., which operated adult residential group homes, allegedly billed Virginia Medicaid (DMAS) for skilled and other nursing services in units of time that exceeded the hours actually worked by its nurses as documented on their time sheets, overbilling $641,396.11 for services impossible to have been performed; it paid $2 million to resolve the civil claims.
WaysToIdentify: Billed nursing time units per licensed nurse per date can be summed across all patients and compared to payroll/timesheet hours, which the provider must retain; totals exceeding hours worked or exceeding a feasible shift are visible before payment. Overlapping units for the same nurse across different group-home residents at the same clock time is a second adjudication-time signal, as is billing skilled nursing on dates a licensed nurse was not scheduled.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit at rendering-nurse-per-date level: aggregate all time units billed across residents, flag totals above a feasible shift ceiling or with overlapping time windows, and pend with a request for timesheets/payroll and shift schedules. Add a periodic reconciliation comparing billed nursing hours to submitted payroll hours per facility and per licensed staff, generating overpayment recovery and prepay review when billed hours exceed paid hours.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Aesculap Implant Systems, LLC (medical device company)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Aesculap sold the VEGA Knee System to physicians and hospitals while knowing bone cement did not properly adhere to the implant, causing premature loosening and revision surgeries, and failed to record or report adverse events, resulting in Medicare and Medicaid claims for devices that were not reasonable and necessary; it also paid a Georgia orthopedic surgeon consulting fees, free international travel and entertainment to induce use of the Vega, and separately distributed two devices (ELAN-4 Air Drill and JS Series SterilContainer S2) without FDA clearance after an employee forged clearance documents.
WaysToIdentify: The FDA-clearance element is checkable at coding/coverage setup: a payer can validate that every implant or instrument catalog number billed maps to an active 510(k)/PMA record and refuse coverage for uncleared codes. Device failure signals are visible in claims as an elevated short-interval revision/removal rate for the specific implant identified by UDI/device identifier on the hospital claim, and the kickback element is visible by matching Open Payments consulting/travel/entertainment transfers from the manufacturer to the volume of that implant used by the surgeon.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a device-identifier gate: require UDI/catalog number on implant and high-cost instrument claims, validate it against FDA clearance and GUDID at adjudication, and deny when no active clearance exists. Add a device-outlier surveillance job computing revision-within-interval rates per device identifier versus comparable implants, triggering coverage review and post-payment recovery; and an Open Payments-linked analytic flagging surgeons whose use share of one manufacturer's implant exceeds the calibrated percentile while receiving above-peer transfers, routing to prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Aesculap Implant Systems LLC (medical device manufacturer/distributor)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Aesculap sold its VEGA Knee System prosthetic implants to U.S. physicians and hospitals while knowing bone cement did not properly adhere and the device would loosen and fail prematurely at a higher than acceptable rate, causing claims for non-reasonable/necessary implants and revision surgeries to be billed to Medicare and Medicaid; it also paid a Georgia orthopedic surgeon consulting fees, free international travel and entertainment to induce use of the Vega, and separately distributed two devices (ELAN-4 Air Drill and JS Series SterilContainer S2) after an employee forged FDA clearance documents (employee previously pleaded guilty and was imprisoned). Whistleblowers Marien and McGee receive $4,475,000 of the $38.5M settlement.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion matter: uncleared devices can be caught at adjudication by validating the billed device identifier against FDA clearance records, and premature-failure risk is observable in claims as an above-expected revision or removal rate within a short interval for one implant's UDI. The kickback inducement is observable by joining Open Payments consulting fees, travel and entertainment from the manufacturer to the surgeon's implant-selection share and case volume.
FeaturesToCreate: Require and validate UDI/catalog identifiers on implant claims against GUDID/FDA clearance status, denying claims for devices with no active clearance and pending those with mismatched identifiers. Run device-level revision-rate surveillance (revisions per implant-year by device identifier versus peer implants) that opens coverage reconsideration and recovery, and an Open Payments-to-utilization correlation flag on surgeons for prepay review and a documentation request on medical necessity.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Agendia, Inc. (molecular diagnostics company); Knoxville Comprehensive Breast Center, PLLC; Knoxville Dermatopathology Laboratory, LLC
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Federal Employees Health Benefits Program; other government payors
SchemeSummary: Agendia allegedly caused referring providers to order MammaPrint breast-cancer genomic tests through standing/automatic orders that were not reasonable or medically necessary, and induced referrals with extravagant dinners, improper honoraria, gift cards, per-referral and monthly flat-rate payments, then billed Medicare, Medicaid and other government payors; KCBC and KDL allegedly participated in generating the tainted referrals. Settlements total at least $3,250,000 (Agendia), $322,500 (KCBC) and $207,500 (KDL), with possible additional payments if Agendia is sold.
WaysToIdentify: Standing/automatic orders show up as near-identical ordering patterns: the same test billed for a very high share of a referrer's eligible patients, in tight batches, often without the diagnosis staging or treatment-decision context that makes a genomic assay reasonable and necessary. Referral concentration to one lab plus Open Payments honoraria, meals and gift-card style transfers from that lab to the ordering practices is visible at claim time by joining lab claims to transfer-of-value data. Signed-order documentation requests reveal pre-populated forms lacking individualized clinical rationale.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit for genomic/prognostic assays: require a qualifying diagnosis plus documented treatment-decision indication, and pend claims where the ordering NPI's share of patients receiving the same assay, or the batch-ordering pattern of same-day identical orders, exceeds the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers. Add a referral-integrity flag joining lab-to-referrer Open Payments/marketing-payment data with referral concentration, triggering payment suspension and a request for the signed order and clinical notes.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Cody Lee Anderson (designated personal representative of the estate); Thomas Allen Bateman, Jr. (co-conspirator, named sole beneficiary)
SchemeSummary: Anderson conspired with Bateman to have an 88-year-old Aiken woman, who investigators found lacked the mental capacity to make an informed decision, execute a will leaving her entire estate of roughly $20 million to Bateman, with Anderson named personal representative in line for a 5% fee; both men pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and neither has been sentenced.
WaysToIdentify: This is estate/bank fraud exploiting an incapacitated elderly person; no health care claim was submitted and no payer adjudicated anything, so there is no prepay claims control. If the victim was a plan member, the adjacent signal is a recent claims/encounter history documenting cognitive impairment diagnoses that contradicts a contemporaneous competent legal execution, and abrupt changes to a member's authorized representative or payee.
FeaturesToCreate: For payers that hold representative-payee or authorized-representative records, flag changes of representative, address or beneficiary designation for members with recent dementia/cognitive-impairment diagnosis codes and route to an SIU/adult-protective referral before honoring the change. Otherwise no payer-side claims edit applies; the control belongs to the bank's elder-financial-exploitation monitoring.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Cody Lee Anderson (designated personal representative of the estate); Thomas Allen Bateman, Jr. (sole beneficiary named in the will)
SchemeSummary: During the pandemic a will was executed by an 88-year-old Aiken woman who lacked the mental capacity to make an informed decision, purporting to leave her entire estate (worth approximately $20 million) to Bateman, with Anderson named personal representative in line for a 5% fee of about $1 million; both men were convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud and each sentenced to 24 months in prison plus three years of supervision.
WaysToIdentify: Same conduct as the companion entry at the sentencing stage: an estate/bank fraud with no health care billing and no payer adjudication point, so no prepay claim edit exists. The only payer-adjacent signal is a member with documented cognitive impairment in claims history whose representative, address or designation changes abruptly in favor of an unrelated third party.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a member-level elder-exploitation flag combining recent cognitive-impairment diagnoses with changes to authorized representative, mailing address or payee, holding the change for SIU and adult-protective-services review. No claims-payment control otherwise applies to this case.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Tommie Robinson (physician)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: An Alabama doctor working with telemedicine companies signed pre-populated doctors' orders for DME and cancer-risk genetic testing generated from telemarketing calls to Medicare beneficiaries, without any contact with or medical relationship with the patients; DME suppliers and labs then billed Medicare over $6 million for the medically unnecessary, kickback-tainted orders.
WaysToIdentify: The ordering physician has no prior or contemporaneous evaluation claim for the beneficiaries whose DME and genetic tests he ordered, and his orders span states far outside his practice location, arriving in high-volume batches — all checkable against claims history and geography at adjudication. A single NPI ordering for far more distinct beneficiaries than same-specialty peers, concentrated to a handful of DME suppliers and labs, is the core signal, as is an ordering rate that implies more encounters than a workday allows.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit on DME and hereditary-cancer panel claims requiring a payable evaluation encounter by the ordering NPI with the same beneficiary within a defined lookback; deny or pend and request the order plus the encounter note when absent. Add an ordering-NPI velocity/geography model (distinct beneficiaries per day, beneficiary-state dispersion versus the physician's licensure and practice ZIP, concentration to few supplier/lab TINs) that fires payment suspension for downstream suppliers and labs above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Tommie Robinson (physician)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Robinson, an Alabama doctor, signed pre-populated doctors' orders generated from telemarketing calls to Medicare beneficiaries he never examined or spoke with, authorizing medically unnecessary DME and cancer-risk genetic testing; DME suppliers and labs then billed Medicare over $6 million on those kickback-tainted orders.
WaysToIdentify: Identical mechanic: orders signed with no examination, so no evaluation claim from the ordering NPI exists for those beneficiaries, and beneficiary residence is dispersed nationally rather than clustered near the physician. Batch signing produces implausible orders-per-day counts and extreme concentration of one physician's orders into a small set of DME supplier and lab TINs, all visible pre-payment from claim linkage fields.
FeaturesToCreate: Require a documented, payable encounter between the ordering NPI and beneficiary within a lookback window for braces/orthoses and genetic panels; otherwise deny or pend with a documentation request for the order and clinical note. Build an ordering-physician surveillance job scoring daily distinct-beneficiary order volume, out-of-state beneficiary share and supplier/lab concentration, and auto-suspend payments to the linked suppliers and labs when scores exceed the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Muhammad Adil Quraish (former Air Force dentist); at least four unnamed co-conspirators
PayerName: Small Business Administration (PPP and EIDL pandemic relief programs)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Quraish and at least four co-conspirators submitted PPP and EIDL loan applications for several entities with inflated employee counts and payroll figures, supported by fabricated payroll records and falsified IRS tax forms falsely certified as filed, netting $1,471,599 in relief funds that were partly invested in cryptocurrency.
WaysToIdentify: This is SBA pandemic loan fraud with no health care claim, so no payer adjudication control applies; detection belongs at loan underwriting. Pre-disbursement signals were available: employee counts and payroll on the application could have been verified against IRS transcript data for the certified-as-filed 941s/Schedule C, and multiple entities sharing owners, addresses, bank accounts and applicant IP would have clustered into a single applicant ring.
FeaturesToCreate: At underwriting, require IRS transcript verification of the payroll figures and filing status before disbursement, auto-declining or holding where the application payroll exceeds transcript wages. Add an applicant-graph check clustering applications by owner SSN/EIN, address, bank account and submission IP, holding all related applications when one entity in the cluster fails verification; no payer claims edit applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: West End Services, Inc. (pharmacy); Christopher Leon (owner-pharmacist)
SchemeSummary: The pharmacy and its owner-pharmacist allegedly billed Medicare for prescription drugs - including Latuda, Humira, Abilify, Invega Sustenna, Seroquel, Acyclovir, Flovent and Truvada - that were never actually dispensed to Medicare beneficiaries, and agreed to pay $825,000 based on ability to pay.
WaysToIdentify: Non-dispensing is detectable by reconciling billed NDC quantities against the pharmacy's wholesaler acquisition records — a pharmacy cannot dispense more units of Latuda, Humira or Invega Sustenna than it purchased, and this invoice-versus-claims ratio can be demanded before or shortly after payment. Additional prepay signals: high-cost specialty drug claims for beneficiaries with no supporting prescriber encounter or diagnosis history, refills without corresponding prescriber activity, and beneficiaries residing far from the pharmacy.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an invoice-reconciliation control at pharmacy-NDC-period level comparing billed units to wholesaler/ARCOS-style purchase data, firing prepay suspension and an invoice documentation request when billed units exceed purchases beyond tolerance. Add prepay edits requiring an active prescriber encounter and consistent diagnosis history for high-cost specialty NDCs, plus refill-pattern checks (refills too regular, no beneficiary cost-share collection, beneficiary-to-pharmacy distance) routing outliers to review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Courtesy Transport Services, LLC; Melanie Burger (owner); Dr. John Milanick (owner)
SchemeSummary: Courtesy Transport Services billed Medicare and Florida Medicaid for basic life support, non-emergency ambulance transports that were not medically reasonable and necessary, where patients did not require ambulance transportation, or that were never actually provided; resolved via qui tam settlement totaling $900,000 across the company and its two owners, with the relator receiving about $171,000.
WaysToIdentify: BLS non-emergency transports are only payable when the beneficiary's condition contraindicates other transport, so the payer can test each claim against the beneficiary's concurrent claims history — ambulatory status, absence of a facility admission or dialysis/outpatient service at the destination on that date, and no supporting condition codes or physician certification statement. Phantom trips show up as transports with no matching destination-facility claim on the same date, implausible trips-per-vehicle-per-day, and repetitive origin/destination and mileage patterns.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit for non-emergency BLS: require a valid physician certification statement and a same-date destination service claim, and deny or pend when the beneficiary's history shows ambulatory status or no qualifying condition. Add a supplier-level analytic on trips per vehicle/crew per day, repeat-transport counts per beneficiary versus peers, and destination-claim match rate, triggering prepay review and a documentation request for run sheets.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Dr. David Antonio Becerril (licensed Washington physician); Health First Urgent Care (urgent care clinic, Richland and Pasco, WA)
State_County: Washington - Yakima County (Selah/Yakima); Washington - Benton County (Richland); Washington - Franklin County (Pasco); Washington - Spokane County (Spokane)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Unbundling
SchemeSummary: This roundup release covers two health care matters: (1) Dr. David Becerril was convicted at trial on 16 counts for signing false orders in a telemarketing scheme for medically unnecessary genetic tests and back/knee/shoulder/ankle braces for Medicare beneficiaries he never saw or spoke to - including deceased patients and patients with no limbs - being paid per order signed, resulting in over $3.2 million billed to Medicare (sentencing set for January 2026); and (2) Health First Urgent Care agreed to pay $2,807,729 under the False Claims Act for 'unbundling' PCR respiratory and urinary tract infection panel tests and billing each component test individually, plus billing Washington Medicaid for more expensive, medically unnecessary panels.
WaysToIdentify: For the signed-order scheme, the ordering NPI has no encounter with the beneficiaries, and the claims themselves contain disqualifying facts the payer already holds: date of death preceding the order, and amputation/limb-absence history contradicting a brace for that limb. For the unbundling matter, panel component CPTs billed individually for the same beneficiary and date sum to more than the panel code, and respiratory/UTI panel use far above same-specialty peers with routine rather than indication-driven ordering is visible at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits: deny orders/services with a service date after the beneficiary's date of death; deny limb-specific orthotics where history shows amputation or absent limb; and require an evaluation encounter by the ordering NPI within a lookback for braces and genetic panels, with per-order payment suspension of the billing supplier/lab above the calibrated ordering-velocity percentile. Add a component-to-panel rebundling edit that aggregates same-day same-beneficiary component tests into the panel code and pays the panel rate, plus a medical-necessity edit requiring a qualifying diagnosis and documented indication for multiplex PCR panels.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Rodolfo Rivera (Amtrak employee); Kevin Frink (Amtrak employee); Quinton Johnson (Amtrak employee); David McBrien (Amtrak employee); Gregory Richardson (Amtrak employee); Michael Toal (Amtrak employee); Damany Walker (Amtrak employee); Timothy Bogen (Amtrak employee); Dion Jacob (Amtrak employee); David Lonergan (Amtrak employee); Punson Figueroa (acupuncturist); Michael DeNicola (podiatrist)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Amtrak employees took cash kickbacks from health care providers (including an acupuncturist and a podiatrist) in exchange for letting the providers bill the Amtrak employee health plan for services that were never rendered and were not medically necessary; Rivera also recruited other employees whose plan IDs were used for the false claims. Claims tied to Rivera, his dependent and his recruits caused over $2 million in plan payments, and the overall conspiracy caused over $11 million in fraudulent payments; co-defendant acupuncturist Figueroa received 34 months in prison while Rivera awaits sentencing and nine co-defendants remain charged.
WaysToIdentify: Kickback-driven ID lending shows as concentrated clusters of plan members from one employer and worksite all treating at the same small set of providers, with high visit counts, no cost-share collection, and services (acupuncture, podiatry) billed on dates the member was on shift or geographically elsewhere per timekeeping data the plan sponsor holds. Members whose dependents also suddenly appear at the same providers, and providers whose patient panel is almost entirely one employer's members, are visible pre-payment from claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a provider-panel concentration analytic per provider TIN computing share of claims from a single employer group and referral-recruiter clustering of member IDs, firing prepay review and payment suspension above the calibrated percentile. Add a member-level utilization edit (visits per member per period for acupuncture/podiatry versus peers, no copay collected, service dates conflicting with employer timekeeping/shift data) that triggers verification-of-services letters to members and a documentation request for treatment notes before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Anthony Saloka (Amtrak employee/insurance beneficiary); Punson Figueroa (acupuncturist); Michael DeNicola (podiatrist)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Saloka, an Amtrak employee, took thousands of dollars in cash kickbacks from providers (including an acupuncturist and a podiatrist) in exchange for letting them use his personal and health insurance information to bill the Amtrak health plan for services never rendered or medically unnecessary; the plan paid over $11 million on fraudulent claims tied to the scheme's providers. Co-conspirator Figueroa was sentenced to 34 months; DeNicola's sentencing is pending.
WaysToIdentify: The tell is a single member ID appearing on high-frequency claims from a small cluster of unrelated providers (acupuncture, podiatry) with implausible visit cadence and no referral or diagnosis continuity, plus the member's own employer-plan enrollment showing he lives/works far from the billing addresses. At adjudication the payer can see repeated same-code visits, no supporting E/M or imaging trail, and the same handful of member IDs recurring across the same provider group - a hallmark of member-recruiter kickback rings. Member-verification letters or EOB attestations ('did you receive this service?') would have surfaced the phantom encounters before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a member-provider concentration model: per member per rolling period, count distinct visits and providers and flag members in the top calibrated percentile of visit frequency for modality codes (acupuncture, chiro, podiatry routine foot care); simultaneously build a provider-side check for share of revenue concentrated in a few member IDs from one employer group. Firing combinations route the provider's claims to prepay review with mandatory records and trigger automated member verification letters; sustained non-response suspends payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Kevin Frink (Amtrak employee); Michael Toal (Amtrak employee); David McBrien (Amtrak employee); Damany Walker (Amtrak employee); David Lonergan (Amtrak employee); Quinton Johnson (Amtrak employee, charged); Gregory Richardson (charged); Timothy Bogen (charged); Dion Jacob (charged); Rodolfo Rivera (pleaded guilty); Anthony Saloka (pleaded guilty); Punson Figueroa (acupuncturist); Michael DeNicola (podiatrist)
State_County: New Jersey - Essex County (Newark); New Jersey - Burlington County (Willingboro); New Jersey - Monmouth County (Hazlet); New York - Queens County (Rockaway Park)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Amtrak employees took thousands of dollars in cash kickbacks from health care providers (including acupuncturist Punson Figueroa and podiatrist Michael DeNicola) in exchange for allowing their Amtrak employee health plan to be billed for services never rendered and not medically necessary; the plan paid over $11 million in fraudulent claims. Figueroa was previously sentenced to 34 months; sentencings of the five employee defendants remain pending.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: employees selling their member IDs produce clusters of members from one employer, all billed repeatedly by the same acupuncturist/podiatrist with impossible service frequency and no clinical progression. A payer can detect it prepay from member-level visit-density outliers within a single employer group and from provider panels whose members are overwhelmingly drawn from one employer, plus geographic mismatch between member residence and clinic. Member verification mailings and interviews confirm services never rendered before further payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement an employer-group/provider affinity edit: for each provider, compute the share of claims from a single employer group and the distinct-member count, and flag providers where a small number of members from one group drive the top calibrated percentile of paid dollars. Pair with per-member visit-frequency caps for modality codes that trigger prepay documentation requests and automated 'services received?' verification; failed verification triggers payment suspension and SIU referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Alaska
FraudEntity: Dr. Claribel Tan (rheumatologist, clinic owner/operator); Daniel Tan (husband, office and management work for the clinic)
PayerName: More than 10 health insurance plans (not individually named)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Drug_Prescriptions; Upcoding; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: A rheumatologist and her husband billed more than 10 insurance plans for full injections of costly injectable medications while actually underdosing patients, substituting free samples, expired, or other patients' medication - claiming 4,829 units billed against only 369 units purchased - and also billed for longer office visits and services never provided, causing about $12.5 million in losses; they then overstated clinic drug expenses on 2014, 2015 and 2017 tax returns and failed to file returns for 2018-2021, costing the IRS about $4.25 million. Figures cover both defendants jointly, who each pleaded guilty and agreed to forfeit $10,471,106, pay $6,300,849 toward restitution and $1,855,144 in False Claims Act civil settlement; a linked release notes the doctor was later sentenced to 78 months in prison.
WaysToIdentify: The decisive signal is a drug-purchase-versus-units-billed reconciliation: billed J-code units for infused/injected biologics vastly exceeded documented acquisition from wholesalers/specialty distributors (4,829 vs 369 units), which payers can test using 340B/wholesaler invoice requests or supplier data at credentialing and audit. Prepay, the practice also showed level-4/5 E/M concentration and per-patient drug unit volumes above same-specialty rheumatology peers, and drug-administration codes without matching visit documentation. Invoice-to-claim reconciliation is normally a post-payment/audit route, but high J-code volume can trigger it prospectively.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a buy-and-bill reconciliation control: per provider per drug NDC/J-code per period, compare billed units against invoice/acquisition units obtained via a mandatory documentation request for practices whose billed units exceed the calibrated peer percentile; a shortfall places the provider on prepay review for all J-codes. Add an E/M distribution edit flagging upcoded level concentration versus same-specialty peers and an edit requiring administration-code/visit-note pairing.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Northwest Anesthesiology and Pain Services (NWAP) (anesthesiology service provider); Donald Carmichael (former president); Stacey Green (independent contractor manager); Remedy Physician Solutions (contractor company)
SchemeSummary: NWAP paid approximately $1.8 million in 'productivity' bonuses to its independently contracted pain management practices that were actually calculated from lab referral revenue minus costs, allegedly functioning as thinly veiled kickbacks for lab referrals, creating improper financial relationships under the Stark Law and tainting Medicare reimbursement claims; NWAP self-disclosed and paid $999,999.
WaysToIdentify: This is a Stark/AKS financial-relationship problem visible at enrolment and credentialing: the lab's contracts with contracted pain practices tied 'productivity' bonuses to referred lab revenue, which a payer can detect by requesting compensation methodology in provider agreements and by comparing each referring practice's lab-referral volume to its own bonus/ownership disclosures. Prepay, the referral pattern shows near-100% of a practice's toxicology/lab referrals routed to one lab with volume far above same-specialty peers. Full proof of the compensation formula usually requires audit or self-disclosure, so this is a hybrid prepay-signal/post-pay-audit control.
FeaturesToCreate: At enrolment, capture structured disclosure of physician compensation arrangements and lab ownership/referral relationships; auto-flag any arrangement where compensation varies with volume or value of referrals for legal review before claims are paid. Add a referral-concentration monitor: per referring NPI, compute share of lab/toxicology referrals to a single TIN and referrals-per-patient versus peers, and place outlier lab claims on prepay medical-necessity and relationship review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Armand Ntchana (APRN, owner); Integrated Procare Services, LLC (psychiatric medication management practice); Brookside Residential Care Home, LLC; 134 Franklin Street Extension, LLC; Riverview Residential Care Home, LLC; 92 Lexington Avenue, LLC
State_County: Connecticut - Wethersfield; Connecticut - Danbury; Connecticut - New Haven
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; Upcoding; Falsify certificate; Unbundling
SchemeSummary: Ntchana and his psychiatric medication management practice billed Medicare and Connecticut Medicaid listing Ntchana as rendering provider for services never provided - impossible hours per day, while he was out of the country or absent, for hospitalized or deceased patients, and for staff-called medication refills - creating false or no medical records; they also billed for patients seen by an unlicensed individual and billed both E/M and psychotherapy for visits where only E/M was provided. Settlement of $614,427.51 plus interest covers Ntchana and his related entities, with a two-year DSS suspension and permanent withdrawal from Connecticut Medicaid.
WaysToIdentify: Impossible-day arithmetic is directly computable at adjudication: sum the time-based psychotherapy and E/M service minutes billed under one rendering NPI per date and flag days exceeding plausible working hours. Cross-checks catch the rest - claims dated while the physician was abroad (compare to travel/absence, or simply to zero-activity gaps), service dates overlapping inpatient stays for the same member, dates after the member's date of death, and E/M plus psychotherapy add-on billed where only medication management occurred. Rendering-provider licensure files also expose services actually delivered by unlicensed staff.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a per-rendering-NPI per-date time accumulator across all time-based codes that denies or pends claims once billed minutes exceed a calibrated daily maximum, and an eligibility-conflict edit denying professional visit claims dated after date of death or during an inpatient facility stay for the same member. Add a code-pair edit requiring documented separate psychotherapy time when psychotherapy is billed with E/M, and a credentialing edit blocking payment when the rendering NPI lacks an active license for the billed service.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division (District of Maryland)
FraudEntity: James Vincent Campbell (CEO and founder of Axim Fringe Solutions Group, LLC); Axim Fringe Solutions Group, LLC (employee benefits processor)
SchemeSummary: Campbell's company processed employee benefits for federal contractors, receiving client funds meant for health insurance premiums and 401(k) contributions and pooling them in a master trust account before forwarding them to carriers and retirement accounts. Instead of taking only the contractual $40 per employee per month fee, he allegedly made 135 unauthorized withdrawals totaling $2,486,905 from the trust account, spending the money on big game hunting trips, taxidermy, jewelry, casino gambling, and payments to his girlfriend; eleven money laundering counts accompany the ERISA theft count.
WaysToIdentify: There is no claims-payment component: this is fiduciary theft from an ERISA master trust by a third-party benefits administrator, not provider billing. Detection sits with plan sponsors, carriers and the fiduciary controls over the trust account: reconcile client remittances received against premiums actually forwarded to carriers and 401(k) recordkeepers, and monitor withdrawals exceeding the contractual per-employee-per-month administrative fee. Carrier-side premium delinquency/lapse notices and unremitted 401(k) contribution reports are the earliest external signals.
FeaturesToCreate: For payer/carrier operations, build a premium-remittance reconciliation monitor per plan sponsor comparing expected premium (enrolled lives x rate) against funds received from the TPA, firing on shortfalls or late remittances and auto-notifying the sponsor and DOL-referral queue. In TPA vendor oversight, require monthly trust-account attestations and compute administrative withdrawals versus contractual fee x covered lives, suspending TPA authority to disburse when the variance exceeds the contract.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Kevin Lamorris McKenzie (Chief Operating Officer then CEO of Apache Behavioral Health Services); Corina Martinez (co-defendant, controlled Evolved Health Care Inc.); Helping Everyday Youth (HEDY); Evolved Health Care Inc. (EHI)
State_County: Arizona - Pima County (Tucson); Arizona - White Mountain Apache Tribe
SchemeSummary: As COO and then CEO of Apache Behavioral Health Services, McKenzie used two sham vendor contracts to divert tribal healthcare funds to himself: ABHS paid over $35 million to Helping Everyday Youth, which under a secret side agreement kicked back roughly $16 million to a shell company McKenzie controlled, and ABHS paid about $16.5 million to co-defendant Corina Martinez's Evolved Health Care Inc. under phony employee-referral contracts under which no employees were ever referred and no services performed, with proceeds split between them (cash, $800,000 of McKenzie's credit card bills, a $128,000 Rolls Royce and a $928,000 home). Figures reflect the combined scheme; the $33,155,701 restitution and forfeitures were ordered against McKenzie.
WaysToIdentify: No payer claim adjudication is involved - this is embezzlement of tribal healthcare funds through sham vendor contracts, so the controls are grantee/vendor financial oversight rather than prepay claim edits. The observable signals are a new vendor receiving an outsized share of an entity's disbursements, contracts for 'employee referrals' with no deliverables, common addresses/officers between the vendor and an executive-controlled shell, and executive-related-party disclosures omitted from conflict-of-interest filings. Follow-the-money review of vendor payments versus documented services is the post-payment route.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a vendor-integrity screen for funded entities: match vendor TINs, addresses, incorporation officers and bank accounts against officer/board related-party registries and flag any vendor whose payments exceed a calibrated share of total disbursements or lacks itemized deliverables. Fire a funds-hold and mandatory independent audit for contracts with no measurable output (referrals delivered, encounters produced) before further draws are released.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Alexandra Gehrke (owner of Apex Medical LLC and Viking Medical Consultants LLC); Jeffrey King (co-owner of graft application company); Apex Medical LLC; Viking Medical Consultants LLC
PayerName: Medicare; TRICARE; CHAMPVA; commercial insurance plans
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Upcoding; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Gehrke's companies paid medically untrained sales reps kickbacks to find elderly and hospice patients with wounds and order oversized (4x6 cm or larger) amniotic wound grafts from a specific distributor, from which Gehrke received over $279 million in kickbacks; patients were then referred to King's company, whose nurse practitioners were directed to apply all ordered grafts regardless of medical necessity, and $1.21 billion in claims were billed to Medicare, TRICARE, CHAMPVA and commercial insurers, which paid $614.99 million. Restitution figures span both defendants ($614,990,420 and $605,690,110) plus over $410 million in agreed forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: The claims picture screams before payment: billed amniotic/skin-substitute graft units per patient and per applicator size at the top of the national distribution, near-exclusive use of the largest-size product from one distributor, application to hospice-enrolled and homebound elderly patients, and grafts billed without wound-measurement documentation or any prior conservative-care trail. Payer data also shows an ordering-clinician cohort of NPs whose graft volume vastly exceeds same-specialty peers and orders originating from non-clinical sales-rep referral patterns. Concurrent enrollment in hospice for wound-related care is a direct eligibility conflict checkable at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit on skin-substitute HCPCS codes requiring prior authorization with wound measurements, photographs, and documented conservative care; auto-deny sq-cm units exceeding documented wound area and deny applications for members with an active hospice election for a related terminal condition. Add a provider/product-concentration monitor (units per patient, single-distributor share, per-NPI graft dollars versus peers) that triggers payment suspension and referral when multiple flags coincide.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Mary Blakley (principal of medical clinic business, self-described 'Doctor Mary'); Fred Blakley (principal); Janmarie Lanzo (clinic worker/product seller)
State_County: Arizona - Lake Havasu City (defendants' base); clients throughout the United States
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: The Blakleys ran clinics charging clients nationwide roughly $300, usually in cash, for sham 'full body scans' performed on conventional ultrasound machines that they falsely claimed contained Mary Blakley's 'smart chip technology' capable of diagnosing, treating and curing cancer and other diseases; based on the bogus scan results they and Lanzo sold supplements, the cosmetic cream Aetheion, and the veterinary dewormer fenbendazole as human cancer treatments, bolstered by fabricated credentials (a nonexistent Karolinska Institutet Ph.D.) and concealment tactics such as claiming to be doing only research, using coded language, keeping no records, and requiring membership/confidentiality agreements. All three pleaded guilty; Fred Blakley also pleaded guilty to felon-in-possession of firearms.
WaysToIdentify: This was a cash, off-claims consumer scheme - no insurer paid claims - so payer prepay controls largely do not apply; the detection route is licensure/credential verification and consumer/FDA complaint monitoring plus advertising surveillance for cancer-cure claims. If any such operation ever enrolls, the credentialing screen catches a nonexistent Karolinska Ph.D. via primary-source degree verification and an unregistered 'smart chip' ultrasound device with no FDA clearance. Post hoc, cash-only pricing, membership/confidentiality agreements and absent medical records are the audit signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Enforce primary-source verification of every claimed degree, license and board certification at enrolment and re-credentialing, auto-rejecting unverifiable foreign institutions, and screen billed diagnostic devices against FDA clearance/registration data with denial of claims for unlisted device technologies. Add a marketing-surveillance feed that flags enrolled or applicant entities advertising cure claims or unapproved therapies for credentialing hold and state-board referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Kevin Paul McMains (Army veteran, benefits claimant)
PayerName: Medicare; Department of Veterans Affairs; Social Security Administration
SchemeSummary: Over nearly 14 years McMains obtained more than $779,000 in VA disability benefits by submitting fabricated documents and making false statements to the VA and to medical professionals that post-traumatic stress left him unable to work or care for himself, and by falsely claiming he had been awarded a Purple Heart as proof of service-connected injury; the false disability status also qualified him for Social Security disability benefits and Medicare coverage. He was ordered to repay $378,380.82 to VA, $357,847.80 to SSA, and $43,451.56 to CMS.
WaysToIdentify: This is benefit eligibility fraud against VA/SSA with derivative Medicare entitlement rather than provider billing, so the control belongs at eligibility determination: verify claimed decorations (Purple Heart) against DoD service records and verify submitted medical documents directly with the issuing clinician rather than accepting claimant-supplied copies. Cross-agency data matching would show the claimed total inability to work against IRS/SSA wage and self-employment earnings records. Continuing-eligibility reviews with earnings matches are the post-award route to stop ongoing payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an automated document-authentication and records-match step in disability adjudication: hash/verify claimant-submitted provider letters against primary-source clinician confirmation and validate decoration/service claims against DoD personnel data, holding award until both clear. Add a recurring earnings-versus-disability match (SSA/IRS wage and 1099 data) that suspends benefits and derivative Medicare entitlement pending review when reported activity contradicts the certified limitation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: John R. Manning (licensed medical doctor)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Drug_Prescriptions
SchemeSummary: Dr. Manning worked for multiple 'telemedicine' companies and signed doctor orders/prescriptions for durable medical equipment, topical creams, and cancer genetic tests based on only a brief conversation with patients or no conversation at all, in exchange for over $812,000 in kickbacks; the orders caused at least $41 million in false Medicare claims, of which Medicare paid over $19 million. He was ordered to pay $19,780,565.44 restitution plus $812,303.41 forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: One ordering NPI generating orders for DME braces, topical compounded creams and hereditary cancer panels across many states and many unrelated suppliers, with no prior or subsequent office visit for those members, is directly observable at adjudication. Telehealth claims are absent or reduced to a single brief code, the beneficiary-to-ordering-physician distance is large, and the same NPI's order volume sits far above same-specialty peers. Supplier-side concentration on a single ordering physician confirms the telemarketing pattern before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-physician surveillance model: per ordering NPI per month, compute distinct beneficiaries, distinct supplier TINs, states covered, share of orders lacking any evaluative encounter with that NPI within a lookback window, and rank against same-specialty peers; outliers trigger prepay review of all downstream DME/genetic/compound claims. Add a hard prepay edit denying DME, cancer genetic panels and compounded creams when no qualifying face-to-face or telehealth encounter with the ordering provider exists, and suspend suppliers whose orders concentrate on flagged NPIs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Athira Pharma Inc.; Leen Kawas (former CEO)
PayerName: National Institutes of Health; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
FraudType: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
FraudTypeAll: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Athira Pharma failed to disclose to NIH and the HHS Office of Research Integrity allegations that its former CEO had falsified and manipulated scientific images in her dissertation and published papers, which were cited in NIH grant applications (including a grant NIH funded in 2019) and in progress reports and institutional assurances; the company paid $4,068,698 to resolve FCA claims brought by a qui tam whistleblower who received $203,434.
WaysToIdentify: No claims payment is involved - this is a grant-integrity/False Claims Act matter about non-disclosure of research misconduct allegations in NIH applications and progress reports. The detectable signal is institutional certification of research integrity in eRA submissions contradicted by pending misconduct allegations, image-duplication detected by forensic screening of figures in cited publications, and journal expressions of concern or retraction notices tied to key personnel. Whistleblower/qui tam and ORI referral are the realistic routes.
FeaturesToCreate: For grant-making payers, build an automated pre-award integrity screen: match key personnel and cited publications against retraction/expression-of-concern databases, PubPeer-style image-integrity flags and ORI/institutional misconduct disclosures, and hold award or continuation funding pending certification review when hits occur. Require an affirmative, machine-checked disclosure attestation each progress report, with funds suspension for undisclosed pending allegations.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
SchemeSummary: Not a fraud case: press release announcing the appointment of Michael DiGiacomo as U.S. Attorney for the Western District of New York; it only mentions health care fraud among his past prosecution areas generally.
WaysToIdentify: Not a fraud case - this is a press release announcing a U.S. Attorney appointment, with no claims, payer, provider or loss. There is nothing for a payer to detect and no billing pattern to model.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies; exclude such announcements from case-derived rule mining so they do not pollute training or rule inventories.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Austin Emergency Center, LLC; Austin ER, LLC; AEC ER 4, LLC; Pahala Ventures, LLC; AEC Physicians, PLLC; AEC Pflugerville, LLC (collectively 'Austin Emergency Center', operator of standalone emergency medical facilities)
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Austin Emergency Center allegedly charged FEHBP more for certain COVID-19 tests than it charged cash-paying patients (June 18, 2020 - April 2, 2021) and up-coded evaluation and management services billed for drive-through COVID-19 screening (April 13, 2020 - April 2, 2021), collecting inflated reimbursements from the federal employee health program.
WaysToIdentify: Two checkable signals: the facility's cash/self-pay price for the same COVID test CPT (published under price-transparency and cash-price posting rules) was lower than what it billed the federal plan, and its E/M level distribution for drive-through screening encounters was concentrated at high levels inconsistent with a swab-only encounter with no exam or MDM. Both are computable at adjudication from the claim plus the provider's posted cash price file.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a cash-price parity edit: ingest each facility's posted self-pay/cash price file, compare the billed/allowed amount per COVID test CPT, and pend or reprice claims where the plan is charged above the posted cash price. Add a site-of-service E/M edit that denies or downcodes level-3+ E/M billed with COVID specimen-collection codes at drive-through/mobile places of service unless records documenting exam and medical decision-making are supplied on request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dr. Mark Malone (pain management doctor, founder of Advanced Pain Care); Advanced Pain Care and related entities including Mark Malone M.D., P.A., Round Rock Surgery Center, LLC, APC-Amarillo Surgical Operating Company, LLC, Killeen Surgical Operating Company, LLC, Waco Surgical Operating Company, LLC, Southwest Surgical Operating Company, LLC, Shoal Creek Pharmacy Operations, LLC, Palo Duro Pharmacy Operations, LLC, APC Pharmacy, LLC, Advanced Anesthesiology, Advanced Health Holdings, LLC, Advanced RX Pharmacy, APC Investments LLC, APC360 LLC, 6000 South Mopac APC LLC, MMJ Partners, LP, MMC Holdco, LLC
State_County: Texas - Austin, Amarillo, Waco, and Houston areas
PayerName: Medicare; Texas Medicaid; TRICARE; Federal Employees Health Benefits Program; Department of Veterans Affairs
SchemeSummary: The government alleged the pain practice billed Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE and FEHBP for concurrent presumptive and definitive urine drug tests on the same patient on the same date of service without reviewing presumptive results to determine whether definitive testing was medically necessary, and billed the VA for definitive drug testing using separate CPT codes for individual analytes (CPT 803XX series) rather than appropriate codes, between January 3, 2017 and December 31, 2021.
WaysToIdentify: Same-date presumptive plus definitive urine drug testing billed reflexively for essentially every patient is visible at adjudication as a code-pair pattern with near-100% concurrency and no documentation that presumptive results were reviewed. The VA billing shows analyte-by-analyte CPT 803XX unbundling instead of the appropriate definitive panel code, detectable as an abnormally high number of drug-class line items per specimen versus peers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a reflex-testing edit: per patient-date, deny definitive drug-test codes billed with presumptive codes unless a documented review of presumptive results and patient-specific medical necessity is supplied, and monitor per-ordering-NPI concurrency rate against same-specialty peers for prepay review. Add an unbundling edit that aggregates 803XX analyte lines per specimen and reprices to the appropriate definitive panel code when the analyte count exceeds the panel definition.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Thomasina E. Amponsah (unlicensed individual posing as registered nurse/licensed practical nurse)
State_County: Maryland - Baltimore County; Maryland - Baltimore City
FraudTypeAll: IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions
SchemeSummary: Amponsah, who never held any nursing license, used stolen Maryland and Florida nursing license numbers and duplicated license images belonging to two identity victims, plus fabricated resumes and false claims of a Florida State University nursing degree, to be hired as an RN/LPN at no less than 40 Maryland facilities (mostly skilled nursing facilities, plus nursing homes and a Baltimore City public school) directly and through a staffing agency; the facilities billed Medicare and Medicaid for services she purportedly rendered and she earned at least $100,000 in wages. She also forged a physician's signature on a controlled-substance form for Tramadol faxed to a pharmacy and falsified medical records after failing to administer prescribed medications. A later release in the document notes she was sentenced to 38 months.
WaysToIdentify: The core signal is licensure verification: the license numbers she used belonged to other people, so an automated primary-source match of name, date of birth and license number against Maryland and Florida nursing boards (and Nursys) fails immediately, as would degree verification with Florida State. Payers and facilities can also detect one license number active concurrently at many unrelated employers and staffing-agency placements, and the pharmacy side shows a controlled-substance fax whose prescriber signature and DEA/NPI do not match the prescriber of record.
FeaturesToCreate: Require automated primary-source license verification (Nursys/state board API matching name+DOB+license number+image) at hire, at staffing-agency placement and at each payer credentialing/revalidation, blocking claims that list an unverified caregiver and firing an alert when one license number appears at multiple concurrent employers. On the pharmacy side, build a prescriber-authentication edit that pends faxed controlled-substance prescriptions where prescriber identifiers, DEA registration or signature template do not match the on-file prescriber, with callback verification required.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Thomasina E. Amponsah (unlicensed individual posing as registered nurse/licensed practical nurse)
State_County: Maryland - Baltimore County; Maryland - Baltimore City
SchemeSummary: Amponsah used two stolen nursing license numbers and duplicated license images, plus fabricated resumes and educational histories, to obtain employment as an RN/LPN at no less than 40 Maryland facilities (mostly skilled nursing facilities) and a Baltimore City public school, earning over $145,000 in wages; the facilities billed Medicare and Medicaid for the services she purportedly provided. She also forged a physician's signature on a Tramadol prescription faxed to a pharmacy and falsified medical records to conceal unadministered medications.
WaysToIdentify: Identical mechanic to the companion case: stolen nursing license numbers and duplicated license images pass only because verification is document-based rather than primary-source. Automated Nursys/state-board matching on name, DOB and license number, plus image-duplication detection across submitted credential files, catches it at hire and at credentialing; concurrent employment of one license number across ~40 facilities is another computable flag. Facility Medicare/Medicaid claims for services by an unlicensed staffer are then blockable before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a credential-integrity service: primary-source license verification with identity match, perceptual-hash comparison of uploaded license images against previously submitted images to detect reuse, and a cross-employer concurrency monitor that suspends a caregiver record when one license appears at implausibly many simultaneous employers. Tie facility claim payment to an all-staff verified-license roster, pending claims naming unverified staff, and add prescriber-signature authentication for faxed controlled-substance orders.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Matthew Hightower; Davon Carter (shooter); Clifton Mosley (accomplice)
SchemeSummary: Hightower, then under federal indictment for a health care fraud scheme and a murder, conspired from jail to kill a federal witness who had given law enforcement information about the health care fraud scheme; the hired shooter killed the witness's neighbor, Latrina Ashburne, by mistake. The document provides no details of the underlying health care fraud billing, payer, or amount.
WaysToIdentify: The document describes witness murder-for-hire arising from an unrelated indictment and gives no billing, payer, provider type or loss detail, so there is no claims-payment mechanic to detect prepay. The only payer-relevant hook is that a provider under indictment for health care fraud should already be on payment suspension.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an automated adverse-action feed (indictments, arrests, exclusion and state-board actions matched to enrolled NPIs/TINs) that triggers credible-allegation-of-fraud payment suspension and prepay review of all pending claims for the affected provider and its affiliated TINs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Samrat Mukherjee (licensed paramedic falsely posing as a medical doctor)
State_County: Louisiana - East Baton Rouge Parish (Baton Rouge)
PayerName: Medicaid (Louisiana); Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: A licensed paramedic created a fake medical degree and residency match letter to pose as a physician, obtaining physician privileges and badges at hospitals and at Acadian Ambulance, then called in and wrote prescriptions for himself and others while falsely claiming to be two doctors (including forging an oncologist's signature on an Ondansetron-ODT prescription), causing pharmacies to submit reimbursement claims to Medicaid and BCBSLA.
WaysToIdentify: A fabricated medical degree and residency match letter fail primary-source verification against the medical school, ECFMG/NRMP and the state medical board, and the impostor held no physician NPI or DEA registration of his own - so pharmacy claims carrying his prescriptions would show prescriber identifiers that do not validate or that belong to other physicians. Signals at adjudication include prescriptions where the prescribing NPI/DEA does not match the name on the script, self-prescribing (prescriber and member are the same person), and one prescriber identifier used from geographically inconsistent origination points.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-validation prepay edit for pharmacy claims: reject or pend when the prescriber NPI/DEA is inactive, mismatched to the prescriber name, not licensed for the drug class, or identical to the patient (self-prescribing), with callback verification for faxed controlled substances. At facility/ambulance privileging and payer credentialing, require automated primary-source verification of degree, residency match and board licensure before any privileges or claim payment tied to that clinician.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: Med-Surg Physician Group Inc. (medical practice); Oluyemisi Sangodeyi, M.D. (owner)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (West Virginia Medicaid / Bureau for Medical Services)
SchemeSummary: Med-Surg routinely appended HCPCS code Q3014 (telehealth originating site facility fee) to Medicare and Medicaid claims for telehealth visits where the patient was at home, a location for which the facility fee is not payable, collecting $76,191.35; the practice and its owner also falsely certified compliance with program requirements and agreed to pay $152,382.70 to resolve FCA allegations.
WaysToIdentify: This is a pure code-eligibility error checkable on the claim face: Q3014 originating-site facility fee is payable only when the patient is at an eligible facility, so any Q3014 line paired with a home place of service (POS 10, or a professional telehealth claim indicating patient home) is unpayable. The payer also sees the same practice appending Q3014 to essentially all telehealth claims, a distributional outlier versus peers.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a hard prepay edit denying HCPCS Q3014 when the associated telehealth encounter's place of service or patient-location modifier indicates the patient's home, or when no eligible originating-site facility NPI is present on the claim. Add a provider-level monitor of Q3014-to-telehealth-claim ratio against peers to trigger recovery review and a compliance-certification/documentation request for outliers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Miguel Saravia (CEO of Dana Group Associates; former COO of Prime Behavioral Health)
SchemeSummary: Saravia directed untrained staff to enter CPT codes for therapy services that were never provided and to upcode psychotherapy visit codes, submitting false claims to health care benefit programs for treatment not rendered or more complex than delivered; he was sentenced to 3.5 months in prison and ordered to pay $561,141.89 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay profiling of the practice's psychotherapy code mix would show a distribution skewed to the longest-duration codes (e.g. 90837/60-minute and high-level E/M) versus same-specialty peers, plus implausible daily service-minute totals per rendering NPI once billed units are summed against a workday. Cross-checking the rendering NPI on the claim against state licensure/supervision files would also reveal therapy billed under credentials of staff not qualified to deliver it, and time-in-day overlaps for the same clinician.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider/day feature that sums implied service minutes from all timed psychotherapy and E/M codes and fires a prepay edit when the total exceeds a feasible clinical day; add a provider-month code-mix outlier score for share of highest-duration psychotherapy codes versus same-specialty peers, above the calibrated percentile, routing to prepay medical-record request for session notes with start/stop times. Add a credentialing cross-edit rejecting timed psychotherapy where the rendering NPI lacks an active licence/supervision link on file.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Hemal Patel
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
