SchemeSummary: Patel allegedly received kickbacks for referring home care patients to home care agencies, forged physician signatures on eligibility certification forms, and used individuals' personal identifying information without their knowledge to enroll them for home care services while they were living out of the country; Medicaid was billed roughly $1,069,384 for home care services never provided.
WaysToIdentify: At authorisation time, the certifying physician's signature and NPI can be validated against the physician's own claim history - a certifier who has no evaluation/office-visit claim for that beneficiary in the lookback window, or who suddenly certifies for many unrelated agencies, is a forged-certification signal. Beneficiary absence from the country is visible by matching member IDs against travel/immigration or by the total absence of any other in-country claim activity during the service span, and by referral concentration linking one referrer to a handful of agencies.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a certification-integrity edit: for each home care authorisation, require a paid face-to-face encounter claim from the certifying NPI within the lookback period and flag certifier-agency pairs whose referral volume is concentrated above the calibrated percentile; suspect certifiers get signature-verification and documentation requests before authorisation. Add a beneficiary-activity check that suspends payment when home care is billed for a member with no other in-state claim or encounter footprint during the service window, and hold enrolment of members whose PII was submitted without a verifiable contact/consent record.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Ulma Form Works, Inc. (manufacturer and supplier of concrete formwork, shoring and temporary scaffolding systems)
SchemeSummary: Ulma Form Works applied for and received a $2 million PPP loan in January 2021 by falsely certifying it had no more than 300 employees, when counting its affiliates and their foreign-based employees it exceeded the limit; it then obtained full forgiveness of the loan plus accrued interest, and resolved the resulting FCA qui tam suit for $2,902,795 (relator share $290,279).
WaysToIdentify: This is a federal loan (PPP) affiliation/size certification case, not a claims-payment scheme, so no payer adjudication control applies. The detectable signal sits at loan underwriting and forgiveness review: the applicant's corporate parentage and worldwide employee count are visible from Dun & Bradstreet/ownership registries, foreign parent filings, and payroll tax filings for affiliates, none of which were reconciled against the 300-employee certification.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control is an ownership/affiliation screen in the enrolment or funding pipeline: resolve applicant EIN to its ultimate parent via corporate-registry and ownership-graph data, aggregate employee counts across all affiliates including foreign entities, and block forgiveness/payment pending manual size review when the aggregated count exceeds the programme cap. The same ownership-graph resolution should be reused for payer provider enrolment to detect undisclosed common control.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Delaware
FraudEntity: BioReference Health LLC, formerly BioReference Laboratories Inc. (clinical laboratory); OPKO Health Inc. (parent company)
SchemeSummary: The government alleged that BioReference routinely performed and billed federal health care programs for the more expensive complete blood count (CBC) with automated white blood cell differential test when providers had actually ordered the cheaper CBC without differential, making the tests billed medically unnecessary and unordered. Resolved via a $704,349 False Claims Act settlement from a qui tam suit, with the relator receiving $112,694.
WaysToIdentify: The signal is a lab whose share of CBC-with-differential (85025) versus CBC-without (85027) is far above same-specialty peer labs, and, more decisively, a mismatch between the ordering provider's requisition/order data and the code billed. Payers can compare the lab's billed panel code against the order captured in the electronic requisition or the ordering physician's own diagnosis/order pattern for that member and date.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab-NPI monthly ratio feature (differential vs non-differential CBC, and analogous upgraded-panel pairs) scored against peer labs, firing a documentation request for the signed requisitions when above the calibrated percentile. Add a claim-level prepay edit that denies or pends the higher-paying panel variant when the linked electronic order or requisition on file specifies the lower-level test, and sample-audit labs with no retrievable order record.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Armen Muradyan (owner/operator of Genex Laboratories Inc.); Genex Laboratories Inc.
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Muradyan, barred by Medicare from submitting claims, paid a long-time friend $2,000/month to pose as owner of his Burbank blood-testing lab Genex Laboratories and to file the Medicare enrollment paperwork; Medicare reimbursements for blood testing were wired to bank accounts in the nominee's name but controlled by Muradyan, and Genex income was reported on the nominee's returns, evading about $11.2 million in taxes on roughly $23.9 million of unreported income. He also obtained a $99,900 SBA EIDL loan by falsely claiming his entity GenMed had employees and $800,000 in 2019 income.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the nominee-owner pattern is visible by matching the applicant's addresses, phone numbers, bank routing/account details, prior enrolment records and business filings against those of excluded or previously revoked individuals - here the barred principal's identifiers would tie to the lab's address, equipment lease or payment account. A nominal owner with no relevant licence, no industry history, and a modest fixed monthly income stream also shows up as an ownership record inconsistent with the operational footprint.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment ownership-graph screen that resolves every listed owner, authorised official, address, phone, EFT bank account and managing employee against exclusion/revocation lists and against identifiers of previously revoked entities, and auto-suspends payment pending on-site verification when any link is found. Add a post-enrolment monitor that flags EFT accounts receiving payments where the signatory or transfer beneficiary differs from the enrolled owner, and re-verify ownership when reassignment or ownership change is filed shortly after a related party's suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Danielle Molinari
SchemeSummary: Molinari joined a conspiracy to obtain medically unnecessary oxycodone prescriptions, filled them, and then resold the pills to another individual for cash, distributing approximately 4,665 oxycodone pills between February 2019 and March 2023.
WaysToIdentify: At point of sale, PDMP and pharmacy claim data show a member filling repeated high-MME oxycodone quantities with early refills, cash or single-prescriber sourcing, and no supporting pain-diagnosis or procedure history - the classic diversion profile. Prescriber-level review shows a small set of patients receiving near-identical high-dose oxycodone regimens with no imaging, therapy or specialist claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a member-level controlled-substance monitor computing cumulative daily MME, refill-too-soon intervals, prescriber/pharmacy counts and absence of supporting diagnosis claims, firing a prepay edit requiring prior authorisation once the composite score passes the calibrated threshold. Add a prescriber panel feature flagging clinicians whose share of patients on high-MME oxycodone without supporting workup exceeds same-specialty peers, for prepay review and PDMP referral.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Belinda Jo Juarez (majority owner and CEO of Superior Home Health Service); Superior Home Health Service
SchemeSummary: The owner/CEO of a San Antonio home health company continued deducting health insurance premiums from employee paychecks after she stopped remitting payments to the insurers (leading insurers to cancel coverage), without telling employees their coverage was inactive, and also withheld federal payroll taxes from paychecks without remitting them to the IRS. She was ordered to pay $617,738.65 restitution to former employees and $3,667,098.88 restitution to the IRS, plus a $20,000 fine.
WaysToIdentify: This is employer payroll-tax and premium-remittance theft, not billing of claims, so no claim-adjudication edit catches it; the insurer's own premium-receivable and eligibility systems carry the signal - premiums stopped arriving while the employer continued to submit enrolment and the group was cancelled without employee notice. Post-payment/administrative route: reconcile group billing arrears against active member eligibility files and IRS payroll filings.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control at the insurer: an automated premium-delinquency to eligibility reconciliation that, when a group's remittance lapses, triggers direct written notice to each covered employee and freezes the employer's ability to file new enrolments; pair with a rule that any group cancellation for non-payment generates member-level notification and a claims-hold advisory. No payer-side claims edit applies to the unremitted payroll taxes; that is an IRS filing-mismatch control.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
FraudEntity: Jacobo Melcer (owner/operator of two durable medical equipment companies)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Melcer owned two DME companies that billed Medicare $5,885,382 (paid $3,479,303) for orthotic braces, paying over $227,000 in kickbacks to companies for referrals of Medicare beneficiaries and DME prescriptions signed by physicians with no legitimate doctor-patient relationship or examination; he also sold the two DME companies to a co-conspirator to place them under a nominee owner and conceal true ownership from Medicare after the co-conspirator was suspended as a provider.
WaysToIdentify: Orthotic-brace claims from these suppliers would show ordering physicians located far from the beneficiary, no prior or contemporaneous office-visit claim from the ordering NPI for that member, and a handful of prescribers concentrated across many unrelated suppliers - the signature of purchased, telemarketed prescriptions. Undisclosed ownership is catchable at change-of-ownership review by matching new owner identifiers, addresses, bank accounts and phones to a currently suspended provider.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a brace-claim prepay edit that requires an evaluation claim from the ordering NPI for the same beneficiary within the lookback window and pends claims where prescriber-beneficiary distance and prescriber-supplier concentration exceed calibrated percentiles, with an ABN/medical-record documentation request. Add a change-of-ownership screen resolving new owners, managing employees and payment accounts against sanctioned/suspended-provider identifiers, auto-suspending payments pending verification when a link exists, plus a growth-velocity trigger on brace HCPCS volume for new suppliers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Athira Pharma, Inc. (Bothell, WA biopharmaceutical company); Leen Kawas (former Chief Executive Officer)
PayerName: National Institutes of Health (NIH) / U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Athira Pharma allegedly obtained NIH research grants for age-related cognitive decline studies (including a grant funded in 2019) while failing to disclose to NIH and the HHS Office of Research Integrity, in grant applications, Research Progress Performance Reports, Small Business Organization Statements and annual reports, that its then-CEO Leen Kawas had allegedly falsified and manipulated scientific images in her doctoral dissertation and in published papers cited in those applications. The company paid $4,068,698 to resolve False Claims Act allegations raised in a qui tam suit, with the relator receiving $203,434.
WaysToIdentify: No claims-payment component: this is grant-application non-disclosure of research misconduct, detectable at grant peer review and progress-report stage. The signal is available from ORI/institutional misconduct inquiries, journal expressions of concern or retraction notices on the papers cited in the application, and image-integrity screening of figures in the cited publications and the PI's dissertation.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control is a pre-award and continuation integrity screen: automatically resolve every publication cited in an application or progress report to retraction/correction/expression-of-concern feeds and to open institutional or ORI misconduct records for the named PI/key personnel, and hold award or the next-year disbursement pending certification review when a hit appears. Add image-duplication/manipulation screening of figures in cited works and require affirmative attestation of any pending misconduct proceeding.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Niranjan Mittal (cardiologist, operator of Brooklyn medical clinic)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Mittal disguised kickbacks as office-space 'rent' payments to other providers to induce patient referrals to his Brooklyn clinic, then had staff order unnecessary diagnostic tests and office visits and fabricate patients' recorded symptoms to justify medically unnecessary peripheral vascular interventional procedures; insurers paid over $40 million between 2016 and 2023 for claims tied to those referred patients.
WaysToIdentify: Peripheral vascular intervention volume per physician, and repeat interventions on the same limb within short intervals, stand far above same-specialty peers and are traceable prepay via procedure codes plus the absence of documented failed conservative therapy or objective vascular testing. The kickback leg shows as payments styled as rent: referring practices concentrated in the referral graph, with lease/rent relationships disclosed or discoverable at credentialing, and referral share from those practices out of proportion to geography.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a provider-month feature counting peripheral vascular interventions per unique patient, repeat-intervention intervals per limb, and the ratio of interventions to prior diagnostic vascular studies; fire a prepay documentation request (ABI/duplex results, conservative-care history, symptom documentation) and a prior-authorisation edit when above calibrated percentiles. Add a referral-concentration graph flagging clinics where a small set of referrers supply most interventional volume and where a financial relationship (rent/lease/space sharing) exists, routing to Stark/AKS review before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Zakia Khan (owner of Happy Family Social Adult Day Care Center Inc., Family Social Adult Day Care Center Inc., a home health care fiscal intermediary, and Tanwee Services Inc.); Seema Memon (employee); Amran Hashmi (employee)
State_County: New York - Kings County (Brooklyn), Coney Island
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Khan owned two Coney Island social adult day care centers and a home health fiscal intermediary; she and her marketers paid cash kickbacks and bribes to Medicaid recipients to enroll, then billed Medicaid roughly $68 million for social adult day care services that were either never provided or were induced by the kickbacks, laundering the proceeds through multiple business entities (including Tanwee Services Inc.) to generate the cash for the bribes. Khan agreed to forfeit $5 million including properties and over $300,000 in seized cash and gold; two employee co-defendants also pleaded guilty and eleven others await trial.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals: explosive enrolment growth at a small number of centres, members travelling implausible distances to attend, attendance rosters with identical sign-in patterns, and heavy overlap between the day-care centre's enrollees and the affiliated fiscal intermediary's home-care members - shared ownership makes that overlap visible from enrolment ownership data. Beneficiary-side, kickback recruitment shows as members with attendance billed on days they have conflicting inpatient/other-provider claims, plus complaint and interview evidence from member outreach surveys.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a centre-day attendance verification edit: compare billed attendance units against biometric/electronic sign-in records and deny or pend units with no matching check-in, and flag centres whose per-member monthly units, enrolment growth rate or member travel distance exceed calibrated percentiles. Add an ownership-graph feature computing member overlap between commonly owned day-care centres and fiscal intermediaries, and place payment suspension plus member-verification interviews on centres above threshold.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Avanish Kumar Jha (co-owner, Dhrishti Pharma International); Rajnish Kumar Jha (co-owner, Dhrishti Pharma International); Dhrishti Pharma International
SchemeSummary: Two brothers operating Dhrishti Pharma International in India advertised prescription drugs online to U.S. buyers and shipped counterfeit and adulterated medicines, including vials labeled as the cancer drug Keytruda that actually contained over-the-counter heartburn medicine and no active ingredient; payments came via wire transfers, direct money exchanges and U.S.-based intermediaries collecting cash, with packaging designed to evade customs detection. Each brother was sentenced to 30 months and fined $50,000 (total $100,000), with $81,596 restitution to Merck to be considered later.
WaysToIdentify: No payer claims are involved - this is direct-to-consumer sale of counterfeit drugs from offshore sellers paid by wire and cash. Detection sits with import screening, payment processors and manufacturer serialisation: parcels from unregistered foreign shippers, online pharmacy sites without VIPPS/state licensure, and DSCSA serial numbers on Keytruda vials that do not resolve to a legitimate distribution record.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable controls: a serialisation/pedigree verification service that flags vials whose DSCSA serial numbers are unissued, duplicated or outside the authorised distribution chain, and payment-processor rules blocking merchant accounts tied to unlicensed online pharmacy domains. For payers, add a pharmacy-claim edit rejecting high-cost biologics dispensed by pharmacies not in the manufacturer's authorised distributor/specialty network.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Willie F. Murray, Jr. (registered agent and manager of Lab Tess, LLC); Lab Tess, LLC
State_County: Florida - Broward County (West Park); Florida - Charlotte County (Punta Gorda); Florida - Palm Beach County (Belle Glade, South Bay)
PayerName: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) COVID-19 Uninsured Program
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Murray used Lab Tess, LLC, which provided no actual COVID-19 testing, to submit more than 126,000 fraudulent reimbursement claims to HRSA for COVID-19 testing of uninsured individuals, using personal identifying information of Florida state prisoners, deceased persons, and people falsely reported as tested at homeless shelters and electrical substations, collecting about $5,671,611 that he partly used to buy South Florida real estate.
WaysToIdentify: Claim-volume velocity for a brand-new lab with no prior claim history, no CLIA capacity commensurate with 126,000 tests, and no matching specimen-collection or ordering-provider records is visible before payment. Identity misuse is caught by batch-matching claimed patients against the Death Master File, incarcerated-population files, and duplicate-address clusters (shelters, non-residential addresses such as substations), plus repeated members with no other claim history anywhere.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment-plus-velocity gate for uninsured-programme labs: cap and pend payment when a provider's weekly claim count exceeds the throughput implied by its CLIA certificate and reported instrumentation, requiring attestation and site verification. Add prepay identity edits that deny claims whose patient matches the Death Master File after the service date, matches a state incarceration roster on the service date, or belongs to an address cluster with anomalous patient counts, and require ordering-provider NPI plus specimen-collection evidence on every claim.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Favorite Home Care, LLC; Larry Sakson (co-owner); Olena Radionovsky (co-owner); Marina Sakson (employee/manager); Michael Radionovsky (employee/manager)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges the owners and managers of Favorite Home Care each personally placed electronic visit verification calls attesting they were delivering home care services to clients when they were not present, after which the company billed Medicaid and a Medicaid MCO and received payment for services never rendered.
WaysToIdentify: EVV telemetry itself carries the fraud: caller ID/GPS shows visits attested from the same device or phone number for many different clients, from the owner's/manager's own line, or from locations distant from the client's home, and multiple simultaneous or overlapping visits by one caregiver. Cross-matching the attesting caregiver ID against payroll and against the agency's owner/manager roster exposes principals logging clinical visits at scale.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an EVV-to-claim reconciliation edit that denies units without a matching check-in/check-out pair and pends visits whose GPS/caller ID is outside a tolerance of the client's registered address or duplicates another concurrent visit by the same caregiver. Add a caregiver-level feature flagging attestation from a single device/number across many clients and from IDs matching owners/managers, triggering payment suspension and client-contact verification for the agency.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Arkan Fadhel (owner, Queen City Transportation, Inc.); Queen City Transportation, Inc.
SchemeSummary: Fadhel, owner of a non-emergency Medicaid transportation company that drove beneficiaries mainly to methadone clinics, submitted false attestation records to Medical Answering Service claiming rides that never occurred and billing group rides as if each passenger had been transported separately, causing a Medicaid loss over $250,000. He was sentenced to three years supervised release with 12 months home incarceration, 400 hours community service, $781,186.80 forfeiture and $250,000 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Trip-level data allows matching each billed ride to a clinic encounter claim on the same date - rides with no corresponding methadone/clinic visit are phantom. Group rides are exposed by comparing pickup/drop times, GPS or vehicle assignment across claims: multiple single-passenger claims for the same vehicle and overlapping time window on the same route should have been billed as a shared trip.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit that requires a same-date service encounter for the destination provider before paying an NEMT trip leg, and denies legs with no matching encounter. Add a vehicle/driver/time-window clustering feature that groups claims sharing vehicle, driver, date and route window and repriced them to group-ride rates, firing a documentation request (signed trip logs, GPS telematics) and prepay review when a provider's single-passenger share exceeds same-market peers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Maureen Holleran (workers' compensation claims handler for Insurance Company 1)
PayerName: Insurance Company 1 (unnamed Canadian-headquartered workers' compensation insurer)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: As a remote workers' compensation claims handler, Holleran entered more than 1,200 fabricated claims (fictitious lost wages, medical supply and copay reimbursements) each kept under her $2,000 no-approval authority, using fake claimant email accounts to register in the insurer's client portal and route roughly $2.37 million in payments to her own bank accounts; she failed to report about $1,592,095 of the embezzled funds on 2020-2022 tax returns, with about $545,792 in tax due, and was sentenced to 18 months for filing a false tax return.
WaysToIdentify: This is internal embezzlement by a claims adjuster, detectable inside the insurer's own payment system: over a thousand claims all priced just below the handler's $2,000 no-approval authority, claimant portal registrations using email domains/patterns controlled by one user, and payment bank accounts repeated across unrelated claimants and matching an employee's own account. Duplicate payee bank details and no supporting provider claim or employer first-report-of-injury are the strongest prepay signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a payee-account dedup and employee-match control that blocks disbursement when the payee bank account, address, phone or email matches another claimant or any employee HR record, and require dual approval for any payment to a repeated account. Add an authority-threshold-clustering monitor per handler (share of approvals in the band just below their limit, count of self-created claimants, claims with no employer FROI or provider bill on file), auto-suspending the handler's payment authority for investigation when above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Zaven Yeghiazaryan (business owner)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud; Other - Unknown
SchemeSummary: Defendant used shell companies and false identities to defraud the SBA's Economic Injury Disaster Loan program and the Pandemic Unemployment Assistance program, and also participated in a scheme to defraud Medicaid; he pleaded guilty to 13 counts including conspiracy, health care fraud, wire fraud and money laundering, with restitution of $334,905.
WaysToIdentify: The EIDL and PUA legs are loan/benefit programmes with no payer adjudication, caught by cross-programme identity and entity screening (shell entities with recent registration dates, no payroll tax filings, shared addresses/IPs/bank accounts across many applications). The Medicaid leg is catchable at enrolment: newly formed entities whose owners, addresses, phones and EFT accounts cluster with other applicants and with the loan-fraud shells, and whose billing begins at high velocity with no verifiable site.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment entity-resolution screen linking applicant owners, addresses, phones, IP/device fingerprints and EFT accounts into clusters; auto-hold enrolment and prepay all claims when an applicant shares identifiers with other recent applicants or with known shell-entity registries, pending site visit. Add a new-provider payment ceiling with velocity monitoring that suspends payment when first-90-day claim volume or dollars exceed peer norms for the specialty.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Zaven Yeghiazaryan (business owner)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendant used shell companies and false identities to defraud government programs, including the SBA's Economic Injury Disaster Loan program and Pandemic Unemployment Assistance, and also admitted participating in a scheme to defraud Medicaid; proceeds were laundered. Ordered to pay $118,205.94 restitution plus $151,300 in fines and assessments.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: SBA EIDL and PUA fraud have no claim-adjudication touchpoint, so the control is identity/entity screening at application - shell companies with recent formation, no payroll history, and shared bank accounts, addresses and devices across applications. For the Medicaid leg, the pre-payment signal is a newly enrolled provider or member whose identifiers cluster with those shells and whose billing has no verifiable service footprint.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a shared identity-graph screen across provider enrolment and member enrolment (owner SSN/EIN, address, phone, email, IP/device, EFT account), blocking enrolment and pending claims when clusters exceed the calibrated linkage threshold and requiring in-person or site verification. Add new-entity payment throttles with velocity-based suspension, and route entities linked to laundering typologies (rapid pass-through of receipts to personal accounts) to prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: C.R. Bard, Inc.; Liberator Medical Supply, Inc.; Liberator Holdings; Rochester Medical Corporation
SchemeSummary: Bard and its Liberator affiliates allegedly gave urology practice groups discounts, excessive free samples and cost savings on in-office urological supplies to induce them to adopt Bard's 'Link' prescription form as the standard form for intermittent catheters, steering patients' catheter prescriptions to Bard products and to Bard's own DME subsidiary Liberator Medical, which billed Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE. Resolved for $17 million following a qui tam suit by a former 180 Medical employee.
WaysToIdentify: The steering shows up in claims as an abrupt, near-total shift in catheter brand/HCPCS supplier mix among a set of urology practices, with prescriptions from those practices concentrating on one manufacturer's affiliated DME supplier. Free-goods and discount inducements are visible from manufacturer transparency/Open Payments and rebate reporting, and from practices receiving in-office supplies at values inconsistent with their purchase records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a referral-steering feature at the ordering-practice/quarter level computing the share of intermittent-catheter prescriptions routed to a single manufacturer-affiliated supplier, and flag step-changes and shares above same-specialty peers for AKS review before continued payment. Cross-join Open Payments/free-sample and discount data to those practices, firing an investigative hold and documentation request on the affiliated supplier's claims where financial-relationship value and steering share co-occur.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
FraudEntity: American Psychiatric Centers, Inc., d/b/a Comprehensive Psychiatric Services (CPS) (behavioral medicine provider)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Medi-Cal); TRICARE; Veterans Affairs health care programs; Federal Employees Health Benefits Program
SchemeSummary: CPS billed government health care payors using psychotherapy 'add-on' CPT codes 90833 and 90836 alongside evaluation and management visits where its providers either never performed the psychotherapy services described or failed to sufficiently document them; CPS will pay $2,615,569.32 to the United States and $134,430.68 to California.
WaysToIdentify: Add-on psychotherapy codes 90833/90836 billed with nearly every E/M visit is a mechanical outlier: compute the ratio of add-on psychotherapy to E/M visits per rendering provider against same-specialty peers, and check whether the E/M level's documented time plus the add-on's required minutes fit the provider's billed day. Providers whose add-on attachment rate approaches 100% and whose implied daily minutes are infeasible should be pended for records before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider/month attachment-rate feature (share of E/M visits carrying 90833/90836/90838) plus a per-day implied-minutes sum across all timed codes; fire a prepay documentation request for session notes with start/stop times and separate psychotherapy content when the attachment rate or daily minutes exceed the calibrated peer percentile. Add a claim-level edit denying the add-on where the paired E/M's time already consumes the encounter, and escalate persistent outliers to prepay review of all behavioural claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Advoque Safeguard LLC (mask manufacturer); Jason Azevedo (owner/manager); Andrew Stack (owner/manager); Paul Shrater (owner/manager); JDM Supply LLC (distributor); Daniel Motha; Jeffrey Motha; Jason Colantuoni
SchemeSummary: Advoque Safeguard manufactured facemasks that were falsely represented as NIOSH-approved N95 respirators and JDM Supply sold hundreds of thousands of them to a Massachusetts hospital during the early COVID-19 pandemic; NIOSH lab testing showed filtration efficiency of only 83.94%-93.24%, below the 95% N95 requirement, and the hospital paid for but never used the masks. Figures span multiple corporate and individual defendants (fines totaling about $1.03 million); one defendant also pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit price gouging.
WaysToIdentify: This is a product-misbranding/procurement fraud rather than a claim-adjudication fraud, so the payer-side hook is the supply chain and any respirator/PPE pass-through billing: verify the claimed NIOSH approval number and manufacturer on the FDA/NIOSH Certified Equipment List and the CDC counterfeit-respirator list before purchase order or before reimbursing PPE add-on codes, and check whether the seller is a listed FDA device establishment. Signals available pre-payment include a distributor with no device establishment registration, a NIOSH approval number that does not match the manufacturer of record, unit prices far above pre-pandemic baselines, and brand-new supplier entity registered weeks before the sale. Otherwise this is caught post-payment via lab testing and recall/False Claims recovery.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a supplier/product validation service keyed on (NDC/UDI or catalog number, manufacturer, NIOSH approval number) that cross-references the NIOSH Certified Equipment List, FDA establishment registration and recall/counterfeit feeds; any PPE purchase order or PPE-related claim line whose approval number is absent, mismatched, or on a counterfeit alert is hard-stopped pending certificate-of-conformance documentation. Add a price-outlier monitor on PPE line items comparing unit price to the pre-emergency rolling median and to same-product peers, flagging above-calibrated-percentile prices for manual procurement/claims review and price-gouging referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Advoque Safeguard LLC (mask manufacturer); Jason Azevedo (owner/manager); Paul Shrater (owner/manager); Andrew Stack (owner/manager); JDM Supply LLC (distributor); Daniel Motha; Jeffrey Motha; Jason Colantuoni
SchemeSummary: Advoque Safeguard LLC manufactured facemasks and, with distributor JDM Supply LLC, sold hundreds of thousands of them to a hospital in spring 2020 falsely represented as NIOSH-approved N95 respirators; NIOSH lab testing showed filtration efficiency of only 83.94%-93.24%, below the 95% N95 requirement. The company and three owner/managers pleaded guilty to misbranded-device charges; a second company and three other individuals pleaded guilty earlier, one to conspiracy to commit price gouging.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: a manufacturer/distributor pair sold non-conforming respirators as NIOSH-approved N95s, which is visible at procurement/credentialing time rather than at adjudication. A payer or hospital could match the asserted NIOSH approval number and manufacturer against the NIOSH Certified Equipment List and FDA device establishment registrations, and note that neither entity had a history of respirator approvals before spring 2020. Definitive proof requires lab filtration testing, so the residual route is post-payment recovery plus sample testing of high-volume PPE lots.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a pre-purchase/pre-pay device-conformance edit: for any respirator or regulated device line, require a resolvable NIOSH approval number plus FDA registration for the named manufacturer, and suspend payment when the seller is not the approval holder or an authorized distributor of record. Layer an entity-age and product-history rule that routes first-time PPE suppliers formed within the recent lookback window to documentation request (certificate of conformance, lot test reports) before any payment or reimbursement of PPE pass-through.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Adam Wayne Owens (owner of marketing companies)
SchemeSummary: Owens used California marketing companies to identify Medicare beneficiaries and pass their personal and medical information to cancer genetic testing (CGX) companies, which mailed at-home test kits and billed Medicare; Owens received $1,700-$2,000 per reimbursed test, routed through a New Zealand company under a sham marketing contract and false hourly invoices to disguise the kickbacks, causing over $10 million in Medicare losses.
WaysToIdentify: The pre-pay signals are structural: CGX panels billed for beneficiaries with no cancer diagnosis history, no treating-physician relationship, ordering providers geographically remote from the beneficiary, and kits mailed after telemarketing contact rather than an office visit. Concentration analysis on the ordering NPI (one physician ordering high-cost hereditary cancer panels across many states with no prior claims for those patients) and on beneficiary clustering by marketing lead source is visible at adjudication. The offshore sham marketing contract and per-test kickbacks are only provable post-payment via financial records and interviews.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit on hereditary cancer panel codes requiring, in the claim history window, an evaluation-and-management encounter with the ordering NPI and a cancer or family-history diagnosis supporting the panel; claims failing both conditions are pended for medical-record and order documentation. Add ordering-provider surveillance computing distinct-beneficiary count, state dispersion, and share of CGX orders with no prior relationship versus same-specialty peers, plus lab-level detection of beneficiary cohorts arriving in bursts from the same mailing/lead source, triggering prepay review or payment suspension of the lab.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; USAO - Central District of California
FraudEntity: Juan Carlos Esparza (owner of House of Angels Hospice); Petros Fichidzhyan; Karpis Srapyan; Susanna Harutyunyan; Mihran Panosyan; House of Angels Hospice
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Valley Village/greater Los Angeles)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants operated four sham hospice companies that billed Medicare nearly $16 million for hospice services that were medically unnecessary and never provided, using foreign nationals' identities as nominee owners to open bank accounts, enroll with Medicare, sign leases, and obtain cell phones; proceeds were laundered through shell company accounts and assets (Esparza bought a $90,000 vehicle). Figures span multiple co-defendants; Fichidzhyan received the longest sentence, 12 years.
WaysToIdentify: Enrolment-time signals dominate: four newly enrolled hospices with nominee owners who are foreign nationals not physically in the country, addresses/leases and phone numbers sharing landlords, IP addresses or registered agents, and bank accounts opened by third parties. At adjudication, hospice election claims appear for beneficiaries with no supporting terminal-diagnosis history, no prior hospitalization or physician contact, and often concurrent claims from other providers inconsistent with hospice election. Rapid post-enrolment billing ramp for a brand-new hospice is a strong prepay flag.
FeaturesToCreate: At enrolment, run identity and presence verification on owners (SSA/DHS travel or death/exit data, credit-header residency) and cluster new applications by address, phone, IP, bank routing, registered agent and lease landlord; matched clusters go to site visit and application hold. At claims, apply a new-provider prepay review regime on hospice elections for the first period of billing, firing when the beneficiary lacks a terminal-illness diagnosis trail or the certifying physician has no prior claims for that beneficiary, and suspend payments when a cluster fires.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California
FraudEntity: Mihran Panosyan (money launderer); Petros Fichidzhyan (co-defendant)
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Winnetka/greater Los Angeles)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Co-defendants used identities of foreign nationals who had left the U.S. to set up and operate sham hospice companies, then billed Medicare roughly $16 million for hospice services for patients who were not terminally ill and never requested or received care; Panosyan laundered over $4.6 million of the proceeds through accounts of the purported foreign owners, the sham hospices, and shell corporations to buy real estate, private school tuition, and personal expenses. Co-defendant Fichidzhyan previously pleaded guilty and received 12 years.
WaysToIdentify: Identical mechanic to the companion case: sham hospices enrolled under identities of foreign nationals who had left the country, billing for beneficiaries never terminally ill and never seen. Pre-pay detectable via owner identity/presence verification at enrolment, shared-infrastructure clustering across the four entities, and beneficiary-level checks that hospice elections lack any terminal diagnosis, prior hospitalization, or certifying-physician relationship. Money laundering through shell corporations is a post-payment financial-analysis route (bank subpoenas, asset tracing).
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment identity control that verifies owner presence and identity against immigration/exit and death data and holds applications whose owners cannot be verified as physically present; combine with a graph clustering job on addresses, phones, bank accounts and registered agents linking multiple hospice applications. Pair with a prepay hospice-election edit requiring documented terminal diagnosis and a prior claims relationship with the certifying physician, escalating to suspension and credible-allegation-of-fraud referral when a linked cluster bills concurrently.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Petros Fichidzhyan (controlled sham hospice entities and a home health care agency)
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Granada Hills / greater Los Angeles)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Fichidzhyan and co-schemers controlled sham hospice companies that billed Medicare for hospice services never provided and not medically necessary, using foreign nationals' PII to open bank accounts, enroll with Medicare and sign leases, and misappropriating the identities of several doctors (two deceased) to submit claims; Medicare paid nearly $16 million, of which he received about $7 million with $5.3 million laundered through a dozen shell/third-party accounts, plus over $1 million to his home health agency using a doctor's name to falsely certify beneficiaries.
WaysToIdentify: Two hard prepay signals exist here: certifying physician NPIs belonging to deceased or non-participating doctors, and hospice/home-health certifications from physicians with no other claim history for that beneficiary. Both are checkable at adjudication against the provider enrolment file, SSA/NPPES death and deactivation data, and the beneficiary's claim history. Nominee foreign-national ownership and shared leases/bank accounts across the entities are catchable at enrolment through identity verification and cluster analysis.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a hard prepay edit rejecting any hospice election or home-health certification where the attending/certifying NPI is deceased, deactivated, or has no active enrolment on the service date, and pend where the certifier has zero prior encounters with that beneficiary. Add a physician-identity misuse monitor that alerts the physician of record when certification volume spikes or when certifications originate from an agency the physician has never billed with, and suspend the agency's payments pending signature and record validation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: American Furniture Rentals, Inc. (furniture rental company, Pennsauken, New Jersey)
SchemeSummary: AFR applied for and received a $2 million PPP loan in January 2021, falsely certifying eligibility despite having more than 300 employees (the eligibility cap at the time), then obtained full forgiveness of the loan plus accrued interest; the False Claims Act qui tam matter settled for $2,907,703.
WaysToIdentify: No health-care claim component: this is PPP loan eligibility fraud resolved under the False Claims Act. The signal was available at loan underwriting and forgiveness review by comparing the borrower's certified employee count against payroll tax filings (941s), state wage records, and affiliate rosters, which would have exposed a headcount above the eligibility cap. No payer-side claims control applies.
FeaturesToCreate: For the loan program administrator, build an eligibility cross-check that joins the applicant EIN to IRS payroll filings and state unemployment wage data plus common-ownership affiliate mapping, computing total employees across affiliates and firing when the certified figure understates the computed figure; hold forgiveness pending reconciliation. Nearest payer-side analogue: reconcile provider-reported staffing/FTE data on cost reports and relief-fund attestations against payroll data before disbursement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Krishna Gidwani (co-owner/operator of DME company); Raju Sharma (co-conspirator)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Gidwani and Sharma allegedly owned and operated a DME company that paid telemarketing companies for orthotic brace orders (ankle, wrist, knee, back), then shipped braces Medicare beneficiaries did not need or want and billed Medicare over $4 million; the doctors whose signatures appeared on the orders often never treated the beneficiaries or prescribed the equipment.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals: orthotic brace claims (L-codes for ankle, wrist, knee, back braces) where the ordering physician has no prior or contemporaneous encounter with the beneficiary, beneficiaries clustered nationwide around one supplier, and multiple braces per beneficiary in short windows. Ordering-NPI concentration - a handful of physicians signing orders across many states for a single supplier - is visible in the claims graph at adjudication, as is a new supplier's steep post-enrolment ramp in a single L-code family. Telemarketing payments themselves are post-payment financial evidence.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit on orthotic L-codes requiring a face-to-face or telehealth E/M claim with the ordering NPI within the required lookback and a supporting musculoskeletal diagnosis; failures pend for medical records and signed order review. Add supplier-level analytics computing share of claims tied to a small set of ordering NPIs, beneficiary geographic dispersion, and braces-per-beneficiary versus same-specialty DME peers, firing prepay review or suspension above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Krishna Gidwani (DME company owner/operator); Raju Sharma (co-conspirator, DME company owner/operator)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Gidwani and co-conspirator Raju Sharma owned and operated a DME company that paid telemarketing companies for orders for orthotic braces (ankle, wrist, knee, back), then billed Medicare over $4 million for braces beneficiaries did not need or want; the doctors whose signatures appeared on the orders often never treated the beneficiaries or prescribed the equipment.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic: telemarketer-sourced orthotic brace orders bearing physician signatures where no encounter occurred. Detectable prepay by joining each DME claim's ordering NPI to that beneficiary's encounter history (no E/M with the ordering physician), by high concentration of one supplier's volume in a few ordering NPIs, and by beneficiaries spread far from both the supplier and the ordering physician. Multiple distinct braces per beneficiary within a short window is an additional adjudication-time flag.
FeaturesToCreate: Deploy a claim-line edit denying/pending orthotic brace codes lacking a qualifying encounter with the ordering provider and a supporting diagnosis, with a documentation request for the signed order and clinical notes. Complement with a supplier scorecard (ordering-NPI concentration index, cross-state beneficiary dispersion, brace-per-beneficiary rate, post-enrolment growth slope) that moves outliers onto prepay review and, on physician attestation of forged signatures, payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Krishna Gidwani (owner/operator of DME company); Raju Sharma (co-conspirator)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Gidwani and co-conspirators owned and operated a DME company that paid telemarketing companies for orders for orthotic braces (ankle, wrist, knee, back), then billed Medicare over $4 million for braces beneficiaries did not need or want, using DME orders bearing signatures of doctors who often never treated or prescribed for those beneficiaries.
WaysToIdentify: Identical brace-mill mechanic: signed orders from physicians who never treated the beneficiary, generated by paid telemarketing leads. The payer can see at adjudication that the ordering NPI has no claim history with the beneficiary, that the supplier's orders funnel through a tiny set of signing physicians, and that beneficiaries are geographically scattered relative to the supplier. Physician outreach/attestation campaigns on top-signing NPIs confirm the forgery before further payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build the ordering-relationship prepay edit (no E/M with ordering NPI within lookback, or diagnosis not supporting the brace) with automatic documentation request; add an automated physician-verification workflow that mails/portals attestation requests to NPIs whose brace-order volume exceeds their peer-specialty norm. Suspend the supplier's payments when attestation is denied or unreturned, and register the involved NPIs on a prepay watchlist across all suppliers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Eric Strom Holland (operator of unlicensed virtual pain clinic)
SchemeSummary: Holland ran an unlicensed, entirely virtual pain clinic and recruited temporary doctors by falsely telling them the clinic had a physical location, that patients had been physically examined by nurse practitioners, that patients had standing relationships with long-term physicians, and that abuse safeguards such as urine screens were in place; the deceived doctors issued more than 900 prescriptions for over 100,000 oxycodone tablets (street value over $4 million), and Holland routinely failed to pay the doctors as promised.
WaysToIdentify: Even without a payer bill, the controllable data is prescribing: a PDMP/pharmacy view shows a single clinic address (unlicensed, no physical site) generating high-volume oxycodone prescriptions from rotating short-tenure prescribers, all patients cash-pay, no accompanying E/M or urine drug screen claims, and long-distance patient travel to fill. State licensure/facility registration files would show no licensed pain clinic at the address. These signals are visible to plans, PBMs and PDMP administrators before dispensing.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a clinic-address-level controlled-substance monitor joining PDMP/pharmacy claims to prescriber licensure and facility registration, computing MED per patient, prescriber-turnover rate at the address, share of opioid prescriptions with no companion E/M or toxicology claim, and patient-to-pharmacy distance; fire when the address has no licensed facility registration or exceeds peer thresholds. Action: prescriber/pharmacy alert plus prior-authorization or pharmacy-lock edit on opioid claims from that address pending verification of a legitimate practice site and examination records.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Fouodzing Mbord (home health aide/caregiver)
SchemeSummary: No billing scheme; a home health aide providing 24-hour care to a bedridden stroke victim was captured on home security cameras striking the vulnerable adult on two occasions in November 2023 and threatening to do it again. He pleaded guilty to abuse of a vulnerable adult and received a 180-day jail sentence suspended in full with one year of probation; the case was investigated in part by the D.C. OIG Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.
WaysToIdentify: There is no billing scheme here, so no prepay claims edit would have caught it; the abuse was detected by home video and reported. Payer-adjacent signals that can be systematized are workforce screening at hire (state abuse registry, exclusion list, criminal history, prior MFCU findings) and complaint/EVV pattern review, plus incident and injury reporting from the member's other claims (ED visits or injury diagnoses during an aide-covered shift). The realistic route is post-service: complaint intake and MFCU referral.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a caregiver-level screening service that re-runs exclusion list, state abuse/neglect registry and licensure checks on a recurring cadence and blocks claims naming a disqualified aide as the service provider. Add a member-safety trigger that correlates EVV-attributed shifts with new injury/ED claims or complaint records for the same member and opens an urgent quality-of-care investigation and MFCU referral rather than a payment edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Carson Tahoe Health System (owner of Carson Tahoe Physician Clinics and Carson Tahoe Continuing Care Hospital); Carson Tahoe Physician Clinics; Carson Tahoe Continuing Care Hospital
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Carson Tahoe Health System and two affiliated entities obtained four Paycheck Protection Program loans in May 2020 and February 2021 totaling $5,077,011 plus a $2 million second loan, and had them forgiven, despite allegedly being ineligible because their combined size under SBA affiliation rules exceeded program limits; the forgiven principal, interest and lender fees cost the government $7,267,009, resolved by an $8,876,475.45 False Claims Act settlement arising from a qui tam suit.
WaysToIdentify: No claims-payment mechanic: this is PPP eligibility fraud under SBA affiliation rules, resolved via FCA settlement. It was detectable at underwriting/forgiveness by aggregating employee counts across commonly controlled affiliates using the health system's ownership disclosures, Medicare cost report related-organization schedules, IRS payroll filings and system-wide W-2 counts. No payer-side prepay claims control applies.
FeaturesToCreate: For the loan administrator, implement affiliation-aware size testing: resolve applicant EIN to a corporate family via ownership registries and Medicare/Medicaid ownership disclosures, sum affiliate employees from payroll tax and state wage data, and block disbursement or forgiveness when the aggregate exceeds the program cap. Payer-side analogue: reconcile provider-submitted ownership/control disclosures with cost report related-party schedules and flag inconsistencies for enrolment review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Catholic Health System, Inc. (CHS) and its affiliated hospitals
SchemeSummary: CHS and its affiliated hospitals allegedly maintained compensation arrangements with non-employee physicians for administrative services that were not commercially reasonable or exceeded fair market value; those physicians then referred laboratory testing, hospital services and medical supplies to CHS, which billed Medicare for the referred services in violation of the Stark Law. Resolved by a $3,293,122.66 civil settlement following a qui tam suit by relator Gary Tucker.
WaysToIdentify: This Stark/kickback arrangement is visible in the payer's own data as referral concentration: non-employee physicians holding administrative-services contracts with a hospital whose lab, imaging and supply referrals to that hospital exceed same-specialty peer patterns, especially where the physician's paid administrative hours are implausible relative to their clinical claim volume. Ownership/compensation relationships are reportable (Open Payments, hospital financial-relationship disclosures) and can be joined to referral flows at adjudication. Fair-market-value and commercial-reasonableness findings generally require post-payment audit and were surfaced by a whistleblower.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a referral-relationship graph linking each referring NPI to hospital/lab/DME billing entities and to disclosed compensation arrangements (Open Payments, contract registry), computing the physician's share of referrals to the paying entity versus same-specialty peers and the ratio of administrative compensation to documented clinical time. Fire above the calibrated percentile into a Stark/AKS documentation request for the written arrangement, time logs and FMV opinion, and hold claims for designated health services from flagged physician-entity pairs pending review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
FraudEntity: Centers Healthcare (operator of 44 related skilled nursing facilities)
State_County: New York - Albany, Essex, Fulton, Jefferson, Oneida, Onondaga, Otsego, Rensselaer, Schenectady, Ulster, Warren, and Washington counties; Rhode Island; Kansas; Missouri
SchemeSummary: Centers Healthcare admitted that Medicare cost reports submitted for 44 commonly owned/controlled skilled nursing facilities contained false statements or omitted material information about transactions with related organizations, which SNFs must disclose at the lower of actual cost or market price; management reviewed the reports and knew or should have known of the falsities. Resolved for $6,063,500 under the False Claims Act.
WaysToIdentify: This is a cost-report fraud, so the control lives in cost-report intake rather than claim adjudication: related-organization schedules (Worksheet A-8-2) for 44 commonly owned SNFs can be cross-checked against ownership/control disclosures, secretary-of-state and PECOS ownership data, and vendor names appearing in each other's filings to detect undisclosed related parties and costs booked above the lower of cost or market. Comparing per-diem management, therapy, staffing-agency and rent costs across commonly owned facilities and against non-affiliated peers exposes inflated related-party charges before settlement.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a cost-report edit that resolves every vendor on each SNF's cost report against a common-ownership graph (PECOS ownership, state corporate filings, shared officers/addresses) and fires when a material vendor is related but not disclosed on the related-organization schedule, or when related-party unit costs exceed market benchmarks and peer commonly owned facilities. Action: hold interim-rate settlement and issue a documentation request for related-party cost buildups; escalate systematically filed chains to audit.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Cemhan "Jimmy" Biricik (sole member and CEO of Fast Lab Technologies, LLC); Dr. Martin Perlin (Medical Director and ordering physician); Fast Lab Technologies, LLC
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; TRICARE; private health insurers
SchemeSummary: Fast Lab operated a website offering "free" COVID-19 tests and harvested visitors' insurance information, then billed Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE and private insurers for antigen and PCR tests across multiple dates per beneficiary, falsely representing that antigen tests were observed by medical professionals, that saliva samples were collected, and that PCR testing was performed - none of which occurred; claims were often submitted before kits were even delivered, and Dr. Perlin was listed as ordering physician without any treating relationship. Over $500 million billed, more than $50 million paid.
WaysToIdentify: Several signals are visible at adjudication: claims with service dates preceding kit shipment/delivery dates, repeated COVID antigen and PCR claims for the same beneficiary across many dates from a single lab, one ordering physician NPI attached to essentially all claims with no treating relationship, and antigen codes billed as professionally observed by an entity with no clinical site or staff. Beneficiary cohorts arriving from a single website lead source, and beneficiaries who never requested tests (complaint and Explanation-of-Benefits feedback), corroborate. Lab enrolment data would show no CLIA capacity matching the PCR volume billed.
FeaturesToCreate: Build prepay edits for COVID testing: deny/pend claims where the same lab bills repeat antigen or PCR tests for a beneficiary above the calibrated frequency, where the service date precedes the shipment/delivery date on the lab's own supply data, and where the observed-administration modifier is used by a supplier with no site-of-service or staffing on file. Add ordering-NPI concentration and CLIA-capacity-versus-volume checks that trigger payment suspension and beneficiary verification outreach for labs above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Cashmir Chinedu Luke (CEO, sole owner and billing representative of Four Corners Health LLC); Four Corners Health LLC
State_County: California - Fresno County; California - Tulare County; California - Merced County; California - Mariposa County; California - Madera County; California - San Francisco County; California - Contra Costa County
PayerName: Department of Veterans Affairs (Veterans Community Care Program)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Retention of Overpayment
SchemeSummary: Luke, sole owner of Four Corners Health LLC, submitted roughly 10,000 false claims to the VA's third-party benefits administrator under the Veterans Community Care Program for in-home care hours never rendered - duplicate claims, days caretakers were not present, hours beyond those worked, and care for veterans who had already died - collecting $7 million into a bank account he solely controlled, then spending it on personal expenses or transferring it across accounts in Asia and Africa while deceiving the administrator's recovery efforts.
WaysToIdentify: All four abuse patterns are detectable prepay from claims data alone: exact duplicate claims (same veteran, date, hours), billed hours exceeding EVV-verified caregiver clock-in/out, dates of service after the veteran's date of death, and aggregate caregiver hours exceeding feasible hours per day. Cross-referencing the administrator's authorization records and the enrolment/death file at adjudication would have stopped the majority of the roughly 10,000 claims. Repayment evasion and offshore transfers are post-payment recovery issues.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement four prepay edits keyed on (veteran, date, caregiver): exact/near-duplicate detection, date-of-death check against the eligibility and death file, EVV reconciliation denying billed hours in excess of verified visit minutes, and a caregiver-day-hours cap that flags impossible aggregate hours across veterans. Combine failures into an agency-level score that triggers payment suspension and prepay review of all claims for single-owner agencies with rapid volume growth.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Gary Cox (CEO of Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)); Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care benefit programs; VA; other insurers
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Cox operated DMERx, an internet platform that generated fraudulent doctors' orders for medically unnecessary orthotic braces and pain creams for Medicare beneficiaries recruited via mailers, TV ads, and offshore call centers; telemedicine companies paid doctors to sign orders without examinations, and DME suppliers and pharmacies paid kickbacks for the orders and billed Medicare and other insurers over $1 billion, of which more than $360 million was paid.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals: a single order-generation platform's fingerprint across thousands of claims - the same small set of telemedicine physician NPIs signing orders for beneficiaries nationwide, no E/M encounter or only a brief telehealth code with no follow-up, and identical L-code brace and compounded pain-cream combinations across unrelated suppliers and pharmacies. Beneficiary recruitment via mailers and offshore call centers shows up as geographic dispersion and bursty enrollment cohorts shared by multiple suppliers. Kickback payments themselves surface post-payment through financial records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a cross-supplier ordering-provider graph: for each signing NPI compute distinct suppliers/pharmacies served, distinct states, orders per active practice day, and share of orders with no prior beneficiary relationship; above the calibrated percentile, place the NPI on a prepay hold list so every downstream brace/pain-cream claim citing that NPI pends for documentation. Add an edit requiring a qualifying encounter and supporting diagnosis for L-codes and compounded topical analgesics, and suspend suppliers whose volume is concentrated in flagged NPIs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Gary Cox (CEO of Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)); Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)
State_County: Florida - Miami-Dade County (Miami); Arizona - Maricopa County
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care benefit programs (including VA); other insurers
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Cox operated DMERx, an internet-based platform that generated false doctors' orders falsely representing that physicians had examined Medicare beneficiaries, when telemedicine companies paid doctors to sign orders after brief or no patient contact; Cox connected DME suppliers, pharmacies, and marketers with these telemedicine companies in exchange for kickbacks, and the suppliers billed Medicare and other insurers over $1 billion for orthotic braces, pain creams, and other items, receiving over $360 million.
WaysToIdentify: The platform's output is statistically distinctive at adjudication: bulk orders signed by a few telemedicine physicians for beneficiaries they never examined, distributed to many unaffiliated DME suppliers and pharmacies that share the same signing NPIs and the same product mix. No prior beneficiary-physician claim history, minimal or absent telehealth E/M, and cross-state dispersion are all observable before payment. Physician attestation campaigns on the top signing NPIs confirm no examination occurred.
FeaturesToCreate: Create a signing-provider risk engine that scores each ordering NPI on orders-per-day, downstream-supplier breadth, no-prior-relationship rate and product concentration, and auto-pends all claims naming high-scoring NPIs pending signed order and clinical documentation. Add a supplier/pharmacy-side edit: when a payee's claims share the same flagged NPI cohort above the calibrated share, trigger prepay review and payment suspension pending kickback/marketing-contract disclosure.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Gary Cox (CEO of Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)); Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)
PayerName: Medicare;TRICARE;Department of Veterans Affairs health programs;other insurers
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Cox ran DMERx, an internet-based platform that generated false doctors' orders falsely representing that physicians had examined Medicare beneficiaries recruited via misleading mailers, TV ads and offshore call centers; he connected DME suppliers, pharmacies and marketers with telemedicine companies that took kickbacks to have doctors sign orders without regard to medical necessity, and the suppliers and pharmacies then billed Medicare and other insurers more than $1 billion, collecting over $360 million.
WaysToIdentify: Same DMERx mechanic across multiple payers, so the strongest signal is cross-payer/cross-supplier reuse of a small set of signing physician NPIs paired with mailer- and call-center-sourced beneficiaries in bursts. At adjudication one can see absent or token telehealth encounters, no prior beneficiary-physician relationship, formulaic brace-plus-pain-cream bundles, and identical order templates across unrelated suppliers. Kickbacks between the platform, telemedicine firms and suppliers are post-payment financial findings.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a shared prepay watchlist of ordering NPIs derived from graph metrics (suppliers served, states, daily order volume, share without prior relationship) that pends brace and compounded-cream claims for documentation, and share the list across Medicare, TRICARE and VA community-care adjudication. Add a beneficiary-cohort burst detector that flags groups of beneficiaries first appearing on multiple suppliers' claims within the same short window via the same ordering NPI, escalating to supplier payment suspension and beneficiary verification calls.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Thomas Stafford (Chief Executive Officer and President of Information Systems Staffing, Inc.); Information Systems Staffing, Inc.
SchemeSummary: Stafford, CEO of an IT staffing company, allegedly caused the company to fail to pay over approximately $2,008,046.63 in trust fund taxes (Social Security, Medicare and federal income tax withholdings from employee paychecks) to the IRS from Q1 2019 through Q4 2024, while using company bank accounts to pay personal expenses; he also allegedly understated income and concealed control of properties in a 2023 Chapter 13 bankruptcy filing.
WaysToIdentify: This is employment-tax and bankruptcy fraud with no claims-payment component, so no payer adjudication control would have caught it; the detection route is IRS matching of W-2 withholding reported by the employer against Form 941 filings and trust-fund deposits, plus bankruptcy schedules cross-checked against property records and bank data. A payer-side analogue is enrolment screening: a contracted staffing/provider entity with unpaid federal tax liens or unfiled payroll returns is a financial-instability and diversion risk.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment/revalidation screen that runs the entity and its owners against federal/state tax lien, judgment and bankruptcy filing feeds and flags mismatches between W-2 aggregate withholding and 941 filings where the data is available; fire a credentialing review and require a corporate financial attestation. Otherwise state plainly no claims-payment control applies to this case.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Dr. Kingsley R. Chin (Founder, President and CEO of SpineFrontier, Inc.); SpineFrontier, Inc. (medical device company)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: SpineFrontier offered spine surgeons purported product-development consulting arrangements; Chin directed employees to report to CMS's Open Payments Program a $4,750 payment made to a surgeon on Jan. 19, 2016 as a 'consulting' fee, though he knew no actual consulting work had been performed, concealing the true nature of the payment required to be publicly disclosed under the Physician Payment Sunshine Act.
WaysToIdentify: The signal is a manufacturer-to-surgeon payment stream reported to Open Payments as 'consulting' with no deliverable, sitting alongside the same surgeons' implant utilization; a payer can join Open Payments general/consulting payments by physician NPI to its own claims for that manufacturer's implant codes and see that payment recipients drive disproportionate device volume. Pre-payment, the credentialing and prior-authorization files for high-cost spine implants can be checked for undisclosed vendor financial relationships.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a physician-level monthly join of Open Payments payments (by paying manufacturer, nature-of-payment) to implant/spine surgery claims; compute the share of a surgeon's implant volume tied to manufacturers paying them and flag surgeons above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers for prepay review of medical necessity. Additionally flag manufacturers whose consulting payments cluster in small round amounts across many surgeons with no reported research output, and route to SIU/AKS referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Dr. Kingsley R. Chin (Founder, President and CEO of SpineFrontier, Inc.); SpineFrontier, Inc.; KICVentures
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Chin, CEO of medical device maker SpineFrontier, offered surgeons purported product-development consulting engagements and directed employees to report a $4,750 payment to a surgeon on Jan. 19, 2016 as a 'consulting' fee in CMS Open Payments reporting under the Physician Payment Sunshine Act, though he knew no actual consulting work had been performed. He was sentenced to one year supervised release (first six months home confinement), a $9,500 fine, plus $40,000 personally and $855,000 from his company KICVentures in a related civil settlement.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the SpineFrontier consulting-fee case: sham 'consulting' payments disclosed under the Sunshine Act to disguise referral inducements to implanting surgeons. Payers can detect it by linking Open Payments records to their own device and surgery claims to find surgeons whose implant selection tracks the paying manufacturer, and by requiring disclosure of vendor financial ties at credentialing and for implant prior authorization.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a surgeon-manufacturer influence score: per NPI, compute payment dollars/counts by manufacturer from Open Payments and the concentration of that manufacturer's devices in the surgeon's implant claims; fire prepay medical-necessity documentation requests on implant claims where concentration and payment both exceed calibrated percentiles. Flag manufacturers with many small uniform 'consulting' payments lacking documented work product for AKS referral and possible network termination.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
SchemeSummary: Not a fraud case: this press release announces the appointment of Charles Neil Floyd as interim U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Washington and describes his career, with no fraud scheme described.
WaysToIdentify: This is a personnel announcement, not a fraud case; there is no scheme, no claims and nothing for a payer to detect. No pre-payment or post-payment signal exists.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. If ingesting DOJ press releases into an intelligence pipeline, add a classifier that drops non-case items (appointments, awards, annual round-ups) before they generate provider risk flags.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Steven Osbey (co-owner, Reign & Inspirations, LLC); Aljihad Shabazz (co-owner); Reign & Inspirations, LLC (clinic)
SchemeSummary: Co-owners of a Charlotte clinic billed NC Medicaid for in-home physician visits that never occurred, submitting more than 30,000 hours of purported visits, at times billing over 100 one-hour in-home visits by a single physician in one day. Osbey consented to a $4,711,159 civil judgment; co-owner Shabazz pleaded guilty to health care fraud conspiracy and money laundering and received 52 months in prison.
WaysToIdentify: The scheme is visible arithmetically at adjudication: a single physician NPI billing over 100 one-hour in-home visit units in one calendar day exceeds the hours in a day, and cumulative 30,000 hours far exceeds any plausible provider-day capacity. Time-based home-visit codes also permit overlap checks (two visits at different addresses at the same time) and travel-feasibility checks between patient addresses.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a provider-day time-accumulator: for each rendering NPI and date of service, sum the time implied by all time-based E/M and home-visit codes plus the units billed, and hard-deny or pend claims that push the day above a calibrated maximum billable-hours threshold. Add an overlap edit for same-NPI concurrent home visits at distinct patient addresses and a travel-time feasibility check; repeated firing triggers payment suspension and a records request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Chesapeake Regional Medical Center (hospital, formerly Chesapeake Regional Hospital); Javaid Perwaiz (physician, OB/GYN with privileges at CRMC)
