PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Virginia Department of Medical Assistance Services); TRICARE; Anthem; Optima; Humana; Cigna; Aetna; United
SchemeSummary: CRMC allegedly kept granting and re-credentialing privileges to Dr. Javaid Perwaiz from 1984 to 2019 despite knowing he had been terminated elsewhere for unnecessary surgeries and had federal felony convictions, and collected roughly $18.5 million from Medicare, Medicaid/Virginia DMAS, TRICARE and commercial insurers for his medically unnecessary hysterectomies and other procedures, elective pre-39-week inductions/C-sections supported by obstetric flowsheets with fabricated due dates (about 64% of reviewed 2019 Medicaid forms altered), sterilizations of Medicaid patients without valid consent forms, and inpatient-only surgeries misclassified and billed as outpatient. Perwaiz was separately convicted in 2020 on 52 counts and sentenced to 59 years; the hospital is now indicted for health care fraud and conspiracy.
WaysToIdentify: Two independently checkable signals: credentialing data (the surgeon's federal felony convictions, prior termination for unnecessary surgery, NPDB and exclusion/licensure adverse-action reports) should have blocked privileging and facility claims tied to him; and claims patterns showing hysterectomy, sterilization and pre-39-week induction/C-section rates far above same-specialty peers, with sterilization claims lacking valid Medicaid consent forms and inpatient-only procedures billed as outpatient. Consent-form and gestational-age documentation are requestable pre-payment on these specific code families.
FeaturesToCreate: Run continuous NPDB/OIG-LEIE/state licensure/criminal-record monitoring on all privileged and rendering NPIs and auto-pend facility and professional claims where the operating physician has an unresolved adverse action. Add prepay edits: sterilization claims require an attached valid consent form dated within the required window; early elective induction/C-section claims require documented gestational age and medical indication; and Medicare inpatient-only procedure codes billed as outpatient are denied. Layer a per-surgeon hysterectomy/C-section rate outlier model versus same-specialty peers driving prepay medical-necessity review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: David Neel (sole owner and operator of Siesta Health LLC, Healthy Sleep LLC, and Healthy Sleep Partners, LLC)
SchemeSummary: Neel, owner of several central Virginia sleep disorder centers, withheld at least $311,985 in federal trust fund taxes from employees' wages (issuing W-2s reflecting the withholding) but never filed Form 941s or paid the funds over to the IRS, and also failed to pay at least $148,558 of the employer's Medicare and Social Security share, using company funds instead for personal expenses such as rent on a horse farm, life insurance, tuition, and a truck.
WaysToIdentify: Pure employment-tax fraud (withholding W-2 amounts, never filing 941s, diverting funds personally) with no billed claims at issue, so it is not detectable at claim adjudication; the detection route is IRS matching of aggregate W-2 withholding to filed 941s and deposits. A payer sees only indirect signals such as tax liens against the sleep-center entity and owner-level commingling.
FeaturesToCreate: Add tax-lien, judgment and bankruptcy feeds plus owner-level financial screening to provider enrolment and revalidation, flagging entities with liens or unfiled payroll returns for credentialing review and enhanced payment monitoring. Otherwise no claims-payment control applies to this mechanic.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Dr. Stanley L. Librach (physician); Dr. Asim Muhammad Ali (physician); Jerry Dale Leech (chiropractor); Denis J. Mikhlin (business owner); Central Diagnostic Laboratory (CDL)
State_County: Missouri - St. Louis County (Chesterfield, Creve Coeur); Missouri - St. Louis
SchemeSummary: Physicians Librach and Ali and chiropractor Leech referred urine samples to Central Diagnostic Laboratory in exchange for kickbacks routed to entities owned by Leech and Mikhlin (including Ali paying the wages of Librach's clinic employees), with CDL billing Medicare and Medicaid for the testing; in a second scheme the doctors pre-signed oxycodone and other controlled-substance prescriptions one day a week without examining patients or reviewing charts, knowing pharmacies would bill Medicare and Medicaid. Librach was sentenced to 5 years and ordered to repay $2.87 million; co-defendant Mikhlin was previously sentenced to 9 years and ordered to repay $181,265, and other defendants await sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: Referral-concentration data shows the tell: nearly all of one lab's urine drug-testing volume originating from a handful of clinics, with standing-order-like panel uniformity and testing billed for chiropractic patients where UDT has no plausible role. The pre-signed prescription scheme is visible as a single prescriber issuing controlled-substance scripts clustered on one weekday, with no corresponding office-visit claim for the patient near the fill date, and per-prescriber opioid MME volume far above peers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build referral-concentration monitoring: per lab TIN, compute the share of definitive/presumptive UDT revenue from each ordering NPI and flag pairs above the calibrated percentile, cross-checked against common ownership/employment and payroll links between ordering and lab entities; pend those lab claims for prepay review. Separately, per prescriber, compute day-of-week concentration of controlled-substance fills, fills without a preceding E/M encounter claim, and MME per patient versus peers; fire prepay pharmacy edits requiring encounter linkage and refer to the state PDMP/licensing board.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Wyoming
FraudEntity: Sean P. Madigan (coffee shop operator); Victoria Madigan (spouse)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: A married couple failed to disclose income from their Cheyenne Frontier Mall coffee shop when certifying eligibility for Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher assistance from the Cheyenne Housing Authority (a HUD-jurisdiction matter), and Sean Madigan used the coffee shop to fraudulently obtain State of Wyoming COVID-19 business relief grant funds, spending a material portion on household living expenses rather than business purposes. Both received five years supervised probation; restitution figures span both defendants ($161,175 to the State of Wyoming from Sean plus $12,864 joint and several to the Cheyenne Housing Authority).
WaysToIdentify: This is HUD housing-voucher eligibility fraud plus a state COVID business-grant fraud, with no health care claims, so there is no payer adjudication control; detection sits with the housing authority and grant administrator matching self-certified income against IRS/state wage, business-license and merchant-deposit data, and testing grant spending against business bank records. Post-award, bank-statement review shows grant funds moving to household expenses.
FeaturesToCreate: For benefit-eligibility programs, build an automated income-verification match at each recertification against state wage records, business registration/sales-tax filings and 1099-K merchant data, flagging any undisclosed business entity tied to the applicant's SSN. For relief grants, require and automatically parse business bank statements to test that disbursed funds were spent on business expenses, holding tranches until verified. No health-payer claim edit applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Clarence W. Brown III (chiropractor, owner of Dr. CB3 Wellness, Inc. and Apex Integrated Medical Center, Ltd.); Dr. CB3 Wellness, Inc.; Apex Integrated Medical Center, Ltd.
PayerName: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Illinois
SchemeSummary: Brown submitted more than 6,000 fraudulent claims to Blue Cross Blue Shield of Illinois through his two Chicago clinics for health care services never provided, including services purportedly rendered while he was on international vacations or while his medical license was suspended, netting nearly $2.1 million used for a house, a $100,000 BMW, vacations and luxury shopping.
WaysToIdentify: Two hard, pre-payment verifiable facts: the rendering provider's license was suspended on many dates of service, and he was outside the country on others. License status is available from state board feeds at adjudication; absence can be surfaced by impossible-day patterns (high volume with no gaps) and, once suspected, by travel/immigration or credit-card data in investigation.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a license-status edit that validates each claim's date of service against the rendering provider's licensure and sanction effective/end dates from state board and LEIE feeds, auto-denying services rendered during suspension and suspending payment on the TIN when hits recur. Add a solo-provider capacity model per NPI-day (visits, implied minutes, patients per hour) versus same-specialty peers, pending claims above the calibrated percentile for attendance documentation such as signed encounter logs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Zishan Alvi (owner/operator of Chicago Covid-19 testing laboratory)
State_County: Illinois - Cook County (Chicago); defendant resided in Inverness, Ill.
PayerName: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Alvi's Chicago lab submitted tens of thousands of claims to HRSA's Covid-19 program for tests that were never performed or were inconclusive because he diluted test reagents to cut costs, while releasing negative results to patients and lying to lab directors to conceal it; HRSA paid the lab over $14 million. He was sentenced to 84 months, ordered to pay over $14.1 million restitution and forfeit over $8 million in cash plus three vehicles.
WaysToIdentify: Volume and quality signals are visible before payment: claim counts per accessioned specimen and per instrument/testing capacity for the lab's CLIA certificate, negative-result rates and turnaround times far outside peer distributions, and a positivity rate implausibly low for the community prevalence. Under the HRSA uninsured program, patient attestation and specimen-collection records were required and could have been sampled pre-payment; reagent dilution itself is only provable via proficiency testing and lab records post-payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab capacity/plausibility engine: per CLIA-certified lab per day, compare billed test volume against certificated test menu, staffing and instrument throughput, and compute positivity and inconclusive rates versus regional peers; pend claims above the calibrated volume percentile or with anomalous positivity for prepay documentation of accession logs and result reports. Add duplicate-detection on patient/date/test triples and require unique specimen identifiers on claims, with payment suspension on repeated failure and a referral for CLIA proficiency-testing review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Zishan Alvi (owner and operator of Chicago laboratory)
PayerName: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) COVID-19 uninsured program
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Alvi's Chicago lab billed HRSA for COVID-19 tests that were never performed or were diluted to save costs, releasing negative results to patients even when specimens were untested or results inconclusive, and he lied to lab directors to conceal it; HRSA paid over $14 million. Restitution of $14,199,217 plus forfeiture of approximately $6.8 million cash, a Range Rover, and over $630,000 from an E-Trade account were ordered.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion count: a single lab billing an emergency uninsured-testing program for enormous test volumes that exceed its CLIA-certified instrument and staffing capacity, with implausibly uniform negative results and no verifiable specimen accession trail. Pre-payment, HRSA-style programs can sample-verify patient attestations and accession numbers; the reagent dilution is provable only post-payment through lab records and proficiency testing.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement per-lab throughput ceilings derived from CLIA certificate, instrument inventory and reported staffing, auto-pending any day's claims above the ceiling; require a unique specimen accession ID per claim line and deny duplicates or reused IDs. Add peer-relative positivity/inconclusive-rate outlier scoring that triggers prepay documentation requests and, on repeat, payment suspension pending an on-site or records audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
FraudEntity: Fernando Valenzuela Ayub (owner/operator of DME companies); co-conspirators (nominee owners of DME companies); sham marketing companies
State_County: California - San Diego County (Chula Vista/San Diego)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Valenzuela and co-conspirators operated multiple DME companies that billed Medicare roughly $51 million (paid ~$20 million) for orthotic braces obtained through $3.7 million in kickbacks to sham marketing companies supplying bogus prescriptions; after his companies were suspended from billing, he placed new DME companies in nominee owners' names while retaining control and laundered at least $14 million of Medicare proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: The reincarnation pattern is the key pre-payment signal: after suspension, new DME PTANs enrolled under nominee owners while sharing addresses, phone numbers, bank accounts, billing agents and beneficiary populations with the suspended entities. Also visible is orthotic brace billing driven by a few marketing-sourced prescribers with no prior treating relationship, brace volume per prescriber far above peers, and identical code combinations across thousands of beneficiaries.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an entity-resolution graph across enrolment records (address, phone, bank account, EFT, billing agent, authorized officials, prior PTANs) and auto-hold enrolment and payments for any new DME applicant linked to a suspended, revoked or excluded entity. Add a prepay orthotic-brace edit requiring a documented treating relationship (prior E/M with the ordering NPI) and flag prescriber-supplier pairs and per-prescriber brace volumes above calibrated percentiles for prepay review; monitor for common beneficiary overlap between the suspended and new suppliers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Thomas K. Weir (majority owner, Oakley Pharmacy d/b/a Dale Hollow Pharmacy and Clay County Xpress Pharmacy); William L. Donaldson (former owner and pharmacist of Dale Hollow Pharmacy, then Donaldson Pharmacy); Pamela Spivey (co-owner of Clay County Xpress Pharmacy); Charles Robert 'Bobby' Oakley (minority owner, Dale Hollow Pharmacy); John Polston (pharmacist-in-charge); Michael Griffith (pharmacist-in-charge)
SchemeSummary: Owners and pharmacists-in-charge of two Celina, Tennessee pharmacies dispensed high volumes of controlled substances despite obvious signs of abuse and diversion, and billed Medicare Part D and TennCare for medically unnecessary combinations of controlled substances; they also paid patient co-payments, paid cash and gave 'Monkey Bucks' redeemable for cash to induce patients to fill prescriptions there, and Donaldson received kickbacks for recruiting patients. Weir agreed to pay $1,419,974 restitution and forfeit pharmacy-related properties; six defendants pleaded guilty in total, none yet sentenced.
WaysToIdentify: Pharmacy-level dispensing data shows the pattern before payment: an outsized share of revenue in opioids/benzodiazepines, high rates of the classic dangerous combination therapy, long-distance patients travelling past nearer pharmacies, cash-equivalent inducements reflected in zero copay collection, and duplicate-therapy claims paid without intervention. Copay waiver and 'Monkey Bucks' inducements are inferable from systematically zero patient responsibility and from patient interviews at audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pharmacy risk score per NPI: controlled-substance share of scripts, opioid+benzo+muscle-relaxant concurrency rate per patient, mean patient-to-pharmacy distance, prescriber concentration, and share of claims with zero collected copay; fire prepay edits denying dangerous-combination claims absent documented justification and pend high-scoring pharmacies for audit or payment suspension. Add a prescriber-side edit requiring an examination/E/M encounter linked to controlled-substance scripts and flag prescribers whose scripts cluster on a single weekday.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dempsey Spears (owner of Transitional Life Counseling and Consultation and Spears Community Services)
State_County: Texas - Galveston County (Texas City); Texas - Dallas County (Mesquite); Texas - Harris County (Houston)
SchemeSummary: Owner of two mental health clinics allegedly billed Medicare roughly $4 million (paid about $1.5 million) for psychotherapy services never provided, continuing to bill under the identities of seven licensed clinical social workers after they resigned, and submitting claims for beneficiaries who were already deceased on the dates of the billed treatment.
WaysToIdentify: Two deterministic pre-payment checks would have stopped this: dates of service after the rendering clinician's employment/roster end date and license reassignment (and, more simply, after they were no longer affiliated or credentialed), and dates of service after the beneficiary's date of death from the eligibility/master death file. Volume per clinician also exceeded feasible psychotherapy hours per day.
FeaturesToCreate: Add a hard prepay edit denying any claim whose date of service follows the beneficiary's recorded date of death, and a roster-affiliation edit validating that the rendering NPI is actively credentialed and affiliated with the billing TIN on the date of service, with an attestation-refresh workflow when clinicians depart. Layer a per-clinician daily therapy-minutes accumulator that pends claims exceeding calibrated maximum billable hours and triggers payment suspension on repeat hits.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Dr. David Antonio Becerril (licensed Washington physician who signed prescriptions); Real Time Physicians, LLC (telemarketing company); Marc Sporn (former owner of Real Time Physicians, LLC)
State_County: Washington - Yakima County (Selah); Idaho - Kootenai County (Coeur d'Alene); Florida - Palm Beach County (Delray Beach)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Phantom Claims; Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Real Time Physicians telemarketers cold-called elderly Medicare beneficiaries to harvest their personal and Medicare beneficiary numbers, then had Dr. Becerril certify pre-prepared prescriptions through an internet portal (reviewed on average 26 seconds each) for genetic tests and back, knee, shoulder and ankle braces for patients he never contacted, including deceased patients and amputees; Real Time sold the prescriptions to genetic testing labs and DME suppliers who billed Medicare over $3.2 million (paid over $1.3 million) and shared proceeds, with Becerril paid $20 per prescription totaling over $37,000. Sentencing figures span two defendants: Becerril awaits sentencing (convicted at trial), while Real Time owner Marc Sporn was previously sentenced to 14 years.
WaysToIdentify: Order-level metadata is the giveaway: one physician certifying thousands of portal orders with review times measured in seconds, no prior or concurrent E/M claim with the beneficiary, patients spread nationwide with no geographic relationship to the prescriber, orders for deceased beneficiaries, and knee/ankle braces for amputees. Beneficiary-complaint feeds about cold calls and requests for Medicare numbers provide an early independent signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a telehealth-ordering integrity model per ordering NPI: count of orders, orders per active day, share with no antecedent E/M encounter, beneficiary geographic dispersion, and share flowing to a small set of labs/DME suppliers; auto-pend downstream genetic-test and brace claims from prescribers above the calibrated percentile pending documentation of the patient encounter. Add hard edits for date-of-service-after-death and clinical-impossibility pairs (laterality/amputation status versus braced limb, prior amputation history in claims), and cluster suppliers sharing the same prescriber pool for coordinated prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Samad Khan, M.D. (physician, owner of SK Primary Care, PLLC); SK Primary Care, PLLC
State_County: Texas - Collin County (Frisco); Texas (dozens of COVID-19 testing sites statewide)
PayerName: HRSA COVID-19 Claims Reimbursement to Health Care Providers and Facilities for Testing, Treatment, and Vaccine Administration for the Uninsured Program
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Phantom Claims; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: At walk-up/drive-through COVID-19 test sites staffed by medical assistants, specimen collection (properly CPT 99211) was instead billed to the HRSA Uninsured Program as Level 2-5 evaluation and management office visits with Khan as sole rendering provider - approximately 400,000 claims from April 2020 to October 2021 - even though no physician or qualified health professional ever saw the patients; a second E/M 'encounter' was also billed for phoning or texting test results by staff who often never spoke to the patient.
WaysToIdentify: The distribution of E/M levels is the signal: essentially every COVID collection encounter billed as level 2-5 E/M by a single rendering NPI across hundreds of thousands of claims, with no site-of-service or staffing consistent with physician evaluation, and specimen-collection codes almost never used. A second E/M billed for result notification produces same-patient duplicate E/M pairs days apart with no separately identifiable service, and the single-provider volume vastly exceeds feasible daily encounters.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-NPI E/M profile that computes level distribution and daily encounter counts versus same-specialty peers and against a feasible-encounters-per-day ceiling; auto-downcode or pend claims when a provider's COVID-test-site E/M claims exceed the ceiling or when level distribution sits above the calibrated percentile with no supporting diagnosis complexity. Add edits requiring specimen-collection codes for test-site encounters, denying a second E/M for result communication on the same episode, and flagging any NPI listed as sole rendering provider across multiple physical sites on the same day for payment suspension and records request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Hector Villegas-Alvarez
SchemeSummary: Not a health care fraud case: defendant was indicted for assaulting an ICE deportation officer while resisting arrest, causing a broken nose and concussion.
WaysToIdentify: This is an assault-on-a-federal-officer prosecution with no claims, provider or payer involvement, so there is nothing detectable pre-payment.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. In intelligence intake, filter non-health-care-fraud prosecutions so they do not generate provider risk scores.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Jerry Joseph Bruggeman, M.D. (physician)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: A telehealth company aggregated Medicare beneficiary information from marketing companies, generated assessments and orders, and paid Bruggeman roughly $29,440 to sign over 3,100 orders for cancer/pharmacogenetic testing and orthotic braces through an online portal without any patient contact; the resulting 8,700+ claims caused Medicare Part B to pay $1,055,303 for genetic testing and $551,105 for DME.
WaysToIdentify: Detectable pre-payment from order metadata and claim linkage: a single physician signing thousands of cancer/pharmacogenomic and brace orders with no telehealth or office-visit claim for those beneficiaries, patients drawn from nationwide marketing lists rather than a local panel, and the resulting claims concentrated in a handful of labs and suppliers. Per-order payment to the signer is not on the claim, but the volume-without-encounter pattern and supplier-prescriber concentration are.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a prepay edit that denies or pends high-cost genetic testing and orthotic brace claims when no E/M or telehealth encounter claim exists between the ordering NPI and the beneficiary within a defined lookback, requiring documentation of medical necessity and patient contact. Add prescriber-level scoring on order volume, distinct downstream billers, and beneficiary geographic dispersion versus peers, plus a supplier-side check flagging billers whose orders concentrate on a few prolific out-of-area prescribers for coordinated review and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Community Health Care Solutions, LLC (Shreveport counseling service); Estate of Yolanda Burnom (deceased owner/operator)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Upcoding; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Community Health and its owner paid Medicaid recipients financial incentives to hand over their patient information, then billed Louisiana Medicaid for crisis intervention services (the highest-reimbursing code) that never occurred, with counselors instructed to cut-and-paste generic notes into patient files; many counselors never met the patients. The estate and company agreed to pay $4.6 million after Burnom died following a 2022 federal indictment.
WaysToIdentify: Coding-mix data shows near-exclusive use of the highest-reimbursing crisis-intervention code, which by definition should be episodic, plus per-counselor daily service volumes exceeding feasible hours and services billed for beneficiaries the counselor never met. Cloned documentation is detectable on prepay records review as byte-identical progress notes across patients, and patient-recruitment payments surface via beneficiary interviews and clusters of new members enrolled from the same recruiter address.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a provider-level code-mix monitor for behavioral health: share of billing in crisis-intervention/highest-intensity codes versus same-specialty peers, and repeat crisis claims per beneficiary per period; pend claims above the calibrated percentile for prepay records review. Add a per-counselor daily minutes accumulator with hard denial above feasible hours, and an automated note-similarity check (text-hash/near-duplicate scoring) on submitted documentation that triggers payment suspension and beneficiary verification calls when clone rates are high.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: C&J Welding & Construction (subsidiary of Rema Tip Top of America, Inc.); Industrial Services Group, Inc. d/b/a Universal Blastco (subsidiary of Rema); NexGen Industrial Services, Inc. (subsidiary of Rema)
PayerName: Small Business Administration (U.S. government - Paycheck Protection Program)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Three subsidiaries of Rema Tip Top of America applied for five PPP loans while knowingly failing to disclose their corporate affiliates, falsely certifying eligibility even though their combined employee counts/revenues exceeded PPP size limits; they received a total of about $8.85 million in loan forgiveness and interest (plus over $209,000 in lender processing fees paid by the U.S.) and paid $13 million to settle FCA claims brought by a qui tam relator, who received $2.34 million.
WaysToIdentify: This is a loan-program eligibility fraud, not a claims-payment scheme: the observable signal is the affiliation/size certification on the PPP application versus corporate ownership data. SBA could have run the applicant EINs and addresses against Dun & Bradstreet/corporate-family trees, SAM.gov parent-entity registrations, and IRS/state UI wage filings to detect that five loans traced to subsidiaries of one foreign-owned parent whose combined headcount exceeded size limits.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pre-disbursement affiliation-graph check: cluster loan applications by shared parent EIN, common officers/registered agents, address and bank-account overlap, and sum affiliate employee counts from UI wage data before approving any loan or forgiveness; fire a hold and manual size-standard review when the cluster's aggregate headcount/revenue exceeds the program limit. Apply the same clustering again at forgiveness stage, since forgiveness is a second payment event, and hold lender processing fees pending resolution.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Nnwood Pharmacy; Cheryl Brew Greenleaf (owner); Wendell Kirk Greenleaf (owner)
SchemeSummary: Civil complaint alleges the pharmacy and its owners dispensed hydrocodone, carisoprodol and other Schedule II-IV controlled substances without legitimate medical purpose - filling prescriptions purportedly written by physicians hundreds of miles away, by OB/GYNs for male customers, and under invalid DEA registration numbers (99 allegedly fraudulent prescriptions seized during a 2021 inspection warrant) - and failed to keep required CSA records.
WaysToIdentify: Every element was visible on the claim: prescriber DEA number validity, prescriber specialty, prescriber-to-pharmacy geographic distance, and drug/patient-sex incompatibility. A payer or PDMP could flag hydrocodone/carisoprodol fills written by OB/GYNs for male patients, prescribers hundreds of miles away, and DEA registrations that are invalid, expired or not authorized for the schedule dispensed.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay pharmacy edits: (1) validate prescriber DEA/NPI against the active DEA registration file including schedule authority and reject on invalid/expired; (2) compute prescriber-patient-pharmacy distance and specialty-plausibility (e.g., OB/GYN prescribing scheduled opioids to male members) and deny or pend for documentation; (3) pharmacy-level scorecard on share of controlled fills from out-of-area or specialty-mismatched prescribers and 'trinity' combinations, triggering payment suspension and an on-site CSA records audit above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Keke Komeko Johnson (Compliance Director, Life Touch LLC); Francine Sims Super (office manager, Life Touch LLC); Life Touch LLC
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Leaders of a Kinston substance abuse treatment company used Medicaid reimbursement funds to buy more than $1 million in gift cards (sometimes routed through personal bank accounts) and handed them weekly to patients based on the number of days they attended, so Life Touch could bill Medicaid for more service days; Johnson lied to Medicaid auditors and Super created false documents, and both took unreported kickbacks from a drug-testing lab (1st Choice Healthcare Services) and failed to file tax returns.
WaysToIdentify: Attendance-driven gift-card inducements show up as implausibly perfect per-patient attendance and near-maximum billable days per member, plus a cost-report/bank trail of large gift-card purchases funded by Medicaid deposits. The paired lab arrangement is visible as a single drug-testing lab receiving essentially all of this program's specimens with definitive testing on nearly every visit.
FeaturesToCreate: Provider-month analytics: compute distribution of billed service days per member and flag programs whose members cluster at the maximum allowable days with abnormally low no-show variance versus same-specialty peers; flag single-lab referral concentration from one SUD program. Fire prepay review/documentation request for attendance sign-in sheets, and cross-check the provider's disclosed expenditures and bank records for stored-value/gift-card purchases during audit; auditor-statement inconsistencies should trigger payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Christopher R. Parks (compounding pharmacy owner)
SchemeSummary: Parks, a compounding pharmacy owner, was convicted in October 2023 of Conspiracy to Offer and Pay Health Care Kickbacks and sentenced to 18 months in prison with more than $6.4 million in restitution ordered. After release he paid only $8,450 toward restitution while concealing checking accounts and businesses through which over $560,000 was deposited and withdrawn (more than $320,000 in cash) between March 2024 and June 2025, and transferred assets to family; he was sentenced to an additional 15 months for violating supervised release.
WaysToIdentify: The underlying kickback scheme was a compounding-pharmacy referral arrangement detectable prepay through marketer-sourced prescriptions, formulaic high-cost compound combinations and one-to-few prescriber concentration. The supervised-release/restitution-evasion conduct has no payer-side claims signal; it is caught post-payment by monitoring exclusion status and by tracing new bank accounts and successor entities the debtor controls.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay: flag compound claims whose ingredients match high-reimbursement templates and whose prescribers concentrate in a small marketer-linked set; require dispensing documentation and patient attestation before payment. Post-payment: run a recurring screen matching convicted/excluded individuals to new NPIs, EINs, bank routing/account numbers and family-member owners on enrolment files, and auto-deny enrolment plus refer for restitution offset when a match hits.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Lakshmi Bethi, DMD (dentist/owner); New Haven Dental LLC; New Haven Family Dental LLC; New Haven Family Dental Group LLC
PayerName: Medicaid (Connecticut Medical Assistance Program / Connecticut Dental Health Partnership)
SchemeSummary: Bethi and her dental practices paid a third-party patient recruiting company $110 per Connecticut Medicaid patient referred whenever that patient received services beyond routine preventive care, then billed CTMAP for those services while impliedly certifying no kickbacks were paid; she paid over $360,000 in kickbacks and Medicaid reimbursed about $2.2 million. The $608,296.39 civil settlement resolved FCA claims for 2019-2023 conduct, and in the related criminal case Bethi received two years' probation plus a $500,000 forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: Per-patient recruiting fees produce a distinctive pattern: sudden influx of new Medicaid members from outside the practice's normal service radius, and a very high conversion rate from a prophy/exam visit to billable restorative or surgical care because payment only triggered on services beyond prevention. Enrolment-time disclosure of marketing contracts and the practice's paid-vendor ledger would show the per-head fee structure.
FeaturesToCreate: Practice-quarter model: compute new-member share, mean travel distance, and ratio of members receiving beyond-preventive treatment to members seen, compared to same-specialty Medicaid peers; fire a prepay documentation/medical-necessity review and a marketing-contract disclosure request when multiple indicators exceed the calibrated percentile. Add an attestation edit requiring disclosure of any per-patient marketing compensation and cluster practices sharing the same recruiting vendor's address, phone or payments.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Dent Plus Family Dentistry, PLLC (dissolved dental practice, Stamford); L&M Family Dentistry, LLC (dissolved dental practice, New Haven); Ivan Makar, DDS (owner); Oleg Losin, DDS (owner)
State_County: Connecticut - Stamford (Fairfield County); Connecticut - New Haven (New Haven County)
SchemeSummary: Two dental practices and their dentist owners paid a third-party patient recruiting company a per-patient fee for each Connecticut Medicaid patient referred to them, then billed the Connecticut Medical Assistance Program for dental services while impliedly certifying no kickbacks were paid, in violation of the CTDHP provider manual's ban on per-patient referral compensation; Makar and Losin jointly paid $714,446.27 to resolve federal and state False Claims Act allegations without admitting liability.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the paired case: per-patient referral compensation banned by the CTDHP provider manual, visible as bursts of new Medicaid patients arriving from a common recruiter's catchment, shared transport/appointment-scheduling patterns across unrelated practices, and high treatment-conversion rates. The recruiter link is confirmable by finding the same vendor paid by multiple practices in AP records obtained at credentialing or audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a shared-recruiter graph: link practices by common referral vendor identifiers, patient-cohort overlap and same-day multi-practice patient batches; combine with new-patient surge and out-of-radius member share to fire prepay review. Require an annual signed disclosure of all patient-marketing arrangements as a condition of claim payment, and treat undisclosed per-patient fee contracts as grounds for payment suspension and AKS referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Genco Lab, LLC (reference laboratory); Paul Conroy (majority owner); Tricia Conroy (Chief Operating Officer); Charles Orefice (part owner)
SchemeSummary: Genco Lab billed Medicare and Connecticut Medicaid for medically unnecessary urine drug tests, including tests done solely for 'residential monitoring' of sober-home residents (explicitly non-covered), and routinely billed both presumptive screening and the more expensive definitive confirmation test on the same patient the same day without any practitioner reviewing the screening result to justify the confirmatory test. The lab and its three owners/officers agreed to pay $1,255,825 collectively.
WaysToIdentify: Both mechanics are fully visible on claims: presumptive screen and definitive confirmation codes for the same member on the same date with no intervening practitioner order, and specimens whose ordering entity is a sober home / residential monitoring program rather than a treating clinician of a covered service. Reflex-testing patterns show as near-100% confirmation rates and standing panels of the same analytes for every member regardless of history.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: deny definitive UDT billed same-date-of-service as presumptive from the same lab unless a documented practitioner reflex order is attached; require the ordering NPI to be an enrolled treating clinician and deny where the order originates from a residential/monitoring facility with no covered service. Lab-month analytics on confirmation-to-screen ratio, analytes per specimen and member test frequency versus peers, with prepay review above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Jesse Foote (controlled marketing company and DME suppliers)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Foote bought patient leads and pre-written doctors' orders for orthotic braces from overseas telemarketing call centers, paid kickbacks to telemedicine companies which bribed doctors to sign DME orders without patient contact or medical-necessity assessment, then sold the signed orders to DME suppliers (including his own) that billed Medicare, TRICARE and private insurers more than $7.8 million.
WaysToIdentify: The signature is a small set of ordering physicians generating brace orders for members spread nationwide with no prior or subsequent clinical relationship, and no telehealth or office E/M claim from that physician for the same member. Multiple DME suppliers billing off the same physicians' orders, sharing addresses, owners or billing agents, is visible in enrolment and claims data at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit on orthotic/brace HCPCS: require a paid qualifying encounter by the ordering NPI within a lookback window and reject orders where ordering-physician-to-beneficiary distance and state count exceed plausible practice patterns. Ordering-physician velocity model (braces ordered per day, distinct suppliers served, share of members with no other claims from that NPI) triggering prepay suspension of all downstream supplier claims and revocation review; cluster suppliers by shared billing agent/telemarketing lead source.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Pain Management, LLC; Halina Snowball, M.D. (owner, physiatrist)
FraudTypeAll: Unbundling; Phantom Claims; Retention of Overpayment
SchemeSummary: Snowball and her pain management practice appended Modifier 25 to evaluation and management claims billed alongside pain injections to Medicare, claiming separately identifiable E&M services that were not actually provided; after being notified in November 2019 of improper Modifier 25 use and assessed an overpayment, they continued the improper billing until August 2023 and paid $427,129.11 to resolve liability.
WaysToIdentify: Modifier 25 misuse is measurable at adjudication: the share of E/M claims carrying modifier 25 when billed same-day with a procedure, per provider versus same-specialty peers. Critically, this payer had already notified the provider and assessed an overpayment in 2019, so its own audit-outcome data should have driven a prepay control rather than allowing four more years of identical billing.
FeaturesToCreate: Provider-quarter metric: proportion of pain-injection encounters with a same-day modifier-25 E/M, benchmarked to same-specialty peers; above the calibrated percentile place the provider on prepay documentation review requiring the separate E/M note before payment. Add a rule that any provider with a prior education letter or assessed overpayment on a specific code/modifier is auto-enrolled in prepay review for that code for a defined period, with continued aberrance escalating to suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Mercer (US), LLC (consulting company/government contractor)
SchemeSummary: Mercer invoiced the Defense Health Agency monthly under a Blanket Purchase Agreement for Health Plan Innovative Support consulting services, billing the labor of 11 employees and subcontractor employees at higher hourly labor-category rates than their actual education and experience qualified them for; Mercer self-disclosed and paid $456,796.50 to resolve contract and unjust enrichment claims.
WaysToIdentify: This is contractor labor-rate mischarging, not clinical claims: the signal is invoiced labor category versus each named employee's actual degree and years of experience, which the payer holds in resumes/key-personnel submissions. Reconciling monthly invoice line items to the contract's labor-category qualification matrix and to the approved personnel roster would have surfaced the mismatch before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an invoice-to-roster edit for services contracts: for each billed labor hour, match employee ID to the approved qualification file and compute whether the billed category's education/experience floor is met; suspend payment on non-conforming lines and request substantiating credentials. Add periodic sampling audits of subcontractor personnel, since substitutions after award are the common failure point.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Trivikram Reddy (licensed nurse practitioner, owner of medical clinics); co-conspirators including two family members
PayerName: Medicare; Blue Cross Blue Shield of Texas; Aetna; UnitedHealthcare; Humana; Cigna
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Reddy, a nurse practitioner, and co-conspirators submitted false patient bills to Medicare and five commercial insurers using the provider numbers of six doctors as the purported treating physicians, though none of those doctors provided billable services at his clinics; fake medical records were manufactured when federal agents inquired, and proceeds were laundered into nearly 200 bank accounts in India. Following his 2020 guilty plea, 2021 sentence of 20 years and over $50 million restitution order, a civil forfeiture judgment in March 2025 required return of up to $41,237,703.16 from the Indian accounts (stipulated by Reddy and two family members).
WaysToIdentify: Rendering-provider identity misuse is detectable prepay: physicians listed as treating provider on claims from clinics they have no reassignment or employment link to, no corresponding presence in the clinic's location/schedule, and volumes exceeding feasible hours per day per NPI. Payment routing to accounts with rapid outbound foreign wires and a beneficiary population with no local footprint are additional pre-payment enrolment signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: reject claims where the rendering NPI has no active reassignment/affiliation to the billing TIN, and pend where the rendering NPI's aggregate same-day billed time across all sites exceeds feasible service minutes. Cross-payer/commercial-plan sharing of the same rendering NPI appearing at unrelated TINs, plus bank-account velocity screening at enrolment, should trigger payment suspension and provider-attestation outreach directly to the named physicians rather than to the clinic.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin; U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Consumer Protection Branch, with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Wisconsin
FraudEntity: KBWB Operations LLC, d/b/a Atrium Health and Senior Living (nursing facility operator/owner); Kevin Breslin (former Chief Executive Officer, Managing Member and part owner)
State_County: Wisconsin; New Jersey - Little Falls (corporate headquarters); Wisconsin - Appleton (Midwest corporate office); Michigan
FraudTypeAll: Other - Unknown; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Breslin and KBWB-Atrium, which operated 23 Wisconsin skilled nursing facilities funded primarily by Medicare and Medicaid, diverted CMS funds meant for facility operations and resident care to owner distributions, guaranteed payments and personal expenses, leaving vendors and third-party administrators unpaid (including employee insurance premiums and 401(k) withholdings); Breslin also directed that income and employment taxes withheld from employee paychecks not be paid to the IRS. Both defendants pleaded guilty to health care fraud and tax conspiracy and await sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: Diversion of operating funds is visible in cost reports and financial filings before further payment: owner distributions and guaranteed payments rising while accounts payable, insurance premiums and payroll-tax deposits go unpaid. External signals available prepay include vendor liens/judgments, lapsed employee benefit filings (Form 5500/401(k) delinquency), IRS trust-fund tax delinquency notices, and staffing-level and complaint data from state survey agencies.
FeaturesToCreate: Chain-level financial monitoring: for each commonly owned SNF group, compute related-party distributions as a share of Medicare/Medicaid revenue, days payable outstanding, and payroll-tax/benefit-remittance delinquency flags from cross-agency feeds; fire enhanced oversight, escrow or payment suspension when distributions rise while payables and staffing deteriorate. Require related-party transaction disclosure as a condition of continued enrolment and re-verify at each ownership change.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Wisconsin; Department of Justice Civil Division
FraudEntity: KBWB Operations LLC, d/b/a Atrium Health and Senior Living (operator/owner of skilled nursing facilities); Kevin Breslin (former chief executive officer and managing member)
State_County: Wisconsin; New Jersey - Little Falls (corporate headquarters); Wisconsin - Appleton (Midwest corporate office); Michigan
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: KBWB-Atrium operated 23 Wisconsin skilled nursing facilities funded primarily by Medicare and Medicaid; Breslin diverted CMS funds intended for resident care to personal expenses and multi-million-dollar owner distributions, concealing from CMS that funds were not used for care and that vendors and taxes went unpaid, and also diverted employee health premiums, 401(k) contributions and resident account funds while directing that withheld employment taxes not be paid to the IRS. Restitution of $146 million and $8.4 million forfeiture were ordered against both Breslin and the corporation (same amounts, not cumulative).
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case and detectable from the same data: CMS funds certified for resident care while owner distributions surge and vendors, employee health premiums, 401(k) withholdings, resident trust accounts and withheld employment taxes go unpaid. Resident personal-fund account shortfalls and unpaid-premium complaints reach state survey and DOL/IRS systems well before the loss reached $146 million.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a cross-agency solvency/diversion dashboard keyed to the owning chain: inputs are cost-report related-party distributions, Form 5500 and trust-fund tax delinquency, vendor judgment filings, resident trust-fund audit exceptions and staffing hours per resident day; firing thresholds set on deterioration versus the chain's own baseline and peer chains. Action is heightened enrolment review, periodic payment escrow or suspension pending an independent monitor, plus mandatory attestation that CMS funds were applied to operations.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Todd Faustin (current NYC Department of Correction officer); Jovanny Concepcion (former DOC correction officer); Steven Murphy (former DOC correction officer)
State_County: New York - Bronx County (Rikers Island, New York City)
PayerName: New York State Workers' Compensation Board (benefits paid from the New York City Treasury)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Three Rikers Island correction officers allegedly falsely claimed they were injured on duty during use-of-force incidents with incarcerated individuals, making false statements to the New York State Workers' Compensation Board, their own physicians, and independent medical examiners to obtain years of workers' compensation medical care and cash benefits paid from the New York City Treasury. Amounts span three defendants: Faustin $469,705.39, Concepcion $232,427.97, and Murphy $294,037.83; an attached later release states Faustin was sentenced to 15 months in prison.
WaysToIdentify: This is workers' compensation benefit fraud detectable prepay through inconsistency between the claimed injury and objective evidence: the employer's use-of-force reports, incident video, body-worn/facility camera footage and witness statements versus the claimant's narrative to the Board, treating physicians and IMEs. Continued cash-benefit payments over years with unchanged subjective complaints, no objective imaging findings, and outside activity (secondary employment, social media, surveillance) are the ongoing signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Claim-level intake edit: require the employer's incident report and available video to be attached and cross-read against the claimant's stated mechanism of injury before the first indemnity payment, flagging narrative conflicts for investigation. Build a long-duration-claim review queue keyed on duration of total disability beyond expected recovery for the diagnosis, IMEs whose findings conflict with treating notes, and cross-match to payroll/UI wage data for concurrent earnings; fire suspension of cash benefits pending examination.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
FraudEntity: Luis Enrique Villegas Brownell; Kassandra Sanchez
State_County: California - San Diego County (San Diego/San Ysidro Port of Entry)
SchemeSummary: Villegas, a Mexican citizen without legal status, and his girlfriend Sanchez allegedly stole the identity documents of Sanchez's brother, used them to obtain a California DMV ID card bearing Villegas's photo, and used that fraudulent identity to cross the border more than 50 times, smuggle an undocumented immigrant, and fraudulently obtain California public benefits including Medi-Cal coverage.
WaysToIdentify: This is eligibility/identity fraud at enrolment rather than a provider billing scheme: the signal is one SSN/identity document supporting two distinct biometric or photo identities and conflicting DMV, SSA and immigration records. Cross-matching the Medi-Cal applicant's SSN and name against SSA Numident, DMV photo/facial-recognition duplicates and border-crossing records would show the same SSN tied to two faces and to an individual whose sibling is the true owner.
FeaturesToCreate: Enrolment identity-proofing edit: run applicant SSN/name/DOB through SSA verification and a DMV photo-duplicate/facial-match service; fire a hold and in-person documentation request when one identifier maps to multiple photos, when the applicant's asserted identity is also actively enrolled or filing elsewhere, or when address/household data conflicts. Add periodic re-verification sweeps of active enrollees against SSA death/mismatch and duplicate-photo results.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Robert Maxwell (promoter/investment solicitor)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Maxwell solicited over $12.5 million from investors during the early COVID-19 pandemic by falsely claiming he had a Chinese manufacturing contract and a domestic sales agreement for PPE (masks, gloves) and was producing an at-home anti-coronavirus aerosol product with a Texas plant and out-of-state distributor; he used fabricated bank records, agreements and other documents and false claims of retailer sell-outs to obtain funds, then pocketed the money as no product ever existed.
WaysToIdentify: Pure investment fraud with no health-plan claims component, so no payer adjudication control applies; the deceit lived in fabricated bank statements, supply contracts and distributor agreements shown to private investors. Detection routes are investor/escrow-side: independent confirmation of bank balances directly with the institution, verification of the Chinese manufacturer and Texas plant's existence and capacity, FDA/EPA registration checks for an antiviral aerosol claim, and SEC/state securities filing review.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side claims edit applies. Nearest applicable control is a procurement/grant vetting check for PPE and COVID-product buyers: verify supplier registration, manufacturing capacity and FDA/EPA product registration, confirm bank documents directly with issuing institutions rather than accepting borrower-supplied PDFs, and require escrowed milestone payment against verified delivery.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
SchemeSummary: Not a fraud case document: this is a press release announcing the swearing in of Craig H. Missakian as U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California, which mentions only in passing his prior leadership of an investigation into a nationwide health care fraud scheme involving over $100 million in fraudulent Medicare claims, with no defendants or case details given.
WaysToIdentify: Not a fraud case: this is a personnel announcement press release with no defendants, claims or payer loss described, so there is nothing to detect prepay.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. If a control must be named, the nearest is ordinary large-dollar Medicare claim analytics on the unrelated $100 million scheme alluded to in passing, which cannot be specified from this document.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Fernando Espinosa Leon (owner, Global Medical Supply Inc.); Global Medical Supply Inc.
SchemeSummary: Espinosa Leon used his company Global Medical Supply Inc. and stolen personally identifiable information of Medicare beneficiaries and medical practitioners to submit, through a third-party biller, more than $7.6 million in claims for durable medical equipment that was never prescribed or supplied; over $4 million was paid into a bank account he controlled.
WaysToIdentify: Classic phantom-DME billing on stolen identities, visible at adjudication: ordering NPIs who deny/never order such equipment, beneficiaries geographically remote from the supplier with no related clinical claims, no qualifying face-to-face encounter, and abrupt post-enrolment claim volume from a new supplier. Enrolment-side signals include a virtual or non-conforming business location, a shared third-party biller, and payments routing to a single individual-controlled account.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits for new/recently enrolled DME suppliers: cap payment pending site verification, require an ordering-NPI qualifying encounter within the lookback window, and reject claims where the ordering physician's specialty/location makes the order implausible or where the beneficiary has no other claims in the state. Add velocity triggers (claims per day, distinct beneficiaries per ordering NPI, submitted dollars in first 90 days) that auto-suspend payment and initiate beneficiary and physician verification letters.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Summit BHC New Jersey, LLC, d/b/a Seabrook (drug and alcohol rehabilitation facility)
PayerName: Veterans Health Administration Community Care Program; New Jersey Medicaid
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Seabrook billed the VHA Community Care Program and New Jersey Medicaid for short-term residential treatment and partial hospitalization services for which it held no license or contract, concealed the unlicensed services from state inspectors, lacked sufficient properly credentialed staff, claimed to provide specialized veteran care that was identical to standard care, and kept false and inadequate treatment records. Resolved by a $19.75 million FCA settlement from a qui tam suit, with the relator receiving about $3,555,137.
WaysToIdentify: Licensure and contract scope were checkable before any payment: the facility billed residential and partial-hospitalization levels of care for which it held no state license and no VA Community Care contract authorization. Staffing credential rosters versus the program's required clinician mix, and specialty 'veteran program' codes billed with services identical to standard care, are further prepay signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a service-to-licensure edit: for each billed level-of-care code, verify against the state licensing file that the facility's license category and bed authorization cover that service on the date of service, and against the network contract that the level of care is authorized; hard-deny non-covered scope. Add a staffing-credential attestation cross-check (licensed clinician FTEs per census pulled from credentialing data) and prepay documentation review of treatment plans for programs billing specialty/enhanced rates.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: CVS Pharmacy Inc. (pharmacy chain)
SchemeSummary: CVS allegedly billed Medi-Cal for 'Code 1' formulary drugs without confirming or documenting the required approved diagnoses, and in some cases dispensed drugs for nonapproved diagnoses without submitting the required justification request to DHCS, then billed the program for those prescriptions. Resolved for $18,282,280 to the U.S. and California, with about $3.3 million to the whistleblower pharmacist.
WaysToIdentify: Medi-Cal's Code 1 rules make this adjudicable: payment requires an approved diagnosis on file or an approved treatment authorization request, so claims lacking a documented approved indication should never have paid. The signal is Code 1 drug claims with no diagnosis submitted or with a member diagnosis history inconsistent with the approved indication and no corresponding TAR.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit for Code 1 formulary drugs: require a diagnosis code on the pharmacy claim and validate it against the approved-indication table, cross-referencing the member's medical-claim diagnosis history; deny when neither an approved diagnosis nor an approved authorization request exists. Add a chain/store-level metric on share of Code 1 fills paid without diagnosis substantiation to target audits and recoupment where legacy claims already paid.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jacquelyn Farrish (Medicaid Consumer Directed Care Program recipient/timesheet approver)
SchemeSummary: Farrish enrolled in Virginia Medicaid's Consumer Directed Care Program and listed her estranged husband A.L., who lived in another part of the state, as her paid personal care attendant; she then submitted and approved fraudulent timesheets using his personal information claiming 9,819 hours of personal care services that were never provided, causing $116,536 in Medicaid losses.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment the consumer-directed program has both the member's address and the attendant's address plus the family relationship attestation; an attendant whose residence is hundreds of miles from the member and who is the spouse/legally responsible relative is a hard eligibility and feasibility conflict visible before the first timesheet is paid. At adjudication, the same person being both the employer-of-record approving timesheets and the beneficiary receiving care, plus implausible hour volumes (near-continuous coverage, hours exceeding the authorized plan of care), are all in the fiscal-agent timesheet data. No EVV geolocation records would exist matching the attendant to the member's home.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment-time edit in the fiscal-employer-agent system that geocodes attendant and member addresses and flags pairs beyond a calibrated commute distance, plus a relationship/self-approval edit that blocks a case where the approver, member and payee resolve to the same household or the attendant is a spouse barred from payment; hold claims pending manual review. Add a per-member per-period hour accumulator that suspends payment when billed hours exceed the authorized service plan or overlap the attendant's other employment/claims, and require EVV check-in/out geocoordinates within a radius of the member's residence as a condition of payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jacquelyn Farrish (Medicaid Consumer Directed Care recipient)
SchemeSummary: Farrish enrolled in Virginia Medicaid's Consumer Directed Care Program and listed her estranged husband, who lived hundreds of miles away, as her paid personal care attendant, then submitted and approved fraudulent timesheets using his personal information for 9,819 hours of personal care/respite services never rendered, causing $116,536 in Medicaid losses; sentenced to five years' probation with 12 months home detention and $116,536 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic: the consumer-directed enrolment file contains the attendant's address, SSN and relationship to the member, so a spouse living hundreds of miles away being paid as attendant is detectable at enrolment rather than after 9,819 hours were billed. Timesheet data shows the member self-approving her own attendant's hours and cumulative hours far above the authorized plan of care and above same-program peers. Absence of any EVV location or telephony call originating at the member's home corroborates non-delivery pre-payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement enrolment screening that geocodes member/attendant address pairs and blocks or pends payment beyond a calibrated distance, and a conflict-of-interest edit where employer-of-record, beneficiary and payee are the same person or spouses. Layer a cumulative-hours edit per member per authorization period that suspends payment and triggers a documentation/EVV-record request when billed hours exceed authorized units or exceed the same-program peer percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota
FraudEntity: Moktar Hassan Aden (owner, Brilliant Minds Services LLC); Mustafa Dayib Ali; Khalid Ahmed Dayib; Abdifitah Mohamud Mohamed (operator, Foundation First Services LLC); Christopher Adesoji Falade (operator, Faladcare Inc.); Emmanuel Oluwademilade Falade (operator, Faladcare Inc.); Asad Ahmed Adow (owner, Leo Human Services LLC); Anwar Ahmed Adow (owner, Liberty Plus LLC)
State_County: Minnesota - Ramsey County (St. Paul); Minnesota - Hennepin County (Brooklyn Park); Minnesota - Anoka County (Blaine); Minnesota - Ramsey County (Roseville)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Upcoding; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Eight defendants operating four Minnesota Medicaid Housing Stabilization Services providers (Brilliant Minds ~$2.3M, Faladcare ~$2.2M, Leo Human Services ~$2.7M, Liberty Plus ~$1.2M) obtained beneficiary names from addiction treatment centers and other facilities, then submitted inflated and fabricated reimbursement claims for housing consultation, transition and sustaining services that were largely never provided; one owner also had employees manufacture false service notes to survive potential DHS audits, and proceeds were diverted to employees/co-conspirators, real estate, luxury car leases and personal AmEx charges. Figures span four companies and eight defendants.
WaysToIdentify: Newly enrolled Housing Stabilization Services providers with no service history, shared addresses/bank accounts/phone numbers and rapid revenue ramp to millions within months are visible in enrolment and claims-volume data before payment. Referral concentration is another signal: large blocks of members whose claims trace to a handful of addiction treatment centers or shelters, many of whom also have claims from other HSS providers for the same dates, and members lacking any documented needs assessment or housing-focused plan authorizing the service. Duplicate/templated service notes only surface on documentation request, so pair the volume trigger with prepay records review.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a new-provider ramp monitor for HSS: per-NPI monthly paid amount and distinct-member count with a velocity trigger that routes the provider to prepay documentation review (assessment, person-centered plan, dated service notes) once billing accelerates above the calibrated new-enroller percentile. Add prepay edits for member-level duplicate transition/sustaining units across providers on the same date, missing authorization/assessment on file, and units-per-consultant-day exceeding what one staffer could deliver; plus enrolment link analysis on shared address, bank account, phone and owner identity to cluster and suspend affiliated shells together.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Live Wire, LLC (Vermont-based defense contractor)
SchemeSummary: Live Wire, LLC sold electronic communications headsets to the U.S. Army under government contracts and submitted claims for payment for headsets that had not been tested to the required military specifications and were non-compliant; the company self-disclosed the testing failure and agreed to pay $628,328 under the False Claims Act.
WaysToIdentify: This is government procurement (defense contract) fraud, not health care claims - the false statement is a certification that headsets met military specification testing. The payer-side analogue is invoice-payment certification: the contracting officer could require and match test reports/certificates of conformance to each lot before paying, and flag invoices where no test artifact exists for the serial/lot numbers delivered. Detection otherwise depends on self-disclosure or acceptance testing.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control: an accounts-payable edit that will not release payment on a spec-critical line item until a matching lot/serial-level test report or certificate of conformance has been uploaded and the testing lab is on an approved list. Add a periodic sampling program that pulls delivered units for independent spec testing and suspends further payments to the vendor on any failure.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Adrienne Ponzo (loan application preparer); unnamed co-conspirators (recruiters)
State_County: New Jersey - Camden County (Camden); Delaware - New Castle County (Bear)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Ponzo's co-conspirators recruited owners of shell or barely-operating companies, and Ponzo prepared and electronically submitted fraudulent PPP and EIDL applications to the SBA and PPP lenders, fabricating bank statements and tax returns to support them; 14 loans totaling nearly $1.5 million were obtained and Ponzo kept a share of the proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: No health care claims component - this is SBA PPP/EIDL loan fraud. The lender/SBA could have caught it pre-disbursement by verifying submitted bank statements and tax returns directly against IRS transcripts and bank-provided data, and by flagging clusters of applications sharing the same preparer, IP address, email domain, phone or bank account across otherwise unrelated shell companies with no payroll filings.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pre-disbursement application-linkage engine keyed on preparer identity, IP/device, contact details, bank routing/account and business address, which pends any application belonging to a cluster above the calibrated size. Require automated IRS transcript and bank-account verification of claimed payroll/revenue, with disbursement blocked where the submitted documents do not reconcile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs (Civil Division)
FraudEntity: More than 600 unnamed defendants in over 280 enforcement actions, including multiple nursing home operators
SchemeSummary: Annual report summarizing DOJ elder fraud and abuse enforcement: more than 280 actions against over 600 defendants, domestic and transnational, who stole or attempted to steal over $2 billion from more than one million older Americans, and actions holding nursing home operators accountable for grossly substandard care billed to Medicare and Medicaid. No single scheme mechanics are described.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual enforcement round-up rather than a single scheme, so there is no specific pre-payment signal to reconstruct. The generalizable payer-side hooks are: linking survey/staffing/quality data (deficiency citations, staffing hours per resident day, ownership changes) to facility payment, and screening for the identity-theft-driven billing patterns typical of elder-targeted schemes such as claims for beneficiaries with no prior relationship to the biller.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control: a facility-level quality-and-staffing feed that pends or flags nursing-home claims for review when reported staffing hours cannot support the billed census or when immediate-jeopardy/substandard-care citations are open. Additionally, a beneficiary-level alert when a new provider bills for a member outside the member's historical geographic and provider network, routing to prepay verification and beneficiary contact.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General / Office of Public Affairs
FraudEntity: More than 20 unnamed doctors and clinics that performed transgender medical procedures on children
SchemeSummary: DOJ announced it issued more than 20 subpoenas to doctors and clinics that performed transgender medical procedures on children, as part of investigations into potential health care fraud and false statements; no billing mechanics, amounts, or defendants are identified.
WaysToIdentify: No scheme mechanics, defendants, or billed amounts are described - this is an announcement of investigative subpoenas, so there is nothing to catch pre-payment from this record. If specific allegations were that services were billed under codes not matching the procedure performed or with false diagnosis attestation, the payer route would be diagnosis-to-procedure consistency and prior-authorization documentation matching.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control: a prepay code-to-diagnosis and age consistency edit for procedures with coverage criteria tied to documented clinical findings, pending claims that lack a matching authorization or diagnosis. Otherwise no payer-side control can be derived from this case.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs (Civil Division; Criminal Division, Fraud Section)
SchemeSummary: Announcement of a new DOJ/DHS cross-agency Trade Fraud Task Force to pursue importers who evade tariffs and customs duties and smuggle prohibited goods, using Tariff Act collection actions, False Claims Act suits, and parallel criminal prosecutions; no specific defendant, health care service, or fraud amount is identified.
WaysToIdentify: No health care claims payment component - this concerns customs/tariff evasion by importers and is enforced through Tariff Act collection and FCA suits. The analogous pre-payment control sits with CBP entry data (declared value, country of origin, HTS classification) rather than any insurer.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side health care control applies. The nearest analogue is an entry-level import screening rule comparing declared unit values and origin against comparable-commodity distributions and transshipment patterns, holding release/liquidation for review on outliers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Forefront Dermatology S.C. (owner/operator of Henghold Dermatology); Henghold Surgery Center LLC (ambulatory surgery center, wholly owned by William B. Henghold, M.D.)
SchemeSummary: A dermatology practice and affiliated ambulatory surgery center allegedly billed Medicare for wound repairs following Mohs micrographic skin cancer surgery using inaccurate, higher-paying codes - coding linear repairs as flap repairs and smaller flap repairs as larger flap repairs. Resolved for $847,394 under the False Claims Act following a qui tam suit by a former employee, who receives $152,531.
WaysToIdentify: Upcoding of repair type after Mohs is visible in claims: the ratio of flap-repair codes to simple/linear closure codes per Mohs surgeon, and the distribution of repair sizes (larger flap tiers) versus same-specialty peers, are computable before payment. Defect-size codes billed can also be checked against the number of Mohs stages/blocks billed on the same date - large flap tiers reported with single-stage, small-lesion Mohs are internally inconsistent. Confirmation requires the operative note, so a prepay documentation request on outliers closes it.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a per-NPI, per-facility monthly metric of flap/graft closure codes as a share of all post-Mohs repairs and mean billed repair size, with a trigger at the calibrated same-specialty percentile that puts the provider on prepay operative-note review for those code pairs. Add a claim-line edit flagging repair-size tier inconsistent with the Mohs stage/lesion codes billed on the same date and same anatomic site, pending the claim for documentation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Genetic Technological Innovations, LLC (GTI) (diagnostic laboratory)
SchemeSummary: GTI paid a purported infection-prevention/marketing company $4,000-$4,500 per month per long-term care facility under a sham Marketing Services Agreement as disguised payment for laboratory test referrals; the company swabbed nursing home residents for COVID-19 and GTI then 'stacked' medically unnecessary respiratory pathogen panels on the same specimens for every resident regardless of symptoms, billing Medicare at roughly 10 times the COVID-19 test reimbursement.
WaysToIdentify: The stacking pattern is directly visible in claims: the same specimen date and same facility population showing a COVID-19 test plus a large respiratory pathogen panel for essentially every resident, with no symptom-bearing diagnosis codes and no variation by clinical presentation, is detectable at adjudication. Facility-level saturation (RPP billed for nearly 100% of residents at a long-term care site) and reimbursement per specimen far above peers are strong prepay flags. The sham per-facility marketing fee is found in the lab's contracts and ledgers, so pair claims flags with a credentialing/AKS attestation review and post-pay contract audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a specimen-level reflex-testing edit: when a high-cost multiplex respiratory panel is billed on the same date/specimen as a COVID-19 test, require a symptomatic diagnosis and treating-clinician order, and deny or pend absent both. Add a facility-cohort saturation metric (share of residents at a single congregate site receiving RPP from one lab per month) that suspends the lab's RPP payments and triggers a medical-necessity documentation request and AKS review of any per-facility marketing agreements.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Indiana
FraudEntity: Patients Choice Laboratories (PCL) (diagnostic laboratory)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims
