SchemeSummary: PCL allegedly paid a purported infection prevention company $5,000/month under a sham Marketing Services Agreement (about $1.86 million total) and paid 1099 sales representatives at least $372,000 in volume-based commissions in exchange for laboratory test referrals; the company swabbed long-term care residents for COVID-19 and PCL used the same specimens to bill Medicare over $6 million for thousands of medically unnecessary respiratory pathogen panels at 43 facilities, sometimes billing RPPs without performing any COVID-19 test.
WaysToIdentify: Same detectable pattern: one lab billing thousands of respiratory pathogen panels concentrated at a defined set of long-term care facilities, with near-universal panel use per resident, no symptomatic diagnoses, and in some cases RPP billed with no corresponding COVID-19 test despite the swabbing pretext. Volume-based 1099 commission arrangements and flat per-facility 'marketing' fees are visible in credentialing disclosures and financial records, so a targeted contract request during enrolment revalidation adds confirmation.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a prepay medical-necessity edit requiring symptomatic diagnosis plus a documented ordering clinician for multiplex respiratory panels, with automatic denial when the panel appears without any corresponding COVID test or clinician order for congregate-care specimens. Add a lab-level facility-concentration and per-resident panel-rate monitor that triggers payment suspension and a request for marketing/sales-rep compensation agreements when panel rates at referring facilities exceed the calibrated peer percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section and U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Done Global Inc. (California digital health company); Mindful Mental Wellness P.A. (Florida medical practice); Ruthia He (founder and CEO of Done Global, previously convicted); David Brody (former clinical president of Done Global, previously convicted)
SchemeSummary: Done Global operated a subscription-based 'digital health' ADHD platform in which members paid a monthly fee and prescribers were instructed to issue Adderall and other stimulant prescriptions without legitimate medical purpose - often with no examination, no pre-existing practitioner-patient relationship, and sometimes based only on a short video/audio contact or none at all - resulting in over 40 million pills prescribed and more than $100 million in revenue. Done Global and Mindful Mental Wellness allegedly deceived pharmacies (incorporating MMW to bypass pharmacies that had blocked Done-affiliated prescriptions) and conspired to submit false claims to Medicare, Medicaid and commercial insurers, plus altering and destroying records after a grand jury subpoena; the company defendants are charged while founder Ruthia He and clinical president David Brody were previously convicted.
WaysToIdentify: Pharmacy claims data shows the signal before payment: a small set of prescribers generating extreme volumes of Schedule II stimulant prescriptions to geographically dispersed, mostly young adult patients with no prior treatment history, no covered E/M or telehealth encounter on file, and standardized dose/quantity patterns. The absence of any billed evaluation encounter preceding a controlled-substance fill, and PDMP data showing new-patient stimulant starts far above peers, are both available at adjudication. Re-emergence of the same prescriber roster under a new corporate entity (MMW) after pharmacies blocked the original is detectable by linking prescriber NPIs across billing entities.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-level controlled-substance monitor computing monthly stimulant prescriptions, distinct patients, new-start rate, patient geographic spread and share of fills with no antecedent billed encounter; firing above the calibrated peer percentile places the prescriber's stimulant claims on prepay review or prior authorization. Add a pharmacy-benefit edit requiring a documented, billed telehealth or in-person evaluation within a defined lookback before paying an initial stimulant fill, and an entity-linkage rule that carries an existing block/flag to any new billing entity sharing prescriber NPIs, ownership or platform identifiers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey; U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Diopsys Inc. (medical device company)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Diopsys allegedly caused eye-care providers to bill Medicare and Medicaid for medically unnecessary electroretinography (ERG) vision testing using its NOVA device, which the FDA had cleared only for visual evoked potential testing, and made substantial unapproved changes to the device without required FDA submission. Resolved by a qui tam civil settlement of $1,225,000 guaranteed plus up to $13,025,000 contingent payments.
WaysToIdentify: Coverage can be tied to device clearance: a payer can maintain the FDA-cleared indication for the specific device model used and deny ERG codes when the only device in the practice is cleared for VEP only, using the manufacturer/model reported on the claim or captured at credentialing. Claims-side signals include ERG billed for nearly every patient visit, ERG on patients without a covered retinal-disease diagnosis, and abrupt adoption clusters across many unrelated small practices seeded by one vendor's sales program. The FDA-submission failure itself is regulatory and only fully verifiable outside claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a device-to-code coverage table keyed to FDA clearance and require the device make/model on ERG claim lines; deny or pend lines where the reported device lacks clearance for the billed test. Add a per-provider ERG-per-patient-visit rate and diagnosis-eligibility edit that pends claims lacking a qualifying retinal diagnosis, plus a vendor-cluster alert that flags simultaneous ERG billing onset across practices sharing a single equipment supplier for coordinated prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Diopsys, Inc. (medical device company)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Diopsys allegedly caused eye-care providers to bill Medicare and Medicaid for medically unnecessary electroretinography (ERG) vision tests performed with its NOVA device, which was FDA-cleared only for visual evoked potential testing, and made substantial device changes never submitted to FDA. Resolved by a qui tam settlement with $1,225,000 guaranteed and up to $13,025,000 contingent payments (total up to $14.25 million).
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the related settlement: the payer can compare the billed ERG code against the FDA-cleared indication of the device model actually in use, information obtainable at credentialing or by requiring device identification on the claim. High-yield claims signals are ERG performed on a near-universal share of visits, absence of qualifying retinal pathology diagnoses, and synchronized billing onset across unrelated practices following one manufacturer's placement campaign.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a prepay edit that denies ERG codes when the reported device model/UDI is not cleared for that test, and requires a qualifying diagnosis and prior imaging/exam findings for coverage. Add manufacturer-cluster analytics that group practices by equipment vendor and trigger prepay medical-necessity documentation review when ERG-per-visit rates exceed the calibrated peer percentile within a cluster.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: James Rausch (director of operations and sales, Northeast region, mobile medical diagnostics company)
State_County: Massachusetts - Suffolk County (Boston); New York - Suffolk County (Port Jefferson Station)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Rausch and co-conspirators at a mobile medical diagnostics company paid doctors cash and check kickbacks based on the volume of transcranial doppler brain scans they ordered, disguising the payments as fair-market-value space rental and administrative service agreements; the medically unnecessary TCD scans generated about $70.6 million in Medicare claims, of which Medicare paid about $27.2 million.
WaysToIdentify: Ordering-physician concentration is visible pre-payment: a mobile diagnostics company whose transcranial doppler volume traces to a small number of high-volume ordering physicians, each ordering TCD for an outsized share of their panel and without stroke/cerebrovascular indications, is an outlier pattern in claims. Space-rental and administrative-services agreements between the testing company and its referrers are disclosable at credentialing and revalidation; rent paid to the same physicians who order the tests, scaling with order volume, is the tell. Financial confirmation of the kickback requires records review, so combine claims flags with an agreement request.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-physician/testing-entity dyad metric: TCD studies per ordering NPI per month, share of that physician's patients tested, and share of the testing entity's volume from its top referrers, firing above the calibrated peer percentile to place the entity's TCD claims on prepay medical-necessity review. Add a credentialing rule requiring disclosure of any lease or administrative-services payments to referral sources, with automated cross-check flagging referrers who also receive payments and referring those dyads for AKS investigation and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Farrukh Jarar Ali (owner of ProMD Solutions); Cle'Esther Davenport (owner, Davenport House LLC); Ira Denny (nurse practitioner); Tyler Kontos; Joel "Max" Kupetz; Jorge Kinds (nurse practitioner); Gina Palacios (nurse practitioner)
State_County: Arizona - Maricopa County (Phoenix, Peoria, Surprise, Mesa, Scottsdale)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System - AHCCCS); TRICARE; CHAMPVA; commercial insurers
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Seven Arizona defendants charged in related takedown cases: Ali's Pakistan-based billing/credentialing firm enrolled 41 sham substance-abuse clinics with AHCCCS and billed ~$650M for addiction treatment never provided to homeless and Native American patients, creating false therapy notes for audits ($564M paid, $24.5M to Ali personally); Davenport took ~$739,000 in kickbacks for referring sober-home residents to Tusa Integrated Clinic (~$1.58M paid by AHCCCS); and Kontos, Kupetz, Kinds, Denny and Palacios billed Medicare, TRICARE, CHAMPVA and commercial insurers over $1 billion (plus $209M and $59M respectively for Denny and Palacios) for medically unnecessary amniotic wound allografts applied to elderly and hospice patients by nurse practitioners at the direction of untrained sales reps paid via kickbacks. Amounts span multiple defendants; $7.2M in crypto and bank accounts seized.
WaysToIdentify: Enrolment analytics would have surfaced 41 behavioral-health clinics credentialed and billed by a single offshore billing/credentialing agent sharing addresses, phones, bank accounts and NPI-application IP addresses - a cluster that could be pended before any high-dollar payment. Claims signals include implausible therapy hours per clinician per day, a beneficiary population concentrated among homeless and tribal members recruited through sober homes with duplicate billing across clinics for the same dates, and, for the wound-graft arm, extreme per-patient amniotic allograft units billed by nurse practitioners on hospice/elderly patients with square-centimeter amounts exceeding plausible wound size. Both arms show explosive new-provider revenue ramps detectable within the first billing cycles.
FeaturesToCreate: Build enrolment link analysis clustering applications by billing agent, address, phone, bank account and submission IP, with automatic prepay review or payment suspension for high-dollar behavioral-health claims from any cluster above the calibrated size; combine with a new-provider revenue-velocity trigger. Add prepay edits for provider-level therapy units exceeding staffed clinician capacity per day, cross-provider duplicate service dates per member, and skin-substitute claims where billed square centimeters, application frequency, or concurrent hospice election are inconsistent - pending payment for wound measurements, photographs and treating-physician orders.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: John Patterson, M.D. (physician); Nursemind Home Care Inc. (hospice); Zenia Chavez (owner of Nursemind Home Care, Inc.)
SchemeSummary: Dr. Patterson allegedly accepted kickbacks from Nursemind Home Care Inc., an El Paso hospice, in exchange for certifying patients as eligible for hospice services when they were not, causing false claims to be submitted to Medicare; he agreed to pay $468,626 to settle FCA allegations, while hospice owner Zenia Chavez pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit illegal remunerations.
WaysToIdentify: Certifying-physician concentration is visible before payment: one physician certifying an outsized share of a single hospice's admissions, with certified patients whose diagnoses and prior claims history show no terminal decline, and with unusually long lengths of stay or live discharges. Financial relationships between the hospice and the certifying physician (medical-director or consulting payments not proportionate to work) are disclosable at enrolment and in the hospice's cost report. The kickback itself needs records review, so pair the certification-pattern flag with a documentation and agreement request before paying.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a certifying-physician/hospice dyad metric computing share of the hospice's certifications from each physician, beneficiary six-month-prognosis plausibility from prior diagnosis/utilization history, long-stay and live-discharge rates; above the calibrated peer percentile, place new admissions on prepay review requiring the certification narrative and clinical records. Add an enrolment cross-check flagging hospices whose certifying physicians also receive medical-director or other payments, routing to AKS review and, where certifications are unsupported, suspension of election-period payments.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Ali Rashan (medical doctor, CEO and founder of ClearMD); ClearMD (COVID-19 testing provider)
State_County: New York - New York County (New York City)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Unbundling; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Rashan allegedly directed his COVID-19 testing company ClearMD to bill insurers for thousands of evaluation and management services never performed and to bill two to four COVID-19 testing codes when only a single test was administered; when insurers requested documentation, staff wrote software to auto-generate fabricated medical records that were submitted to justify retaining roughly $24 million in payments.
WaysToIdentify: Both mechanics are pure claims-data patterns: a COVID-testing entity billing an E/M service on nearly every specimen - often with no qualified clinician attached and identical code levels - and billing two to four COVID test codes for a single collection date on the same patient are detectable at adjudication. Unit-per-specimen and E/M-attachment rates versus other testing sites are computable per NPI per week. The auto-generated records defeat retrospective document review, so the control must be prepay volume/edit-based rather than reliance on requested charts.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit limiting COVID-19 test codes to one payable unit per patient per collection date and denying duplicate/overlapping methodology codes on the same specimen; and a second edit denying E/M billed by a testing-only entity absent an identified rendering clinician and documented separate evaluation. Add an NPI-level ratio monitor (E/M claims per test claim, test units per patient-day) that triggers payment suspension when it exceeds the calibrated peer percentile, and treat identical templated notes across patients as a fraud indicator rather than substantiation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Duane Dixon (doctor); Wendell Lewis Randall (former doctor); Charles Wilson Adams, Jr. (falsely held out as trained medical professional); Debra Shaffer (nurse practitioner); John Gregory Barnes (L5 owner); Jennifer Adams (former COO); L5 Medical Holdings, LLC d/b/a Pain Care Center
State_County: Virginia - Lynchburg; Virginia - Madison Heights (Amherst County); Virginia - Christiansburg (Montgomery County); Virginia - Blacksburg (Montgomery County); Virginia - Woodlawn (Carroll County)
SchemeSummary: At L5 Medical Holdings pain clinics, Dr. Duane Dixon pre-signed dozens of blank prescriptions that clinic staff filled out for Schedule II opioids (fentanyl, oxycodone) and gave to patients who never saw a qualified provider, and shared his DEA registration number so unauthorized providers could prescribe Suboxone; to obtain insurance payments he also approved and signed patient files, including another doctor's records, for patients he had not treated. Dixon received 40 months, a $35,000 fine and $200,000 forfeiture; co-defendants Randall (18 months) and Charles Adams (24 months) were also sentenced, and the owner, COO and L5 itself pled guilty awaiting sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: Prescription and claims data show one physician's DEA number attached to Schedule II volumes and to Suboxone prescriptions written on dates and locations where he had no billed encounter, and to patients with no E/M claim from him at all - a prescriber-to-encounter mismatch computable at adjudication. Also visible: signatures/attestations on records for patients whose visits were billed by a different NPI, and clinic-level opioid prescribing per patient far above pain-management peers. PDMP-to-claims linkage flags prescriptions issued while the prescriber was demonstrably not practicing.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-encounter linkage edit that pends or denies controlled-substance pharmacy claims where no encounter by that prescriber exists for the patient within a defined lookback, and flags a single DEA number used across multiple mid-level or unauthorized providers/locations. Add clinic-level opioid MME-per-patient and Schedule II scripts-per-prescriber-day monitors that trigger prepay review of the practice's professional claims plus a records request comparing rendering-provider attestation to the billed NPI, escalating to prescriber payment suspension and DEA referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Alexander Baldonado, M.D. (physician)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: A Queens physician took cash kickbacks from two related New York laboratories and from a DME supplier to order medically unnecessary cancer genetic and other lab tests and orthotic braces for Medicare/Medicaid beneficiaries he never treated - many recruited at COVID-19 testing events at assisted living facilities, adult day care centers and a retirement community - and also billed Medicare for lengthy office visits he never provided, causing over $24 million in claims and more than $2.1 million in Medicare payments.
WaysToIdentify: The ordering physician's claims show hereditary cancer panels, other lab tests and orthotic braces ordered for large numbers of beneficiaries with no prior or concurrent treating relationship, many clustered by assisted-living/adult-day-care addresses and by event dates, alongside high-level office visit codes billed at volumes exceeding available clinic hours. Genetic-panel orders without a cancer diagnosis or documented family history, and multiple braces per beneficiary from a single supplier, are all prepay-detectable. Supplier/lab-to-orderer concentration (one physician driving most of two labs' and one DME company's volume) is likewise computable before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-physician edit that denies or pends high-cost genetic panels and orthotic braces when the ordering NPI has no prior qualifying encounter with the beneficiary and the claim lacks a supporting diagnosis/family-history indicator, and caps braces per beneficiary per period across suppliers. Add a physician time-plausibility check (billed E/M minutes plus test-order volume per day versus feasible hours) and an orderer-concentration metric per lab/DME supplier; exceeding the calibrated percentile triggers payment suspension for that dyad and a records/medical-necessity request, plus AKS referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (federal grand jury in California)
FraudEntity: Violetta Mailyan (doctor, owner and operator of Healthy Way Medical Center); Healthy Way Medical Center
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Superseding indictment alleges the owner of Healthy Way Medical Center billed Medicare more than $45 million for Botox injections that were medically unnecessary or never provided, including claims for dates when she or the beneficiary was traveling internationally, when the beneficiary was in federal prison, and when the clinic was closed; she also allegedly produced falsified medical records in response to a grand jury subpoena.
WaysToIdentify: The impossible-day signals were all visible prepay: claim dates while the beneficiary was incarcerated (CMS inmate/Prisoner file), while the beneficiary or the billing/rendering provider was outside the country (CBP/passport travel data, or provider absence inferred from zero-claim gaps at other sites), and dates when the clinic was closed (weekends/holidays, posted hours, utility or badge data). Botox volume per NPI versus same-specialty peers and per-beneficiary injection frequency far above the calibrated percentile is also a prepay screen. Falsified records surfaced only after subpoena, but a pre-payment documentation request on the outlier population would have forced early production.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a claim-line eligibility/impossible-day edit that denies or pends any date of service where the beneficiary appears on the incarceration or deceased file, or where the rendering NPI has documented out-of-country travel, plus a service-date-versus-practice-calendar edit flagging dates the practice reports as closed. Add a provider-level Botox/J-code utilization outlier model (units per beneficiary per year, share of panel receiving injections versus same-specialty peers) that triggers prepay review and a medical-records request, escalating to payment suspension on credible fraud.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Gabriel Alejandro Hernandez-Roman (emergency room resident doctor)
State_County: Iowa - Linn County (Cedar Rapids); Iowa - Johnson County (Iowa City)
SchemeSummary: A resident ER doctor knowingly accessed the protected health information of multiple women who were not his patients at two Iowa hospitals under false pretenses, asked one victim to falsely tell the hospital she had consented, shared a patient photograph via SnapChat with no medical purpose, and made false statements to the Iowa Board of Medicine; no billing or payer loss was involved.
WaysToIdentify: No claims-payment component: this is unauthorized PHI access and false statements to a licensing board, with no billing or payer loss. The detectable signal lives in EHR audit logs — record access by a clinician with no encounter, order, or care-team relationship to the patient — and in state-board disciplinary and NPDB feeds at credentialing time.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control: an EHR access-audit rule that joins each record-view event to the patient's active encounters, orders and care-team assignments and fires a privacy investigation when a user views records with no treatment relationship, weighted for same-sex/age-pattern browsing. At credentialing, automate NPDB/state-board query refresh so board findings and false-statement adjudications block or flag network participation.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: David M. Young M.D. (physician)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Young signed thousands of prescriptions and medical records for orthotic braces and cancer genetic tests for over 13,000 Medicare beneficiaries (including undercover agents) he never saw, spoke to, or treated, falsely certifying medical necessity, diagnoses and plans of care; brace suppliers and labs used these prescriptions to bill Medicare more than $70 million while Young was paid about $475,000 for signing.
WaysToIdentify: Wholly visible prepay: one ordering NPI appears as certifier on braces and hereditary cancer panels for thousands of beneficiaries spread across many states with no companion E/M claim from that NPI and no prior treating relationship in claims history. Telemedicine-only or absent encounter, distance between ordering provider and beneficiary, and concentration of the same ordering NPI across a handful of DME suppliers and labs are all computable at adjudication. The undercover-agent beneficiaries would themselves have flagged as members with no clinical history matching the order.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-provider linkage edit: for DME braces (L-codes) and hereditary cancer panels, require a paid E/M or covered telehealth encounter with the ordering NPI within a lookback window; if absent, deny prepay pending records. Add a certifier-network model computing per-ordering-NPI counts of unique beneficiaries, distinct states, distinct billing suppliers/labs, and share of orders with no prior relationship versus same-specialty peers, firing prepay review of all downstream supplier/lab claims tied to that NPI and referral for revocation.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Wendell Lewis Randall (physician, sole owner of National Institute of Toxicology, PLLC); National Institute of Toxicology, PLLC
SchemeSummary: Randall, sole physician/owner of National Institute of Toxicology, prescribed opioids and other controlled substances without regard to medical necessity and required every patient to submit to definitive urine drug tests at each visit, run by his in-house lab, billing Medicare and NC Medicaid at the highest-reimbursing code for nearly all Medicare/Medicaid patients; he obtained $753,446.70 from Medicare and $1,296,300.77 from Medicaid and used proceeds for purchases including a $97,000 building near his home.
WaysToIdentify: The signature is reflexive definitive UDT at every visit from an in-office lab: near-1.0 ratio of definitive drug-test claims to office visits, and use of the highest-tier definitive code (largest analyte class count) for essentially the entire panel, versus same-specialty peers. Self-referral to a commonly owned lab is visible from shared address, TIN, and ownership data on the CMS-855 enrollment. Pair with the prescriber's controlled-substance volume and MME per patient from Part D/state PDMP.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-level edit computing definitive UDT claims per patient encounter and the share billed at the top analyte tier; when both exceed the calibrated percentile against same-specialty peers, deny or pend the definitive test lines and allow only presumptive testing pending documentation of individualized medical necessity. Add a linkage rule flagging labs sharing address/TIN/ownership with the ordering practice and route their claims to prepay review, plus a PDMP-linked high-MME prescriber flag.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Alexander Baldonado, M.D. (physician)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Physician took cash kickbacks from two New York laboratories to order expensive cancer genetic tests and other lab tests for Medicare beneficiaries recruited at COVID-19 testing events held at assisted living facilities, adult day care centers and a retirement community, without treating, examining or even speaking to them; he also billed Medicare for lengthy office visits never provided and took cash bribes from a DME supplier for signing prescriptions for medically unnecessary orthotic braces, causing over $24 million in claims and $2.2 million in Medicare payments.
WaysToIdentify: Detectable prepay through clustering: many beneficiaries residing at the same assisted living/adult day/retirement addresses receive identical high-cost cancer panels ordered by a single physician on the same or adjacent dates, alongside COVID test claims, with no prior treating relationship. The same physician also bills top-level prolonged E/M for those beneficiaries — implausible time-in-day totals per rendering NPI per date. Kickbacks themselves need post-payment proof, but the referral concentration between the physician, two labs and one DME supplier is computable at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a cohort-clustering detector keyed on beneficiary residence address plus ordering NPI plus test code, firing when a single orderer generates same-code high-cost genetic panels for many co-resident beneficiaries within a short window; pend the lab and DME lines and request the ordering record. Add a per-rendering-NPI daily time-accumulation edit that denies E/M levels whose summed typical minutes exceed a plausible workday, and a referral-concentration score (share of a lab's or supplier's volume from one orderer) triggering prepay review and suspension.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (DOJ-HHS False Claims Act Working Group)
SchemeSummary: Not a specific fraud case: DOJ and HHS announced the creation of a joint False Claims Act Working Group and listed priority enforcement areas (Medicare Advantage, drug/device pricing and rebate arrangements, network adequacy, kickbacks tied to drugs/devices/DME, defective devices, and EHR manipulation driving utilization).
WaysToIdentify: Not a specific fraud case — it is an enforcement-priority announcement with no claims, provider or loss mechanics to detect. No case-level payer detection applies.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control: maintain a mapped portfolio of prepay and post-pay analytics covering the named priority areas — MA risk-adjustment diagnosis validation (chart-unsupported HCCs), drug/device price-and-rebate reporting reconciliation, network-adequacy access audits, referral-concentration kickback scoring, and EHR-driven upcoding/cloned-note detection — each with an owner and a fire-to-action path.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (Office of Public Affairs)
FraudEntity: Peter Roussonicolos (silent-partner owner of five DME suppliers); unnamed co-conspirators serving as nominee owners
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Roussonicolos secretly owned and operated five durable medical equipment suppliers through paid nominee owners and falsified Medicare enrollment forms and bank records to hide that his felony convictions made him ineligible to enroll; the companies submitted roughly $61.5 million in claims for medically unnecessary DME (paid about $26.7 million), with beneficiary referrals obtained through kickbacks and bribes paid to patient recruiters. Restitution of $21,195,540.18 and forfeiture of $2,514,040 were ordered against him.
WaysToIdentify: Catchable at enrollment: nominee-owner structures show up as new DME suppliers sharing addresses, phone numbers, bank accounts, billing agents, surety bonds and IP/submitter IDs with each other and with a previously excluded or convicted individual; the hidden owner appears in corporate registry, UCC and bank signatory records not matching the CMS-855S disclosure. Post-enrollment, the five suppliers billing identical L-code mixes with overlapping beneficiaries and recruiter-sourced referrals is a prepay signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrollment-time entity-resolution graph linking applicants by address, phone, bank routing/account, EFT payee, submitter ID, registered agent and owner identity, and auto-refer any applicant linked to an excluded/convicted person or to a common nominee for site visit and denial; screen all disclosed and inferred owners against LEIE, GSA and criminal-history sources continuously. Layer a new-supplier prepay hold with escalating documentation requests when claim ramp rate, beneficiary overlap across linked suppliers, and single-recruiter beneficiary concentration exceed calibrated percentiles.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Karen Gaston (controlled LNK, Elegant Clinical, Ruby Red LLC, and Diamond Shine LLC)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Gaston submitted PPP and EIDL loan applications for four entities she controlled (some non-operational or with no employees), falsely stating that all were active operating businesses, inflating employee counts and wages, attaching fraudulent tax returns, and falsely listing a family member as a part owner; she spread applications across separate financial institutions and spent the $1,163,910 received on cars, travel, jewelry and her home mortgage. Sentenced to three years probation with four weekends of incarceration, 10 months home detention, full restitution, and forfeiture of a $39,521.63 ring.
WaysToIdentify: No payer-side claims component: this is SBA PPP/EIDL loan fraud, not health care billing. The detectable signals sat with the lenders and SBA — applicant entities with no payroll filings, tax transcripts that do not match IRS records, duplicate applications for related entities across multiple banks, and shared addresses/owners/bank accounts.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer claims control applies. Nearest equivalent: at the funding agency, an application-time edit that reconciles claimed wages and employee counts against IRS transcript and state wage-report data, plus cross-lender entity resolution on EIN, owner SSN, address and bank account to flag multiple applications by one controller; mismatch or duplication holds disbursement pending verification.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Shiva Akula (hospice owner); Michelle Andre
SchemeSummary: Annual FY2024 collections release: after a trial and guilty verdict, the office's Monetary Penalties and Recovery Unit collected approximately $3.7 million in restitution to Medicare from hospice owner Shiva Akula, restraining and turning over his assets including hospice licenses; separately it forfeited approximately $34,570 in proceeds from Michelle Andre, who pleaded guilty to distributing misbranded injectable contraceptives to patients. Figures span two unrelated defendants and no billing scheme mechanics or loss amounts are described.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual collections round-up covering two unrelated defendants with no billing mechanics described, so nothing case-specific is detectable. The generally applicable prepay signals for the hospice component are long-stay non-terminal patients, high continuous/general-inpatient day share, and physician certifications without supporting decline documentation; the misbranded-injectable component is caught through drug pedigree/NDC and licensure checks rather than claim analytics.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable controls: a hospice provider-level model on median length of stay, share of beneficiaries exceeding long-stay thresholds, live-discharge rate and GIP/continuous-care day share versus peers, firing prepay medical-record review and payment suspension on credible allegation. For drugs, an NDC-validity and licensed-supplier edit denying claims for products not in the approved drug file or dispensed by unlicensed/unauthorized entities.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Tyreek Rasheed Exum; Anthony Wandland, Jr. (co-defendant who supplied stolen identities)
State_County: North Carolina - Greene County (Snow Hill); Illinois - Cook County (Chicago)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Exum and Wandland used over 20 stolen identities plus co-conspirators' identities to file Economic Injury Disaster Loan and Pandemic Unemployment Assistance applications containing false income, employment and business information; Wandland supplied the identities for a cut of proceeds, and Exum routed nearly $1 million in loan proceeds through his own, nominee, family/friend and stolen-identity bank accounts, moving funds via PayPal, CashApp, debit cards and ATM withdrawals.
WaysToIdentify: No health care claims component: EIDL and Pandemic Unemployment Assistance fraud using stolen identities. Detectable at application by the benefit agencies through identity-proofing failures, SSNs and names that do not match SSA/state wage records, and many applications routing to a common set of bank accounts, IP addresses, devices and phone numbers.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer claims control applies. Nearest equivalent for any benefit payer: application-time identity verification against authoritative sources plus a payment-routing graph that counts distinct applicant identities sharing a bank account, debit card, device fingerprint or IP; exceeding the calibrated threshold holds disbursement and triggers manual identity proofing.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dr. Tajul Shams Chowdhury (physician, owner of Center for Pain Management); Mohammad Imtiaz Chowdhury (purported pharmacy marketer, son)
SchemeSummary: A physician referred prescriptions for costly compounded drugs from his Edinburg pain management clinic to local pharmacies, and the pharmacy paid $6.6 million in kickbacks to his son, who posed as a pharmacy marketer.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signal is extreme referral concentration: a single pain clinic prescriber accounts for an outsized share of one pharmacy's high-cost compounded drug claims, with per-claim amounts and refill counts far above peers and a narrow set of expensive compound formulas. The kickback conduit — the prescriber's son on the pharmacy's payroll as a 'marketer' — is discoverable from ownership/employee disclosures, corporate filings and shared surname/address matching against the prescriber's identity.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-pharmacy dyad model computing each pharmacy's claim-dollar share from a single prescriber, average compound claim cost and formula concentration, firing prepay review and prior authorization on compounded claims when the dyad exceeds the calibrated percentile. Add a relationship-screening rule matching pharmacy owners, employees and marketing contractors against high-volume prescribers' names, addresses and family links, routing matches to kickback investigation.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Louisiana
SchemeSummary: Not a fraud case: personnel announcement of Ellison C. Travis's appointment as Acting U.S. Attorney for the Middle District of Louisiana.
WaysToIdentify: Not a fraud case — a personnel announcement. Nothing to detect and no payer data involved.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Nabeen Leigh Singha
SchemeSummary: Not a health care fraud case: defendant pleaded guilty to production, receipt and possession of child pornography after exchanging sexually explicit messages with two minors, paying them to produce explicit images, and paying an intermediary for explicit material of four additional minors.
WaysToIdentify: Not a health care fraud case and no claims were submitted; there is no payer-side signal. If the defendant were an enrolled provider, the only payer-relevant hook would be criminal-history and licensure monitoring.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer claims control applies. Nearest equivalent: continuous criminal-conviction, exclusion-list and licensure monitoring of enrolled providers and their employees, auto-terminating participation on a disqualifying conviction.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Carrie Musselman (chiropractor)
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Chiropractor billed Medicare and private insurers for services falsely represented as performed by physicians when they were actually delivered by nurse practitioners and physician assistants (triggering higher reimbursement), billed placement of electroacupuncture devices as surgically implanted neurostimulators, and billed for neurostimulators and allergy injections never provided (patients instead received unapproved 'experimental' oral drops). Convicted at trial of health care fraud and five wire fraud counts; a related release notes she was later sentenced to 20 months and ordered to repay more than $2.3 million.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay-visible: services billed under a physician NPI on dates when the practice's only clinicians present were NPs/PAs — testable against the practice's rostered staff, licensure files and the volume-per-physician-day implied by claims. Billing implanted neurostimulator codes from a chiropractic-owned office with no facility, anesthesia, or operative claim on the same date is an internally inconsistent claim combination. Allergy-injection and neurostimulator claims with no corresponding drug/device NDC or HCPCS supply line, and no supplier invoice, are also checkable prepay.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider plausibility edit comparing billed rendering NPIs against the practice's credentialed staff roster and per-provider daily service totals, denying or pending physician-rate claims that exceed plausible physician presence and requiring incident-to documentation. Add code-consistency edits: deny neurostimulator implantation codes billed by non-surgical specialties or without a same-date facility/anesthesia/device-supply claim, and deny injection administration codes lacking a paired drug/device line.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Carrie Musselman (chiropractor)
SchemeSummary: Chiropractor billed Medicare and twelve other insurers for services as if performed by medical doctors when they were actually performed by mid-level providers (triggering automatic higher reimbursement), billed for allergy injections never given (patients instead received unapproved experimental oral drops), and billed placement of an electroacupuncture device as a surgically implanted neurostimulator, a service that otherwise would not have been payable.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the related case and equally visible prepay: claims billed at physician rates while the actual renderers were mid-levels, detectable by reconciling rendering NPIs against the practice's credentialed roster, licensure type, and implied physician service-hours per day. Neurostimulator implant codes billed by a chiropractic practice with no operative, facility or device-supply line is a code-eligibility contradiction; allergy injections with no drug supply line or purchase volume to support them is another.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a rendering-identity/scope edit that cross-checks each claim's rendering NPI against taxonomy, state scope of practice and the practice's roster, pending physician-rate payment when the service could not have been personally performed. Add specialty-eligibility edits denying implanted neurostimulator and allergy-immunotherapy administration codes absent same-date device/drug supply lines and a facility claim, and reconcile billed injection units against distributor purchase data on audit.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Darius Moore (patient recruiter / "body broker")
SchemeSummary: Moore worked as a "body broker," conspiring with sober living home/addiction treatment facility owners to refer patients for drug addiction treatment; the facilities billed the patients' private insurance for the treatment and paid Moore a share of the insurance proceeds, totaling nearly $500,000 in kickbacks. He was also convicted of a separate firearms offense committed while on pretrial release.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals of body-brokering: clusters of newly enrolled, out-of-state members with recently purchased individual policies all admitting to the same facility/sober-home pair, often with premiums paid by a third party, plus repeat admissions of the same members cycling between facilities. Facility claim patterns show high-cost UDT and residential day billing per admission and a small number of referral sources supplying most admissions.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an admission-cohort model per facility computing share of admissions from out-of-area members, days from policy effective date to admission, third-party premium payment flags, and readmission cycling across affiliated facilities; exceeding the calibrated percentile triggers prepay review, verification of the member's residence and referral source, and documentation requests. Add a referral-source concentration score and flag any facility payments to individuals who are not licensed clinicians for kickback investigation.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Alabama
FraudEntity: Exactech Inc. (medical device manufacturer, Gainesville, Florida)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
SchemeSummary: Exactech allegedly knew as early as January 2008 that its finned tibial tray knee-replacement component failed prematurely at an unacceptable rate, and as early as January 2019 that the polyethylene component in its Logic and Truliant knee systems did likewise, yet continued marketing and selling them for total-knee replacement surgeries on Medicare, Medicaid and VA beneficiaries, causing claims for devices that were not reasonable and necessary. Resolved via $8 million settlement ($7,640,000 federal share, $360,000 state share) in Chapter 11 bankruptcy, arising from qui tam suits in Alabama and Maryland.
WaysToIdentify: Not detectable in a single claim: the device was FDA-cleared and the implant claims looked normal. The route is post-payment device-outcome surveillance — linking implanted device identifiers (UDI/lot on the operative claim or hospital implant log) to subsequent revision-surgery claims to compute time-to-revision by device model versus comparators, plus monitoring MAUDE complaint volumes and manufacturer internal knowledge surfaced by qui tam.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a device-registry analytic that joins UDI/device model captured at implant to downstream revision/removal claims for the same beneficiary and joint, computing model-level revision hazard rates versus peer devices; when a model exceeds the calibrated benchmark, open a manufacturer FCA/recovery referral and flag the model for prior authorization. Require UDI capture on implant claims as a prepay data-completeness edit so the linkage is possible.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Michael Roberts (executive director and co-owner of Progressive Alternatives); Larry Keith Gildersleeve III (co-owner/purchaser)
State_County: Ohio - Lake County; Ohio - Ashtabula County
SchemeSummary: Roberts, executive director and co-owner of Progressive Alternatives, an in-home care business serving people with developmental disabilities, withheld payroll taxes from employees' wages (reflected on paychecks and W-2s given to employees) but never filed W-2 forms with the government or remitted the required quarterly employment tax payments to the IRS; the scheme surfaced when an employee preparing to retire in 2017 found the payroll taxes had not been paid. Restitution figures combine Roberts ($322,718.56) and co-owner spouse Gildersleeve ($692,697.50), each sentenced to 24 months.
WaysToIdentify: No claims-payment fraud: this is employment-tax theft by a home-care employer, with the loss to IRS and employees, not to the payer. Detectable by tax authorities from a filer that shows wage withholding on W-2s issued to employees but no filed W-2/W-3 or Form 941 deposits, and by the payer only indirectly through payroll-tax noncompliance signals during provider financial screening.
FeaturesToCreate: No direct payer claims control; nearest payer-side check is an enrollment/revalidation financial-integrity screen that verifies the provider's employment-tax filing status and any federal tax liens for Medicaid/Medicare home-care participation, flagging nonfilers for corrective action. At the tax agency, an automated edit comparing employee-reported withholding on returns against employer 941/W-2 filings, firing when withholding is claimed with no matching employer remittance.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Dafud Iza (executive vice president of an insurance brokerage firm)
PayerName: Affordable Care Act federal premium subsidies (federal government/ACA insurance plan)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Iza and accomplices at an insurance brokerage submitted false ACA plan applications that inflated the incomes of ineligible, often homeless or substance-affected consumers (and used mismatched addresses and Social Security numbers) so the federal government would pay premium subsidies; the brokerage collected millions in commissions from the insurer, and the government paid at least $133.9 million in subsidies. Street marketers paid bribes to induce enrollment.
WaysToIdentify: Fully checkable at enrollment: applications reporting income implausibly clustered just above the subsidy-eligibility floor, with income attestations that fail IRS/SSA and Equifax data-matching, mismatched or shelter/PO-box addresses, and SSN-name mismatches. Broker-level clustering — one NPN or brokerage submitting many such applications, repeatedly switching enrollees' plans or agents of record — is visible before subsidies are paid.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an application-time edit that scores each enrollment on income-attestation deviation from IRS/SSA data, proximity of attested income to the eligibility threshold, address reuse across unrelated applicants, and SSN/name mismatch; failures require documentary income verification before advance premium tax credits begin. Add a broker/agent-level anomaly model on volume, data-match failure rate, threshold-clustering and unauthorized agent-of-record changes, suspending the broker's marketplace access and withholding commissions pending review.[detect]

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Eye Consultants of Pennsylvania, PC (ECOP) (ophthalmology practice)
SchemeSummary: ECOP billed Medicare Part B for Evaluation & Management services on the same date of service as bilateral eye injections for beneficiaries, contrary to Medicare billing rules, and agreed to pay $790,000 to resolve False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: Pure claim-edit issue, visible at adjudication: E/M billed on the same date of service as bilateral intravitreal injections for the same beneficiary and provider, without a valid modifier or documented separately identifiable service, contrary to NCCI/global-period rules. Provider-level rate of same-day E/M-plus-injection pairs versus same-specialty peers identifies the systematic biller.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement an NCCI/global-surgery bundling edit that automatically denies same-date E/M lines paired with eye injection procedure codes for the same beneficiary/provider unless a supported modifier is present, and validate modifier use by sampling records. Add a provider scorecard on the share of injection encounters carrying a separately billed E/M and modifier-override frequency, referring outliers above the calibrated percentile for prepay documentation review and overpayment recovery.[detect]

Soleyman Cohen-Sedgh, Farid Pakravan, Farhad Manavi; Hemisphere GNSS (USA) Inc.; Andrew Maloney and Capstone Diagnostics; Provista Health LLC and Patrick Britton-Harr (owner); CityMD entities (City Medical of the Upper East Side PLLC, Summit Medical Group P.A., Summit Health Management LLC, Village Practice Management Company LLC); Sikorsky Support Services Inc. and Derco Aerospace Inc.; Austal USA LLC; Insect Shield LLC and Estate of Richard Lane; Georgia Institute of Technology and Georgia Tech Research Corp.; Guidehouse Inc.; Nan McKay; Insight Global LLC; Gen Digital Inc. (formerly Symantec Corp.); City of Los Angeles; Hilcorp San Juan L.P.; XTO Energy Inc.; Hahn Air Lines GmbH and Hahn Air USA Inc.; Consolidated Nuclear Security LLC; AECOM
Service: Pharmacy; Laboratory; GeneticTesting; NursingHome; Hospice; BehavioralHealth; SubstanceUseTreatment; PhysicianPractice; Hospital; Dental; Device, DME
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Drug_Prescriptions; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Upcoding; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Retention of Overpayment; Falsify certificate; Other - Unknown
SchemeSummary: Annual DOJ report: False Claims Act settlements and judgments exceeded $2.9 billion in FY2024 (over $1.67 billion health care related) across 558 resolutions and 979 new qui tam suits, spanning opioid over-dispensing and unlawful prescribing (Endo/Opana ER, Rite Aid controlled substances, Dr. Gerber), billing for medically unnecessary or never-provided services (Grand Health Care therapy quotas, Acadia inpatient behavioral health, Crossroads billing exams for check-ins, Walgreens prescriptions never picked up, unnecessary respiratory panel and cancer genomic tests), kickback and Stark Law arrangements (Community Health Network above-FMV physician pay, DaVita, Oak Street Health agent payments, Paksn medical directorships, RDx commissions/MSO payments, Innovasis surgeon inducements), Medicare Advantage and rebate-reporting misconduct, retained overpayments (Gentiva hospice, USFHP plans), plus pandemic PPP/COVID-testing and cybersecurity, procurement and royalty matters. Figures are cumulative across many defendants; the 42-month prison term is Dr. Gerber's related criminal sentence.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual DOJ round-up rather than a single case, so there is no one mechanic to edit against; the recurring signals across its components are, however, all payer-observable: opioid dispensing volumes and MME/day per prescriber and pharmacy, therapy minutes clustered at the top RUG/quota threshold, inpatient behavioral length-of-stay and admission-criteria documentation, dispensed-but-never-picked-up prescriptions still billed, and physician compensation above fair market value or in excess of collections in credentialing/Stark disclosures. Retained-overpayment components are only detectable post-payment via credit-balance and self-audit reporting timelines.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a provider-level composite risk board that scores each enrolled entity on peer-relative dispensing MME, therapy-minute clustering at reimbursement thresholds, inpatient behavioral readmission/LOS outliers, and Part D reversal-without-return reconciliation, firing prepay review when multiple domains exceed calibrated percentiles. Add a Stark/AKS attestation feed at credentialing that compares physician compensation to collections and to same-specialty FMV bands, and a 60-day overpayment clock that flags unreturned identified credit balances for demand letters.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Helen Zervas (optometrist, owner of Family Eye Care)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Optometrist billed Medicaid (300+ claims) and Medicare (30+ claims) for insertion of amniotic membrane to the eye surface when the treatment was never provided or was not medically necessary; she then conspired with a senior state Office of Policy and Management official and a state representative, paying them through Family Eye Care to pressure state employees to interfere with the Medicaid billing audit.
WaysToIdentify: Amniotic membrane insertion (e.g., CPT 65778/65779 plus the Q-code product) is a low-frequency procedure; a single optometrist accounting for hundreds of such claims is a stark volume and specialty-scope outlier visible at adjudication. Payers can also reconcile billed membrane units against the provider's purchase invoices from the tissue supplier, and check scope-of-practice rules for optometrists performing the procedure. The audit-interference conduct is only reachable post-payment, but the audit itself should have been protected from external inquiry by logging contacts.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: cap and manually review amniotic membrane/tissue-graft claims when a provider's per-beneficiary or monthly volume exceeds the calibrated same-specialty percentile, and require the tissue product invoice/lot number on the claim, denying when lot data are absent or duplicated across patients. Add a scope-of-practice edit blocking the procedure code for non-authorized taxonomies, and an audit-integrity control that logs and escalates any third-party or political inquiry into an open provider audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Donald Calvin Saunders (organizer/leader); Vanessa Ragin-Boatright; Dajuan Strickland; Cynthia Jenkins Harris; Latarsa Hitchcock; Stephanie Corbett; Karen McClary; David Corey Hill; Crystal Sherrell Jackson (owner, Jackson Consulting Services LLC); Nirvana Hyperbaric Institute, LLC; Roger Hunter (owner); Dr. Herminia De Guzman Ferreras; Steven Osbey (clinic co-owner); Benson I. Ejindu (DME business operator); LabXperior Corporation; Tina Ball (owner)
State_County: North Carolina - Mecklenburg County (Charlotte); South Carolina
PayerName: South Carolina Medicaid; North Carolina Medicaid; Medicare
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; FakeEncounter; Upcoding; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Eight defendants were charged with conspiring to bill South Carolina Medicaid more than $21 million for behavioral health services that were inflated or never rendered, buying and selling Medicaid beneficiaries' personal identifying information (including fictitious beneficiaries created by investigators), paying kickbacks for providers' NPI numbers (some obtained by tricking professionals with fake job applications), creating fictitious service notes, and laundering proceeds disguised as consulting contracts and payroll. Separately, Crystal Jackson allegedly billed NC Medicaid over $1.9 million (paid $1.6 million) through Jackson Consulting Services for psychotherapy and high-level urine drug tests that were unnecessary or never provided, using beneficiary identities including more than a dozen incarcerated or deceased persons; the release also reports civil False Claims Act resolutions totaling about $5.1 million (Nirvana Hyperbaric $200,000, Steven Osbey $4.7 million judgment for phantom physician home visits, LabXperior/Tina Ball $235,000) plus a filed complaint against a DME operator for billing more expensive supplies than provided.  Figures span multiple defendants and separate schemes.
WaysToIdentify: Multi-state Medicaid claims can be screened against eligibility, death-master and correctional-custody files to catch billing for deceased or incarcerated beneficiaries, and against NPI-to-employer consistency to catch NPIs rented or harvested through fake job applications. Rendering-provider NPIs appearing suddenly at unrelated new entities, and high-complexity urine drug testing paired with every psychotherapy visit, are both visible pre-payment. Investigator-created fictitious beneficiary IDs surfacing on claims is itself a decisive detection signal if the sentinel IDs are wired into adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Build prepay eligibility edits denying claims whose service dates fall inside a date-of-death or incarceration window, plus a sentinel-ID tripwire that suspends and refers any provider billing a decoy beneficiary. Add an NPI-affiliation monitor that flags rendering NPIs newly linked to a group with no prior claim history or with implausible geography, and a definitive-UDT frequency edit requiring documentation when presumptive/definitive test rates exceed same-specialty percentiles; new behavioral-health enrollees go on prepay review with service-note sampling.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Sanjeev Kumar (gynecologist)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a Memphis gynecologist performed medically unnecessary gynecologic procedures using single-use medical devices that he stored in unsanitary conditions and reused on patients instead of disposing of or properly reprocessing them, then billed Medicare and Medicaid as though the procedures were medically necessary and a new or properly reprocessed device had been used each time; charged with 27 counts of adulteration/misbranding of medical devices.
WaysToIdentify: Single-use device reuse is visible as a mismatch between the count of procedures billed and the provider's documented device purchases or the absence of any billed/supplied disposable per encounter, which a payer can test by requesting purchase invoices. The medical-necessity side shows as an outlier rate of the same gynecologic procedure per patient and repeat procedures at short intervals versus same-specialty peers. Sanitary-condition and adulteration facts come from site visits and FDA/board referrals rather than claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: for procedures requiring a single-use disposable, compare the provider's monthly procedure volume against supplier purchase records or billed device units and suspend payment with a documentation request when procedures exceed devices acquired. Add a per-beneficiary repeat-procedure frequency edit for gynecologic procedures with automatic records review above the calibrated percentile, and route sanitation/reuse allegations to a site-visit and licensing-board referral queue.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: George Nathaniel Boykins (Qualified Mental Health Professional)
State_County: Virginia - Richmond; Virginia - Chesterfield County (North Chesterfield)
SchemeSummary: Boykins, a Qualified Mental Health Professional, caused his multiple employers to submit Medicaid claims for Mental Health Skill-Building Services he never provided - including on dates he was outside the United States, for different recipients at the same date and time across employers, and once while he was being interviewed by law enforcement.
WaysToIdentify: The decisive signals are all in the claim data: the same rendering clinician billed by two or more employers for different recipients at overlapping times, and service dates that fall while he was abroad, which can be tested against impossible-day totals and, where available, EVV geolocation. Cumulative billed hours per clinician per day exceeding a feasible workday is computable pre-payment across all payers of the same Medicaid program.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-clinician daily-hours aggregator across all billing entities that denies or suspends claims when summed units exceed a feasible workday or when two encounters overlap in time for different recipients. Require EVV check-in/out with geolocation for skill-building services and auto-deny units lacking a matching visit record; flag clinicians whose billed days form continuous blocks with no gaps for documentation request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
FraudEntity: Precious Cruse (owner and operator of Caring Through Love, a prenatal care coordination company); Caring Through Love
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Cruse recruited pregnant women and young mothers into her prenatal care coordination company by offering free baby items (car seats, pack 'n plays, diapers, wipes) as inducements, then used their personal information to bill Medicaid for prenatal care coordination services that were never provided; proceeds funded luxury travel, designer clothing and an $18,000 custom diamond necklace and bracelet.
WaysToIdentify: Inducement schemes show up as explosive enrollee growth at one small care-coordination provider concentrated in a narrow geography and referral source, with claims for every enrollee at the maximum allowed units and little or no downstream prenatal care claims from OB providers. Beneficiary outreach or verification letters asking whether coordination visits occurred is a cheap pre-payment test for new providers.
FeaturesToCreate: Place newly enrolled prenatal care-coordination providers on prepay review with a documented-visit note and beneficiary attestation required for payment. Build a provider-level monitor computing new-member growth rate, share of members billed at maximum units, and absence of corroborating prenatal claims from a distinct OB provider, firing suspension and a beneficiary-verification mailing when several exceed calibrated thresholds; screen marketing/gift expenditures at enrollment as an AKS attestation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
FraudEntity: Markita Barnes (owner and operator of Here for You, a prenatal care coordination company)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Barnes lured pregnant women and young mothers into her prenatal care coordination company with cash enrollment bonuses and free baby items, then used their personal information to bill Wisconsin Medicaid for care coordination services never provided, often backdating claims to months before the client was even enrolled; proceeds funded luxury travel, designer clothing, and a $75,000 Mercedes.
WaysToIdentify: The backdating is directly detectable: service dates precede the client's enrollment/assignment date with that provider, and often precede the pregnancy episode itself, all checkable at adjudication. Cash enrollment bonuses show as clustered same-day sign-ups from one recruiter and a member roster far larger than the provider's staffed capacity.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit denying any care-coordination claim whose date of service precedes the member's enrollment/assignment effective date with the billing provider or falls outside the documented pregnancy/postpartum window. Add a capacity check comparing billed coordination hours to credentialed staff FTEs and a same-day mass-enrollment detector, both triggering payment suspension and beneficiary verification letters.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Indiana
SchemeSummary: A general office-activity press release noting that, during the government shutdown (Oct 1 - Nov 12, 2025), the Civil Division resolved a $9.6 million health care fraud settlement under the False Claims Act and Anti-Kickback Statute; no defendant, payer, service type, or scheme mechanics are described.
WaysToIdentify: This is a general office-activity press release with no defendant, payer, service line, or scheme mechanics described, so no case-specific pre-payment signal can be derived; the only route is the post-payment qui tam/settlement channel that produced it.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies to this item as written. The nearest applicable control is a standing intake process that converts FCA/AKS settlement terms into concrete prepay edits and provider watchlist entries once the underlying mechanics are published.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota
FraudEntity: Asha Farhan Hassan (owner, Smart Therapy LLC); Smart Therapy LLC
PayerName: Minnesota Medicaid (Minnesota Health Care Programs/Minnesota DHS); UCare; USDA Federal Child Nutrition Program (via Feeding Our Future/MDE)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Upcoding; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Hassan enrolled Smart Therapy LLC as an EIDBI autism provider (concealing co-owners, one excluded by DHS), recruited Somali-community children by paying parents $300-$1,500 monthly cash kickbacks, used a QSP to get every child qualified for autism services, staffed 'behavioral technicians' with untrained teenage relatives, and billed Minnesota Medicaid/DHS and UCare for the maximum authorized ABA therapy hours - including services never rendered and claims bearing forged provider/QSP signatures - collecting over $14 million, some of which was wired abroad to buy real estate in Kenya. She also used Smart Therapy as a Feeding Our Future child-nutrition site, submitting fake meal counts, rosters and S&S Catering invoices for nearly 200,000 meals worth about $465,000.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment the ownership disclosure could have been cross-matched to the state exclusion list, which would have exposed the concealed excluded co-owner. In claims, one provider having nearly every child qualified by a single QSP assessor and billed at the maximum authorized ABA hours, with technician hours exceeding credentialed staff capacity and technicians who are minors/relatives, is all computable pre-payment; forged QSP and provider signatures on authorizations can be tested by signature/credential verification. Parent cash kickbacks surface through beneficiary interviews and shared-address clustering.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment control that resolves all disclosed and inferred owners/managers (address, phone, bank account, tax ID overlap) against exclusion lists and denies or revokes on match. Add an EIDBI/ABA analytic firing when a provider's share of members billed at maximum authorized units, single-assessor qualification concentration, or billed technician hours per staff FTE exceed calibrated percentiles, with automatic prepay suspension, signature verification on authorizations, and cross-program linkage to child-nutrition site rosters at the same address.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Vincent Thayer (owner, Patient Payment Agent d/b/a My Community Testing); Sevendik Huseynov (owner and CEO, Vonyes, Inc.); Clinton Johnson Christian (nurse); Dr. Yasmin Pirani (physician); Patrick Omeife
Service: PhysicianPractice; DME; Telehealth; Laboratory; Hospital; Optometry
State_County: California - Santa Clara County (San Jose, Sunnyvale); California - Solano County (Fairfield)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Medi-Cal); HRSA COVID-19 Uninsured Program; Medicare Advantage Organizations (Medicare Part C plans); COVID-19 Provider Relief Fund
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Device, DME; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Drug_Prescriptions
SchemeSummary: Five separate Northern District of California cases charged as part of the 2025 National Health Care Fraud Takedown: Thayer billed Medicare, Medi-Cal and the HRSA COVID-19 Uninsured Program about $68.2 million (approx. $11.75 million paid) for office visits that never occurred, using a stolen doctor's identity to enroll his purported COVID-testing company; Huseynov's Vonyes submitted over 7,200 claims worth more than $137 million to at least eight Medicare Advantage Organizations for braces never supplied or needed (about $761,037 paid); nurse Christian withdrew hydromorphone vials by falsely claiming a patient needed them and refilled them with saline; Dr. Pirani was paid by a telemedicine company to sign medically unnecessary DME prescriptions and false diagnoses for beneficiaries she never examined, supporting about $32.5 million in DME billing to Medicare ($35.2 million scheme); Omeife laundered approximately $33,765 fraudulently obtained from the COVID-19 Provider Relief Fund in a stolen optometrist's name via a romance-scam money mule and Bitcoin, part of at least $1.6 million in related fraudulent PRF disbursements. Figures span multiple defendants.
WaysToIdentify: Enrolment identity-proofing is the common failure: companies were enrolled using a stolen physician's and a stolen optometrist's identities, which contact-verification calls to the licensee of record, bank-account/address matching and license-board cross-checks would expose before any claim paid. In claims, brace and office-visit volumes implausible for the staff and location, telehealth-ordered DME where no encounter exists between the ordering physician and the beneficiary, and duplicate billing of the same visits to Medicare, Medi-Cal and the HRSA uninsured program are all pre-payment signals. Drug diversion by the nurse is caught by dispensing-cabinet/waste reconciliation, not claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement enrolment identity verification that calls the licensee at their board-registered contact, matches EFT account ownership to the disclosed owner, and holds first payments pending verification; auto-deny COVID/uninsured-program claims duplicating a claim for the same beneficiary-date already paid by Medicare or Medicaid. Add a DME prepay edit requiring an ordering-provider encounter with the beneficiary within a lookback window and flagging ordering NPIs whose orders concentrate at one telemedicine entity or exceed same-specialty percentiles; refer controlled-substance waste discrepancies from facility ADC logs to investigators.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: 2818 JFK Pharmacy LLC; 518 Summit Care Pharmacy LLC; 1850 Greenville Pharmacy LLC; 327 Alexandria Pharmacy LLC; 516 Broadway Care Pharmacy LLC
State_County: New Jersey - Hudson County (Jersey City); New Jersey - Hudson County (Bayonne); New Jersey - Union County (Elizabeth)
PayerName: Medicare Part D; New Jersey Medicaid
SchemeSummary: Five pharmacies billed Medicare Part D and New Jersey Medicaid for prescription drugs never dispensed to beneficiaries; wholesaler inventory records showed they had not purchased enough medication to fill the prescriptions billed. The five entities agreed to pay a combined $1,935,000 ($1,000,000; $600,000; $133,000; $101,000; $101,000).
WaysToIdentify: Billed drug quantities can be reconciled against wholesaler acquisition data (ARCOS/837-independent purchase reporting or supplier invoices requested from the pharmacy) - a pharmacy cannot dispense more units than it bought. Pre-payment flags include NDC-level billed units exceeding plausible inventory, high-cost drug concentration, and dispensing without corresponding prescriber e-prescribing records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an invoice-versus-claims reconciliation engine at pharmacy-NDC-month granularity: cumulative billed units minus documented purchases; when the gap exceeds a calibrated tolerance, suspend payment and issue a purchase-invoice documentation request. Add prepay edits for missing/unmatched prescriber e-prescription records and for beneficiaries with no other claim activity in the pharmacy's service area.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Charles P. Kasbee, Jr. (marketer)
State_County: Florida - Palm Beach County (Palm Beach Shores); New Jersey
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Kasbee used marketing call centers using deceptive telemarketing to harvest Medicare beneficiaries' personal and medical information, arranged for cancer genetic (CGX) test kits to be mailed to those beneficiaries, and had completed kits shipped to a lab that billed Medicare for medically unnecessary tests; he received over $1,200 per reimbursed test, disguised in contracts and false invoices as 'expenses,' causing over $4.8 million in Medicare losses.
WaysToIdentify: CGX claims arriving for beneficiaries who have no cancer diagnosis, no treating-oncologist relationship, and whose ordering physician is a distant telemarketing-linked provider are visible at adjudication; geographic dispersion between beneficiary, ordering provider and lab is a strong pre-payment marker. Payer complaint lines and beneficiary reports of unsolicited test kits give early warning; per-test 'marketing' payments appear only in post-payment financial review.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit for hereditary-cancer panels requiring a cancer or documented family-history diagnosis plus an ordering provider with a prior E/M relationship with the beneficiary within a lookback window; deny or pend for records otherwise. Add a lab-level analytic on ordering-provider concentration, beneficiary-to-lab distance and unsolicited-kit complaint counts, triggering prepay review and an AKS marketing-contract audit when above calibrated percentiles.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Ted Albin (operator of Grapevine Professional Services, medical billing company; co-owner of DME supply companies); Erin Foley (sister, co-owner of DME supply companies); Grapevine Professional Services; Liberty Bell Medical; Skye Medical; Priority Medical
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Albin used his medical billing company Grapevine to submit thousands of Medicare claims for orthotic braces (back, knee, wrist, shoulder) on behalf of DME supply companies, including three he and his sister owned, based on prescriptions purchased through kickbacks and in some cases generated with forged doctor signatures and without regard to medical necessity; the DME companies billed Medicare over $38 million and were paid over $12 million.
WaysToIdentify: Brace claims from multiple DME suppliers routed through one billing company, sharing ordering physicians, addresses and bank accounts, and with sibling/common ownership, are linkable at enrolment and adjudication. Ordering physicians whose brace-order volume dwarfs their peers, or who order for beneficiaries in states they never practice in, indicate purchased or forged orders; signature verification against the prescriber's on-file exemplar and prescriber outreach are cheap pre-payment tests.
