FeaturesToCreate: Build a supplier-affiliation graph keyed on billing agent, owner identity, address, phone and EFT account that pools brace billing across related suppliers and applies aggregate prepay review when pooled volume or ordering-provider overlap exceeds calibrated percentiles. Add an ordering-provider validation service that pends orthotic claims for prescriber confirmation when the ordering NPI's brace-order rate is an outlier or when beneficiary-prescriber distance is implausible.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Mark Weinberger (beneficial owner and/or managing employee of DME company)
State_County: South Carolina - Greenville County (Greenville); Florida - Palm Beach County (Lake Worth Beach)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Weinberger, excluded from Medicare for at least 15 years due to a prior conviction, allegedly concealed his ownership/control of a Medicare-enrolled DME company via a false enrollment document, then used call centers (including one in Greenville, SC) to generate doctors' orders for orthotic braces and billed Medicare about $6.7 million in claims procured by kickbacks and bribes and medically unnecessary; Medicare paid roughly $3.4 million.
WaysToIdentify: An excluded individual concealing ownership is catchable at enrolment by resolving indirect owners, managers, authorized officials, addresses, phones and bank accounts against the exclusion database and prior revoked-provider records, and by site visits confirming who actually controls the business. In claims, brace volumes generated by out-of-state call centers show as ordering-provider concentration and beneficiary-supplier geographic dispersion before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Enrolment control: fuzzy-match all disclosed and inferred owners/officers/agents (name, SSN, DOB, address, phone, EFT) against exclusion and prior-revocation lists, plus adverse-media/affiliate linkage, and deny enrolment or revoke with payment suspension on match. Layer a new-supplier prepay hold on orthotic claims until a site visit and first-claim audit clear, and flag suppliers whose orders trace to a small set of call-center-linked ordering NPIs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Alexis Garcia (manager/director of Tape Drywall Services Inc.); Tape Drywall Services Inc.
PayerName: IRS (United States); workers' compensation insurance companies
SchemeSummary: Garcia and a co-conspirator ran an off-the-books cash payroll for construction workers through Tape Drywall Services: they cashed over 3,600 contractor checks totaling about $28 million, kept a fee, and distributed cash to foremen to pay workers, never reporting wages or withholding Social Security, Medicare and income taxes, causing over $4.2 million in tax loss; they also understated payroll to workers' compensation insurers to lower premiums.
WaysToIdentify: This is an off-the-books payroll, tax and workers'-compensation premium fraud with no health care claims submitted, so there is no pre-payment claims signal for a health payer; detection sits with IRS wage-reporting mismatches, check-cashing/CTR patterns at the check casher, and comparison of insurer-reported payroll to contract volumes and certified payrolls.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side claims control applies. The nearest control is a workers'-compensation carrier premium-audit rule comparing declared payroll to state wage filings, subcontractor payment records and job-site headcounts, firing an audit when declared payroll per contract dollar falls below industry benchmarks.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Eric Van Vleet (operator of Hype Med LLC); Hype Med LLC
State_County: Florida - Palm Beach County (Delray Beach); New Jersey - Middlesex County (Edison)
SchemeSummary: Van Vleet's company Hype Med used call centers to pressure Medicare beneficiaries into accepting expensive compounded creams, migraine medication and a prescription 'foot soak,' then sent call recordings and pre-marked prescription pads to telemedicine companies that were paid kickbacks and in turn paid doctors to approve the prescriptions; the prescriptions were routed to pharmacies including Apogee Bio-Pharm, which billed Medicare and kicked back a share of reimbursements (at least $343,683.69 to Hype Med), with Medicare paying at least $1,399,812.52.
WaysToIdentify: Compounded topical creams, 'foot soaks' and similar high-cost non-formulary items concentrated at a few pharmacies, with prescribers who never had an in-person or documented telehealth encounter with the beneficiary and who prescribe across many distant states, are visible at Part D adjudication. Beneficiary complaints about telemarketing calls and identical prescription templates (same drug mix, same quantities, same refills) across unrelated patients are strong pre-payment markers.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit requiring prior authorization for high-cost compounded topicals with a documented prescriber-beneficiary encounter within a lookback window and denial where the prescriber's state/geography does not match the beneficiary. Add pharmacy- and prescriber-level analytics on compound-claim concentration, template-identical formulations and prescriber-pharmacy pairing exclusivity, triggering payment suspension and an AKS contract/financial-flow audit above calibrated percentiles.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Corey Alston; Latresia A. Wilson (co-defendant); companies they owned and controlled
FraudTypeAll: IdentityFraud; Phantom Claims; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Alston and co-defendant Wilson unlawfully purchased Medicare beneficiary identification numbers and, through companies they owned, used that information to bill Medicare over $8.4 million for COVID-19 test kits that beneficiaries never requested and that were ineligible for reimbursement; Medicare paid over $2.6 million.
WaysToIdentify: Claims for COVID test kits mailed to beneficiaries who never requested them show as unsolicited-item patterns: no ordering-provider relationship, no prior claims from the beneficiary in that region, bulk identical claims across purchased beneficiary IDs, and duplicate kit claims for the same member within short windows. Beneficiary MSN complaints and the ineligibility of the billed item under the benefit are both checkable before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit denying test-kit/OTC claims for codes not covered under the benefit and rejecting duplicates beyond the allowed per-member frequency. Add a provider-level analytic on share of beneficiaries with no prior claim relationship, geographic dispersion and same-day claim bursts across sequential beneficiary IDs, firing payment suspension plus beneficiary verification mailing; cross-check enrolled entity owners against known ID-purchase networks.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
FraudEntity: Michael G.V. Comino (fifty percent owner of Kestrel Medical LLC); Kestrel Medical LLC (DME supplier); unnamed co-defendant (co-owner)
SchemeSummary: Comino supplied 'leads' and signed doctors' orders for orthotic braces to Kestrel Medical LLC, a DME supplier he came to half-own, in exchange for kickback payments funneled to two companies he owned and disguised as invoices for marketing hours; Kestrel billed and Medicare paid over $2 million for the resulting DME claims.
WaysToIdentify: The tell is that the lead-generator/order-signer is also a part owner of the supplier receiving the claims - detectable by matching supplier ownership disclosures against the entities receiving 'marketing' payments and against the NPIs appearing as ordering or referral sources. In claims, a supplier whose brace orders trace overwhelmingly to one lead source, with flat per-order payments disguised as hourly marketing invoices, is reviewable pre-payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ownership-versus-referral-source conflict check: flag and pend claims where the ordering provider, marketer or lead vendor shares ownership, address or bank account with the billing supplier, requiring an AKS safe-harbor attestation and contract production. Add a referral-concentration metric per supplier (share of orders from a single source) that triggers prepay review above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Thomas Farese (investor in DME supply company); Aaron Williamsky (owner/operator); Nadia Levit (owner/operator); Patsy Truglia (business partner, convicted)
State_County: New Jersey; Florida - Broward County (Fort Lauderdale)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Farese invested in a DME supply company run by Williamsky, Levit and others that billed Medicare and other insurers for orthotic knee, elbow and back braces that patients did not want or need, obtained through a kickback scheme; after learning of his co-conspirators' April 2019 arrests, Farese received $495,000 of the scheme's proceeds into his bank account, pleading guilty to money laundering and being ordered to pay $1,314,000 restitution plus $495,000 forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the other brace mills: orthotic claims for beneficiaries with no ordering-provider encounter, orders sourced from kickback-paid lead vendors, and a supplier whose investor/owner set overlaps with other suppliers already under investigation. Once co-conspirators were arrested, ongoing payments to affiliated entities and post-arrest transfers of proceeds should have triggered an affiliate-based payment suspension rather than continued payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Maintain an affiliation graph linking suppliers by owners, investors, addresses, EFT accounts and billing agents, and automatically extend payment suspension to all affiliated TINs when any node is indicted or has payments suspended. Keep the standing orthotic prepay edit requiring a documented ordering-provider encounter and beneficiary confirmation of medical need before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Alan Swiss (operator of Tropical Medical Marketing, Inc., Modern Medical Equipment, Inc., and A&E Medical, Inc.); Erin Foley (co-defendant, billing company operator); Ted Albin (co-defendant, billing company operator)
State_County: Florida - Palm Beach County (West Palm Beach)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicare Advantage (private insurers under Medicare Part C)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Swiss ran a call center that cold-called Medicare beneficiaries and used their personal/medical information without consent to generate DME prescriptions, then sold those prescriptions to co-conspirators who obtained purported provider signatures/authorizations; he also ran two DME supply companies that submitted over $18 million in claims to Medicare Part B and Medicare Advantage plans through his co-defendants' billing company, with Medicare paying nearly $6 million. He was ordered to forfeit $6,650,929.76 and pay an equal amount in restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Prescriptions manufactured by a call center appear as ordering NPIs signing brace orders in volumes and geographies inconsistent with their practice, beneficiaries with no encounter history with the signer, and identical order templates across many patients; the same billing company submitting for multiple related suppliers links the network at enrolment. Beneficiary complaints about cold calls and MSN entries for braces never wanted give early, pre-payment warning when routed into the edit logic.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: pend orthotic claims where no encounter exists between the ordering provider and beneficiary in the lookback window, where the ordering NPI's order volume or out-of-state share exceeds calibrated percentiles, or where the order signature/authorization fails prescriber confirmation. Add cross-payer sharing so Medicare Advantage plans and FFS pool supplier/billing-agent affiliation and complaint signals, and suspend all suppliers sharing a billing agent once one is flagged.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Lino Mallari Gutierrez, a/k/a 'Joe Gutierrez' (licensed broker; operator of sham DME companies)
State_County: Florida - Martin County (Palm City); Florida - Middle District of Florida
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Gutierrez created sham DME companies that shipped orthotic braces to Medicare beneficiaries who did not want or need them, obtaining beneficiaries through overseas telemarketing call centers and stolen personal identifying information, and paying kickbacks to other companies for signed doctors' orders procured via fraudulent telemedicine outfits; over $10.8 million in false Medicare claims were submitted and the proceeds were laundered, while he filed false records with his broker employer and a regulatory body to hide his ownership.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the sham suppliers share addresses, bank accounts, phone numbers, mail drops and a nominee/beneficial owner network with previously revoked DME PTANs, and the owner concealed ownership on the 855S — resolvable by cross-matching 855S disclosable parties against corporate registries, licensing records and prior revocation lists. At adjudication the pattern is unmistakable: L-code orthotic braces billed nationwide to beneficiaries with no geographic or care relationship to the supplier, ordered by a tiny set of telemedicine prescribers who each 'order' braces for hundreds of beneficiaries with no prior or subsequent visit, often multiple braces per beneficiary and duplicate HICNs across sibling suppliers. Beneficiary complaint intake ('I never ordered this') and identity-theft flags on the beneficiary IDs add corroboration prepay.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment graph-linkage screen keyed on address/phone/bank/registered-agent/owner identity that scores new DME applicants for shared identifiers with revoked or high-risk suppliers, holding the PTAN for site visit and beneficial-ownership verification. At claim level, build a prepay edit on orthotic brace HCPCS that computes, per ordering NPI, the share of orders with no evaluation/management encounter with that beneficiary in the prior and following look-back window, the beneficiary-state-to-supplier-state distance distribution, and the count of distinct suppliers sharing that prescriber; claims from prescribers above the calibrated percentile suspend for documentation of a bona fide clinical encounter, and suppliers with beneficiary-ID overlap to other flagged suppliers go to payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Leo Joseph Govoni (co-founder of Center for Special Needs Trust Administration); John Leo Witeck (accountant at CSNT); Center for Special Needs Trust Administration (CSNT)
State_County: Florida - Pinellas County (Clearwater); Florida - Hillsborough County (Tampa)
SchemeSummary: Defendants allegedly misappropriated over $100 million in client-beneficiary funds from a nonprofit special needs trust administrator managing about 2,100 trusts, concealing the theft with complex financial transactions and fraudulent account statements showing false balances to disabled victims; Govoni used the money for real estate, private jets, a brewery, and personal debts, and separately allegedly committed bank fraud on a $3 million mortgage refinance and laundered $205,054.
WaysToIdentify: No health-care claims-payment component: this is embezzlement from a special-needs trust administrator, detectable through fiduciary audit, not claim adjudication. The observable route is post-hoc: annual independent reconciliation of pooled-trust bank/custodial balances to per-beneficiary statement balances, and trustee bonding/audit filings required by state courts and Medicaid third-party-trust rules. Bank-side signals (transfers from trust accounts to owner-controlled LLCs, real estate and aircraft purchases) would be caught by AML monitoring.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest payer-side control: for Medicaid agencies that approve (d)(4)(A)/(d)(4)(C) pooled trusts, require and automatically track annual third-party attestation reconciling custodial cash to sum of beneficiary sub-account balances, firing a review when the reconciliation is missing, late, or shows an unexplained delta. Add a rule flagging trust-administrator disbursements to entities sharing officers with the administrator; no claim-level edit applies.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Pinellas Eye Care, P.A. d/b/a Gulfcoast Eye Care (ophthalmology practice)
State_County: Florida - Pinellas County (Pinellas Park, St. Petersburg); Florida - Pinellas County (Palm Harbor)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Gulfcoast Eye and a third-party TCD provider performed trans-cranial doppler ultrasounds on thousands of patients and billed Medicare/Medicaid hundreds of dollars per test, pre-assigning patients a qualifying diagnosis (occlusion and stenosis of cerebral arteries) before results were received even though nearly no patient had that condition; Gulfcoast Eye paid the TCD provider based on the volume/value of tests ordered and referred patients to the provider's preferred radiology group, violating the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law. Settled for $615,000 ($602,046 to the U.S., $12,953 to Florida), with a whistleblower receiving $116,850.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication the tell is diagnosis-result decoupling: essentially every trans-cranial doppler claim from this practice carries the same qualifying cerebral occlusion/stenosis ICD-10 code, at a positivity rate far above same-specialty and same-test peers, and the diagnosis appears on the ordering claim before any interpretive report exists. Also visible: an ophthalmology practice ordering high-volume vascular ultrasound at a rate far above optometry/ophthalmology peers, a single third-party mobile TCD entity appearing under many practices, and concentration of downstream radiology referrals into one group (a Stark/AKS financial-relationship signal available from the practice's own disclosures and from referral-concentration analytics).
FeaturesToCreate: Build a per-provider diagnosis-positivity monitor: unit of observation = ordering NPI × TCD/vascular-ultrasound CPT, computing the fraction of tests carrying the coverage-qualifying diagnosis and the practice's test-per-1,000-patient rate versus same-specialty peers; above the calibrated percentile, apply a prepay documentation request for the interpretive report supporting the diagnosis. Add a referral-concentration edit that fires when >a calibrated share of a practice's imaging referrals route to one entity that also supplies staff/equipment to the practice, routing to Stark/AKS review and, for repeat offenders, prepay review of all TCD claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Pinellas Eye Care, P.A. d/b/a Gulfcoast Eye Care (ophthalmology practice)
State_County: Florida - Pinellas County (Pinellas Park, Palm Harbor, St. Petersburg)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Gulfcoast Eye and a third-party TCD provider performed trans-cranial doppler ultrasounds on thousands of patients and billed Medicare and Medicaid hundreds of dollars per test, pre-assigning patients a qualifying diagnosis (occlusion and stenosis of cerebral arteries) before results were available even though nearly all patients did not have that condition; Gulfcoast paid the third-party provider based on the volume/value of tests ordered and referred patients to its preferred radiology group, implicating the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law. Settlement of $615,000 ($602,046 federal, $12,953 Florida), with $116,850 to the qui tam whistleblower.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: near-100% attachment of the coverage-qualifying cerebral occlusion/stenosis diagnosis to every trans-cranial doppler claim, with the diagnosis assigned before results existed — detectable prepay by comparing per-provider diagnosis-positivity rates against same-specialty peers and by requesting the interpretive report. Secondary signals: an eye practice ordering vascular ultrasound volumes far above peers, one mobile TCD vendor recurring across many ordering practices, and referral concentration to a single radiology group indicating a volume-based financial relationship.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement an ordering-NPI × test-code positivity and utilization outlier model (share of tests billed with the qualifying diagnosis; tests per 1,000 attributed patients versus peers) that triggers prepay documentation requests for the signed interpretation and medical-necessity note. Pair it with a vendor-linkage rule flagging practices whose imaging/diagnostic services are performed by a third party that is also the source of the referrals or is compensated per test, routing to AKS/Stark investigation and suspension of the affected test codes.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: OHM Pharmacy Services, aka "Benzer," aka "Auburndale" (Florida-based pharmacy)
SchemeSummary: The pharmacy dispensed the high-priced naloxone auto-injector Evzio and, to obtain insurer coverage, completed and signed prior authorization forms in place of prescribing physicians (sometimes without authorization), making it appear physicians submitted them, and included false statements that patients had already tried and failed Narcan/naloxone. Resolution combined a criminal guilty plea with $82,000 restitution plus one year probation and a $1,018,000 False Claims Act civil settlement (whistleblower share $285,040).
WaysToIdentify: Prior-authorization metadata is the carrier: PA forms for the high-cost naloxone auto-injector arrive from the dispensing pharmacy's fax/portal account or IP rather than the prescriber's, are submitted in bursts, and reuse identical step-therapy language ('failed Narcan') across unrelated patients. That claimed prior trial is falsifiable prepay against the plan's own Part D claim history — most patients have no prior naloxone/Narcan fill. Also visible: one pharmacy accounting for an extreme share of national Evzio volume with the same handful of prescribers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a PA-integrity check: unit = PA request, computing submitter identity/channel versus the attesting prescriber's registered contact, template-similarity of free-text across requests, and whether the asserted prior therapy is corroborated by pharmacy claim history for that member; mismatch on submitter or absent corroborating prior fill auto-denies or pends the PA pending prescriber attestation. Add a pharmacy-level monitor for concentration in a single high-cost brand NDC and PA-approval volume versus peers, triggering prepay review of all claims for that NDC.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: OHM Pharmacy Services, aka "Benzer," aka "Auburndale" (Florida-based pharmacy)
SchemeSummary: The pharmacy dispensed the high-priced naloxone auto-injector Evzio and, to obtain insurer coverage, completed and signed prior authorization forms in place of prescribing physicians (sometimes without physician authorization), making it appear a physician submitted them, and included false statements such as that patients had previously tried and failed Narcan/naloxone, causing Medicare Part D and other insurers to reimburse the claims. Resolution includes $82,000 criminal restitution plus $1,018,000 False Claims Act civil settlement, of which the whistleblower receives $285,040.
WaysToIdentify: Identical mechanic: the pharmacy authored and signed prescriber PA forms for Evzio, so the PA's submission channel, fax header and IP trace to the pharmacy, not the physician's office, and the 'tried and failed Narcan/naloxone' assertion contradicts the member's own Part D fill history. Extreme concentration of a single very-high-cost NDC in one pharmacy, with repeated identical PA narratives, is visible before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Automate PA provenance validation (submitter identity/fax/IP vs prescriber of record; prescriber callback or e-signature verification for high-cost NDCs) and step-therapy auto-verification against internal pharmacy claim history, denying or pending PAs whose asserted prior therapy has no corroborating fill. Layer a pharmacy outlier report on share-of-revenue from one NDC and PA-approval rate versus peers, escalating to prepay review and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Sehrelina Tardo (senior accountant at a car dealership)
SchemeSummary: As senior accountant at a New Orleans car dealership, Tardo embezzled customer cash down payments and deposits for herself and concealed the theft with fake journal entries of customer transactions in the employer's books; she agreed to pay $535,750.77 restitution to the dealership. No health care service or payer involved.
WaysToIdentify: No payer, no claims: embezzlement of customer cash deposits at a car dealership concealed by false journal entries — detectable only by employer-side controls (segregation of duties between cash receipt and ledger posting, daily deposit-to-DMS reconciliation, surprise audit of voided/adjusting entries by the accountant who books them). Nothing is visible at claim adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest analogous control, if any payer wanted it, is an internal-accounting rule that flags journal entries created and approved by the same user against customer deposit accounts and any cash receipt lacking a matching bank deposit within one business day.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: Yolanda Dupont (nominee owner of Allstar Medical Supply Corp.); Allstar Medical Supply Corp.
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Dupont acted as nominee owner of Allstar Medical Supply Corp., a purported New Hampshire DME company, to conceal the true owners and falsely certified no false claims would be submitted; she and co-conspirators billed Medicare approximately $3.3 million for orthotic braces that were medically unnecessary and often unwanted, collecting at least $1.6 million.
WaysToIdentify: Enrolment screening is the choke point: the 855S listed a nominee owner while the true owners were concealed, so identity/ownership verification (credit-header and corporate-registry match on the applicant, prior involvement of the same address, phone, bank account or accountant with other DME PTANs) plus an unannounced site visit to the claimed New Hampshire location would have exposed a shell. Post-enrolment, first-90-day billing behavior — immediate high-volume orthotic brace claims to out-of-state beneficiaries from a handful of telemedicine prescribers, with no local referral base — is visible before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a nominee-owner risk score at enrolment combining applicant age/credit-history thinness, absence of prior health-care industry footprint, shared identifiers with other applicants, and site-visit outcome; high scores require verified beneficial-ownership documentation before PTAN activation. Add a new-supplier ramp edit: for DME PTANs within their first billing months, cap payment and auto-suspend when brace-code volume, out-of-state beneficiary share, or prescriber concentration exceeds calibrated percentiles for new suppliers, with prepay documentation review and beneficiary contact.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: Georgina Exposito (owner of 3rd Party Services of Florida); 3rd Party Services of Florida
SchemeSummary: Exposito and her company allegedly altered patients' medical diagnoses in prior authorization requests submitted on behalf of pharmacies, including PerforMix Specialty Pharmacy, a compounding pharmacy in Amherst, NH, causing false claims to be submitted to Medicare and TRICARE; she agreed to pay $400,000 under the False Claims Act following a whistleblower suit.
WaysToIdentify: The signal is diagnosis substitution inside prior-authorization packets submitted by a third-party PA-services vendor on behalf of compounding pharmacies: the diagnosis asserted on the PA does not appear anywhere in the patient's medical or claims history from the named prescriber. Comparing PA-stated diagnoses to the member's historical diagnosis profile, and tracing PA submitter identity to a vendor rather than the prescriber's office, is doable prepay. Vendor fingerprinting — one fax number/portal account submitting PAs across many unrelated pharmacies and prescribers with unusually high approval rates — is another prepay flag.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a PA diagnosis-corroboration edit: for each PA on compounded or high-cost drugs, check whether the asserted qualifying diagnosis appears in the member's prior claims history from the attesting prescriber or any provider; absent corroboration, pend for medical records rather than auto-approve. Add submitter-entity analytics that cluster PAs by fax/IP/agent account and flag third-party submitters whose diagnosis-change rate or approval rate exceeds the calibrated percentile, suspending auto-approval for that channel.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Julian Lopez (seller of Medicare beneficiary information); One Medical Services (durable medical equipment company)
SchemeSummary: Lopez obtained Medicare beneficiary identification cards and sold beneficiaries' personal information to One Medical Services, a sham DME company, which used the data to bill Medicare over $3.2 million for orthotic braces that were never provided and were medically unnecessary.
WaysToIdentify: Beneficiary-identifier misuse is detectable prepay: the same beneficiary IDs, harvested and sold in bulk, appear across a cluster of DME suppliers in short windows, with the supplier located far from the beneficiary and no ordering physician with any prior encounter history for that patient. Brace claims for beneficiaries who have no matching diagnosis, no prior musculoskeletal care, and often multiple braces on the same date are also visible. Beneficiary complaints and 'services I never received' hotline reports corroborate that nothing was delivered; proof-of-delivery is absent on request.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-ID compromise monitor: unit = beneficiary ID, counting distinct DME suppliers, distinct states, and brace HCPCS billed within a rolling window; when counts exceed the calibrated percentile, tag the ID and route all further DME claims to prepay review with proof-of-delivery and signed-order requests. Add a supplier-level edit that suspends payment when a supplier's share of claims on tagged/compromised IDs, or its share of beneficiaries with no prior encounter with the ordering NPI, exceeds peer-calibrated thresholds.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Shekhar Thakur (physician, owner of Parkside Medical)
SchemeSummary: Physician at his own Battle Creek clinic routinely prescribed Schedule II opioids, benzodiazepines and other controlled substances without legitimate medical purpose - no physical exam, records review or verification, and despite failed urine drug screens indicating abuse or diversion - resulting in a Controlled Substances Act civil suit resolved for $705,075 and permanent surrender of DEA registration.
WaysToIdentify: PDMP and pharmacy-claim data show the pattern prepay: a single prescriber writing high-MME Schedule II opioids plus concurrent benzodiazepines to a large panel, with short intervals, high cash/out-of-area patient share, and no corresponding office-visit or exam claims. Failed or inconsistent urine drug screens on file alongside continued escalating prescribing is a documented red flag visible in the practice's own lab claims. Missing E/M encounters paired with active prescriptions is a direct claims-level contradiction.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-level controlled-substance risk monitor joining PDMP dispensing to medical claims: compute per-prescriber average daily MME, opioid+benzodiazepine co-prescribing rate, share of prescriptions with no E/M encounter in the look-back window, and patient travel distance, versus same-specialty peers. Above calibrated percentiles, trigger prescriber education/audit, prior authorization on further opioid claims for that prescriber's patients, and referral to DEA/licensure; pend pharmacy claims tied to prescribers under active review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire; Justice Department Tax Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: Andrew Park (co-founder and CEO of a startup technology company)
SchemeSummary: As CEO responsible for company finances, Park withheld Social Security, Medicare and income taxes from employees' wages from 2014 through Q3 2021 but never paid them over to the IRS, also failing to pay the employer's matching share, and did not file his own individual returns from 2013-2020 despite a ~$250,000 annual salary, causing over $14 million in tax loss. He was ordered to pay $639,821.78 restitution plus a $15,000 fine.
WaysToIdentify: Pure employment-tax and personal income-tax fraud with no health-care claim — not detectable by a payer. IRS-side detection is automatic: W-2/W-3 wage totals reported to SSA versus Form 941 filings and EFTPS deposits for the same EIN, plus non-filer scoring for a person with reported six-figure W-2 wages and no 1040.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The applicable government control is an automated 941-to-W-2 reconciliation per EIN that opens a trust-fund-recovery case when withheld amounts reported on W-2s exceed deposits, plus non-filer flags where third-party wage reports exist without a filed return.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: Andrew Park (co-founder and CEO of a startup technology company)
SchemeSummary: As CEO of a startup software company, Park withheld federal, state and local payroll taxes (including Social Security and Medicare withholdings) from employees' wages from 2014 through Q3 2021 but never paid them over to the IRS, using the funds as capital for the business, and also failed to file personal returns from 2013-2020 despite a ~$250,000 annual salary, causing over $14.7 million in tax loss; ordered to pay $639,821.78 restitution plus a $15,000 fine.
WaysToIdentify: Same as the companion entry: no claims, no payer — payroll trust-fund diversion and non-filing. Visible only to the tax authority via mismatch between W-2/W-3 reported withholding for the EIN and actual 941 filings/EFTPS deposits, and via non-filer scoring against third-party wage reports.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Build (at IRS) an EIN-level automated deposit-versus-reported-withholding variance monitor that escalates persistent multi-quarter shortfalls to responsible-person assessment, and a non-filer trigger for individuals with substantial reported wages and no return.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon
FraudEntity: Pamela J. Kahut (former Chief Financial Officer, Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission)
PayerName: Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission self-funded health care benefit program (health benefit trust account)
SchemeSummary: As CFO, Kahut controlled the employer's self-funded health benefit trust account and wrote checks/withdrew approximately $211,083 from it between October 2014 and September 2020, including a $2,812.85 check for her spouse's long-term care insurance premium, plus paying off her pension loans and credit card bills.
WaysToIdentify: This is misappropriation from a self-funded plan's trust account by the plan sponsor's CFO, not a false claim, so no adjudication edit sees it; it surfaces through bank-level and plan-accounting controls — checks drawn on the benefit trust payable to the CFO, her creditors, or an unrelated long-term-care insurer, and disbursements not matching any TPA-adjudicated claim funding request. Reconciling trust disbursements to the TPA's paid-claims register plus admin fees leaves an unexplained residual.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a benefit-trust disbursement reconciliation control: unit = each disbursement from the plan's trust account, matched to a TPA claim-funding wire, stop-loss premium, or approved admin invoice; any payee not on an approved-payee whitelist, or any month where disbursements exceed adjudicated paid claims plus fees beyond tolerance, fires an alert to the plan fiduciary and auditor. Require dual signature/approval separated from the person who reconciles the account.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon
FraudEntity: Pamela J. Kahut (Chief Financial Officer, Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission)
State_County: Oregon - Clackamas County (Wilsonville); Oregon - Multnomah County (Portland)
PayerName: Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission self-funded health care benefit program (health benefit trust account funded in part by federal grant money)
FraudType: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
FraudTypeAll: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
SchemeSummary: As CFO of the Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission, Kahut controlled the agency's self-funded health benefit trust account (funded partly with federal grant money) and stole $211,083.27 from it over roughly six years, using the money to pay her spouse's long-term care premiums, pay off her pension loans, and pay her personal credit card bills.
WaysToIdentify: No claim-adjudication signal: the CFO wrote checks directly from a self-funded health benefit trust partly funded by federal grants. Detection routes are the annual Single Audit / OMB grant audit, bank monitoring for trust-account checks payable to insiders or their personal creditors, and monthly reconciliation of trust outflows to the TPA's paid-claims and premium records.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement automated payee screening on benefit-trust and grant-funded accounts that flags any disbursement to an employee, employee's spouse, or an employee's known creditor, and any check lacking a matching claim-funding or invoice record; flags block release pending second-signature approval. Add a monthly variance monitor of trust outflow versus adjudicated claims plus fees, with unexplained residuals reported to the audit committee and grantor agency.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jennifer Adams (Chief Operating Officer and practice manager, L5 Medical Holdings d/b/a Pain Care Centers); John Barnes (owner, L5 Medical Holdings); L5 Medical Holdings d/b/a Pain Care Centers; Dr. Wendell Randall (practitioner)
State_County: Virginia - Woodlawn; Virginia - Lynchburg; Virginia - Madison Heights; Virginia - Blacksburg; Virginia - Christiansburg
SchemeSummary: As COO of pain clinics owned by a non-medical former mortgage broker, Adams directed non-medical staff to override providers' medical decisions on opioid and Suboxone prescribing, knew the clinics used doctors' DEA prescribing credentials to issue Suboxone prescriptions for patients those doctors never saw, and implemented urine drug-testing policies that improperly inflated bills to medical insurers.
WaysToIdentify: Two prepay-visible contradictions: buprenorphine/Suboxone prescriptions written under a physician's DEA number for patients with no corresponding encounter claim from that physician (and often on dates the physician had no claims at the clinic at all), and a rigid urine-drug-testing profile where nearly every patient receives the same large definitive multi-drug panel at every visit regardless of history. Lay ownership and non-clinical control of prescribing shows up in enrolment/ownership disclosures for a clinic owned by a non-licensed person, and in prescriber-to-clinic volume ratios that are physically implausible per provider-day. UDT units per patient-year versus same-specialty peers is a direct outlier metric.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescription-to-encounter linkage edit for controlled substances and MAT: for each prescription attributed to a DEA/NPI, require a same-patient encounter by that prescriber within the look-back window; unmatched prescriptions pend and the prescriber's volume-per-workday is scored against a plausibility ceiling. Add a UDT profile edit computing, per clinic, definitive-panel frequency and analyte count per patient-year and the share of patients receiving the identical panel, above calibrated percentiles requiring prepay documentation of individualized testing rationale; flag clinics whose disclosed owners hold no clinical license for enhanced review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Jariatu Jalloh (community support worker)
SchemeSummary: While employed as a community support worker for a D.C. Mental Health Rehabilitation Service provider, Jalloh submitted encounter notes claiming an hour or more of community support services for Medicaid beneficiaries she never met or met only briefly, causing D.C. Medicaid to pay over $234,500 on fraudulent CSW claims.
WaysToIdentify: Encounter-level time arithmetic exposes it prepay: the worker's billed community-support units per day exceed feasible working hours, include overlapping or back-to-back sessions at geographically incompatible locations, and cluster on identical durations (uniform 60-minute notes). Notes submitted in batches long after the service date, and beneficiaries with no other service history who suddenly receive daily CSW hours, are further flags; beneficiary verification letters and GPS/EVV data confirm no visit occurred.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-staff daily-capacity edit: unit = staff NPI/employee ID × date, summing billed CSW units and flagging totals above a feasible-hours ceiling, overlapping time spans, and travel-time-infeasible location pairs; violations deny or pend prepay. Add electronic visit verification for community-based behavioral health so claims without a matching time-and-location check-in are not payable, plus a per-worker note-uniformity metric (identical duration/text similarity) that triggers documentation audit and beneficiary confirmation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Wendy Nicole Villatoro (former D.C. Homeland Security Commissioner and former USDA employee)
PayerName: Small Business Administration (PPP/EIDL); private financial institutions
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Villatoro submitted eight PPP loan applications to financial institutions and 15 EIDL applications to the SBA containing materially false statements, including loans on behalf of fake businesses and inflated employee counts, payroll, revenue and cost of goods sold; she attempted to obtain between $2.6 million and $5.5 million and received over $844,000, which she spent on student loans, a BMW SUV and luxury goods.
WaysToIdentify: Not a health-care claim scheme: this is SBA PPP/EIDL loan fraud. Pre-disbursement detection is available from data the lender/SBA already holds — applicant EIN and payroll figures verifiable against IRS 941/W-2 transcripts and state UI wage filings, business existence verifiable against state registration and formation date, and duplicate-applicant detection across 23 applications sharing one SSN, bank account, address, phone or IP.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pre-disbursement verification pipeline: for each application, auto-match claimed payroll/revenue to IRS transcript and state UI wage data and reject or manually review on material variance; block applications for entities formed after the eligibility date or absent from state registries. Add cross-application entity resolution on SSN/EIN/bank account/address/device-IP that holds funding when one identity appears across multiple applications or when the same bank account receives multiple program disbursements.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Delaware
FraudEntity: Sandra Jackson (former Delaware nurse practitioner)
SchemeSummary: Nurse practitioner digitally signed hundreds of pre-populated orders for genetic testing and durable medical equipment for Delaware Medicare beneficiaries she never examined and had no relationship with, signing within seconds of opening and providing no follow-up care; Medicare paid about $520,000 on the resulting claims. Resolved as a civil False Claims Act settlement with no determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: Order provenance is measurable: the NP signed pre-populated orders in seconds via a telemedicine platform, so platform audit logs (time-open-to-signature, orders signed per session/day) plus claims data showing no E/M encounter by that NP with the beneficiary before or after the order reveal the absence of a treating relationship. Volume implausibility — hundreds of genetic-test and DME orders from one mid-level provider for out-of-state beneficiaries, concentrated into a few labs/suppliers — is visible before payment. Cancer-panel/PGx testing with no oncology or supporting diagnosis history for the beneficiary is an additional prepay flag.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a treating-relationship edit for high-risk order-driven services (hereditary cancer/PGx panels, orthotic braces): deny or pend when the ordering NPI has no E/M or telehealth encounter claim with that beneficiary in the look-back window, and when the ordering NPI's daily order count or lab/supplier concentration exceeds calibrated peer percentiles. Require submission of the signed order with authorship/timestamp metadata for flagged prescribers, and place labs/suppliers whose orders come predominantly from such prescribers on prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana; U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, Fort Worth Division
FraudEntity: Carlos A. Lopez (former DOJ Trial Attorney/federal prosecutor); Barrett R. Howell (Dallas-based criminal defense attorney)
State_County: Texas - Dallas County (Dallas); Texas - Tarrant County (Fort Worth)
SchemeSummary: A bill of information charges a former DOJ prosecutor with unauthorized disposal of government records for deleting text messages with a defense attorney from his government-issued phone in April 2023, after a district judge in an underlying health care fraud prosecution ordered production of their communications; the defense attorney is charged with aiding and abetting by deleting the same messages from his own phone. The conduct concerns obstruction/record destruction, not billing fraud.
WaysToIdentify: No claims-payment component: this is destruction of government records and obstruction arising from a health-care fraud prosecution, not billing conduct. Detection lies with agency device management and e-discovery — mobile-device management backup and retention policies that preserve texts on government phones, litigation-hold enforcement, and audit logs showing deletion after a preservation order.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side claim control applies. The applicable control is enforced server-side archiving of all government-issued device communications with immutable retention and automated alerts when messages are deleted on a device subject to an active litigation hold.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Anna Elperin (osteopathic physician, owner of Awake Health, PLLC)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges the physician improperly performed DOT commercial driver's license physicals and certified applicants as physically qualified when they were not, failing to transmit required certification data to DOT; separately she kept a pre-signed prescription pad at her clinic allowing staff to write themselves controlled-substance prescriptions and signed prescriptions for staff and others that she then took for her own personal use.
WaysToIdentify: The DOT certification side is not a claims-payment scheme, but the pre-signed pad is visible in PDMP and pharmacy claims data: controlled-substance prescriptions written under one prescriber's DEA number where the patient is an employee at the same practice address, or dispensed to the prescriber herself or immediate family, and prescriptions issued on dates with no corresponding office visit claim for that patient. Also detectable at credentialing time by cross-checking DOT National Registry certification submissions against the examiner's exam volume. Enrolment-time route: state medical board and DOT National Registry status feeds.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-level PDMP/pharmacy-claims edit that flags controlled-substance fills where patient address/phone/employer matches the prescribing practice, where prescriber and patient share surname or the prescriber is the patient, or where no E/M encounter exists for that patient within a calibrated lookback window; fire a prepay pharmacy edit plus a documentation request for the chart note. Add a self/family-prescribing counter per DEA number that triggers referral above the same-specialty peer percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Stephanie L. Roberts (executive director of Cancer Services of Gaston County)
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Other - Unknown
SchemeSummary: As executive director of a non-profit providing support and resources to cancer patients, Roberts embezzled more than $136,000 from the organization between January 2016 and January 2022, failed to remit over $200,000 in payroll taxes withheld from employees' paychecks to the IRS, and filed false personal income tax returns overstating tax withheld and paid. She pleaded guilty to theft in connection with health care, failure to pay over trust fund taxes, and filing a false return, and was ordered to pay $157,722.69 restitution to the non-profit and $62,612 to the IRS.
WaysToIdentify: This is embezzlement from a nonprofit plus payroll-tax and personal income-tax fraud, not a claims-payment scheme, so no prepay claim edit would have caught it. The detectable route is IRS matching of Form 941 withholding against W-2 wage reports and against deposits, and grantor/payer oversight of the nonprofit's Form 990 and audited financials showing officer withdrawals and accrued unpaid payroll taxes.
FeaturesToCreate: For payers or grantors that fund nonprofit entities, build an entity-level financial-integrity monitor that compares reported payroll withholding to remittance records and flags accrued tax liabilities, single-signatory disbursements to the executive director, and missing independent audits; action is a payment hold on further grant draws and a documentation request. Otherwise state that this is a tax/IRS control, not a payer claim edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
FraudEntity: Rafael Castro (VA benefits recipient, former Veterans Health Administration and IRS employee); Miriam Castro (wife, designated primary caregiver)
PayerName: Department of Veterans Affairs (Caregiver Support Program)
SchemeSummary: Rafael Castro falsely told the VA at least six times that he was unemployed and needed high-level assistance with daily activities such as dressing and grooming, qualifying his wife Miriam for Caregiver Support Program payments equivalent to a full-time 40-hour-per-week home health aide, while he actually worked full time for the Veterans Health Administration and later the IRS; the couple collected more than $130,000 in caregiver benefits over roughly six years.
WaysToIdentify: The claim is a self-attested need for full-time personal assistance while the beneficiary was concurrently a full-time federal employee, which is visible by matching the caregiver-program applicant against federal payroll and wage-reporting data at eligibility determination and at each annual reassessment. A second signal is the mismatch between claimed total dependence in ADLs and the veteran's own encounter record, which shows no corresponding functional-status documentation or care utilization.
FeaturesToCreate: At enrolment and reassessment, run an automated wage/employment match (federal payroll, state new-hire and quarterly wage files) for both the veteran and the paid caregiver, and fire a hold when a beneficiary certified at the highest assistance tier shows concurrent full-time employment earnings. Add a consistency edit comparing certified ADL dependency tier against clinical encounter and DME/home-care utilization, requiring an in-person functional assessment before the tier is renewed.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Irene Oluwatoyin Oshiyoye (operator); Dr. Adekunle Oshiyoye (deceased, operator); Advance Visiting Physicians, P.C.
State_County: Michigan - Oakland County (Farmington Hills); Southeast Michigan
SchemeSummary: Operator of Advance Visiting Physicians allegedly billed Medicare and Michigan Medicaid for home health visits that were actually performed by unlicensed and unsupervised foreign doctors, contrary to program rules; resolved via a $250,000 False Claims Act settlement based on ability to pay, following a qui tam suit.
WaysToIdentify: Every home visit claim carries a rendering-provider NPI; the payer can match each rendering NPI against state licensure files and, where a supervising-physician arrangement is claimed, verify the supervisor's own claim volume for the same day. Red flags include a single billing physician's NPI attached to visit volumes physically impossible in a day, visits at dispersed addresses within implausible travel times, and rendering clinicians with no active state license or with foreign-credential-only status.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit that rejects home-visit claims whose rendering NPI lacks an active in-state license on the date of service, and a per-billing-NPI daily capacity/geo-feasibility check (visits per day and drive-time between successive service addresses) that suspends payment above the calibrated feasibility bound. Add a credentialing check requiring the roster of all clinicians performing visits, with supervision attestations reverified periodically.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Oleg Beretsky (owner of Obest, Inc.); Obest, Inc.
State_County: New York - Nassau County (Plainview); New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Queens County
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Beretsky, through Obest Inc., cultivated control over elderly Russian-speaking Medicare beneficiaries identified via a nonprofit senior services employee, then steered them only to doctors, social workers, pain specialists and diagnostic companies who paid him kickbacks based on patient volume or Medicare reimbursement; he also pushed providers to bill Medicare for unnecessary or never-rendered services, generating over $22 million in claims and $12.4 million in payments, which he laundered through cash payments to relatives and family-name accounts.
WaysToIdentify: The signature is a tight closed referral cluster: a defined cohort of beneficiaries (here elderly, same language group, recruited via one nonprofit) whose claims across many unrelated specialties all trace back to the same small set of providers, with near-identical service bundles and shared addresses, phone numbers or billing agents. Beneficiary-level network analysis at adjudication shows implausibly high provider-sharing concordance, and repeat use of the same marketer-linked entities. Kickback payments themselves surface only post-payment via financial records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-cohort graph feature: cluster beneficiaries by shared provider sets, and compute for each provider group the share of its patients that also appear at the other members of the cluster versus geographic base rates; fire prepay review and a documentation request on all providers in clusters above the calibrated percentile. Layer an entity-linkage check (shared address/phone/bank account/billing agent across referring and rendering NPIs) that suspends payment pending ownership disclosure.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Florence Ndubizu (co-owner and pharmacist-in-charge, Healthcare Pharmacy); Healthcare Pharmacy
SchemeSummary: Pharmacist-in-charge and co-owner of a single-location Trenton pharmacy, with employee conspirators at her direction, filled fraudulent oxycodone prescriptions outside the usual course of professional practice, diverting millions of dosage units (including over 800,000 pills in 2014) to street-level dealers, and manipulated pharmacy records to evade state and federal reporting requirements; a DEA inventory audit found more than 64,000 oxycodone pills diverted between April 2015 and August 2017. Her husband and co-owner was separately convicted of tax evasion.
WaysToIdentify: Dispensing volume is the signal: a single-location pharmacy dispensing hundreds of thousands of oxycodone dosage units a year, far above same-size peers, with a high share of cash-pay high-dose immediate-release oxycodone, patients travelling long distances, and heavy concentration on a few prescribers. PDMP and ARCOS/wholesaler purchase data compared to dispensed quantities exposes both the diversion and the record manipulation (purchases exceeding reported dispensing).
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pharmacy-level monthly monitor computing controlled-substance dosage units per prescription and per pharmacy, share of oxycodone in total volume, cash-pay share, prescriber concentration, and mean patient-to-pharmacy distance versus same-size peers; fire network suspension/prepay review above the calibrated percentile. Add a reconciliation edit comparing wholesaler purchase quantities to PDMP-reported dispensing, flagging unexplained gaps for on-site inventory audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Kevin Aguilar
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Aguilar conspired to submit seven fraudulent PPP loan applications and three fraudulent EIDL applications on behalf of four businesses, obtaining approximately $3.3 million in PPP funds and $450,000 in EIDL funds, then laundered the proceeds through other businesses he created to appear legitimate and spent them on Texas residential properties, a $100,000 truck, and personal expenses.
WaysToIdentify: This is pure pandemic loan fraud with no health-care claims component, so no payer claim edit applies. Prepayment detection sits with the lender/SBA: cross-check applicant payroll figures against IRS Form 941/W-2 filings and state wage records, and detect one applicant filing multiple applications across several entities using shared addresses, bank accounts, IP addresses and EINs.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control is a loan-underwriting duplicate-and-verification engine: key each application on principal SSN, EIN, bank account, address and device/IP, block funding where the same controlling person appears on multiple applications or where reported payroll exceeds IRS-verified wage filings, and require tax-transcript match before disbursement. No payer-side claim control applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Vishnudat Seodat (internist/physician)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Seodat, a Long Island internist, ordered hundreds of medically unnecessary transcranial doppler brain scans using false diagnoses for a mobile medical diagnostics company, receiving approximately $100 in cash per test; a co-conspirator billed Medicare and private insurers roughly $1 million for the scans. He was sentenced to two years of supervised release (one year home confinement) plus a $50,000 fine, $52,100 forfeiture and $342,876 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Transcranial doppler is a low-volume test; a mobile diagnostics company billing ~$1M concentrated among a handful of referring internists, with each referrer ordering hundreds of scans, is visible at adjudication. Supporting signals: the diagnosis codes used to justify the scan appear only on the ordering claim and nowhere else in the patient's history, no neurology consult or follow-up imaging, and no change in treatment after the scan.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-physician-level rate feature for TCD/mobile diagnostic CPT codes (tests per 100 patients, share of panel receiving the test, referral concentration into one supplier NPI) and fire prepay review with medical-record request above the same-specialty peer percentile. Add a diagnosis-corroboration edit that denies pending documentation when the justifying diagnosis appears on no other claim in the member's history and no downstream neurologic care follows.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Dr. Kenneth Fishberger (internist)
State_County: New York - Suffolk County (East Setauket, Long Island)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Fishberger, a Long Island internist, used false diagnoses to order hundreds of medically unnecessary transcranial doppler brain scans for a mobile medical diagnostics company, which billed Medicare and private insurers approximately $891,978; he received cash kickbacks of about $100 per test. Sentenced to two years supervised release (one year home confinement), $50,000 fine, $48,000 forfeiture and $342,876 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as its co-defendant case: a mobile diagnostics supplier with nearly all volume funneled from a small ring of internists ordering hundreds of transcranial doppler scans each, using boilerplate justifying diagnoses absent from the rest of the patient record. At adjudication the payer sees per-referrer test rates far above same-specialty peers and no neurologic workup or follow-up around the scan.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a supplier-referrer concentration metric (share of a mobile diagnostics supplier's claims from top referrers, and each referrer's TCD tests per attributed patient) with prepay suspension and records request above the calibrated percentile. Pair with an edit requiring documented symptoms/prior neurologic evaluation coded elsewhere in the member's history before TCD is payable.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Delaware
FraudEntity: Jordona Ndon (former nurse practitioner)
SchemeSummary: Nurse practitioner digitally signed hundreds of orders for medically unnecessary orthotic braces for Delaware Medicare beneficiaries she never physically examined, after telemedicine calls often under two minutes, with order information pre-populated by unqualified telemarketers, enabling Medicare billing for the braces.
WaysToIdentify: The orders are visible as one nurse practitioner signing hundreds of brace orders for beneficiaries scattered across a state with whom she has no prior or subsequent relationship, tied to telehealth encounters of extremely short duration and to a small set of DME suppliers. Prepay signals: no established-patient history, no prior visit for the affected joint, out-of-area beneficiary geography, and repeated identical order text across patients.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-clinician monitor for orthotic/brace HCPCS: count distinct beneficiaries ordered per month, share with no prior encounter with that clinician, telehealth encounter length where available, and geographic dispersion; suspend DME claims linked to clinicians above the calibrated percentile and require the signed clinical note. Add a prepay edit denying brace claims where the ordering NPI has no evaluation claim for that member within a lookback window, and a supplier-side check on referral concentration into a single telemarketing-linked clinician pool.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Montana
FraudEntity: Tristan Ashley Svejkovsky (nurse practitioner)
PayerName: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Montana
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Upcoding; IdentityFraud; Drug_Prescriptions; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Nurse practitioner billed Blue Cross Blue Shield of Montana for 158 vitamin B-12 injections that never occurred, inflating units from 1 to 1,000 per injection (raising payment from ~$4.88 to $4,880) and later claiming $15 million per injection, and backdated claims to appear before her license suspension; she also wrote at least 28 controlled-substance prescriptions using a friend's DEA registration number after surrendering her own. Total billed $62,310,000 with $613,108 paid.
WaysToIdentify: Units-per-claim are absurd on their face: 1,000 units of a B-12 injection, and later billed amounts of $15 million per injection, are catchable by a units-versus-MUE/charge-plausibility edit before a dollar moves. Backdating is visible by comparing dates of service to the license-suspension date in the state board feed and to the claim submission date; the DEA-number misuse is visible by verifying that the prescriber NPI on controlled-substance claims owns the DEA number presented.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay units and charge sanity edit per procedure code (units above the medically unlikely maximum, or billed charge above a calibrated multiple of the allowed amount) that hard-denies and routes to review. Add an eligibility-date edit that denies claims whose date of service precedes suspension but is submitted after it unless documentation is supplied, and an NPI-to-DEA ownership match on controlled-substance prescriptions that rejects mismatches.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Joseph Schwartz (owner/operator of Skyline Management Group LLC); Skyline Management Group LLC
State_County: New Jersey - Essex County (Newark); nursing/rehabilitation facilities in 11 states
SchemeSummary: Schwartz, owner/operator of Skyline Management Group, withheld trust fund employment taxes from the pay of employees at nursing and rehabilitation facilities in 11 states but failed to pay over more than $38 million to the IRS, and also failed to file the required annual Form 5500 report for the company's 401K plan for 2018.
WaysToIdentify: This is employment-tax fraud by a facility chain, not claim fraud, so prepay claim edits do not reach it; the IRS route is matching Form 941 withholding and W-2 filings against actual deposits per EIN, and the DOL route is missing Form 5500 filings. A payer can still see the correlated risk: a multi-state chain with unpaid trust-fund taxes, missing 5500s, wage garnishment/lien filings and staffing-cost anomalies in cost reports.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a chain-level financial-viability monitor for institutional providers using cost-report payroll versus reported withholding, federal/state tax lien filings, missing Form 5500 filings and payroll-service termination signals; fire enhanced oversight, escrow of payments, or a change-of-ownership review rather than a claim denial. Primary enforcement remains an IRS deposit-versus-withholding match.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Rodney L. Yentzer (former owner of Pain Medicine of York/All Better Wellness); John H. Johnson (physician, 'Physician 1'); Paula Z. Johnson (physician, 'Physician 2'); Florentina Mayko (former CEO of PMY); Pain Medicine of York (PMY, a/k/a All Better Wellness)
PayerName: Medicare; Pennsylvania Medicaid; private insurance companies; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (COVID-19 provider relief funds)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Yentzer, who controlled the Pain Medicine of York pain clinics, agreed with physician John H. Johnson to order multiple urine drug tests for every chronic opioid patient at every office visit regardless of individualized need; the specimens were routed to PMY's in-house lab so PMY collected the payments, billing Medicare over $10 million from mid-2017 through 2019 (Medicare paid over $4 million), plus Pennsylvania Medicaid and private insurers. Proceeds funded luxury goods and were funneled to the incarcerated Johnson and his wife, who was put on the PMY payroll as a no-work employee to shield income from his restitution obligation; Yentzer also kept over $191,000 in HHS COVID-19 provider stimulus funds after PMY had closed. Figures span four sentenced defendants (Yentzer 42 months, Johnson 97 months, Mayko 30 months, Paula Johnson probation), and the settlement total aggregates their restitution, fines and civil settlement payments.
WaysToIdentify: The mechanic is reflex, per-visit definitive urine drug testing for every chronic opioid patient routed to a clinic-owned in-house lab, which shows at adjudication as a near-100% testing rate per office visit, identical large test panels for every patient regardless of risk, and lab claims billed under an NPI sharing address and ownership with the referring pain clinic. Also checkable: the practice's self-referral/ownership disclosure, and retention of COVID provider-relief funds after the practice ceased billing.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a per-provider UDT intensity feature (definitive drug tests per patient per year, tests per E/M visit, distinct analytes per panel, share of panels identical across patients) with prepay review and a records request above the same-specialty peer percentile, plus a hard edit on multiple definitive panels per encounter. Add an ownership-linkage flag when referring practice and lab share address, TIN or owners, and a relief-fund reconciliation that recoups when a recipient TIN stops submitting claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Martin Elling (former senior partner, McKinsey & Company); McKinsey & Company
SchemeSummary: Elling, who directed McKinsey's consulting engagements advising Purdue Pharma on how to 'turbocharge' OxyContin sales by targeting high-value prescribers, learned of investigations into Purdue and deliberately deleted a 'Purdue' folder, documents and Outlook emails from his McKinsey laptop between April and September 2018 to impede the DOJ investigation. He pled guilty to obstruction; McKinsey had separately agreed the prior month to pay $650 million to resolve criminal and civil investigations.
WaysToIdentify: No claims-payment component: this is obstruction of justice by a management consultant and opioid-marketing conduct by a manufacturer, so no payer prepay edit would have caught it. The nearest payer-visible signal is manufacturer-driven prescribing patterns — high-value-prescriber targeting shows up as concentrated growth in high-dose long-acting opioid prescribing among a small set of prescribers with heavy manufacturer sales/payment contact.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control: a prescriber-level opioid monitor joining pharmacy claims MME per patient per day, share of long-acting opioids, and Open Payments manufacturer payment/detailing intensity, firing prior authorization and prescriber outreach above the calibrated percentile. No payer control addresses the obstruction conduct itself.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Martin Elling (former senior partner, McKinsey & Company); McKinsey & Company (consulting firm to Purdue Pharma)
SchemeSummary: Elling, who directed McKinsey's client-service team on roughly 30 Purdue Pharma engagements (including the 2013 'Evolve to Excellence' project to boost OxyContin sales by targeting High Value Prescribers), deleted a 'Purdue' folder with over 100 documents and a Purdue Outlook email folder from his McKinsey laptop between April and September 2018 while aware of investigations into Purdue's opioid conduct; he pleaded guilty to obstruction and was sentenced to six months' prison, two years' supervised release with 1,000 hours community service, and a $40,000 fine (McKinsey separately paid $650 million in 2024 to resolve related criminal and civil investigations).
WaysToIdentify: Same as the companion case: obstruction and consulting-driven opioid promotion, with no claim submitted to a payer, so nothing was catchable at adjudication. Payers could only observe the downstream effect — abnormal growth in OxyContin and high-MME prescribing concentrated in prescribers identified as high-value targets.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber trend feature on brand-specific long-acting opioid volume and MME growth versus same-specialty peers, joined to manufacturer payment data, triggering prior authorization, formulary step edits and prescriber audit. State plainly that the obstruction offense has no payer-side control.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Miranda Rachel Briggs, a/k/a Miranda Rachel Fisher (former spouse of deceased veteran)
State_County: Georgia - Chatham County (Savannah); Georgia - Effingham County (Rincon)
PayerName: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA Dependency and Indemnity Compensation; CHAMPVA)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: After divorcing an Army veteran and being removed from his VA benefits, Briggs falsely claimed to be his surviving spouse following his 2018 death, submitting paperwork asserting they were married until death and legally changing her surname to his, thereby obtaining approximately $80,000 in VA Dependency and Indemnity Compensation and about $49,000 in CHAMPVA medical care benefits.
WaysToIdentify: The claimed relationship is contradicted by records already held: the veteran's file showed the spouse had been removed on divorce, and a state vital-records marriage/divorce match would show no marriage subsisting at death. A surname change filed shortly before or after the claim, and a prior dependency record showing termination for divorce, are both visible at eligibility adjudication before survivor benefits or CHAMPVA cards issue.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an eligibility edit for survivor/dependent benefit applications that compares the claimed marital status against prior dependency-termination reason codes in the beneficiary's own file and against state vital-records divorce/marriage data, holding payment when a prior 'divorce' termination exists without a documented remarriage. Add a name-change alert (surname adopted within a short window of the claim) and require certified marriage certificate and death-linked documentation before CHAMPVA enrolment activates.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Craig A. Spiegel (pediatrician); April Bingham (co-defendant)
SchemeSummary: Pediatrician issued prescriptions for opioids, benzodiazepines and stimulants with no legitimate medical purpose to adult women (many former patients) in exchange for sex acts, nude photos or cash, and prescribed to co-defendant Bingham using the names of her ex-husband, mother and friends to exploit their insurance benefits; Medicare, Missouri Medicaid and Illinois Medicaid lost $114,480. Bingham was separately sentenced to 21 months; Spiegel awaits sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: A pediatrician writing opioid, benzodiazepine and stimulant prescriptions to adult women is a specialty/age mismatch visible in PDMP and pharmacy claims at point of adjudication, together with no corresponding office-visit claims for those patients. The identity misuse is visible as prescriptions dispensed under a member's ID for a drug regimen inconsistent with that member's other claims, and as several members at different addresses sharing one prescriber and identical regimens.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-specialty/patient-age plausibility edit that flags controlled-substance claims where the prescriber's specialty and the patient's age band are incompatible (pediatrician to adults) and where no E/M encounter exists for that patient-prescriber pair in a lookback window; deny pending documentation. Add an identity-consistency check comparing dispensed controlled-substance regimen to the member's own diagnosis/encounter history and flagging clusters of members sharing one prescriber, one pharmacy and identical regimens.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Konstantinos "Kosta" Diamantis (Deputy Secretary, Connecticut Office of Policy and Management); Christopher Ziogas (State Representative, attorney); Helen Zervas (optometrist and owner of Family Eye Care, charged separately)
State_County: Connecticut - Hartford County (Farmington); Connecticut - Hartford County (Bristol)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: An optometrist who had fraudulently overbilled Connecticut Medicaid for services not provided or not medically necessary paid $95,000 in bribes, routed through her fiance (a state representative), to a state OPM deputy secretary who pressured DSS officials to cancel the pending Medicaid billing audit and accept a favorable $599,810 settlement; the officials also lied to the FBI and one omitted the bribe income from his 2020 tax return.
WaysToIdentify: Two separable problems: the underlying overbilling was detectable at adjudication (exam and testing volumes per provider-day above peers, services with no supporting record, repeat visual-field/imaging testing per patient), and the bribery was detectable in audit-governance data — an open audit closed or settled after external political intervention, with settlement authority exercised outside normal delegation. The bribe payments themselves surface only post-payment via bank records and the fiance's practice checks.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a provider-level utilization monitor for optometry (encounters per provider-day, tests per patient per year, share of claims with no distinct documentation) with prepay review above the calibrated percentile. Separately harden audit workflow controls: log every external contact and settlement-authority override on an open audit, require dual independent sign-off and an integrity-office review for any audit cancellation or discounted settlement, and auto-alert on cases closed after non-program contacts.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
