FraudEntity: Christopher Ziogas (former Connecticut State Representative); Helen Zervas (optometrist and owner of Family Eye Care); Konstantinos Diamantis (senior official, CT Office of Policy and Management - charged by indictment)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Retention of Overpayment; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Optometrist Helen Zervas fraudulently overbilled Connecticut Medicaid for eye care services she did not provide or that were not medically necessary; when DSS noticed an audit of Family Eye Care's billing in January 2020, she and her fiance, State Representative Christopher Ziogas, paid bribes totaling $95,000 (payments of $20,000, $10,000 and $65,000, reimbursed by Family Eye Care checks) to OPM official Konstantinos Diamantis, who pressured DSS officials to cancel the audit and accept a $599,810 settlement. Ziogas also committed bank fraud by negotiating a $5,500 check from a client trust to Diamantis and lied to federal agents; Zervas has pleaded guilty and Diamantis is awaiting trial.
WaysToIdentify: The billing itself was catchable prepay: eye exam and diagnostic-testing volumes per provider-day and repeat testing frequency per patient far above same-specialty Medicaid peers, and claims for services with no corresponding chart entry. The bribery is only visible post-payment/administratively — an audit cancelled and settled at a steep discount following contact from outside the agency, plus practice checks reimbursing personal payments to an official.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement optometry-specific prepay edits: cap payable diagnostic tests per member per period without documented medical necessity, and flag providers above the calibrated percentile on encounters per day and tests per encounter for prepay record review. Add an audit-integrity control that requires independent approval and audit-committee review for any cancellation or below-extrapolation settlement of an open provider audit, with automated alerts when external officials contact case staff and when provider-linked disbursements match official payees.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Stephen D. Meis, M.D. (Medical Director, Golden Sunrise Pharmaceutical Inc. and Golden Sunrise Nutraceutical Inc.); Huu Tieu (Chief Executive Officer); Golden Sunrise Pharmaceutical Inc.; Golden Sunrise Nutraceutical Inc.
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Meis, medical director of Golden Sunrise, and CEO Huu Tieu sold and mailed boxes of herbal drug vials (including 'Imunstem') marketed as an 'Emergency D-Virus Plan of Care' COVID-19 treatment, with labeling falsely claiming FDA approval as a prescription medicine and efficacy against the virus; no Golden Sunrise product was ever FDA approved. Meis pleaded guilty to introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce; co-defendant Tieu was previously sentenced to 18 months in prison.
WaysToIdentify: The products were unapproved herbal drugs marketed as FDA-approved COVID treatments and sold direct to consumers, so there may be no payer claim at all; where reimbursement was sought, the signal is a claim carrying an NDC or compound description that is absent from the FDA approved-drug/NDC directory or flagged in FDA warning-letter and import-alert feeds. Marketing claims of FDA approval for an unlisted product are detectable at formulary/coverage-file load, before any payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay pharmacy/medical-benefit edit that validates every submitted NDC or product identifier against the FDA NDC directory and approved-drug and unapproved-drug lists, hard-denying products with no approval basis and auto-blocking any NDC appearing in FDA warning letters or import alerts. Add a coverage-file gate that requires FDA approval status and an evidence review before any COVID-treatment product is added, plus member-alert referral for cash-market unapproved-cure marketing.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Richard E. Moore (executive vice president and part owner of Nexus Services Inc.); Nexus Services Inc.
SchemeSummary: Moore, who controlled the finances of Nexus Services Inc., withheld Social Security, Medicare and income taxes from employees' wages but failed to pay those funds over to the IRS and failed to file quarterly employment tax returns for many quarters from Q1 2015 through Q1 2024, causing a tax loss of about $3.1 million.
WaysToIdentify: No claims-payment component: this is employment tax fraud against the IRS, detectable from the payer side by reconciling W-2/Form 941 filings - employer issued W-2s showing withholding while no matching 941 returns or EFTPS deposits exist for the same quarters. The signal is a non-filer/underdeposit gap on the employer's EIN across consecutive quarters, visible at return-processing time rather than in any claim.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an EIN-level quarterly reconciliation job that joins W-2/W-3 wage-and-withholding totals to filed Form 941 liabilities and deposited funds, and fires when withholding is reported at the annual level but quarterly returns or deposits are missing for two or more consecutive quarters. Action: automatic non-filer notice and referral to a trust-fund recovery examination before further refunds or credits are allowed. No payer-side medical claim control applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Western District of Virginia; Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs
FraudEntity: Richard Moore (executive vice president and part owner of Nexus Services Inc.); Nexus Services Inc.
SchemeSummary: Moore, part owner and EVP of Nexus Services Inc., withheld Social Security, Medicare and income taxes from employees' wages for many quarters from Q1 2015 through Q1 2024 but failed to pay them to the IRS or file employment tax returns, causing about $3.1 million in tax loss while spending company funds on luxury cars, his wedding, and publishing his spouse's book.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case and again not a health-claims scheme: withheld trust-fund taxes were never remitted and 941s were never filed while the company continued to run payroll and make large discretionary disbursements. IRS-side signals are the W-2-to-941 mismatch on the EIN plus continued payroll activity with zero deposits; the luxury spending is only visible post-payment through bank records.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement an EIN trust-fund monitor computing, per quarter, expected withholding from payroll/W-2 data minus actual EFTPS deposits, flagging repeat-quarter gaps and escalating where the same responsible officer appears on multiple delinquent EINs. Action: automated non-filer assessment, responsible-person identification, and freeze on any related-entity refunds pending examination.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Marlenin Vito (Medicaid Coordinator at a Stamford assisted living facility; later bookkeeper at an alarm company and a law firm)
State_County: Connecticut - Fairfield County (Stamford); Connecticut - Hartford County (Hartford); New York - Westchester County (White Plains)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: As Medicaid coordinator at a Stamford assisted living facility, Vito generated roughly 500 checks from the facility's system, forged a coworker's signature, cashed them purportedly to give cash to residents, kept the money (~$310,820), and covered it up with false debits to residents' patient trust account ledgers and fabricated account statements; she also pocketed residents' COVID-19 Economic Impact Payments and continued deducting for cancelled supplemental insurance. After termination she stole approximately $23,558 from a White Plains alarm company (false overtime and company-funded product orders) and about $27,179 from a Hartford law firm via forged 'Petty Cash' checks; figures span all three victim companies.
WaysToIdentify: This is internal embezzlement of resident trust funds rather than false claims, but a payer/regulator can see it: patient trust fund reconciliations show hundreds of cash disbursement checks signed with one countersignature, resident ledger debits with no resident receipt, and continued premium/insurance deductions for a cancelled policy. Facility cost reports and the required resident-funds surety/quarterly accounting are the data carriers; also EIP deposits to resident accounts followed immediately by cash withdrawals.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a resident-trust-account audit routine per facility: count and value checks payable to cash or to a single employee per month, test signature/countersignature pairs against authorised signer files, and compare ledger debits to signed resident receipts and bank statements. Fire when cash-check volume or per-employee disbursement share exceeds the calibrated percentile versus peer facilities, or when a resident's federal benefit deposit is withdrawn as cash within days - action: documentation request for the trust-fund reconciliation and referral to state survey/MFCU.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Michael W. Luehrsen
SchemeSummary: Luehrsen pleaded guilty to perjury for falsely testifying at his prior trial that he was out of town when an altered compound prescription form was faxed from his father's Buffalo-area home; the underlying trial involved conspiracy to commit health care fraud tied to altered compounded-drug prescriptions. He agreed to pay approximately $2 million in restitution and forfeit approximately $2 million in assets.
WaysToIdentify: The underlying scheme was alteration of compounded-drug prescription forms, which a PBM can see prepay: the same faxed prescription template with modified drug/ingredient lines, high-reimbursement compound NDC combinations, and fax origination numbers not associated with the prescriber's registered practice location. Compare the prescriber's NPI/DEA address of record and normal prescribing mix to the compound claims being submitted.
FeaturesToCreate: At adjudication, edit compound claims on prescriber-plus-pharmacy pairs where the compound ingredient mix or reimbursement per script exceeds the same-specialty peer percentile, or where the originating fax/e-script source does not match the prescriber's enrolled practice location. Fire a prepay documentation request for the original signed prescription and prescriber attestation, and suspend payment on the pharmacy's compound claims while the prescriber is contacted directly.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Timothy Craig Jolloff; Lisa Ann Jolloff
PayerName: Small Business Administration (SBA); PPP approved lenders
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Married couple submitted false EIDL and PPP applications to the SBA and PPP lenders, misstating employee counts, average monthly payroll, gross revenue and cost of goods sold, and falsely certifying how proceeds would be used, obtaining eleven EIDLs, eight PPP loans and EIDL advances totaling about $3.4 million that they spent on boats, real estate, vehicles, jewelry and unrelated businesses; both defendants were sentenced (97 months and 36 months) and ordered to pay $3.4 million restitution plus $3.4 million forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: Not a health-claims case: SBA loan fraud. Detectable at underwriting by cross-checking applicant-stated employee counts, payroll and gross revenue against IRS Form 941/W-2 transcripts and filed returns, and by de-duplicating applications across shared EIN, address, bank account, phone and principal identities - eleven EIDLs plus eight PPP loans to one couple should have collided in an entity/identity graph.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pre-disbursement rules engine: (1) require IRS transcript match of payroll to stated average monthly payroll with tolerance, flagging mismatch; (2) an identity/entity graph keyed on SSN, EIN, address, bank routing/account, device and phone that fires when the same principal or bank account appears on multiple loan applications. Action: hold disbursement pending documentation, and post-disbursement trace of proceeds to asset purchases for clawback.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Marcus Asay (founder and chairman); Antonio Gastelum (COO, CFO and Compliance Officer); Agricultural Contracting Services Association dba American Labor Alliance (ALA) (company)
FraudTypeAll: Other - Unknown; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Through ALA, the defendants sold three sham products to workers and businesses: a purported 401(k) retirement plan whose contributions (over $620,000 in losses to more than 3,000 people) were spent on personal and business expenses and covered up with premiums from other schemes; workers' compensation coverage falsely certified on certificates of insurance and policy declarations as backed by national insurers, generating $2.25 million in premiums; and bogus Affordable Care Act hardship exemptions sold for a few hundred dollars although only government agencies can issue them. Asay also laundered pension funds through multiple bank accounts; figures and penalties span both individuals and the corporate defendant (corporate fine $2.5 million plus $69,250 restitution each from Asay and ALA).
WaysToIdentify: No payer adjudication occurred - the defendants were the fake payer selling sham 401(k), workers' comp and ACA-exemption products. Detection sits with regulators and with providers/employers verifying coverage: certificates of insurance naming national carriers can be validated against the named carrier's policy system, retirement contributions can be reconciled to trustee/custodian statements and Form 5500 filings, and ACA hardship exemptions exist only in the federal exemption registry.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a coverage-verification API check for any presented certificate of insurance or exemption number: query the named carrier's policy master and the federal exemption registry, and flag any certificate whose policy number is absent or whose issuing entity is not a licensed carrier in the state. Additionally reconcile withheld retirement contributions to custodian deposit records and fire when withholding occurs with no matching trust deposit; action: regulator referral and suspension of the entity's ability to be accepted as a coverage source.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Ruthia He (founder and CEO of Done); David Brody (clinical president of Done); Done (California-based digital health company)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Through the telehealth company Done, He and Brody used over $40 million of deceptive social-media and keyword advertising to recruit drug seekers into a monthly subscription, capped initial appointments at under half a typical psychiatric exam, refused to pay for follow-up care, paid nurse practitioners up to $60,000/month to refill prescriptions without clinical interaction, and used an 'auto-refill' feature that issued Adderall prescriptions for years (including for deceased patients), distributing over 40 million stimulant pills. To keep subscribers paying, they submitted false prior authorization requests to insurers falsely claiming DSM-5 diagnosis practices, urine drug screens, and prior failed non-stimulant trials, causing Medicare, Medicaid and commercial insurers to pay over roughly $14 million; He also moved operations to China, used disappearing-message apps, deleted documents and wired over $1 million to a Chinese shell company to obstruct the investigation.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals are dense: prior-authorization requests from one telehealth group asserting identical DSM-5 workups, urine drug screens and prior non-stimulant failures with no corresponding UDS lab claims or prior non-stimulant pharmacy fills in the member's own history; stimulant scripts written by a handful of NPs at volumes far above same-specialty peers; visit durations billed below the minimum for the psychiatric evaluation code; and refills continuing past the member's date of death. Cross-checking PA attestations against the plan's own claims history for that member is the single strongest catch.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an auto-verification layer on stimulant PAs: for each request, look up member claim history for a UDS claim and a prior non-stimulant trial fill and for an E/M encounter of adequate duration; deny or route to clinical review when attested elements are absent from the payer's own data. Add prescriber-level monitors for controlled-substance scripts per NP per month, share of new starts with no follow-up visit within the expected interval, and any fill dated after a date-of-death match - action: prepay suspension of the group's stimulant claims and PA privileges pending records.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Alan Redmond (principal architect/controller of the businesses); Arthur Walsh (senior executive); Jesus Barrera (senior executive); Albert Groff (head sales agent and manager); Bene Market LLC (company); Seguro Medico LLC d/b/a Quick Health, Q Health, Benefits Now, Express Benefits, YourBenefits4U (company)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants ran a boiler-room call center near Reading, PA that bought live transferred calls from lead generators and used bait-and-switch pitches - falsely claiming to be the 'national enrollment center for health insurance' working with 30+ A-rated carriers - to sell consumers limited benefit discount health/dental plans misrepresented as comprehensive major medical insurance, collecting tens of millions in commissions; tactics included unlicensed sales staff, churning/policy-flipping, double-billing, altering recorded sales calls to deceive regulators, and nominee ownership to conceal Redmond's control. Redmond also allegedly withheld over $1.2 million in trust fund taxes from employee wages between 2019 and 2022 without paying the IRS.
WaysToIdentify: Mostly a consumer-deception and trust-fund-tax case, not claims submission - the product sold was a limited-benefit discount plan, so there are no provider claims to edit. Payer-adjacent detection: state DOI licensure files show unlicensed sellers writing business, carrier commission systems show churning (same consumer replaced repeatedly within short intervals) and duplicate monthly draws on the same cardholder, and the marketing scripts claim carrier affiliations that carriers can disprove. The withheld payroll taxes are caught by the W-2-to-941 reconciliation.
FeaturesToCreate: For entities that pay commissions or process member drafts, build a producer-level monitor: verify every writing agent's ID against state licensure feeds prepay of commission, and compute per-consumer replacement/cancel-rebuy counts and duplicate-draft rates per agency, firing above the calibrated percentile. Action: withhold commissions and refer to state DOI; separately run the EIN W-2-versus-941 withholding gap check for the trust-fund tax exposure.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; USAO - Central District of California
FraudEntity: Juan Carlos Esparza (owner of House of Angels Hospice); Petros Fichidzhyan; Karpis Srapyan; Susanna Harutyunyan; Mihran Panosyan; House of Angels Hospice
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Valley Village, Winnetka, Granada Hills)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Defendants operated four sham hospice companies that billed Medicare roughly $16 million for hospice services that were medically unnecessary and never provided, using foreign nationals' identities as straw owners to enroll with Medicare, open bank accounts and sign leases, then laundered the proceeds through shell company accounts and assets. Restitution totals span five defendants ($1,825,012; $2,822,963; $3,203,574; $4,680,146; $17,129,060), plus $2,920,383 seized and forfeiture of two homes; longest sentence was 12 years (Fichidzhyan).
WaysToIdentify: Enrolment-time signals dominate: four new hospices with owners who are recent foreign-national identities holding no clinical or industry history, shared addresses, sequential bank accounts and leases signed by the same agent, and no verifiable medical director. Post-enrolment, claims show hospice election periods with no visit-level activity, no attending physician relationship, and beneficiaries who simultaneously have unrelated Part A/B utilisation inconsistent with terminal care.
FeaturesToCreate: At enrolment, build an owner/identity graph across new hospice applications keyed on SSN/ITIN, address, phone, bank account and notary/agent, and require in-person site verification plus identity-proofing when a listed owner is newly created or appears on multiple applications; hold billing privileges until cleared. For newly enrolled hospices, apply a prepay review flag on all claims for an initial period and fire when election periods lack any documented visit encounters or when beneficiaries show concurrent curative-intent utilisation - action: payment suspension and revocation referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Edward Cannatelli; Robbyn Cannatelli; Thomas Farese; Virginia Lockett; Patsy Truglia (co-conspirator, previously pleaded guilty); LouTricia Morgan (co-conspirator, previously pleaded guilty)
State_County: Florida - Hillsborough County (Tampa); Florida - Broward County (Parkland, Fort Lauderdale, Margate, Sunrise)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants ran a telemarketing operation that harvested Medicare beneficiaries' names, dates of birth and Medicare ID numbers to generate medically unnecessary orthotic brace orders, then sent them to purported telemedicine vendors that paid kickbacks to physicians who signed the orders without contacting beneficiaries; the signed orders supported bogus DME claims spread across three DME storefronts controlled by the conspirators to avoid Medicare scrutiny. Two co-conspirators (Truglia and Morgan) previously pleaded guilty in separate cases.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay claim-graph signals: brace claims where the ordering physician is in a different state from the beneficiary and has no prior or subsequent E/M relationship with that beneficiary, one telemedicine physician ordering across hundreds of unrelated beneficiaries, and identical brace code sets (multiple joints per beneficiary) repeating verbatim. Splitting volume across three DME storefronts is itself detectable by linking the storefronts on shared owners, addresses, bank accounts and the same ordering-physician pool.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-ordering-physician relationship edit that denies or pends orthotic DME claims where no covered E/M encounter with the ordering NPI exists in a defined lookback and the geographic distance exceeds a calibrated threshold. Add a supplier-cluster detector that links DME NPIs by shared ownership, address, bank account and overlapping ordering-physician set and aggregates their volume for outlier scoring; action: prepay review of the whole cluster, plus documentation request for the order and beneficiary contact attestation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Demitrious Gilmore (owner of WM Wellness, LLC and Gilmorehands, Inc. d/b/a Work-Med); Gary Martin (owner of medical clinics); Damon Heath Roberts (co-defendant, pleaded guilty); Khadeer Khan Mohammed (owner of American Premier Labs LLC); Olatunbosun Osukoya (owner of Ayo Biometrics, LLC d/b/a Cambridge Diagnostics)
State_County: Texas - Lubbock County (Lubbock); Texas - Collin County (McKinney, Plano); Texas - Dallas County (Richardson)
PayerName: Medicare; TRICARE; Department of Labor Office of Workers Compensation Program (DOL-OWCP); other private insurers
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Four separately indicted Northern District of Texas defendants collectively billed roughly $210 million: Gilmore billed DOL-OWCP about $19 million ($17 million paid) for custom knee braces, physical therapy (including hours billed while the claimant was in surgery), PRP treatments and at-home ultrasonic devices that were unnecessary or never provided; Martin allegedly funneled Medicare beneficiary information (including deceased beneficiaries) to co-conspirators who billed over $73 million for over-the-counter COVID-19 tests and paid him kickbacks off the reimbursements; Mohammed used stolen physician identifiers to submit about $93 million ($65 million paid) in Medicare claims for genetic testing never ordered or performed; and Osukoya billed over $25 million to Medicare, TRICARE and other insurers for EEG testing, paying over $450,000 in kickbacks disguised as loans, medical directorships and consulting fees and falsifying diagnoses. Over $1 million was seized from Gilmore's accounts and nearly $6 million from Mohammed's.
WaysToIdentify: Each strand has a prepay tell: DOL-OWCP therapy hours overlapping a facility surgery claim for the same claimant on the same date; COVID test claims tied to beneficiaries whose date of death precedes the service date and to beneficiary lists funnelled from one recruiter; genetic testing billed under physician identifiers with no ordering encounter and volumes wildly off the physician's specialty norm; and EEG billing concentrated on referrers receiving 'loan', directorship or consulting payments disclosable in ownership/financial-relationship data.
FeaturesToCreate: Build (1) a same-claimant temporal conflict edit that denies therapy/office services overlapping an inpatient/operative claim window; (2) a date-of-death and beneficiary-ID-reuse edit on test claims, plus a recruiter-linkage graph over beneficiary lists shared across billing NPIs; (3) an ordering-physician validation edit requiring a documented ordering encounter and firing when a physician's genetic-test order volume exceeds the same-specialty peer percentile, with fraud-hold on the lab. Action: prepay suspension of the billing NPI and revocation review, with referral where identifiers appear stolen.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Dr. Shakeeb Chinoy (physician); Dr. Sunil Manjila-Varghese (physician); Rommel Harvey (clinic owner/operator); Gregory Sparks (patient recruiter)
State_County: Michigan - Wayne County (Detroit); Michigan - Oakland County (Bloomfield Hills); Michigan - Washtenaw County (Ann Arbor)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges two doctors, a clinic owner/operator and a patient recruiter conspired to issue thousands of opioid prescriptions (over 400,000 dosage units of Schedule II opioids, street value over $7 million) to purported patients with no legitimate medical need, and that Medicare and Medicaid were billed over $1 million for medically unnecessary prescription and maintenance medications.
WaysToIdentify: PDMP-plus-claims joins show it prepay: two prescribers issuing Schedule II opioid dosage units far above same-specialty peers, a high share of patients travelling long distances or sharing a single recruiter's address, cash-heavy visits with cookie-cutter same-day E/M codes, and pharmacy concentration where a handful of pharmacies fill nearly all scripts. Diagnosis support for chronic opioid therapy is absent from the member's other claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-level controlled-substance surveillance job computing MME per patient per month, share of patients on high-dose opioids, patient-address clustering and pharmacy concentration, and fire above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers. On fire, apply prepay pend on the practice's E/M and the linked pharmacy's opioid claims with a documentation request for treatment plans and PDMP reconciliation; refer for DEA/MFCU action and consider prescriber payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dera Ogudo (operator of United Palliative & Hospice Company); Victoria Martinez (operator); Evelyn Shaw (hospital discharge coordinator); Hattie Banks; Lydia Obere; Cheryl Brooks; Ena Cowart; United Palliative & Hospice Company; Residential Hospice; Cedar Hospice

SchemeSummary: Seven defendants allegedly billed Medicare and Medicaid more than $110 million for hospice services for patients who were not terminally ill; UPHC marketers told beneficiaries they qualified for hospice, the owner paid kickbacks to group home owners and a hospital discharge coordinator for patient referrals and bribed a physician to falsely certify and re-certify terminal illness. After a search of UPHC, the operators opened new hospice companies under straw owners and laundered Medicare reimbursements through controlled accounts to conceal ownership.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals: hospice census dominated by beneficiaries referred from a small set of group homes and one hospital discharge coordinator, one physician certifying and re-certifying terminal illness for an outsized share of the census, live-discharge and long-length-of-stay rates far above peers, and beneficiaries with no prior hospice-consistent diagnosis trajectory. After the search warrant, the reopening under straw owners is catchable at enrolment by ownership-graph matching to the sanctioned entity's addresses, staff, medical director and bank accounts.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a hospice certification-concentration monitor (share of certs by one physician, referral-source concentration, beneficiaries alive past the calibrated percentile of expected stay) that triggers prepay medical-record review of certifications and payment suspension. Separately, at enrolment run a successor-entity detector linking new applications to prior investigated/revoked providers on address, phone, bank account, medical director, employees and managing-employee identity, and deny or hold billing privileges pending on-site verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Lindsay N. McCray (also known as Lindsay Rogers) (employee of a medical practice); Alexandra M. Christensen; Heather T. Bradley (also known as Heather Thomas); Jennifer E. Purves
SchemeSummary: While employed by a medical practice, McCray allegedly forged controlled substance prescriptions using the names, signatures, and DEA registration numbers of the practice's two physicians without their knowledge, causing over 300,000 hydrocodone and over 30,000 oxycodone pills to be unlawfully dispensed; she also allegedly distributed amphetamine with Bradley and Purves, and conspired with Christensen.
WaysToIdentify: Payer/PBM-side prepay: script volume attributed to two physicians' DEA numbers spikes far above their historical and peer baselines, with fills for individuals who have no encounter history with that practice and often no coverage relationship at all. Cash-pay fills bypass claims, so the PDMP is the primary data carrier - prescriber-level dispensing counts reported there can be pushed back to the prescriber for confirmation.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-identity integrity monitor that compares controlled-substance fill volume per DEA/NPI against that prescriber's own historical baseline and specialty peers, and fires on step-change increases or on fills for patients with no prior encounter with that prescriber's TIN. On fire, pend the pharmacy claims, send an automated prescriber-verification request ('did you write these?'), and notify PDMP/DEA; add an alert for prescriptions whose patient identity cannot be resolved to a real member record.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Lindsay N. McCray (also known as Lindsay Rogers) (medical practice employee); Alexandra M. Christensen; Heather T. Bradley (also known as Heather Thomas); Jennifer E. Purves
SchemeSummary: While employed at a medical practice, McCray forged controlled substance prescriptions using the names, signatures and DEA registration numbers of the practice's two physicians, issuing them in the names of non-patients or fictitious persons; area pharmacies dispensed over 300,000 hydrocodone and over 30,000 oxycodone pills, which Christensen and others picked up and resold for shared profit, while Bradley and Purves filled Adderall/amphetamine prescriptions in their own and others' names for resale with payments passing through McCray.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: forged scripts under two physicians' DEA numbers dispensed to non-patients and fictitious names. Observable prepay at the pharmacy/PBM layer are repeated fills for patients with no encounter history with the prescriber, multiple different patients picking up at the same pharmacy on the same days by the same individuals, identical directions and quantities across scripts, and fictitious patient identities that fail eligibility/identity resolution.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement (1) a prescriber-baseline step-change edit on controlled-substance volume per DEA number with automated prescriber verification before payment; (2) an identity-resolution edit rejecting fills where patient demographics do not resolve to a verified member/person record; (3) a pharmacy-level pickup-clustering report over shared payer/pickup identifiers. Action: prepay pend on the affected DEA number's scripts and referral to DEA and the state board.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Raef Hamaed (pharmacist/pharmacy owner); Tarek Fakhuri (pharmacist/pharmacy owner); Ali Abdelrazzaq (pharmacist/pharmacy owner); Kindy Ghussin (pharmacist/pharmacy owner); Eastside Pharmacy; Harper Drugs; Wayne Campus Pharmacy; Heartland Pharmacy; Heartland Pharmacy 2
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan
SchemeSummary: Four pharmacist owners of five pharmacies in Michigan and Ohio billed Medicare, Medicaid, and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan for prescription medications that were never actually dispensed, causing over $13 million in collective losses; all four were convicted at trial and sentenced (longest sentence 10 years for Hamaed, plus 7 years, 5 years 5 months, and 2 years for the others).
WaysToIdentify: Non-dispensing is detectable prepay through inventory-versus-billing logic: aggregate NDC units billed by each pharmacy far exceed wholesaler acquisition data (ARCOS/834-type purchase records) for the same NDCs, and refill patterns are too regular (exact 30-day cadence, no gaps, no partial fills). Also visible are beneficiaries with no corresponding prescriber encounter or who live implausibly far from the pharmacy, and five pharmacies under common ownership showing the same signature pattern.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a monthly per-pharmacy, per-NDC billed-units-versus-purchased-units reconciliation using wholesaler purchase data, firing when billed units exceed purchases beyond tolerance, and aggregate across commonly owned NPIs. Combine with a refill-regularity and beneficiary-distance score; on fire, place the pharmacy on prepay review with documentation requests for signature logs and acquisition invoices, and suspend payment where the inventory gap persists.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: John Ageudo Rodriguez (pharmacist, owner of Pharr Family Pharmacy); Mohammad Imtiaz Chowdhury (marketer); Hector de la Cruz Jr. (marketer); Alex Flores Jr. (marketer)

SchemeSummary: Pharmacist-owner of Pharr Family Pharmacy paid kickbacks, via marketers, to medical providers who referred compounded drug prescriptions to his pharmacy, then billed more than $110 million in compound drug claims to the Department of Labor, TRICARE and Medicare. Four defendants pleaded guilty; sentences ranged from 30 to 60 months.
WaysToIdentify: Compound kickback schemes show prepay as extreme reimbursement-per-claim, a narrow set of high-margin compound formulations, and referral concentration - a small number of prescribers accounting for nearly all of one pharmacy's compound volume, often out-of-state and outside the therapeutic specialty, with marketer-driven patient cohorts appearing in bursts. Cross-payer view (DOL-OWCP, TRICARE, Medicare) is important because the pharmacy shifted the same formulations across programs.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a compound-claim outlier engine at pharmacy level: average paid per compound claim, share of revenue from the top compound formulations, and Herfindahl-style prescriber concentration versus peers; fire above the calibrated percentile. On fire, apply prepay documentation review requiring proof of patient-specific medical necessity and prescriber attestation of no financial relationship, and check prescriber-to-pharmacy financial ties; suspend payment and refer for kickback investigation where marketer payments are found.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: Joseph Huff (pharmacist); Jenifer Huff (spouse)
State_County: Kentucky - Simpson County (Franklin); Kentucky - Warren County
PayerName: Kentucky Medicaid; unnamed commercial insurance companies

SchemeSummary: A pharmacist and his wife diverted oxycodone and hydrocodone from their pharmacy (the wife trading pills for cocaine, meth and marijuana), billed Kentucky Medicaid for prescriptions never ordered by a prescriber, billed insurers for brand-name Adderall while dispensing generic, billed for medication never dispensed, falsely reported a pharmacy robbery to DEA, and used another provider's name and NPI to issue prescriptions. Restitution totaled $17,518.19 (Joseph) plus $5,730.43 (Jenifer); sentences were 3 years and 2 years respectively.
WaysToIdentify: Several distinct prepay tells: claims billed with brand NDCs while acquisition records show only generic purchases (brand/generic NDC-versus-inventory mismatch); scripts billed under a prescriber NPI who has no relationship to the member and can be verified by outreach; billed units exceeding purchased units for the diverted opioids; and a reported robbery used to explain inventory loss that should trigger reconciliation rather than close it.
FeaturesToCreate: Build per-pharmacy NDC-level reconciliation of billed brand versus purchased brand units (fires on any material brand-billed/generic-purchased gap and on billed-exceeds-purchased for controlled substances), plus a prescriber-validation edit rejecting claims whose prescriber NPI has no encounter/relationship history with the member. Action: prepay pend and automated prescriber verification; on inventory loss reports, auto-open an audit that reconciles ARCOS purchases, dispensing records and claims.

SchemeSummary: Owners and staff of now-closed Florida for-profit nursing schools sold fraudulent nursing diplomas and transcripts (approximately 7,300 fake diplomas) falsely showing that purchasers had completed required coursework and clinical training; buyers used the documents to qualify for the NCLEX exam, obtain RN/LPN licenses in states including Florida, California and Pennsylvania (including multi-state compact licenses), and then obtain nursing jobs, salaries and benefits from unwitting health care employers nationwide. Figures span 12 defendants; only Herline Lochard has been sentenced (13 months) after pleading guilty, Patrick Buchanan pleaded guilty and awaits sentencing, and the remaining defendants are charged by indictment or information.
WaysToIdentify: No claims payment - this is credential fraud, and the payer-relevant control is at credentialing/enrolment: licences issued to candidates whose diploma and clinical hours come from a small set of schools with implausible graduate volume, transcripts that cannot be confirmed by primary-source verification, and NCLEX candidates whose program attendance dates conflict with employment history in another state. Nurse-compact and board databases plus school-level graduate counts carry the signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Make primary-source verification mandatory and automated in credentialing: verify diploma and clinical-hour transcripts directly with the institution's registrar API, and flag any applicant whose program is on a high-risk school list built from graduate-volume-per-faculty and NCLEX pass-rate anomalies. Fire a hold on network participation/billing privileges until verification returns, and run a retroactive sweep of already-credentialed staff from flagged schools with claims-payment suspension for services rendered by unverified licensees.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Shontavia Riddick
PayerName: North Carolina Department of Commerce, Division of Employment Security (NCDES)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Riddick submitted more than 65 fraudulent pandemic unemployment benefit claims to the North Carolina Division of Employment Security, requesting over $340,000 by making false representations about the applicants' employment and supplying fraudulent supporting documents.
WaysToIdentify: Not a medical-claims case: pandemic unemployment insurance fraud. Detectable pre-payment by cross-matching claimant-reported employer and wages against state quarterly wage records (no wage record for the claimed employer), and by de-duplicating on the filer's IP/device, bank account or debit-card routing, mailing address and phone across 65+ claims filed by one person. Supporting documents can be checked against employer verification responses before first payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pre-payment UI adjudication rules set: (1) require wage-record match for the claimed employer and hold claims with no match pending employer verification; (2) an identity/payment-instrument graph that fires when more than a small number of distinct claimants share a bank account, address, phone, device fingerprint or IP. Action: suspend first payment and route to identity verification and document authentication before release.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida; U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Absolute Physical & Aquatic Therapy, LLC (physical therapy billing company); Chipley Physical Therapy, LLC (outpatient physical/aquatic therapy provider); Ruben Laurel (owner/operator of both entities); Lorrie Laurel (physical therapist, co-owner of CPT)
State_County: Florida - Chipley, Marianna and Bonifay (Florida panhandle)
SchemeSummary: Government's False Claims Act complaint alleges the defendants submitted 613 claims to the United States for physical therapy services purportedly rendered by physical therapist Lorrie Laurel at Chipley Physical Therapy while she was actually out of the country, including on cruises to Mexico, Jamaica, Aruba and the Bahamas, between July 2019 and March 2024; a later related release notes the defendants collectively agreed to pay $754,722.88 to resolve the litigation.
WaysToIdentify: Every claim named a specific treating physical therapist (rendering NPI) on dates when that therapist was physically outside the country - detectable by cross-checking rendering-provider claim volume against absence evidence, and more cheaply by the pattern signal: continuous same-therapist billing with no gaps, including on dates where the same NPI appears as sole renderer for implausibly long service-minute totals. Timed-unit PT codes billed under one NPI can be summed per day and compared to a feasible workday. CBP/travel data is not payer data, but sudden identical-daily-pattern billing and later beneficiary/therapist interviews close it post-pay.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-NPI per-day capacity edit: sum billed timed PT units plus untimed procedures per rendering NPI per date of service across all TINs, convert to minutes, and pend claims exceeding a calibrated feasible-day threshold or where one NPI is the sole renderer for an entire clinic's panel every business day. Add a 'renderer identity attestation' documentation request (signed treatment notes with therapist credentials and time in/out) when a solo-renderer clinic shows zero absence days over long periods versus same-specialty peers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Community Health System (hospital system operating Community Regional Medical Center and Clovis Community Medical Center); Physician Network Advantage Inc. (affiliate health care technology business)
PayerName: Medicare; other governmental health care programs
SchemeSummary: The United States alleged Community Health System and its affiliate PNA induced Fresno-area physicians to refer patients to Community facilities by providing extravagant perks (expensive wine, liquor, cigars and meals in a custom-built lounge called HQ2), subsidies for electronic health records technology and equipment in physicians' private offices, and bonuses ostensibly for clinical integration activities that actually rewarded referrals; the resulting referred hospital services were billed to Medicare and other federal programs in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law. Settled for $31.5 million, with qui tam relator Michael Terpening receiving about $5 million.
WaysToIdentify: This is a Stark/AKS relationship case, visible not in claim lines but in the financial-relationship data the hospital must disclose: EHR-subsidy agreements, office equipment provided to referring physicians' private practices, and 'clinical integration' bonus payments. A payer can require and analyze physician financial-relationship disclosures at hospital enrollment/revalidation and correlate each subsidized physician's referral share into the sponsoring system before paying designated health services. Qui tam and expense-ledger review (a custom lounge cost center) are post-payment routes.
FeaturesToCreate: Create a financial-relationship registry keyed to (hospital TIN, referring physician NPI) populated from mandatory Stark/EHR-donation and physician-compensation disclosures, then compute for each disclosed physician the share and volume of designated health services referred into the donor system, trended pre/post agreement date. Fire a review flag and a DHS claim hold when referral share jumps above the calibrated percentile after an agreement start or where compensation varies with referral volume; require attestation of fair market value and non-volume-based compensation at revalidation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Felipe Ruiz (podiatrist at West Coast Podiatry Inc.); Jose Gabriel Aguirre (skin graft sales representative); West Coast Podiatry Inc.
State_County: California - Fresno County; California - Madera County; California - Stanislaus County
SchemeSummary: Podiatrist Ruiz bought skin grafts from sales representative Aguirre and let Aguirre - an unlicensed person who patients called 'Dr. Gabe' - apply the grafts to Medicare and Medi-Cal beneficiaries without Ruiz present; claims were then submitted falsely representing that Ruiz performed the applications, and Ruiz paid Aguirre a share of the millions in resulting payments. Both defendants were charged (indicted April 2025), pleaded guilty in September 2025, and each was sentenced to 63 months in a scheme described as $3.2 million.
WaysToIdentify: Skin-substitute graft applications billed under one podiatrist's NPI at volumes and product spend far above same-specialty peers, with graft product units purchased from a single distributor and applications occurring at times/places where the billing podiatrist is simultaneously billing elsewhere. Q-code product spend per beneficiary and per rendering NPI per day, plus 'incident to' supervision rules, are all adjudication-visible. Sales-rep involvement surfaces on records review showing no physician signature or an unlicensed applicator's handwriting.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-NPI daily capacity and place-of-service concurrency edit for CPT 15271-15278 with paired Q-code units: pend when one NPI's graft applications per day, or graft product dollars per beneficiary, exceed the calibrated same-specialty percentile, or when the same NPI bills applications at two locations in overlapping windows. Trigger a prepay documentation request for wound measurements, product lot/invoice, and the credentialed applicator's identity; suspend on evidence of application by unlicensed personnel.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Felipe Ruiz (podiatrist, West Coast Podiatry Inc.); Jose Gabriel Aguirre (skin graft sales representative); West Coast Podiatry Inc. (podiatric medical practice)
State_County: California - Fresno County; California - Madera County; California - Stanislaus County
SchemeSummary: Podiatrist Ruiz bought skin grafts from sales representative Aguirre and let Aguirre, who was not a licensed health care provider, apply the grafts to Medicare and Medi-Cal beneficiaries; claims were then submitted falsely representing that Ruiz performed the graft applications, and after Medicare/Medi-Cal paid Ruiz he passed payments to Aguirre. Both defendants pleaded guilty and each was later sentenced to 63 months in a scheme described as involving $3.2 million.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic: claims assert the podiatrist personally performed skin-graft applications actually done by an unlicensed sales rep, so the payer sees outlier graft volume and product spend concentrated on one NPI with a single graft supplier, and geographic/time impossibility across service sites. Supervision and licensure requirements for skin-substitute application are checkable at adjudication against state licensure files for anyone documented as applying. Confirmation requires records review or beneficiary interviews (patients knew the applicator as 'Dr. Gabe').
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a graft-application integrity edit: per rendering NPI per date, count 15271-15278 applications and sum associated Q-code allowed amounts, flag above calibrated same-specialty percentile or where per-beneficiary graft spend is an extreme outlier; also flag overlapping service times across POS. Route flagged claims to prepay documentation request requiring the applicator's name and license number, and validate that name against state licensure and payer credentialing files before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Kelo White; Donald Ray Pierre; Ifeanyi Vincent Ntukogu (pharmacist)
State_County: California - Fresno County (Fresno); California - Madera County (Madera)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: White and Pierre obtained more than 450,000 oxycodone and hydrocodone pills using prescriptions bearing forged signatures of more than 10 doctors; pharmacist Ntukogu vetted and filled the prescriptions to avoid regulatory red flags in exchange for cash, and the pills were resold for profit. Sentences span three defendants: White 90 months, Ntukogu 87 months, Pierre 112 months.
WaysToIdentify: Prescriber-side signal: hundreds of thousands of oxycodone/hydrocodone units dispensed by one pharmacy under prescriptions attributed to 10+ prescribers whose own PDMP/claims histories show little or no opioid prescribing, out-of-area prescriber-patient distances, cash-pay or uniform high-quantity/high-MME prescriptions, and duplicate prescriber signature images. A payer or PDMP analytic can compare each pharmacy's opioid share and prescriber mix against peers and verify prescriptions with the named prescribers before paying.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pharmacy-prescriber concordance check: for each dispensing NPI, compute opioid share of scripts, average MME per script, patient-prescriber distance, and the fraction of opioid volume attributed to prescribers whose specialty/claim history is inconsistent with that prescribing; fire when multiple metrics exceed calibrated peer percentiles. Action is prepay suspension of opioid claims plus mandatory prescriber verification (call-back/e-prescribe-only requirement), and referral of the pharmacist to licensure/DEA.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Lilit Gagikovna Baltaian (physician)
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Porter Ranch/Los Angeles)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: A licensed California physician falsely certified Medicare beneficiaries as needing home health care - including pre-signing blank, undated certification forms that four Los Angeles-area home health agencies then falsified to show she had examined patients and made supporting clinical findings - enabling the agencies to bill Medicare about $1.5 million; she took cash payments for the referrals and separately billed Medicare for signing the certifications.
WaysToIdentify: One certifying physician's NPI appears on plans of care for many unrelated home health agencies with no corresponding face-to-face evaluation claim in her own claim history, and her certification-signing claims cluster in batches. Pre-signed blank forms show as certifications with dates that precede or do not match any documented encounter, and as identical clinical findings across patients. All of this is visible at adjudication by joining HHA claim certifying-physician fields to physician E/M claim history.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a certification-linkage edit: for each home health episode, require a matching face-to-face encounter claim by the certifying NPI within the required window; deny or pend when absent. Add a certifying-physician monitor computing distinct HHAs served, episodes certified per month, and share of certifications lacking an encounter versus peers, firing prepay review of all episodes tied to that NPI and a documentation request for signed, dated F2F notes.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Prescriptions Plus (pharmacy, Gastonia, N.C.)
SchemeSummary: Pharmacy agreed to pay $204,000 in civil penalties for failing to maintain complete and accurate Controlled Substances Act records of oxycodone and alprazolam received and distributed and failing to monitor its staff pharmacist, which the government alleged negligently enabled illegal distribution of those drugs; the pharmacy also entered a Memorandum of Agreement with DEA.
WaysToIdentify: This is a DEA recordkeeping/diversion civil penalty rather than a claims-payment fraud, so there is no claim edit that catches it directly; the payer-side analogue is monitoring the pharmacy's controlled-substance dispensing profile and reconciling purchased inventory (ARCOS/wholesaler data) to dispensed claims. Large unexplained gaps between acquisitions of oxycodone/alprazolam and billed dispensing, plus one staff pharmacist accounting for the bulk of controlled fills, are the observable signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an inventory-to-claims reconciliation for pharmacy network participants: per NDC per quarter, compare wholesaler/ARCOS acquisition units to units dispensed on adjudicated claims and flag unexplained shrinkage above a calibrated tolerance. Also compute controlled-fill concentration by individual pharmacist ID on the claim; fire network audit, corrective action plan, and prepay review of controlled-substance claims when either metric breaches.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Genexe, LLC (d/b/a Genexe Health, marketing company); Immerge, Inc. (parent company); Jason Green (CEO); Jason Gross (COO)
State_County: Pennsylvania - Philadelphia County (Eastern District of Pennsylvania); Colorado - Arapahoe County (Greenwood Village)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Marketing company Genexe and parent Immerge, with executives Green and Gross, paid independent contractors with no medical training to collect cheek-swab DNA samples from Medicare beneficiaries at malls, churches, retirement homes and nursing facilities, then paid kickbacks to telemedicine providers/physicians for orders for medically unnecessary CGx and PGx genetic tests; labs billed Medicare (often over $6,000 per test) and kicked back $800-$2,000 per swab to Genexe. Settled for $6 million under the False Claims Act, with about $1.3 million going to four whistleblower relators.
WaysToIdentify: Claims show CGx/PGx panels ordered by a small set of telehealth physicians for beneficiaries hundreds of miles away, with no prior treating relationship, no oncology/cancer diagnosis history, and no follow-up care or treatment change after the result. Specimen-collection venues (malls, churches, nursing facilities) show up as clustered service dates and addresses and as bursts of identical panels billed by the same lab. Marketing-company kickbacks per swab are detectable pre-pay through these ordering-pattern signals and lab-marketer contract disclosure at enrollment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an order-legitimacy edit for CGx/PGx codes: deny or pend when the ordering NPI has no prior E/M with the beneficiary in a lookback window, when ordering is via a telehealth-only NPI outside the beneficiary's region, or when the beneficiary lacks a supporting diagnosis history. Add lab-level monitors for same-day clustered collections at one geography and share of volume from a single marketing entity, firing prepay suspension and a request for the signed order, medical record, and marketer compensation arrangement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Patrick C. Moore Jr. (kickback broker/recruiter network organizer)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Moore directed a network of recruiters to induce Medicare beneficiaries to accept medically unnecessary genetic tests, receiving about $4.3 million in kickbacks from co-conspirators for supplying beneficiary insurance information, DNA specimens and doctors' orders, and paying kickbacks down to recruiters. Associated laboratories billed Medicare about $24 million and were paid about $7.2 million; Moore created sham invoices showing fabricated hours worked to disguise per-referral payments.
WaysToIdentify: Recruiter-driven volume shows as many labs billing high-dollar genetic panels for the same cohort of beneficiaries, orders concentrated in a few physicians who never treated them, and repeat/duplicate panels on the same beneficiary across labs. The sham 'hourly' invoices are post-payment evidence, but per-referral economics are inferable pre-pay from the tight correlation between one intermediary's beneficiary list and multiple labs' claims. Payment-to-billed ratios and lack of any follow-on clinical care are adjudication-visible.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a beneficiary-level duplicate-panel and orphan-order edit: deny repeat CGx/PGx panels on the same beneficiary within the clinically implausible window regardless of billing lab, and pend panels whose ordering NPI has no treating-relationship claim. Add a network-graph monitor linking beneficiaries shared across otherwise unrelated labs to common ordering NPIs; when a cluster exceeds the calibrated threshold, place involved labs on prepay review with documentation requests and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Kenneth Terrell Harrison (owner); Aurtism, LLC (outpatient behavioral health counseling service)
PayerName: Medicaid (Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System - AHCCCS, American Indian Health Plan)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Harrison concealed his ownership of Aurtism, LLC when it enrolled as an AHCCCS provider in 2019 because his criminal history would have disqualified it, then obtained AHCCCS ID numbers for enrollees (mostly American Indian Health Plan members), some obtained fraudulently, and billed AHCCCS $6,538,485 for behavioral health counseling services that were never provided.
WaysToIdentify: Two catchable points: enrollment, where undisclosed ownership by an individual with disqualifying criminal history is detectable by requiring full owner/managing-employee disclosure and running background/exclusion and address/phone-linkage checks against known bad actors; and adjudication, where a new agency bills millions in counseling units for a narrow member population (American Indian Health Plan) with rendering-clinician hours exceeding feasible workdays and members whose eligibility records were manipulated. Member outreach/EOB verification confirms services never occurred.
FeaturesToCreate: At enrollment/revalidation, require and verify all 5%+ owners and managing employees against criminal-history, exclusion and prior-adverse-action files plus shared-identifier linkage (address, phone, bank account, EIN) to previously denied entities; deny or place a payment hold on mismatch. At adjudication, monitor new behavioral-health providers for units per rendering clinician per day, member-eligibility-record recency, and month-over-month billing ramp; fire prepay review, session-note documentation requests, and payment suspension for credible fraud allegation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Nita Almuete Paddit Palma (concealed owner of Magnolia Gardens Hospice and C@A Hospice); Percy Dean Abrams (marketer); Magnolia Gardens Hospice; C@A Hospice
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Palma, excluded from Medicare due to prior kickback convictions, secretly bought two hospices through her daughter and husband and concealed her ownership, then paid marketers including Abrams up to $1,000 per month per referred patient; marketers falsely told non-terminal patients they did not need to be dying to enroll and forwarded their identifying information, allowing Palma to bill Medicare roughly $6,000 per patient month for a total of about $10.6 million in hospice claims, and fake patient charts were created and submitted when Medicare requested supporting documentation. Palma received 108 months and $8,270,032 restitution; Abrams received three years probation with two years home confinement.
WaysToIdentify: An excluded individual's control was hidden behind family-member owners - catchable at enrollment by requiring disclosure of all owners, managing employees and their family relationships, and by linkage checks (shared addresses, phones, bank accounts, prior CHOW history) against the exclusion list. At adjudication, hospice claims show long lengths of stay with no decline, live discharges, non-terminal diagnoses, and marketer-driven admission clusters; certifications lack valid face-to-face visits. The fabricated charts submitted on ADR are detectable by internal inconsistency and identical templated narratives.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ownership-integrity screen: match all disclosed owners/managers plus their linked identifiers and immediate relatives against exclusion and prior-fraud files, and hold payments for any hospice whose ownership shares identifiers with an excluded party. Add hospice claim edits for missing/invalid F2F certification, cap-relevant long-stay and live-discharge rates above the calibrated percentile, and admission clustering by referral source; fire prepay ADR with authenticity checks (metadata, duplicate-narrative detection) and suspension on findings.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Bayonne Drydock and Repair Corporation (government contractor); Bayonne Drydock's Risk Manager
SchemeSummary: Bayonne Drydock used subcontractors owned and/or controlled by its own Risk Manager to perform work on Navy ship government contracts, and those subcontractors employed approximately 52 individuals not authorized to work in the United States; the company paid $4,043,810.56 to resolve False Claims Act allegations, and the Risk Manager previously pleaded guilty to knowingly hiring and continuing to employ unauthorized aliens.
WaysToIdentify: No health-care claims-payment component: this is a federal procurement False Claims Act matter about self-dealing subcontracts and unauthorized workers on Navy contracts. The catchable signals sit in contract administration - undisclosed conflicts of interest where a company officer owns subcontractors, and unverified employment eligibility of subcontractor labor - visible from mandatory organizational-conflict-of-interest disclosures, subcontractor ownership data, and E-Verify status.
FeaturesToCreate: For contract-paying agencies (analogue for payers: vendor/subcontractor integrity), build a conflict-of-interest screen matching officers/employees of the prime against ownership records of all subcontractors and flagging any match before invoice approval, plus a subcontractor-level requirement for E-Verify attestation. Fire invoice hold and contracting-officer review on any owner-identifier match or missing eligibility attestation; no direct claims edit applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
FraudEntity: Mohammed Kazim Ali (co-owner, Noah Associates); Justin Hanson (co-owner, Noah Associates); Noah Associates (clinical laboratory)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Ali and Hanson, owners of Milwaukee-area lab Noah Associates, paid over $400,000 in kickbacks to the owner of a substance use treatment clinic for referrals of Medicaid and Medicare patients for urine drug testing; the tests were not physician-ordered or medically necessary and were billed using a physician's credentials without authorization (continuing even after the physician objected), yielding over $2.2 million in program payments. Ali was sentenced to 15 months, ordered to pay over $2.2 million restitution plus a $75,000 fine; Hanson pleaded guilty and awaited sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: The lab's Medicaid/Medicare urine drug testing volume is concentrated in patients from a single SUD clinic and billed under a physician's NPI that the lab was not authorized to use - detectable by measuring referral concentration per ordering NPI and by verifying with the named ordering physician (who had objected). Payments flowing from the lab to the referring clinic owner are visible only on audit, but the one-source referral pattern, uniform high-complexity definitive panels, and standing-order uniformity are prepay signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab referral-concentration and order-authenticity check: per lab NPI, compute the share of UDT claims attributable to a single ordering NPI or clinic TIN and flag above the calibrated percentile; require an ordering-provider verification (e-signature or portal attestation) before paying definitive UDT for high-concentration pairs. Provide an ordering-physician dispute channel that immediately suspends payment on claims using that NPI and triggers investigation of lab-clinic financial arrangements.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Substance Abuse Treatment Labs; Paul Fribush (owner)
SchemeSummary: The lab and its owner allegedly billed North Carolina Medicaid for the highest-reimbursing level of urine drug screening tests despite clear indications the tests were not medically necessary, collecting the top payment rate; they agreed to pay $850,000 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: Every patient receiving the highest-tier definitive drug-testing code regardless of clinical presentation is a distribution anomaly: near-100% use of the top-paying UDT code, uniform large analyte counts, and testing frequency identical across a whole panel of patients, all visible on claim lines at adjudication. Peer comparison of code-tier mix among labs serving SUD clinics isolates it before payment; medical necessity is confirmed by requesting the ordering rationale and prior test results.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a UDT code-tier distribution edit: per lab (and per ordering clinic), compute the share of definitive testing billed at the highest analyte-count tier and tests per patient per month, and pend claims when both exceed the calibrated same-peer percentile or when top-tier billing is not preceded by a presumptive screen or documented individualized order. Action: prepay downcode/deny to the supported tier pending documentation request for patient-specific medical necessity.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Jasmine Hoyle (owner of Harvest Focused & Consulting Services, LLC and The Ultimate Sacrifice); Harvest Focused & Consulting Services, LLC; The Ultimate Sacrifice
SchemeSummary: Hoyle, through two Winston-Salem companies she owned, billed North Carolina Medicaid for urine drug tests and office visits that were never performed - including 97 claims for a beneficiary who had never heard of the companies and provided no urine - collecting over $6 million that she laundered into personal purchases such as a Dodge Challenger.
WaysToIdentify: Claims for urine drug tests and office visits with no plausible encounter trail: no ordering provider with a treating relationship, beneficiaries geographically remote from the company, and repeat high-frequency testing (97 claims on one member) that no clinical pathway supports. Beneficiary verification letters/EOB response and specimen-tracking (no collection site, no chain of custody) would have exposed it before payment; the two commonly-owned entities billing the same members is another adjudication-visible link.
FeaturesToCreate: Build per-beneficiary UDT frequency and encounter-linkage edits: cap and pend UDT claims exceeding a calibrated per-member-per-month frequency, deny when no ordering provider encounter exists in a lookback window, and flag when the same members are billed by multiple commonly-owned TINs. Add automated beneficiary verification mailings/portal confirmation for new labs with steep billing ramps, with payment suspension when verifications come back negative.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Jasmine Hoyle (owner/operator of Harvest Focused & Consulting Services, LLC and The Ultimate Sacrifice); LaTameria Davis (former business partner); Harvest Focused & Consulting Services, LLC; The Ultimate Sacrifice
State_County: North Carolina - Forsyth County (Winston-Salem); North Carolina - Guilford County (Greensboro)
SchemeSummary: Hoyle, through two Winston-Salem businesses she owned, billed North Carolina Medicaid for services never performed, largely urine drug testing screens - including 97 claims for a beneficiary who never received services or provided urine - collecting over $6 million that she spent on personal items such as a Dodge Challenger. She was sentenced to 44 months and $6,299,738.89 restitution; co-defendant LaTameria Davis pleaded guilty to conspiracy and awaits sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: phantom UDT screens and office visits from a newly enrolled owner-operated lab with explosive billing growth, no ordering-provider treating relationship, extreme per-member claim counts, and members who deny any contact. Ownership linkage between the two Winston-Salem entities (shared owner, address, bank account) shows a single scheme split across TINs to dilute outlier detection.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a common-ownership aggregation rule so outlier and frequency edits are computed across all TINs sharing owner/address/bank identifiers, not per TIN. Combine with per-member UDT frequency caps, an orphan-order denial (no ordering-provider encounter), and a new-provider ramp monitor; when triggered, place the provider group on prepay review with beneficiary-verification letters and suspend payment on negative or non-responsive verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Fred Beans Holdings, Inc.; Auto Express Enterprises, Inc.; Autorent of Doylestown Inc.; McCafferty Autorent Inc.; Noble Advertising, Inc.
SchemeSummary: Five affiliated Bucks County, PA car-related companies each applied for and received roughly $973,395 in PPP loans in April 2020, falsely certifying eligibility even though, counting affiliates, they had more than 500 employees; they then obtained forgiveness of the full loan amounts plus interest. The qui tam False Claims Act matter settled for $1,427,869 total across all defendants, with the relator receiving $142,786.
WaysToIdentify: No health-care claim payment involved: this is PPP loan eligibility fraud where five affiliated companies each certified fewer than 500 employees while their affiliate group exceeded the cap. The catchable signal is affiliation - common ownership, shared addresses, shared officers and shared payroll agents across the five applications - plus payroll-tax filings that reconcile group headcount, all available at underwriting.
FeaturesToCreate: For loan/grant programs, build an affiliation-aggregation screen at application: cluster applicants by owner TIN/SSN, officers, address, bank account and payroll provider, sum reported employees and payroll across the cluster, and reject or refer for manual underwriting when the aggregated headcount exceeds the size standard or when multiple near-identical loan amounts appear in one cluster. Verify headcount against IRS 941/state UI wage records before forgiveness. No payer claims control applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jamahl Rennelle Burch, aka Jarod or Jerrod Burch
PayerName: Virginia Medicaid; Virginia Employment Commission (state unemployment insurance and Federal Pandemic Unemployment Compensation)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Burch recruited Medicaid recipients into Virginia Medicaid's consumer directed care program, designated numerous individuals as personal care attendants, and used the recipients' and purported PCAs' personal identifying information to create accounts and submit and approve fraudulent timesheets for thousands of hours of personal and respite care that were never provided, causing at least $936,950.70 in Medicaid payments; he also used two purported PCAs' identities to file fraudulent unemployment claims yielding $15,720 in UI/FPUC benefits.
WaysToIdentify: Consumer-directed timesheets were created and approved by the same actor using recipients' and attendants' stolen identities, so the payer can see one device/IP/email/phone submitting and approving timesheets across many unrelated recipients, attendants billing overlapping or impossible hours across multiple members, and attendant identities with no independent contact history. EVV location/time data and duplicate bank-account routing for attendant pay are the strongest prepay signals; the parallel UI claims filed on the same identities show as cross-program identifier reuse.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an identity/self-approval control for consumer-directed programs: flag and hold any timesheet where submitter and approver share a device fingerprint, IP, phone, email or bank account, or where one identifier appears across recipients in unrelated households. Add attendant-hour aggregation across all members to deny overlapping or beyond-feasible-day hours, require EVV geolocation match to the member's residence, and refer identifier clusters to cross-program (Medicaid/UI) matching.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Jeremiah Yzaguirre (operator, Southwest Medical Homepatient); Maria Luisa Yzaguirre (operator, Southwest Medical Homepatient); Southwest Medical Homepatient (DME company)
SchemeSummary: The husband-and-wife operators of DME provider Southwest Medical Homepatient billed Medicare approximately $14 million for power wheelchairs, parts and repairs for only 37 beneficiaries between 2019 and 2023, including about $736,072 for one beneficiary by falsely claiming to have replaced expensive parts hundreds of times; the parts and repairs were never provided and proceeds bought cryptocurrency, a vehicle, electronics, collectibles and purses.
WaysToIdentify: Extreme dollars-per-beneficiary: ~$14M across only 37 beneficiaries, with one beneficiary at $736K from the same expensive wheelchair parts replaced hundreds of times. Repeat-replacement counts per HCPCS per beneficiary, replacement intervals far shorter than the part's expected life, and repair billing without a base-equipment history are all computable at adjudication before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a DME repair/replacement frequency edit: per beneficiary per HCPCS, count lifetime replacements and compare to expected useful life and calibrated peer replacement rates; deny or pend when counts or per-beneficiary annual allowed dollars exceed thresholds, and when repairs are billed without a documented base wheelchair or with no corresponding delivery. Add a supplier-level metric of allowed dollars per unique beneficiary versus peers, triggering prepay review, delivery-proof/serial-number documentation requests, and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Ester N. Mbaya (president of Cool Waters, LLC, home health care agency)
SchemeSummary: As president of home health agency Cool Waters, LLC, Mbaya submitted Medicaid claims for home health services that were never provided or were inflated, obtaining over $1 million; she also submitted altered bank statements and falsified paychecks to four financial institutions to obtain loans and lines of credit.
WaysToIdentify: Claim-side signals: visits billed for dates with no EVV check-in, aide hours exceeding feasible schedules, billed units above authorized plan-of-care amounts, and services for members who were hospitalized or otherwise unavailable. Peer comparison of units per member per month and certification/plan-of-care completeness for a small agency with fast revenue growth flags it prepay; the bank-statement and paycheck falsification is a lender-side matter, though the same fabricated payroll would fail a payroll-to-claims reconciliation on audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement an EVV-to-claim reconciliation that denies home health visit lines lacking a matching verified visit record, plus edits capping billed units at the authorized plan-of-care and rejecting service dates overlapping inpatient stays.
