Add an agency-level payroll-to-billed-hours reconciliation at audit (state UI wage data versus billed aide hours) and place agencies with unexplained gaps or outlier units-per-member on prepay documentation review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Thelma "Wendy" Epps (Licensed Alcohol and Drug Abuse Counselor, owner of Miracles to Destiny LLC); Miracles to Destiny LLC; Dennis Tomczak (LADC, Medicaid provider); Shawn Tyson (LADC, Medicaid provider)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: After Connecticut Medicaid suspended Epps as a provider for a credible fraud allegation, she arranged for two other licensed counselors (Tomczak and Tyson) to bill Medicaid under their own provider numbers for psychotherapy counseling she purportedly performed, paying Tomczak 25% of Medicaid receipts; Epps also used Tyson's portal login to submit claims, and many of the billed psychotherapy sessions (including some dated on holidays) were never provided at all. Medicaid paid $330,547.71 through Tomczak's number, $7,879.40 for Tyson-attributed services billed under Tomczak, and $663,081.32 through Tyson's number; Epps was sentenced to 27 months and ordered to pay $1,001,058.43 restitution, while Tomczak and Tyson pleaded guilty and await sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: Epps was already payment-suspended, so the signal is a suspended/excluded individual's fingerprints appearing behind other NPIs: shared billing IP address and portal credentials, shared practice address/phone/bank routing with the suspended provider, and a step-change in Tomczak's and Tyson's psychotherapy volume beginning the month after Epps's suspension. Session-level impossibilities are also visible prepay - psychotherapy units on federal/state holidays, and rendering-hour totals per counselor exceeding a plausible workday. The 25% revenue split is only visible post-pay via bank records, but the suspension-adjacent billing surge is prepay-detectable.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a suspended/excluded-affiliate linkage engine: for every excluded, suspended or credibly-alleged provider, hash their address, phone, TIN, bank account, portal login ID and submitter IP, and match against all incoming claim submissions; a hit triggers prepay suspension of the linked NPI and a records request. Add a rendering-provider capacity edit that sums timed psychotherapy units per NPI per calendar day and denies/pends when total minutes exceed a calibrated workday ceiling or fall on dates the provider had no active roster, plus a holiday/date-of-service reasonableness flag, and a change-of-behavior monitor firing on volume jumps versus the provider's own 12-month baseline and same-specialty peers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Commonwealth Care Alliance, Inc. (acquirer/successor); Reliance HMO, Inc. (Medicare Advantage plan operator)
SchemeSummary: Reliance HMO paid cash to healthcare professionals and administrative staff at physician practices for contact information of patients who signed 'permission to contact' cards, and paid four physicians/practices $2,500 each characterized as advances on 'coordination of care' services, allegedly to induce enrollment of Medicare beneficiaries in Reliance's Medicare Advantage plan, for which CMS pays monthly capitated payments. CCA, which acquired a 70% stake in Reliance in 2022, self-disclosed and paid $520,355.65.
WaysToIdentify: This is a Medicare Advantage marketing-kickback scheme, so the payer-side signals are enrolment-pattern rather than claim-line: enrolment applications for a given plan concentrated among a handful of source practices, high shares of enrolees whose 'permission to contact' leads trace to the same clinic staff, and paired financial records showing lump 'coordination of care' advances to physicians who then generate enrolments. CMS can see beneficiary-to-referring-practice concentration and agent/broker attribution in enrolment files before capitation flows.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment-source concentration monitor: unit of observation is plan-month by originating practice/TIN, computing share of new enrolees whose lead source, PCP-of-record or agent maps to that practice, firing when concentration exceeds the calibrated percentile versus peer plans in the same market. Pair it with a vendor-payment screen that reconciles plan general-ledger payments to physicians/practices (rent, 'coordination of care', advances) against enrolment counts from those same practices, and pend capitation for review plus require a written fair-market-value/personal-services agreement when correlation is high.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Gerald Congdon, M.D.; Coastal Urgent Care LLC; Coastal Wellness Center LLC; Gbenga Aluko, M.D.; Eagle Medical Center PC; Anup Banerjee, M.D.; Gastonia Medical Specialty Clinic P.A.; Omar Hussain (laboratory marketer); Curis Healthcare Inc. (marketing company); Saeed Medical Group Ltd. d/b/a Alliance Immediate and Primary Care
State_County: South Carolina - Georgetown County (Pawleys Island); South Carolina - Horry County (Myrtle Beach); South Carolina - Anderson County (Anderson); North Carolina - Mecklenburg County (Charlotte); North Carolina - Gaston County (Gastonia); Illinois - Cook County (Chicago)
SchemeSummary: Physicians and their practices allegedly received remuneration disguised as office space rent, phlebotomy and toxicology payments from an Anderson, S.C. laboratory in exchange for ordering lab tests, while a marketer and his company took volume-based commissions from that lab and paid cash to a clinic for test orders, resulting in false Medicare and TRICARE lab claims; the $1,913,808 total spans all settling defendants (Congdon $400,000, Aluko $250,000, Banerjee $206,000, Hussain/Curis $817,808, and Saeed Medical Group with Hussain/Curis $240,000).
WaysToIdentify: Detectable prepay from referral-concentration and ordering-pattern data: a single lab receives an outsized share of one physician's orders, and the ordering physicians' toxicology/definitive-drug-test panel volumes and panel breadth jump versus same-specialty peers with no diagnosis support. The disguised remuneration (rent, phlebotomy, toxicology fees) is visible at credentialing/disclosure time as lab-to-referrer payment relationships and as lab lease agreements at referrer addresses; the cash-to-clinic and volume-based marketer commissions surface post-pay in bank and 1099 records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab-referrer concentration edit: per ordering NPI per quarter, compute Herfindahl concentration of lab referrals and the ratio of high-value toxicology/definitive panels to peer median, flagging pairs above the calibrated percentile for prepay documentation request (medical necessity, treatment plan). Add a relationship screen that joins lab ownership, lease and service-agreement disclosures, shared addresses and lab-issued 1099/commission payments to referring NPIs, and suspend payment on claim streams where the lab pays the referrer, and where marketer compensation is per-test rather than fixed.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Health Net Federal Services, LLC (TRICARE managed care support contractor); Centene Corporation (corporate parent)
State_County: California - Sacramento County (Rancho Cordova); Missouri - St. Louis
PayerName: TRICARE (Defense Health Agency, U.S. Department of Defense)
SchemeSummary: HNFS allegedly falsely certified in required annual reports to the Defense Health Agency that it complied with cybersecurity controls in its contract to administer the TRICARE program, when it had failed to timely scan for and remediate known vulnerabilities and ignored third-party and internal audit findings on access controls, firewalls, patch management and password policies; HNFS and parent Centene agreed to pay $11,253,400 to resolve False Claims Act liability.
WaysToIdentify: No clinical claim is at issue - the false statement is an annual cybersecurity compliance certification by a TRICARE contractor, so it is caught at contract administration rather than claim adjudication. The observable signals are the contractor's own vulnerability-scan cadence and remediation logs, unresolved third-party and internal audit findings, and configuration evidence for access control, firewall, patching and password policy, which contradict the attestation on file.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an attestation-versus-evidence reconciliation control for contractor payments: unit of observation is contractor-year, ingesting scan frequency, mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities, and open audit findings from required artifact submissions, and firing when self-certified compliance is asserted while artifacts are missing, stale, or show unremediated findings. Action is to withhold the compliance-linked portion of the administrative fee and require independent third-party validation before release.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Gerald Congdon, M.D.; Coastal Urgent Care, LLC; Coastal Wellness Center, LLC; Gbenga Aluko, M.D.; Eagle Medical Center, PC; Anup Banerjee, M.D.; Gastonia Medical Specialty Clinic P.A.; Omar Hussain (laboratory marketer); Curis Healthcare Inc. (marketing company); Saeed Medical Group Ltd. d/b/a Alliance Immediate and Primary Care
State_County: South Carolina - Pawleys Island; South Carolina - Myrtle Beach; South Carolina - Anderson; North Carolina - Charlotte; North Carolina - Gastonia; Illinois - Chicago
SchemeSummary: Physicians and their practices allegedly received remuneration from an Anderson, S.C. laboratory disguised as office space rental, phlebotomy, and toxicology payments in exchange for ordering lab tests, while marketer Omar Hussain and Curis Healthcare received volume-based commissions from the lab and paid cash to Saeed Medical Group for test orders; resulting lab claims were billed to Medicare and TRICARE. Settlements total $1,913,808 across all defendants ($400,000 Congdon, $250,000 Aluko, $206,000 Banerjee, $817,808 Hussain/Curis, $240,000 Saeed/Hussain/Curis).
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: the lab's payments to referring physicians are dressed up as rent, phlebotomy and toxicology fees, while a marketer earns per-test commissions and pays a clinic cash for orders. Prepay signals are extreme referral concentration from a few practices into one out-of-area lab, toxicology panel volume and breadth far above same-specialty peers, and disclosed or discoverable lease/service arrangements between the lab and its referrers; the cash payments appear post-pay in financial records and 1099s.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement an ordering-physician/lab dyad analytic: compute per-dyad referral share, distance from patient population, and toxicology panel intensity versus specialty peers, and pend claims above the calibrated percentile pending medical-necessity documentation. Layer a financial-relationship rule that flags any lab claim where the lab has a lease, phlebotomy, service or commission payment relationship with the ordering NPI or its marketing intermediary, requiring fair-market-value and non-volume-based compensation attestation before payment resumes.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Amstrong Chapajong (personal care aide and community support worker)
SchemeSummary: Chapajong, working as a personal care aide and community support worker, submitted false timesheets to his employers claiming to have provided in-person personal care and telephonic behavioral health services to multiple D.C. Medicaid beneficiaries at the same time from different locations, causing D.C. Medicaid to pay $113,243 for duplicative services never rendered.
WaysToIdentify: The overlapping shifts are fully visible prepay because both employers bill Medicaid with the same aide/community-support worker identity: the same rendering staff member appears on concurrent time-based units for different beneficiaries at different locations on the same date and hour. Aggregate daily hours per worker across all employing agencies also exceed a feasible workday, and EVV timestamps/GPS for the personal care visits conflict with the telephonic behavioral health encounter times.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a cross-agency caregiver-overlap edit: key time-based personal care and community support claims by rendering-staff identifier (SSN/license/EVV worker ID) and interval, and deny or pend any claim whose service interval overlaps another paid or pending interval for that worker, regardless of billing TIN. Add a daily and weekly hours-per-worker ceiling edit and an EVV-versus-claim reconciliation that requires visit-level GPS/telephony evidence before payment for flagged dates.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nevada
FraudEntity: David Ralph Webber (owner/operator of Passion Plus Enterprises Inc. and Whole Science Health); Passion Plus Enterprises Inc.; Whole Science Health
SchemeSummary: Webber allegedly imported hundreds of thousands of capsules containing sildenafil and tadalafil from Indian manufacturers without FDA registration or a wholesale/prescription license, had packaging falsely labeled '100% Natural' with false ingredients and no prescription requirement, and sold them under brand names such as 'Kinky Kong' and 'Stif' to smoke shops, convenience stores, adult novelty stores and directly to consumers via his website, generating over $2.5 million in revenue.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health-plan claim here - unlicensed importation and retail sale of unapproved drug products containing sildenafil/tadalafil to smoke shops and consumers, so the enforcement route is FDA import screening and state wholesale licensure, not claim adjudication. Observable signals are import entries from foreign manufacturers lacking FDA registration, an importer without a wholesale distributor or pharmacy license, and '100% natural' supplement labeling inconsistent with declared ingredients.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest payer-side control is a licensure and product-integrity screen: cross-check any entity billing or supplying drug products against state wholesale/pharmacy licensure and FDA establishment registration, and block payment or network participation on mismatch. For non-payer enforcement, build an import-entry rule linking consignee licensure status to product category and flagging supplement-labeled entries whose supplier ships known PDE-5 API for laboratory verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Xuhan Zhang a/k/a "Shelia Zhang" a/k/a "Xuhan Mei" (medical doctor); Jing Qi Mei (office manager, billing)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a physician and her office-manager husband billed Medicare and Blue Cross Blue Shield roughly $20 million (about $6.5 million paid) for inpatient hospital physician services never rendered - including after the hospital closed, for patients actually residing in nursing homes, for deceased patients, and for more than 24 hours of services in a single day; charges include aggravated identity theft and money laundering, and about $6 million in bank funds plus a Tesla Cybertruck were seized.
WaysToIdentify: Every element is detectable at adjudication: inpatient E/M professional claims with a place-of-service hospital whose facility CCN was terminated or reported closed on the date of service; dates of service after the beneficiary's date of death in the eligibility/DMF file; professional inpatient visits for beneficiaries with concurrent nursing-facility or long-term-care residency claims; and summed timed/visit units implying more than 24 hours of provider work in one day.
FeaturesToCreate: Build four prepay edits keyed to claim line: (1) deny when POS/facility identifier maps to a facility with a closure or termination effective date on or before the date of service; (2) deny when date of service is after date of death; (3) pend inpatient professional visits that conflict with an overlapping institutional stay of a different type for the same beneficiary; (4) compute per-rendering-NPI per-day aggregate service time from RVU/time-typical values and suspend payment with a records request when it exceeds a calibrated 24-hour feasibility ceiling.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Wendy Gibson-Fitzgerald
State_County: North Carolina - Guilford County (High Point); North Carolina - Forsyth County (Winston-Salem)
SchemeSummary: Gibson-Fitzgerald used a victim's personal identifying information to take out loans and obtain credit cards in the victim's name, secured high-interest loans against the victim company's equipment and accounts receivable, and made hundreds of unauthorized money transfers from the victim's personal and business accounts into her own accounts, spending the $466,776.79 on trips and retail shopping; no health care payer was involved (she had a prior 2012 health care fraud/kickback conviction).
WaysToIdentify: No health care payer is involved - this is identity theft, consumer/commercial lending fraud and embezzlement from a business, so no claim-adjudication signal exists. The only payer-adjacent fact is the defendant's prior health care fraud and kickback conviction, which is an exclusion-list and credentialing signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Applicable control is an ongoing exclusion/conviction rescreen: re-run all owners, officers, managing employees and billing agents of enrolled providers against OIG LEIE, SAM and court/conviction feeds monthly, and auto-suspend billing privileges and payments when a health care fraud conviction or exclusion appears. Otherwise no payer-side control applies to this conduct.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Casey Mahoney (owner/operator of Healing Path Detox LLC and Get Real Recovery Inc.)
State_County: California - Orange County (Huntington Beach, San Juan Capistrano)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Upcoding; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Mahoney paid nearly $2.9 million in kickbacks to 'body brokers' who recruited patients with lucrative insurance policies to his two Orange County addiction treatment facilities, concealing the payments through sham fixed-fee contracts while actually negotiating amounts based on patients' insurance reimbursements and billable treatment days; brokers paid patients cash and even supplied drugs so patients would qualify for higher-paying levels of care.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals in the insurer's own data: patients enrolled in rich individual policies shortly before admission (often with premiums paid by a third party), travelling long distances to two commonly-owned Orange County facilities, and repeated admissions cycling through the same facilities. Level-of-care escalation is visible as drug-positive toxicology at admission for patients whose intake history did not support it, plus billing concentrated in the highest-paying residential/detox day rates and frequent definitive urine drug testing. Broker payments themselves surface in the facility's ledgers - obtainable via audit or, post-pay, financial records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an admission-provenance model at the facility level: compute share of admissions with policies effective within a short window before admission, third-party premium payment, out-of-state/long-distance residence, and readmission cycling, firing at the calibrated percentile to trigger prepay review and pre-authorization requirements. Add a level-of-care justification edit requiring ASAM criteria documentation and admission toxicology consistency before paying residential/detox day rates, and a marketing-expense audit rule requiring fixed, FMV, non-volume-based referral-source contracts as a condition of network payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Paul Njoku (owner and CEO of Opnet Health Care Services Inc., d/b/a P & P Health Care Services); Opnet Health Care Services Inc. d/b/a P & P Health Care Services
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Njoku, owner/CEO of a Houston home health agency, billed Medicare over $400,000 (receiving over $360,000) for home health services without maintaining required documentation, then fabricated records in response to a Medicare records request by cutting out old doctor and nurse signatures and taping them onto newly created physician orders, nursing notes and assessments - including continued use of a registered nurse's signature after she left in 2017. A witness also testified he bribed a doctor to approve home health services.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay-detectable through certification and workforce integrity: home health episodes certified by a physician with little or no documented face-to-face encounter claim for the beneficiary, and nursing/therapy visits attributed to a clinician whose license or agency employment/roster ended before the dates of service. In the documentation response, forged records show as identical reused signature images, mismatched fonts/paper artifacts and signature dates inconsistent with the signer's employment period - detectable by image-hash comparison during the records review rather than only after payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a certifying-physician linkage edit that requires a matching face-to-face encounter claim from the certifying NPI within the allowed window and denies episodes lacking it, plus a referral-concentration flag when one physician certifies an outsized share of a single agency's episodes. Add a clinician-eligibility edit checking rendering license status and agency roster/termination dates against dates of service, and in medical-review workflows run perceptual-hash comparison of signature blocks across submitted documents, escalating duplicate-signature-image hits to payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Sally Njume-Tatsing (owner/operator of three Labelle Home Health agencies)
State_County: Ohio - Franklin County (Reynoldsburg); Ohio - Knox County (Mt. Vernon); Ohio - Cuyahoga County (Parma)
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Owner of three Labelle Home Health agencies personally did all Medicaid billing for nursing services while living out of state, inflating hours of home health aide services, billing registered-nurse rates for care actually provided by licensed practical nurses, and billing for patients who were deceased or ineligible for Medicaid, resulting in $5.7 million in losses.
WaysToIdentify: All three mechanics are adjudication-visible: claims for beneficiaries whose eligibility segment is closed or whose date of death precedes the service date; RN-rate procedure codes billed on dates when only LPN staff were on the agency's roster or where the rendering clinician's license is LPN not RN; and aide-hour totals per beneficiary per day/week far above the authorized plan-of-care units and peer distributions. Billing all performed remotely by an out-of-state owner also shows as a single submitter IP/credential across three separate agency TINs.
FeaturesToCreate: Deploy prepay edits: (1) eligibility/date-of-death gate on every date of service; (2) credential-to-code consistency check joining the rendering clinician's licence type to the skilled-nursing rate code, denying RN-rate lines rendered by LPNs; (3) authorized-units cap comparing billed aide hours to the approved service authorization and pending overages. Add a common-control detector clustering agencies by shared owner, submitter credential and IP, and applying a combined prepay review and records request to the cluster.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: M&Y Care, LLC (home health care provider)
SchemeSummary: M&Y Care allegedly billed Medicare and Michigan Medicaid under CPT code G0156 (home health aide services under a home health plan of care) for services actually rendered by insufficiently trained staff, when it should have billed the non-skilled care rate that was about 74% lower; resolved via a $334,807.20 FCA settlement arising from a qui tam suit.
WaysToIdentify: The distinguishing fact is staff qualification: G0156 home health aide services under a plan of care require trained aides supervised under a skilled plan, so the payer can compare the rendering staff's training/certification records and the presence of a skilled discipline on the plan of care against the code billed. Prepay signals are G0156 volume with no concurrent skilled nursing/therapy visits and an agency whose payroll roster shows uncertified staff, with the code mix shifted almost entirely to the higher-paying aide code versus peers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a code-versus-qualification edit: for each G0156 line, require an active certified/trained aide identifier on the agency roster and a concurrent skilled discipline visit within the episode, otherwise reprice to the non-skilled personal care rate or pend for documentation. Add an agency-level code-mix monitor computing the share of aide services billed at the skilled-plan rate versus same-state peers and triggering a training-records request when above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Desert Imaging Services, L.P.; In Tandem Solutions Group, LLC; Leroy Candelaria; Donald Burris; Vox Intus, LLC; East El Paso Physician's Medical Center, LLC d/b/a Foundation Surgical Hospital of El Paso
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Upcoding; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Desert Imaging billed medical imaging services under Foundation Surgical Hospital's NPI as hospital outpatient services, even though the patients had no connection to the hospital, to obtain higher federal health care program reimbursement rates; the hospital kept 17% of the payments in exchange for the use of its NPI. Settlement amounts span multiple defendants: $693,913 (Desert Imaging/In Tandem/Candelaria), $325,000 forfeiture (Burris/Vox Intus), and a $2,081,739 consent judgment against the hospital.  Resolved a qui tam suit.
WaysToIdentify: Fully visible in claims: hospital outpatient imaging billed under the hospital's NPI/CCN for beneficiaries with no other encounter at that hospital, and with service-facility addresses (or the equipment/technician location) that are the independent imaging center's, not the hospital's. Also detectable are professional/technical component pairs where the interpreting physician is affiliated only with the imaging company, geographic implausibility between beneficiary residence and the hospital, and a step-change in the hospital's outpatient imaging volume after the arrangement began. The 17% fee split appears post-pay in financial records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a place-of-service/service-facility validation edit: deny or pend hospital outpatient (facility-rate) imaging claims whose service-facility address, NPI-registered practice location, or rendering technician/equipment registration is not an enrolled location of that CCN. Add a beneficiary-linkage rule requiring at least one other encounter or registration record at the billing hospital within a defined window, and a hospital-level outpatient-imaging volume change monitor that triggers site-of-service audit and payment suspension for outlier facilities.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dr. Ajay Aggarwal (anesthesiologist and pain medicine physician); Ajay Aggarwal (sole proprietorship); PRWCSWTX LLC (The Pain Relief & Wellness Center)
State_County: Texas - Harris County (Houston/Bellaire); Texas - Brazoria County (Lake Jackson); Texas - Matagorda County (Van Vleck)
PayerName: Medicare; U.S. Department of Labor Office of Workers' Compensation Programs
SchemeSummary: Aggarwal allegedly billed Medicare and DOL workers' compensation programs for surgical implantation of neurostimulator electrodes - invasive operating-room procedures paying thousands of dollars each - when patients actually received electro-acupuncture devices placed in his clinic by inserting monofilament wire a few millimeters into the ear and taping the device behind the ear with no incision. He agreed to pay $2,053,515 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay-detectable via site-of-service and code-context mismatch: surgical neurostimulator electrode implantation codes billed with an office place of service, no operating room or facility claim, no anesthesia claim, and no corresponding implantable-device invoice or HCPCS device code. Volume per physician per day for a supposedly invasive procedure also far exceeds same-specialty peers, and repeat 'implantations' on the same beneficiary within short intervals are inconsistent with a permanent implant.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit that denies neurostimulator implantation CPT codes when place of service is office/clinic and no paired facility, anesthesia, or implantable-device claim/invoice exists, routing them to the correct acupuncture/electro-acupuncture device coding. Add a per-provider frequency and repeat-implant analytic across Medicare and workers' compensation claim feeds, suspending payment and requesting operative reports and device serial-number invoices for providers above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dr. Benjamin Tiongson (pain management physician); Pain Reduction Center P.A. (his medical practice entity)
State_County: Texas - Harris County (Houston), Fort Bend County (Sugar Land), Katy
SchemeSummary: Physician allegedly billed Medicare for surgical implantation of neurostimulator electrodes (an invasive operating-room procedure paying thousands of dollars each) when in fact patients only received electro-acupuncture devices inserted a few millimeters into the ear and taped behind the ear in his clinic, with no incision made.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic: high-paying surgical implantation codes submitted for a non-incisional, clinic-applied ear device. Adjudication-visible signals are office place of service, absence of any facility or anesthesia claim, absence of an implantable device HCPCS line or purchase invoice, and implausible per-day volumes and repeat implantations on the same beneficiary versus same-specialty peers.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a site-of-service and device-evidence edit that denies neurostimulator electrode implantation codes billed in office POS without paired facility/anesthesia claims and a documented implantable device with invoice/serial number. Add a provider-level outlier and repeat-procedure monitor on these codes, firing above the calibrated percentile to pend claims and issue an operative-report and device-purchase documentation request before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division / U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Christopher Obaze (owner and pharmacist-in-charge, Chrisco Pharmacy); Chrisco Pharmacy; co-conspirators including a pharmacy technician
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Obaze ran Chrisco Pharmacy as a 'ghosting pharmacy,' buying hydrocodone and oxycodone from wholesalers and reselling at least 2,268,700 pills in bulk to drug traffickers with no physicians, patients, or prescriptions involved; he hid the activity by reporting no dispensing to the Texas prescription monitoring program, structuring cash deposits with false bank documents, and aiding false tax returns understating pharmacy gross receipts.
WaysToIdentify: Diversion at a 'ghosting pharmacy' shows as a purchase-versus-dispense mismatch: ARCOS/wholesaler purchase data show massive hydrocodone/oxycodone acquisition while the pharmacy reports essentially zero dispensing to the state PMP and submits few or no third-party claims for those NDCs. Prescriber-level support is absent entirely, and banking behavior shows structured cash deposits - a post-pay/financial signal, but the purchase-to-dispense gap is available prospectively from wholesaler and PMP feeds.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a controlled-substance reconciliation engine at pharmacy-NDC-month level: compare wholesaler/ARCOS purchase quantities to PMP-reported dispensations plus billed claims, and flag any pharmacy whose unaccounted-for volume exceeds a calibrated tolerance for immediate on-site audit, DEA referral, and suspension of network participation and payment. Add a zero-or-near-zero PMP reporting flag for pharmacies with active controlled-substance purchases, and a cash-only/no-claims dispensing ratio outlier check.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Dorian Farmer (owner of several businesses, including Titleist Technologies, Inc. d/b/a Summit Joint Performance)
SchemeSummary: Farmer, owner of several businesses, withheld employment trust fund taxes (Social Security/Medicare) from employees' pay but, instead of remitting them to the IRS, embezzled the funds for personal use, took large unreported cash distributions from one business, and failed to file tax returns for himself and Titleist Technologies for tax year 2000, causing a total tax loss of $806,653.
WaysToIdentify: Pure employment-tax embezzlement and non-filing; no health care claim, provider enrolment or payer payment is implicated, so no claim-adjudication signal exists. Detection sits with IRS matching of W-2 withholding reported by employees against Form 941 deposits and missing-return indicators.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side claims control applies. The nearest applicable control is a provider-enrolment financial-integrity screen that checks enrolling or revalidating entities and their owners against federal/state tax-lien, unfiled-return and trust-fund-penalty indicators, requiring resolution or a payment plan as a condition of continued billing privileges.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Christina Ann Mobley, also known as Kris Mobley (business manager/bookkeeper of a Fortuna construction company)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: As business manager who assumed bookkeeping duties at a Fortuna, Calif. construction company, Mobley allegedly diverted company funds to herself by directing company checks and electronic payments to her personal credit card accounts, using the company credit card for casino cash advances and personal travel, writing company checks to herself, and inflating her vacation time, hours and bonuses plus issuing duplicate payroll checks in the company payroll system, embezzling more than $500,000 between January 2022 and November 2024. No health care payer was involved.
WaysToIdentify: No health care payer is involved - this is internal embezzlement from a private construction company via self-directed payments, card misuse and duplicate payroll checks. It would be caught by employer-side controls (segregation of duties, bank-account whitelisting, payroll change review), not by any claim edit.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies to the fraud itself; the transferable control for payers and providers is an internal-disbursement monitor that flags payments to bank/card accounts matching an employee's own account, duplicate payroll runs for the same employee-period, and self-approved payroll or bonus changes, routing them to dual approval before release.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Javier Alfonso Nunez Suarez (beneficiary)
SchemeSummary: Defendant, a Colombian national illegally residing in Houston, allegedly impersonated a U.S. citizen to fraudulently apply for and obtain SSA disability benefits in February 2016, then used that status to qualify for Medicaid, continuing to collect both until his arrest for a total theft of government funds exceeding $588,000.
WaysToIdentify: Detectable at eligibility determination rather than claim adjudication: the identity used did not match SSA records for the claimed citizen, and cross-checks of SSN issuance data, immigration/SAVE status, and biometric/photo or wage-history consistency would show the applicant's earnings and residency history diverging from the identity claimed. Continued dual SSA-disability and Medicaid payments over years also present a long-running eligibility redetermination gap.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an eligibility identity-verification control: at application and each redetermination, match applicant SSN, name, date of birth and citizenship attestation against SSA Enumeration/Numident and DHS SAVE, and suspend benefit and Medicaid capitation/claim payment on any mismatch pending in-person documentary verification. Add a duplicate-identity detector clustering applications by SSN, address, phone and bank account across SSA and Medicaid files, flagging cases where the same SSN shows conflicting demographic or wage history.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Ana Juanita Andrade-Reyes (owner of shell construction company)
State_County: Florida - Duval County (Jacksonville); various Florida counties
PayerName: Internal Revenue Service (IRS); workers' compensation insurance carrier
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Defendant set up a shell construction company and bought a minimal workers' compensation policy (payroll of $169,400, premium ~$11,352), then 'rented' certificates of insurance to dozens of work crews so contractors would believe the crews were insured and employed by the shell company. Contractors issued payroll checks (~$8 million total) to the shell company; she cashed them, kept about 6%, and distributed cash to workers without withholding or reporting payroll taxes, evading $2,048,182 in Social Security, Medicare and income tax withholding, and depriving the insurer of about $591,978 in proper premiums.
WaysToIdentify: This is a payroll-tax and workers'-comp premium fraud with no health claims component; the payer-side analogue is the workers' compensation carrier and state wage/UI data. The carrier could have caught it by comparing the policy's declared payroll ($169,400) against the volume and dollar value of certificates of insurance issued to unrelated contractors and against checks deposited to the insured's account, and by noting that a single small construction insured was named on dozens of unrelated jobsites. IRS/state cross-match of Form 941/W-2 filings against the ~$8 million of 1099/check payments received by the shell entity would also have flagged the missing withholding pre-audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a carrier-side certificate-of-insurance monitor: unit of observation is the policy; compute count of distinct certificate holders/jobsites and estimated exposed payroll implied by those jobs versus declared payroll, and fire a mid-term premium audit or policy suspension when the ratio exceeds the calibrated percentile for same-class construction policies. Add a data-match rule that flags any insured whose deposited receipts or 1099-reported income greatly exceeds reported payroll with no 941 filings, routing to audit before renewal.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division; Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Krishnaswami Sriram (medical doctor)
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Doctor evaded roughly $1.6 million in taxes, penalties and interest by transferring rental properties in name only to his children, moving about $600,000 to accounts in India, and omitting accounts and property from IRS submissions; he also admitted falsifying medical records to bill Medicare $136,980.36 for in-home physician visits purportedly provided to beneficiaries who were actually inpatients elsewhere or deceased.
WaysToIdentify: The Medicare component is fully detectable prepay: home-visit E/M claims (99341-99350) with dates of service after the beneficiary's date of death in the Medicare enrollment/EDB file, or overlapping an active Part A inpatient or SNF stay, are contradictions inside Medicare's own data. The tax evasion piece is not payer-detectable and belongs to IRS asset/offer-in-compromise verification.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits on the claim line: deny any home/domiciliary visit whose DOS is after the beneficiary date of death, and deny or suspend home-visit claims whose DOS falls inside an inpatient/SNF/hospice institutional claim span. Add a provider-level counter of such conflicts and trigger prepay documentation review of all home-visit claims for providers above the calibrated peer percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division; Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Krishnaswami Sriram (doctor)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Doctor billed Medicare $136,980.36 for in-home physician visits that never occurred, claiming to treat beneficiaries on dates when they were dead or residing in inpatient facilities, supported by false statements in medical records; he separately evaded roughly $1.6 million in taxes by transferring rental properties to his children in name only, moving about $700,000 to accounts in India, and omitting assets from an IRS offer-in-compromise.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: home-visit claims billed for deceased beneficiaries and for beneficiaries who were inpatients on the service date, both verifiable against the enrollment date-of-death field and concurrent Part A institutional claims at adjudication. The falsified records only surface on documentation request, but the date conflicts alone justify prepay review.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement date-of-death and institutional-overlap edits for place-of-service 12/13/14 E/M codes, denying conflicting lines outright. Track per-NPI rates of home-visit claims per beneficiary-day and share of visits conflicting with institutional stays; providers above the peer percentile go on prepay medical-record review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Kartik Bhatia (DME company owner/operator); Raju Sharma (co-conspirator)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Bhatia and co-conspirators operated DME companies that paid telemarketing firms for orthotic brace orders (ankle, wrist, knee, back) and billed Medicare over $2 million for braces beneficiaries did not need or want, with doctors' signatures on orders from physicians who never treated or prescribed for the beneficiaries; after CMS suspended payments to his company, he opened a new DME company to continue the same billing. He also made false statements to law enforcement.
WaysToIdentify: Orthotic brace claims (L-codes for ankle, wrist, knee, back) clustered on a small set of ordering NPIs with no prior treatment relationship to the beneficiary are visible prepay: check whether the ordering physician has any evaluation/management claim history for that beneficiary, and whether ordering physicians are geographically remote from the beneficiary. Critically, the re-enrollment of a new DME entity by a principal whose prior supplier was payment-suspended is catchable at enrollment via ownership/officer, address, phone, and bank-account matching.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: suspend brace L-code claims where the ordering NPI has no prior office/telehealth encounter with the beneficiary within a lookback window, or where multi-brace 'combo' orders exceed the peer percentile per ordering NPI. Enrollment control: graph-match new DME applications on owner/officer SSN, address, phone, bank account and billing agent against suspended or revoked suppliers and deny/hold pending review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Minhaj Feroz Muhammad (owner/controller of clinical laboratories); Sufyan Feroze (owner/controller of clinical laboratories)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Two brothers allegedly owned and controlled, sometimes through straw owners, four clinical laboratories in Illinois and California that submitted over $293 million in claims to Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for COVID-19 laboratory testing never performed, collecting about $65 million, then moved proceeds between their labs and businesses to buy overseas real estate, gold bars, luxury watches and vehicles.
WaysToIdentify: Rapid ramp-up of COVID test billing volume with no corresponding ordering-provider footprint, specimen collection sites, or beneficiary encounter history is visible prepay, as is billing volume implausible for the lab's staffing, CLIA certificate scope and site capacity. Straw ownership is detectable at enrollment by matching listed owners against the true controlling parties through shared addresses, bank accounts, and cross-lab billing-agent and claim-pattern identity across the four labs.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab capacity model: per CLIA/NPI compute daily test volume, distinct beneficiary states, and tests per FTE/analyzer against the certificate scope, and auto-suspend payment when volume exceeds the calibrated capacity or growth percentile. Add an entity-linkage feature clustering labs on shared bank accounts, addresses, billing agents and overlapping beneficiary rosters and place linked clusters on prepay review with documentation requests for requisitions and result reports.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Cassandra Marie Strube (administrator at nursing and senior living facilities)
SchemeSummary: While employed as an administrator at at least five nursing and senior living facilities, Strube stole fentanyl patches, hydrocodone, morphine, and oxycodone from the facilities' narcotics emergency kits and locked medication carts and rooms; she was sentenced to three years' probation and ordered to pay $1,975.61 restitution, a $5,000 fine, and a $200 special assessment.
WaysToIdentify: This is internal drug diversion by a facility administrator, not billed claims, so it is not visible at adjudication; the detection route is facility controlled-substance inventory reconciliation and PDMP/dispensing-to-administration matching after the fact. Signals include emergency-kit and cart counts that do not reconcile to MAR administrations, repeated 'wastage' or missing patches, and the same employee present across multiple facilities with discrepancies.
FeaturesToCreate: Require and ingest per-facility controlled-substance reconciliation feeds: unit of observation is drug-facility-shift; compute dispensed/kit-stocked units minus MAR-documented administrations plus witnessed waste, and fire an alert when unexplained variance exceeds the calibrated threshold. Add a cross-facility employee-linkage rule that aggregates variance by staff member on duty and refers repeat outliers to the MFCU and licensing board.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Mohammed Asif (owner and director of American Labworks LLC); American Labworks LLC (diagnostic testing laboratory)
SchemeSummary: Asif, listed as owner/director of American Labworks LLC in Everett, WA, allegedly conspired to bill Medicare more than $8.7 million (over $1.1 million paid) for COVID-19 and respiratory illness lab tests that were never ordered or performed, using referring-physician names without authorization, including dates of service after the beneficiary or the referring physician had died; he withdrew $260,000 from the lab's account and returned to India.
WaysToIdentify: Fully prepay-detectable: claim lines carrying a referring-physician NPI that is deceased or has no other claim relationship with the beneficiary, and service dates after the beneficiary's date of death, are contradictions in Medicare's own enrollment and PECOS data. Also check that the lab's CLIA/test-site license is active and in scope on the date of service, and monitor rapid draw-down of payments by a foreign-resident owner.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits: reject lab claims where ordering NPI date of death precedes DOS, where beneficiary date of death precedes DOS, or where the ordering NPI has zero encounter claims with that beneficiary in the lookback window. Add an active-CLIA/license-on-DOS edit and auto-suspend payments to any lab exceeding the calibrated percentile for share of claims tied to a single or unverified ordering NPI, with a requisition documentation request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Mohammed Asif (owner and director of American Labworks LLC); American Labworks LLC (diagnostic testing laboratory)
SchemeSummary: Asif, owner/director of American Labworks LLC in Everett, WA, conspired to bill Medicare more than $8.7 million for COVID-19 and other respiratory illness lab tests that were never ordered or performed, using referring-physician names without authorization (some physicians and beneficiaries were deceased on the claimed service dates) and continuing after the lab's test-site license expired; Medicare paid over $1.1 million, which Asif withdrew from the lab's bank account, including a $260,000 withdrawal before fleeing to India.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic: deceased referring physicians and deceased beneficiaries on service dates, plus continued billing after the test-site license expired, all verifiable at adjudication from PECOS, enrollment date-of-death and CLIA status files. Physician complaints of unauthorized NPI use and absent requisitions provide corroboration on documentation request.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a license-validity edit that denies lab claims with DOS outside the CLIA/test-site effective period, and date-of-death edits on both beneficiary and ordering NPI. Add an ordering-NPI concentration and 'no prior relationship' feature that triggers prepay suspension and requisition/result documentation requests before any further payment release.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Indiana
FraudEntity: Patients Choice Laboratories (PCL) (diagnostic laboratory)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: PCL allegedly used a $5,000/month sham 'Marketing Services Agreement' with an infection prevention company (paying it about $1.86 million total) and paid 1099 sales reps commissions of at least $372,000 based on referral volume, to obtain referrals for respiratory pathogen panels; the company swabbed long-term care residents for COVID-19 and PCL used the same specimens to bill Medicare for medically unnecessary RPPs at 43 facilities (sometimes billing RPPs with no COVID test performed), collecting over $6 million.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals: respiratory pathogen panel claims billed in bulk for long-term-care residents from a handful of facilities, RPPs billed without a paired COVID test or diagnosis supporting panel-level testing, and near-identical panel utilization per resident regardless of symptoms. The kickback structure (flat-fee marketing agreement plus per-referral 1099 commissions) is only visible in the lab's contracts and payment ledgers, so that is a post-payment/audit or whistleblower route, but the utilization pattern alone supports prepay review.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an RPP medical-necessity edit: unit of observation is beneficiary-DOS; require a documented symptom/diagnosis code and flag RPPs billed without a same-episode COVID or targeted test, denying or pending lines that fail. Add a facility-cluster feature computing share of a lab's RPP volume from a small set of LTC facilities and per-resident RPP frequency versus peers, triggering prepay review plus a request for the lab's marketing and sales-compensation agreements.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Timothy Mark Anderson (Iowa licensed attorney providing Medicaid eligibility planning services)
SchemeSummary: Attorney assisting elderly clients with Iowa Medicaid nursing home eligibility took a $186,000 check from a client and transferred her a wrecked, inoperable 1961 Rolls Royce, then submitted documents to Iowa Medicaid falsely valuing the car at $194,000 so the couple's over $400,000 in assets would be sheltered under the one-automobile exclusion and Father-1 would qualify for Medicaid-funded nursing home care.
WaysToIdentify: Detectable at eligibility determination, not claim adjudication: the asset workup showed a $186,000 transfer out and a claimed $194,000 vehicle under the one-automobile exclusion, a valuation wildly inconsistent with a 1961 vehicle's condition and with any independent valuation guide or title/registration record. The same attorney appearing as representative across many LTC eligibility applications with unusual exclusion claims is a second, list-level signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an eligibility-application edit: when a claimed excluded asset's declared value exceeds the calibrated percentile of book value for that make/model/year, or when a large cash transfer within the lookback window is offset by an asset acquisition of similar value, auto-require independent appraisal and title/inspection documents before approval. Add a representative-level analytic aggregating applications by preparer attorney/agent and flagging preparers with outlier rates of high-value exclusion claims for audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Kevin M. Whitman (individual falsely claiming to be a physician)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Whitman, not a licensed physician and without a DEA registration, allegedly posed as a medical doctor and used a DEA Registration Number belonging to Strong Memorial Hospital to issue 177 Schedule II prescriptions (173 for oxycodone, 38,067 dosage units) to nine individuals; a fake University of Rochester Medical School diploma was recovered from his residence.
WaysToIdentify: Detectable at dispensing and in PDMP data: Schedule II prescriptions written under a hospital's institutional DEA number but signed by a prescriber name with no matching state medical license or individual DEA registration, and 177 scripts to only nine patients at high dosage units. Pharmacies could have validated prescriber license/DEA at fill; PDMP could flag an institutional DEA number generating outpatient oxycodone scripts for a narrow patient set.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay/point-of-sale edit: validate the prescriber's individual DEA registration and active state license against the name on the script and reject controlled-substance claims where the DEA number is institutional or the prescriber identity does not resolve. Add a PDMP monitor computing per-DEA-number outpatient CII volume, patient count, and dosage units, alerting the registrant hospital and DEA when an institutional number exceeds the calibrated pattern.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Charmaine Gatlin (former Chief Operating Officer of Jackson Health Foundation)
State_County: Florida - Miami-Dade County (Miami); Florida - Broward County (Weston)
SchemeSummary: As COO of the Jackson Health Foundation, the nonprofit fundraising arm of Miami's Jackson Health System, Gatlin allegedly approved and submitted at least $3.6 million in false vendor invoices for goods and services never provided to the Foundation, including roughly $2 million to a Georgia audiovisual vendor that kicked back $1 million to her, plus invoices used to buy designer goods from Louis Vuitton, Gucci and Apple and a rose gold golf cart delivered to her home; charged as wire fraud conspiracy, wire fraud and money laundering.
WaysToIdentify: No health-insurance claims are involved; this is vendor-invoice embezzlement inside a hospital foundation, so no payer adjudication control applies. Detection sits with the organization's accounts-payable controls: new vendors added and approved by the same executive who approves payment, invoices lacking purchase orders or receiving evidence, vendor addresses/bank accounts matching an employee, and consumer-retail purchases run through vendor accounts.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement AP anomaly controls at the paying organization: unit of observation is invoice; fire when the requester and approver are the same person, when a vendor is new within a short window and receives outsized payments, or when vendor bank/address data matches employee records, holding disbursement pending independent verification. Add merchant-category screening on card and vendor payments to route luxury-retail purchases to internal audit.

WaysToIdentify: Not a fraud case — it is a personnel announcement about a U.S. Attorney being sworn in, with no claims, provider or payment component. There is nothing for a payer to detect.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Lino Mallari Gutierrez a/k/a 'Joe Gutierrez' (owner/operator of two DME companies); unnamed co-conspirators (straw owners)
State_County: Florida - Martin County (Palm City); Florida - Middle District of Florida
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Gutierrez and co-conspirators operated two DME companies held in the names of straw owners and billed Medicare more than $10.9 million (over $5 million paid) for medically unnecessary orthotic braces. They paid kickbacks to marketing companies that used call centers to solicit Medicare beneficiaries and telemedicine companies to obtain signed doctors' orders, and Gutierrez filed false records with his employer and a regulatory organization and moved Medicare proceeds between accounts after learning of law enforcement action.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals: brace L-code claims where the ordering physician's only contact was a brief telehealth encounter from a telemarketing-sourced call center, orders concentrated on a few telemedicine NPIs, and beneficiaries geographically dispersed far from the supplier. Straw ownership is catchable at enrollment by matching listed owners against the true controller through shared addresses, phones, bank accounts and prior enrollment history and by verifying disclosure filings.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: pend brace claims whose ordering NPI is a telehealth-only prescriber with no in-person or longitudinal encounter history with the beneficiary, and cap/deny multi-brace bundles above the peer percentile per ordering NPI. Enrollment control: run identity/ownership graph checks on DME applications (owner, officer, address, bank, billing agent) and require site visits plus payment holds for suppliers whose brace-to-total-billing mix and telehealth ordering share exceed calibrated thresholds.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Paul Njoku (owner and CEO of Opnet Health Care Services Inc., d/b/a P & P Health Care Services); Opnet Health Care Services Inc. d/b/a P & P Health Care Services
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Njoku's home health agency billed Medicare over $400,000 (receiving over $360,000) for home health services without maintaining required documentation; when Medicare requested records, he and others cut out and taped old physician/nurse signatures onto newly created doctors' orders, nursing notes and assessments, including using a departed nurse's signature without consent, and bribed a doctor to approve home health services.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay detectable through targeted documentation review: a new or low-volume HHA billing episodes with a single certifying physician, and a documentation response containing cut-and-pasted, photocopied or misaligned signatures and notes signed by a nurse no longer employed on the date of service. Cross-check certifying physician face-to-face encounter claims and nurse license/employment dates against visit notes.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay documentation-request workflow for HHAs above the peer percentile on episodes per certifying physician and on new-provider billing ramp; require submission of orders, F2F encounter notes and visit logs before payment. Add automated authenticity checks on submitted records: signature-image hashing to detect reuse of identical signature bitmaps across documents and validation that each signer's license and employment period covers the documented visit date, with clinician-attribution mismatches triggering payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Ndubuisi Joseph Okafor, M.D. (sole practitioner and owner of Okafor Medical Associates)
SchemeSummary: Okafor, sole owner of an internal medicine clinic in Northwest Washington D.C., prescribed oxycodone and promethazine with codeine for cash after minimal or no examination, including to undercover agents, confidential sources, and individuals using false identities whom he knew were diverting the drugs; the scheme spanned at least 45 states and hundreds of thousands of units. He also created backdated medical records for one patient after a complaint was filed with the D.C. Board of Health.
WaysToIdentify: Visible in PDMP and pharmacy claims before further fills: one internal-medicine NPI issuing oxycodone and promethazine-with-codeine to patients drawn from dozens of states, cash-pay visits with no corresponding E/M claims, high units per prescription, and multiple patients sharing addresses or presenting inconsistent identities. Backdated records only appear on audit, so records authenticity is a post-hoc route.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber controlled-substance profile: per NPI compute share of CII/cough-syrup scripts, MME per patient, patient count outside the practice's home state/radius, and absence of paired office-visit claims, firing an alert and pharmacy point-of-sale hold when multiple indicators exceed calibrated peer percentiles. Add a patient-identity dedup check across scripts (shared address/phone, mismatched demographics) and refer flagged prescribers to licensing board and DEA.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division (Fraud Section); U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
SchemeSummary: Not a specific fraud case: the Justice Department announced the expansion of its Health Care Fraud Unit's New England Strike Force into the District of Massachusetts, noting that in FY 2025 the U.S. Attorney's Office's Health Care Fraud and Affirmative Civil Enforcement Units recovered more than $450 million in fraudulently obtained funds.
WaysToIdentify: Not a specific fraud case — it is an announcement of a strike-force expansion and an annual recovery total, with no identifiable scheme mechanic, provider or claim set. No pre-payment signal exists to detect.
FeaturesToCreate: No case-specific control applies; the nearest applicable payer action is to align referral pipelines and data-sharing with the strike force's geography (e.g., routing regional outlier provider lists from existing prepay analytics to that office). Tag the item as a non-case press release and exclude from feature derivation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois; Justice Department Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Offices for the Northern District of Illinois, Middle District of Florida, District of Maryland, Eastern District of New York and Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Walgreens Boots Alliance Inc.; Walgreen Co. and various subsidiaries (national pharmacy chain)
State_County: Nationwide (United States), including Illinois; Florida; Maryland; New York (Eastern District); Virginia
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; other federal health care programs (TRICARE/Defense Health Agency, OPM, DOL programs referenced)
SchemeSummary: DOJ civil False Claims Act/Controlled Substances Act complaint alleging Walgreens pharmacists filled millions of controlled substance prescriptions (excessive opioid quantities, early refills, opioid/benzodiazepine/muscle relaxant 'trinity' combinations) despite clear red flags of illegitimacy, while corporate policies pressured pharmacists to fill quickly and withheld prescriber information, then billed Medicare, Medicaid and other federal health programs for those unlawful prescriptions. Case originated from four qui tam whistleblower suits, now consolidated with U.S. intervention; no liability determination yet.
WaysToIdentify: All the red flags cited are present in pharmacy claims data at adjudication: excessive daily MME, early refills before the prior day's-supply is exhausted, concurrent opioid+benzodiazepine+muscle relaxant 'trinity' fills, long travel distances between patient, prescriber and pharmacy, and cash-then-bill patterns. A payer can also see store-level and prescriber-level concentration of these patterns and the absence of documented resolution of red flags.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay POS edits: reject or require prior authorization for fills exceeding the calibrated MME threshold, refills before the calibrated percent of days supply elapsed, and trinity combinations without an override reason code documenting the pharmacist's red-flag resolution. Add store- and chain-level scorecards on rate of red-flag fills and per-prescriber concentration, with network-level corrective action, payment suspension, or exclusion referral for outliers.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Vida Med Center LLC (purported DME company); Med-Union Medical Center, Inc. (purported DME company)
SchemeSummary: Two Medicare-enrolled DME companies allegedly submitted a combined $33 million in false claims for durable medical equipment that was medically unnecessary and not provided as represented (Vida Med billed $14.1M and was paid $8.76M; Med-Union billed $19.0M and was paid $14.2M, all paid claims resting on prescriptions from a single provider). The government filed two civil forfeiture complaints seeking $967,760.37 and $10,014,325.40 in fraud proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay detectable: every paid claim rested on prescriptions from a single ordering provider, an extreme ordering-NPI concentration measurable at adjudication, coupled with high per-beneficiary equipment volume, beneficiaries far from the supplier, and no prior treatment relationship between the ordering provider and the beneficiaries. Delivery-proof and medical-necessity failures surface on documentation request before payment release.
FeaturesToCreate: Compute per-supplier Herfindahl-style concentration of ordering NPIs and the share of billed dollars from the top ordering provider; when concentration and growth exceed calibrated percentiles, place the supplier on prepay review requiring proof of delivery and medical-necessity documentation. Add reciprocal ordering-provider monitoring that suspends payment when one NPI's DME order volume exceeds same-specialty peer percentiles or lacks corresponding E/M encounters.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Marieva Briceno (owner of three purported medical clinics)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Briceno owned three purported medical clinics in the Detroit area that paid Medicare beneficiaries to undergo unnecessary tests and procedures, then billed Medicare approximately $5,460,323 for those medically unnecessary services, of which Medicare paid about $2,998,322 (Briceno personally received about $513,200). She later concealed the fraud on her naturalization application; after a 2012 guilty plea and 60-month sentence, a court revoked her U.S. citizenship on Nov. 17, 2025.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals: clinics with beneficiary rosters that are shared across the owner's multiple clinic NPIs, patients traveling long distances, uniform batteries of diagnostic tests per visit regardless of diagnosis, and beneficiaries appearing at several unrelated clinics on the same day — a marker of paid patient recruitment. Beneficiary interviews and complaint data about cash payments provide confirmation; common ownership across the three clinics is verifiable at enrollment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-sharing/recruitment detector: unit of observation is beneficiary-month; flag beneficiaries appearing across multiple commonly-owned clinics and clinics whose share of such shared beneficiaries or same-day test-battery uniformity exceeds calibrated peer percentiles, triggering prepay review and beneficiary verification letters. Link clinics by owner/address/bank at enrollment so suspensions apply to all entities of the same principal.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida; Justice Department Civil Division, Office of Immigration Litigation
FraudEntity: Marieva Briceno (owner of three purported medical clinics)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Briceno owned three purported medical clinics in the Detroit area that paid Medicare beneficiaries to undergo medically unnecessary tests and procedures, and she and co-conspirators billed Medicare approximately $5.46 million for those services, of which Medicare paid about $3 million (Briceno personally received roughly $513,200). She pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit health care fraud in 2012 and received 60 months; on Nov. 17, 2025 a court revoked her U.S. citizenship because she had concealed the fraud during naturalization.
WaysToIdentify: The signature signal is beneficiary sharing and travel: the same small pool of Medicare beneficiaries appearing across three commonly-owned Detroit clinics receiving identical diagnostic test batteries, often with beneficiaries residing far from the clinic or clustered by recruiter address. Enrollment data linking the three clinics to one owner plus abnormally high tests-per-beneficiary and high new-patient-to-test conversion is visible at adjudication. Payment of beneficiaries is only provable by interview, but the claim pattern (no treatment following abnormal test results, no continuity of care) is prepay-visible.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a common-ownership cluster entity (link clinics by owner/officer TIN, address, bank account from PECOS) and compute per-cluster shared-beneficiary rate, diagnostic tests per beneficiary per quarter, and beneficiary-to-clinic distance distribution versus same-specialty peers; fire prepay review when multiple metrics exceed calibrated percentiles. Add a beneficiary-level edit for repeated identical test panels at commonly-owned sites with no follow-up treatment claims, requiring records before payment. On naturalization/exclusion checks, re-screen owners of clustered high-risk clinics at revalidation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs / Criminal Division (Money Laundering and Asset Recovery Section)
FraudEntity: Bernard L. Madoff (chairman, Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities LLC); The Western Union Company; Olalekan Jacob Ponle; Aydin Kalantarov, Zaur Kalantarli and Ali Kalantarli; Michael Little; Thuy Tien Luong (nail salon owner); Richard J. Sherwood and Thomas K. Lagan (attorneys)
FraudTypeAll: Other - Unknown; Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: General DOJ Asset Forfeiture Program announcement, not a single health care fraud case: it reports that over $12 billion in forfeited assets has been paid to crime victims (over $735.3 million in FY2024-early FY2025) and summarizes unrelated remission examples, including the Madoff Ponzi scheme, Western Union consumer fraud, business email compromise scams (one against a health care company that wired $1,652,254 to fraudulent malpractice-insurance wire instructions, of which $1,100,694 was recovered), fictitious-corporation EIDL loan fraud, bogus fuel tax credit refund fraud, forced labor, and estate embezzlement.
WaysToIdentify: No payer claims-payment component: this is a DOJ asset forfeiture/remission announcement covering Ponzi, wire, EIDL and tax matters. The only health-care-adjacent element is a business email compromise that redirected a company's insurance premium wire, which is treasury/vendor-payment controls, not claim adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control is payer-side vendor and payee integrity: verify any change to bank routing details for provider or vendor payments through out-of-band callback to a pre-registered number, hold the first payment after any EFT change for a cooling-off period, and alert when multiple providers point to one newly added bank account. No claims edit applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Dr. Scott Taggart Roethle (telemedicine physician, anesthesiologist)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Drug_Prescriptions
SchemeSummary: A telemedicine doctor contracted with multiple health care companies and, via electronic portals, signed orders for medically unnecessary durable medical equipment, pain creams and genetic tests for thousands of patients he never evaluated or followed up with, receiving roughly $30 per order and $674,000 total from five companies; Medicare paid at least $1.5 million on his orders, with the government asserting total loss of $7 million to $9.5 million.
WaysToIdentify: The ordering physician's NPI appears as ordering provider on thousands of DME, compounded pain cream and genetic test claims with no corresponding evaluation or management claim by him or anyone in his group, and with beneficiaries scattered nationwide across many states. Order volume per day per ordering NPI and the ratio of orders to billed patient encounters are both computable at adjudication before the supplier claim is paid.
FeaturesToCreate: For each ordering NPI, compute per-day and per-month counts of DME/genetic/compound orders, the share of ordered items with no prior E/M or telehealth visit by that NPI within a look-back window, count of distinct billing suppliers relying on that NPI, and geographic spread of beneficiaries; fire a prepay edit denying or pending supplier claims whose ordering NPI exceeds calibrated peer percentiles on order-without-visit share. Escalate ordering NPIs used by three or more unrelated suppliers to payment suspension and records request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: Jacqueline Brewster (travel nurse at Raleigh General Hospital)
SchemeSummary: A travel nurse used her own biometrics plus patients' individually identifiable health information to check out hydromorphone from automated dispensing cabinets at Raleigh General Hospital, siphoned off part of each vial and diluted the remainder to look full, then canceled/nulled the transactions to hide the diversion for her personal use.
WaysToIdentify: This is internal drug diversion, not a claim-payment scheme, so it is invisible in claims; the detectable data is the automated dispensing cabinet audit trail — high hydromorphone withdrawal counts per nurse-shift, frequent cancel/null transactions, withdrawals under patients not assigned to that nurse, and mismatch between cabinet dispenses and eMAR administrations/wastage witnessing. Pharmacy inventory reconciliation and patient pain-score non-response provide corroboration post hoc.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a nurse-shift level diversion model joining ADC transaction logs, staffing/assignment rosters and eMAR: compute controlled-substance withdrawals per shift, cancelled/nulled transaction rate, unwitnessed waste rate, and dispenses for non-assigned patients, all normalized to unit peers; fire an alert and pharmacy audit plus cabinet access review above calibrated percentiles. Payer-side, no prepay claim edit applies; add post-pay review of 340B/inventory reconciliation for units with anomalies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Timothy Gaines Pollard (owner, Tim Pollard Construction)
SchemeSummary: Owner of a residential remodeling and fence installation business withheld federal income, Social Security and Medicare employment taxes from employees' paychecks from 2019 through 2021 but never remitted them to the United States, instead using the funds for personal expenses, causing a tax loss over $400,000.
WaysToIdentify: Pure employment tax fraud by a remodeling and fence business with no claims submitted to any health plan; nothing in claims adjudication would surface it. Detection route is IRS matching of W-2 withholding reported to Social Security against Form 941 deposits.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. If any payer relationship existed, the nearest analogue is enrollment-time and revalidation screening of an owner's tax-lien/unremitted-payroll-tax status as a financial-risk factor feeding elevated review category.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Seoul Medical Group Inc. (Medicare Advantage provider); Advanced Medical Management Inc. (wholly-owned subsidiary); Dr. Min Young Cha (founder and former president); Renaissance Imaging Medical Associates Inc. (radiology group)
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Los Angeles/Koreatown; Northridge)
SchemeSummary: Seoul Medical Group and Dr. Cha allegedly submitted diagnosis codes for two severe spinal conditions (spinal enthesopathy and sacroiliitis) for patients who did not have them, inflating risk scores so CMS paid Medicare Advantage plans more, a portion of which was passed to Seoul Medical Group; when an MA Plan questioned the enthesopathy diagnoses, Renaissance Imaging created radiology reports appearing to support them. Settlement totals $62.85 million across defendants ($58.74M Seoul/AMM, $1.76M Cha, $2.35M Renaissance).
WaysToIdentify: Risk-adjustment abuse shows as a sudden, group-wide spike in the prevalence of two narrow, high-RAF spinal codes (spinal enthesopathy, sacroiliitis) among one provider group's MA members, far above same-region same-specialty peers, and codes appearing only on chart-review/addenda rather than on treatment-bearing encounters. Absence of corroborating claims (no imaging at the time, no spine-directed therapy or specialist care) and retro-dated radiology reports supplied only after a plan query are strong prepay/pre-submission signals inside the plan's encounter pipeline.
