FeaturesToCreate: At the provider-group level, compute prevalence and year-over-year delta for each high-RAF diagnosis versus peers, plus the share of those diagnoses lacking any supporting service claim (imaging, injection, PT, specialist visit) within a look-back/look-forward window; suppress unsupported codes from RAF submission and open targeted chart validation above calibrated percentiles. Flag radiology reports whose creation/interpretation date postdates the plan's diagnosis inquiry, and audit addendum-only diagnoses from vendors.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (federal jury in Detroit)
FraudEntity: Sherif Khalil (owner/operator of Spectra Clinical Labs); Spectra Clinical Labs
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Gardena; Redondo Beach)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Upcoding; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Khalil, owner of Spectra Clinical Labs, paid marketers a percentage of Medicare reimbursements—concealed by routing payments through nominally independent marketing companies he secretly controlled—to induce orders for the highest-reimbursing urine drug testing panels; marketers trained doctors' office staff to send Spectra orders for medically unnecessary tests physicians never authorized, causing Medicare to pay over $4 million.
WaysToIdentify: The lab's mix is skewed to the highest-reimbursing definitive UDT panels with near-uniform panel size per beneficiary regardless of clinical context, and referrals concentrate in a handful of practices whose staff — not the physician — generated orders. Payer can see reflex-to-definitive without presumptive testing, identical panels across unrelated diagnoses, and ordering NPIs whose UDT volume is wildly out of line with their own visit volume; percentage-of-collections marketing paid through shell entities is visible in enrollment/ownership disclosures and post-pay financial audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Per billing lab, compute distribution of UDT panel tiers, mean analytes per specimen, share of definitive tests without a preceding presumptive test or documented medical necessity diagnosis, and Herfindahl concentration of ordering NPIs; fire prepay pend and documentation request on high-tier panels above calibrated peer percentiles. Add an ordering-NPI edit comparing UDT orders to that NPI's own E/M encounters, and cross-reference lab-disclosed contractor addresses/officers against the lab's own owners to detect self-controlled marketing entities at enrollment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Fadel Alshalabi (owner/CEO, Crestar Labs, LLC); Samuel Harris (owner, Flojo Recruiting d/b/a Secure Health); Benjamin Toh, M.D. (telemedicine doctor); Edward D. Klapp (former VP of Sales, Crestar Labs); Melissa L. Chastain (owner/CEO, Genetix LLC); Roger Allison (President, Genetix); Dakota White (former Director of Client Services/VP Operations, Crestar Labs); Robert Alan Richardson (principal, Freedom Medical Labs, LLC); Edward Burch (principal, Freedom Medical Labs, LLC); Elizabeth H. Turner (owner, Advanced Tele-Genetic Counseling)
State_County: Tennessee - Spring Hill (Maury/Williamson County); Texas; Maryland; Utah; South Carolina; Illinois - Chicago
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Marketing companies recruited elderly and low-income Medicare/Medicaid beneficiaries at senior health fairs, door-to-door and in low-income neighborhoods to collect genetic samples; purported telemedicine doctors such as Dr. Toh were paid $20 per order to sign lab orders for patients they never contacted, and Crestar Labs billed Medicare and Medicaid often over $10,000 per genetic test, then paid over $12 million in kickbacks to the marketers. Across the conspiracy over $129 million was billed and over $35 million paid; Alshalabi got 5 years, Harris 30 months, Toh 13 months plus $495,000 restitution, with restitution for Alshalabi and Harris and sentences for seven other defendants pending.
WaysToIdentify: Cancer/hereditary panel claims billed at very high unit values for beneficiaries with no oncologist, no family-history workup and no treating relationship, all funneled through a handful of telemedicine ordering NPIs signing hundreds of orders per day across many states. Recruitment shows up as tight geographic clusters of beneficiaries (same neighborhoods, senior centers) sharing an ordering NPI and specimen collection date; kickbacks to marketers are visible only in post-pay financial records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-NPI daily order counter and an order-without-encounter ratio for molecular/genetic CPT codes, plus a beneficiary-cluster detector keying on collection date, ZIP cluster and shared ordering NPI; auto-pend high-dollar genetic claims failing the treating-relationship test and demand the physician's evaluation record before payment. Cap and prepay-review new labs whose genetic billing per beneficiary exceeds calibrated peer percentiles, and place payment suspension on labs whose top ordering NPIs are shared with other flagged labs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Laboratory Corporation of America Holdings; Laboratory Corporation of America; Labcorp Tennessee, LLC; University Health System, Inc. (operator of University of Tennessee Medical Center)
SchemeSummary: UHS and Labcorp Tennessee allegedly held, or cancelled and resubmitted, physician orders for Caris laboratory tests until more than 14 days after a Medicare beneficiary's hospital discharge, circumventing Medicare's Date of Service/14-Day Rule so the lab could bill Medicare directly instead of billing the hospital; they paid $388,667.17 to resolve a qui tam suit (relator received $73,846.76), while Caris separately paid $2.8M in EDNY.
WaysToIdentify: The 14-Day Rule violation is arithmetically visible: compare the lab claim's date of service and specimen collection date to the beneficiary's inpatient discharge date on the hospital claim, and look for order/claim dates clustering just past day 14. Systematic clustering of specimen-collection-to-billing intervals at 15-16 days post-discharge for one lab, plus cancelled-and-resubmitted claim histories for the same specimen, is detectable at adjudication once inpatient stay data is joined.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a claim-level edit joining outpatient reference-lab claims to the beneficiary's recent inpatient/outpatient discharge record: if specimen collection occurred during or within 14 days of the stay, deny the lab's direct bill and route to the hospital as bundled. Add a lab-level monitor for the distribution of days-from-discharge-to-DOS spiking immediately after day 14, and a duplicate/void-and-rebill detector on the same specimen ID or accession, both triggering audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Christopher Grottenthaler (former CEO, True Health Diagnostics, LLC); Hong Davis, M.D. (physician); Elizabeth Seymour, M.D. (physician); Courtney Love (former True Health Account Executive/marketer); Stephen Kash (former True Health Director of Strategic Accounts/marketer); Laura Howard (former Boston Heart Area Sales Manager/marketer); Jeffrey Parnell (former Boston Heart sales representative/marketer); Stanley Jones (part-owner, LGRB Management Services LLC); Jordan Perkins (co-owner, Next Level Healthcare Consultants LLC); Ruben Marioni (co-owner, Next Level Healthcare Consultants LLC)
State_County: Texas - Collin County (Frisco, Plano); Texas - Denton County (Denton); Texas - Dallas County (Dallas); Texas - Milam County (Rockdale); Massachusetts - Middlesex County (Framingham)
SchemeSummary: Marketers, including employees of laboratory True Health Diagnostics and Boston Heart Diagnostics, paid physicians kickbacks disguised as investment distributions from purported management service organizations (Ascend MSO, Herculis MG, Eridanus MG) to induce referrals of lab tests to True Health, Boston Heart, and Little River Healthcare, which were then billed to Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE; the CEO also arranged kickbacks disguised as consulting fees, processing/handling fees, and copay/deductible waivers. Settlements total $6,068,462 across the CEO ($4.25M), two physicians ($358,842), and seven marketers ($1,459,620).
WaysToIdentify: Kickbacks dressed as MSO investment distributions leave two traces: physician-owners appearing in ownership disclosures of management entities whose only economic activity tracks their referral volume, and referral volume to the specific labs rising in lockstep with distributions. At adjudication the payer can see abrupt shifts of a physician's entire lab book to one out-of-state lab, high-dollar cardiovascular/panel testing per patient, and zero patient cost-share collection (copay/deductible waiver) on those claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Correlate, per referring NPI, monthly test volume/allowed dollars to each lab and flag step changes plus single-lab concentration above calibrated peer percentiles; cross-match physician ownership disclosures and MSO/officer names against lab owners and marketer entities at enrollment to build a relationship graph and pend claims where a referral crosses a financial-interest edge. Add a routine-waiver detector comparing billed patient responsibility to amounts actually collected (remittance/EOB data or lab's own zero-balance pattern), triggering documentation request and referral to SIU.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Munef Fadhel (owner, Great Lake Transportation, Inc.); Great Lake Transportation, Inc.
SchemeSummary: Fadhel, an owner of Great Lake Transportation, a company providing rides to Medicaid beneficiaries, submitted false records certifying shared rides as individual rides so as to obtain the higher per-trip reimbursement rate, causing a Medicaid loss over $95,000.
WaysToIdentify: Shared rides billed as individual trips are detectable by overlapping trip records: two or more beneficiaries with the same vehicle/driver, same pickup or drop-off address and overlapping time windows, each billed the solo per-trip rate. Trip logs, GPS/telematics and driver IDs submitted with NEMT claims carry the signal at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: At the trip level, cluster claims by driver ID, vehicle, date and time window with pickup/dropoff geocoding; when two or more beneficiaries fall in the same vehicle-time cluster, auto-reprice to the shared-ride rate and deny the excess. Add a provider-level monitor for share of trips billed solo versus peers serving the same facilities, firing prepay review and a request for GPS/manifest records.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Munef Fadhel (owner, Great Lake Transportation, Inc.); Great Lake Transportation, Inc.
SchemeSummary: Fadhel, an owner of a non-emergency medical transportation company serving Medicaid beneficiaries, submitted false records certifying shared rides as individual rides to obtain a higher reimbursement rate, causing over $95,000 in Medicaid losses; he was sentenced to one year probation.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: solo-rate billing for rides physically shared. Payer can detect it prepay by joining trip manifests, driver/vehicle identifiers and GPS timestamps and finding multiple beneficiaries transported in one vehicle over the same interval to the same destination facility.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a vehicle-time clustering edit on NEMT claims (driver+vehicle+date+overlapping time+matching origin/destination) that automatically downcodes to the shared-ride rate; hold claims lacking driver/vehicle/GPS fields pending manifest submission. Track provider-level solo-trip percentage against peers and open audit above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Dr. Henry Goolsby (physician); Patricia Lenae Goolsby (co-founder); Infinite Health Integrative Medical Center (clinic)
SchemeSummary: The physician, his wife and their clinic billed Medicare for surgically implanted neurostimulator electrodes (a procedure requiring a surgery center) when they had actually applied single-use, non-covered 'P-Stim' electro-acupuncture devices behind patients' ears in the office; they agreed to pay $450,000 under the False Claims Act.
WaysToIdentify: Implanted neurostimulator electrode codes billed with an office place of service by a practice with no surgical suite, no anesthesia claim, no facility claim and no implantable device invoice is a self-contradictory claim pattern visible at adjudication. Repetition of the same high-value implant code for the same beneficiary at short intervals (impossible for a true implant) further confirms the P-Stim substitution.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit: deny surgically-implanted neurostimulator/electrode codes when place of service is office, when no companion anesthesia/facility claim exists, or when the same code repeats for the same beneficiary inside a clinically implausible interval; require device invoice/serial number documentation for payment. Add a provider-level counter of implant codes per practice with no ASC affiliation, firing SIU review and prepayment review status.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Charles McKinley Griffin (owner/operator, Transformation Services); Tika Michelle Griffin (owner/operator and president, Transformation Services); Kirk Nathan Evans; Transformation Services
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Charles and Tika Griffin operated Transformation Services, which recruited Medicaid beneficiaries from disadvantaged backgrounds as clients and then submitted bills and records to South Carolina Medicaid for behavioral health services never rendered, and used unlicensed counselors; the entity was set up with Tika Griffin as president after Charles Griffin was barred as a Medicaid provider, concealing his role. All three defendants pleaded guilty; loss at least $246,335.
WaysToIdentify: Two independent prepay signals: rendering-provider identifiers that do not match any active state license for the billed behavioral health service, and a newly enrolled entity whose president/address/phone/bank account link to an already-excluded or terminated provider. Service volume implausible for the staff roster (units per counselor per day) and identical session notes across recruited beneficiaries round it out.
FeaturesToCreate: At enrollment, graph-match new applicants' officers, addresses, phones, bank accounts and email domains against the exclusion/termination list and deny or flag for site visit on any match to a barred individual. At adjudication, validate every rendering NPI against the state licensure file for the billed behavioral health code set and deny unlicensed renderers; add a per-rendering-provider daily service-units cap versus calibrated peers that pends claims and requests attendance documentation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Andrew Voegel-Podadera (anesthesiology resident); Pinnacle Health PC (Seattle-based healthcare provider)
SchemeSummary: Two matters: an anesthesiology resident at Seattle Children's, Harborview and UW Medical Center allegedly diverted fentanyl, hydromorphone and other narcotics for his own use over at least a year by obtaining controlled substances by fraud, sometimes using them while treating patients; separately, Pinnacle Health PC billed Medicare and TRICARE more than $500,000 for an injectable amniotic fluid product (FlowerAmnioFlo) that was experimental and not approved for any diagnosis, resolving False Claims Act liability for $1,115,976.
WaysToIdentify: For the resident diversion, claims show nothing; the signal is in ADC/anesthesia records — controlled substance withdrawals per case versus peer anesthesiologists, waste without witness, and cases where documented administration is less than dispensed. For the amniotic fluid injections, the payer can see an unclassified/experimental biologic billed under a miscellaneous or unlisted code with no FDA approval or covered indication, at high dollars, concentrated in one practice.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a provider-level controlled-substance reconciliation model (dispensed vs administered vs wasted per case, normalized to same-specialty clinicians) generating pharmacy audit alerts, since no prepay claim edit exists. Separately, maintain a coverage table for amniotic/placental and other investigational biologics: hard-deny unlisted/miscellaneous J-codes for non-approved products, require product name, NDC and invoice on the claim, and pend high-dollar unlisted-code claims from any single practice above calibrated volume.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Mindpath Care Centers, North Carolina, PLLC (behavioral health practice); Jeff Williams (former officer); Abigail Sheriff (former officer); Sarah Williams (former officer)
SchemeSummary: The government alleged that Mindpath, North Carolina's largest behavioral health practice, billed Medicare for psychotherapy and medication management sessions without documentation of separate and distinct psychotherapy treatments (separate time), ignoring repeated internal employee complaints about billing fraud; the practice and three former officers paid $1.9 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations arising from a whistleblower suit.
WaysToIdentify: The mechanic is billing an add-on psychotherapy code alongside E/M medication management without separate, timed psychotherapy documentation, so it appears as a practice whose psychotherapy-with-E/M pairing rate and average units-per-prescriber-day far exceed same-specialty peers, sometimes exceeding available clinical minutes in a day. Time-in-session math (sum of timed code minutes per clinician per day versus scheduled hours) is computable prepay from claims alone; internal whistleblower complaints indicate the payer should also weight prior compliance history.
FeaturesToCreate: At clinician-day level, sum minutes implied by all timed codes plus E/M and flag days exceeding plausible working minutes; at practice level compute the share of med-management visits carrying an add-on psychotherapy code versus peers. Above calibrated percentiles, place the practice on prepayment review requiring timed psychotherapy notes (start/stop times, distinct treatment plan) before paying the add-on.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Magaly Travieso (advanced practitioner registered nurse, owner of ProMed Healthcare, L.L.C.); Yudorki Ramirez (former spouse, money laundering); ProMed Healthcare, L.L.C.
PayerName: Medicare; Medicare Advantage Plans; Florida Medicaid; commercial insurance
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Travieso, an APRN who owned ProMed Healthcare clinic, billed over $20 million (receiving over $10 million) to commercial insurers, Medicare/Medicare Advantage and Medicaid for back and shoulder braces, physical therapy and psychosocial rehabilitation/mental health services that were medically unnecessary or never provided, paying patients kickbacks and fabricating progress notes with copied stock patient quotes (including typos) across dozens of elderly patients' records; her former spouse Ramirez laundered roughly $2.07 million of the proceeds into investment accounts and used funds for homes and a Range Rover, with over $6 million in assets forfeited across both defendants (9 years for Travieso, 3 years for Ramirez).
WaysToIdentify: One APRN-owned clinic billing across three unrelated service lines — orthotic braces, PT and psychosocial rehab — for the same elderly beneficiaries is a scope/mix anomaly visible at adjudication, as is service volume exceeding the licensed staff's possible hours. Templated documentation is detectable when records are pulled: identical patient quotes and repeated typos across many charts, i.e., near-duplicate note text; multi-payer coordination would show the same beneficiaries billed identically to Medicare, MA, Medicaid and commercial plans.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a provider service-mix breadth check (distinct unrelated benefit categories billed under one enrollment) and a clinician-day capacity check on timed units versus licensed staff FTE; exceeding calibrated peer percentiles triggers prepayment review with mandatory records. On received documentation, run text-similarity/shingle hashing across the provider's notes and fire on high near-duplicate rates; add a beneficiary-kickback signal (same beneficiaries repeatedly appearing with braces plus behavioral health at one address) and move the provider to payment suspension pending investigation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Magaly Travieso (advanced practitioner registered nurse, owner of ProMed Healthcare, L.L.C.); Yudorki Ramirez (former spouse); ProMed Healthcare, L.L.C.
PayerName: Medicare; Medicare Advantage Plans; Medicaid (Florida); commercial insurance
SchemeSummary: Travieso, an APRN who owned ProMed Healthcare, allegedly submitted over $20 million in fraudulent claims to commercial insurers, Medicare/Medicare Advantage and Medicaid for back and shoulder braces, physical therapy, psychosocial rehabilitation and other mental health services, collecting over $10 million; she and her former spouse Ramirez then allegedly laundered the proceeds into a Range Rover, two Miami residences and investment accounts, leading to seizure of the vehicle and over $4 million from bank accounts.
WaysToIdentify: Same scheme as the companion case: implausible cross-benefit billing (braces, PT, psychosocial rehab) from a single small clinic, with billed units per clinician per day beyond physical capacity and beneficiaries who never received the devices. Rapid ramp in monthly allowed dollars for a newly high-volume APRN-owned enrollment, plus overlap of the same beneficiary rosters across payers, is visible before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Deploy a new-provider velocity monitor (monthly allowed dollars and distinct HCPCS families versus peers with the same specialty and enrollment age) that auto-pends claims on step-change growth; couple it with a clinician-capacity edit on timed units. Add prepay verification for orthotic HCPCS from non-DME-accredited billers, and refer to SIU with payment suspension when device delivery documentation and proof-of-delivery signatures cannot be produced.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Nathan Mathews (owner, Emerald Lane Therapy Services and co-owner, Stars & Stripes Therapy); Jimmie Mathews (co-owner, Stars & Stripes Therapy); Amber Delger (subsequent co-owner, Emerald Lane Therapy Services); Emerald Lane Therapy Services; Stars & Stripes Therapy
SchemeSummary: Owners of two Lawton massage therapy businesses scheduled TRICARE beneficiaries for multiple appointments months in advance and continued billing the Defense Health Agency as if care was delivered even when beneficiaries missed appointments or stopped coming; Emerald Lane also billed under the NPI of an occupational therapist who no longer worked there. The two companies billed over $7 million and were reimbursed nearly $3 million; restitution figures ($1,410,255.66, $632,026.43 and $653,269.00) and sentences (87, 42 and 26 months) span the three defendants.
WaysToIdentify: Billing for pre-scheduled appointments that never occurred shows as perfectly regular, calendar-like claim series per beneficiary continuing without interruption for months, including on holidays or after the beneficiary moved or deployed; beneficiary attestation surveys and explanation-of-benefits confirmations would break it. The NPI misuse is detectable at adjudication by checking whether the rendering provider is still affiliated with the billing entity and whether that NPI's total daily units are physically possible.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a per-beneficiary regularity/periodicity score on repetitive therapy claims (fixed-interval, fixed-unit series with zero gaps and no discharge) that pends the series and triggers a beneficiary verification letter above the calibrated threshold. Validate rendering NPI-to-billing-TIN affiliation and license status on every claim, denying claims for renderers with terminated affiliation, and cap rendering-NPI daily units at a physically possible maximum with prepay pend on breach.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Junyi Liu a/k/a 'Jenny' (licensed acupuncturist, leader of scheme); Noemi Algodon; Mohamed Elmandouh; Gerard Estrella; Ramon Garcia III; Henler Datu Tahil; Jonathan Laqui; Mitzy Baldovino
State_County: New York - New York County (Manhattan); New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Queens County (Queens)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Liu operated acupuncture/physical therapy offices in Manhattan, Brooklyn and Queens that billed Medicare and other insurers for services either not rendered or not as represented, using partner licensed therapists/acupuncturists' provider enrollments and fabricated medical documentation; cash kickbacks were paid to patients to supply insurance information (some never even visited the offices) and kickbacks of cash and wine were given to insurer employees. Liu separately obtained fraudulent COVID-19 unemployment benefits for herself and a family member; restitution of $23,855,425 to insurers, $40,075 to NY DOL, and $15,368,171 forfeiture relate to Liu, with seven co-defendants also pleading guilty.
WaysToIdentify: The scheme rents licensed acupuncturists'/therapists' enrollments across three boroughs, so the signal is one NPI billing implausible daily volumes at multiple locations, shared billing addresses/bank accounts/billing agents across nominally separate practices, and beneficiaries whose only claims are these services with no referring physician. Patient-recruitment kickbacks surface via beneficiary verification letters showing members who never visited; the bribed insurer employees are an internal-controls matter detectable by reviewing which adjudicators repeatedly overrode edits for these providers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-NPI multi-site capacity edit (sum of timed units and locations per NPI per day) plus an ownership/payment graph linking practices by address, phone, bank account and billing agent, pending claims from clusters exceeding calibrated peer percentiles. Add automated beneficiary verification sampling for high-frequency acupuncture/PT series, and an internal audit rule flagging adjudicators/staff with anomalous override or pend-release rates for specific providers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Manishkumar Patel (leader of scheme, script seller)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Drug_Prescriptions; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Patel and a coconspirator obtained DME, pharmaceutical and lab-test scripts by having call centers cold-call Medicare beneficiaries, then converting the call data into orders via cursory telemedicine visits, 'doctor chasing' (doctors signing without seeing patients), or outright forgery, and sold those scripts to DME suppliers, pharmacies and labs that billed Medicare; payments for the scripts were disguised as flat-rate marketing contracts to conceal kickbacks, causing about $48 million in Medicare losses. Patel was ordered to pay $48,150,692.49 restitution and forfeit $6,839,900.
WaysToIdentify: The signal is a single ordering NPI whose orders fan out across unrelated DME suppliers, pharmacies and labs in many states with no prior treating relationship — visible at adjudication by joining the ordering NPI on DME/lab/pharmacy claims to that NPI's own E/M history for the same beneficiary. Telehealth E/M claims billed the same day as high-value braces, topical creams or cancer panels, with the telehealth visit and the item ordered from different geographies, plus beneficiaries clustering to a handful of marketing-linked suppliers, are all pre-pay observable. Forged/'doctor-chased' orders also surface as beneficiary and physician complaints and as orders signed by physicians whose claim history shows no telehealth activity at all.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-physician fan-out edit: per ordering NPI per month, count distinct billing suppliers, distinct states of beneficiary residence, and share of ordered items with no prior face-to-face E/M by that NPI or their group; suspend payment and request the order plus visit documentation when the composite exceeds the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers. Add a claim-level pairing edit that flags DME/lab/pharmacy claims whose only supporting encounter is a telehealth E/M under the calibrated minimum duration or billed by a telemedicine entity with no other care for that beneficiary. Feed physician/beneficiary complaint intake into the same score so complaint volume triggers prepay review of all downstream suppliers sharing that ordering NPI.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Zakia Khan (owner of Happy Family Social Adult Day Care Center Inc., Family Social Adult Day Care Center Inc., Responsible Care Staffing Inc., and Tanwee Services Inc.); marketers employed by Khan; co-defendants
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Khan and marketers she employed paid cash kickbacks and bribes to Medicaid recipients to enroll at her two Brooklyn social adult day care centers, then billed Medicaid over $68 million for social adult day care services that were never provided or were induced by the kickbacks; multiple business entities, including a home health fiscal intermediary and a shell company, were used to launder proceeds and generate the cash for bribes. Khan agreed to forfeit $5 million including two properties, cash and gold jewelry.
WaysToIdentify: Social adult day care billing is attendance-driven, so the payer can compare billed attendance days per site against licensed capacity, staffing rosters and building hours — sustained billing above physical capacity is a pre-pay arithmetic check. Rapid enrollment surges of members recruited by marketers, high geographic dispersion of members relative to the center, and overlap of the same members with a related fiscal intermediary or home health entity under common ownership/address are visible in enrollment and claim data. Kickbacks to members are best confirmed post-pay via member interviews and cash-flow tracing, but the shell-entity common-ownership link is detectable at enrolment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a site-day capacity edit: for each center and service date, sum billed attendance units and compare to licensed capacity times operating hours; deny or pend the excess and require sign-in sheets. Add an enrollment-velocity monitor per center (new members per month, share recruited within a short window, travel distance) that triggers prepay documentation review and member verification calls above the calibrated percentile, and a common-ownership graph linking the center, fiscal intermediaries and shell entities by owner, EIN, address, phone and bank account to force consolidated review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maine
FraudEntity: Joseph Dobie
SchemeSummary: Dobie allegedly used another person's identity to fraudulently obtain Medicaid and SNAP benefits, and was charged by complaint with aggravated identity theft, false statements relating to health care matters, and unlawful use of SNAP benefits as part of the 2025 National Health Care Fraud Takedown.
WaysToIdentify: This is eligibility/identity fraud rather than provider billing: the catchable signal is at enrolment, where the applicant's SSN, name and date of birth do not match the SSA/Death Master and credit-header records, or the same SSN is already active in another state or under another name. Duplicate-identity detection across Medicaid and SNAP eligibility files, and address/phone reuse across cases, are pre-payment checks. Confirmation typically requires identity verification with the true holder.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an eligibility-side identity proofing check that scores every new or renewing application against SSA verification, cross-state duplicate SSN/DOB matches, and reuse of address, phone or bank account across unrelated cases; hold benefit issuance and require in-person identity documents when any hard mismatch or duplicate fires. Add a periodic sweep of active cases against updated death and cross-state enrollment files to suspend issuance mid-cycle.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
SchemeSummary: Not a fraud case: this is a personnel announcement naming Lisa G. Johnston Acting United States Attorney for the Southern District of West Virginia.
WaysToIdentify: No fraud and no claims-payment component — this is a personnel announcement naming an Acting U.S. Attorney, so no payer-side detection signal exists.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. If desired, exclude such press releases from fraud-intelligence ingestion by a source classifier so they do not generate spurious provider risk scores.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Arkansas
FraudEntity: Krameelah Banks (psychologist, owner and operator of Arkansas Behavioral Center)
PayerName: Medicare; Arkansas Blue Cross and Blue Shield
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Banks allegedly billed Medicare and Arkansas Blue Cross for thousands of hours of ongoing psychotherapy in the names of referral patients who were seen only once for pre-surgical psychological evaluations, including billing while vacationing in Florida and Mexico, more than 24 hours of services in a single day, and over 130 sessions for patients who had died, causing over $500,000 in losses; she allegedly created fictitious records to answer claim inquiries and misled the FBI by blaming her calendaring software.
WaysToIdentify: All the tells are arithmetic on the claim line: summed timed psychotherapy units per rendering NPI per day exceeding a plausible workday, service dates after the beneficiary's date of death, and repeated 60-minute sessions for patients whose only other history with that provider is a single pre-surgical evaluation. Provider travel is inferable from a gap between service-date claims and any location/geolocation data, but the impossible-day and post-death checks alone are pre-pay deniable using the eligibility death file and time-unit accumulation.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider daily time accumulator that sums all timed-code minutes across payers-in-network per NPI per date and denies or pends lines once the total exceeds a plausible workday, plus a hard prepay edit denying any service date on or after the eligibility death date. Add a longitudinal profile edit: when a beneficiary's psychotherapy series follows a single evaluation code with no interval progress-note documentation on file, pend and issue a records request, and route providers whose submitted records show identical templated text to investigation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: LiveCare Inc. (remote patient monitoring provider)
SchemeSummary: LiveCare Inc., which provides remote patient monitoring services to Type 2 diabetes patients, allegedly paid a marketing service for referrals of Medicare beneficiaries, causing claims tainted by kickbacks to be submitted to Medicare; resolved through a qui tam civil settlement of up to $4.9 million with no determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: Remote patient monitoring claims concentrated on beneficiaries all sourced from one marketing vendor show up as an abrupt enrollment surge with near-identical diagnosis coding and near-universal billing of the maximum monthly RPM management minutes. At credentialing, ask for and screen marketing agreements for per-referral or per-enrolled-patient compensation; flat 'per lead' terms are the kickback signal. Kickback payments themselves are usually post-pay findings via vendor invoices and bank records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an RPM utilization profile per supplier: share of beneficiaries billed the maximum treatment-management tier, monthly enrollment growth, and concentration of referring NPIs or beneficiary acquisition channels; above the calibrated percentile versus peers, pend claims and request the patient consent, device-transmission logs and any marketing contract. At enrolment/revalidation, require disclosure of marketing arrangements and flag per-referral or per-enrollee compensation structures for review before claims are paid.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Dr. Eric Edward Haeger (physician, sleep clinic owner/supervisor)
SchemeSummary: Physician bought over 500 used, recalled Philips CPAP/BiPAP devices from online resellers, had staff pry out the recalled sound-abatement foam with screwdrivers and hooks outside any clean room, then dispensed the refurbished devices to Washington State Medicaid patients at his sleep clinic and billed Medicaid representing them as new devices in good working order.
WaysToIdentify: Billing new-equipment HCPCS codes requires a serial number and acquisition trail; the payer can require serial numbers on PAP claims and match them against manufacturer recall and prior-billing registries — a serial already billed to another beneficiary or listed on an FDA recall is a prepay denial. Supplier purchase invoices showing acquisition from online resellers rather than authorized distributors, and margins far above peer acquisition cost, are auditable at revalidation. Physical refurbishment is only provable on site inspection, the post-pay route.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a serial-number edit for capped-rental and purchased DME: require the device serial on the claim, deny when the serial is absent, previously billed to a different beneficiary, or appears on an active FDA recall list, and flag new-vs-used modifier mismatches. Add a supplier-level check comparing invoiced acquisition sources against authorized-distributor lists at revalidation, triggering prepay review and site inspection when secondary-market purchases are detected.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Eric Ndungu Mwangi (Kenyan national, owner of Linear Diagnostics); Linear Diagnostics (LD); Davendra Rampersaud (Guyanese national, owner of Caribbean Medical Supplies, Inc.); Caribbean Medical Supplies, Inc. (CMS)
PayerName: U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) - KEMSA Medical Commodities Program
FraudType: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
FraudTypeAll: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Mwangi and his company Linear Diagnostics systematically stole USAID-funded HIV test kits and other health commodities intended for Kenya's government supply authority (KEMSA), selling them to Rampersaud and his Guyanese company CMS for over $177,000; Rampersaud fraudulently obtained a 'Letter of Authority' as an authorized distributor to win a sole-source contract with the Guyana Ministry of Health and resold the stolen USAID commodities to the Guyanese government. Rampersaud pleaded guilty, received credit for time served, three years supervised release and an $84,000 fine; Mwangi remains charged and is awaiting trial in Kenya.
WaysToIdentify: No health-plan claims were paid — this is theft and diversion of donor-funded commodities plus fraudulent distributor authorization, so the controls are grant/supply-chain, not claim adjudication. The observable signals are inventory reconciliation gaps between shipped and received quantities at the recipient authority, and unverified 'Letter of Authority' documents presented in sole-source procurement.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control: a commodity reconciliation feature that matches donor shipment manifests to recipient warehouse receipts and downstream dispensing counts by lot/serial, firing on unexplained variance, plus an authenticity check that verifies claimed distributor authorization letters directly with the named manufacturer before any sole-source award. No claim-level payer edit applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Dr. Benjamin Tekippe (chiropractor, owner of Metairie Chiropractic & Rehab)
State_County: Louisiana - Orleans Parish (New Orleans); Louisiana - Jefferson Parish (Metairie)
PayerName: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana; Louisiana unemployment insurance program
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Chiropractor recruited BCBSLA-insured patients at schools, public events and via social media with offers of 'free' chiropractic massages, then billed BCBSLA over $2.3 million (about $740,000 paid) for thousands of chiropractic services never performed, including on dates he was on vacation, out of the office or incarcerated; he fabricated patient records in staff handwriting to defeat an insurer audit. He also falsely certified weekly unemployment during COVID-19 while billing, collecting $12,952 in benefits.
WaysToIdentify: Service dates while the provider was incarcerated or out of the country are catchable by cross-checking billed dates against public incarceration records and against the provider's own absence of any other activity, and by an impossible-volume check on daily patient counts per solo practitioner. Mass enrollment of new members recruited at schools and events shows as a spike of first-time patients with identical code sets and no cost sharing collected. Fabricated audit records surface post-pay, but records with uniform handwriting/templates and no contemporaneous scheduling data are a review trigger.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider daily-capacity edit (distinct beneficiaries and total timed units per NPI per date) that pends claims above the calibrated percentile for solo chiropractic peers, and a provider-availability edit that denies dates matching incarceration, license lapse or verified absence records. Add a new-patient surge monitor plus beneficiary verification letters ("were you seen on these dates?") issued prepay when a practice's new-patient share and per-patient visit counts both exceed peer percentiles.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Dr. Benjamin Tekippe (chiropractor and owner of Metairie Chiropractic & Rehab)
PayerName: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana; Louisiana unemployment insurance program
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Chiropractor lured BCBSLA members with 'free' massages, then billed the insurer for non-covered full-body massages performed by massage therapists plus thousands of chiropractic services never performed - including on dates he was on vacation in Aruba or incarcerated - and fabricated/rewrote patient records to survive an insurer audit; he also filed false weekly COVID-era unemployment certifications claiming to be unemployed while billing for services, collecting $12,952.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic: billed dates when the provider was in Aruba or incarcerated, plus volumes exceeding a solo practitioner's day, are both computable prepay; and non-covered massage delivered by massage therapists is detectable when the rendering credential on file is not eligible for the billed chiropractic manipulation code. Free-service recruitment shows as zero patient responsibility with high visit counts per newly enrolled member. Record rewriting is a post-pay audit finding.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a credential-to-code edit that denies manipulative/therapy codes when the rendering provider's licensed scope does not permit them and when supervision requirements are unmet, and a provider-availability edit denying dates matching incarceration or verified absence. Layer a daily-capacity accumulator and a beneficiary attestation mailing triggered prepay for practices with outlier visits-per-member and outlier new-patient acquisition rates.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Louisiana; Justice Department Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Adrian Dexter Talbot M.D. (owner/operator of Medex Clinical Consultants); Medex Clinical Consultants
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Louisiana); Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana
SchemeSummary: Talbot ran a cash-based clinic issuing prescriptions for Schedule II opioids; after taking a full-time job elsewhere in 2015 he pre-signed prescriptions (and directed a hired practitioner to do the same) for individuals he never examined, falsified patient records to make it appear exams occurred, and the prescriptions were then filled using patients' insurance, causing Medicare, Louisiana Medicaid, and BCBS of Louisiana to be billed over $5.4 million for over 1.8 million doses of controlled substances.
WaysToIdentify: Pharmacy claims carry the prescriber NPI, so the payer can test whether the prescriber has any billed E/M encounter with that member near the fill date — controlled-substance fills with no supporting visit history are the core prepay signal. Sequential prescription numbers, identical quantities and dates spread across many patients indicate pre-signed pads, and the prescriber's own claims showing full-time employment elsewhere (or no clinic claims at all) contradicts an active cash clinic. Aggregate MME per prescriber versus specialty peers is visible at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-integrity edit on Schedule II fills: require an E/M encounter by the prescriber or their group within the lookback window, and pend fills lacking one; compute per-prescriber monthly MME, patient count, distance travelled by patients and share of cash-clinic patients, suspending payment above calibrated peer percentiles pending chart review. Add a pre-signing detector that flags prescriptions from one prescriber sharing identical drug/quantity/directions across many members with clustered written dates, and cross-check the prescriber's asserted practice location against PDMP and claim-based activity.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Michael L. Riggins (owner of Bluewater Healthcare); Bluewater Healthcare
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Riggins, owner of DME supplier Bluewater Healthcare, paid for doctors' orders for medically unnecessary durable medical equipment and tricked physicians into signing DME orders and certificates of medical necessity, then billed Medicare over $3.8 million and was reimbursed over $1.8 million despite hundreds of complaints about the fraudulent orders.
WaysToIdentify: Complaint intake is the loudest signal here: hundreds of physician and beneficiary complaints about orders they never authorized should have suspended payment before further claims were paid. At adjudication, the supplier's orders concentrate on a few ordering NPIs with no treating relationship to the beneficiary, and braces are ordered for beneficiaries with no relevant diagnosis or prior conservative care. Payment for orders is proven post-pay via bank records and marketing invoices.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a complaint-linked suspension rule: when verified 'order not mine' complaints against a supplier or ordering NPI exceed a calibrated rate per thousand claims, place the supplier on prepay review or payment suspension automatically. Add a supplier-level ordering-concentration and clinical-support edit (share of items from top ordering NPIs, share with no prior E/M or supporting diagnosis) that pends claims and demands the signed order plus the medical record before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana; U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Scharmaine Lawson Baker (nurse practitioner, independent contractor for telehealth company)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Nurse practitioner signed hundreds of orders for medically unnecessary cancer genetic tests after phone calls typically under 60 seconds, without exams, falsely diagnosing patients (e.g., male patients with cervical cancer) to justify testing; she took kickbacks from the telehealth company, causing over $12.1 million in Medicare claims with labs receiving over $1.5 million.
WaysToIdentify: Diagnosis-to-sex and diagnosis-to-code coherence is a hard prepay edit — cervical cancer diagnoses on male beneficiaries, or hereditary cancer panels with no personal/family history codes, can be denied at adjudication. The ordering NP's telehealth claims, if billed at all, show durations and volumes incompatible with real assessments, and hundreds of panel orders from one mid-level with no oncology or genetics practice pattern is a peer outlier. Kickbacks from the telehealth entity are traced post-pay.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a clinical-plausibility edit for high-cost genetic panels: deny/pend when diagnosis conflicts with beneficiary sex or age, when no qualifying personal or family history diagnosis is present, or when no counseling/E/M encounter by the ordering provider exists. Add an ordering-provider concentration score (panel orders per month, share to a single lab, share with sub-minute or absent encounters) that triggers payment suspension for the lab's claims from that NPI and a documentation request for the order and chart.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana; U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Shanone Chatman-Ashley (nurse practitioner, independent contractor for telehealth companies)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Working as a contractor for telehealth companies, the nurse practitioner signed more than 1,000 orders for medically unnecessary knee braces, suspension sleeves and other DME for Medicare beneficiaries she never examined, falsely certifying she had consulted with and assessed them, causing over $2 million in claims and over $1 million in reimbursements, in exchange for kickbacks from the telehealth companies.
WaysToIdentify: A single nurse practitioner contracted to telehealth companies generating over a thousand brace orders across many states and suppliers is a fan-out outlier computable at adjudication from the ordering NPI on DME claims. Supporting signals: no E/M claim by that NPI for the beneficiary, orders for multiple braces per beneficiary on one date, and beneficiaries geographically remote from the certifying provider. Kickback flows are post-pay bank-record work.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-NPI velocity and geography edit for orthotics: per NPI per month compute distinct beneficiaries, distinct states, distinct billing suppliers, braces per beneficiary, and share with no prior face-to-face or documented telehealth encounter; pend all downstream DME claims above the calibrated percentile and require the certification plus encounter record. Add a per-beneficiary duplicate-brace edit denying multiple same-anatomy orthotics within the reasonable-useful-lifetime window.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: Dr. James Charasika (physician); Louisville Patient Centered Medical Home, P.S.C. (LPCMH) (practice)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleged that Dr. Charasika and his practice billed Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE as if the physician personally performed medical services when the services were actually rendered by nurse practitioners, without satisfying the conditions permitting billing at the higher physician rate. Resolved for $250,000 in a qui tam action, with relators receiving over $35,000 and the Kentucky Medicaid Fraud Control Unit over $68,000.
WaysToIdentify: The signal is billing under the physician NPI on dates and times when the rendering work was done by NPs — detectable by comparing the physician's claimed daily service volume to a plausible personal workday, and by the absence of any claims under the employed NPs' own NPIs despite payroll/credentialing showing them active. Missing supervision/incident-to modifiers combined with services on dates the physician was not on site is checkable prepay if a provider roster and modifier are required.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an incident-to/supervision edit: require the rendering provider identifier and, where a physician NPI is billed, verify the practice's credentialed NP/PA roster and physician presence, pending claims where the physician's aggregate daily volume exceeds plausible capacity or where employed mid-levels submit no claims of their own. Compute a practice-level ratio of physician-rate lines to physician availability and refer above-percentile practices for prepay documentation of who performed each service.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Mississippi
FraudEntity: Reginald Fullwood, Jr. (owner of Jackson Medical Supply); Jackson Medical Supply (durable medical equipment company)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Fullwood paid kickbacks to a marketer for completed doctors' orders so his DME company, Jackson Medical Supply, could bill Medicare and Medicare Advantage for medically unnecessary or ineligible orthotic braces; after Medicare began investigating, he opened a second entity under a nominee owner and continued the same kickback-for-orders billing, totaling about $12.4 million billed and $6.4 million reimbursed.
WaysToIdentify: Orthotic braces sourced from one marketer show as extreme concentration of ordering NPIs and near-identical code combinations per beneficiary; eligibility problems (items within reuse windows, deceased or hospice/inpatient beneficiaries) are prepay deniable. Critically, the reincarnation under a nominee owner is catchable at enrolment by matching the new applicant's address, phone, bank account, billing agent, employees and item mix to the entity already under investigation.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment identity-linkage graph that blocks or places on prepay review any new DME application sharing address, phone, bank account, billing service, NPI staff, or ownership relations with a supplier under investigation or previously revoked, including nominee-owner patterns. Add a supplier-level brace profile edit (top-referrer concentration, braces per beneficiary, reuse-window and inpatient/hospice overlap) that suspends payment above calibrated peer percentiles pending records, and share both signals with Medicare Advantage plans.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Mahlega Abdsharafat, aka "Mallie Sharafat"; Creative Hospice Care, Inc. and affiliated companies (Creative Hospice entities)
SchemeSummary: Creative Hospice and its owner allegedly paid medical directors monthly stipends and a signing bonus that rose or fell with the number of hospice patients each director referred, inducing referrals and causing false claims to federal health care programs; resolved for $9.2 million with over $1.5 million paid to three qui tam relators.
WaysToIdentify: The arrangement is visible in the correlation between a medical director's stipend and his referral volume — payer-side, the proxy is that a small number of certifying/attending physicians account for most of the hospice's admissions and that those physicians are also the hospice's paid contractors, disclosable at enrolment/revalidation. Rising admission counts tracking new director contracts, plus long lengths of stay and low live-discharge rates, are prepay profileable; the compensation-to-volume link itself usually requires contract and payroll review.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a certifying-physician concentration monitor per hospice: share of admissions from physicians with a financial relationship disclosed to the payer, month-over-month admission growth per such physician, and comparison to peer hospices; above the calibrated percentile, pend claims and request the medical-director agreements and time logs. Require disclosure of medical-director compensation terms at enrolment and flag agreements whose payment varies with patient census for review before claims are paid.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Petros Fichidzhyan (operator of sham hospice companies and owner of a home health care agency)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Fichidzhyan and co-schemers operated a series of sham hospice companies, using stolen identities of foreign nationals as nominee owners (to open bank accounts and sign leases) and misappropriating doctors' identifying information to certify that hospice care was needed, then billed Medicare for hospice services for patients who were not terminally ill and never received care; Medicare paid nearly $16 million, of which he personally received nearly $7 million laundered through a dozen shell and third-party accounts. He also obtained over $1 million for his home health agency by fraudulently using a doctor's name to certify beneficiaries, paying the doctor $11,000 to cover it up.
WaysToIdentify: Provider-enrolment screening is where this dies: nominee owners are foreign nationals with stolen identities, so SSA/passport identity verification, in-person interview and site visits would fail, and the entities share addresses, leases, bank accounts and billing patterns. At adjudication, hospice election claims certified by physicians who have no other treating relationship with the beneficiary — or whose NPI is being used across several unrelated hospices — plus beneficiaries with no terminal diagnosis history and no prior hospital/oncology utilization, are prepay flags.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment control that identity-proofs every disclosed owner against SSA/immigration and death files, requires a verified site visit, and blocks applications sharing address, bank account, phone or billing agent with existing or revoked hospice/home-health entities. At adjudication, add a certifying-physician edit that suspends hospice election claims when the certifying NPI has no prior claims for the beneficiary or certifies for multiple unrelated new hospices, and a clinical-history edit pending payment when no terminal-illness diagnosis or supporting utilization exists; notify physicians of certifications filed in their name.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Chaudhry Shabbir Ahmed (nominee owner of Dune Medical Supply, LLC and Prospect Health Solutions, Inc.); Dune Medical Supply, LLC; Prospect Health Solutions, Inc.
State_County: North Carolina - Guilford County (High Point); Florida - Broward County (Fort Lauderdale)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Ahmed used a sham purchase agreement to pose as sole owner of two DME companies (while a co-conspirator retained control), including on Medicare enrollment documents; the companies billed Medicare over $100 million for durable medical equipment beneficiaries never received, requested, needed, or that was never ordered, and Medicare deposited over $33 million into company accounts from which Ahmed withdrew large cash sums (e.g., $400,000 and $500,000).
WaysToIdentify: Ownership misrepresentation is detectable at enrolment: verify the purchase agreement, source of funds, and continuing control by the prior owner via bank signatory, lease, phone and management-company links, and screen the true controller against exclusion/revocation lists. Post-enrolment, a new-owner DME supplier ramping to nine-figure billing in a short period, with beneficiaries scattered nationwide, no prior treating relationships, and large cash withdrawals from the receiving account, is a payment-suspension case well before $33 million is paid.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a billing-velocity autopilot for newly enrolled or newly transferred DME suppliers: model claims and paid dollars per week against the supplier's tenure and peer distribution and auto-place on prepay review or suspension when growth exceeds the calibrated percentile, releasing only after proof-of-delivery and beneficiary verification sampling. At enrolment, require and verify ownership-change documentation (funding source, bank signatories, lease, management contracts) and link-analyze applicants to prior owners and known bad actors before granting billing privileges.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Daniel Gonzalez-Munguia, aka "Alejandro Vasquez" (operator of online drug business)
SchemeSummary: Defendant operated an online drug business from Mexico from 2012 to 2021 selling bottles of Pentobarbital, a controlled substance sold in Mexico for euthanizing animals, to hundreds of buyers in the U.S. and worldwide for use in committing suicide; he shipped it disguised as a cosmetic product and used intermediaries to smuggle it into the U.S. Many buyers consumed the product and died.
WaysToIdentify: No payer or claim is involved — this is unlawful international distribution of a controlled substance direct to consumers, so there is no adjudication signal. Detection routes are customs/parcel interdiction of mislabeled shipments, payment-processor and marketplace monitoring of the seller's accounts, and DEA import controls.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side claim edit applies. The nearest analogous control is a pharmacy-network/PBM check that flags dispensing or purchase of veterinary-labeled controlled substances by non-veterinary entities and reconciles licensed distributors' pentobarbital acquisition against ARCOS-type reporting; otherwise this is a law-enforcement and customs control.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nebraska
FraudEntity: Paul M. Hughes; The Hughes and Company Foundation USA Coalition Company; The Hughes and Company Foundation USA Coalition- Virtual Infirmary
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Hughes submitted a false NPI application to CMS falsely claiming to be a physician and Advanced Registered Nurse Practitioner, obtained an NPI number, and then used it to submit fake prescriptions to pharmacies, including a fraudulent electronic prescription for a Schedule III controlled substance listing a real doctor as the prescriber.
WaysToIdentify: The NPI application itself carried the signal: a claimed physician/ARNP taxonomy with no matching active state license number in the state board licensure file, and a credential attestation that never verified against primary-source licensure data. At the pharmacy end, e-prescriptions for a Schedule III arrived under an NPI whose taxonomy/DEA registration did not support controlled-substance prescribing, and one prescription named a real doctor as prescriber while routing from a different NPI/e-prescribing account.
FeaturesToCreate: At enrolment, auto-verify every NPI/PECOS application's claimed prescriber taxonomy against primary-source state licensure and DEA registration files; mismatch or no-hit puts the NPI in a non-prescribing status and blocks pharmacy claim adjudication. At claim time, deny (prepay edit) any controlled-substance pharmacy claim where the prescriber NPI has no active DEA registration/schedule authority or where the prescriber NPI on the claim differs from the account credential that transmitted the SCRIPT message, and alert the named physician.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (sentenced in Tampa, Florida)
FraudEntity: Robert Desselle (marketer)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Desselle paid non-medical marketers to recruit Medicare beneficiaries at grocery stores, pharmacies and car dealerships into medically unnecessary genetic tests, then bribed a telemedicine company to generate doctors' orders; clinical laboratories paid him kickbacks for the referrals and billed Medicare $11.5 million, of which Medicare paid $4.5 million and Desselle personally received over $2.1 million. Restitution of $4.5 million plus $2.1 million forfeiture were ordered.
WaysToIdentify: Claims data shows high-volume CGx/PGx panels for beneficiaries with no treating-physician relationship: the ordering NPI is a telemedicine physician with no prior or subsequent E/M claim for that beneficiary, geographically remote, and ordering across many unrelated labs. Beneficiary clustering by recruitment site (many enrollees sharing a marketer's ZIP/date-of-service cluster) and absence of any oncology/hereditary-risk diagnosis history are visible before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-physician concentration model: per ordering NPI per month, compute count of high-cost genetic panels, share with no E/M encounter by the orderer within a lookback window, and beneficiary-state dispersion; above the calibrated percentile, suspend payment and issue a documentation request for the order and medical record. Add a prepay edit denying CGx panels lacking a qualifying diagnosis plus a treating-relationship encounter, and flag labs whose referral volume is concentrated in a few marketer-linked ordering NPIs for kickback review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Shahram Naghshbandi (laboratory marketer); John Bello (laboratory marketer); RiteRx4U LLC (marketing company); Dr. Abbesalom Ghermay (physician); Dr. James Cook (physician); Family Medical Centers, P.C. (medical practice); Dr. Daniel Theesfeld (physician); H8 Pain Management Center of Texas PLLC (medical practice); Troy Belton (medical practice owner); Advantage Medical Group (outpatient clinic)
State_County: Texas - Tarrant County (Fort Worth); Texas - Collin County (Plano); Texas - Gregg County (Longview); Texas - Harris County (Houston); Texas - Dallas County (Dallas); Texas - Denton County (Denton); Virginia - Chesterfield County (Chesterfield/Chester); Virginia - Richmond; South Carolina - Richland County (Columbia); New Jersey - Union County (Kenilworth); Florida - Orange County (Orlando)
SchemeSummary: Lab marketers and their companies paid physicians and clinic owners kickbacks disguised as investment distributions/returns from purported management service organizations (MSOs) in exchange for ordering clinical laboratory testing from labs in New Jersey, Texas, Virginia and Florida; the labs paid the marketers commissions based on reimbursement, and the tainted referrals produced false Medicare lab-testing claims. Six settling parties and associated entities agreed to pay a combined $1,137,914 (Naghshbandi $400,000 plus 10-year exclusion, Bello/RiteRx4U $140,000, Ghermay $228,482, Cook/Family Medical Centers $206,987, Theesfeld/H8 Pain Management $99,125, Belton/Advantage Medical Group $63,320).
WaysToIdentify: The kickback is disguised as MSO investment returns, so the payer signal is the referral pattern: ordering physicians whose lab-test ordering volume and test mix (expensive panels) jump abruptly and route almost exclusively to one out-of-state lab, versus same-specialty peers. Ownership/investment disclosures at enrolment and out-of-state lab claims for in-state patients are visible prepay; the actual MSO payments generally surface only post-payment via bank records, whistleblowers, or Open Payments/tax-record review.
FeaturesToCreate: Per ordering NPI, compute monthly lab-referral concentration (share to a single lab TIN), out-of-state lab share, cost per patient for lab panels, and change-point detection versus that NPI's own baseline and specialty peers; firing cases go to prepay review with a documentation request for medical necessity and a financial-relationship attestation. Maintain a lab-marketer/MSO entity graph from enrolment ownership disclosures and deny or suspend claims where an ordering provider has an undisclosed financial link to the billing lab.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Amanda Nicole Manatt (registered nurse)
State_County: Iowa - Marshall County (Marshalltown); Iowa - Story County
SchemeSummary: A registered nurse working at two Iowa hospitals obtained controlled substances, including fentanyl and hydromorphone (Dilaudid), that were intended for patients and took them for her own use, and falsely documented in a patient record that a controlled substance had been administered.
WaysToIdentify: This is drug diversion inside a facility; the payer sees little directly, but the hospital's dispensing/ADC (Pyxis) records versus the eMAR expose the nurse: overrides, withdrawals not matched to an administration, and wastage without witness, concentrated on one clinician. Payer-side, charge lines for administered controlled substances that exceed documented administration on the record are detectable in a post-payment record audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Require facilities to run per-nurse-per-shift reconciliation of ADC withdrawals to eMAR administrations and documented waste, firing on override rate, unwitnessed waste, and withdrawal-without-administration counts above peer percentile on the same unit; positive cases trigger internal referral and payer notification. For the payer, add a post-payment audit sampling controlled-substance charge lines against MAR entries at facilities with reported diversion events, with recoupment where administration is undocumented.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Amanda Nicole Manatt (registered nurse)
State_County: Iowa - Marshall County (Marshalltown); Iowa - Story County (Ames)
SchemeSummary: An ER registered nurse obtained controlled substances (fentanyl, hydromorphone, morphine) in patients' names at two Iowa hospitals, documented them in medical records as administered to patients, and diverted them for her own use; the false records caused health care benefit programs to be billed for drugs never administered. Restitution of $5,258.20 plus a $5,500 fine and $300 assessment were ordered.
WaysToIdentify: Same diversion mechanic with a direct billing effect: drugs charged as administered were never given, so line-level pharmacy charges exist with no clinically coherent context (opioid administrations to ED patients whose diagnoses/vitals/orders do not support them, repeated across one nurse's shifts). Prepay, the payer can only see anomalous controlled-substance charge intensity per encounter; confirmation requires MAR/ADC records, so the practical route is a targeted post-payment audit triggered by that signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an encounter-level edit computing opioid administration units per ED visit against diagnosis-adjusted peer norms, and a facility-level metric of controlled-substance charge intensity per ED encounter by administering clinician ID where captured; outliers trigger a documentation request for the MAR and ADC dispensing log with prepay suspension for that facility's flagged claims. Recoup lines where administration cannot be evidenced and refer for diversion investigation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Joel Smithers (physician)
SchemeSummary: Smithers ran a Martinsville medical office where he prescribed Schedule II controlled substances (oxymorphone, oxycodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl) to every patient, distributing over 500,000 pills to patients who traveled hundreds of miles; he accepted no insurance and collected over $700,000 in cash and credit card payments. Convicted at retrial of 466 counts of illegal prescribing plus maintaining a drug-involved premises and sentenced to 40 years.
WaysToIdentify: Even with a cash-only practice, the prescriptions land in PDMP and pharmacy claims: one prescriber writing Schedule II opioids to essentially 100% of patients, with high MME per day, long-distance patient travel (patient ZIP far from prescriber ZIP), and cash-pay dispensing clusters. Pharmacy claims paid by the plan for prescriptions from that NPI, plus PDMP dispensing counts versus same-specialty peers, are visible before further payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Per prescriber NPI per month, compute share of patients receiving Schedule II opioids, average daily MME, mean patient-to-prescriber distance, count of distinct dispensing pharmacies, and share of patients traveling over the calibrated distance percentile; above threshold, place the prescriber on prepay review and refer to PDMP/board and DEA. Add a pharmacy-side edit requiring pharmacist attestation/denial for opioid claims from prescribers on the high-risk list.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Benjamin Jamal Washington (scheme leader)
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Los Angeles); Maryland - Prince George's County (Hyattsville)
SchemeSummary: Washington and co-conspirators stole doctors' personal identifiers (NPI, DEA numbers), obtained fake driver's licenses and paid telecom employees for SIM swaps to hijack physicians' phone numbers, then opened fraudulent e-prescribing accounts in the doctors' names and issued at least 5,600 fraudulent prescriptions for oxycodone and promethazine with codeine, which they picked up at pharmacies nationwide and resold for profit.
WaysToIdentify: The fingerprint is identity hijack of prescribers: new e-prescribing accounts enrolled under existing NPIs with changed phone numbers, emails, and addresses just before a burst of oxycodone and promethazine-codeine prescriptions dispensed at pharmacies far from the prescriber's practice and outside the prescriber's specialty pattern. Pharmacy claims show one prescriber NPI suddenly appearing at many distant pharmacies with cash or unusual payment patterns.
FeaturesToCreate: Monitor e-prescribing/EHR account provisioning events against the provider master file: fire on demographic change (phone, email, address, MFA device) followed within a short window by controlled-substance prescribing volume above the prescriber's own baseline, and require out-of-band re-verification with the licensed provider before scripts transmit. At adjudication, add a prepay edit suspending controlled-substance claims when prescriber-pharmacy distance and pharmacy-count-per-prescriber exceed calibrated percentiles, and notify the prescriber of record.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Jariatu Jalloh (community support worker employed by a District Mental Health Rehabilitation Service provider)
SchemeSummary: While working as a community support worker for a D.C. Mental Health Rehabilitation Service provider, Jalloh allegedly submitted encounter notes for community support services she never provided and overbilled for services she claimed to provide, causing the D.C. Medicaid program to pay over $234,500.
WaysToIdentify: Phantom community-support encounters show up as impossible service-day arithmetic for one worker: billed units per day exceeding a feasible workday, overlapping encounter times across beneficiaries, and services billed on days the worker had no location evidence. Higher-level codes billed uniformly (no variation in duration) against the same beneficiary panel is another prepay-visible pattern.
FeaturesToCreate: Per rendering-staff identifier per date, sum billed service units/time across all beneficiaries and flag totals above a feasible-day threshold or with time overlaps; auto-deny overlapping units and suspend the remainder pending encounter notes. Add a distribution check on billed duration/level per worker versus agency and program peers, firing on near-constant maximum-unit billing, with a documentation request for progress notes and a supervisory attestation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Carolyn Bryant-Taylor (former director and corporate officer/owner-operator); Kafomdi "Josephine" Okocha (owner-operator); Samuel Okocha (owner-operator); Shekita Gore a.k.a. Shekita Steele (director of nursing); Elizabeth Ilome (nurse/personal care employee); Eno Utuk (nurse/personal care employee); 1st Adult N Pediatric Healthcare Service (Medicaid-enrolled home health agency)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Upcoding; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Owners and staff of a Medicaid-enrolled home health agency billed Virginia Medicaid for private duty nursing, personal care and respite services that were never provided or were billed in excess of what was delivered; Bryant-Taylor and Josephine Okocha paid patients' parents/guardians for blank, pre-signed nursing notes that employees then filled out to support the false claims. Bryant-Taylor is the first of six charged co-conspirators to plead guilty.
WaysToIdentify: Private duty nursing and personal care billed in excess of hours actually delivered is visible as aide/nurse schedule impossibilities, hours billed exceeding authorized plan-of-care hours, and billing while the beneficiary had an inpatient or ED claim on the same dates. Pre-signed blank notes yield tell-tale documentation: identical signatures/dates across many visits and notes with uniform vitals, detectable via a targeted record request before payment for flagged agencies.
FeaturesToCreate: Build prepay edits: (1) deny hours exceeding the authorized service plan or overlapping with facility claims for the same beneficiary; (2) per caregiver ID per day, sum hours across beneficiaries and flag over a feasible-day maximum with time overlap detection using EVV timestamps; (3) flag agencies where EVV records are missing or where visit check-in/out geolocation does not match the beneficiary address. Firing agencies go to prepay documentation review and payment suspension pending nursing-note audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Le Thu (doctor)
