SchemeSummary: A Boston doctor signed, or had untrained individuals sign, false medical documentation and orders for Medicare beneficiaries' genetic testing, falsely certifying she had consulted with and examined patients and would use results for treatment, when she never communicated with them; third-party laboratories then billed Medicare approximately $35.3 million on these orders, of which Medicare paid about $25.3 million.
WaysToIdentify: One physician signing orders for thousands of beneficiaries she never contacted is measurable prepay: no E/M or telehealth claim from that NPI for the beneficiaries she ordered for, ordering volume orders of magnitude above same-specialty peers, and orders spread across multiple unrelated labs and states. Labs' claims share a single ordering NPI at extreme concentration, and the certification of treating relationship is contradicted by the claim history.
FeaturesToCreate: Per ordering NPI per month, compute count of genetic-test orders, percentage with no accompanying qualifying encounter claim by that NPI within the lookback window, distinct billing labs, and beneficiary state dispersion; when the no-encounter share and volume exceed calibrated percentiles, suspend payment on all downstream lab claims citing that NPI and request the signed order plus records. Also apply a claim-level prepay edit requiring an encounter link and cancer/hereditary-risk diagnosis for high-cost panels.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Rodrigo de Medeiros Siqueira (owner of Rodrigo Beauty Inc.); Rodrigo Beauty Inc.
SchemeSummary: Med spa owner, not licensed to prescribe, dispense or administer prescription drugs, allegedly injected clients with unapproved botulinum toxin obtained from illegitimate foreign sources while falsely representing himself as a licensed medical professional and misrepresenting the identity and source of the products; numerous clients developed botulism. Charged with misbranding a drug after shipment in interstate commerce with intent to defraud; agreed to plead guilty.
WaysToIdentify: Largely a cash-pay med-spa/FDA misbranding case with no payer claims, so prepay claim edits are not the primary route; the observable signals are an unlicensed owner performing injections and product sourced outside the legitimate US supply chain. A payer or state could catch it via credentialing/licensure checks on any enrolled entity and via product-serialization/wholesaler purchase records, plus adverse-event (botulism) clusters reported to public health.
FeaturesToCreate: For any enrolled or credentialed injectable-service entity, require primary-source license verification for every individual who administers drugs and verify botulinum-toxin purchases against authorized US distributor records; unverifiable supply or unlicensed administrator blocks enrolment and denies claims. Add a public-health/payer feed linking adverse-event or ED-diagnosis clusters (botulism, injection complications) back to the facility for investigation referral; note that for pure cash practices only licensure/enforcement controls apply.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia; U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, Norfolk Division
FraudEntity: Chesapeake Regional Medical Center (aka Chesapeake General Hospital, Chesapeake Regional Healthcare) (hospital); Dr. Javaid Perwaiz (physician with privileges at CRMC)
PayerName: Medicaid; health care benefit programs/insurance companies
SchemeSummary: CRMC was indicted for conspiracy and health care fraud for billing insurers and health care benefit programs for surgeries and procedures performed at its facility by Dr. Javaid Perwaiz, including medically unnecessary hysterectomies and other irreversible surgeries, elective inductions before 39 weeks without medical justification, and sterilizations of Medicaid patients lacking consent forms signed 30 days in advance; CRMC received about $18.5 million in reimbursements from 2010 to 2019 for Perwaiz's procedures. Perwaiz was separately convicted in November 2020 of 52 counts, about 38 involving procedures at CRMC.
WaysToIdentify: Facility claims data exposed the pattern: one surgeon's hysterectomy, sterilization, and elective-induction volume per patient panel far above same-specialty peers at the same hospital, high rates of inductions coded before 39 weeks without a qualifying maternal/fetal indication, and repeat surgeries on the same patients. For Medicaid sterilizations, the required consent form with a 30-day waiting period is a checkable claim attachment — claims paid without a valid, timely signed consent were payable-in-error prepay.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: deny Medicaid sterilization claims unless a validated consent form is on file with a signature date at least the required interval before the procedure date, matching patient and procedure. Build a surgeon-level outlier monitor per facility for hysterectomy/sterilization/early-induction rates and diagnosis-support ratios versus same-specialty peers, firing a prepay medical-necessity documentation review on that surgeon's and the facility's related claims, and escalate to the facility's governing body.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Delaware
FraudEntity: Ty Mauldin (medical biller and credentialer)
SchemeSummary: A medical biller/credentialer allegedly used the names and licensure information of medical professionals he worked with to order thousands of opioid pills from wholesale pharmaceutical suppliers and prescribe himself opioids; he also falsified his own electronic medical records and forged documents to pose as a cancer patient needing pain management (getting an intrathecal pain pump and opioids paid for by his private insurer), and falsely presented himself as a licensed nurse/certified medical assistant to perform Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation therapy on patients, billing Medicaid for it.
WaysToIdentify: Several checkable signals: wholesale controlled-substance orders placed under prescriber licenses by a non-clinical biller (DEA ARCOS/wholesaler ship-to inconsistent with the registrant's practice address), prescriptions written to a self-related patient identity, and TMS services billed with a rendering provider whose license cannot be primary-source verified. The pain-pump implant claim rests on a cancer history absent from the insurer's own longitudinal claims (no oncology encounters, imaging, or chemotherapy claims).
FeaturesToCreate: Add prepay edits: deny/suspend claims where the rendering or supervising NPI's license is not verified active for that service (TMS requires licensed clinician), and deny prescriber-written prescriptions where prescriber and patient identity match or share address/SSN. Build a clinical-coherence edit for high-cost implants (intrathecal pump) requiring corroborating diagnosis history in prior claims; absence triggers documentation request and record authentication, plus a feed comparing wholesaler shipments per DEA registrant to that registrant's own prescribing/practice location.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
FraudEntity: Scott Newcombe (owner of SJ Healthcare Management Services, LLC; office manager and health care claims biller); SJ Healthcare Management Services, LLC
SchemeSummary: As office manager and billing agent for two Plattsburgh physicians' practices through his company SJHMS, Newcombe submitted false claims to public and private insurers for services never provided and for services billed at higher rates than actually delivered, including claims for procedures purportedly performed on himself that never occurred. He was sentenced to 1 year probation and $34,583.21 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: A third-party biller submitting for two practices produced detectable artifacts: claims where the patient is the biller himself or a household member, upward drift in E/M level distribution after the billing agent took over, and services billed on dates with no corresponding scheduling/encounter record. Cross-payer, the same billing TIN's claim mix shifted versus specialty peers.
FeaturesToCreate: Flag claims where the subscriber/patient identity matches the submitting billing agent's principals or their dependents (identity match on name, SSN, address) and route to prepay review. Monitor E/M level distribution per practice NPI with change-point detection against its own pre-period and specialty peers, and per billing-agent submitter ID across all client practices; firing submitters get prepay documentation requests on sampled claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Alabama
FraudEntity: Exactech, Inc. (medical device manufacturer, Gainesville, Florida)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
SchemeSummary: Exactech allegedly knew as early as January 2008 that its finned tibial tray, and as early as January 2019 that the polyethylene components in its Logic and Truliant knee systems, failed prematurely at higher-than-acceptable rates, yet continued marketing and selling them for total-knee replacements on Medicare, Medicaid and VA beneficiaries, causing false claims for devices that were not reasonable and necessary. Resolved for $8 million ($7.64M federal share, $360,000 state share) under the False Claims Act following two qui tam suits.
WaysToIdentify: This is manufacturer-caused false claims for defective implants; payers can see it in device-level revision-surgery outcomes: linking implant UDI/catalog numbers on hospital claims to subsequent revision-knee claims yields premature-failure rates per device model versus comparators. Signals also include FDA MAUDE complaint density and internal manufacturer knowledge, which the payer learns post-payment via qui tam or recall notices.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a device-outcome surveillance pipeline: require UDI/device identifiers on implant claims, compute per-model time-to-revision survival curves versus same-category peers, and fire when the revision hazard exceeds the calibrated percentile, triggering a coverage review and FCA referral. Add a prepay edit denying claims for devices under recall or on a non-covered-device list from the recall/FDA feed, with post-payment recovery against the manufacturer for pre-flag claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Michigan; U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan
FraudEntity: The Prometheus Group (medical device manufacturer); Richard Poore (president and sole owner)
SchemeSummary: A New Hampshire manufacturer of rectal therapeutic systems and its sole owner allegedly instructed health care providers to reuse FDA-cleared single-user rectal pressure sensors and single-use anorectal manometry catheters on multiple patients (covering probes with a glove or condom) to cut overhead costs; the resulting pelvic muscle rehabilitation services billed to Medicare were alleged to be not reasonable or necessary and thus false claims. Prometheus and Poore agreed to pay $550,000.
WaysToIdentify: Reuse of single-use sensors/catheters shows up as a supply-to-service mismatch: a practice bills far more anorectal manometry and pelvic-rehab sessions than its documented purchases of single-use catheters/probes could support, and the manufacturer's shipment volumes are low relative to procedure counts billed by its customers. Prepay, high per-patient session counts for pelvic muscle rehabilitation versus peers is visible; the reuse instruction itself surfaced via a whistleblower, i.e., post-payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a consumable-reconciliation audit: for procedures requiring a single-use device, compare each provider's billed procedure counts to purchase/shipment records obtained from manufacturers or distributors and fire when procedures exceed devices purchased; positive cases get a documentation/attestation request and prepay hold. Complement with a provider-level outlier check on pelvic-muscle-rehab and manometry units per patient versus same-specialty peers, and open manufacturer-level FCA inquiry when multiple customers of one manufacturer fire.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: Pedro Reyes (owner of durable medical equipment businesses)
State_County: Kentucky - Hardin County (Elizabethtown); Kentucky - Jefferson County (Louisville)
SchemeSummary: Through multiple Kentucky companies, Reyes fraudulently billed Medicare for orthopedic durable medical equipment (back, knee and shoulder braces) that was medically unnecessary, unwanted by the patients, and never prescribed by their medical providers; he was sentenced to 33 months and ordered to pay $6,004,916 in restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Classic brace-mill pattern visible prepay: newly enrolled DME suppliers under common ownership billing multi-brace combinations (back, knee, shoulder) to beneficiaries spread nationally, with ordering physicians who have no prior treatment relationship and often no orthopedic diagnosis history. Duplicate braces per beneficiary across the related companies and telemarketing-sourced beneficiary clusters are detectable before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Per supplier, compute braces per beneficiary, share of beneficiaries with no prior musculoskeletal diagnosis or orderer encounter, beneficiary geographic dispersion, and ownership links to other suppliers; new suppliers exceeding calibrated growth/percentile thresholds go on prepay review with mandatory order and medical-record submission. Add claim-level edits: deny multi-brace same-day combinations without a supporting diagnosis and orderer encounter, and deny where the same beneficiary already received the same HCPCS within its reasonable-useful-lifetime window, plus beneficiary confirmation letters.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: Shafi Abbas (owner of Aidmen Medical Equipment LLC and Justright Medical Equipment LLC); Aidmen Medical Equipment LLC; Justright Medical Equipment LLC
SchemeSummary: Abbas, through his two DME companies, billed Medicare for durable medical equipment that was medically unnecessary, unwanted by the patients, and not prescribed by their medical providers, then transferred the fraud proceeds (over $10,000 per transaction) in money-laundering transactions.
WaysToIdentify: Same unwanted-and-unordered DME mechanic across two commonly owned companies: rapid billing ramp from newly enrolled suppliers, ordering NPIs with no encounter claim for the beneficiary, beneficiaries far from the supplier, and near-identical HCPCS mixes across both TINs sharing an owner, address, or bank account. Money-laundering transfers are post-payment (bank data), but the claim pattern and the shared-identity enrolment links are prepay signals.
FeaturesToCreate: At enrolment, graph suppliers on owner, address, phone, bank account, and billing-agent identifiers and inherit risk across the cluster; a flagged cluster puts all member TINs on prepay review. At adjudication, edit for orders lacking a documented treating-provider encounter and for supplier ramp rate above the calibrated percentile, with payment suspension plus beneficiary verification letters before release of funds.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Fairfax Radiological Consultants, PLLC, formerly known as Fairfax Radiological Consultants, P.C. (radiology medical group)
PayerName: Small Business Administration - Paycheck Protection Program
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Radiology group obtained a $6.8 million PPP loan in April 2020 based on its 2019 payroll of over 500 employees when it actually employed fewer than 100, then in April 2021 falsely represented eligible payroll costs for 98 employees in its forgiveness application to obtain full forgiveness, though it was only entitled to $4,945,860.
WaysToIdentify: No health-care claims component — this is PPP loan and forgiveness fraud against SBA. It was catchable at underwriting and forgiveness by cross-checking the applicant's claimed employee count and payroll against IRS Form 941/W-2 filings and state unemployment-insurance wage records for the same quarters; the 500-versus-under-100 discrepancy would appear immediately.
FeaturesToCreate: For loan/forgiveness programs, build an automated third-party payroll verification: match applicant EIN to IRS 941 and state UI wage-base employee counts and total wages per quarter, and hold disbursement or forgiveness when the application overstates employees or eligible payroll beyond a tolerance. No payer claims control applies; the nearest payer-side analogue is verifying provider-reported staffing/cost-report headcount against payroll tax filings.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: PenRad Technologies, Inc. (medical software company headquartered in Raleigh, N.C.)
SchemeSummary: PenRad's Series 7 software sometimes installed the Tyrer-Cusick breast cancer risk calculator with 'competing mortality' disabled without telling customers, producing inflated patient risk scores; at least one provider consequently ordered medically unnecessary breast MRIs that were billed to Medicare and MassHealth, making PenRad liable under the False Claims Act for causing false claims (resolved for $529,069 following a qui tam suit).
WaysToIdentify: Payer-visible signal is a surge in screening breast MRIs ordered for average-risk women at specific sites: high-risk-justified MRI claims whose beneficiaries lack qualifying genetic, family-history, or prior-cancer indicators in claims history, clustered at providers using one vendor's risk-calculator software. The software defect itself is only knowable post-payment (qui tam/vendor disclosure), but the ordering-pattern anomaly is detectable prepay.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit for breast MRI: require a documented qualifying high-risk indication (diagnosis code, genetic result, or prior malignancy) present in claim history or attached risk score with the calculation method; absent that, deny or request documentation. Add a facility-level monitor of screening-MRI rate per mammography volume versus peers, with drill-down on the risk-assessment software/version so vendor-linked clusters trigger recovery and referral against the software supplier.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California
FraudEntity: Seoul Medical Group Inc. (Medicare Advantage provider); Advanced Medical Management Inc. (subsidiary); Dr. Min Young Cha (former president and majority owner); Renaissance Imaging Medical Associates Inc. (radiology group)
SchemeSummary: Seoul Medical Group and its owner allegedly submitted diagnosis codes for two severe spinal conditions (spinal enthesopathy and sacroiliitis) for patients who did not have them, inflating beneficiaries' risk scores so CMS paid Medicare Advantage plans more, with the plans passing a portion of the increased payment to Seoul; when an MA Plan questioned the enthesopathy coding, Renaissance Imaging created radiology reports appearing to support the diagnosis. Settlement totals $62.85M across defendants ($58,740,000 by Seoul/Advanced Medical Management, $1,760,000 by Dr. Cha, $2,350,000 by Renaissance Imaging).
WaysToIdentify: Risk-adjustment diagnoses that appear only on provider-generated encounter data and never recur in any other setting are visible in the MA encounter feed: cluster the plan's chart-review/EDPS submissions by submitting provider and HCC and look for a single group contributing a spike in spinal enthesopathy (M46.0x) and sacroiliitis codes far above same-specialty peers, with no matching imaging, procedure, DME or specialist follow-on claims for the same members. The retro-dated radiology reports are catchable by comparing report creation/authoring metadata and imaging claim dates to the date the plan first queried the diagnosis. Payment inflation flows through the risk score, so the primary route is a prepay encounter-data edit plus a pre-submission audit before the risk-score run.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a provider-HCC concentration monitor: unit = (submitting TIN, HCC, sweep period); compute the share of the plan's members receiving that HCC solely from this TIN and the fraction with no corroborating clinical claim (imaging, injection, PT, rheumatology visit) within a trailing window; fire above the calibrated percentile to hold those diagnoses out of the risk-score submission and open a medical-record request. Add a second edit that flags any imaging report supplied as diagnosis support whose service date postdates the plan's query or whose report authoring date is after the encounter's original submission, routing to SIU.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Dr. Mark Shermer (Memphis nephrologist)
SchemeSummary: A Memphis nephrologist allegedly billed Medicare for end-stage renal disease treatment visits to dialysis patients that he never actually performed; the allegations were raised in a qui tam False Claims Act suit and resolved for $375,296.90 without a determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: ESRD monthly capitation/visit codes (MCP tiers) are countable per physician per patient-month, and phantom visits show up as impossible service volume: count distinct dialysis patients billed at the highest visit tier per month per NPI and divide by plausible clinic hours, and cross-check the dialysis facility's own treatment records/place-of-service dates against the physician's claimed visit dates. Also look for MCP billed for months where the patient had no dialysis treatment claims, was hospitalized, or was concurrently billed by another nephrologist.
FeaturesToCreate: Unit = (nephrologist NPI, beneficiary, month): fire a prepay edit when the MCP tier billed implies more face-to-face visits than the facility's dialysis session records support, when the same beneficiary-month is billed by two physicians, or when the patient was inpatient/absent for the claimed visit dates. Add an NPI-level capacity feature (total MCP patient-months and implied visit hours per day versus same-specialty peers) that triggers prepay documentation review of visit notes.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Nakita Cannady (owner and operator of What About Us In-Home Healthcare)
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Cannady billed Cigna for 24 hours a day of in-home custodial care for mostly elderly patients when they had actually received only 8 or 12 hours a day, and separately submitted six PPP/EIDL applications for four businesses she controlled containing false dates of operation, revenues, employee counts and payroll figures; restitution totaled $193,508.10 to Cigna and $346,882.13 to the SBA.
WaysToIdentify: Billing 24 hours/day of custodial care per member per day is detectable at adjudication by summing all attendant-hour units per beneficiary per date and comparing to the authorized hours on the plan's own service authorization; the paid authorization said 8 or 12 hours. Cross-check aide-level totals too: the same caregiver IDs cannot cover 24-hour shifts across multiple members. The PPP/EIDL side is not a payer matter, but the SBA loan data (employee counts, payroll) can be compared to the payer's own remitted volumes as a corroboration signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: unit = (member, date of service); sum personal-care/home-health hour units across all lines and reject or pend anything exceeding the authorized daily hours on the active authorization, with a hard cap edit at 24 hours and a caregiver-level constraint that no single aide ID exceeds plausible daily hours across all members. Add a provider-level monitor on average billed hours per member-day trending upward versus authorization to trigger a records/timesheet request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Manuel Delgado (contractor/inspector for Board of Certification/Accreditation, International)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Delgado, a contractor performing CMS quality-standard accreditation inspections of DME companies for BOC, took cash bribes from DME company owners to expedite accreditation so they could enroll and bill Medicare, and also formed DME companies in family members' names, inspected and accredited them himself, then sold them as Medicare-enrolled suppliers; the accredited companies were valued at over $1.4 million.
WaysToIdentify: This is an enrolment/credentialing control, not a claims edit: the accrediting inspector and the applicant were related. Screen accreditation records for inspector-to-supplier relationships (shared surnames, addresses, phone numbers, registered-agent or corporate-officer overlap in Secretary of State filings) and for inspectors whose approval rate, inspection duration and time-to-accreditation are outliers versus peer inspectors. Also flag newly accredited suppliers that change ownership shortly after enrolment - the sell-on of enrolled shells.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an accreditation-integrity model: unit = (inspector, accredited supplier); compute conflict-of-interest matches across name/address/phone/officer data, inspector approval rate and median days-to-accreditation versus peers, and fire to withhold billing privileges pending re-inspection by an independent surveyor. Second control: unit = supplier PTAN; flag change-of-ownership or authorized-official change within a short window of initial accreditation and place a prepay review/payment hold until revalidation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (National Rapid Response Strike Force)
FraudEntity: Sophie Toya, M.D. (physician who signed orthotic brace prescriptions)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Patients recruited through deceptive TV ads for 'free' back braces were routed to telemedicine companies; Toya signed over 7,900 orthotic brace prescriptions for more than 2,600 Medicare beneficiaries after minute-long calls or no contact at all, falsely attesting medical necessity, diagnoses and plans of care. Brace supply companies used the prescriptions to bill Medicare over $6.3 million, and Toya was paid about $120,000 by the telemedicine companies for signing.
WaysToIdentify: The signature volume is the signal: one ordering NPI attached to thousands of orthotic brace claims across thousands of beneficiaries nationwide, with no prior or subsequent E/M relationship with any of them and beneficiary residences far outside the prescriber's service area. At adjudication, brace claims (L-code back/knee/wrist braces) can be tested for an ordering provider whose only claim history with the member is a brief telehealth encounter or none at all, and for multiple braces per beneficiary in a short window.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: unit = (orthotic brace claim); deny/pend when the ordering NPI has no in-person or substantive E/M claim for that beneficiary within the lookback window, or when beneficiary-to-prescriber distance and the prescriber's cross-state beneficiary count exceed calibrated percentiles. Add a prescriber-level velocity feature (distinct DMEPOS orders per day and per beneficiary, share of same-HCPCS orders, share tied to a single telemedicine entity) that suspends payment on all downstream suppliers using that NPI and triggers documentation requests for the telehealth encounter record.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Nabil Fakih (pharmacist, pharmacy owner/operator)
SchemeSummary: Fakih billed Medicare for high-reimbursing prescription drugs (blood thinners, lung disease inhalers) that his Dearborn Heights pharmacy never dispensed and lacked the inventory to dispense, concealing the scheme by manipulating inventory purchase records and diverting proceeds for personal use; ordered to pay $4M restitution plus $726,364.96 and four properties forfeited.
WaysToIdentify: Dispensing without inventory is provable pre-payment by reconciling billed NDC units against wholesaler acquisition data (ARCOS/wholesaler invoices) for the same NDC and period; a pharmacy billing high-cost anticoagulants and inhalers far in excess of purchases cannot have dispensed them. Also visible: the pharmacy's dispensing mix concentrated in a few high-reimbursement NDCs versus peer pharmacies of similar size, refills at implausibly perfect intervals, and no beneficiary cost-share collection evidence.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an inventory-reconciliation feature: unit = (pharmacy NPI, NDC, month); compute billed units minus wholesaler-purchased units and fire a prepay suspension plus invoice request when billed materially exceeds purchases. Add a high-cost-drug concentration score (share of revenue from top NDCs, growth rate, beneficiaries per prescriber) versus same-size peers, escalating to prepay review of dispensing logs and signature records.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Walgreens Boots Alliance (pharmacy chain); Dr. Edward Lubin (pain management physician); Bluestone Physician Services (geriatric provider); Daniel Hurt (owner of Fountain Health Services LLC, Verify Health, Landmark Diagnostics LLC, First Choice Laboratory LLC, Sonoran Desert Pathology Associates LLC); Robert J. Remington and New Horizons Computer Learning Center franchises (Jacksonville and Orlando); Miles Partnership, LLC; H. Lee Moffitt Cancer and Research Center; Baptist Health System
Service: Pharmacy; PhysicianPractice; GeneticTesting; Laboratory; Hospital; Telehealth
State_County: Florida - Hillsborough County (Tampa); Florida - Duval County (Jacksonville); Florida - Orange County (Orlando)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; other federal health care programs; Department of Veterans Affairs (Post-9/11 GI Bill); Small Business Administration (PPP)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Upcoding; Drug_Prescriptions; FakeEncounter; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Annual MDFL collections release summarizing multiple resolutions: Walgreens billed Medicare/Medicaid $106.8M worth of prescriptions that were processed but never picked up by beneficiaries (2009-2020); Dr. Edward Lubin took Insys speaker-program kickbacks to prescribe the opioid Subsys ($1.5M); Bluestone Physician Services billed unnecessary or upcoded monthly visits to assisted-living residents ($14.9M); Daniel Hurt used telemarketers and telemedicine prescribers to generate medically unnecessary cancer genomic tests billed to Medicare through his labs and a hospital, paying kickbacks (~$27M, plus criminal guilty plea); Moffitt Cancer Center billed federal programs for clinical-trial items that should have been billed to trial sponsors ($19.56M); Baptist Health offered patient discounts as inducements ($1.5M); non-health-care matters included a New Horizons GI Bill subsidy case ($1.35M) and a Miles Partnership PPP second-draw loan obtained despite FARA ineligibility ($2.28M). Figures span multiple defendants.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual round-up of separate resolutions, so no single control applies; each component has its own prepay signal. Walgreens' never-picked-up prescriptions are catchable by reconciling adjudicated claims against dispensing/return-to-stock events and auto-reversing claims not picked up within the return-to-stock window. Bluestone-style ALF visits are catchable by per-facility, per-day E/M level and visit-frequency profiling; Hurt's genomic tests by telemarketer-sourced orders with no treating relationship; Moffitt by clinical-trial enrolment flags (modifier/condition codes and NCT identifiers) that should route the item to the sponsor; Insys speaker fees are visible in Open Payments matched to Subsys prescribing volume.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a suite: (a) pharmacy claim-reversal monitor - unit = (Rx claim); auto-recoup when no pickup/dispense confirmation within the return-to-stock window; (b) ALF panel edit - unit = (prescriber, facility, month); flag monthly high-level E/M for nearly all residents versus peers and request notes; (c) genetic-test edit requiring an ordering provider with a treating-relationship claim; (d) research-billing edit requiring trial modifier/NCT reconciliation against sponsor-funded item lists; (e) Open Payments-to-prescribing correlation score triggering prepay review of the drug's claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Mohammed Rahman (controlled Caltech Trading Corporation); Caltech Trading Corporation
SchemeSummary: Rahman, through Caltech Trading Corporation, induced about 60 South Korean victims to invest toward a purported $1 million purchase of Brazilian sugar under a fraudulent agreement promising a 100 percent return; instead the wired funds went into his personal bank account for expenses including his mortgage, and he altered bank statements to conceal it.
WaysToIdentify: No payer or health-care claims component exists - this is an investment/wire fraud against private investors, detectable only by banks and securities regulators (funds routed to a personal account rather than an escrow or trade account, altered bank statements). There is no adjudication-time signal for a health payer.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest analogue is a payment-integrity control on payee banking: verify that remittance accounts are titled to the enrolled legal entity and flag payments routed to personal or newly opened accounts, plus manual review of any submitted bank documentation for alteration.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Mohammed Rahman (controller of Caltech Trading Corporation); Caltech Trading Corporation
SchemeSummary: Rahman, through Caltech Trading Corporation, and associates in South Korea induced roughly 60 South Korean victims to invest in a purported $1 million purchase of Brazilian sugar under a fraudulent agreement promising a 100% return; the funds were instead wired to Rahman's personal bank account and spent on personal expenses including his mortgage, with bank statements altered to conceal the diversion. Restitution of $1,393,200 and forfeiture of $1,000,000 were ordered.
WaysToIdentify: Same matter as the companion case: pure wire fraud on private investors with no claims submitted to any health plan, so nothing was catchable at adjudication. Detection sits with financial institutions (personal-account receipt of pooled investor funds, altered statements) and with securities/commodities regulators.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. If a control must be mapped, enforce entity-name-to-bank-account matching and alteration screening on any financial documents submitted during provider enrolment or payment setup.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Ramon Apellaniz (a/k/a 'Kristopher Rockefeller', de facto operator of Minds Cornerstone under pseudonym; former operator of The Gemini Project, LLC); Suhail Aponte (sole principal and registered agent of Minds Cornerstone LLC); Minds Cornerstone LLC dba Minds Cornerstone Behavior Therapy Services
PayerName: Medicaid (Connecticut Medical Assistance Program / HUSKY, Connecticut Department of Social Services)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate; Unbundling
SchemeSummary: Apellaniz, an unlicensed provider running Minds Cornerstone under a pseudonym (including while incarcerated) with owner Aponte, billed Connecticut Medicaid roughly $1.88 million for applied behavior analysis services to autistic children that were never rendered - services for which payroll shows no employee was paid, BCBA supervision billed without the corresponding technician code, and services purportedly given to patients who were actually inpatient in a hospital. Apellaniz had earlier been convicted in state court for a similar $909,268 scheme through The Gemini Project and used Minds Cornerstone funds to pay part of that restitution; both defendants pleaded guilty federally and agreed to forfeit about $469,000 plus bank accounts and two Hartford land parcels.
WaysToIdentify: Several signals were visible pre-payment: the rendering/supervising individual was unlicensed and operating under a pseudonym, so identity and license verification against the state licensing board and BCBA registry at enrolment would have failed, and the principal had a prior state Medicaid fraud conviction that exclusion/adverse-action screening should have surfaced. At adjudication, BCBA supervision codes billed with no corresponding technician direct-service code on the same date, and ABA services on dates when the child had an inpatient hospital claim, are hard edits. Payroll-versus-claims reconciliation (no employee paid for billed hours) is a records-request test.
FeaturesToCreate: Enrolment control: unit = (provider, owner, rendering NPI); run identity proofing plus license/certification and OIG-LEIE/state-exclusion and criminal-conviction matching, including pseudonym/alias and incarceration-record checks, and deny or revoke on hit. Prepay edits: reject ABA supervision codes lacking a paired technician service line for the same beneficiary-date; reject any outpatient behavioral service overlapping an inpatient stay; and add a rendering-staff capacity check comparing billed service hours to credentialed staff on file, escalating to a payroll/timesheet documentation request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Habroon Habib (owner/formed company); Around the World Solutions LLC
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Device, DME; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Habib formed Around the World Solutions LLC at a shared office space in Middletown and billed Medicare Advantage plan sponsors for orthotics purportedly supplied to more than 400 Medicare beneficiaries nationwide who never requested or received them; approximately $680,000 in plan checks were deposited into the company account and $425,000 was wired out to financial institutions in Pakistan.
WaysToIdentify: A brand-new supplier at a shared/virtual office space billing orthotics for hundreds of beneficiaries scattered nationwide within months of enrolment is an enrolment-plus-velocity signal: the practice address maps to a mail-drop/coworking suite shared by other billing entities, there is no ordering-provider relationship, and beneficiaries are far outside any plausible service radius. Site verification and beneficiary-geography dispersion are both available before payment; outbound wires to foreign banks are a bank-side signal that arrives after payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Enrolment control: unit = supplier location; match the practice address against coworking/virtual-office and mail-drop registries and against other enrolled suppliers at the same suite, and require an unannounced site visit before releasing billing privileges. Prepay control: unit = (new supplier, first 6 months); compute claim velocity, distinct-state beneficiary count, median beneficiary-to-supplier distance and share of orders from prescribers with no other relationship to the supplier's members, and place a payment hold with proof-of-delivery and beneficiary-verification requests when above calibrated percentiles.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Neuro Stat Analytical Solutions, LLC (Neurostat) (Texas-based Air Force contractor)
PayerName: United States Air Force / Department of Defense (Defense Health Agency)
SchemeSummary: Neurostat, which contracted with the Air Force to develop and implement psychological assessments and occupational health stress screening tools, allegedly paid more than $1 million to a federal employee between 2016 and 2021 in exchange for preferential treatment on federal contracts awarded to or performed by the company; it agreed to pay $1.2 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations and to cooperate in the ongoing investigation of individuals.
WaysToIdentify: This is contractor procurement corruption, not claims fraud: a vendor paying a federal employee for favorable treatment on contract awards. The detectable signals sit in procurement and financial data - a single contracting official repeatedly steering awards to one vendor, sole-source or unusually narrow solicitations, and payments from the vendor to a government employee visible in financial-disclosure filings and bank records. Nothing surfaces at claim adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a procurement-integrity analytic rather than a claims edit: unit = (contracting official, vendor); compute award concentration, sole-source rate, and modification/price-growth versus peer officials, and cross-match vendor disbursements against employee financial-disclosure and payroll identities to trigger suspension of award actions pending IG review. Nearest payer-side analogue: conflict-of-interest attestation and vendor-to-employee payment matching before contract award or provider network approval.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota
FraudEntity: Gabriel Adam Alexander Luthor, a.k.a. Gabriel Adam Alexander Langford (co-founder of Golden Victory Medical, LLC); Elizabeth Christine Brown (co-founder of Golden Victory Medical, LLC); Golden Victory Medical, LLC
SchemeSummary: Through Golden Victory Medical, LLC, the couple allegedly billed Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for neurofeedback therapy using inapplicable CPT codes, code combinations that cannot be billed together, and codes reflecting longer service durations than actually provided, continuing after warnings from insurers, an auditor, and CMS; proceeds (~$15M loss) were moved between bank accounts and used to buy an Eden Prairie mansion and pay living expenses.
WaysToIdentify: Neurofeedback billed under inapplicable codes with mutually exclusive combinations and inflated time units is entirely visible at adjudication: NCCI procedure-to-procedure and MUE edits catch the impossible pairs and unit counts, and time-based code reconciliation catches billed minutes exceeding the provider's total available clinic minutes per day. Crucially, the payer, an auditor and CMS had already warned this provider - prior audit findings and warning letters should have driven the provider onto prepay review instead of continuing auto-adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Turn on and log NCCI PTP/MUE and time-unit edits for neurofeedback/biofeedback and psych testing codes: unit = (claim, rendering NPI, date); deny lines whose summed timed units exceed the provider's plausible daily minutes or that pair non-billable code combinations. Add a recidivism control: unit = provider; when a provider has prior audit findings or education letters on the same code family and continues billing the same pattern, automatically place the provider on prepay documentation review or payment suspension rather than sending another letter.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota
FraudEntity: Tammy Wadsworth (founder and owner of Pain, Injury and Brain Centers of America); Pain, Injury and Brain Centers of America (PIBCOA)
SchemeSummary: Wadsworth founded PIBCOA and sold franchises (charging owners $60,000-$250,000 plus royalties and equipment costs) for clinics offering purported 'A.I. Myoneurvascular Therapy,' falsely claiming low-voltage electrode treatment could cure Alzheimer's, autism and other conditions with a 95% success rate; the devices she sold franchisees were relabeled with PIBCOA labels after manufacturer serial numbers and product information were removed, and she laundered proceeds into real estate and a Mercedes. Loss to franchise owners was $887,061 actual and more than $2 million total.
WaysToIdentify: The victims here are franchise buyers, not a payer, so the core fraud has no claim component; however the relabeled devices and the cure claims for Alzheimer's/autism are catchable if any franchise clinic sought reimbursement - unregistered device labeling, missing FDA clearance for the claimed indication, and unlisted/miscellaneous HCPCS codes with unsupported indications. Watch for new clinics from a single franchisor billing an identical unusual code set with identical narratives.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: unit = (device/HCPCS, indication); deny electro-stimulation device or therapy claims billed for indications with no FDA-cleared or covered use, and require manufacturer, model and serial number on the claim, rejecting relabeled or unverifiable device identifiers against the FDA/GUDID registry. Add a franchisor-cluster feature grouping providers by shared corporate parent, billing template and address lineage, routing new clusters to prepay review; otherwise this scheme is a consumer-protection matter, not a payer one.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Mississippi
FraudEntity: Willie De Gibbs (owner/beneficial owner of seven DME supply companies)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Gibbs paid kickbacks for fraudulent doctors' orders and used them to bill Medicare over $19 million for medically unnecessary orthotic braces for beneficiaries who did not request or need them, submitting claims through seven DME supply companies, four of which he controlled through straw owners.
WaysToIdentify: Common-control across seven supplier PTANs behind straw owners is visible at enrolment through shared addresses, phone numbers, bank accounts, billing agents, authorized officials and Secretary-of-State officers; the same orders and prescribers appearing across all seven confirms the ring. At adjudication, the brace claims share a small set of ordering NPIs with no treating relationship, beneficiaries did not request the items, and per-beneficiary duplicate braces across sibling suppliers are detectable.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a supplier-affiliation graph: nodes = PTANs, owners, addresses, phones, bank/EFT accounts, billing agents; fire when a cluster exceeds the calibrated size or when a new supplier links to an entity already under review, and apply the payment hold or revocation across the whole cluster. Prepay edits: deny orthotic claims where the ordering NPI has no treating-relationship claim, cap same-anatomic-site braces per beneficiary across all affiliated suppliers, and require proof of delivery plus beneficiary contact verification on flagged clusters.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Mississippi
FraudEntity: Rajwinder Kaur; Kawaldeep Singh; Narinder Kaur; Prabhdeep Momi; Bobby Babber; Priyalpreet Babber; Gurinder Babber; Mehaknoor Babber; Navdeep Basra (former Medicaid recipients; officers/registered agents/members/owners of convenience stores, gas stations, liquor stores, restaurants and other businesses)
SchemeSummary: The settling former Medicaid recipients, who owned or were officers of convenience stores, gas stations, liquor stores and restaurants, allegedly understated their household earned income on Mississippi Medicaid applications and renewals to create eligibility for their dependents, causing the state Medicaid agency to pay health coverage benefits they were not entitled to; the nine defendants collectively agreed to pay $173,627.
WaysToIdentify: This is beneficiary eligibility fraud, catchable at application/renewal rather than in claims: applicants declared low earned income while being owners or officers of retail businesses. Eligibility determination can be run against state wage/quarterly UI records, tax filings, Secretary-of-State officer/owner registries and business license data, plus federal income data hub sources, to detect self-employment income omitted from the application.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an eligibility verification rule: unit = (application/renewal, household member); cross-match declared income against UI wage records, state tax data and business-registry officer/ownership records, and fire when the applicant is a registered owner/officer of an active business with no reported self-employment income, pending manual verification before approval. Add periodic re-verification that re-runs the match mid-certification and triggers a redetermination and recovery referral on new hits.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Deer Valley Home Health Services LLC (DVHH) (home health care company); unnamed contractor/employee (purported applied behavior analysis provider)
SchemeSummary: A home health company billed Missouri Medicaid for applied behavior analysis therapy, assessments and treatment plans purportedly rendered by a contractor-turned-employee who had inflated his educational credentials and was not qualified to provide the services, and who also billed more than 24 hours of service in a single day; the company agreed to repay $534,475.
WaysToIdentify: Two checkable things: the rendering provider's credentials (claimed degree/BCBA status) were false, verifiable at credentialing through primary-source degree and certification verification with the awarding institution and the BACB registry; and he billed more than 24 hours of service in a day, an arithmetic impossibility detectable by summing timed ABA units per rendering NPI per date. Assessment and treatment-plan codes billed by a provider whose credential type is not eligible for those codes is also a prepay edit.
FeaturesToCreate: Credentialing control: unit = rendering individual; require primary-source verification of degree and certification (institution and BACB/state board) before adding to the provider file, with automatic re-verification and claim rejection when credentials lapse or fail verification. Prepay edits: reject when summed timed units per rendering NPI per date exceed available hours, and reject ABA assessment/plan-of-care codes billed under a credential type not authorized for them, routing the provider to documentation review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana; U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Jamie P. McNamara (operator/owner of laboratories in Louisiana and Texas)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: McNamara ran labs in Louisiana and Texas that obtained cancer and cardiovascular genetic testing orders from telemarketing call centers, with orders signed by purported telemedicine doctors who never treated or consulted the beneficiaries; he paid kickbacks disguised via sham contracts, shifted billing among his labs to evade scrutiny, and concealed his ownership by listing family members as owners. The labs billed Medicare over $174 million in about 18 months and were reimbursed over $55 million; the government seized luxury vehicles and over $7 million in bank accounts.
WaysToIdentify: Prepay signals: hereditary-cancer and cardiac panel claims where the ordering NPI has no treating-relationship claim for the beneficiary, orders concentrated from a handful of telemedicine NPIs, beneficiaries spread nationwide with no local clinical footprint, and no follow-up genetic counseling or treatment change after a result. Ownership concealment is catchable at enrolment via identity/family-relationship and address/phone matching plus prior-lab lineage, and billing-shifting across sibling labs is visible when the same order-source prescribers and beneficiaries move between related TINs after a review begins.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: unit = (genetic test claim); pend or deny CPT 81xxx/PLA panels when the ordering NPI lacks a qualifying treating encounter with the beneficiary in the lookback window, when the ordering NPI's cross-state ordering volume and per-day order count exceed calibrated percentiles, or when the same panel is duplicated for the beneficiary. Build a lab-affiliation graph on owners, family names, addresses, bank accounts and billing agents that transfers review status and payment suspension across sibling labs, and monitor abrupt migration of a prescriber cohort's volume from one TIN to an affiliated TIN as a suspension trigger.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Jamie P. McNamara (operator/owner of laboratories)
State_County: Louisiana - New Orleans (Eastern District of Louisiana); Texas
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: McNamara ran labs in Louisiana and Texas that billed Medicare over $174 million (receiving over $55 million) for cancer and cardiovascular genetic testing ordered via aggressive telemarketing, with orders signed by telemedicine doctors who never treated or consulted the beneficiaries; he paid kickbacks disguised as sham contracts, shifted billing among labs to evade scrutiny, and concealed his ownership by listing family members as owners on Medicare documents. Restitution of over $55 million plus $7 million forfeiture was ordered.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic: telemarketer-sourced genetic panels signed by telemedicine prescribers with no treating relationship, disguised kickbacks via sham marketing/consulting contracts, and hidden ownership via family nominees. All three are observable pre-payment - the missing treating-encounter claim for the ordering NPI, extreme per-prescriber order velocity and beneficiary geographic dispersion, and enrolment-time ownership matching against relatives and prior sanctioned labs.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a treating-relationship prepay edit on high-cost molecular panels (deny/pend absent a qualifying E/M by the ordering NPI) plus an ordering-provider velocity and dispersion score that suspends payment on all labs fed by that NPI. Add enrolment screening that resolves beneficial ownership through family/address/phone/bank linkage to previously sanctioned or reviewed labs, and require disclosure of marketing contracts with per-order or percentage-of-revenue compensation as a condition of billing.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Jamie P. McNamara (operator/owner of laboratories)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: McNamara operated laboratories in Louisiana and Texas that billed Medicare over $174 million (receiving over $55 million) for cancer and cardiovascular genetic testing, using doctors' orders obtained from telemarketers and call centers and signed by telemedicine doctors who never treated or consulted the beneficiaries; he paid kickbacks disguised as sham contracts, shifted billing among his labs to evade scrutiny, and hid his ownership by listing family members as owners on Medicare documents.
WaysToIdentify: Identical scheme profile: call-center-generated orders, telemedicine signatures without any patient consultation, kickbacks papered as contracts, and nominee owners. Pre-payment the payer can see genetic panel claims whose ordering NPI has no encounter history with the beneficiary, a tiny set of prescribers driving nearly all of a lab's volume, nationwide beneficiary spread relative to the lab's location, and rapid ramp-up of a newly enrolled lab's high-cost panel billing.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab-level prepay scorecard: unit = (lab TIN, month); features include share of claims from top-5 ordering NPIs, share of orders lacking a treating encounter, beneficiary state dispersion, revenue concentration in a few panel codes, and month-over-month growth; above the calibrated percentile, place the lab on prepay documentation review or payment suspension. Pair with a claim-level edit denying panels without a documented treating relationship and with an enrolment beneficial-ownership graph that blocks re-entry through family-named entities.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Christopher Lee Carroll (co-owner, Square One Group LLC and Whiskey Dix Big Truck Repair LLC); George Reed (co-owner, Square One Group LLC); Whiskey Dix Big Truck Repair LLC (company)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Carroll and Reed, owners of a timeshare exit company, submitted a false April 2020 PPP loan application for $1.2 million that listed their wives as owners to conceal Carroll's status as a paroled felon, then falsely certified in a forgiveness application that the funds went to payroll while Carroll instead used them to start a trucking company and cut employee health insurance; they later obtained a second PPP loan of over $1.6 million and took $660,000 in owner draws. Carroll was sentenced to 108 months and $3 million restitution and Reed to time served with the same $3 million restitution; unrelated Clean Air Act and witness-tampering counts were also part of Carroll's conviction.
WaysToIdentify: No health-claims component: this is a PPP loan and forgiveness fraud. The catchable signals sit with the SBA/lender at application - ownership listed as the wives while the operating control and signatures trace to a paroled felon (a disqualifier), and forgiveness certifications contradicted by payroll tax filings (941s) and the fact that employee health insurance was cancelled while $660,000 in owner draws left the account. A second loan to the same EIN/affiliated entity should have tripped a duplicate-borrower check.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a loan-underwriting entity-resolution check: match applicant officers, address, phone, bank account and IP against criminal-history/debarment attestations and against other applications, firing when a declared owner's spouse or associate is a disqualified person or when the same EIN/bank account appears on more than one loan. At forgiveness, reconcile claimed payroll to IRS 941/state wage data and to bank outflows, holding forgiveness for documentation where owner draws or non-payroll transfers exceed reported payroll.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: David M. Anderson (physician)
SchemeSummary: A Morgantown physician filed false federal tax returns over a four-year period that understated his taxable income and included false claims to reduce his tax liability, causing an IRS loss of $143,599; he was sentenced to six months in prison plus three years of supervised release.
WaysToIdentify: Pure individual income tax fraud with no payer claim component; the detection route is IRS-side, comparing reported taxable income to third-party reporting (1099s, insurer/payer remittance totals, merchant card receipts) for the practice. A payer contributes only by making its annual paid-claims totals per TIN available for such matching.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side prepay control applies. Nearest applicable control: an annual reconciliation feed of paid amounts per provider TIN/NPI to tax authorities, plus a credentialing flag when a provider is convicted of a tax or fraud offence so the exclusion/revalidation workflow starts.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: CIE Tours International Inc. (tour company owned by the government of Ireland)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: CIE Tours International applied for and obtained two PPP loans totaling $3,410,300 and then obtained full forgiveness, despite being ineligible because it was owned by the government of Ireland and exceeded PPP employee size limits; resolved via False Claims Act qui tam settlement of $4,428,985.04, with the relator receiving $428,985.
WaysToIdentify: No health claims: PPP eligibility fraud by a foreign-government-owned tour operator. The observable signals at application were the ownership chain (owned by the government of Ireland, so ineligible) and affiliated-entity headcount exceeding size limits, both testable against corporate registry/affiliation data and payroll filings rather than the borrower's self-certification.
FeaturesToCreate: Add an eligibility-screen at loan application that resolves ultimate beneficial ownership against foreign-state-ownership and affiliate registries, and aggregates employee counts across all commonly-controlled EINs from wage-reporting data; fire a manual review hold before disbursement and again before forgiveness when either test fails self-certification.

FraudEntity: Michael Kiszka; Gregory Kubina
State_County: New Jersey - Morris County (East Hanover); New Jersey - Ocean County (Whiting)
SchemeSummary: Two defendants allegedly obtained high-dosage oxycodone pills from several New Jersey doctors - Kiszka directly from certain doctors and by purchasing pills Kubina obtained from other doctors - and resold them to street-level drug users, diverting over 10,000 pills beginning around April 2024.
WaysToIdentify: Diversion is visible in PDMP and pharmacy claim data before payment: two individuals obtaining high-dose oxycodone from several unconnected prescribers with overlapping fill dates, cash or short-interval refills, and travel distance between patient home, prescriber and pharmacy. Multi-provider 'doctor shopping' counts and MME per day per beneficiary are computable at point of adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-level prepay edit computing distinct prescribers and pharmacies for schedule II opioids in a rolling window plus cumulative daily MME; fire a pharmacy-level reject/prior-authorisation requirement above the calibrated percentile versus peers and route the prescriber cluster to investigation. Add a prescriber-level report of patients shared with other high-MME prescribers.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

SchemeSummary: Life Touch, a North Carolina substance abuse treatment company, and its owner/managers/compliance officer allegedly paid patients more than $1 million in gift cards based on the number of days per week they attended services, generating over $25 million in Medicaid payments, while staff also took kickbacks from a drug-testing lab and lied to Medicaid auditors (two defendants also charged with failure to file tax returns). Separately, Randal Wood bought beneficiary information and prefilled orders from marketing entities that waived copays and pressured beneficiaries, then used a 'doctor chase' model to get physicians to sign or alter orders, collecting over $39 million from Medicare for medically unnecessary braces and compression devices; seven Raleigh-area mental health practitioners also pleaded guilty to falsifying health care documents for two Medicaid mental health providers. Figures span multiple defendants: $25 million (Life Touch) plus $39 million (Wood DME), with more than $6 million in assets seized.
WaysToIdentify: Attendance-driven gift-card inducements show up as implausibly perfect attendance: the same cohort of beneficiaries billed the maximum days per week for long unbroken stretches, high units per patient-day, and patients travelling far to a single clinic. The lab kickback shows as near-100% of the clinic's definitive drug tests routed to one lab with high panel-size per test; the DME arm shows one-to-many physician signing of prefilled brace/compression orders and copay waivers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a facility-level intensity model on attendance/units per enrolled beneficiary per week and the share of beneficiaries at maximum billable frequency, plus a referral-concentration ratio from clinic to single laboratory TIN; fire prepay review and documentation requests (sign-in sheets, treatment plans) above the calibrated peer percentile. For DME, edit on ordering-physician order volume per day and on braces ordered for beneficiaries with no prior treating relationship, suspending payment pending signed medical-necessity records; flag copay-waiver patterns from zero patient-responsibility remittances.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Alexis Garcia (manager/director of operations, Tape Drywall Services Inc.); Tape Drywall Services Inc.
SchemeSummary: Garcia and a co-conspirator cashed more than 3,600 checks totaling about $28 million received by Tape Drywall Services from general contractors at a check cashing business, then distributed cash to foremen to pay construction workers off the books, failing to report wages or withhold and remit FICA and federal income taxes, causing over $4.2 million in loss to the IRS and also understating payroll to avoid workers' compensation insurance costs.
WaysToIdentify: No payer claims involved - off-books cash payroll and workers' compensation premium evasion. The signals are financial: millions in check-cashing-business negotiations by a contractor whose 941 wage reports are tiny relative to contract revenue, and workers' comp payroll audits inconsistent with the general contractors' 1099 payments.
FeaturesToCreate: No health-payer prepay control applies. Nearest control for a workers' comp carrier: build a premium-audit rule comparing insured-reported payroll to third-party revenue and wage data plus check-cashing/currency-transaction patterns, firing an audit hold and premium recalculation when the revenue-to-payroll ratio is an outlier versus same-trade peers.

(owner/operator, Detroit Hoover Pharmacy); Durand Bynum (patient recruiter); Ebony Daniels (patient recruiter); Allen Satawhite (patient recruiter); P & A Aftercare (clinic); Villa Financial Services LLC; Villa Olympia Investment LLC; six Villa nursing homes (The Ambassador, Father Murray, Imperial, Regency, St. Joseph's, Westland); Wahid Makki; Zainab (Zeinab) Makki; Kirtland Corp. aka New Millennium Drugs (pharmacy); Western Wayne Pharmacy, LLC
State_County: Michigan - Wayne County (Detroit, Canton, Dearborn Heights, Westland); Michigan - Oakland County (Southfield, Lake Orion); Michigan - Macomb County (Eastpointe)
SchemeSummary: Three Eastern District of Michigan matters announced in the 2025 national takedown: four defendants were charged in a superseding indictment alleging the owner of P & A Aftercare paid doctors cash to write over 1.9 million Oxycodone, Percocet and Norco prescriptions for 'fake' patients recruited by Bynum, Daniels and Satawhite, with pharmacist Ahmad filling those prescriptions at Detroit Hoover Pharmacy outside legitimate practice; separately, Villa Financial Services, Villa Olympia Investment and six Villa nursing homes agreed to pay $4.5 million for billing Medicare/Michigan Medicaid while providing grossly substandard or absent resident care, and Wahid and Zainab Makki with their two pharmacies agreed to pay $1.5 million for billing Medicare and Medicaid for prescription drugs never dispensed (figures span multiple defendants).
WaysToIdentify: The pill-mill leg is visible prepay in prescriber/pharmacy analytics: a small clinic generating extreme oxycodone/Norco volumes, a single pharmacy filling a dominant share of one prescriber's controlled scripts, cash-paid patients travelling long distances, and 'patients' with no other medical claim history. The nursing-home substandard-care leg is best caught by joining survey/staffing data (PBJ hours, immediate-jeopardy citations) to per-diem billing; the never-dispensed drugs leg is caught by comparing dispensed NDC volumes to wholesaler acquisition data (invoice-vs-billed reconciliation), largely post-pay.
FeaturesToCreate: Build prescriber-pharmacy dyad edits: share of a prescriber's schedule II volume filled by one pharmacy, patients with no non-pharmacy encounter claims, and beneficiary-prescriber distance - firing prepay suspension and DEA referral. Build a pharmacy invoice-reconciliation audit that flags billed units exceeding purchased units per NDC, and a nursing-home payment-integrity flag joining staffing hours per resident day and serious deficiency citations to trigger medical review of per-diem claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section (Health Care Fraud Unit), 50 U.S. Attorneys' Offices and 12 State Attorneys General's Offices
FraudEntity: 324 charged defendants nationwide, including 96 doctors, nurse practitioners, pharmacists and other licensed medical professionals; 19 defendants in Operation Gold Rush (foreign straw owners of medical supply companies and a banker); 5 defendants including owners/executives of Pakistani marketing organizations; a Pakistan/UAE-based billing company owner and Arizona substance abuse treatment center owners; 7 wound care defendants including 5 medical professionals; owner of telemedicine and DME companies (Southern District of Florida); 3 defendants including business owners and a pharmacist (Western District of Tennessee)
State_County: Nationwide - 50 federal districts (including New York, Illinois, California, Florida, New Jersey, Arizona, Nevada, Texas, Tennessee, Washington)

SchemeSummary: Nationwide 2025 takedown charging 324 defendants with over $14.6 billion in intended loss: Operation Gold Rush used foreign straw owners of dozens of medical supply companies and over one million stolen American identities to bill Medicare $10.6 billion for urinary catheters and other DME, laundering proceeds into cryptocurrency and foreign shell companies; other schemes included AI-generated fake beneficiary consent recordings feeding $703 million in nominee-owned DME/lab claims, $650 million in fraudulent Arizona Medicaid substance abuse treatment billing with kickbacks for homeless and Native American patient referrals, $1.1 billion in medically unnecessary amniotic wound allografts on hospice patients, 15 million diverted opioid pills, and $1.17 billion in telemedicine/genetic testing claims. Figures aggregate across all 324 defendants; civil charges against 20 defendants ($14.2M) and civil settlements with 106 defendants totaling $34.3M were also announced, with $245 million in assets seized.
WaysToIdentify: Straw-owner enrolment is detectable at credentialing: shared addresses, phones, bank accounts and IPs across dozens of newly enrolled supplier NPIs, foreign-resident owners, recently purchased dormant entities, and no local physical inspection. At adjudication, the billing pattern is unmistakable - catheter and DME volumes per beneficiary far above peers, beneficiaries spread across states with no treating-physician relationship, ordering NPIs whose own claim history shows no such patients, and identical 'consent' recordings reused across beneficiaries.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment link-analysis engine clustering applicant NPIs on address, phone, bank, EIN, owner identity and login IP, auto-placing new-supplier clusters on prepay review or payment hold pending site visit. Add adjudication edits on units per beneficiary per period, share of beneficiaries with no prior claim from the ordering physician, and geographic dispersion of a supplier's beneficiaries; add audio-fingerprint/duplicate-hash detection on submitted consent recordings and a beneficiary-verification outreach sample before release of payment.

FraudEntity: Leland Roberts (co-owner, CEO and later consultant to Luminus Diagnostics); Dr. Marion Lee (co-owner and medical advisor to Luminus Diagnostics); Steven D. Peyroux (chiropractor and purported health care consultant); Zoe Francis (chief operating officer, Institute of Women and Ethnic Studies)
State_County: Louisiana - Orleans Parish (New Orleans); Georgia - Tift County (Tifton)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
SchemeSummary: Four EDLA defendants charged as part of the 2025 national takedown: Roberts and Lee, co-owners of Luminus Diagnostics in Tifton, GA, allegedly paid/received kickbacks for genetic testing orders (including via purported telemedicine), used 'dummy proof' order forms with prepopulated diagnosis codes, and routed tests through another lab under a sham contract, causing over $30 million (Roberts) and about $24 million (Lee) in false Medicare claims with roughly $4.4 million and $4 million paid; Peyroux allegedly paid kickbacks for Medicare beneficiary identifiers and fabricated recordings of purported beneficiaries to bill about $12.1 million (about $11 million paid) for unrequested over-the-counter COVID-19 tests, using sham agreements and false audit responses to conceal it; Francis allegedly embezzled HHS-grant and other federal funds from a New Orleans non-profit for personal events and Amazon purchases. Figures span multiple defendants and the two Luminus co-owners' billing overlaps.
WaysToIdentify: Kickback-driven genetic testing shows as orders concentrated from a handful of telemedicine prescribers who have no other treating relationship with the beneficiary, identical prepopulated diagnosis codes across thousands of requisitions, and cancer-panel volumes far above peer labs. The sham pass-through to another lab appears as reference-lab billing where the performing site differs from the billing TIN; the OTC COVID-test leg appears as high test-kit counts per beneficiary with no beneficiary request and fabricated consent recordings.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab-level ordering-concentration and diagnosis-homogeneity check: distinct ordering NPIs, share of claims from telehealth-only orderers, and entropy of ICD codes on requisitions; fire prepay medical review requiring the signed order and the treating-encounter note. Add per-beneficiary frequency caps and duplicate-supplier detection for OTC test kits, plus duplicate-hash checks on consent audio and a place-of-service/performing-lab mismatch edit for pass-through billing.

SchemeSummary: Thirteen defendants charged in five Northern District of Illinois cases totaling more than $1.83 billion billed and over $865 million paid: a Pakistan-based call center stole Medicare beneficiary IDs and used AI-faked consents to generate roughly $703 million in DME, OTC COVID-19 test kit, and genetic testing claims (about $418 million paid) plus kickbacks for selling beneficiary data; a physician and associates used patient lists from a former hospital employer and non-operational Texas labs to bill the HRSA COVID-19 Uninsured Program about $894 million ($293 million paid); a staffing operator caused a lab to bill about $233 million to HRSA for specimens never collected from often nonexistent patients ($154 million paid, $60 million to him); a lab billed Medicare and BCBS of Illinois over $72 million for COVID tests never provided ($9.7 million paid); and one defendant imported unapproved foreign Botox/Sotox and dispensed it without prescriptions. Proceeds were laundered through U.S. bank accounts; roughly $106 million in assets seized in two of the cases.
WaysToIdentify: All five schemes are visible prepay in claim metadata: stolen beneficiary IDs surface as claims for beneficiaries far from the supplier with no ordering-physician relationship and reused AI 'consent' files; the HRSA Uninsured Program billings surface as a physician submitting hundreds of thousands of specimens through Texas labs with no facility activity, no matching patient encounters, and patient lists identical to a former employer's roster; the never-provided COVID tests surface as billed test volumes exceeding lab capacity/purchased reagent quantities.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab/supplier capacity-plausibility edit: daily tests billed per accession versus staffed capacity and reagent purchases, and claims per rendering NPI per day, holding payment above plausible limits. Add a duplicate-patient-roster detector (overlap of a new biller's patient set with another entity's historical panel), beneficiary-supplier distance and no-prior-relationship edits, consent-audio duplicate hashing, and pre-disbursement bank-account/ownership link clustering for programs that pay uninsured claims without beneficiary cost-sharing.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: David Fuhrmann (national sales director of mobile medical diagnostics company)
State_County: New York - Suffolk County (Port Jefferson); Massachusetts - Suffolk County (Boston)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Sales director for a mobile diagnostics company allegedly paid doctors cash and checks per transcranial doppler (TCD) ultrasound they ordered, disguised through sham rental and administrative services agreements purporting to be fair-market-value payments, generating roughly $70.6 million in Medicare billing for medically unnecessary brain scans.
WaysToIdentify: Per-test payments to ordering doctors show up as an extreme ordering-volume concentration: a mobile diagnostics TIN whose TCD ultrasound claims come from a small set of physicians whose ordering volume tracks linearly with payments received, with TCDs ordered for patients lacking any neurologic diagnosis or follow-up. Sham 'rental/administrative services' agreements are visible at contract review and in Open Payments/vendor payment records; the medical-necessity failure is visible from diagnosis codes and absence of any resulting treatment change.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-physician profile per test code: TCD studies ordered per physician versus same-specialty peers, share of a supplier's volume from top orderers, and the proportion of studies with no supporting neurologic diagnosis or downstream care - firing prepay medical-necessity review and documentation requests. Add a financial-relationship cross-check that flags claims where the ordering physician receives payments from the billing supplier (lease/services agreements) for anti-kickback review before payment.

SchemeSummary: Nearly 50 defendants charged across 22 SDTX cases in the 2025 national takedown, with over $360 million billed to Medicare/Medicaid and roughly 12 million controlled-substance pills diverted: Ogudo/Martinez enrolled non-terminally-ill elderly beneficiaries in United Palliative & Hospice while paying kickbacks to group-home owners, a psychiatric hospital discharge coordinator, and physician Munoz to certify terminal illness ($110 million); Jenson and Romero billed over $90 million for skin-substitute products for patients with no qualifying wounds and falsified records to show chronic, improving wounds; Harper billed $115 million for kickback-induced, medically unnecessary genetic/diagnostic lab tests through shell companies and a fraudulent equipment loan; Mitchell collected $9.9 million from the COVID-19 Uninsured Program for in-office consultations never provided; Johnson billed Medicaid $793,804 (receiving $331,112) for mental health therapy never provided; and pill-mill/pharmacy rings (Peterson, Qayum, Bowers, Stokes, Sampson, Betts et al.) sold opioid prescriptions for cash and diverted millions of doses to the black market.
