WaysToIdentify: Each leg has a prepay signature: hospice enrollees drawn disproportionately from a few group homes and one psychiatric hospital discharge coordinator, with long lengths of stay, live discharges and no decline in status, certified by a single physician; skin-substitute claims with huge product units per patient and no qualifying chronic-wound diagnosis or debridement history; a lab billing kickback-driven genetic panels via shell TINs with a tiny set of orderers; COVID Uninsured Program consultations billed with no supporting encounter data; and opioid prescribers/pharmacies with extreme MME and cash-pay patients.
FeaturesToCreate: Build hospice admission-source concentration and certification-physician concentration metrics plus long-stay/live-discharge rates, firing prepay medical review of the terminal-illness certification. Add a skin-substitute edit on units/sq cm per wound and required qualifying wound diagnosis with prior conservative-care claims; add lab shell-entity link clustering on address/bank/owner; add prescriber MME and single-pharmacy-share edits with payment suspension and DEA referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nevada
FraudEntity: Mary Huntly (nurse practitioner, owner of wound care company)
SchemeSummary: A Las Vegas nurse practitioner applied medically unnecessary amniotic wound allografts to Medicare beneficiaries obtained through illegal kickbacks and bribes, and her wound care company billed Medicare approximately $14.3 million, of which Medicare paid about $9.1 million.
WaysToIdentify: Amniotic allograft overuse is visible at adjudication: very high units/square centimetres of skin-substitute product per beneficiary, applications repeated at short intervals, patients with no qualifying chronic non-healing wound diagnosis or prior debridement/offloading claims, and a single mid-level practitioner accounting for extreme product spend versus peers. Kickback-sourced patients appear as beneficiaries with no prior relationship to the practice and clustered referral sources.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a practitioner-level skin-substitute check computing product units per beneficiary and per wound area, application frequency, and share of applications lacking a qualifying wound diagnosis with documented failed conservative care; fire a prepay documentation request (wound measurements, photos, treatment history) and place outlier NPIs on prepay review. Add a referral-source concentration flag where a high share of beneficiaries arrive from a single marketer or entity.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Vermont
FraudEntity: Adnan S. Khan, M.D. (owner/physician, New England Medicine and Counseling Associates); New England Medicine and Counseling Associates (NEMCA)
SchemeSummary: Khan, through his NEMCA network of New England clinics, required patients to pay $250 in cash for high-dose buprenorphine prescriptions, falsified medical records to justify the prescribing, and lowered dosages for patients who could not pay in full; he diverted the cash proceeds for personal use including an airplane and properties, and was ordered to forfeit $75,000 plus a $20,000 fine.
WaysToIdentify: Cash-only buprenorphine dosing is detectable through PDMP and pharmacy data even where the visit was not billed: a clinic network whose patients receive high-dose buprenorphine with dose changes that track payment rather than clinical course, no corresponding office-visit claims to any payer, and no counselling or toxicology claims. Prescriber-level dose distribution far above buprenorphine peers plus long patient travel distances are computable prepay at the pharmacy claim.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-level buprenorphine profile: mean daily dose distribution versus peers, share of patients above high-dose thresholds, absence of associated evaluation/counselling or toxicology claims, and patient travel distance; fire prior authorisation on high-dose fills requiring the treatment plan and visit note. Flag clinics whose prescription volume greatly exceeds their billed encounter volume for state licensing/DEA referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut

State_County: Connecticut - New Haven County (New Haven, Danbury)
SchemeSummary: A New Haven/Danbury psychiatrist issued medically unnecessary prescriptions, including controlled substances such as excessive benzodiazepines and 'holy trinity' combinations, without legitimate medical purpose and without adequate records, causing Cornerstone Pharmacy (Whalley Drug) to submit false claims to Medicare and Medicaid, and also billed Medicare and Medicaid for medically unnecessary office visits tied to those prescriptions. Syed paid $455,439.26 and accepted a 20-year program exclusion; the pharmacy and its owner separately paid $120,000 in April 2024.

FeaturesToCreate: Build a concurrency edit at claim level firing on overlapping opioid + benzodiazepine (+ muscle relaxant) days supply per beneficiary-prescriber, with prescriber-level rate versus same-specialty peers, resulting in prior authorisation and a records request. Add a linked-billing check comparing a prescriber's E/M claim dates to fill dates and templated-note indicators (identical durations/no vitals), routing high-rate prescribers to prepay review and exclusion referral.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey

FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Williamsky opened or purchased more than twenty New Jersey DME companies using nominee/straw owners to hide his ownership, submitted fraudulent doctors' orders and claims to Medicare for orthotic braces, and closed companies one-by-one to evade Medicare audits and recoupment. Orders were generated by marketing companies cold-calling elderly beneficiaries offering free braces, with per-patient kickbacks disguised in sham contracts as 'business process outsourcing' and 'marketing expenses,' and proceeds laundered through overseas shell corporations and foreign real estate.
WaysToIdentify: The straw-ownership network is detectable at enrolment: twenty-plus DME suppliers sharing addresses, phones, bank accounts, billing agents and beneficiary overlap, with nominee owners of little means and rapid open-close cycles timed to audits. At adjudication, brace claims arrive for beneficiaries with no prior orthopaedic care, from a few high-volume signing physicians who never treated them, and marketer payments booked as 'business process outsourcing' are visible on contract/financial review.
FeaturesToCreate: Build enrolment link-analysis clustering supplier applications on address, phone, bank account, EIN, authorised official and billing-agent identity, plus a successor-entity rule flagging new NPIs sharing identifiers with recently closed or audited suppliers - action: payment hold and site visit before first payment. Add prepay brace edits on ordering-physician volume per day, ordering-physician-beneficiary prior-relationship absence, and beneficiary-supplier distance, escalating to prepay review and suspension for cluster members.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Pain Specialists, P.A. (pain clinic with locations in Northfield, Vineland, and Cape May Courthouse, NJ)
State_County: New Jersey - Atlantic County (Northfield); New Jersey - Cumberland County (Vineland); New Jersey - Cape May County (Cape May Courthouse)
PayerName: Medicare; New Jersey Medicaid; private insurance plans
SchemeSummary: The clinic billed Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers using its owner-physician's NPI for services and procedures requiring his in-person consultation or direct supervision on dates when he was traveling and not present, collecting about $58,365; the related civil settlement covered listing a physician as rendering provider for services actually performed by non-physician practitioners with no physician in the office, contrary to Medicare incident-to and Medicaid own-NPI billing rules. Corporate defendant agreed to $58,365.26 restitution, an $81,711.36 fine and a $240,000 civil settlement.
WaysToIdentify: The billing physician's NPI appears as rendering provider on dates he was out of the country, which is testable against travel/absence evidence and, more practically, against internal inconsistencies: incident-to and direct-supervision codes billed on days when no other claim, no facility log, and no supervising presence exists. A payer can also compare the practice's mix of mid-level-performed services to claims submitted under the physician NPI with no NPP claims at all.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider presence check: per NPI per date of service, count supervision-required or E/M codes and cross-check for the same NPI billing simultaneously at other locations or for gaps consistent with absence; also compute the ratio of physician-NPI claims to employed-NPP claims at the practice TIN. Fire a prepay documentation request for supervision attestation and daily schedules when supervision-required volume under one NPI is implausible or when the practice bills no NPP-rendered lines despite an NPP roster.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Medsinbox Pharmacy LTC LLC, d/b/a Farmacia San Antonio (pharmacy)
PayerName: Medicare Part D; New Jersey Medicaid
SchemeSummary: Pharmacy submitted claims to Medicare Part D and New Jersey Medicaid for prescription drugs never dispensed to beneficiaries; inventory records showed it had not purchased enough medication from wholesalers to fill the prescriptions billed. Resolved for $625,000 under the False Claims Act with no determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: Phantom dispensing is detectable prepay by reconciling billed NDC units against wholesaler acquisition data (ARCOS, 340B/wholesaler purchase feeds, or pharmacy-supplied invoices) - a pharmacy cannot dispense more units of an NDC than it bought. Additional signals: dispensing volume out of line with store size and foot traffic, and high-cost NDCs with no purchase history at all.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pharmacy-NDC inventory reconciliation engine: per pharmacy per NDC per rolling period, sum billed units and compare with purchased units from wholesaler/acquisition data, computing a dispensed-to-purchased ratio. Fire a prepay suspension and invoice-production request when the ratio exceeds unity beyond tolerance or when a high-cost NDC is billed with zero recorded purchases.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Nestor E. Jaime (pharmacy owner)
SchemeSummary: Through a Paterson, NJ pharmacy he owned, Jaime submitted hundreds of false Medicare claims for Dificid (over $4,000 per prescription) that the pharmacy never purchased or dispensed, for dozens of beneficiaries who were never prescribed it, falsely listing providers' unique provider numbers to make the prescriptions appear legitimate; Medicare paid at least ~$2.5 million, spent on luxury vehicles and personal expenses.
WaysToIdentify: A single independent pharmacy billing hundreds of Dificid claims at >$4,000 each is a glaring high-cost-NDC concentration outlier versus same-region peers, and none of it is backed by wholesaler purchases. The listed prescribers can also be canvassed cheaply: prescriber NPIs appearing on the pharmacy's claims with no corresponding office-visit or C. difficile diagnosis history for those beneficiaries.
FeaturesToCreate: Build two prepay edits: (1) high-cost-NDC concentration - per pharmacy, the share of paid dollars from a single expensive NDC and its z-score versus peer pharmacies, with automatic prepay review above the calibrated percentile; (2) prescription-provenance linkage - require, for flagged high-cost NDCs, a matching diagnosis and recent encounter for the same beneficiary from the listed prescriber, and suspend payment plus send prescriber-verification letters when absent.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Robert Lake (licensed prosthetist and orthotist, owner of TRISETO, ORTHO WORKS, and CRANIAL SCIENTIFIC); Patrick Haydel (co-conspirator, pleaded guilty)
State_County: Louisiana - Terrebonne Parish (Houma); New York - Nassau County (East Rockaway)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Lake, a licensed prosthetist/orthotist operating DME supply companies, purchased doctors' orders for medically unnecessary orthotic braces and billed Medicare; after Medicare revoked his company's enrollment, he sold the (sometimes manipulated or unsigned) doctors' orders through his marketing company for kickbacks. Lake and co-conspirator Haydel submitted over $17 million in fraudulent DME claims, receiving over $8 million; Lake transferred over $2 million to a Philippine account after a search warrant on Haydel's business.
WaysToIdentify: Two signals were available prepay: orders sourced from a marketing entity rather than a treating relationship (orthotic braces with no prior office visit, no musculoskeletal diagnosis, and one physician ordering for beneficiaries scattered nationwide), and continuity of billing after enrolment revocation through successor/related supplier NPIs sharing address, bank account, principals or phone. Signed-order anomalies (identical signature images, unsigned or altered orders) are visible on documentation review.
FeaturesToCreate: Build (1) a common-ownership/successor-entity graph over enrolment data (address, phone, bank routing, owners, licensees) that blocks payment to any new supplier NPI linked to a revoked entity; (2) an ordering-physician-to-supplier concentration edit for orthotic HCPCS - per ordering NPI, count distinct suppliers, geographic dispersion of beneficiaries, and absence of a prior in-person encounter or supporting diagnosis - firing prepay documentation requests and payment suspension above calibrated thresholds.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Rachel Collins (licensed professional counselor and owner of Rachel Collins, LPC Counseling Services LLC)
State_County: Connecticut - New Haven County (North Haven; Hamden)
SchemeSummary: Collins, an individually enrolled Connecticut Medicaid behavioral health clinician, submitted more than 17,000 claims under her own provider number for psychotherapy sessions that never occurred - billing 12 to 24+ hours per day, on holidays, weekends, while working full-time for another provider, while vacationing out of state (e.g., 96 claims during a Disney World trip in March 2023, paid $9,349.90), and for clients she never treated or who were hospitalized - obtaining $1,647,031.51 from Medicaid. She also collected $41,182 in Connecticut unemployment benefits by falsely certifying she performed no work.
WaysToIdentify: Everything needed was on the claims themselves: time-based psychotherapy units summing to 12-24+ hours in a single day for one solo NPI, service dates on holidays and weekends, and dates falling inside travel windows, plus claims for members who were inpatient on the same date. Cross-payer/cross-employer overlap (billing solo while W-2 employed full-time elsewhere) and claims for members with no other treatment history complete the picture.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider daily-capacity edit: per NPI per date, convert time-based codes to minutes, and deny or pend any day exceeding a physically plausible workday, with escalation when the pattern repeats. Add conflict edits that pend claims when the same date has (a) an inpatient/institutional claim for the member, (b) concurrent claims for the same NPI under another employer's TIN, or (c) geolocation conflicts, and auto-suspend payments plus request session notes when a provider trips the capacity edit repeatedly.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Advanced Dental Center PC (dental practice); Tal Yossefi, DMD (owner); Elad Yossefi, DDS (owner); Nazneen Jaffri, DDS (dental provider)

Pair with an enrolment-time attestation and audit trigger requiring disclosure of any per-patient marketing arrangement, with recovery under the false-certification theory.

State_County: Iowa - Dubuque County (Dubuque); Wisconsin - Grant County (Platteville)

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Shanone Chatman-Ashley (nurse practitioner, independent contractor for telehealth companies)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Nurse practitioner working as an independent contractor for purported telehealth companies signed more than 1,000 orders for knee braces, suspension sleeves and other DME for Medicare beneficiaries she never examined (including a left knee brace for a patient whose left leg was amputated), falsely certifying she had consulted with and assessed them; she received kickbacks from the companies, and the orders caused over $2 million in fraudulent Medicare claims and over $1 million paid.

Concentration of one ordering NPI across a handful of supplier NPIs indicates a paid-order pipeline.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
FraudEntity: Anja Salamack (psychiatric nurse practitioner)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Drug_Prescriptions; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: A psychiatric nurse practitioner living in Florida but claiming to practice in Albany billed New York health care benefit programs, including Medicare, for psychotherapy and evaluation/management services she never rendered, causing $163,639.58 in losses; she also issued 108 amphetamine (Adderall) prescriptions in the name of a person who had not been her patient since 2016, at a relative's request, and misused $48,670 in COVID-19 Provider Relief Funds. Provider Relief Fund misuse is detected through post-payment attestation audit and revenue-loss reconciliation.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-relationship edit for controlled substances: pend or deny stimulant fills where PDMP/claims show no qualifying encounter with the prescriber within the lookback window. Add a residency/place-of-service consistency edit comparing provider practice address, licensure state, and POS on time-based behavioral claims, pending claims with no in-state encounter footprint; route COVID relief attestations to a post-payment revenue-reconciliation audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota
FraudEntity: NUWAY Alliance, Inc. (substance use disorder treatment provider)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; Unbundling
SchemeSummary: NUWAY Alliance paid Medicaid patients (in the form of compensation, e.g. housing/other value) to seek reimbursable intensive outpatient substance use disorder treatment, violating the Anti-Kickback Statute, and also double-billed Medicaid for the same period of treatment time as distinct billable units, billing for IOP services not actually provided. Resolved by an $18.5 million civil FCA settlement plus a 5-year Corporate Integrity Agreement.
WaysToIdentify: Two distinct prepay-visible signals: overlapping/duplicated billable units for the same patient and same clock time (IOP session units billed twice or unbundled into separate codes on one date) and free housing or other value given to Medicaid patients contingent on entering reimbursable treatment, which surfaces in enrolment/marketing materials, patient cohorts sharing sober-home addresses, and rapid re-admission cycling. Address clustering of members across affiliated housing plus census-versus-billed-hours mismatch is computable from claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a same-day time-overlap edit for IOP/group codes: per member per date, sum billable minutes across all codes and providers and deny units exceeding the program's authorized daily maximum or overlapping in wall-clock time. Add a patient-inducement analytic clustering members by residential address and affiliation to the treatment entity, computing share of the provider's census living in affiliated housing and readmission cycling, firing documentation requests and prepay review above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Michelle Forsythe (licensed mental health counselor)
PayerName: Two unnamed commercial health insurance companies
SchemeSummary: Licensed mental health counselor allegedly used the names and insurance policy information of 22 individuals, without their knowledge, to bill two health insurance companies for counseling sessions she never provided, including for a person she had never treated; the insurers electronically transferred payments to her, and the government seeks forfeiture of $483,511.44 in proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: Members billed for sessions they never attended can be caught prepay by patterns: a solo counselor's panel where many members have no other claims history with the provider, no referral, and no cost-share activity, plus daily time units exceeding a plausible workday. Post-adjudication EOB verification letters to a sample of the counselor's members is the direct confirmation route, and member complaints about services never received are a high-value trigger.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a solo-provider anomaly bundle: per NPI, compute daily billed minutes, share of panel members with only this provider's claims and no other utilization, and new-member spike rate; pend payment above the calibrated percentile and auto-issue member verification letters with a response window. Escalate to prepay suspension when any member denies receiving services or when the same member's session dates conflict with other providers' claims.

FraudEntity: American Health Foundation Inc. (nonprofit owner); AHF Management Corporation (managing entity); AHF Montgomery Inc. d/b/a Cheltenham Nursing and Rehabilitation Center (nursing home); AHF Ohio Inc. d/b/a The Sanctuary at Wilmington Place (nursing home); AHF Ohio Inc. d/b/a Samaritan Care Center and Villa (nursing home)
State_County: Pennsylvania - Philadelphia County (Philadelphia); Ohio - Montgomery County (Dayton); Ohio - Medina County (Medina); Ohio - Franklin County (Dublin)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleged that three AHF-affiliated skilled nursing facilities billed Medicare and Medicaid for skilled nursing services that were grossly substandard - inadequate staffing and infection control, unsanitary/pest-infested buildings, unnecessary antibiotic, antipsychotic, antianxiety and hypnotic medications, and missing resident care plans and assessments - thereby obtaining federal payments for care that failed to meet required standards. The AHF entities collectively agreed to pay $3.61 million and enter a five-year chain-wide quality-of-care Corporate Integrity Agreement with HHS-OIG.
WaysToIdentify: Worthless-services quality failures are visible pre-payment by joining claim streams to survey/enforcement data and MDS/staffing feeds: PBJ-derived nurse hours per resident day far below same-state peers, repeat immediate-jeopardy or infection-control citations, and MDS records lacking required comprehensive assessments/care plans for residents whose per-diems are being billed. Pharmacy claim data for the same residents showing chain-wide antipsychotic, benzodiazepine, hypnotic and antibiotic prescribing rates above the calibrated percentile is a second observable signal available at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a facility-month quality composite (PBJ staffing hours per resident day, survey deficiency severity history, share of residents with no current MDS assessment or care plan, and psychotropic/antibiotic prescribing rates versus same-state peers) keyed on the facility CCN, and flag facilities in the adverse tail. Firing routes the facility's RUG/PDPM per-diem claims to prepay medical review requiring the care plan and assessment for each billed resident, and triggers a chain-level rollup review across all commonly owned CCNs.  Persistent failure supports payment suspension pending a quality CIA.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Ronald F. Ambrosia (physician)
SchemeSummary: Physician allegedly billed Medicare for application of single-use percutaneous electrical nerve stimulation devices (P-Stim) taped behind patients' ears in an office setting as if they were surgically implanted neurostimulators, using higher-paying surgical codes despite no surgery, anesthesia, or operating room, contrary to CMS guidance.
WaysToIdentify: The tell is site-of-service and code-set mismatch: implanted-neurostimulator surgical CPT codes billed with POS office, no anesthesia, no facility claim, no implantable device HCPCS on the same or nearby claim, and often no operative report. Volume of these surgical codes per rendering NPI per day is physically implausible for true implant procedures, and CMS has published guidance that P-Stim/auricular electro-acupuncture devices are not billable as implanted neurostimulators.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit at claim line level: deny or pend implanted peripheral-nerve/neurostimulator implantation CPTs when POS is office/home, no companion anesthesia claim or facility claim exists for the same beneficiary-date, and no implantable device code is present. Add a provider-month counter of such codes per rendering NPI; above the calibrated peer percentile, place the NPI on prepay documentation review demanding the operative note and device invoice/serial number.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Mohammed Ahmad (licensed physician/telemedicine contractor); Lifeline Recruiting Inc. (Florida-based DME/telemedicine company); Alicia Hiller (owner of Lifeline Recruiting)
SchemeSummary: Lifeline Recruiting bought leads of Medicare beneficiaries and used call centers to target those eligible for orthotic braces and other DME, then sent pre-completed orders to physician Ahmad, who signed them certifying the DME as medically necessary and falsely indicating he had examined patients and performed tests; the signed orders generated approximately $267,402 in claims to Medicare, of which about $126,643 was paid.
WaysToIdentify: Look at the ordering physician as the unit: a single NPI signing orthotic/DME orders for geographically dispersed beneficiaries with no corresponding evaluation claim (no office or telehealth E/M in a lookback window) and no prior treating relationship. Cluster the DME claims by ordering NPI and observe the fan-out to many unrelated suppliers plus concentration of a narrow brace HCPCS set arriving in bursts after lead-buying campaigns.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: pend brace/orthotic HCPCS when the ordering NPI has no paid E/M or telehealth encounter for that beneficiary within the lookback, or when the beneficiary's residence is beyond the calibrated distance from the ordering NPI's practice. Add an ordering-NPI monthly scorecard (distinct beneficiaries, distinct supplier NPIs, share of orders lacking any encounter) and auto-suspend new orders from NPIs above the calibrated percentile pending records showing the exam and tests certified.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Sidney L. Glover, Jr. (sole owner of Teaching Excellence, LLC)
PayerName: Medicaid (Ohio Medicaid, via Ohio Department of Disabilities)
SchemeSummary: Glover, sole owner of a home healthcare business serving individuals with disabilities that was funded largely through the Ohio Department of Disabilities/Ohio Medicaid, failed to report more than $1 million in gross business receipts for 2015-2017 on his federal income tax returns and spent some of the unreported earnings on personal expenses, causing about $155,000 in unpaid taxes.
WaysToIdentify: This is income-tax evasion on lawfully earned Medicaid revenue, so there is no claims-payment control that detects it; the route is a data-match between state Medicaid paid-amount totals per provider TIN and IRS/state receipts reported, which is post-payment and inter-agency. A payer-side proxy is owner-level financial screening at revalidation (personal expenditures funded from the provider account, commingled business/personal banking).
FeaturesToCreate: Build an annual reconciliation extract of paid dollars per provider TIN/owner SSN shared with tax authorities under an existing data-sharing agreement, flagging providers whose reported receipts differ materially from payer-paid amounts. On the payer side, require enrolled agency provider owners to attest to and reconcile revenue at revalidation and flag failure-to-file indicators for enhanced screening rather than payment action.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Daniel R. Hitlan (owner of small businesses)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Hitlan obtained three fraudulent Paycheck Protection Program loans for small businesses he owned by creating fictitious payroll documents and forms; IRS records showed no payroll, withholdings, or return filings for the entities. He spent the proceeds on Rolex watches, a Cadillac Escalade, a vintage Corvette, and real estate.
WaysToIdentify: No payer claims component: this is SBA PPP loan fraud. It was detectable at underwriting by cross-matching the applicant EIN against IRS payroll filings (Form 941, W-2/W-3) and state unemployment wage records - the entities had no payroll history at all - and by detecting one owner submitting multiple applications across related entities.
FeaturesToCreate: For the grant/loan program: an application-level verification service that requires an IRS transcript or state wage-record match for claimed payroll before disbursement, and a common-owner/common-bank-account dedupe across applications. No health-payer control applies; the nearest analogue is owner-level cross-entity linkage at provider enrolment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Richard Swenson, M.D. (physician at Accident Care and Treatment Center, Inc.)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleged that Dr. Swenson failed to maintain DEA Forms 222 for certain purchases of Hydrocodone/Acetaminophen (Schedule II) and failed to keep required purchase records for Schedule III and IV controlled substances at his Oklahoma City practice; he paid $130,000 in civil penalties without admitting liability and agreed to permanently stop dispensing and administering controlled substances.
WaysToIdentify: This is a Controlled Substances Act recordkeeping case rather than a false-claim case, but it is observable from data payers and regulators already hold: DEA ARCOS purchase volumes for the registrant compared to dispensing/administration records and to claims showing office-administered controlled substances. A gap between quantities purchased and quantities documented as dispensed is the signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a registrant-level reconciliation comparing controlled-substance acquisition (ARCOS/wholesaler data) with dispensed/administered quantities evidenced in claims and PDMP records; flag unexplained variance for an on-site records audit. For the payer, add a credentialing check that the practice holds current DEA registration and passes recordkeeping audit before paying for in-office controlled-substance administration.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Alexander Frank
SchemeSummary: Frank was indicted on 25 counts of health care fraud for billing Medicare approximately $3.2 million for face-to-face visits with beneficiaries in skilled nursing facilities that he never performed or performed only in part.
WaysToIdentify: Face-to-face SNF visit codes are checkable against independent facility data before payment: the beneficiary must be a resident on the service date (matching SNF per-diem/MDS records), and the rendering physician's daily visit count and total implied minutes must be feasible. Concentration of a single NPI billing high-level subsequent-visit codes across many facilities on the same day, and visits on dates the beneficiary was hospitalized or discharged, are the observable flags.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits: (a) deny SNF visit codes where no overlapping SNF stay exists for the beneficiary on the date of service or an inpatient/hospice overlap exists; (b) compute per rendering-NPI-day the count of nursing-facility visits and implied service minutes and pend claims above the feasibility ceiling. Providers repeatedly firing go on prepay documentation review requiring signed, dated progress notes with facility sign-in logs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Natasha Allmon (behavioral health counselor)
SchemeSummary: A behavioral health counselor submitted thousands of false claims to Blue Cross Blue Shield for 60-minute psychiatric counseling sessions purportedly provided to her own family members nearly every day of the year, including claims totaling more than 24 hours of treatment in a single day, billing about $1.4 million and collecting roughly $1.1 million.
WaysToIdentify: Two signals are visible at adjudication: implied service time per rendering provider per day exceeding a feasible workday (summing timed psychotherapy units), and a family/household relationship between the rendering provider and the members treated, detectable via shared surname, address, subscriber/dependent linkage on the same policy. Near-daily 60-minute sessions for the same small set of members every day of the year is also an outlier frequency pattern.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider-day minute accumulator across all timed psychotherapy codes and hard-deny/pend claims once cumulative minutes exceed a feasible day. Add a relationship edit that flags claims where the rendering provider shares subscriber policy, address or surname with the patient, and pend for self/family-treatment review; combine with a member-year session-frequency outlier flag for documentation request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Dr. Naveed Aslam (licensed oncologist); Somerset Hematology and Oncology, P.C. (his medical practice)
State_County: Michigan - Oakland County (West Bloomfield); Michigan - Wayne County (Detroit)
SchemeSummary: An oncologist used his medical practice's access to purchase expensive prescription cancer drugs from his supplier, then diverted and resold more than $17 million of those drugs outside the FDA-regulated supply chain through co-conspirators' company to end customers who could not otherwise obtain them, personally profiting over $2.6 million.
WaysToIdentify: Diversion shows as acquisition-versus-administration imbalance: the practice's purchases of high-cost oncology drugs from wholesalers (837/ASP or wholesaler data, DSCSA transaction records) vastly exceed units billed as administered to patients. Payers can also see the buy-and-bill mix - J-code units billed per infusion-eligible patient panel - and downstream sales appearing from an entity with no dispensing licence.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a practice-level monthly reconciliation of purchased units (wholesaler/DSCSA feed or invoice submission requirement) against J-code units billed for administration; flag material unexplained surplus for investigation and require invoice submission as a condition of payment for high-cost biologics. Add a licence check that purchasers/resellers in the DSCSA chain hold valid wholesale distributor licences, flagging unlicensed downstream buyers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Timothy Doyle (operations manager)
State_County: Massachusetts - Suffolk County (Boston); New York - Suffolk County (Selden)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Doyle and managers of a mobile medical diagnostics company paid doctors cash and checks per transcranial doppler (TCD) brain scan ordered, disguising the per-test payments as sham space rental and administrative service agreements at purported fair market value; the medically unnecessary TCD scans generated about $70.6 million in Medicare billings, of which Medicare paid roughly $27.2 million to the TCD company.
WaysToIdentify: The scheme's fingerprint is a single mobile diagnostics company billing one narrow test (TCD) at enormous volume concentrated among a small set of ordering physicians, with the same physicians simultaneously receiving space-rental/administrative payments that track test counts. Ordering-volume-per-physician outliers, absence of neurologic indications in the diagnosis history, and lack of any follow-up treatment for abnormal findings are all visible in claims before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-physician/testing-entity dyad model: tests per ordering NPI per month, share of the entity's revenue from the top few orderers, and share of scans with no supporting neurologic diagnosis or subsequent related care; fire prepay review above the calibrated percentile. Require the mobile diagnostic entity to disclose all financial arrangements with ordering physicians at enrolment and run per-test-correlation analysis on rental payments; unresolved concentration triggers payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Faith Newton (operator of Arbor Homecare Services LLC); Winnie Waruru (co-defendant); Arbor Homecare Services LLC
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Newton used Arbor Homecare Services to bill MassHealth at least $100 million for home health nursing visits and home health aide services that never occurred, directing staff to create copy-and-paste falsified nursing notes, paying kickbacks for patient referrals, creating sham employment of patients' family members as aides, pressuring doctors to sign unnecessary Plans of Care, and forging training documents for uncertified aides; she also wrote herself and her husband backdated $2 million checks from the payroll account. Newton was sentenced to 12 years, a $250,000 fine and $99,734,517 restitution; co-defendant Waruru pleaded guilty and awaits sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: Massive, fast revenue ramp at one agency plus visit-level implausibility: EVV records absent or mismatched to billed visits, aides billed while beneficiary was inpatient, aides who are the patient's own household members, and aide NPIs/employee IDs with billed hours exceeding a feasible workday. Nursing notes that are byte-identical across visits and patients are detectable by text-similarity scoring on submitted documentation, and aide certification can be verified against state registries at enrolment.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits: deny visits with no matching EVV check-in/out geolocated at the member's address, deny overlapping-hour claims per caregiver, and flag caregiver-patient household/relationship matches for review. Add an agency-level growth-and-concentration monitor (month-over-month paid growth, referral-source concentration, share of Plans of Care signed by a small set of physicians) and place fast-growing agencies on prepay review with near-duplicate-text detection on nursing notes; aide certification registry match required before hours are payable.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Eric Karlewicz a/k/a 'Anthony Mazza' (operator of marketing company Empire Pain Center Holdings LLC); Nicco Romanowski (operator of Empire Pain Center Holdings LLC); Empire Pain Center Holdings LLC (marketing company)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Operators of a New Jersey marketing company cold-called Medicare and TRICARE beneficiaries to pressure them into accepting back, shoulder and knee braces, then paid kickbacks to telemedicine companies which paid doctors to sign DME prescriptions without medical necessity and often without speaking to patients; the orders were sold to DME suppliers nationwide who billed Medicare and TRICARE over $127 million and kicked back a share (over $63 million) to Empire. Both defendants were ordered to pay $127.6 million restitution jointly, plus forfeitures of over $63 million (Karlewicz) and over $5.5 million (Romanowski), and Karlewicz/Empire consented to a $63.8 million False Claims Act judgment.
WaysToIdentify: Brace claims traceable to telemarketing-plus-telemedicine mills share a signature: a small pool of ordering NPIs writing orders for beneficiaries spread across many states and many unrelated supplier NPIs, with no prior treating relationship and often no telehealth encounter claim of adequate duration. Cross-payer view (Medicare plus TRICARE) shows the same orderers and the same lead-source clustering.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit pending L-code brace claims where the ordering NPI has no qualifying encounter with that beneficiary in the lookback, or where the ordering NPI's distinct-supplier and distinct-state counts exceed the calibrated percentile. Build an orderer-supplier bipartite network score updated nightly; when a supplier's volume is dominated by flagged orderers, suspend payment and demand the order documentation and proof of beneficiary contact.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Paul Richard Randall; Kyrollos Mekail; Patricia Anderson; Monte Vista Pharmacy
State_County: California - Orange County (Orange); California - Riverside County (Moreno Valley); California - Los Angeles County (West Hills)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants exploited Medi-Cal's temporary suspension of prior-authorization requirements to bill, through Monte Vista Pharmacy, more than $269 million (paid over $178 million) from May 2022 to April 2023 for 19 high-reimbursement, non-contracted generic drugs (including an over-the-counter vitamin, Folite) that were medically unnecessary and often never dispensed to patients; prescriptions were procured by kickbacks and proceeds were laundered through a third party to pay co-schemer Anderson. Randall charged by complaint; Anderson charged by information; Mekail pleaded guilty in August 2024 and awaits sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: When prior authorization is suspended, the compensating control is post-adjudication anomaly monitoring: a single pharmacy NPI capturing an outsized share of statewide spend on a narrow list of non-contracted high-cost generics (including an OTC vitamin) within months, with per-beneficiary quantities and refill frequencies far above peers and prescriptions concentrated among few prescribers. Beneficiary confirmation surveys and prescriber outreach would show drugs never received.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pharmacy-NDC-month surveillance feed that computes each pharmacy's share of program spend by NDC, deviation from same-region peer mix, prescriber concentration and per-member days-supply, and auto-imposes a targeted prior-authorization requirement or payment suspension on the flagged pharmacy-NDC pairs even while general PA is waived. Add a rule that non-contracted/OTC NDCs above a spend velocity trigger require proof of dispensing (signature log) before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Marielys Feliciano Rodriguez (owner of shell construction company)
State_County: Florida - Orange County (Orlando); various Florida counties
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Rodriguez set up a shell construction company, bought a minimal workers' compensation policy in its name, and 'rented' certificates of insurance to dozens of subcontractor work crews, falsely representing to contractors that the crews were her employees. Contractors issued payroll checks to the shell company (about $13 million cashed); she cashed them and paid crews in cash minus a ~6% fee, with no wages reported and over $3 million in payroll taxes (Social Security, Medicare, income tax) unpaid, and defrauding the workers' comp carrier of premium.
WaysToIdentify: No health-claims component: this is workers'-compensation premium fraud and payroll-tax evasion. It was detectable by the carrier and tax authority through mismatch between the policy's declared payroll and the volume of certificates of insurance issued/checks flowing to the shell entity, plus zero 941/state wage filings against millions in check-cashing activity at a check casher.
FeaturesToCreate: For the comp carrier: an underwriting/audit rule comparing declared payroll to third-party evidence (bank deposits, state wage records, count of certificate-of-insurance requests per policy) and flagging policies with minimum premium but wide certificate distribution for mandatory audit. Cross-agency: flag entities with large check-casher activity and no payroll filings. No payer-side health claim control applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
FraudEntity: Michael Brier (owner); Recovery Connections Centers of America, Inc. (RCCA)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; other private health insurers
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Brier and his addiction-treatment chain RCCA billed Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for 45-minute counseling sessions when patients actually received sessions of 5-15 minutes or none at all, with staff directed to move patients through quickly; they also submitted a Medicare enrollment application concealing Brier's role and his prior federal tax conviction. Brier got 98 months and $3,515,100 restitution plus roughly $1 million forfeiture; RCCA received probation and the same $3,515,100 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Time-based counseling codes can be tested for feasibility at adjudication: total billed minutes per counselor per day, and per-facility ratio of billed 45-minute units to available staffed clinician hours, will exceed what the roster can deliver when 5-15 minute sessions are upcoded. Separately, the enrolment application was falsifiable-detectable: ownership/managing-employee disclosure screened against federal conviction and exclusion databases would have surfaced the concealed principal's tax conviction and hidden control.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-clinician-day and facility-day minute accumulator across timed psychotherapy/counseling codes, comparing billed minutes to licensed-staff hours reported by the facility; pend claims above feasibility and request session start/stop times and notes. At enrolment/revalidation, run automated identity resolution on all owners, officers and managing employees (including prior names, shared addresses, bank signatories) against conviction and exclusion data, and deny or revoke on undisclosed principals.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Armen Muradyan (owner/operator of Genex Laboratories); Genex Laboratories
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Muradyan secretly owned and controlled Genex Laboratories, a blood testing lab, using a paid nominee to pose as owner and hold bank accounts that received more than $23 million in Medicare reimbursements; he gave the nominee false financial summaries so Genex income went unreported, omitted Genex activity from his own returns (tax loss over $8.5 million federal and $2.7 million California), and obtained nearly $100,000 in COVID EIDL funds via an application for a fictitious company with fabricated employees and income.
WaysToIdentify: Hidden true ownership is detectable at enrolment through identity-resolution: the nominee owner had no industry history, and bank accounts, addresses, phone numbers and prior entity filings link back to the real controller (often already known from prior entities). Payment-flow signals also show it - reimbursements sweeping out of the lab account to entities associated with the undisclosed principal, plus test-mix and per-beneficiary volume outliers typical of a controlled lab.
FeaturesToCreate: At enrolment/revalidation for labs, require and automatically verify all direct/indirect owners, managing employees and bank-account signatories, scoring nominee risk (owner with no prior claims/tax footprint, shared address/phone/IP with previously sanctioned entities) and holding the billing privilege pending verification. Add a payment-destination control: flag when EFT account holder differs from the enrolled owner or changes shortly after enrolment, and suspend payment pending verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Hassan Abdellatif, aka 'Eric' (owner/operator of El Milagro Mini Market, Supermercado El Grande, Star Mini Market, In & Out Grocery, and Harding Grocery); eight unnamed co-defendant store owners/workers
PayerName: USDA Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) program
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Convenience-store owner and eight co-defendants let customers use federally funded WIC checks to pay for items not eligible under the program, often at inflated prices, then redeemed the vouchers for cash reimbursement; ten stores redeemed over $19 million in WIC checks over eight years, with more than $6.5 million at two of Abdellatif's stores alone. He was also convicted of willfully failing to file corporate tax returns.
WaysToIdentify: WIC voucher redemption, not health claims: the signal is at the redeeming vendor level - redemption dollars per store far above same-size authorized peers, average voucher redeemed at or near the maximum allowable price, and redemption volume inconsistent with the store's authorized-food purchase invoices from wholesalers. Common ownership across ten stores showing correlated patterns is an additional enrolment-time flag.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a vendor-month redemption analytics engine: dollars per voucher versus peer price benchmarks, redemption totals versus wholesaler invoice evidence for WIC-eligible stock, and owner-linkage clustering across stores; fire a compliance buy/inventory audit and withhold redemption above the calibrated percentile. Require periodic invoice submission as a condition of continued vendor authorization, with disqualification for unsupported redemptions.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Raju Sharma (owner of Pharmagears, LLC and RR Medco, LLC); Pharmagears, LLC; RR Medco, LLC
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Sharma contracted with telemarketing companies that generated DME orders (back and knee braces) by targeting Medicare beneficiaries, paying the marketers on a per-lead/per-order basis while nominally contracting for a flat fee; he then billed Medicare through Pharmagears, RR Medco and related companies for medically unnecessary equipment that beneficiaries did not want or could not use, ordered by practitioners who never examined them or through unauthorized use of practitioners' NPIs, billing about $29.6 million and collecting about $15.8 million used to buy Ferraris, a Mercedes and Rolex watches.
WaysToIdentify: Same brace-mill signature: supplier claims concentrated in a few L-codes, ordered by NPIs with no encounter history with the beneficiary, beneficiaries far from the ordering practitioner, and some orders using practitioner NPIs whose owners never billed anything else consistent with DME ordering. Practitioner complaints of NPI misuse and beneficiary complaints of unwanted deliveries are additional pre-payment flags in the contractor's complaint data.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: pend brace HCPCS where no qualifying face-to-face encounter claim exists for the ordering NPI-beneficiary pair or the beneficiary-orderer distance exceeds the calibrated threshold. Build a supplier scorecard (L-code concentration, orderer fan-in, share of orders from NPIs with no other clinical claims, complaint counts) and auto-suspend payments for new suppliers above the calibrated percentile pending records and beneficiary verification calls.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Raju Sharma (owner of Pharmagears, LLC and RR Medco, LLC); Pharmagears, LLC; RR Medco, LLC
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Sharma allegedly contracted with telemarketing companies that generated DME orders (back and knee braces) by targeting Medicare beneficiaries, paying the marketers per lead/order rather than the flat fee stated in contracts, then billed Medicare approximately $29.6 million (paid ~$15.8 million) for medically unnecessary DME ordered by practitioners who never examined the beneficiaries or through unauthorized use of practitioners' NPIs; proceeds bought two Ferraris, a Mercedes-Benz and Rolex watches, which were subject to seizure warrants.
WaysToIdentify: Identical mechanic to the companion case: verify at adjudication that the ordering practitioner actually saw the beneficiary (presence of an E/M or qualifying telehealth claim), that the beneficiary lives within plausible distance, and that the ordering NPI's brace-order volume and supplier fan-out are within peer range. Marketing arrangements paying per lead/order are detectable at enrolment by requiring disclosure of marketing contracts and comparing invoices to order counts.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement the encounter-linkage and distance prepay edit for orthotic L-codes plus an ordering-NPI velocity flag, and a supplier-level new-enrollee payment cap with 100% prepay review during the initial period. Require suppliers to disclose marketing vendor contracts and payment records at enrolment; detected per-order compensation triggers referral and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Kelley Oliver-Hollis (owner, Serenitycare LLC)
PayerName: Medicaid (Pennsylvania Home and Community-Based Services Waiver Program); Social Security Administration
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Oliver-Hollis, an enrolled Medicaid provider operating group homes for intellectually disabled adults under Pennsylvania's HCBS Waiver Program, submitted weekly claims for HCBS benefits that falsely represented the homes were staffed with adequate workers as the program required, while the homes were understaffed and fell into unsanitary, unsafe disrepair. She also acknowledged 39 additional counts including false statements on health care matters, money laundering, and misuse of Social Security benefits as a representative payee.
WaysToIdentify: HCBS residential claims assert required staffing ratios, which is testable pre-payment: compare billed resident-days per home to submitted staffing rosters/timesheets and EVV or shift-log data, and flag homes where billed days imply more staffed hours than payroll evidences. Licensing inspection findings (unsafe/unsanitary conditions) and complaint records joined to the provider ID are further pre-payment flags, as is the same individual serving as SSA representative payee for residents whose funds she controlled.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a home-week control comparing billed HCBS resident-days against staff hours evidenced by EVV/payroll for that site and against the ratio required by the waiver; fire a prepay documentation request for staffing records and withhold payment where the ratio cannot be substantiated. Add a provider-level risk trigger from state licensing deficiency and complaint feeds that moves the provider to prepay review, and flag providers who are also representative payees for their own residents for financial-exploitation review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Ohio; U.S. District Court, Southern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Sharon Romaine Ward (owner of Halo Home Healthcare); Halo Home Healthcare
State_County: Ohio - Butler County (West Chester); Ohio - Hamilton County (Cincinnati)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Ohio Department of Medicaid); Department of Veterans Affairs health care programs
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Ward founded Halo Home Healthcare in 2015 while excluded from federal health care programs due to a prior felony prescription-forgery conviction, concealing her ownership, and the company submitted at least 92,770 Medicaid claims totaling $8,556,776.58 for home health services not performed - including continuing to bill Medicaid while a patient was hospitalized - and employed over 50 workers with disqualifying criminal histories; she also gave false information to her business tax preparer causing false returns. Restitution figures span Ohio Medicaid ($8,403,299.24), the VA, and the IRS ($81,617).
WaysToIdentify: Enrollment screening should have matched the owner and any indirect/nominee owners against the LEIE, state Medicaid exclusion list and criminal-history results, and the concealed-ownership pattern would surface by matching Secretary of State officers, tax filings, addresses and bank accounts to the disclosed owner. At adjudication, home-health visit claims overlapping a paid inpatient stay for the same beneficiary are directly visible, as are aide identities that match exclusion or disqualifying-background lists.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a monthly re-screen job that hashes and matches every disclosed owner, managing employee and billing staff plus corporate address/phone/EIN neighbors against LEIE/state exclusion and background-disqualification files, firing a payment suspension and revalidation on hit. Add a prepay edit that denies HomeHealth/PersonalCare visit lines whose dates of service fall inside an adjudicated inpatient or institutional stay for the same member, and an aide-level edit rejecting lines whose rendering aide ID is on the disqualified-worker roster.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Kansas
FraudEntity: Daniel Reif, Inc., d/b/a The Medicine Shoppe (retail pharmacy); Daniel Reif (owner and Pharmacist-in-Charge)
SchemeSummary: The pharmacy allegedly failed to maintain complete and accurate records and inventories of controlled substances and failed to keep certification records for retail sales required by the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act, in violation of the civil recordkeeping provisions of the Controlled Substances Act; it agreed to pay $200,000 to resolve the allegations.
WaysToIdentify: This is a CSA/CMEA recordkeeping civil case with no claims-payment component, so the payer route is indirect: reconcile the pharmacy's controlled-substance acquisition (ARCOS/wholesaler purchase data, 222/CSOS records) against dispensing claims volume and look for unexplained gaps, and treat DEA inspection findings as a credentialing event. Pseudoephedrine retail logbook/NPLEx certification failures are found on inspection, not in claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pharmacy-level purchase-to-dispense reconciliation that compares wholesaler controlled-substance acquisition volume by NDC/schedule to paid and cash-reported dispensing, flagging unreconciled variance above the calibrated percentile for audit and documentation request. Add a credentialing feed that ingests DEA administrative actions/inspection findings and triggers network review or on-site record audit of inventory and CMEA logs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Adnan Arshad, aka 'Eddie' (owner of MTK Taxi LLC and part owner of All-Star Taxi LLC); five unnamed co-conspirators who previously pleaded guilty
State_County: New York - Suffolk County (Montauk, Ronkonkoma, Mount Sinai, Long Island); New York - New York City
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Upcoding; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Arshad, owner/part-owner of Long Island ambulette/taxi companies, paid kickbacks to Medicaid beneficiaries to order medical transportation (largely to methadone/addiction treatment centers) from his companies, then billed Medicaid roughly $20 million for rides that generally were never provided - including claims for at least two deceased beneficiaries and for hospitalized or incarcerated individuals. He also inflated claims by directing beneficiaries to request rides to New York City clinics and list false addresses to obtain higher long-distance reimbursement rates (over $16 million billed for trips to three NYC treatment centers), and laundered proceeds into homes, luxury cars, and more transport vehicles; five co-conspirators also pleaded guilty.
WaysToIdentify: Rides billed for members with a date of death before service, or with concurrent inpatient/incarceration status, are detectable in eligibility and Vital Statistics/corrections data at adjudication. Mileage/origin-destination anomalies are visible when a member's billed pickup address does not match the eligibility address of record and the destination is a distant NYC clinic while equivalent in-county treatment centers exist, and per-member ride counts and paired billing to a handful of clinics stand out against peer transport providers.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits: deny transportation lines with DOS after date of death, during a paid inpatient stay, or during a corrections-custody span; deny long-distance/mileage-modifier lines where the billed origin ZIP differs from the member's eligibility address ZIP without an authorized address change. Add a provider-level cluster score (share of trips to a small set of distant destinations, repeat-member concentration, rides per member per week versus same-county peers) that triggers prepay review and trip-log/signature documentation requests.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Andrew Do (owner and operator of three mail-order pharmacies); Family Care Investments d/b/a Value Pharmacy
SchemeSummary: Do, who owned three mail-order pharmacies in Orange County, California, allegedly paid kickbacks to induce referrals of prescriptions for compounded topical creams, filled those prescriptions, and billed Medicare for reimbursement; the resulting claims were alleged to be false under the False Claims Act. He agreed to pay $600,000 based on inability to pay, with the qui tam relator receiving up to $100,000.
WaysToIdentify: Mail-order compounded topical cream billing shows a distinctive prepay signature: a small pharmacy, high-cost compound NDC/HCPCS mix, prescribers geographically distant from the pharmacy and from patients, and referral concentration in a few marketers' prescriber panels. Kickback payments themselves are only provable post-payment, but the referral concentration and prescriber-distance pattern are visible at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pharmacy-month model computing share of revenue from compounded topical/high-cost ingredient claims, count of distinct prescribers with prescriber-to-pharmacy distance above the calibrated threshold, and Herfindahl concentration of prescribers; fire prepay review with medical-necessity and patient-contact documentation requests. Add an ingredient-cost outlier edit that pends compound claims exceeding same-formulation peer cost percentiles pending pricing substantiation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Raheel Naviwala (owner of marketing companies and a DME supply company)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Naviwala bought lists of Medicare beneficiaries and used telemarketers to pitch orthotic braces, pre-filling prescriptions for the highest-paying braces; he paid telemedicine doctors to sign the prescriptions without speaking to patients, then sold the signed orders to DME suppliers (disguised as marketing/consulting fees via sham contracts and invoices) that billed Medicare, TRICARE and other insurers. He also owned a DME supplier that billed Medicare for up to nine braces per patient and hid his ownership behind nominee owners; insurers paid at least ~$100 million tied to his companies and he pocketed over $10 million.
WaysToIdentify: Orthotic brace claims tied to telemedicine orders show a signature payers can see prepay: one ordering NPI signing orders across many states with no prior or subsequent treatment relationship with the patient, extremely short or no telehealth encounter claim, and multiple braces per beneficiary in a short window. Ownership concealment behind nominees is catchable at enrollment by matching addresses, phones, bank accounts and shared management across supplier applications.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits: deny/pend brace HCPCS lines where the ordering NPI has no qualifying E/M or telehealth encounter with the member in the lookback window, where the ordering NPI's state/patient-distance and beneficiary count exceed calibrated peer percentiles, or where cumulative distinct brace codes per member per period exceed clinical norms. At enrollment, run an entity-resolution graph on supplier addresses/phones/bank accounts/officers to detect nominee networks and place new suppliers with graph links to flagged entities on prepay review or hold.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Daniel Dadoun (owner of several New Jersey businesses)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Dadoun submitted false PPP loan applications for his New Jersey businesses to obtain over $3.2 million, then filed fraudulent loan forgiveness applications misrepresenting payroll expenses and employee counts, supported by falsified tax documents and altered bank statements; he pleaded guilty to bank fraud and money laundering.
WaysToIdentify: No payer-side claims component; this is PPP bank/loan fraud with falsified tax documents and altered bank statements. Detection belongs to the lender/SBA: verify reported payroll against IRS Form 941 transcripts and state wage records, and re-verify bank statements directly with the depository at forgiveness.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer control applies. Nearest analogue for a health payer is an enrollment-integrity check that verifies a provider's claimed payroll/staffing against state wage and IRS transcript data and cross-checks bank/ownership documents for alteration before granting billing privileges or advance payments.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Daniel Dadoun (owner of several New Jersey businesses)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Dadoun submitted false PPP loan applications for his New Jersey businesses, obtaining over $3.2 million, then filed fraudulent loan forgiveness applications misrepresenting payroll expenses and employee counts, supported by falsified tax documents and altered bank statements; he pleaded guilty to bank fraud and money laundering and was ordered to pay $3,239,773 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Same as the companion case: pure PPP loan and forgiveness fraud with no claims adjudication involved. Lender/SBA controls - IRS 941 transcript matching, state unemployment wage-base matching, and direct bank verification of statements - are the detection path.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer control applies. If mapped to a payer, implement automated third-party verification of payroll/employee counts and bank documents before any relief, advance or accelerated payment program disbursement, with duplicate-application detection across affiliated EINs and shared owners.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Hawaii
FraudEntity: Stephen Timothy Wells (owner of Oahu Spine and Rehab)
State_County: Hawaii - Honolulu County (Oahu: Kailua and Aiea)
SchemeSummary: Wells, owner of a physical therapy clinic with Kailua and Aiea locations, used unqualified personnel (massage therapists, athletic trainers, personal trainers, and one person with no license or certification) to deliver physical therapy, then billed TRICARE and Medicare as though licensed practitioners had provided the services; he was ordered to pay $392,157.20 in restitution and 9 months in prison.
WaysToIdentify: The claims listed licensed practitioners as rendering providers while unlicensed massage therapists and trainers performed the work; payers can compare the rendering NPI's billed treatment minutes/units per day against the physically possible workday and against staff rosters submitted at credentialing. State licensure boards' data plus site-visit staff rosters reveal that clinic headcount cannot support billed volume across two locations.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider capacity edit: for each NPI-day, sum timed therapy units across all locations and pend/deny when total treatment minutes exceed the feasible workday or when the same NPI bills concurrently at two service locations. Add a roster-reconciliation check requiring each therapy claim's rendering NPI to appear on the clinic's credentialed licensed-staff roster with an active license on the DOS, and request treatment logs with signatures when clinic units-per-licensed-FTE exceed same-specialty peers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Nosson Sklar, a/k/a "Nathan Sklar" (owner and CEO of physical rehabilitation company)
PayerName: Three unnamed health benefit programs (federal health care programs referenced by HHS-OIG)
SchemeSummary: Sklar, owner/CEO of a company operating physical rehabilitation facilities around New York City, submitted or caused submission of more than $20 million in claims to three health benefit programs listing a physician (Victim-1) as the rendering provider, using forged/unauthorized physician signatures, though that doctor did not provide the services or work with the company; roughly $12.4 million was paid.
WaysToIdentify: A single physician NPI appearing as rendering provider on $20M of rehab claims for an entity he has no affiliation with is visible prepay by comparing the billing entity's TIN to the physician's own historical affiliations, addresses and claim patterns. A sudden new TIN-to-NPI pairing with high volume, plus the physician's own separate practice billing elsewhere at the same times, are strong prepay signals; physician-attestation outreach confirms it.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a TIN/NPI affiliation-change monitor: when a rendering NPI newly appears under a billing TIN and volume ramps above the calibrated percentile within the first months, pend claims and send an automated attestation notice to the physician's board-of-record address before payment. Add a concurrency edit flagging the same rendering NPI billing at multiple unaffiliated service locations on the same date, and a signature-verification documentation request on pended claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: John Drivas (owner and operator of Red's Sandwich Shop, Red's Kitchen and Tavern, and Red's Seabrook)
State_County: Massachusetts - Salem; Massachusetts - Peabody; New Hampshire - Seabrook
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Restaurant owner paid $1,496,417 in under-the-table wages to employees without reporting them or paying over federal employment taxes (causing over $439,000 in IRS losses), and collected Massachusetts state and local meals taxes from customers but intentionally omitted $1,596,775 of those taxes from monthly reports and payments to the Massachusetts Department of Revenue.
WaysToIdentify: No health care payer involvement: this is employment-tax and state meals-tax evasion by a restaurant. Detection is via IRS/state revenue analytics - comparing reported wages to POS gross receipts and merchant-processor data, and comparing collected meals tax on POS records to remitted amounts.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The analogous control is a revenue-agency edit comparing third-party payment-processor gross receipts and POS tax-collected totals against filed returns, flagging remittance ratios below the industry-calibrated norm for audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Patrick Boyd (co-owner, Safe Chain Solutions); Charles Boyd (co-owner, Safe Chain Solutions); Adam Brosius (co-owner/CEO, pleaded guilty); Safe Chain Solutions (pharmaceutical wholesaler); Peter Khaim (owner, Boulevard 9229 - supplier); Gentek (supplier)
State_County: Maryland - Talbot County (Easton); Florida - Broward County (Fort Lauderdale) and South Florida; nationwide distribution
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: The Boyd brothers, through their wholesale company Safe Chain Solutions, bought more than $92 million in black-market HIV medications from at least five suppliers (over $35 million from Boulevard 9229 and over $42 million from Gentek) that had been acquired from patients on the street through 'buyback' schemes, had prescription labels stripped and were repackaged in scavenged cardboard boxes; they resold the misbranded, sometimes tampered or wrong-drug bottles to thousands of pharmacies nationwide using falsified pedigree paperwork to make them appear sourced from legitimate distributors, and failed to report pharmacy complaints to the FDA. Two owners were convicted at trial; co-owner Adam Brosius previously pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy.
WaysToIdentify: Diverted HIV drugs re-entering the supply chain leave traceable signals: DSCSA pedigree/transaction-history chains that dead-end at unknown small wholesalers, serial numbers already recorded as dispensed to a patient, and pharmacies acquiring high-cost antiretrovirals from non-authorized distributors at below-market cost. Payers can see the downstream side as members with paid ARV fills whose dispensed serialized packages later reappear, and as pharmacies whose ARV purchase sources are not on the manufacturer's authorized distributor list.
FeaturesToCreate: Build serialization/pedigree verification at the point of claim: require the dispensing pharmacy's supplier to be on an authorized-distributor whitelist for the NDC, and reject or pend claims for high-cost specialty NDCs sourced from unlisted wholesalers. Add a duplicate-serial detector that fires when a package identifier is reported dispensed more than once or reappears after a prior paid claim, plus a member-level 'buyback' signal (repeated full ARV fills with no lab/visit utilization) referred to investigation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Kafomdi "Josephine" Okocha (co-owner, 1st Adult N Pediatric Healthcare Service); Samuel Okocha (co-owner); Carolyn Bryant-Taylor (co-owner/operator); Shekita Gore a.k.a. Shekita Steele (director of nursing); Elizabeth Ilome (nurse/personal care employee); Eno Utuk (nurse/personal care employee); 1st Adult N Pediatric Healthcare Service (Medicaid-enrolled home health agency)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Upcoding; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Owners and staff of a Medicaid-enrolled home health agency providing private duty nursing, personal care and respite care billed Virginia Medicaid for nursing services never provided or in excess of what was provided, supporting the claims with falsified records; owners paid parents/guardians of patients for blank, pre-signed nursing notes that were then filled out to document the fraudulent billing. Two owners pled guilty on this date, a third pled guilty the prior week, and three other charged defendants have pending charges; the $10 million figure is the total attributed to the scheme.
WaysToIdentify: Billed private-duty nursing and personal-care hours can be reconciled prepay against EVV check-in/out records, nurse licensure status, and per-nurse daily hour totals across all patients; hours billed with no EVV event or exceeding a feasible workday are visible before payment. Pre-signed blank notes show up as documentation whose signature dates cluster or precede service dates, detectable on targeted documentation requests to high-outlier agencies.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: deny or pend PDN/personal-care units lacking a matched EVV visit with corroborating start/stop, and deny units where the rendering caregiver's summed hours across members exceed the calibrated daily maximum or overlap in time. Add an agency-level score (hours per member per week vs peers, share of claims without EVV, guardian-paid relationships) that triggers prepay documentation review of nursing notes with signature/date consistency checks.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
FraudEntity: Brandon Nowak (officer/operator, Alternative Integrative Medicine, LLC d/b/a AIM Health); Jason Simmons (officer/operator, Alternative Integrative Medicine, LLC d/b/a AIM Health); Alternative Integrative Medicine, LLC d/b/a AIM Health
PayerName: Medicare; Medicare Advantage; Medicaid Managed Care; four unnamed private insurers
SchemeSummary: Owners of a Warwick pain management clinic allegedly told patients massage therapy was insured and then billed Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid Managed Care and four private insurers for covered services never provided - acupuncture, physical therapy, and evaluation and management office visits - as well as infrared therapy, hot/cold therapy, therapeutic activity and self-care training that the clinic had no qualified providers to deliver.
WaysToIdentify: The clinic billed acupuncture, therapy and E/M codes for which it had no licensed/qualified provider - a mismatch between the credentialed staff roster's license types and the CPT codes submitted, visible at adjudication. Also visible: high-frequency modality codes (infrared, hot/cold, therapeutic activity, self-care training) billed to every patient on every visit with E/M on the same day, far above same-specialty peer patterns, and non-covered massage delivered but billed as covered services.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a scope-of-practice/code-to-roster edit: reject claim lines whose CPT requires a license type (acupuncturist, PT, OT) not present on the billing group's credentialed roster on the DOS. Add a per-visit modality-bundle detector flagging providers whose share of visits containing the same fixed set of modality codes plus same-day E/M exceeds the calibrated peer percentile, firing prepay review with treatment-record and patient-attestation requests.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
