FraudEntity: Dr. Kamal Kabakibou (pain-management physician); Kamal Kabakibou, M.D., P.C. d/b/a The Center for Pain Management (medical practice)
State_County: Georgia - Atlanta (Fulton County); Georgia - Blue Ridge (Fannin County)
PayerName: Medicare; TRICARE; U.S. Department of Labor Office of Workers' Compensation Programs
SchemeSummary: The government alleged the doctor's pain clinics used an in-house lab to perform medically unnecessary and duplicative urine drug tests billed to Medicare, TRICARE and the Department of Labor, and that he pre-signed Schedule II opioid prescriptions left for nurse practitioners to dispense while he was out of the country. The practice and doctor jointly pay $3.5 million, with 5 years of DEA monitoring reports and a 3-year HHS-OIG integrity agreement.
WaysToIdentify: Definitive/presumptive urine drug testing done at an in-house lab shows prepay signals: uniform high-frequency testing intervals per patient regardless of risk, presumptive and definitive panels on the same specimen, duplicate panels within short windows, and a physician-owned lab receiving essentially all of the practice's referrals. Pre-signed Schedule II prescriptions are detectable by matching prescription/dispense dates to the prescriber's absence - e.g., no billed encounters by that NPI on or around those dates, and PDMP entries while no corresponding visit exists.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits: limit definitive UDT panels per member per period, deny same-specimen presumptive-plus-definitive and duplicate panels, and pend claims where the ordering physician has a financial interest in the performing lab (self-referral/ownership disclosure match). Build a prescriber-absence check linking PDMP/Part D Schedule II fills to the prescriber's own claim activity, flagging opioid prescriptions issued on dates the prescriber rendered no services for chart review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Office of Foreign Litigation (in coordination with the Public Ministry of Panama)
FraudEntity: Dr. Rolando Chin (surgeon residing in Panama); nearly 40 other Panamanian defendants including doctors, pharmacies, corporations and a hospital
PayerName: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs - Foreign Medical Program
SchemeSummary: Panamanian doctors and pharmacies submitted false and inflated claims to the VA's Foreign Medical Program, which pays for care of U.S. veterans living abroad, including claims for services never rendered and medicines never received as well as deceptive billing for services performed; Dr. Chin pleaded guilty in Panama to fraud charges and entered a restitution agreement with the United States, and VA's suspension of the roughly 40 defendants is projected to save almost $25 million in FY2025 FMP expenditures.
WaysToIdentify: Foreign Medical Program claims are paper/manual and beneficiary-reimbursed, so controls must sit at intake: check for provider concentration (a small set of Panamanian clinics/pharmacies billing most veterans in-country), duplicate or sequential invoice numbering, identical service bundles across unrelated patients, and services/medicines a veteran can be asked to confirm receipt of. Inflated per-visit pricing versus local-market fee benchmarks is visible before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an FMP prepay analytics layer: normalize foreign invoices to structured codes, compute per-provider price versus country/market benchmark and per-veteran service frequency, and pend claims above the calibrated percentile pending beneficiary confirmation of receipt. Add duplicate-invoice and template-detection (same amounts/line sets across patients) plus a provider watchlist that suspends payment to foreign providers under investigation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Matthew Brown (owner/operator of Elite Payroll and other businesses); Elite Payroll
State_County: Florida - Martin County; Florida - St. Lucie County; Florida - Palm Beach County
SchemeSummary: Brown's payroll services company collected the full amount of Social Security, Medicare and federal income taxes withheld from client companies' employees' wages, then filed false employment tax returns with the IRS that substantially underreported the liabilities, paying only the underreported amount and pocketing the difference (e.g., collecting $219,000 for one 2021 quarter but reporting and paying only about $32,000). More than $20 million in withheld taxes was diverted to buy real estate, a yacht, an aircraft and luxury cars including 27 Ferraris.
WaysToIdentify: No health care payer involvement - this is a third-party payroll agent diverting withheld employment taxes. Detection is an IRS control: reconcile aggregate W-2 withholding reported by client employers against 941 filings submitted by the agent, and notify employers directly of amounts reported/paid on their behalf.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest analogue: for entities acting as billing/financial agents on behalf of enrolled providers, require agent registration and send the principal an independent statement of amounts filed/remitted, flagging agents whose reported liabilities diverge from client-level withholding or receipt data.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Amstrong Chapajong (personal care aide and community support worker)
SchemeSummary: Chapajong, working as both a personal care aide and community support worker, billed D.C. Medicaid for overlapping shifts, claiming to provide in-home personal care and behavioral health services to multiple clients in different locations at the same time; Electronic Visit Verification data showed he was usually not near the clients' homes. He was paid $461,369 for the overlapping-hours shifts.
WaysToIdentify: Overlapping shifts by one caregiver are fully visible prepay by intersecting time-stamped units across all members, programs and provider TINs for the same worker ID. EVV geolocation showing the worker not at the member's residence at check-in is available before payment and directly contradicts the claim.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a worker-day timeline engine keyed to caregiver ID/SSN across personal care and behavioral health claim types and across agencies; deny any line whose time interval overlaps another paid or pending line for the same worker. Add an EVV geofence edit that pends units where check-in/out coordinates fall outside the member's service address radius, and suspend a worker with repeated overlap/geofence failures pending investigation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Pfizer Inc. (parent/acquirer); Biohaven Pharmaceutical Holding Company Ltd. (subsidiary, drug manufacturer)
State_County: New York - Erie County (Buffalo); New York - Monroe County (Rochester)
SchemeSummary: Biohaven allegedly paid health care providers speaker-bureau honoraria and high-end restaurant meals to induce them to prescribe the migraine drug Nurtec ODT, including repeat programs with no educational value and programs attended by speakers' spouses, relatives, friends and practice colleagues; resulting prescriptions were billed to Medicare and other federal health care programs. Pfizer, which acquired Biohaven in October 2022 and ended the programs, paid $59,746,277 (about $50.2 million federal, $9.5 million state Medicaid) to resolve the qui tam action, with the whistleblower receiving about $8.4 million.
WaysToIdentify: Speaker-program kickbacks are visible by joining Open Payments (food/beverage and speaking fees by manufacturer and drug) to Part D prescribing: prescribers with repeat honoraria for the same topic whose Nurtec volume jumps after payments. Prepay-detectable at the prescriber level as rapid new-brand share growth concentrated in paid speakers; the manufacturer-side conduct itself is post-payment/FCA territory.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a payment-to-prescribing correlation job: for each drug, link Open Payments records to prescriber-level claim volume and compute pre/post-payment prescribing lift, attendee-repeat counts and meal frequency, flagging prescribers above the calibrated percentile for prepay prior-authorization and medical-necessity review. Add a manufacturer-level monitoring report used to open FCA/CIA referrals and to tighten formulary controls on the affected brand.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Pfizer Inc. (parent/acquirer); Biohaven Pharmaceutical Holding Company Ltd. (wholly-owned subsidiary, drug manufacturer)
SchemeSummary: Biohaven allegedly paid health care providers speaker-bureau honoraria and high-end restaurant meals to induce them to prescribe the migraine drug Nurtec ODT, including sham repeat programs on the same topic and programs attended by speakers' spouses, family and practice colleagues with no educational need; resulting prescriptions were billed to Medicare and other federal health care programs. Resolved by a $59,746,277 FCA settlement (approx. $50.2M federal, $9.5M state Medicaid) from a qui tam suit by a former sales representative who receives ~$8.4M.
WaysToIdentify: Identical mechanic to the companion case: Open Payments speaker-fee and meal records joined to Part D/Medicaid prescribing reveal prescribers whose brand volume rises after honoraria, including repeat same-topic programs and attendees who are the speaker's own colleagues or relatives. Kickback liability is resolved post-payment, but the prescribing-lift signal is available before individual claims pay.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement the payment-to-prescribing lift model (Open Payments joined to prescriber claim history, per drug) with flags for repeat-program attendance and abnormal new-brand growth, routing flagged prescribers' claims to prior authorization and step-therapy edits. Feed the same output into a manufacturer-level dashboard for referral and into targeted documentation requests on flagged prescriptions.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Assertio Therapeutics Inc., f/k/a Depomed Inc. (pharmaceutical manufacturer)
State_County: Illinois - Lake Forest (company headquarters); District of Columbia
SchemeSummary: Assertio (then Depomed) allegedly marketed its fentanyl nasal spray Lazanda to high-volume TIRF prescribers - including some flagged for diversion or later indicted - placing them on speakers' bureaus and advisory boards, and ran a 'Signature Support Program' to secure insurer/Medicare Part D approval, causing 13 prescribers to write Lazanda prescriptions for Medicare and TRICARE beneficiaries without breakthrough cancer pain (the only FDA-approved indication). Resolved for $3.6 million under the FCA, with $657,000 to the qui tam relators.
WaysToIdentify: TIRF products are indicated only for breakthrough cancer pain, so payers can check prepay whether the member has any cancer diagnosis and a qualifying around-the-clock opioid regimen in claims history; absence of both is a clean denial signal. Prescriber-level signals include concentration of TIRF scripts in a handful of high-volume prescribers who also appear in Open Payments as speakers/advisors for that manufacturer, and manufacturer-funded 'support programs' submitting the prior-authorization paperwork.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay prior-authorization edit for TIRF/fentanyl NDCs requiring a cancer diagnosis in the member's claim history plus concurrent long-acting opioid therapy and opioid-tolerance documentation; deny otherwise. Add a prescriber TIRF-concentration monitor cross-joined to Open Payments and PDMP diversion flags that suspends automatic PA approval, forces independent clinical review, and blocks PA submissions originating from manufacturer-sponsored reimbursement-support entities.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Assertio Therapeutics, Inc., formerly known as Depomed, Inc. (pharmaceutical manufacturer)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Assertio (f/k/a Depomed) allegedly marketed its transmucosal immediate-release fentanyl nasal spray Lazanda to high-volume TIRF prescribers, including some flagged for diversion or later indicted, placed them on its speakers' bureau and advisory boards, and ran a 'Signature Support Program' to secure insurance/Medicare Part D approval, causing false claims to Medicare and TRICARE for patients without breakthrough cancer pain; resolved via $3.6 million FCA settlement of a 2017 qui tam suit.
WaysToIdentify: TIRF products are indication-restricted to breakthrough cancer pain, so Part D/TRICARE claims for Lazanda with no cancer diagnosis anywhere in the beneficiary's 12-month diagnostic history and no prior opioid-tolerance evidence are visible at adjudication. Concentration analysis on the prescriber dimension - a handful of NPIs writing the bulk of a manufacturer's TIRF volume - plus cross-matching those NPIs to Open Payments speaker/advisory-board payments from the same manufacturer and to prior-authorization requests submitted with manufacturer hub ('Signature Support') fax numbers or shared contact data, would have surfaced the sponsored-prescriber cluster pre-payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit on TIRF NDCs: deny/pend unless the member has a qualifying malignancy diagnosis in claims history and a concurrent long-acting opioid indicating tolerance; route pends to documentation request. Add a prescriber-level monthly scorecard combining TIRF share-of-panel and off-label rate versus same-specialty peers, joined to Open Payments speaking/consulting receipts from the TIRF manufacturer, and to a flag for PA submissions originating from manufacturer-hub contact identifiers; above the calibrated percentile, place the prescriber's TIRF claims on prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Raad Kouza (pharmacist, pharmacy owner); Ramis Kouza (pharmacy manager)
State_County: Michigan - Wayne County; Michigan - Oakland County
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan
SchemeSummary: Two brothers operating Michigan pharmacies billed Medicare, Medicaid and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan for expensive prescription drugs (antipsychotics, inhalers) that were never dispensed, concealing resulting inventory shortages from multiple auditors, causing over $15 million in losses. Both were ordered to pay approximately $15.5 million in restitution plus the same amount in forfeiture; sentences were 8 years (Raad) and 5 years (Ramis).
WaysToIdentify: Dispensing volume can be reconciled against acquisition: pharmacy claims for antipsychotics and inhalers by NDC compared with wholesaler/ARCOS and 340B/distributor purchase records will not balance when drugs were never bought. Also visible pre-payment are refill-too-soon patterns, high-cost NDC concentration versus peer pharmacies of the same size, and beneficiaries who never picked up (no copay collection, out-of-area members, no matching physician office visit).
FeaturesToCreate: Build a monthly NDC-level inventory reconciliation engine: units billed to all payers minus units purchased from distributors; fire when the unexplained dispensed-over-purchased ratio exceeds the calibrated peer percentile, and place the pharmacy on prepay review or payment suspension for those NDCs. Add a prepay edit flagging high-cost NDC claims where the member has no encounter with the prescriber in the lookback window, and share audit-refusal/inventory-shortfall findings across payers so one auditor's shortfall triggers others' edits.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: John Ageudo Rodriguez (licensed pharmacist, owner of Pharr Family Pharmacy)
SchemeSummary: Rodriguez, a pharmacist who owned Pharr Family Pharmacy, paid over $24 million in kickbacks to marketers who had relationships with physicians and clinics to steer prescriptions for expensive compounded drugs to his pharmacy, which then billed more than $110 million to federal health care programs.
WaysToIdentify: Compounded-drug claims are the signal: a single pharmacy billing enormous per-claim amounts for compounded creams/gels, with prescriptions arriving from a geographically dispersed set of prescribers who share no patients with the pharmacy's local area, indicates marketer-brokered referral flow. Kickbacks show up as abnormal marketing/commission spend relative to revenue in cost or ownership disclosures, and as prescriber panels where nearly all compound scripts route to one out-of-state pharmacy.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit on high-dollar compounded claims requiring the prescriber-patient relationship to be evidenced by a paid office visit and requiring the pharmacy to be within a plausible service radius or have documented mail-order status. Add pharmacy-level analytics: compound share of revenue, average allowed per claim, and prescriber-referral concentration (share of scripts from prescribers with no local patient overlap) versus same-specialty peers; above the calibrated percentile, suspend payment on compound claims pending records and screen the pharmacy's marketer contracts for percentage-based compensation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Cynthia Ann Herrera (pharmacist)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a pharmacist submitted or caused submission of fraudulent Medicaid claims for prescriptions that doctors had never prescribed, using doctors' personal identifying information without consent, resulting in more than $2 million in Medicaid payments between 2018 and 2024.
WaysToIdentify: Prescriber-identity misuse is detectable at adjudication: claims citing a prescriber NPI whose specialty, historical drug mix, or geography does not fit the drug, or whose NPI appears on scripts filled only at one pharmacy while that prescriber has no patient relationship with the member. Provider outreach/attestation letters to the named prescribers and members are the confirmatory step; state PDMP data will show the prescriptions absent from the prescriber's own records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-NPI plausibility edit: pend pharmacy claims where the prescriber NPI is inactive, out-of-state, specialty-implausible for the drug class, deceased, or has no encounter with the member in the lookback; require documentation before payment. Add a monitor computing, per pharmacy, the share of claims whose prescriber NPIs appear at that pharmacy only and are absent from PDMP records; above the calibrated percentile, auto-generate prescriber verification letters and suspend payment on affected claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; USAO - Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Isaiah Okoh (pharmacist); unnamed co-conspirator
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan
SchemeSummary: Okoh, a pharmacist at three Michigan pharmacies, and a co-conspirator submitted claims to Medicare, Medicaid and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan for prescription drugs that were never dispensed and never ordered by any doctor, using forged physician prescriptions to conceal the scheme, causing over $6 million in losses; he was sentenced to 80 months and ordered to pay $3,889,760 restitution plus $3,230,147 forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: Two independent signals were available pre-payment: acquisition-versus-dispensed reconciliation against wholesaler purchase records for the billed NDCs, and prescriber verification, since the underlying prescriptions were forged and would not exist in the named prescribers' records or the PDMP. Common ownership/staffing across the three pharmacies, and the same forged prescriber NPIs appearing across all three, tie the locations together.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement NDC-level purchase-to-billed reconciliation per pharmacy with pend/suspend when unexplained dispensing exceeds the calibrated peer percentile. Add a prescriber-verification edit that pends high-cost claims whose prescriber NPI has no other claim relationship with the member and no PDMP entry, and a common-ownership linkage rule that propagates a flag at any one location to all commonly owned NPIs/TINs for prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: Justin Bell (pharmacist, owner and operator of Georgetown Pharmacy); Georgetown Pharmacy
SchemeSummary: Pharmacist owner of Georgetown Pharmacy solicited unwitting Kentucky Medicaid patients to accept expensive medicated scar pads (reimbursed over $14,000 per box of twelve) that they had no medical need for and in some cases never used or discussed with their providers, then submitted eight claims causing Kentucky Medicaid to pay $118,621.28 for medically unnecessary prescriptions.
WaysToIdentify: Extreme unit price is the trigger: a per-box reimbursement in the thousands for medicated scar pads, billed by a single retail pharmacy to a small number of Medicaid members, is a clear outlier against state peer benchmarks. Absence of any surgical, burn, or wound-related diagnosis or procedure in the member's history, and absence of a prior encounter with the ordering prescriber, indicates no medical need; member interviews confirm they never discussed the product.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit on high-cost topical/wound-product NDCs and HCPCS: require a wound/scar-related diagnosis or recent surgical procedure in claims history plus a documented prescriber encounter, else pend for medical records. Add a pharmacy-level outlier monitor on allowed-dollars-per-claim and on newly billed high-unit-cost NDCs never previously dispensed by that pharmacy; above the calibrated percentile, suspend and send beneficiary verification letters.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Medsinbox Pharmacy LTC LLC d/b/a Farmacia San Antonio (pharmacy)
PayerName: Medicare Part D; Medicaid (New Jersey Medicaid Program)
SchemeSummary: Pharmacy allegedly submitted claims to Medicare Part D and New Jersey Medicaid for prescription drugs never dispensed to beneficiaries; wholesaler inventory records showed it had not purchased enough medication to fill the prescriptions billed. Settled for $625,000 with no determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: The payer itself named the signal: wholesaler inventory records show the pharmacy could not have acquired enough drug to fill what it billed, a reconciliation that can be run pre-payment if purchase data is required as a condition of network participation. Supporting prepay signals include no member cost-share collection, refill-too-soon clusters, and members with no matching prescriber encounter.
FeaturesToCreate: Require pharmacies to submit periodic wholesaler purchase files and run an automated NDC-level billed-versus-purchased reconciliation; pend or suspend claims for NDCs where billed units exceed purchases beyond a tolerance for returns/transfers. Layer a claim-level edit pending high-cost refills where no pickup/copay signal or prescriber encounter exists, with documentation request as the action.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: A Plus Pharmacy LLC (former owner of A Plus Pharmacy, Manalapan, New Jersey)
SchemeSummary: A Plus Pharmacy LLC allegedly submitted claims to Medicare Part D for prescription drugs never dispensed to beneficiaries; wholesaler inventory records showed the pharmacy had not purchased enough of the medications to fill the prescriptions billed. It agreed to pay $350,000 with no admission of liability.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as other non-dispensing pharmacies: Part D claims volume by NDC exceeds what the pharmacy ever purchased from wholesalers, provable from distributor data at or before payment if purchase reporting is a network condition. Refills continuing after a member's death, hospitalization, or nursing-home stay, and absence of copay collection, are additional adjudication-time flags.
FeaturesToCreate: Automate an NDC-level dispensed-versus-acquired ratio per pharmacy per month, firing above the calibrated tolerance into a payment suspension for the implicated NDCs pending purchase-invoice production. Add prepay edits denying refills that overlap inpatient/institutional stays or postdate death, and pending auto-refill patterns with no member contact evidence.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (sentencing in Houston, Southern District of Texas)
FraudEntity: Arthur Billings (owner, operator and pharmacist-in-charge of Health Fit Pharmacy); Deanna Winfield-Gates (relief pharmacist); Jeremy Branch (pharmacist-in-charge, 2017); Frank Cooper (relief pharmacist); Health Fit Pharmacy
State_County: Texas - Harris County (Houston); Texas - Fort Bend County (Missouri City)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; FakeEncounter; IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Health Fit Pharmacy operated as a cash-only pill mill: for hundreds of dollars per prescription it dispensed hydrocodone, oxycodone and other abused drugs to straw 'patients' sent and funded by black-market drug traffickers, who resold the pills; the prescriptions were often fraudulent, written in the names of physicians whose identities had been stolen. More than half a million opioid pills were distributed; owner Billings also made false statements on a disability benefits application. Forfeiture figures ($2.6M, $60,000, $68,931.44, $5,000) and sentences (12 years, 6 years, 22 months, 20 months) span four defendants.
WaysToIdentify: This was a cash-only diversion operation, so little or nothing flowed through payer claims; the primary detection route is PDMP and DEA/ARCOS dispensing data rather than adjudication - a pharmacy with huge Schedule II volume and near-zero insurance billing, out-of-area cash patients, and prescriber NPIs whose owners deny writing the scripts. The one payer-side hook is the disability benefits application, testable by cross-matching claimed inability to work against business ownership and licensure records.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a PDMP/ARCOS-fed monitor computing each pharmacy's Schedule II share, cash-pay share, patient travel distance, and prescriber concentration; fire above the calibrated percentile into a referral and, for any payer claims from that pharmacy, prepay review plus prescriber attestation letters. Separately, run a benefit-eligibility cross-match of disability applicants against corporate registry, licensing, and payroll/provider-enrollment data, pending awards on mismatch.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Samuel "Sam" Khaimov (co-owner of Prime Aid Union City, lead pharmacist of Prime Aid Bronx); Yana Shtindler (administrator of Prime Aid Union City); Ruben Sevumyants (operations manager); Alex Fleyshmakher (employee and on-paper owner of Prime Aid Bronx); Prime Aid Pharmacies
State_County: New Jersey - Hudson County (Union City); New York - Bronx County (Bronx)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; private health benefit providers; pharmacy benefit managers
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Drug_Prescriptions
SchemeSummary: Prime Aid specialty pharmacies billed PBMs, Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for at least $65 million in refills of expensive specialty medications (Hepatitis C, Crohn's, rheumatoid arthritis) that were never dispensed and never even ordered or stocked, and paid bribes (cash, checks, wires, meals, and an employee placed inside a doctor's office) to doctors and their staff to steer prescriptions to the pharmacies; when PBMs audited, employees falsified records and forged shipping records. Khaimov received 87 months and Shtindler 72 months; two co-defendants pleaded guilty and await sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: Specialty drugs are low-volume and high-cost, so billed-versus-acquired reconciliation against wholesaler and specialty-distributor records exposes refills for drugs never stocked. Refill-timing patterns (perfectly regular refills with no gaps, refills for members who had no corresponding specialist visit or lab monitoring for HCV/RA/Crohn's therapy) and forged shipping records that reuse tracking numbers or show impossible delivery patterns are checkable pre-payment via carrier tracking validation. Kickbacks surface as extreme prescriber-referral concentration and as pharmacy employees whose addresses/phones match a prescriber's office.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a specialty-NDC reconciliation engine (billed units vs. distributor purchases) that suspends payment per NDC on unexplained excess, and a prepay edit requiring, for specialty refills, a documented specialist encounter or monitoring lab within the clinical interval. Add automated shipment-proof validation (carrier API check of tracking numbers for existence, weight, and delivery address matching the member) and a prescriber-concentration/entity-linkage monitor flagging pharmacies where a top prescriber shares phone, address, or payroll ties with the pharmacy; fire into prepay review and audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Randy Yost (owner of Randy's Gateway Drug)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Virginia Medicaid); TRICARE; other insurance companies
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Upcoding; Phantom Claims; Retention of Overpayment
SchemeSummary: Pharmacy owner dispensed cheaper generic Schedule II medications (e.g., in place of OxyContin) while billing Medicare, Virginia Medicaid, TRICARE and private insurers for more expensive brand-name drugs; also billed for prescriptions never dispensed, and re-billed medications that patients returned without reversing the original charge. Adjusted government loss of $1,309,515; ordered to pay restitution of $1,035,279.44 to Medicare, $271,274.03 to Virginia Medicaid and $2,961.75 to TRICARE, plus 18 months imprisonment.
WaysToIdentify: Brand-for-generic substitution is detectable by reconciling billed brand NDCs against the pharmacy's purchase history - a pharmacy billing brand OxyContin while buying only generic oxycodone cannot support the claims. Reversal-rate analysis catches the return re-billing: returned/undelivered prescriptions that were never reversed appear as duplicate fills of the same drug for the same member within an implausible interval, and as a reversal rate far below same-size peers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build NDC-level brand-billed-versus-brand-purchased reconciliation per pharmacy, firing above tolerance into suspension of brand claims pending invoices. Add a prepay duplicate/refill-too-soon edit for Schedule II fills and a pharmacy-level monitor of reversal rate and unclaimed-prescription handling versus peers; low reversal rate combined with repeat early fills triggers a documentation request and postpay recovery review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Nyesha D. Paris, aka Nyesha D. Henderson and Nyesha D. Jackson (business owner)
PayerName: Medicaid; Paycheck Protection Program (SBA); Lowe's Home Improvement
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Paris ran more than a dozen fraud schemes causing over $600,000 in losses to 15 victims: she billed Pennsylvania Medicaid nearly $150,000 for home health services purportedly provided by her business but never rendered; obtained over $120,000 in PPP pandemic loans by inflating payroll, submitting fake documents and falsely certifying her companies were operating in February 2020; and stole over $40,000 in merchandise and gift cards from Lowe's using a shell company and fraudulent business accounts. Restitution of $545,993 and a forfeiture judgment of $84,008 were ordered.
WaysToIdentify: The Medicaid piece is catchable at adjudication: a newly enrolled home-health agency with no employed, background-checked, credentialed caregivers on file billing visits, no EVV check-in/check-out records matching the billed units, and members whose other claims show no home-care authorization. Cross-program matching against SBA PPP data (payroll claimed on the loan versus payroll/wage records and the provider's own billed staffing) exposes the inflated-payroll loan; the retail theft has no payer control.
FeaturesToCreate: Require EVV as a condition of payment and build a prepay edit denying home-health units with no matching EVV visit record or no active authorization, plus an enrolment-time edit blocking billing until at least one credentialed, screened caregiver NPI/employee record is on file. Add a new-provider surge monitor (rapid ramp in billed units per caregiver-hour available) that suspends payment pending records, and a data-share match of provider TINs against PPP/loan payroll certifications versus state wage filings.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: James Sessoms
PayerName: Medicaid (Pennsylvania Department of Human Services / HHS); SNAP (USDA)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Sessoms used stolen and fabricated identities, valid SSNs assigned to others, fake driver's licenses bearing his photo, and fraudulent birth certificates for fictitious spouses and children to file false SNAP and Medicaid benefit applications with the Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, obtaining $1,063,633 in benefits and selling the fraudulently obtained SNAP cards for cash at a local supermarket.
WaysToIdentify: This is benefit-eligibility identity fraud at the application stage, not claim billing: it is caught by identity proofing - SSN-to-name-and-DOB verification against SSA, death-master and duplicate-SSN checks, vital-records validation of the submitted birth certificates, and document-authentication of the driver's licenses whose photo repeats across multiple distinct applicant identities. Repeated use of one mailing address, bank account, phone, or device across supposedly unrelated households is the strongest cross-application signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an application-time identity engine: SSA/SSN validation, state vital-records verification for claimed dependents and spouses, and biometric/photo-hash plus device, phone, address and bank-account clustering across all SNAP/Medicaid applications; hold benefit issuance pending manual identity verification when one identifier links to multiple identities. Add an EBT redemption monitor for card-trafficking patterns (whole-balance transactions at a single retailer, cards used far from the enrollee's address) that suspends the card and reopens the eligibility file.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Aboudramane Karamoko; Sekou Fofanah; Shamaire Brown; Quamaire Brown
State_County: New Jersey; New York; Pennsylvania; Indiana; Rhode Island
SchemeSummary: Four Philadelphia defendants conspired to break into approximately 55 UPS warehouses across multiple states, prying open or breaking loading bay doors and targeting parcels labeled 'lithium-ion battery' that contained high-value electronics such as cell phones, stealing about $1,600,157 in merchandise; all four were ordered to pay that amount in restitution and received sentences of 24 to 39 months (longest imposed on Karamoko). Not a health care fraud scheme, though prosecuted by an AUSA of the Health Care Fraud Unit.
WaysToIdentify: No payer-side control applies: this is a cargo-theft/burglary conspiracy against UPS warehouses with no health care claims and no benefit payment involved, prosecuted only incidentally by a health care fraud AUSA. There is nothing observable at claim adjudication, enrolment, or credentialing.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer control applies. The nearest analogue, if any payer nexus were alleged, would be a supply-chain check validating that DME or drug shipments billed to the plan trace to legitimate distributor invoices and carrier delivery confirmations rather than diverted goods.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: James Sessoms
PayerName: Medicaid (Pennsylvania Department of Human Services / HHS); SNAP (USDA)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Sessoms used stolen and fabricated identities, valid SSNs assigned to others, fake driver's licenses bearing his photo, and fraudulent birth certificates for fictitious spouses and children to submit false SNAP and Medicaid benefit applications to the Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, obtaining $1,063,633 in benefits and selling the fraudulently obtained SNAP cards for cash at a local supermarket.
WaysToIdentify: Pure eligibility/identity fraud at intake rather than provider billing: catch it with SSA SSN verification, duplicate-SSN and death-master matching, state vital-records validation of the birth certificates submitted for the fictitious spouse and children, and document/photo authentication that would reveal one photo attached to several distinct identities. Shared addresses, phone numbers, bank accounts and devices across nominally unrelated applications are the clustering signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement an application-time identity-resolution service: validate SSN/name/DOB against SSA, verify each claimed dependent against vital records, hash and compare ID photos, and cluster applications on address, phone, device and account; hold issuance for manual verification whenever one identifier maps to multiple identities. Add EBT-trafficking detection (full-balance swipes at one retailer, geographic mismatch) that suspends the card and triggers eligibility redetermination.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Ghodrat Pirooz Sholevar, M.D. (psychiatrist owner); Nueva Vida Multicultural/Multilingual Behavioral Health, Inc. (mental health clinic company)
PayerName: Medicaid (Community Behavioral Health, Philadelphia Medicaid program administrator)
SchemeSummary: Psychiatrist and his three Northeast Philadelphia clinics billed Medicaid for whole 15-minute 'units' of medication management ('med checks') for children and adults when the appointments were substantially shorter, and falsified start/end clock times in patient records - including overlapping times showing two or three patients seen in the same 15-minute window at two different clinic locations - and billed more med checks than could fit in a workday. Resolved by a $900,000 False Claims Act settlement with the doctor and his company.
WaysToIdentify: Time-based E/M and med-check codes can be tested against the calendar: sum billed time-units per rendering NPI per day and flag totals exceeding a plausible workday, and detect overlapping start/end times, including the same provider billing at two service locations in the same window. Distribution analysis showing near-100% use of the higher time-tier code with no shorter-unit claims, versus same-specialty peers, is visible before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a per-rendering-NPI per-day time accumulator across all sites: deny or pend claims once billed minutes exceed the calibrated daily maximum, and hard-edit any two claims for the same provider with overlapping documented time or impossible travel between locations. Add a code-distribution outlier monitor on time-tiered med-check codes versus same-specialty peers that triggers a records request for start/stop times before payment on subsequent claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Roman Berezhnoy (operator of ransomware affiliate group '8Base'/'Affiliate 2803'); Egor Nikolaevich Glebov (operator of ransomware affiliate group); Evgenii Ptitsyn (alleged Phobos ransomware administrator)
SchemeSummary: Defendants allegedly hacked into more than 1,000 victim networks worldwide - including a children's hospital, other health care providers, and schools - stole and encrypted data with Phobos ransomware, then extorted ransom payments (over $16 million received) in exchange for decryption keys, threatening to publish stolen files on a darknet site if victims did not pay.
WaysToIdentify: This is ransomware extortion, not claims fraud, so there is no adjudication-time signal; detection sits with network security monitoring, threat intelligence, and sanctions/OFAC screening of ransom payments. The only payer-adjacent routes are contractual security attestations at credentialing and watching for post-incident billing anomalies (claim gaps then catch-up surges, or claims submitted from compromised provider credentials).
FeaturesToCreate: No claims edit prevents the intrusion; build instead a credentialing-time security-attestation requirement and a compromised-credential monitor that flags sudden changes in a provider's submitter ID, EFT bank account, IP geography, or batch volume and holds payment pending out-of-band verification. Pair with an EFT-change hold and callback verification to stop payment diversion following provider network compromise.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Puerto Rico
FraudEntity: Raúl D. Villalobos-Meléndez (physician assistant posing as licensed physician)
SchemeSummary: Defendant, licensed only as a physician assistant and never having passed the USMLE, altered his PA license into forged provisional/permanent medical licenses and forged USMLE score reports and a JLDM certification to obtain a paid physician internship position at Hospital del Maestro (June 2023–May 2024), then submitted a CMS-855I enrollment form to CMS listing a false Puerto Rico medical license number and 'General Practitioner' specialty, reassigning his Medicare benefits to Physician HMO.
WaysToIdentify: Enrolment screening catches this: the license number on the CMS-855I can be verified in real time against the state medical board's primary source, and the applicant's identity matched against the board's own licensee record - here the same person held only a PA license, so the physician license number would not validate to him. Cross-checking the NPI's taxonomy, NPPES history, education/ECFMG-USMLE verification, and prior PA-level claims history would show a specialty change with no credential basis.
FeaturesToCreate: Build automated primary-source license verification at enrolment and revalidation: match license number, licensee name, DOB and license type to the state board API, and hard-block enrolment or reassignment when type does not support the claimed specialty or the number is unissued/altered. Add a continuous monitor that flags any NPI whose taxonomy escalates from mid-level to physician without a new verified license, suspending payment on reassigned claims pending credential re-verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Neil K. Anand M.D. (physician, owner of in-house pharmacies)
PayerName: Medicare; U.S. Office of Personnel Management health plans; Independence Blue Cross; Anthem
SchemeSummary: Anand required patients seeking controlled-substance prescriptions to accept 'Goody Bags' of medically unnecessary medications dispensed by his own in-house pharmacies, billing Medicare, OPM plans, Independence Blue Cross and Anthem over $2.3 million; unlicensed medical interns wrote oxycodone prescriptions on blank forms pre-signed by Anand (20,850 tablets for nine patients), and he moved about $1.2 million of proceeds into a relative's account after learning of the investigation.
WaysToIdentify: Look for the tying pattern at adjudication: members receiving controlled-substance prescriptions from one prescriber who simultaneously and uniformly receive a fixed bundle of other medications dispensed by a pharmacy sharing the prescriber's address/ownership. Self-referral to in-house pharmacies is visible through common TIN/address/ownership between prescriber and pharmacy, and the pre-signed-blank scheme shows as prescriptions dated when the prescriber was absent or as volumes exceeding his own encounter counts, plus interns/unlicensed staff appearing as writers in PDMP data.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-pharmacy affiliation flag (shared TIN, address, phone, ownership from enrolment data) and pend claims where an affiliated pharmacy dispenses a repeating multi-drug bundle to controlled-substance patients with no supporting diagnoses. Add a per-prescriber reconciliation of controlled-substance prescriptions against billed encounters for the same member-date; when prescription counts exceed encounters above the calibrated threshold, suspend payment and request charts and signature logs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Dr. Marion Lee (co-owner and medical advisor, Luminus Diagnostics); Luminus Diagnostics
State_County: Georgia - Tift County (Tifton); Louisiana - Orleans Parish (New Orleans)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Lee, co-owner and medical advisor of a Georgia diagnostic lab, paid and received kickbacks to obtain orders for medically unnecessary genetic tests, including through purported telemedicine, using 'dummy proof' order forms with prepopulated diagnosis codes and check-box panels; claims were routed through another Louisiana lab thought more likely to be paid and concealed by a sham contract, resulting in over $24 million billed to Medicare and about $4 million paid.
WaysToIdentify: Genetic-panel claims ordered by telemedicine prescribers with no treating relationship are visible pre-payment: no prior or subsequent encounter with the ordering NPI, one ordering NPI spread across many states and labs, and identical diagnosis-code sets repeating across unrelated beneficiaries - the signature of prepopulated 'dummy proof' order forms. Reflex/pass-through billing shows as the billing lab's claims for tests it did not perform, detectable via referring-lab CLIA mismatch and sudden migration of the same ordering NPIs from one lab TIN to another.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit on high-cost genetic panels requiring a treating-provider encounter with the ordering NPI within a defined lookback and a diagnosis supporting the specific panel; deny or pend for medical necessity documentation otherwise. Add analytics on diagnosis-code entropy per ordering NPI (repeated identical code sets), telehealth-order share, and cross-lab NPI migration/CLIA-versus-performing-site mismatch; above the calibrated percentile, suspend the lab's genetic-testing payments and audit its contracts with marketers and referring labs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Neil K. Anand, M.D. (physician, owner of in-house pharmacies)
PayerName: Medicare; U.S. Office of Personnel Management (federal employee health plans); Independence Blue Cross; Anthem
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Anand billed Medicare, OPM, Independence Blue Cross and Anthem over $2.4 million for 'Goody Bags' of medically unnecessary prescription medications dispensed by pharmacies he owned, enticing patients to accept them by supplying oxycodone (20,850 tablets for nine patients) prescribed outside the usual course of practice; unlicensed medical interns wrote controlled-substance prescriptions on blank forms pre-signed by Anand, and he later moved about $1.2 million of proceeds into a relative's account. Ordered to pay over $2 million restitution and over $2 million forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: Claims data shows one prescriber accounting for nearly all prescriptions dispensed at pharmacies he owns (common ownership/address/TIN linkage between prescriber NPI and pharmacy NPI), with each beneficiary receiving an identical multi-drug 'bag' of high-margin topicals/creams plus a concurrent oxycodone fill. PDMP/Part D data would show extreme oxycodone MME per patient from a single prescriber, and prescriptions signed on dates when the prescriber was not present or written by unlicensed interns (signature/DEA number mismatch, pre-signed blank forms) is detectable via state license checks on the writer.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-pharmacy affiliation graph (shared owners, addresses, bank accounts, corporate filings) and prepay-flag pharmacy claims where the referring prescriber is affiliated and represents an outsized share of that pharmacy's revenue. Add a 'kit' detector clustering identical multi-NDC dispense baskets per beneficiary and a rule firing when a beneficiary receives the basket plus a Schedule II opioid from the same prescriber; suspend payment and require dispensing/medical records. Validate that the prescribing practitioner on each controlled-substance claim holds an active license and DEA registration at the fill date.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia; U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Ndubuisi Joseph Okafor, M.D. (sole practitioner and owner of Okafor Medical Associates)
SchemeSummary: Okafor, sole owner of an internal medicine clinic in Northwest Washington D.C., sold prescriptions for oxycodone and promethazine with codeine for cash to walk-in 'patients' (including FBI undercover agents and confidential sources) after minimal or no examination, and prescribed opioids to individuals using false identities whom he knew were diverting the drugs; conduct spanned at least 45 states and hundreds of thousands of units. He also created backdated medical records for one patient to justify prescribing after a Board of Health complaint.
WaysToIdentify: Prescriber-level PDMP and pharmacy claims show a single internal medicine office writing oxycodone and promethazine-with-codeine to patients whose home ZIP codes span dozens of states, with no corresponding office-visit claims (cash pay) and no diagnostic or imaging workup. Duplicate or mismatched patient identities (same SSN/DOB tied to different names, or names with no payer eligibility history) and pharmacy shopping across distant pharmacies are visible at fill adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Prescriber panel-geography check: compute the distribution of patient residence distance and state count per prescriber per drug class, and flag Schedule II/promethazine-codeine writers above the calibrated peer percentile for out-of-area patients or for opioid fills unaccompanied by any evaluation claim. Add an identity-integrity edit at the pharmacy that fires on SSN/DOB/name mismatch or reused demographics, and trigger a prepay documentation request plus referral of the prescriber to the licensing board and DEA.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Physicians Toxicology Laboratory, LLC (laboratory); Lund Capital Group, LLC (grandparent company); Matthew Ryan Lund (former president of PTL); Thomas C. Lund; Family Health Partners, P.C. (medical practice); Michael J. Septer, D.O. (owner of Family Health Partners); Advanced Pain Solutions, PLLC d/b/a Vitruvian Health (medical practice)
State_County: Michigan - Kent County (Grand Rapids); Michigan - Ionia County (Ionia); Florida - Hillsborough County (Tampa)
SchemeSummary: PTL created requisition forms allowing simultaneous 'blanket' orders of presumptive and definitive urine drug tests for all patients of Michigan medical practices, and placed its own in-office urine collectors who filled out the blanket orders without individualized medical-necessity determinations; PTL then ran and billed Medicare for these non-covered tests, and also billed for urine hormone tests used as specimen validity testing already bundled into UDT reimbursement. PTL and co-defendants pay $4,425,000; two ordering practices previously settled for a total of $188,633.18.
WaysToIdentify: Presumptive and definitive UDT billed on the same date for essentially every patient of a referring practice, with identical CPT combinations and identical diagnosis codes, is the signature of a blanket standing order rather than individualized necessity. Requisition forms with pre-checked panels, and lab-employed collectors physically embedded in referring offices (shared address between lab staff and the practice), are visible at audit and in referral-concentration data; urine hormone/specimen-validity codes billed alongside UDT are a bundling violation catchable by a code-pair edit.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab-plus-referrer unit of observation: compute the share of that referrer's patients receiving both presumptive and definitive UDT on the same date and the reflex-to-definitive rate, and prepay-deny or pend definitive UDT above the calibrated peer percentile pending signed, individualized orders documenting why presumptive was insufficient. Add an NCCI-style bundling edit rejecting specimen-validity/urine hormone assays billed with UDT on the same specimen, and cap UDT frequency per beneficiary per period.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Comprehensive Healthcare Management Services, LLC, d/b/a Brighton Rehabilitation and Wellness Center (nursing home operator); Mt. Lebanon Operations, LLC, d/b/a Mount Lebanon Rehabilitation and Wellness Center (nursing home operator)
State_County: Pennsylvania - Allegheny County (Pittsburgh area, Mt. Lebanon); Pennsylvania - Beaver County (Brighton)
SchemeSummary: Two nursing home operating companies, acting through high-level personnel and employees, falsified staffing sheets and certifications submitted to the Pennsylvania Department of Health and CMS - adding names of people not working or not providing direct patient care - to appear compliant with minimum staffing ratios required as conditions of participation in Medicare and Medicaid, thereby avoiding penalties and continuing to receive federal funds. After a December 2023 jury conviction, Brighton was ordered to pay $12,629,257.46 restitution plus five years probation and Mt. Lebanon $2,721,312.10 plus one year probation.
WaysToIdentify: Reported staffing on cost reports and PBJ/state staffing submissions can be reconciled against payroll tax records, wage data, and licensure files: names listed as direct-care staff who have no payroll entry, no active license, or who are simultaneously reported at another facility are detectable before payment of the period's claims. Administrative/kitchen staff counted as direct care is visible by comparing job codes to hours claimed.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an automated PBJ-to-payroll reconciliation: for each facility-quarter, join reported staff hours to employer payroll/tax filings and state license files, and compute the share of reported hours with no payroll or license match and hours for individuals reported at multiple facilities in overlapping shifts. Fire a compliance hold and condition-of-participation review (with payment suspension for repeated variance) when unmatched hours exceed the calibrated threshold or when reported ratios sit just above the minimum every period.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Toby Weatherbee (member of Plasterer's Local Union #9)
State_County: New York - Western District of New York (Pike, NY)
PayerName: Plaster's Local Union #9 health and welfare fund (union health care benefit program)
SchemeSummary: Weatherbee submitted 12 fraudulent invoices, including a fabricated $6,720 invoice from Dansville Dental Professionals, LLP, to his union's health and welfare fund for reimbursement of out-of-pocket medical expenses he never incurred, converting $44,012 of fund money to his own use. He received two years' probation and was ordered to pay $44,012 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Member-submitted out-of-network reimbursement invoices can be validated against the named provider: verify the practice's TIN/NPI, confirm the invoice number/format and that the provider has any record of the patient, and check whether the same member submitted multiple invoices with sequential or reused numbers and round-dollar totals. Repeat manual reimbursements to one member with no corresponding provider-side claim is the core signal.
FeaturesToCreate: For member-reimbursement claims, build a provider-verification step that matches the billing entity on the receipt to registry data (NPI/TIN/address) and auto-pends any receipt from a provider with no submitted claim history for that member. Add a member-level velocity/aggregate rule (count and dollars of self-submitted receipts per rolling period, duplicate invoice numbers, identical templates) that fires an investigator review and direct provider confirmation before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Cory Lloyd (president of insurance brokerage firm); Steven Strong (CEO of marketing company)
State_County: Florida - Martin County (Stuart); Texas - Tarrant County (Mansfield)
PayerName: Federal government (Affordable Care Act premium subsidies); insurance companies
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants allegedly enrolled low-income and homeless individuals in fully subsidized ACA health plans by submitting false applications overstating projected income (and using mismatched addresses and Social Security numbers) so enrollees would appear eligible for federal premium subsidies; the brokerage collected commissions from insurers and paid Strong commissions for consumer referrals, with street marketers bribing consumers to enroll. Alleged federal subsidy payments totaled at least $161.9 million.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, attested projected income can be cross-checked against IRS/SSA and state wage data; applications that attest income just above the subsidy-eligibility floor while the trusted-data check returns no or near-zero income are the core signal. Broker-level clustering - one NPN/agency submitting many applications sharing addresses, phone numbers, or shelter addresses, with mismatched SSN/name, all at maximum subsidy - is visible before any APTC is paid.
FeaturesToCreate: Build broker/agency-level enrolment analytics: for each writing agent, compute the rate of applications with income attested within a narrow band above the eligibility floor, the rate of data-matching inconsistencies, address/phone reuse across unrelated enrollees, and the share of zero-premium plans; suspend the agent's marketplace access and hold APTC pending DMI resolution when above the calibrated percentile. Add a per-application rule requiring documentary income proof before subsidy payment when trusted data shows income below the attested figure.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (federal jury in West Palm Beach, Florida)
FraudEntity: Cory Lloyd (president of insurance brokerage firm); Steven Strong (CEO of marketing company)
State_County: Florida - Palm Beach County (West Palm Beach); Florida - Martin County (Stuart); Texas - Tarrant County (Mansfield)
PayerName: Affordable Care Act federal premium subsidies (federal government); private insurance companies
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Lloyd and Strong submitted false ACA marketplace enrollment applications for low-income, homeless, and substance-using individuals whose income did not meet the minimum eligibility threshold for fully subsidized plans, using coached answers, mismatched addresses and Social Security numbers, bribes to enrollees, and deliberately doomed Medicaid applications to enable off-cycle enrollment; the federal government paid at least $180 million of over $233 million in subsidies, and Lloyd earned insurer commissions and paid Strong for referrals.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic: attested income clustered just above the subsidy floor while IRS/SSA/state wage data show none, plus reused or shelter addresses, mismatched SSNs, and abandoned Medicaid applications used to manufacture special-enrolment periods. Agent-level concentration of these features, and enrollees with zero claims utilization after enrolment, are all observable before subsidies are disbursed.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement an income-plausibility edit that pends APTC when attested projected income is within a narrow band above the floor and trusted data returns no earnings, requiring documentation before disbursement. Layer an agent scorecard (data-match failure rate, duplicate contact/address clusters, SEP-via-denied-Medicaid rate, commission per enrollee) that triggers agent suspension and retroactive APTC recovery, and flag SEP claims where the Medicaid application was never completed.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Liaquat Cheema (President of AFL Construction Co. Inc.); AFL Construction Co. Inc.
State_County: New York - Queens County; New York - New York County (Southern District of New York)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Cheema, president of a Queens construction company holding ~$12 million in New York City homeless-shelter contracts, submitted fraudulent invoices and supporting documents falsely claiming workers performed work and inflating material costs, using other people's identities (including a Social Security number) as purported workers. Separately, he and others obtained tens of thousands of dollars in Medicaid benefits by submitting false certifications and near-identical employment letters underreporting income and bearing the signature of a deceased 'project manager.'
WaysToIdentify: The Medicaid side is catchable at eligibility determination: employment/income letters from multiple applicants that are near-identical in wording and layout, signed by the same 'manager', and reporting income conveniently below the limit, can be matched against employer payroll/quarterly wage filings and against SSA death records for the signer. The city-contract invoice fraud is a procurement matter - certified payroll names/SSNs can be matched to wage records - not a claims-adjudication control.
FeaturesToCreate: At Medicaid eligibility, auto-verify attested employer income against state quarterly wage and IRS data and pend cases with a variance beyond tolerance; add document-forensics rules that hash/fuzzy-match uploaded employment letters across applications to detect templates and flag reused signer names, plus a check of signer identity against death-master and licensing files. For contract invoicing, run certified-payroll SSN/name validation against wage records before disbursement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Walter Stanzione (principal/leader of Fire Alarm Electrical Corp.); William Neogra (principal of Fire Alarm Electrical Corp.); Fire Alarm Electrical Corp.
PayerName: City of New York agencies (Department of Citywide Administrative Services, Department of Education, Department of Environmental Protection, Department of Sanitation)
SchemeSummary: The two principals of a fire alarm maintenance contractor holding New York City contracts submitted fraudulent invoices to four city agencies over an eleven-year period, buying supplies from legitimate retailers and re-invoicing them through secretly owned shell companies at three to five times the real cost, and altering genuine retailer invoices when city auditors grew suspicious; Stanzione siphoned off much of the proceeds for personal spending. Both defendants pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy; no health care payer was involved.
WaysToIdentify: No health care payer is involved - this is municipal procurement/wire fraud. It would be caught by vendor-side controls: beneficial-ownership disclosure showing the 'suppliers' were shell companies owned by the prime's principals, and price benchmarking of invoiced parts against retail catalog prices. Altered retailer invoices are detectable by requesting confirmation directly from the retailer rather than accepting contractor-supplied copies.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a vendor-graph control on invoice payment: match subcontractor/supplier entities against the prime's registered officers, addresses, bank accounts and corporate filings, and block payment on pass-through markups from related parties. Add a line-item price benchmark against reference catalog pricing that pends invoices whose unit prices exceed the benchmark by more than tolerance and requires retailer-sourced verification. Nearest payer analogue: related-party ownership screening in provider enrolment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
FraudEntity: Nicholas M. Ash
SchemeSummary: Ash allegedly falsely told a Providence VA Medical Center doctor that he had been on a combat deployment to Iraq/the Middle East and suffered PTSD and seizures from an IED blast, in order to obtain veterans' disability compensation and health care benefits; Defense Department records showed he never served outside the United States and was on non-deployable status.
WaysToIdentify: This is benefit-eligibility fraud on self-reported service history, catchable at claim/entitlement adjudication by verifying the asserted combat deployment against DoD personnel records (DD-214, deployment and non-deployable status data) before service-connection and treatment authorization. The signal is a diagnosis and rating narrative built solely on patient self-report of an IED blast with no corroborating record.
FeaturesToCreate: Require automated DoD/DMDC record matching for any claim or clinical encounter whose diagnosis basis is combat exposure: compute a flag when the record shows no OCONUS deployment or non-deployable status while the claim/encounter documents combat trauma, and pend the entitlement decision for corroboration. Route matched discrepancies to the OIG queue and hold retroactive compensation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: Shawn R. Blankenship (licensed nurse practitioner, owner of Holistic Inc.); Holistic Inc. (medical clinic)
State_County: West Virginia - Putnam County (Winfield); West Virginia - Kanawha County (St. Albans)
PayerName: Medicaid (West Virginia Medicaid and its Managed Care Organizations)
SchemeSummary: Blankenship, a nurse practitioner who owned Holistic Inc. clinic (office-based opioid treatment, weight loss and smoking cessation counseling), caused false claims to be submitted to West Virginia Medicaid and its MCOs for services that were never provided and not medically necessary, including three smoking cessation counseling claims and a 15-minute office visit purportedly performed on October 29, 2020 when he and the clinic's other licensed nurse practitioners were in Hilton Head, South Carolina. Losses were approximately $600,000.
WaysToIdentify: Claims listing service dates when the only licensed practitioners at the clinic were out of state are detectable by cross-checking rendering-provider claim dates against travel/absence indicators - most practically, against the provider's own claim activity elsewhere, clinic closure days, and geolocation-independent signals like billing on holidays or dates with implausible daily volume. Smoking-cessation and short office-visit codes billed to every patient in an OBOT panel on the same dates, with no supporting notes, is the other signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider day-level impossibility check: for each NPI-date, count claims and computed service minutes and flag dates exceeding a plausible workday or dates where the NPI is also billing far-away service locations; pend and request signed notes with time stamps. Add a panel-uniformity rule flagging counseling/E-M add-on codes billed to an abnormally high share of a clinic's patients on identical dates versus same-specialty peers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: Clara Ann Mason (veterinarian, DEA-registered practitioner)
SchemeSummary: A licensed veterinarian ordered 14,200 dosage units of hydrocodone/acetaminophen and 1,400 dosage units of oxycodone HCL from a veterinary wholesaler between March 2018 and July 2023, failed to secure them or keep required DEA purchase, dispensing and inventory records, and after a 2023 administrative inspection warrant found at least 6,593 dosage units (9,796 total controlled substance units) unaccounted for, submitted apparently fabricated records claiming she dispensed large opioid quantities to pets before euthanasia; the court entered a $956,709 default judgment of maximum civil penalties.
WaysToIdentify: No payer claims involved - this is DEA registrant diversion/recordkeeping. It is detectable from ARCOS/wholesaler distribution data: a small veterinary practice ordering thousands of hydrocodone and oxycodone dosage units is far above species-and-practice-size peers, and the absence of biennial inventory and dispensing logs is confirmable on inspection. Post-hoc 'records' produced after inspection can be tested for internal inconsistency against euthanasia/appointment logs.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a registrant-level purchase surveillance feed from wholesaler/ARCOS data: compute per-registrant annual dosage units by schedule normalized to practice type and patient volume, and fire an inspection referral when above the calibrated peer percentile or when purchases exist with no reported dispensing records. Add a wholesaler suspicious-order rule that blocks shipment pending justification. No payer claim edit applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: PharmaLogic Holdings Corporation (radiopharmaceutical company) and nine of its acquired subsidiaries
SchemeSummary: Nine entities acquired by PharmaLogic Holdings filed NRC Form 526 certifications falsely claiming small-entity status under 10 C.F.R. 171.16(c), even though they exceeded the size limits, thereby obtaining reduced U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission annual licensing fees; the company agreed to pay $350,000 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: Not a health claims case: it is a false self-certification of small-entity status to obtain reduced regulatory fees. It is catchable at certification intake by cross-referencing the certifying entity against corporate ownership/affiliation records, IRS revenue and employee-count data, and M&A filings showing the licensee is now a subsidiary of a larger parent.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an affiliation-aware size test at fee certification: resolve each licensee to its ultimate parent via corporate registry and ownership disclosures, aggregate parent revenue/employee counts, and auto-reject or pend Form 526 small-entity claims where aggregated size exceeds the regulatory limit. Re-run the test annually and on any change-of-ownership filing. The payer analogue is enrolment-time ownership/affiliation disclosure verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Ankita Singh, M.D. (physician who signed brace orders); Alfonso Bailey (leader) and Eric King and 19 others associated with Eye for Change Youth and Family Services, Inc.; Cleveland Clinic Foundation; Rite Aid Corporation and 10 subsidiaries/affiliates; Elixir Insurance Company, RX Options LLC and RX Solutions LLC (Rite Aid subsidiaries); Gregory Gerber, M.D.
State_County: Ohio - Northern District of Ohio (Cleveland, Akron, Toledo, Youngstown areas)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Ohio); National Institutes of Health (grant funding)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Device, DME; Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Drug_Prescriptions; Retention of Overpayment; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Omnibus office round-up describing several separate health care fraud matters: Dr. Ankita Singh signed over 11,000 orthotic brace orders for ~3,000 Medicare beneficiaries she never examined, causing more than $8 million in fraudulent Medicare claims (26 months prison, $4,470,931.02 restitution); 21 people tied to Eye for Change Youth and Family Services manipulated billing, falsified records and used client identities to bill Ohio Medicaid (Bailey and King each 36 months, $4.5M restitution, $4.3M forfeited); Cleveland Clinic paid $7.6M over false NIH grant applications; Rite Aid entities paid $7.5M for medically unnecessary prescriptions and $101M for misreported Medicare drug rebates; and Dr. Gregory Gerber received 42 months plus $4.7M civil judgment and $861,892.13 restitution for medically unnecessary opioid prescribing.}
WaysToIdentify: This is an omnibus round-up, but the recurring adjudication-visible signals are: one prescriber signing orthotic-brace orders for thousands of beneficiaries with no corresponding E/M encounter and beneficiaries geographically remote from the ordering NPI; behavioral-health claims using client identities with overlapping service times and no session documentation; and pharmacy claims for prescriptions lacking a valid prescriber relationship plus misreported manufacturer rebate/DIR amounts detectable by reconciling reported rebates to manufacturer data.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay DME edit: deny or pend brace claims where the ordering NPI has no evaluation claim for that beneficiary within a look-back window, and flag ordering NPIs whose order counts, beneficiary counts and telehealth-only patient share exceed same-specialty peers - suspend payment above the calibrated percentile. For behavioral health, add duplicate-identity and overlapping-time-slot edits per client and staff NPI; for Part D sponsors, automate rebate/DIR reconciliation against manufacturer-reported amounts with recoupment on variance.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Recovery Centers of America (RCA) / TRC-OC, trading as Recovery Centers of America Holdings, LLC (drug and alcohol treatment provider)
State_County: Pennsylvania - Montgomery County (King of Prussia, corporate headquarters); Pennsylvania; Maryland
PayerName: Federal Employees Health Benefits Program; Medicaid
SchemeSummary: RCA allegedly billed the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program and Medicaid from 2017 through 2019 for drug and alcohol treatment services at certain facilities that it failed to actually provide or document, and separately, DEA audits of its Pennsylvania and Maryland facilities from 2019 to 2024 found unlawful dispensing of controlled substances, missing controlled substances and recordkeeping failures. RCA paid $1 million to resolve the Controlled Substances Act allegations and $1 million for the False Claims Act allegations, with a qui tam whistleblower (a former Outcomes Supervisor) receiving $230,000.
WaysToIdentify: Facility-level billing of per-diem and group/individual therapy units can be tested against staffing rosters and census: billed therapy hours exceeding the clinician hours actually on shift, or every client billed the identical daily service bundle regardless of level of care, indicates undelivered or undocumented services. The controlled-substance side is caught through DEA registrant inventory reconciliation at the facility, not through claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a facility-day reconciliation: sum billed therapy units per site-date and divide by credentialed clinician hours available (from rosters/credentialing files), pending payment when the implied per-clinician workload exceeds a plausible ceiling or when service bundles are identical across the census. Add a documentation-request edit for residential/IOP per-diems lacking a signed daily note, and require periodic controlled-substance inventory attestation for licensed sites.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Health Wealth Safe, Inc.; Dr. Subodh Agrawal (owner)
SchemeSummary: At the direction of owner Dr. Subodh Agrawal, Health Wealth Safe billed Medicare for remote physiologic monitoring services despite failing to supply patients with devices that automatically transmitted readings without human intervention, as Medicare coverage requires, making the claims non-reimbursable; resolved via a $1.29 million qui tam settlement with $238,650 to the relator.
WaysToIdentify: RPM coverage requires a device that auto-transmits at least the minimum days of readings; the payer can require device identifiers and transmission-day counts on or supporting the claim and detect practices billing the monitoring code with no accompanying device supply claim, no device serial, or implausibly perfect monthly billing for every patient. Practices billing RPM to nearly the whole panel every month with no setup/device code is the prepay signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit on RPM codes: require a linked device-supply/setup claim or a submitted device identifier plus attested transmission-day count for the billing period, and deny when absent or below the coverage minimum. Add practice-level analytics on the share of panel billed RPM monthly and the ratio of monitoring-treatment-management codes to device codes versus peers, triggering a records request for raw transmission logs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nevada
FraudEntity: Dr. Samuel R. Chacon (OB-GYN, owner of Women's Health Center of Reno)
PayerName: Medicaid; Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield Healthcare Solutions; Health Plan of Nevada; Molina Healthcare of Nevada; Silversummit Healthplan; Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield of Nevada; Cigna Healthcare
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges an OB-GYN billed Medicaid and multiple commercial plans for medically unnecessary gynecologic tests and surgeries (hysterectomies, anterior/posterior and enterocele repairs, vaginal vault suspensions, bladder slings, urodynamic studies, physical therapy, ultrasounds), falsifying patient medical records to add symptoms patients never reported and misrepresenting diagnoses to patients; some procedures caused serious bodily injury.
WaysToIdentify: Surgeon-level utilization profiling shows an OB-GYN performing hysterectomies, pelvic-floor repairs, slings and urodynamics at rates far above same-specialty peers, often stacked on one patient in short succession and preceded by urodynamic/ultrasound testing on nearly every patient. Prior-authorization review of the submitted records would reveal symptom documentation appearing identically across patients and diagnoses unsupported by the testing.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a surgeon-procedure profile per NPI: rates of hysterectomy and pelvic-floor procedures per 1,000 unique patients, share of patients receiving urodynamics/ultrasound before surgery, and multi-procedure stacking per patient; when above the calibrated peer percentile, place the NPI on prepay medical review with mandatory prior authorization and records submission. Add a template-detection check flagging near-duplicate history/symptom text across different patients' submitted notes.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: Erik X. Alonso (psychotherapist, excluded provider)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims
