SchemeSummary: Alonso, excluded from federal health care programs after a 2015 health care fraud conviction, began working in March 2022 for a New Hampshire-based telehealth mental health provider and provided psychotherapy services billed to New Hampshire Medicaid despite being on the HHS-OIG Exclusion List; he also caused claims for counseling sessions not provided as represented, including sessions in which a patient helped him with personal tasks such as preparing a presidential pardon application and medical licensure documents, causing NH Medicaid to pay about $173,998.83.
WaysToIdentify: The exclusion is a hard, pre-payment fact: screening the rendering and employed-staff NPIs/SSNs against the HHS-OIG LEIE and state exclusion lists monthly (and at hire/credentialing) would have blocked every claim. Session-level fraud shows as billed psychotherapy units overlapping in time, sessions on dates with implausible daily totals, and telehealth claims with no corresponding platform connection log.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a mandatory prepay exclusion edit that matches every rendering, supervising and employed individual on a claim against LEIE/state exclusion files at adjudication and denies with a group-level notice; re-screen the group's full roster monthly and suspend payments if an excluded individual is found. Add telehealth session-integrity edits: overlapping time units per rendering NPI, daily unit ceilings, and a documentation request for platform session logs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maine
FraudEntity: The Opportunity Alliance (residential treatment provider operating Morrison Place)
SchemeSummary: The Opportunity Alliance sent misleading urine drug requisition forms to Morrison Place clients' medical providers and treated individual test orders as standing orders for three presumptive and definitive urine drug tests per week for up to a year, directing a third-party lab to perform and bill Medicare and MaineCare directly for tests that were not medically necessary or validly ordered and instead served as residential monitoring.
WaysToIdentify: Standing-order abuse is visible in claims: a single referring provider or residential program generating a fixed cadence of presumptive plus definitive UDT per client (e.g., three times weekly for a year) with unchanged diagnosis codes and near-100% definitive reflex rate. Requisition forms with pre-checked recurring panels and a residential facility rather than a treating clinician as the effective orderer are catchable at prepay review of the order documentation.
FeaturesToCreate: Compute per-beneficiary UDT frequency and per-referrer definitive-reflex rate, and prepay-pend definitive UDT beyond a calibrated frequency per period or where the same order date recurs mechanically, requiring an individualized, signed order dated near the collection. Flag labs whose referrals concentrate in one residential program and whose beneficiaries all share identical test cadence; deny testing used for program monitoring rather than treatment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Daniel Jacobsen (Licensed Clinical Social Worker/psychotherapist)
SchemeSummary: A licensed clinical social worker billed Virginia Medicaid and Medicare at least $335,824 for psychotherapy services never rendered, including days billed for more than 16 hours of services, and used higher-paying codes for more complex services than provided, supported by fabricated psychotherapy progress notes. He pled guilty, was sentenced to three months, paid restitution/forfeiture/fine, and then paid an additional $449,014.93 civil settlement (total $1,201,174.55).
WaysToIdentify: Time-based psychotherapy codes are directly auditable at adjudication: summing billed service minutes per rendering NPI per day exposes days exceeding 16 hours, and the code mix shift toward longer/complex codes (e.g., 60-minute over 45-minute, add-on crisis codes) is measurable against same-specialty peers. Both are computable before payment from the claim's own units and dates.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an NPI-day minute accumulator across all payers/lines: convert each time-based code to its minimum minutes, sum per rendering provider per date, and auto-deny or pend claims once the daily total exceeds a plausible workday ceiling. Add a code-distribution monitor comparing the provider's long-session/high-complexity share to same-specialty peers, placing outliers on prepay review with a request for time-stamped progress notes.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
FraudEntity: Justin Drew Hanson (co-owner, Noah Associates); Mohammed Kazim Ali (co-owner, Noah Associates); Noah Associates (clinical laboratory)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Hanson and co-owner Ali, of Milwaukee-area clinical lab Noah Associates, paid over $400,000 in kickbacks (concealed by sham agreements) to the owner of a substance use treatment clinic for referrals of Medicaid and Medicare patients for urine drug tests that no physician ordered and that were not medically necessary; the lab collected over $2.2 million. Hanson got 21 months and $2.2M restitution plus a $75,000 fine; Ali was sentenced to 15 months.
WaysToIdentify: Referral concentration is visible at adjudication: nearly all of Noah Associates' UDT volume traced to a single SUD clinic owner, and the ordering NPI on the claims either did not match any physician with an active treatment relationship or showed no corresponding E/M or treatment-plan claim for the same beneficiary near the collection date. Definitive/presumptive UDT units per patient per month and panel breadth also sat far above same-specialty peers. Ownership and sham 'consulting' contracts surface at enrolment/credentialing via common addresses, officers and 1099 flows.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab-level referral-concentration monitor: per billing lab per quarter, compute share of UDT dollars from the top one or two ordering entities and the count of UDT claims lacking any companion E/M/SUD treatment claim for the same beneficiary within a lookback window; when both exceed calibrated percentiles, apply a prepay edit requiring the signed physician order and medical-necessity documentation and route to a kickback review. Add a per-beneficiary-per-month cap edit on definitive UDT drug classes with documentation request above the cap.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Vicki Lynn Dowdy (home health attendant)
SchemeSummary: Dowdy, contracted as a home health attendant for two Medicaid recipients in the Roanoke area, submitted fraudulent timesheets and billed Virginia Medicaid for 1,970.5 hours of personal home health and respite care never rendered, receiving $24,760 in payments.
WaysToIdentify: Attendant-level hour accumulation is fully visible prepay: 1,970.5 hours billed for two recipients implies impossible daily/weekly hour totals for one aide and overlapping service windows. Cross-check billed visit times against EVV check-in/out records, and against the recipients' authorized plan-of-care hours and any concurrent institutional or hospital claims for those beneficiaries.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement an aide-NPI/employee-ID daily and weekly hour aggregator across all recipients and agencies, firing when total hours exceed a physiologically plausible ceiling or when two recipients' service intervals overlap for the same aide; deny or pend those lines prepay. Add an authorization-reconciliation edit that rejects units above the approved plan-of-care hours and an EVV-absent edit that pends claims with no matching telephony/GPS visit record.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Robert Burkich, M.D. (physician); Preventive Medicine Anti-Aging & Chelation, Inc. (his practice)
SchemeSummary: Burkich billed Medicare for chelation therapy using edetate calcium disodium (EDTA) - a drug reimbursable only for lead poisoning or lead encephalopathy - for patients who did not have lead poisoning, falsely representing to Medicare that patients suffered from lead poisoning or other heavy-metal diseases to evade coverage restrictions; he and his practice agreed to pay $700,000 under DOJ ability-to-pay guidelines.
WaysToIdentify: EDTA/chelation claims are covered only for lead toxicity, so the diagnosis code is the hook: look for J0600 (edetate calcium disodium) and chelation administration codes carrying lead-poisoning diagnoses with no supporting blood-lead or heavy-metal laboratory claim history for that beneficiary. A single practice reporting lead poisoning in a large share of its panel is statistically implausible versus same-specialty peers and versus state public-health lead prevalence.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a diagnosis-substantiation prepay edit on chelation drug and infusion codes: require a paid blood-lead or heavy-metal lab claim (or submitted result) for the beneficiary within a defined lookback, else pend for records. Add a provider-level monitor of the share of that provider's beneficiaries with lead-toxicity diagnoses versus peers; above the calibrated percentile, place the provider on prepay review of all chelation claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Daniel Iulian Teutoc (a/k/a "Simon Mikula"); Constantin Calin
State_County: Louisiana - Laplace, Slidell, Harvey, Boutte, Chalmette, and New Orleans (Eastern District of Louisiana)
SchemeSummary: Two Romanian nationals allegedly visited Walmart stores across southeastern Louisiana and used magnets to activate card skimming devices previously installed by co-conspirators at points of sale, electronically capturing customers' credit, debit and EBT card data on their cell phones and forwarding it to a co-conspirator so fraudulent charges could be made.
WaysToIdentify: This is retail card/EBT skimming with no provider claim component, so no health-claim adjudication edit applies; detection sits with the card processor and the EBT program via common-point-of-purchase analytics linking compromised cards to a shared merchant terminal, plus out-of-pattern EBT balance drains and out-of-state ATM/POS use. For the benefit agency, post-compromise the route is card-replacement and transaction-reversal workflows.
FeaturesToCreate: For EBT: build a common-point-of-compromise engine that clusters fraud-reported cards by shared prior terminal/merchant ID and time window, auto-flags that terminal, and forces reissue of all cards that transacted there. Add velocity/geography rules on EBT authorizations (rapid full-balance withdrawals, transactions far from the household's usual merchants) that hold the transaction and trigger cardholder verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: William Skaggs Jr. (owner of Nastar Roofing); Billie Adkison (office administrator/payroll manager); Nastar Roofing
SchemeSummary: Owner and payroll administrator of a roofing company withdrew over $21 million from company bank accounts to pay employees predominantly in cash without withholding Social Security, Medicare and federal income taxes, and filed or caused false employment tax returns that omitted the cash wages, causing a tax loss of nearly $2.5 million. Skaggs received 36 months and Adkison a year and a day.
WaysToIdentify: Pure employment-tax fraud with no health claims; the payer is the IRS. The observable signal is a mismatch between very large cash withdrawals from business accounts (and BSA/CTR filings) and the wages reported on Forms 941/W-2, plus workers' compensation payroll and certified-payroll filings inconsistent with reported wages.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side claims control applies. Nearest applicable control is an IRS/state-workforce cross-file analytic: per EIN per quarter, compare reported 941 wages to bank cash-withdrawal aggregates from CTRs, state unemployment wage records and industry revenue-to-payroll ratios, and open an employment-tax examination when the ratio falls below the calibrated peer percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Anthony Delmaro (owner of Kings Roofing commercial roofing/paving business)
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Delmaro concealed roughly $20.9 million in roofing/paving receipts (2012-2022) by cashing customer checks at check cashers, using UPS-mailbox addresses, an alias ('Sonny Rubino'), and false Forms 1099/W-9 in his father's or a relative's name, and never filed income or payroll returns; by hiding this income he also collected more than $500,000 in Connecticut Husky Health low-income Medicaid benefits from 2019 to April 2025. He agreed to pay $1,129,669 restitution to the IRS and $578,259 to Connecticut Medicaid.
WaysToIdentify: The Medicaid piece is income-eligibility fraud, detectable at enrolment and redetermination rather than in claims: the applicant reported near-zero income while operating a licensed roofing/paving business, used a UPS-mailbox address, and appeared as payer on 1099s issued in relatives' names. Automated wage/asset matches (state wage records, IRS 1099/1040 extracts, business registration and contractor licence files, bank/asset verification) would show self-employment and business receipts absent from the application.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an eligibility-verification rule set: at application and each redetermination, match applicant SSN/name against secretary-of-state and contractor-licence registries, 1099-MISC/NEC payer and payee data, and commercial-address databases; fire when self-attested income is near zero but the applicant is a registered business principal or the mailing address is a commercial mail drop, and suspend enrolment pending documentary income proof. Add an alias/identity-linkage check on shared SSNs, addresses and phone numbers across applications.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Anthony Delmaro (owner/operator of Kings Roofing)
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Delmaro concealed roughly $20.9 million in roofing/paving business receipts from the IRS by cashing customer checks at check cashers, using UPS mailbox addresses, aliases and false Forms 1099/W-9 in his father's and a family member's names, and never filing income or payroll returns; while concealing this income he also collected more than $500,000 in Connecticut Husky Health (Medicaid) low-income medical benefits, and was ordered to repay $1,129,669 to the IRS and $578,259 to Connecticut Medicaid.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: concealed self-employment income used to obtain low-income Medicaid, catchable at enrolment/redetermination via wage, 1099, business-registration and commercial-mailbox matches rather than in claim adjudication. Zero reported income alongside an active contracting business and alias-linked filings is the observable signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement automated income and identity verification at application and redetermination: cross-match to state wage files, IRS 1099/return extracts, contractor licensing and business registries, and commercial-address databases; fire when declared income is inconsistent with matched business activity and hold eligibility pending proof. Periodically re-run matches on the active enrolled population and generate overpayment-recovery referrals where income appears retroactively.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Aaron Rossi (owner/operator of Reditus Labs); Reditus Labs
State_County: Illinois - Peoria County (Peoria); Illinois - Tazewell County (Morton)
PayerName: Medicare; State of Illinois; private health insurance companies
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Through his laboratory Reditus Labs, Rossi submitted COVID-19 test claims with codes for services that were never performed and collected payment from more than one source for the same test, defrauding Medicare, the State of Illinois and private insurers of a combined $525,520.61; he received an additional 37 months in prison and forfeiture of a $1 million recreational vehicle (separate prior fraud case carried 5 years and over $3 million in restitution/fines).
WaysToIdentify: Duplicate-source billing is visible prepay through duplicate-claim logic keyed on beneficiary, specimen/DOS, and test code across Medicare, the state COVID program and, via clearinghouse/all-payer data, commercial payers; the same test billed to a federal program and to a state uninsured-testing fund is a hard duplicate. Phantom codes show up as claim volumes exceeding the lab's reported specimen accessions and instrument throughput, and as add-on/panel codes reported at implausible ratios to the base test.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a cross-payer duplicate detector: hash beneficiary+DOS+test code and reject the second payment path (federal versus state uninsured fund versus commercial) prepay, with attestation that no other payer has been billed. Add a lab-capacity check comparing billed test counts per day to reported CLIA capacity/accession logs, and suspend payment where billed volume exceeds capacity pending an on-site or records audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: RST-Sanexas, Inc. (manufacturer and marketer of electric stimulation devices); Richard Sorgnard (principal owner); Lisa Sorgnard (principal owner); Morhea Sorgnard (principal owner)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Sanexas and its owners marketed the neoGEN-Series electrical stimulation device for uses outside its FDA clearance (acute pain, nerve regrowth, combined with vitamin injections), causing provider customers to bill Medicare for non-covered, medically unnecessary electrical nerve stimulation, vitamin injections, and follow-up ENFD punch-biopsy testing; they also paid volume-based discounts/commissions to provider-owned distributorships and received commissions from a diagnostic lab for referring providers for ENFD testing, in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute. Settlement of $1.5 million, based on ability to pay, is joint across the company and the three owner defendants.
WaysToIdentify: The signal is a sudden clustered adoption of specific electrical-stimulation and ENFD punch-biopsy code combinations by unrelated small practices, all coinciding with one manufacturer's distributor footprint, billed with acute-pain and neuropathy diagnoses outside the device's cleared/covered indication. Marketing-driven waves show up as new-to-code providers with near-identical code triplets (E-stim + vitamin injection + biopsy), and provider-owned distributorships appear in ownership disclosures and 1099/commission records at credentialing.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a code-cluster diffusion monitor: per HCPCS combination, detect statistically abnormal cohorts of providers newly billing the same triplet within a short window and sharing a device supplier, and place that cohort on prepay documentation review for coverage-indication proof. Add a non-covered-technology edit that denies electrical nerve stimulation and photoplethysmography-style codes when the underlying device/technology is not covered, plus an ownership-disclosure edit flagging provider-owned distributor relationships with the referred lab.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Tina Marie Armstrong (owner, Safe at Home Medical Equipment and Supplies, LLC); Safe at Home Medical Equipment and Supplies, LLC; Dee Alice Moton (owner/licensed massage therapist, Flowing Hands Massage Clinical Therapy)
State_County: South Carolina - Florence; South Carolina - Aiken County (Aiken)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Device, DME; Unbundling; Upcoding
SchemeSummary: Two South Carolina defendants charged in the 2025 national takedown: Armstrong allegedly billed Medicare and Medicaid $198,981.55 (of which $104,577.74 was paid) through her DME company for equipment no longer in service, never delivered, or not physician-authorized, and used patient identities; Moton allegedly billed the Veterans Administration $2,373,147.22 over two years through her massage therapy clinic for services never rendered, including mutually exclusive E&M codes, telehealth codes for in-person visits, unauthorized specialized services, and treatments for conditions veterans did not have (e.g., wheelchair therapy for a veteran with no wheelchair).
WaysToIdentify: Both strands are prepay-detectable code-logic and authorization failures: DME claims without a matching physician order/face-to-face encounter claim, rentals continuing after the beneficiary died, moved to a facility or after the item was returned; and clinic claims with mutually exclusive E/M pairs, telehealth POS/modifier on visits also billed as in-person, and therapy codes clinically inconsistent with the member's diagnosis/equipment history. Duplicate billing across Medicare, Medicaid and VA for the same DOS is visible with cross-payer matching.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a DME order-linkage edit requiring a paid physician encounter and written-order record before paying rental/purchase, plus continuous-rental termination logic tied to death, institutional stay and equipment-return data. For clinic claims, build mutually-exclusive/NCCI pair edits, a telehealth-consistency edit (deny when POS/modifier indicates telehealth but an in-person claim exists for the same DOS), and a diagnosis-to-service plausibility edit; combine with cross-payer duplicate DOS matching and place high-scoring providers on prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Alabama
FraudEntity: Saad Enterprises Inc., d/b/a Saad Healthcare (hospice provider)
SchemeSummary: Saad Healthcare allegedly billed Medicare's hospice benefit for 21 patients in Alabama who were not terminally ill (life expectancy over six months) and thus ineligible, despite knowing they did not meet eligibility requirements; resolved for $3 million following a qui tam suit by two former employees who receive $540,000.
WaysToIdentify: Hospice ineligibility is inferable prepay and near-real-time from the certification and utilization record: long stays with no decline in level of care, repeated recertifications, live discharges, absent or boilerplate physician narratives, and non-specific 'debility/failure to thrive' terminal diagnoses. Concurrent claims history showing curative treatment, active dialysis or aggressive workups for the same beneficiary contradicts a six-month prognosis.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-episode monitor computing length of stay beyond the calibrated peer percentile, recertification count, live-discharge rate and share of episodes with non-specific terminal diagnoses per hospice; when thresholds trip, apply prepay medical review of the certification and narrative for continued episodes. Add a contradiction edit flagging hospice episodes with concurrent curative/aggressive treatment claims and pend those periods for records.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Michael Andrew Scott (owner/operator of Trusted Medical Partnership); Trusted Medical Partnership
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Scott told investors that he or his company Trusted Medical Partnership held purchase orders from health care providers for medical devices but lacked capital to fill them, soliciting loans with promises of quick, risk-free returns; the purchase orders were fabricated or doctored, the company conducted no legitimate business, and he spent the roughly $470,000 taken from at least 16 victims on casino gambling, personal expenses, and Ponzi-style payments to earlier investors.
WaysToIdentify: No health-plan claims were submitted; this is an investor-loan Ponzi based on fabricated purchase orders, so no adjudication edit applies. Detection routes are securities/lender-side: verifying purported purchase orders directly with the named provider customers, confirming no corresponding revenue or inventory, and observing bank flows where new investor money pays earlier investors and casinos.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control for a payer or lender doing supplier due diligence: automated verification of claimed purchase orders/contracts against the named counterparty's confirmation and against the supplier's actual claim/shipment history, plus a bank-flow rule flagging deposits from individual investors immediately disbursed to prior investors or gaming merchants.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Philip Yen, M.D. (radiologist; DEA registrant at Sutter Imaging Capitol Pavilion)
SchemeSummary: As the DEA registrant for Sutter Imaging Capitol Pavilion, Dr. Yen allegedly failed to keep the detailed receipt and dispensing records for controlled substances required by the Controlled Substances Act; a 2022 DEA inspection found multiple recordkeeping violations, and he agreed to pay $125,000 in civil penalties and complete CSA training.
WaysToIdentify: This is a DEA recordkeeping violation, not a billing scheme, so claim edits will not catch it; the signal is a reconciliation gap between controlled-substance purchases reported by distributors (ARCOS) for the registrant and dispensing/administration records or claims. A registrant with contrast/sedation purchases but no corresponding administration documentation or biennial inventory is the flag.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a registrant-level purchase-to-dispense reconciliation: per DEA number per period, compare ARCOS/distributor purchase quantities to documented administrations (claims with sedation/anesthesia codes or dispensing records) and flag unexplained variance for inspection scheduling. For the payer, add a documentation request on controlled-substance administration codes from registrants with open DEA compliance findings.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Maine
FraudEntity: SVCMC Inc., formerly known as Saint Vincents Catholic Medical Centers of New York (health plan participating in the Uniformed Services Family Health Plan)
PayerName: TRICARE (Defense Health Agency, Department of Defense) - Uniformed Services Family Health Plan
SchemeSummary: Saint Vincent received capitated payments from the Defense Health Agency to provide care to military retirees and families under the USFHP program; after learning in 2012 that the capitation rates had been miscalculated, producing four years of overpayments, it allegedly concealed the overpayments, kept submitting invoices at the inflated rates, and conspired with the five other USFHP plans to avoid repaying the money. It agreed to pay $29 million, with the qui tam relators receiving $5.655 million.
WaysToIdentify: This is a capitation-rate and overpayment-retention issue on the payer's own side: the rate-setting actuarial recalculation showed the paid PMPM diverged from the correct basis, and the plan kept invoicing at the stale rate. Signals are invoiced rate versus the authoritative contracted rate table, enrollment-count reconciliation, and the absence of a self-report after the plan was notified of the error.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an invoice-to-rate-table validation that recomputes each capitation invoice as authoritative rate x verified eligible member-months and auto-rejects or withholds any line where the billed rate differs from the current approved rate; retain version history so retroactive rate corrections generate automatic recoupment schedules. Add a 60-day self-report clock: once an overpayment is identified in the rate file, open a receivable and offset future capitation payments automatically.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Terrance Owens Elliott, a.k.a. 'Tony Elliott' (church pastor, former San Bernardino City Council candidate, self-appointed trust co-trustee)
SchemeSummary: Elliott allegedly told a long-time friend she would lose her Medicare and Social Security benefits if she took an inheritance directly, set himself up as sole-signatory trustee of a trust holding her money using a fraudulently modified trust agreement, and diverted trust funds and her Social Security payments to his church and personal expenses; in related schemes he took a $65,000 'loan' from another victim's corporation via signed blank checks and caused a nonprofit to issue about 32 checks for fabricated litigation-related debts, totaling roughly $238,563 in losses.
WaysToIdentify: No claims were paid; this is fiduciary/elder financial exploitation involving a trust and diverted Social Security payments, so payer claim edits do not apply. Observable signals are a representative-payee/trustee change followed by redirection of benefit deposits to an account controlled by an unrelated third party, and payments from a nonprofit to a fiduciary's personal or church accounts.
FeaturesToCreate: No health-claims control applies. Nearest control at the benefit agency: a rule that flags any change of direct-deposit routing or representative payee where the new account is not in the beneficiary's name, or is shared with multiple unrelated beneficiaries, and holds the change pending beneficiary contact; add monitoring for a single payee account receiving benefits for unrelated recipients.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey; U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Frank Procopio (leader of '10th and O Crew'); Michael Procopio (co-leader)
SchemeSummary: Frank Procopio, a leader of South Philadelphia's '10th and O Crew,' obtained prescription oxycodone pills from area doctors' offices and, with co-conspirators working in shifts, sold them out of a 24-hour restaurant; law enforcement made a controlled buy and observed him splitting the proceeds. He received 57 months; his brother and co-leader Michael Procopio was convicted and sentenced to 72 months.
WaysToIdentify: Street resale is not visible in adjudication, but the upstream supply is: PDMP data would show the crew's members and straw patients obtaining oxycodone from multiple prescribers and pharmacies with short intervals, high MME, cash payment, and long travel distances, and would show a small set of prescribers accounting for the pills. Payer claims (if any) would show early refills and pharmacy/prescriber shopping.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-level PDMP/claims shopping score using distinct prescribers and pharmacies for opioids in a rolling window, cumulative MME, early-refill overlap and cash-versus-insurance mix; above the calibrated percentile, lock the member to a single prescriber/pharmacy and require prior authorization. Pair with a prescriber-level monitor of opioid volume and share of cash-paid, out-of-area patients, triggering prepay review and referral.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Fraud Section and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Semler Scientific Inc. (device manufacturer); Bard Peripheral Vascular Inc. and related companies (distributor)
SchemeSummary: Semler manufactured and marketed the FloChec and QuantaFlo photoplethysmography devices for diagnosing peripheral arterial disease and, with distributor Bard, told providers that tests using the devices were reimbursable under CPT codes 93922/93923/93924, even though the devices do not perform an ankle brachial index test and Medicare does not cover photoplethysmography, causing providers to submit non-covered claims to Medicare. Semler paid $29.75 million and Bard $7.2 million (total ~$36.95 million) to resolve the qui tam FCA allegations, with relators receiving about $6.5 million.
WaysToIdentify: The signal is mass billing of vascular-study CPT codes (93922/93923/93924) by primary-care and risk-assessment providers who own no vascular lab, in tight clusters tied to one device vendor's rollout, often on the same encounter as annual health-risk assessments. Coverage policy excludes photoplethysmography, so the technology-to-code mismatch is checkable if the device/technology is captured, and abnormal per-provider PAD-testing rates versus peers are visible prepay.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a code-versus-technology edit requiring, for 93922/93923/93924, attestation of an ankle-brachial-index-capable modality and supplier/device identification, denying claims where the registered device performs only photoplethysmography. Add a diffusion monitor detecting cohorts of non-vascular specialties newly billing these codes at rates above the calibrated peer percentile within a short window, and place that cohort on prepay documentation review with recovery referral for prior paid claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Indiana
FraudEntity: James Henley (organizer; claimed CEO of five fake businesses); Jameka Henley (wife, charged); Jimmie Bickers (associate, charged); OnTrack Real Estate Solutions; LDI Investments Corp; Lucario Investments; 317 Traffic; Henley Real Estate Solutions
State_County: Indiana - Marion County (Indianapolis); Indiana - Vanderburgh County (Evansville); Indiana - Johnson County (Greenwood); Indiana - Hendricks County (Plainfield); Kentucky
FraudTypeAll: IdentityFraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Henley, his wife, and an associate used stolen personal information of 76 real people to file 120 pandemic unemployment insurance applications in ten states, collecting $1,119,426 via 65 benefit debit cards; Henley also filed fraudulent deeds with the Marion County Recorder to steal and resell five Indianapolis homes, faked a mortgage payoff to pocket $255,000 in sale proceeds, and drew $98,000 from an attorney's IOLTA trust account to pay his auto loans. Total loss $2,927,758.95; restitution $1,887,426.63 ordered against Henley, whose co-defendants remain charged but not convicted.
WaysToIdentify: No health claims involved; this is stolen-identity pandemic UI fraud plus deed/escrow fraud. The UI side was highly detectable prepay: 120 applications for 76 identities across ten states, sharing IP addresses, phone numbers, bank/debit-card mailing addresses and device fingerprints, with claimant identity data not matching state wage records.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side health control applies. For benefit agencies: build a cross-state identity-and-device deduplication service that clusters UI applications by SSN, mailing address, IP/device fingerprint and card-delivery address, holds payment when a cluster exceeds one claimant per identity or a shared address serves multiple unrelated claimants, and requires documentary identity proofing plus wage-record match before first disbursement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Rotimi Iluyomade (Annandale-based doctor); Obioma Alozie Ndubuka a.k.a. 'Bankroll'; Raymono Alfonzo Russell II; Cameron Isaiah Lewis; Elhadj Malick Diallo; Zion Oluwademilade Adeduwon; Kenechukwu Brian Okwara a.k.a. 'Kene'; Yared Michael Tesfaye a.k.a. 'Yar'
State_County: Virginia - Fairfax County (Annandale); Virginia - Western District of Virginia
SchemeSummary: Co-conspirators visited a doctor's Annandale medical clinic with lists of fake 'patients' using fabricated names and false addresses to obtain fraudulent prescriptions for promethazine-codeine solution, oxycodone pills and hydrocodone-chlorpheniramine ('Tussionex'), which were transmitted to pharmacies across the country (at least 70 filled in the Western District of Virginia) and the drugs then distributed in multiple states; the doctor was convicted of distributing over 7,000 oxycodone pills, 34,000 mL of Tussionex and 107,000 mL of promethazine-codeine, while the seven arrested co-conspirators are charged.
WaysToIdentify: Fabricated patients are detectable at the pharmacy and PDMP layer prepay: prescriptions from one Virginia clinic filled in dozens of far-flung states, patient names/addresses failing identity and address verification, repeated use of the same phone or address across many 'patients,' and one prescriber generating extreme volumes of promethazine-codeine and Tussionex relative to peers. Cash payment and geographic dispersion between prescriber and pharmacy are the strongest markers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-level controlled-substance profile computing volume of opioid/cough-syrup units, number of distinct patients per day, and the geographic spread between prescriber address and dispensing pharmacies; when the out-of-area fill share and volume exceed calibrated percentiles, suspend claim payment for that prescriber's controlled-substance scripts and refer to licensing/DEA. Add a patient-identity validation edit at the pharmacy claim level (address/DOB/SSN verification and duplicate-demographic clustering) that pends fills failing verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee; United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee (Chattanooga)
FraudEntity: Rebekah Proctor (operator of Franklin Springs Academy, a daycare business)
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Proctor, who operated a daycare business, withheld income and FICA taxes from employees' paychecks but willfully failed to account for and pay them over to the IRS (first quarter 2022), and separately submitted PPP loan applications with false certifications (that she was current on federal taxes and would use funds for payroll/business expenses), spending the $105,800 (April 2020) and $118,000 (February 2021) in loan proceeds on personal expenses; she agreed to $893,232.26 restitution to the IRS and $223,800 to the SBA.
WaysToIdentify: No health claims; the payers are the IRS and SBA. The trust-fund piece is visible as withheld amounts on W-2s with no matching 941 deposits for the quarter; the PPP piece was verifiable at underwriting by matching the applicant's certification of tax compliance and payroll figures against IRS transcripts and 941/W-2 filings, and by monitoring disbursement use against payroll bank activity.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side claims control applies. Nearest controls: an IRS rule matching per-EIN W-2 withholding totals to 941 deposits each quarter and auto-opening a trust-fund case on unexplained gaps; and an SBA underwriting edit that blocks disbursement until IRS transcript match confirms filed/paid employment taxes and the stated payroll matches reported wage data, with post-disbursement monitoring for absence of payroll outflows.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota
FraudEntity: Abdinajib Hassan Yussuf (President and CEO, Star Autism Center LLC); Asha Farhan Hassan; Anthony Waddell Jefferson (HSS provider owner); Lester Brown (HSS provider owner); Hassan Ahmed Hussein (co-owner, Pristine Health LLC); Ahmed Abdirashid Mohamed (co-owner, Pristine Health LLC); Kaamil Omar Sallah (owner, SafeLodgings, Inc.); Ultimate Home Health Services LLC
State_County: Minnesota - Hennepin County (Minneapolis); Minnesota - Ramsey County (St. Paul)
PayerName: Medicaid (Minnesota Medical Assistance / Minnesota Health Care Programs - DHS); UCare
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; Upcoding
SchemeSummary: Multiple defendants billed Minnesota Medicaid programs for services not rendered: Yussuf's Star Autism Center used unqualified teenage relatives as 'behavioral technicians,' recruited Somali-community children into EIDBI autism services, paid monthly cash kickbacks to parents scaled to the DHS authorization amount, and submitted inflated claims billed without providers' knowledge, obtaining over $6 million (Hassan separately charged in a $14 million autism scheme plus $465,000 from Feeding Our Future and pleaded guilty). In the Housing Stabilization Services program, Jefferson and Brown flew from Philadelphia to recruit shelter and Section 8 residents as 'The Housing Guys' and fabricated client notes and fake employee signatures ($3.5 million in claims for ~230 beneficiaries); Hussein and Mohamed's Pristine Health worked with Foundation First to fabricate Housing Focused Plans and bill ~$750,000 for ~100 beneficiaries; Sallah's SafeLodgings double-billed overlapping service hours, claiming ~$1.4 million and receiving ~$1.3 million before he fled the country; and a search warrant alleges Ultimate Home Health Services billed over $1.1 million in Integrated Community Supports claims for 13 clients, including services purportedly delivered on nearly every day of a 447-day period and to a client who had died.
WaysToIdentify: At claim adjudication, these schemes leave arithmetic footprints: EIDBI/HSS/ICS units billed on nearly every calendar day for the same client (447 consecutive service days), overlapping service hours for the same staff or same client across programs, service dates after a beneficiary's date of death, and billing under an NPI whose rendering provider never logged an encounter. At enrolment/credentialing, new EIDBI and Housing Stabilization agencies with out-of-state owner addresses (Philadelphia principals billing Minnesota HSS), no prior program history, and rapid ramp to full authorization amounts are visible before the first payment. Kickbacks to parents scaled to the DHS authorization are only detectable post-pay, via bank-record subpoena and beneficiary interviews, but the tell-tale prepay proxy is authorization amount consumed at or near 100% for every client in a clustered geographic/kinship recruitment pool.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-day engine that flags (a) any claim with service date > date of death from the MMIS eligibility/death file, (b) rendering-staff hours summed across all clients/programs exceeding a feasible workday, (c) clients with consecutive-service-day streaks and authorization-utilization ratios above the calibrated percentile versus same-program peers - each firing a prepay suspend and a records request for signed session notes with staff credentials. Add a credentialing rule that scores new EIDBI/HSS/ICS enrolments on out-of-state principal address, shared address/phone/bank account with other new enrolments, and owner overlap with previously sanctioned entities, placing them on 100% prepay review of the first N claims. Add a staff-qualification cross-check that matches each billed behavioral technician to a registry/training record and age, denying claims rendered by unverifiable staff.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Providence Park, Inc., d/b/a Ascension Living Providence Village (skilled nursing facility owner/operator); Ascension Providence, f/k/a Providence Health Services of Waco (acute care hospital owner/operator)
SchemeSummary: A Waco skilled nursing facility allegedly billed federal health care programs for medically unnecessary Ultra-High Resource Utilization Group therapy, while the affiliated acute care hospital allegedly billed individual outpatient therapy when only group therapy was delivered and billed therapy services at three clinics without a physician-signed plan of care; resolved by a $6,526,851.64 payment to the United States and Texas following a qui tam suit and partial self-disclosure.
WaysToIdentify: RUG/PDPM distribution is the signal: a facility whose share of Ultra-High therapy RUGs sits far above same-state SNF peers, with therapy minutes clustering just past the Ultra-High threshold and uniform across clinically dissimilar residents, is visible from MDS assessments matched to claims before payment. On the hospital side, individual therapy codes (97110/97530 one-on-one) billed for many patients in the same time block by the same therapist is arithmetically impossible and detectable from rendering-therapist plus date/time-on-claim data. Absence of a physician-signed plan of care is a documentation condition of payment testable by targeted prepay records request at the three outpatient clinics.
FeaturesToCreate: Compute per-facility monthly Ultra-High/High therapy RUG mix and minutes-just-above-threshold density versus same-state peer distribution; fire prepay review with MDS and therapy-log request when both exceed the calibrated percentile. Build a therapist-day concurrency edit: sum billed one-on-one therapy units per rendering therapist per date; when implied minutes exceed available worked minutes, deny or downcode to group therapy pending logs. Add a plan-of-care attestation edit for outpatient therapy at new or flagged sites requiring physician signature date on file before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Dennis Michael Peyroux (chiropractor, clinic owner)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Peyroux purchased Medicare beneficiary identifiers and fabricated audio recordings of people posing as beneficiaries 'requesting' over-the-counter COVID-19 test kits, then billed Medicare through his chiropractic clinic for kits that were never requested or otherwise ineligible, misappropriating a former nurse practitioner's credentials as the referring provider on thousands of claims; ~$3.3M billed and ~$3.2M paid in about six months, with $3.2M restitution plus over $1M forfeited from bank accounts.
WaysToIdentify: A chiropractic clinic billing thousands of OTC COVID test kits is an immediate specialty/service mismatch - the service has no plausible relationship to the billing taxonomy - and volume ramping from zero to millions in six months is visible in weekly paid-trend monitoring. The referring NP appeared on thousands of claims across a state she had no relationship with; comparing the referring provider's own claim/encounter history (no corresponding office visit, no other referrals, licence status/retirement) to the volume attributed to her exposes credential misappropriation prepay. Beneficiary geography scatter far from the clinic's service area, and beneficiaries with no other claims from that provider, are further prepay signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a taxonomy-vs-service edit that hard-denies OTC test kit/DME-type codes billed by specialties with no plausible scope (chiropractic, etc.) absent explicit program authorization. Build a referring-provider plausibility check: per referring NPI per month, count distinct billing NPIs and claim volume, and require a matching evaluation encounter by that NPI within a lookback window; fire prepay suspension and provider outreach/attestation when the referring NPI's attributed volume exceeds the calibrated percentile or the provider is inactive/retired. Add a beneficiary-distance and new-patient-share monitor with velocity trip-wires that cap payment and trigger review on explosive first-year growth.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Robert Tassin, M.D. (physician, independent contractor for telemedicine companies)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Tassin, working as an independent contractor for purported telemedicine companies, signed doctors' orders for cancer genetic (CGx) tests for Medicare beneficiaries he never saw or spoke with, falsely certifying in medical records that the tests were medically necessary; his orders generated over $6.6 million in claims to Medicare (over $2 million reimbursed) and he was paid roughly $30 per order, totaling $106,757.
WaysToIdentify: One ordering physician appearing on CGx orders for hundreds of geographically scattered beneficiaries, with no corresponding telehealth or office E/M claim for those beneficiaries by that physician, is fully visible in claims prepay. The referring NPI's cross-state beneficiary footprint, licensure states, and the concentration of his orders in a handful of labs are all adjudication-time data. Per-order payments of ~$30 from telemedicine marketing companies are only provable post-pay via bank records, but the ordering pattern alone justifies prepay suspension.
FeaturesToCreate: Per ordering NPI per month, compute distinct CGx-billing labs, distinct beneficiary states, order count, and the share of orders with no companion E/M/telehealth encounter by that NPI within a lookback window; fire prepay suspension of all CGx claims carrying that NPI and a documentation request for the encounter record when the no-encounter share and volume exceed calibrated percentiles. Add a lab-side edit requiring the ordering physician's licence state to include the beneficiary's state. Escalate ordering NPIs whose orders concentrate in a single lab to payment suspension and referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Robert Tassin, M.D. (physician working for purported telemedicine companies)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Through purported telemedicine companies, a physician signed doctors' orders for cancer genetic (CGx) tests for Medicare beneficiaries he never saw or spoke to, falsely certifying in medical records that the tests were medically necessary; he was paid roughly $30 per order, and the orders generated over $6.6 million in claims to Medicare, of which over $2 million was paid.
WaysToIdentify: Identical mechanic to the companion case: a single physician signs CGx orders for beneficiaries he never contacted, so the diagnostic signal is orders without any companion encounter claim by the ordering NPI, extreme beneficiary-state dispersion, and order volume concentrated into one or two labs - all present in claim data before payment. Cancer-genetic testing ordered with no oncology diagnosis history or prior workup in the beneficiary's claim history is an additional prepay medical-necessity flag. The $30-per-order kickback is a post-pay bank-record finding.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement an ordering-provider integrity score per month (distinct labs, beneficiary-state count, order volume, share of orders lacking an E/M by that NPI, share of beneficiaries lacking any cancer/oncology diagnosis history) and suspend prepay all CGx claims bearing NPIs above the calibrated composite percentile pending encounter documentation. Add a beneficiary-level edit denying CGx when no qualifying diagnosis or treating-oncologist relationship exists in claim history. Feed flagged ordering NPIs and their linked labs to a shared watchlist that triggers prepay review of the lab's entire CGx line.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Argosy Investment Partners V, L.P. (Small Business Investment Company); Argosy Investment Partners Parallel V, L.P. (affiliate); AIP-ECS Holdings LLC (portfolio company, PPP borrower)
PayerName: U.S. Small Business Administration (Paycheck Protection Program)
SchemeSummary: AIP-ECS Holdings LLC applied for, received and obtained forgiveness of a $1,205,352 second-draw PPP loan although other companies in its Argosy SBIC corporate group had already received PPP loans that pushed the group over the $4 million second-draw cap, making the loan ineligible. The Argosy entities and AIP-ECS collectively agreed to pay $1.5 million to resolve a qui tam False Claims Act suit, with the relator receiving $150,000.
WaysToIdentify: This is a lending/eligibility case, not a claims-payment case: no payer adjudication exists, so detection sits with the SBA/lender at application, by testing the stated affiliate group against corporate-ownership data (SBIC portfolio filings, EIN and common-control links, prior PPP loan records) to enforce the $4 million second-draw corporate-group cap. The observable signal is the applicant's ownership chain overlapping entities that already drew PPP. Post-award, forgiveness review could have aggregated loans across all entities with a shared controlling parent.
FeaturesToCreate: For payer-side analogues, build an affiliation-aggregation check for any enrolment or funding application: resolve applicant EIN/owner/officer/address to a corporate-group graph and sum prior awards or capitated payments across the group against the programme cap, blocking disbursement and forgiveness when the group total exceeds it. Require a signed affiliate-disclosure schedule and auto-compare it to the resolved ownership graph, flagging any undisclosed affiliate for manual underwriting.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Unified Care Services LLC (skilled nursing facilities chain); Emmanual David (owner); Casa Montana LLC; Geri-Care Inc.; Geri Care V LLC; Pacific Palms Healthcare LLC; Foothill Care Center Inc.; Mount Megiddo LLC; Canyon Properties III LLC; Cloverleaf Enterprises Inc.; Foothill Care Center LLC; Foothill Care Center II LLC; David Kleis III LLC; David Kleis II LLC; Miramonte Enterprises LLC; Washington Enterprises III LLC
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: A Torrance-based skilled nursing facility chain and its affiliates allegedly falsely certified on 2020 PPP loan and loan-forgiveness applications that each entity was a small business with fewer than 500 employees, concealing that they were part of a larger commonly owned and controlled chain that made them ineligible; they agreed to pay $18 million to resolve FCA allegations arising from a qui tam suit, with the whistleblower receiving $2,070,000.
WaysToIdentify: Again a loan-eligibility case rather than claim adjudication, but the payer already holds the disproving data: Medicare/Medicaid SNF enrolment and cost-report files record common ownership and control across a chain and employee/staffing counts (PBJ payroll-based journal data), so an entity-by-entity 'fewer than 500 employees' certification could be tested against the chain's aggregate PBJ headcount at application. The observable signal is many separately certifying facilities sharing officers, managers, and a single management company.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a common-ownership aggregation service that keys facility CCNs to owner/officer/management-company records from enrolment and cost reports, then sums PBJ-derived employee counts across the resolved group; fire an ineligibility flag whenever an entity certifies a size standard that the group total contradicts. Expose this graph as an API to grant/loan programmes and as a prepay risk factor for chain-wide payment review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: Thompson Construction Group Inc. (contractor, Sumter, South Carolina)
State_County: West Virginia - central and southern West Virginia (2016 flood-affected region)
PayerName: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (Community Development Block Grant - Disaster Recovery funds)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
SchemeSummary: Thompson Construction Group was awarded contracts, funded by HUD CDBG-DR disaster recovery grants, to rebuild homes destroyed in the June 2016 West Virginia flooding; it submitted invoices falsely certifying that contractually required crawl space drainage systems and sump pumps had been installed in flood-plain homes and was paid federal funds, when the water management systems were never installed. It agreed to pay $95,535 restitution plus $95,535 in double damages under the False Claims Act.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health-care claim here - it is a HUD construction grant with a false certification of completed work, so the control belongs to the grant administrator's invoice-approval step: paying draw requests only against independent inspection evidence (geotagged photos, sump-pump serial numbers, third-party inspector sign-off) for scope items in flood-plain homes. The observable signal is invoices certifying installed drainage systems with no matching inspection record or materials-purchase documentation.
FeaturesToCreate: For the nearest applicable payer control, build a pay-for-verified-deliverable rule: hold invoice lines for high-risk scope items until a matching independent inspection artifact (photo with geotag/timestamp, serialized equipment record) is linked, and sample-audit a calibrated share of certified units before final payment. Flag contractors whose certified-completion rate outpaces their materials purchases or inspection submissions for full documentation review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Patrick Britton-Harr (owner of Provista Health and AeroVanti Inc.); Provista Health; AeroVanti Inc.
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Britton-Harr allegedly used his company Provista Health to offer COVID-19 screening tests to nursing home patients nationwide and then billed Medicare for expensive respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests that were medically unnecessary, never ordered by a treating physician, and in many cases never performed, including for deceased patients - more than $15 million billed and over $5 million paid. A second indictment charges wire fraud for misappropriating nearly $15 million in upfront payments from about 100 'Top Gun' members of his AeroVanti private jet club, plus obtaining a $1.5 million loan by withholding material information.
WaysToIdentify: Respiratory pathogen panels billed in bulk for nursing-home residents nationwide by one lab with no ordering-physician relationship is visible prepay: RPP claims lacking an ordering NPI who has any encounter with that beneficiary, an RPP-to-COVID-test ratio far above peer labs, and claims with service dates after the beneficiary's date of death. Facility-level clustering (whole census tested the same day at one SNF) and the lab's explosive volume ramp are adjudication-time signals from claim headers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab-claim edit chain: deny RPP/large-panel codes when the paired COVID test is the documented purpose and no ordering physician with a beneficiary relationship exists; deny any service date after date of death; and compute per-lab monthly panel-to-basic-test ratio and same-facility same-day mass-testing density, suspending prepay above calibrated percentiles pending physician orders and specimen/result records. Add a facility-consent/order attestation requirement for nationwide SNF sweep testing before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Patrick Britton-Harr (owner of Provista Health and AeroVanti, Inc.)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: During the COVID-19 pandemic, defendant offered COVID-19 screening to nursing home patients nationwide and, through his company Provista Health, billed Medicare over $15 million for expensive respiratory pathogen panel tests that were medically unnecessary, not ordered by treating physicians, and in many cases never performed - including for deceased patients; Medicare paid over $5 million. A second indictment charges wire fraud for misappropriating roughly $15 million in upfront payments from nearly 100 'Top Gun' members of his private jet club AeroVanti.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion indictment: high-cost respiratory pathogen panels attached to nursing-home COVID screening with no treating-physician order, many tests never performed, and some beneficiaries already deceased. All three are prepay-testable from claim data: missing/implausible ordering NPI, date-of-death conflicts, and per-lab panel-versus-simple-test mix far above peers. Explosive month-over-month growth from a new lab enrolment adds an enrolment-time risk flag.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement date-of-death and eligibility-window hard denials on all lab claims, plus an ordering-provider relationship edit requiring an encounter by the ordering NPI within a lookback window for high-cost panels. Compute per-lab RPP share of total volume and growth velocity versus peer labs; when above the calibrated percentile, apply prepay payment suspension and request signed orders, specimen logs and result reports. Route new labs billing SNF populations across many states into first-N-claims full prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Vascular and Interventional Specialists, LLC (VIS) (endovascular surgery center); Vascular and Spine Institute, Inc. (VSI) (billing entity); Oscar Sosa, M.D. (practitioner); Osmany DeAngelo, D.O. (practitioner)
SchemeSummary: Providers performed hundreds of percutaneous transluminal angioplasties without any diagnostic inquiry or clinical diagnosis supporting medical necessity, then billed Medicare and other federal health programs for the medically unnecessary procedures; resolved for $810,301 following a qui tam suit whose relator receives about $186,369.
WaysToIdentify: Angioplasty without any diagnostic workup shows as a missing-precursor pattern in claim history: PTA/peripheral intervention claims with no preceding non-invasive vascular study (ABI, duplex ultrasound, angiography) and no qualifying PAD/claudication or critical-limb-ischemia diagnosis for that beneficiary. Provider-level concentration - one practice performing hundreds of PTAs with per-beneficiary repeat interventions well above same-specialty peers - is visible before payment. Necessity itself is confirmed only by chart review, sought via prepay documentation request.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a precursor-diagnostics edit: for each PTA/peripheral intervention claim, require a qualifying diagnosis plus a non-invasive vascular study by any provider within a lookback window; otherwise pend the claim and request the diagnostic report and procedure note. Add provider-level metrics (PTAs per 100 patients, repeat interventions per beneficiary per year, share of cases without prior imaging) benchmarked to same-specialty peers, placing outliers above the calibrated percentile on prepay medical-necessity review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Jessa Zayas (CEO and owner of Healing Hands Hospice and Humane Love Hospice); Healing Hands Hospice; Humane Love Hospice
State_County: California - Fresno County; California - Kern County; California - Los Angeles County (Van Nuys)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Zayas, owner of two Van Nuys hospice companies, recruited over 100 residents of Fresno and Kern County retirement homes during after-hours door-knocking visits to obtain their Medicare information, then billed Medicare for hospice care with false representations that the patients were terminally ill and submitted forged physician certifications when Medicare requested supporting documentation; payments went to bank accounts she controlled.
WaysToIdentify: Hospice enrolments harvested by door-knocking at retirement homes produce distinctive prepay patterns: election dates clustering within days for many beneficiaries from a few residential addresses hundreds of miles from the hospice's service area, patients with no prior claims evidencing terminal illness, and unusually long lengths of stay with no decline. Forged physician certifications are catchable at the ADR stage by verifying the certifying physician's signature, NPI status and attesting directly with that physician rather than accepting the submitted form. Beneficiary-side confirmation via a hospice-election notification letter is also a prepay control.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a hospice-election screen that geocodes beneficiary residence against the hospice's approved service area and clusters elections by shared facility address and election date; fire prepay review when out-of-area or address-cluster share exceeds the calibrated percentile. Require, before first payment, a verified certification: match certifying/attending NPI to an active licence and to a prior encounter claim with that beneficiary, and auto-contact the physician to confirm authorship on flagged records. Send election-confirmation letters to beneficiaries/representatives and suspend payment on non-response or denial.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Colorado
FraudEntity: Mt. San Rafael Hospital and Rural Health Clinic; Dr. Sheryll Castro-Flores (physician); Dr. Joseph Jimenez (physician); Dr. Douglas McFarland (physician)
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care programs
SchemeSummary: Three hospital-employed physicians allegedly issued invalid controlled-substance prescriptions, including high-dose opioids and dangerous combinations, without legitimate medical purpose and despite red flags (early refills, cash payments despite insurance, long-distance patients), and the hospital caused claims for those invalid prescriptions to be billed to Medicare and other federal health programs. Combined $650,000 payment across the hospital ($325,000) and the three doctors ($112,500, $112,500, $100,000).
WaysToIdentify: Prescription-level red flags were all in the data the payer holds: MME per day above the calibrated high-dose threshold, concurrent opioid-benzodiazepine (and carisoprodol) combinations, early refills, and beneficiaries travelling implausible distances to a single prescriber. Cash payment despite coverage is visible as pharmacy fills for the same patients falling outside the drug benefit while medical claims continue. Prescriber-level concentration within one hospital's employed staff is detectable at adjudication and at pharmacy point-of-sale.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-patient risk engine on pharmacy and medical claims computing per-patient daily MME, overlapping opioid/benzo/muscle-relaxant days, early-refill ratio, prescriber-patient distance and cash-fill share; fire point-of-sale prepay edits requiring prior authorisation on high-MME and dangerous-combination fills. Aggregate to prescriber level versus same-specialty peers and place outliers on prepay review with medical-record requests, notifying the employing hospital as a compliance obligation. Escalate persistent outliers to payment suspension and licensure/DEA referral.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Charise Valentine (doctor); Michele Ritter (doctor, co-defendant); Iris Winchester (clinic operator); Joyce Robinson (patient recruiter); Orthopedic Medical Building (sham clinic)
State_County: Michigan - Oakland County (Southfield); Michigan - Oakland County (Oak Park)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: At a cash-only sham clinic operating from an Oak Park warehouse, Dr. Valentine issued over 3,000 medically unnecessary opioid prescriptions (more than 200,000 Oxycodone/Oxymorphone pills worth over $5.2 million) to 'patients' brought in by recruiters, who paid $200-500 per prescription based on drug quantity and dosage, plus cash for fabricated medical records; Valentine received about 50% of proceeds (over $500,000 cash) and was paid only when she wrote a prescription. Co-defendants including the clinic operator, another doctor, and a recruiter previously pleaded guilty and were sentenced.
WaysToIdentify: A cash-only clinic that bills nothing leaves its footprint downstream at the pharmacy: one prescriber accounting for enormous oxycodone/oxymorphone volumes, uniform high-quantity high-dose scripts, patients clustered far from the practice address, and a practice location that is a warehouse with no legitimate clinical claim history. Payers and PDMPs can see prescriber volume and patient travel distance before paying the fills; the absence of any E/M claims for those patients from that prescriber is itself the giveaway. Kickback payments per prescription are post-pay bank-record evidence.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a 'prescriber with no encounters' detector: for each prescriber, compare controlled-substance fill volume against E/M/encounter claims for the same patients; when fills are high and encounters near zero, block pharmacy payment pending prior authorisation and chart request. Add prescriber-level oxycodone/oxymorphone dosage-unit volume, mean MME and mean patient-prescriber distance benchmarked to same-specialty peers, plus an address-validation check flagging practice locations that are non-clinical (warehouse/industrial) parcels. Route trip-wires to PDMP and DEA referral alongside the prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Tonmoy Sharma (founder and former CEO, Sovereign Health Group); Paul Jin Sen Khor (cash management and accounts payable supervisor); Sovereign Health Group; Vedanta Laboratories Inc.
State_County: California - Orange County (San Clemente, Tustin, Irvine)
PayerName: Private health insurers (out-of-network commercial plans, including ACA-subsidized private plans)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud; Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Upcoding
SchemeSummary: Sovereign Health Group allegedly submitted over $149 million in fraudulent claims to private insurers for addiction/mental health treatment billed at high out-of-network rates, using a sham 'foundation' to harvest patients' identities and then falsifying insurance applications (fake qualifying life events, misstated income) to surreptitiously enroll patients in ACA-subsidized private plans instead of lower-paying Medicaid. It also billed more than $29 million for comprehensive urinalysis panel tests (through its Vedanta Laboratories) that ordering physicians never authorized or that were billed after physicians left, and paid over $21 million in kickbacks to patient brokers disguised as 'marketing hours' under sham contracts.
WaysToIdentify: For the insurers, the enrolment side is testable at underwriting: many ACA applications sharing a facility's address, phone, email domain or bank/payment instrument, all claiming qualifying life events and income just above Medicaid thresholds, then immediately incurring out-of-network residential treatment claims - a same-day enrol-and-admit pattern. On claims, comprehensive urinalysis panels billed at extreme per-patient frequency with ordering physicians who had already terminated employment (verifiable against licence/credential and employment dates) is a prepay conflict. Broker kickbacks disguised as marketing hours are post-pay, found through contract and payment-record audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment-integrity model that clusters applications by shared contact/address/payment identifiers and third-party assistor, and flags QLE-plus-income-attestation applications followed by out-of-network SUD admission within a short window for eligibility verification before claims pay. Build a UDS frequency and ordering-validity edit: cap definitive comprehensive panels per patient per period without documented rationale, and deny claims whose ordering NPI has no active relationship with the facility on the service date. Add a facility-level out-of-network billing monitor (claims per patient-day, panel spend per admission) that triggers prepay review and a records/contract request covering marketing agreements.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: William Philip Werschler (dermatologist, owner); Spokane Dermatology Clinic; Premier Clinical Research L.L.C.; 3rd and Sherman Plaza L.L.C.
SchemeSummary: Dermatologist applied for COVID-19 Economic Injury Disaster Loans for his dermatology clinic and related businesses, then spent the proceeds on prohibited personal purposes - $252,375 on two Porsche automobiles and $553,143 to purchase two properties across from his clinic - resolving False Claims Act claims and related criminal charges for $1.4 million.
WaysToIdentify: No claims-payment component - this is EIDL misuse of loan proceeds, detectable by the lender/SBA rather than by claim adjudication: post-disbursement transaction monitoring of the loan-funded account would show large luxury-vehicle and real-estate purchases inconsistent with permitted working-capital use. At application, revenue and injury figures could be cross-checked against tax transcripts. Payer-side, none of this touches claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control: require disbursement into a designated account and run automated use-of-proceeds monitoring that flags MCC-coded luxury vehicle, brokerage and real-estate transactions above a threshold, freezing remaining draws and triggering a documentation request. Verify application revenue against IRS transcript data before funding. No payer claims edit applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Dr. Duncan Lahtinen (licensed physician)
SchemeSummary: Dr. Lahtinen issued over 1,400 controlled substance prescriptions to thirteen identified patients between 2017 and 2025 - often dangerous combinations of opioids, benzodiazepines, sedatives, and carisoprodol - ignoring red flags of substance abuse, making him liable for civil penalties under the Controlled Substances Act and False Claims Act; he paid $120,000 in penalties.
WaysToIdentify: The pattern is prescriber-level and visible in pharmacy claims and PDMP data before each fill is paid: a small set of patients receiving sustained opioid plus benzodiazepine plus sedative plus carisoprodol combinations over years, with early refills, escalating MME and overlapping days' supply. Concentration of a prescriber's controlled-substance volume in a handful of long-term patients, with no evidence of taper, referral or urine-drug monitoring claims, is measurable at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement point-of-sale prepay edits denying or pending fills that create opioid+benzodiazepine or opioid+carisoprodol overlap, or push daily MME above the calibrated high-dose threshold, absent prior authorisation. Compute per-prescriber concentration metrics (share of controlled-substance dosage units to top patients, mean overlap days, early-refill rate) versus same-specialty peers and place outliers on prescriber-level prior authorisation plus medical-record request. Auto-generate PDMP/board referral packets when the pattern persists after outreach.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Ashley Hymel (executive assistant at Company 1)
SchemeSummary: Hymel, an executive assistant, allegedly used her employer's company credit card to embezzle at least $130,663.92 from the company, charged by bill of information as wire fraud.
WaysToIdentify: Purely internal corporate embezzlement via a company credit card - there is no payer claim and no adjudication touchpoint, so no payer-side control applies. Detection sits with the employer's expense controls: card transactions lacking receipts or business purpose, personal-merchant MCCs, and spend far above the cardholder's role benchmark, all visible in card-issuer data before reimbursement.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer control applies; the nearest analogue is a corporate card monitoring rule: per cardholder per month, flag personal-category MCCs, transactions without matched receipt/approval within a set period, and spend above role-peer percentile, auto-suspending the card and requiring documentation. Enforce segregation of duties so the cardholder cannot approve their own reconciliations.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Ashley Hymel (executive assistant at Company 1)
SchemeSummary: Hymel, an executive assistant, used her employer's company credit card to embezzle at least $130,663.92 from the employer (Company 1); she pled guilty to wire fraud and agreed to repay the full amount.
WaysToIdentify: Same as the companion charge: employee credit-card embezzlement with no health-care claim and no payer adjudication step, so this is outside payer controls. It is caught by card-level expense monitoring and reconciliation - unsupported charges, personal merchant categories, and approval by the spender herself.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest applicable control is automated card-transaction surveillance (unmatched-receipt aging, personal-MCC flags, spend-versus-role-peer outliers) with automatic card suspension and mandatory independent approval of executive-assistant reconciliations.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Daniel Tharp (managing director, Hangar X Holdings, LLC); Hangar X Holdings, LLC
SchemeSummary: As managing director of Hangar X Holdings, LLC, Tharp was responsible for collecting and paying over the company's trust fund taxes (income, Medicare, and Social Security taxes) withheld from employee wages; from October 2014 through December 2019 the company withheld these taxes but Tharp knowingly failed to remit over $1.2 million to the IRS.
WaysToIdentify: This is trust-fund payroll tax fraud with no claims-payment component, so no payer adjudication control exists; detection belongs to the IRS by matching W-2/Form 941 reported withholding against actual EFTPS deposits and flagging accruing zero-deposit quarters in near-real time. The observable signal is filed returns reporting withheld amounts with no corresponding remittance over consecutive quarters.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer claims edit applies. Nearest control: an automated 941-versus-deposit reconciliation that fires after consecutive quarters of reported-but-unremitted withholding, triggering responsible-person identification and collection action; secondarily, flag employers whose payroll-based staffing data implies withholding far above deposits.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Dr. Sonny Saggar (doctor, operator of St. Louis General Hospital urgent care locations); Renita Barringer (office manager)
State_County: Missouri - St. Louis (downtown St. Louis and Creve Coeur)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
