SchemeSummary: Saggar and his office manager hired assistant physicians (medical school graduates without residency) to see patients at two urgent care/primary care locations but billed Medicare and Missouri Medicaid as if Saggar personally performed the services, even when he was out of town; he paid physicians stipends up to $480/month to sign collaborative practice arrangement forms filed with the state medical board to falsely show supervision, used APs at a non-underserved location, and concealed from Medicaid that a co-conspirator physician with suspended billing privileges was providing services. Loss of $742,528 attributed jointly to Saggar and Barringer (who awaits sentencing).
WaysToIdentify: Compare the rendering/supervising NPI on claims against the physician's verifiable location and activity: Saggar was billed as personally performing services on dates he was out of town, detectable by cross-checking travel/absence indicators, simultaneous billing at two sites, and impossible same-day service volume for one NPI across two clinics. Credentialing data carries the rest: the state medical board's collaborative practice arrangement filings list assistant physicians and their collaborating physicians, and CPA rules restrict AP practice to underserved areas, so the practice's service ZIP can be scored against the state's shortage-area file. Also screen every servicing/ordering provider on claims against the OIG LEIE and the state Medicaid suspended/terminated-provider list, which would have flagged the co-conspirator with suspended billing privileges.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a 'personally performed' plausibility edit per rendering NPI per date: count distinct service locations, total timed/E&M minutes, and flag when one NPI bills as performer at two or more geographically separate sites the same day or exceeds a calibrated same-specialty daily-hours percentile; pend those claims for supervision documentation. Add an enrolment-time linkage that ingests state board collaborative-practice/supervision filings and mid-level rosters, maps each supervising physician to the number of APs and to the shortage-area status of each practice location, and blocks billing under the physician's NPI where the location is not eligible or the supervisor-to-AP ratio exceeds the licensure limit. Run a nightly rendering/ordering/supervising NPI screen against LEIE and state exclusion/suspension files with automatic prepay denial and post-pay recoupment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Dr. Asim Muhammad Ali (physician, owner of Central Diagnostic Laboratory and Institute for Pain Management LLC); Dr. Mohd Azfar Malik (owner of Psych Care Consultants LLC)
PayerName: Medicare; Missouri Medicaid; TRICARE; private health insurers
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Drug_Prescriptions; Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Dr. Ali paid kickbacks for urine specimens referred to his own lab, Central Diagnostic Laboratory, and pre-signed/issued controlled-substance prescriptions for pain-management patients he never examined; in a separate case he performed services for Psych Care Consultants' Medicare patients but billed under Dr. Malik's name and Medicare number for 'annual wellness visits' conducted only by phone. Dr. Malik separately billed Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for in-person services while out of the state or country and for ketamine infusions performed by Ali, who lacked DEA registration. Figures span both defendants: Ali ordered to pay $1,845,916 plus $3,902 restitution; Malik fined $20,000 and ordered to pay $19,442 restitution with five years probation.}
WaysToIdentify: Physician-lab ownership is visible at enrolment: Ali's ordering NPI and Central Diagnostic Laboratory shared ownership/address information in PECOS and state filings, so a self-referral link plus a spike in urine drug testing referrals concentrated from a handful of ordering NPIs is observable prepay. Billing under Dr. Malik's NPI for visits Ali performed shows up as annual wellness visits billed on dates Malik was out of state/country and as telephone-only encounters billed with in-person place-of-service codes; ketamine infusion and controlled-substance claims can be matched to the performing provider's DEA registration status. Absence/location evidence for the physician is partly post-payment, but POS/modifier inconsistency, pre-signed prescription patterns and DEA validation are all prepay signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ownership-graph edit that links ordering physician NPIs to lab TINs via PECOS owner names, addresses and bank data, then computes each lab's share of volume from owner-affiliated orderers and each orderer's toxicology-per-patient rate versus same-specialty peers, pending claims above the calibrated percentile for medical-necessity documentation. Add a place-of-service/modifier consistency edit that denies in-person POS or wellness-visit codes when the only supporting contact is telephonic, and a same-day conflict edit flagging one NPI billed as performer at multiple locations. Validate the performing provider's active DEA registration and scope for any controlled-substance or ketamine infusion claim as a hard prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Omnicare (long-term care pharmacy); CVS Health Corporation (parent company)
SchemeSummary: A civil False Claims Act jury found that Omnicare, the nation's largest long-term care pharmacy, dispensed drugs to elderly and disabled residents of assisted living and other residential long-term care facilities without valid prescriptions, submitting over three million false claims to Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE; damages were assessed at $135,592,814, trebled to $406,778,442, and parent CVS Health was found liable for causing the false claims.
WaysToIdentify: Long-term-care pharmacy claims should be traceable to a valid, current prescriber order; the observable signal is dispensing after the last valid fill/authorization has lapsed - refills beyond the authorized quantity, dispensing on rolling 'standing order' or facility-cycle files with no new prescriber authorization, and prescriber DEA/NPI or prescription dates missing or stale on the claim. At adjudication the payer can compare fill dates to prescription written date and refill authorization count, and check that the prescriber NPI is active and has an encounter relationship with the resident. Full proof requires chart/prescription audit, so the prepay route is targeted documentation requests on the lapsed-authorization subset.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescription-validity engine at the claim line: for each dispense, validate presence and currency of prescriber NPI, written date, days-supply and remaining authorized refills, and deny or pend fills that exceed authorized refills, fall outside the state prescription-validity window, or lack a documented prescriber order. Add a pharmacy-level monitor computing the share of fills that are auto-refill/cycle-fill without a new authorization and the share of residents with no prescriber encounter in the lookback, and trigger prepay documentation review or payment suspension for pharmacies above the calibrated percentile versus LTC pharmacy peers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Shawn Bashir (creator of Success for Kids and Growing Kids Therapy)
State_County: Illinois - Lake County (Grayslake); Illinois - Cook County (Chicago)
SchemeSummary: Bashir allegedly created fictitious entities, Success for Kids and Growing Kids Therapy, purporting to provide early intervention therapy services to children, and submitted about $17.3 million in claims to a private insurer for therapy never provided, causing at least $1.4 million in payments; also charged with two counts of aggravated identity theft.
WaysToIdentify: A brand-new entity billing $17.3 million of pediatric early-intervention therapy is detectable at enrolment and first-billing: no verifiable clinical site, no licensed therapist roster, residential/virtual address, and a billing ramp far above same-specialty new-provider peers. Phantom services show up as claims for members with no other corroborating utilization, identical unit counts across members, and therapy minutes exceeding what the credentialed therapist headcount could physically deliver. Identity misuse is visible when member IDs appear on this provider's claims with no referral, no IFSP/early-intervention authorization, and geographic distance from the member's home.
FeaturesToCreate: Add a new-provider velocity control: for entities within their first year, compute weekly billed amount, distinct members and minutes-per-licensed-therapist, and auto-pend claims above the calibrated new-provider percentile pending site visit and therapist license verification. Build a rendering-capacity edit comparing billed therapy units per day to the number of licensed rendering NPIs on file, and a corroboration edit that pends claims for members with no referral/authorization and no other provider contact in the period, with member outreach verification letters before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Advanced Inventory Management, Inc. (medical device company); Anthony Iaderosa (sole owner and CEO)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: The company imported medical products from international distributors at lower prices, used a hair dryer to remove labels restricting resale to specified foreign countries, and resold the misbranded devices in the U.S. at 35-50% markups, earning about $500,000 in profits while concealing the practice from the FDA and causing false statements to customs agents; resolved via deferred prosecution agreements with a $1 million fine.
WaysToIdentify: This is a product-diversion/misbranding case with no claim-adjudication footprint, so the payer signal is indirect: gray-market devices reach payers through DME suppliers whose acquisition invoices, serial numbers and lot codes do not trace to authorized U.S. distributors, and whose unit costs sit far below the market for the billed HCPCS. Detection is largely post-payment and regulatory (FDA/customs), but payers can require and audit invoice/serial documentation for high-cost device claims and check supplier accreditation and product-listing status at credentialing.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a device-provenance check on high-cost DME/implant HCPCS: require serial/lot and acquisition invoice on the claim or in the audit file, validate the manufacturer/model against the FDA listing and against authorized-distributor lists, and pend claims where provenance is missing or the invoice price falls below the calibrated low percentile for that HCPCS. At credentialing, verify supplier accreditation and add periodic invoice sampling with recoupment for non-U.S.-labeled product.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Mona Ghosh (physician, owner of Progressive Women's Healthcare, S.C.); Progressive Women's Healthcare, S.C.
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Upcoding; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: OB/GYN owner billed Medicaid, TRICARE and private insurers for nonexistent and medically unnecessary procedures (endometrial ablations and biopsies, ultrasounds, vaccinations, blood and STD tests), some performed without patient consent, and inflated the length/complexity of in-office and telemedicine visits using higher-paying codes, supporting the claims with falsified patient medical records.
WaysToIdentify: The signal is procedure-rate outliers within one specialty: endometrial ablation/biopsy, ultrasound, vaccination and STD/blood panel counts per unique patient far above OB/GYN peers, plus repeat ablations on the same patient (an anatomically implausible repetition) and ultrasounds billed on nearly every visit. Upcoding is visible in the E&M level distribution skewed to high levels for both office and telehealth visits, and in telehealth claims billed at levels whose time requirements exceed the documented session length. Falsified records only surface on audit, so the prepay route is targeted record requests on the outlier code families.
FeaturesToCreate: Build per-provider, per-code-family utilization scoring (procedures per unique patient, ultrasound-per-visit ratio, lab panels per patient) benchmarked against same-specialty peers, and pend claims for providers above the calibrated percentile pending records. Add member-history edits: deny/pend repeat endometrial ablation for the same member within the clinically implausible window, and pend where a procedure claim has no supporting diagnosis history or consent documentation. Add an E&M level-distribution monitor by provider and modality that triggers prepay level-of-service review when high-level share exceeds the peer-calibrated threshold.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Kelley Oliver-Hollis (owner of SerenityCare LLC); SerenityCare LLC
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Owner of SerenityCare LLC, a Penn Hills facility serving residents with intellectual disabilities, allegedly overbilled Pennsylvania Medicaid for services provided from December 2016 to July 2023, and made false statements and concealed material facts relating to health care matters; superseding indictment adds money laundering and misuse of Social Security benefits as a representative payee.
WaysToIdentify: Overbilling of residential/ID waiver services is visible as billed units exceeding the authorized service plan and exceeding calendar feasibility - more than 24 hours of billed care per resident per day, units billed while the resident was hospitalized or absent, and staff-to-resident ratios that cannot support the billed hours. Cross-check claims against the state's waiver authorization file, facility census/attendance logs and concurrent institutional claims. Representative-payee/SSA benefit misuse is not a claims signal; that requires referral to SSA-OIG.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an authorization-versus-billed reconciliation for waiver/personal-care lines: compute billed units per member per day against the approved plan of care and hard-deny units exceeding authorization or 24 hours/day, and pend units overlapping inpatient, ER or other facility claims for the same member. Add a facility-level staffing feasibility check comparing total billed direct-care hours to payrolled staff hours reported at enrolment/revalidation, with prepay documentation request or payment suspension when the ratio exceeds the calibrated peer threshold.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Mihir Taneja; Larry Smith (owner of Z Stat Medical, LLC d/b/a Oldsmar Pharmacy); Z Stat Medical, LLC d/b/a Oldsmar Pharmacy; Centurion Compounding, Inc. (marketing company)
State_County: Florida - Hillsborough County (Tampa); Florida - Pinellas County (Oldsmar)
SchemeSummary: Taneja and pharmacy owner Larry Smith negotiated an arrangement paying marketing company Centurion Compounding a percentage of profits from TRICARE claims it referred to Oldsmar Pharmacy, resulting in thousands of TRICARE claims for compounded pain and scar creams tainted by kickbacks from November 2014 to February 2015. Taneja agreed to pay $2 million, Smith previously paid $600,000, and Oldsmar Pharmacy returned over $19 million to TRICARE.
WaysToIdentify: Percentage-of-profit marketing arrangements show up as an abrupt concentration of TRICARE compounded-cream claims at one pharmacy sourced from a small set of out-of-area prescribers, near-identical formulas and ingredient/quantity patterns across beneficiaries, and average reimbursement per claim far above peer pharmacies. Enrolment/contract data can be probed by requiring disclosure of marketing contracts and their compensation basis. Beneficiary contact showing they were cold-called and never examined by the prescriber is also available prepay.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a compound-drug prepay edit: for each pharmacy, compute share of revenue from compounded topical/scar creams, average paid per prescription, distinct-prescriber concentration and prescriber-to-patient geographic distance, and pend or suspend when multiple indicators exceed calibrated peer percentiles. Require signed attestation and disclosure of any marketing/referral arrangement with per-claim or percentage compensation as an enrolment condition, and flag pharmacy-marketer TIN/address/bank-account linkages for prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Henry Ezeonyido (organizer); Brendon Ashe; Aqiyla Atherton (intermediary/recruiter); Darline Cobbler; Ariel Lambert
PayerName: Five unnamed private health insurance companies
SchemeSummary: Ezeonyido submitted over $1 million in false out-of-network reimbursement claims to five private health insurers for expensive medical treatment allegedly received and paid out-of-pocket while traveling abroad (including fake stabbings, gunshot wounds and hit-and-run injuries), supported by fabricated medical records, bank records and foreign police reports, although the purported patients were actually in the U.S.; insurers paid about $655,313, and beneficiaries kicked back a share to Ezeonyido, who kept roughly $396,998. Restitution ($655,313) and forfeiture ($396,998) figures are Ezeonyido's; his four co-defendants received probation.
WaysToIdentify: Foreign out-of-network self-pay reimbursement claims are a narrow, high-risk lane: the tells are multiple unrelated members submitting claims routed through the same submitter, email, address or bank account, dramatic injury narratives (stabbings, gunshots, hit-and-run) from the same foreign facilities, and receipts/police reports with reused formatting or sequential numbering. Payers can verify prepay that the member was actually abroad by checking travel/entry records or asking for passport stamps and boarding passes, and by cross-checking domestic claim activity on the same dates that proves the member was in the U.S.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a member-reimbursement clustering feature that links foreign-claim submissions by shared bank account, address, phone, email, IP, notary or foreign facility name and fires when a cluster exceeds a small number of unrelated members. Add a presence-conflict edit: pend any foreign-treatment reimbursement where the same member has domestic claims or pharmacy fills within the claimed treatment window, and require documentary proof of travel plus direct facility verification before payment; route matched clusters to SIU rather than paying.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: LifeWorks Counseling Associates, PLLC; Dr. David Ferruolo (owner); Erik Alonso (excluded individual providing services)
SchemeSummary: LifeWorks, a New Hampshire telehealth mental health provider, and its owner Dr. David Ferruolo submitted Medicaid claims and received reimbursement for counseling services rendered by Erik Alonso, who had been excluded from federal health care programs by HHS-OIG, making the claims non-reimbursable; they agreed to pay $300,000 based on ability to pay, and Alonso separately pleaded guilty to one count of health care fraud on October 23, 2025.
WaysToIdentify: This is a pure exclusion-screening failure and is fully catchable prepay: the rendering counselor's name/NPI/SSN appears on the HHS-OIG LEIE and state exclusion lists, so any claim naming him as rendering provider is non-reimbursable regardless of supervision. The gap is that telehealth group claims often carry only the group NPI or the owner's NPI, hiding the actual renderer, so the payer must require rendering-provider identification on every behavioral-health line and screen the group's full employee roster monthly.
FeaturesToCreate: Require a rendering-provider NPI on every professional/behavioral-health line and hard-deny lines where the rendering, supervising, ordering or billing entity's owner matches LEIE, SAM, or the state exclusion/termination file, refreshed monthly with name/DOB/SSN fuzzy matching. Add an employment-roster attestation at enrolment and revalidation for group behavioral-health providers, screen every listed clinician and contractor, and suspend payments to the group when an excluded individual is found on the roster pending remediation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: CompreCare Health LLC and its affiliates, d/b/a Meditelecare LLC (telehealth company)
State_County: Kentucky (Bowling Green/Louisville); Connecticut (company base); services provided in at least 17 states
SchemeSummary: Meditelecare billed Medicare for telehealth psychotherapy sessions that did not last the minimum time required for the billed time-based codes, and supported those claims with false time records; the allegations came from a qui tam whistleblower suit and were resolved for $358,514.
WaysToIdentify: Time-based psychotherapy codes have minimum-duration requirements, and telehealth platforms generate objective session-duration metadata (connection start/stop) that can be compared prepay to the billed code tier. Provider-level tells: nearly all sessions billed at the longer tier, back-to-back sessions whose billed minutes exceed the clinician's available workday, and identical documented durations across all patients. Payers can require session start/stop times on telehealth behavioral claims and reconcile aggregate billed minutes against clinician capacity.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a timed-code duration edit: require start/stop time on time-based telehealth psychotherapy lines, deny or downcode when documented duration falls below the code's minimum, and pend when the field is absent. Add a clinician-day capacity check summing billed minutes per rendering NPI per day (including travel/facility rounds) and a distribution monitor on the share of sessions at the longest tier versus same-specialty peers, triggering prepay record and platform-log requests above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Paul Wexler (operator of telemarketing company); Paul Bleignier (operator of telemarketing company; owner of clinical laboratory)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Wexler and Bleignier ran a telemarketing company that solicited Medicare beneficiaries for medically unnecessary cancer genetic (CGx) testing and received kickbacks for referring those beneficiaries to laboratories, causing $17.3 million in Medicare billings and collecting $5.2 million in kickbacks. Separately, Bleignier enrolled his own clinical laboratory in Medicare while using other people's identities to conceal his 5%+ ownership, billing $3,012,156 in kickback-tainted, ineligible claims and being paid $916,106; the sentencing figures span both defendants (4 years for Wexler, 2 years for Bleignier, $1.2M forfeiture each, $5.2M restitution, plus $916,106 additional forfeiture for Bleignier).
WaysToIdentify: CGx claims driven by telemarketing show a distinctive signature prepay: high-cost hereditary cancer panels ordered for beneficiaries with no cancer diagnosis or family-history documentation, ordering physicians located hundreds of miles from the patient with no prior or subsequent treating relationship, and a handful of ordering NPIs feeding many labs. Ownership concealment is catchable at enrolment by verifying 5%-plus owners against identity data, cross-matching owner SSNs/addresses/bank accounts to other enrolled entities and to individuals with prior sanctions, and requiring notarized disclosure with identity proofing.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay medical-necessity edit for hereditary cancer panels requiring a qualifying diagnosis or documented family history and evidence of a treating relationship (prior E&M by the ordering NPI within a lookback), denying or pending otherwise. Add ordering-physician concentration and patient-distance features per lab, plus an enrolment identity/ownership verification that scores owner identity documents, matches owner PII and bank accounts across enrolled entities, and blocks or revokes enrolment where disclosed ownership conflicts with verified identity data; suspend payment on labs whose orders concentrate in telemarketing-linked NPIs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Rashid Naqvi (owner/operator of Elite Diagnostics Inc. and Astro Diagnostics Inc.); Elite Diagnostics Inc.; Astro Diagnostics Inc.
State_County: Missouri - St. Louis (Eastern District of Missouri); Texas - Harris County (Houston area)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Naqvi's two labs submitted 22,898 claims to Medicare totaling $1,974,479 for COVID-19 test kits mailed to beneficiaries who never requested them, using Medicare numbers obtained through $488,435 in kickbacks to co-conspirators; some claims were for patients who had already died, and he produced false authorization records during Medicare audits to conceal the scheme.
WaysToIdentify: Unsolicited mailed COVID test kits are catchable prepay with three deterministic checks: date of service after the beneficiary's date of death in the eligibility/DMF file, no ordering-provider relationship or physician order for the kit, and mass-identical claims (same code, same units, thousands of members) from a lab with no matching specimen-processing footprint. Kickback-sourced beneficiary lists show up as member cohorts clustered geographically or by marketer-linked ordering NPIs, and audit responses consisting of templated 'authorizations' with identical wording are a further tell on documentation review.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement hard prepay edits: deny lines with DOS after date of death using daily-refreshed eligibility/DMF, and deny lab/test-kit claims lacking a valid ordering NPI with a documented patient relationship. Add a lab-level mass-mailing detector computing distinct beneficiaries per day, single-code concentration, share of members with no other claims from the ordering NPI, and duplicate authorization-document hashes on audit responses, with automatic payment suspension and beneficiary verification mailings when thresholds are exceeded.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Murex Management, Inc. (MMI) (management company of ethanol marketing affiliate)
State_County: Texas - Collin County (Plano); Louisiana - Orleans Parish (New Orleans)
PayerName: First NBC Bank; a North Carolina bank
SchemeSummary: MMI and an ethanol producer ('Company A') allegedly created fictitious invoices purporting to reflect ethanol sales between the two companies ('buy/sells'), then sold those sham accounts receivable to financial institutions through a New Orleans online auction marketplace, generating cash flow for Company A and about $6.07 million in profit for MMI; approximately $1.2 billion in fake transactions ended in defaults causing about $73.07 million in losses to First NBC Bank and $8.33 million to a North Carolina bank.
WaysToIdentify: No payer-side control applies: this is a commercial receivables/bank fraud on fictitious ethanol invoices with no health care claim component. The analogous financial-institution control is invoice and counterparty verification - confirming shipments and independent counterparty confirmation before purchasing receivables, and flagging circular buy/sell flows between two related parties.
FeaturesToCreate: No health-plan claims control applies. The nearest analogous control, if the payer purchases or factors receivables, is a counterparty-circularity check that detects offsetting invoice pairs between the same two entities, requires third-party proof of delivery before funding, and suspends funding on concentration or default-rate outliers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Jorge Zamora-Quezada, M.D. (rheumatologist)
State_County: Texas - Hidalgo County (Mission); Rio Grande Valley
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; TRICARE; Blue Cross Blue Shield
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; Drug_Prescriptions; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Rheumatologist falsely diagnosed patients with rheumatoid arthritis so he could bill Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE and Blue Cross Blue Shield for medically unnecessary injections, infusions, x-rays, MRIs and other procedures, fabricating medical records (including using ultrasound images of employees as patient documentation) to support the diagnoses and defeat insurer audits and a grand jury subpoena; over $118 million billed and $28 million paid.
WaysToIdentify: The mechanic is a fabricated chronic diagnosis driving high-cost recurring services, which is visible prepay as an extreme rheumatoid arthritis diagnosis rate and infusion/injection volume per unique patient versus rheumatology peers, plus near-universal RA coding across the panel with no supporting serology or imaging claims. Additional prepay tells: infusion units exceeding drug-acquisition purchases, imaging billed for more patients per day than equipment capacity allows, and duplicate/reused ultrasound image files identified on documentation review. Fabricated records and staff-image reuse are audit findings, so the prepay action is a documentation request plus prior authorization on biologic infusions.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a diagnosis-concentration feature per provider (share of panel with the same high-reimbursement chronic diagnosis, and infusion/injection lines per unique patient) benchmarked to same-specialty peers, firing prepay review above the calibrated percentile. Require diagnosis corroboration for biologic infusion claims (supporting lab/serology or imaging claim history) via prior authorization, and add a drug-inventory reconciliation comparing billed J-code units to distributor purchase data, with payment suspension when billed units exceed documented acquisition.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Jeffrey Paul Madison (hospital CEO, Little River Healthcare); Susan L. Hertzberg (Boston Heart Diagnostics executive); Matthew John Theiler (laboratory sales executive); David Weldon Kraus (laboratory sales executive); Thomas Gray Hardaway; Jeffrey Paul Parnell; Laura Spain Howard; Todd Dean Cook; William Todd Hickman; Christopher Roland Gonzales; Ruben Daniel Marioni; Jordan Joseph Perkins; Elizabeth Ruth Seymour; Linh Ba Nguyen; Thuy Ngoc Nguyen; Joseph Gil Bolin; Heriberto Salinas; Hong Davis; Robert O'Neal (marketer); Peter J. Bennett (attorney, money launderer); Little River Healthcare; Stamford Memorial Hospital; Boston Heart Diagnostics
State_County: Texas - Milam County (Rockdale); Texas - Jones County (Stamford); Massachusetts - Middlesex County (Framingham)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; other federal health care programs
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; Upcoding
SchemeSummary: Two rural Texas hospitals (Little River Healthcare and Stamford Memorial) partnered with clinical lab Boston Heart Diagnostics: BHD processed cardiovascular lipid blood tests for a fee while the hospitals billed insurers for them as higher-paying hospital outpatient services. The hospitals paid a share of lab revenue to marketers running sham management services organizations, which passed kickbacks to referring physicians disguised as MSO 'investment returns'; one attorney laundered at least $2,724,080 of kickback proceeds through sham trusts, shell corporations and his law firm's IOLTA account. Figures span multiple defendants: Madison received 36 months and agreed to pay $5,343,630 under the FCA; Theiler 18 months and a $75,000 fine; Kraus 22 months and a $25,000 fine.
WaysToIdentify: The pass-through mechanic is visible in claim data: small rural hospitals billing high volumes of specialized cardiovascular lipid panels for patients who never appear in their inpatient/outpatient encounter data and who live far outside the hospital's service area, with the actual testing done by an out-of-state reference lab. The observable signals are outpatient lab revenue as a dominant share of a critical-access hospital's billing, referring-physician geography, and hospital-outpatient rates billed for tests performed elsewhere. Kickbacks routed through MSO 'investment returns' surface at credentialing through physician financial-interest disclosures and in ownership/payment records; the laundering trail is post-payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a lab pass-through edit for facility claims: for each facility, compute the share of billed lab lines for members with no other encounter at that facility, the referring-physician distance distribution, and the ratio of reference-lab-performed to in-house tests, and pend or deny facility-rate lab claims where the specimen was neither collected nor analyzed at the facility. Add mandatory disclosure of MSO/management-company financial relationships at credentialing, link referring-physician NPIs to MSO payee entities, and suspend payment on referral streams where a referring physician holds an undisclosed financial interest in the billing chain.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Shelby Lynn Hill (health insurance broker)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Hill, a health insurance broker, obtained a $220,645 PPP loan for a fictitious cattle farm (Plateau Angus Farms) by submitting fake W-2s and Tennessee Secretary of State records claiming 14 employees and $88,000 monthly payroll - listing prospective health insurance customers' identities as employees without authorization - plus a $42,700 PPP loan for a second fictitious company, and misused PPP proceeds of a third entity (Shelby Lynn Hill, MD PLLC) to install a personal swimming pool.
WaysToIdentify: No payer-side claims control applies: this is PPP loan fraud, detectable by the SBA/lender through payroll-tax records - no IRS 941 filings or state wage reports matching the claimed 14 employees and $88,000 monthly payroll, an entity with no filing history, and identities of insurance prospects appearing as employees. The health-plan-adjacent signal is a broker misusing customer PII, which a plan can detect through unusual broker access to member/prospect identity data.
FeaturesToCreate: No claims-payment control applies. The nearest applicable controls are lender-side payroll verification (cross-match applicant payroll to IRS 941/state wage filings before disbursement, deny on mismatch) and, on the payer side, broker/agent access monitoring that flags bulk export or reuse of prospect PII and SSNs by a single broker account and suspends the broker's appointment pending review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Louisiana; U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Darrion Denard Brooks
State_County: Louisiana - East Baton Rouge Parish (Baton Rouge); Texas; Florida; Georgia; Tennessee
SchemeSummary: Brooks and co-conspirators allegedly used fictitious patient identification information and the DEA registration numbers and identifying data of at least five medical professionals, without authorization, to present at least 11 fraudulent prescriptions for codeine and other controlled substances at eight pharmacies in five states, then resold the drugs on the street.
WaysToIdentify: Forged controlled-substance prescriptions using stolen DEA numbers are catchable at the point of dispensing: the prescriber's DEA registration can be validated in real time for active status, state, and schedule authority, and the patient identity can be checked against eligibility/PDMP records. Cross-pharmacy, cross-state signals are decisive - the same prescriber DEA number appearing at pharmacies in five states within days, patients with no prior claim or PDMP history, and cash-pay codeine fills clustered by presenter. PDMP and switch-level data carry these signals before the fill is completed.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a real-time prescriber-validation edit on controlled-substance claims that verifies active DEA registration, schedule authority and state of practice, and rejects mismatches. Add a cross-pharmacy velocity detector on prescriber DEA number and patient identity: fire when one DEA number appears across pharmacies in multiple states within a short window, or when a patient with no verifiable eligibility/PDMP history presents schedule II-V opioid or codeine prescriptions, generating a hard reject plus PDMP/board alert.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dehshid "David" Nourian (pharmacist, owner/operator of three compounding pharmacies)
State_County: Texas - Tarrant County (Fort Worth); Texas - Tarrant County (Arlington)
PayerName: U.S. Department of Labor Office of Workers' Compensation Programs; Blue Cross Blue Shield
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Nourian and co-conspirators paid doctors millions in bribes and kickbacks to prescribe medically unnecessary compound pain creams to injured federal workers; the creams were mixed by untrained teenagers in pharmacy back rooms at ~$15 per prescription and billed to DOL-OWCP and Blue Cross Blue Shield for as much as $16,000 per prescription, totaling over $145 million billed and $90 million paid, with proceeds laundered through shell/holding companies and $24 million in taxes evaded. Restitution of over $115 million plus $405 million forfeiture were imposed.
WaysToIdentify: Compounded pain creams billed at up to $16,000 per prescription are catchable prepay on price and formula: reimbursement per prescription orders of magnitude above the ingredient cost, high-cost bulk ingredient NDCs, and identical multi-ingredient formulas across unrelated injured workers. Referral concentration is the second signal - a small group of prescribers generating nearly all of a pharmacy's compound volume, often with no examination and with patients geographically remote from the prescriber. Kickback payments are visible through required disclosure of marketing/consulting arrangements and, post-payment, through financial flows to shell entities.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a compounded-drug prepay control: require ingredient-level NDCs and quantities, cap or pend claims where paid amount per prescription or per-gram cost exceeds the calibrated peer percentile, and require prior authorization with documented failure of commercially available alternatives. Add prescriber-pharmacy concentration and prescriber-patient distance features per pharmacy, with payment suspension when both exceed thresholds, and mandate disclosure of percentage-based marketing contracts as a condition of participation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Nnamdi Felix Udeagha
State_County: Oklahoma - Eastern District of Oklahoma (Chickasaw Nation); Texas - Humble
SchemeSummary: Business email compromise scheme: conspirators sent the Chickasaw Nation Department of Health emails posing as a legitimate vendor directing payment to bank accounts opened by the conspirators; Udeagha supplied the receiving bank account information used to collect and distribute the diverted payments.
WaysToIdentify: This is a business email compromise against a health department's accounts-payable function, not a claims fraud, so the signal lives in vendor-master and payment operations: an emailed request to change a known vendor's bank account, sent from a lookalike domain, with new account details not matching the vendor's tax ID or historical banking. It is preventable prepayment by out-of-band callback verification to a phone number on file and by dual approval of any banking change.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a vendor-master change control: any bank account, address or remittance-email change triggers a hold on all payments to that vendor until out-of-band verification against previously stored contact data plus dual authorization is recorded. Add automated detection of lookalike sender domains and of new payee accounts receiving first-time payments above a threshold or accounts already linked to other payees, routing those disbursements to manual review before release.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky; U.S. District Court for the Western District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: The Arthritis Knee Pain Centers (AKPC); Dr. John Rush (owner and Chief Executive Officer)
SchemeSummary: Civil False Claims Act complaint alleging that a knee-injection clinic and its owner-physician doubled billable visits by treating each knee of bilateral osteoarthritis patients on separate dates rather than the same visit, and billed Medicare for millions of milliliters of single-use contrast dye claimed as discarded when it was actually reused on other patients.
WaysToIdentify: Bilateral knee injection claims split across two dates of service for the same beneficiary within a short window are visible at adjudication: pair the same HCPCS (e.g., viscosupplement injection/arthrocentesis) with LT and RT modifiers on separate claims days apart and flag the repeating pattern practice-wide rather than one-off. Contrast/drug waste is auditable prepay by summing billed units of single-use vials (JW-modifier discarded units plus administered units) against vials purchasable per the provider's 340B/wholesaler purchase records and per-patient dosing limits.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-level edit that detects same-code opposite-laterality injection claims separated by fewer days than the calibrated clinical norm and, when the provider's share of split-laterality pairs exceeds same-specialty peers, deny the second date pending records. Build a provider-month drug-waste reconciliation: total billed units (administered + JW discarded) of single-use contrast/viscosupplement divided by distinct patients and compared to vial size and to purchase-invoice volumes; overage triggers prepay suspension of the J-code line and an invoice documentation request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Scottie Girl, LLC d/b/a The Breastfeeding Shop (DME supplier); Patricia Gatter (owner)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleged that The Breastfeeding Shop, a DME supplier, billed TRICARE hundreds of dollars more per breast pump than it charged Pennsylvania Medicaid (a prohibited dual fee schedule), and unbundled accessories already included in the standard pre-packaged breast pump kit by billing TRICARE separately for each item as a replacement part; the company and its owner collectively pay $1 million.
WaysToIdentify: Cross-payer price comparison catches the dual fee schedule: compare the supplier's charged/allowed amount per breast pump HCPCS against the same supplier's Medicaid-charged amount and against peer suppliers for the identical code, since TRICARE rules bar charging more than other payers. Unbundling is visible at adjudication because accessory HCPCS codes are billed on the same date or shortly after the pump code even though the kit includes them, and 'replacement part' billing appears before any plausible wear interval.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a supplier-code price parity check that joins TRICARE claim lines to the same NPI/TIN's Medicaid or commercial charge data for identical HCPCS and fires when the TRICARE charge exceeds the lowest other-payer charge, suspending payment above the parity amount. Add a kit-bundling edit that denies accessory/replacement-part codes billed within the kit's included-contents list on or near the pump dispense date absent documentation of loss or defect.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire (with Districts of Vermont and Maine; New England Strike Force)
FraudEntity: Erik Alonso (excluded social worker/psychotherapy provider); Leo Anzivino Jr. (straw owner, Advanced Medical Supply); Manthan Rohit Shah (owner/operator of Mumbai-based pharma company); Evelyn Herrera (owner, Merida Medical Supplies Inc.); Donald Jani (CEO, CSS Pain Relief, Inc.); Joseph Dobie
State_County: New Hampshire - Belknap County (Laconia); Vermont; Maine - Androscoggin County (Lewiston)
PayerName: Medicaid (New Hampshire Medicaid); Medicaid (Maine); Medicare; SNAP
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud; Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Six unrelated New England Strike Force cases totaling over $14 million: an excluded prior health care fraud felon (Alonso) hid his exclusion from a Laconia, NH telehealth psychotherapy provider and billed NH Medicaid for telehealth psychotherapy while exploiting a patient for personal tasks; straw owner Anzivino fronted DME company Advanced Medical Supply, billed Medicare over $6 million in false DME claims and laundered over $3 million through bank transfers with falsified beneficial-ownership documents; Herrera's purported DME firm Merida billed Medicare ~$6.5 million for medically unnecessary wrist, knee and back braces for New England residents and moved proceeds to Mexico property and crypto; Jani's CSS Pain Relief billed Medicare ~$1.9 million using stolen patient and provider identifying information to fake legitimate orders; Shah shipped misbranded drugs and controlled substances (including Ozempic) into the U.S. using fake prescriptions and laundered proceeds through shell companies; Dobie used a stolen identity to obtain Maine Medicaid and SNAP benefits while also drawing SNAP in New York.
WaysToIdentify: Several mechanics here are pure enrolment/credentialing controls: nightly screening of every owner, officer, managing employee and W-2 clinician against the LEIE/SAM exclusion and state-exclusion lists would have surfaced Alonso, and beneficial-ownership verification against corporate filings, bank signatory records and IRS data would have exposed straw owners Anzivino and Ramirez-style figures. New DME NPIs that bill high volumes of braces to beneficiaries clustered far from the supplier's service area, with orders traceable to purchased leads and to prescriber NPIs whose other claims never touch orthotics, are detectable prepay; identity-theft-based ordering shows as prescriber NPIs whose ordering pattern breaks from their historic specialty mix, and cross-program benefit duplication (Maine Medicaid/SNAP plus New York SNAP) is found by interstate identity matching.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a continuous exclusion and ownership monitor that re-screens all disclosed and inferred owners/managers/clinicians against LEIE, state exclusion and death-master files daily and auto-suspends billing privileges plus prepay-holds all claims on a hit. Build a new-supplier surveillance score (months since enrolment, beneficiary geographic dispersion from supplier ZIP, share of claims from prescribers with no prior same-item ordering history, brace-per-beneficiary counts, denied-then-resubmitted claim ratio) that routes above-percentile suppliers to prepay review and requires signed order and delivery-proof documentation; separately run interstate beneficiary identity dedupe on SSN/DOB across state Medicaid and SNAP files.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina; U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Benson I. Ejindu (operator of durable medical equipment business)
SchemeSummary: Complaint alleges Ejindu, through a DME business operated under different names, billed North Carolina Medicaid for high-reimbursing specialized nutritional formula for rare inherited metabolic disorders while recipients actually received lower-reimbursing retail drinks such as Ensure, PediaSure, Boost and Glucerna.
WaysToIdentify: Compare billed medical-food HCPCS for inherited metabolic disorders against each recipient's diagnosis history: claims for metabolic formula on members with no PKU/organic-acidemia diagnosis, no metabolic geneticist or specialty-clinic claims, and no prior-authorization from a metabolic specialist are a prepay red flag. Supplier-level acquisition reconciliation also works: the DME's purchase invoices from the metabolic formula manufacturer will not support the billed units, and multiple NPIs/business names sharing one address, bank account or owner conceal volume.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a diagnosis-and-specialist concordance edit that denies specialized metabolic-formula codes unless the beneficiary has a qualifying metabolic diagnosis on a claim from a metabolic/genetics specialist within the lookback window and a valid prior authorization. Add a supplier-level units-versus-invoice reconciliation requiring manufacturer purchase documentation when billed metabolic-formula units per month exceed the calibrated peer percentile, and link NPIs sharing address/EIN/bank account so the aggregate is scored as one entity.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Aetna Inc. and affiliates (Medicare Advantage insurer); Elevance Health Inc., formerly Anthem (Medicare Advantage insurer); Humana Inc. (Medicare Advantage insurer); eHealth, Inc. and an affiliate (insurance broker); GoHealth, Inc. (insurance broker); SelectQuote Inc. (insurance broker)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: The United States, intervening in a qui tam suit, alleges that Aetna, Elevance/Anthem and Humana paid hundreds of millions of dollars in kickbacks to broker organizations eHealth, GoHealth and SelectQuote in exchange for steering Medicare beneficiaries into their Medicare Advantage plans regardless of suitability, and that Aetna and Humana threatened to withhold those payments to pressure brokers to enroll fewer disabled beneficiaries perceived as less profitable.
WaysToIdentify: This is a plan-and-broker marketing-compensation scheme rather than a claim-level fraud, so the detection surface is the MA plan's broker payment ledger, marketing agreements and enrolment outcomes, reviewable by CMS before capitation flows. Signals: broker-organization payments exceeding regulated commission caps or booked as 'co-op advertising'/'admin fees' with volume-based terms, and enrolment mix by broker showing a deficit of disabled/under-65 or high-risk enrollees versus the market, plus rapid disenrollment and low plan-suitability match.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a broker-compensation audit feed: per plan-broker-year, compute total compensation per enrolment across all payment categories and flag amounts above the regulatory cap or contracts with volume/quality-of-life-of-plan contingencies, triggering marketing-material and contract production. Build a broker-level enrolment-mix monitor comparing the share of disabled/ESRD/high-CMS-risk enrollees and 90-day disenrollment rates against the broker's local market baseline, with above-percentile deviation escalating to a compliance investigation and potential enrolment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: John Christopher Barrilleaux (social worker)
SchemeSummary: A Thibodaux social worker submitted false claims to private insurers for millions of dollars of counseling/healthcare services never provided, and created fake patient notes to support the bills; ordered to pay $4,592,650 restitution plus a $100 special assessment and sentenced to 30 months.
WaysToIdentify: Phantom counseling is visible prepay from time-and-capacity arithmetic: sum billed timed psychotherapy units per rendering clinician per day and flag days exceeding feasible working hours, plus weekend/holiday volumes and identical session lengths for every patient. Cross-check with member-side signals — no other claims contact, deceased or out-of-state members, and members who deny receiving services on verification letters — and request the notes, since fabricated notes are typically cloned with near-identical text.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a clinician-day capacity edit that converts each timed psychotherapy code to minutes, sums per NPI per date, and prepay-suspends claims on dates exceeding the calibrated maximum service hours or where the same member is billed concurrent sessions. Add a solo-provider anomaly score (billed minutes per week, share of patients with no corroborating claims from any other provider, note-text similarity across records obtained) that triggers a documentation request and beneficiary verification mailing before further payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: John Christopher Barrilleaux (social worker)
SchemeSummary: A Thibodaux social worker billed private insurers for millions of dollars of counseling/health care services that were never provided, and fabricated patient notes submitted to the insurers to substantiate the false claims; he was ordered to pay $4,592,650 in restitution and sentenced to 30 months.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: a single social worker's billed therapy minutes per day exceed any feasible schedule, and the members billed show no other clinical footprint, so the fraud is catchable at adjudication from timed-unit totals per NPI per date. Fabricated notes are exposed by a targeted prepay documentation request plus template/text-similarity comparison and beneficiary verification letters asking members to confirm the sessions.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a per-NPI per-date minute accumulator across all timed psychotherapy codes with a prepay suspension when totals exceed the calibrated clinician workday and when concurrent-session overlaps occur. Pair it with a solo-behavioral-health monitor scoring growth in billed minutes, patient-panel size versus peers, and share of members with no other provider claims; above-percentile providers move to 100% prepay review with records requested and note-similarity scoring.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Kevan Andre Hills; Devin Tyrone Stampley, Jr.; Asia Deshan Guess
State_County: Louisiana - East Baton Rouge Parish (Baton Rouge)
PayerName: Medicaid; Paycheck Protection Program; Economic Injury Disaster Loan Program; CARES Act unemployment (Louisiana Workforce Commission; Maine Department of Labor)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Three defendants submitted fraudulent prescriptions for controlled substances (Promethazine with Codeine, Hydrocodone) to pharmacies using the stolen DEA registration numbers and identifying information of licensed physicians, causing Medicaid to be billed for filling them, with the drugs resold; Stampley also burglarized a Louisiana pharmacy. The same defendants separately sought at least $293,498 in PPP/EIDL/CARES unemployment funds using falsified bank statements and tax forms (receiving at least $87,663), while Guess sought $125,978 in PUA benefits from Louisiana and Maine workforce agencies using falsified employment and residency details (receiving at least $15,859). Amounts span multiple defendants.
WaysToIdentify: Forged controlled-substance prescriptions on stolen DEA numbers are detectable at pharmacy claim adjudication: the prescriber NPI/DEA is out of state or far from the pharmacy and member, has no prior treating relationship with the member, and suddenly appears as prescriber of Promethazine-Codeine/hydrocodone at a rate inconsistent with that prescriber's specialty and history. Cross-referencing DEA registration status, licence specialty, PDMP dispensing records and member-prescriber-pharmacy distance triangles catches it before payment; the PPP/EIDL/PUA loan and unemployment fraud is not a payer claims matter and is only addressable by the lending/labor agencies' own identity and payroll verification.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-integrity edit on controlled-substance pharmacy claims that validates DEA registration, state licence, and prescribing-authority scope, and fires when a prescriber's cough-syrup/opioid claim volume or geographic dispersion breaks from that prescriber's own 12-month baseline — action is prepay reject plus an alert to the listed prescriber to confirm authorship. Add a member-level triangulation rule (distinct prescribers, distinct pharmacies, prescriber-member and pharmacy-member distance, early refills) that locks further controlled-substance fills pending review; no payer control applies to the PPP/PUA counts.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Louisiana

State_County: Louisiana - East Baton Rouge Parish (Baton Rouge)
PayerName: Medicaid; Paycheck Protection Program (PPP); Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) Program; CARES Act unemployment benefits (Louisiana Workforce Commission; Maine Department of Labor)

SchemeSummary: The three defendants submitted fraudulent prescriptions for controlled substances (Promethazine with Codeine, Hydrocodone) to pharmacies using the stolen DEA registration numbers and identifying information of licensed physicians and other providers, causing Medicaid to be billed for filling them, and Stampley also burglarized a Louisiana pharmacy to obtain drugs for resale. Hills and Stampley separately sought at least $293,498 in PPP/EIDL and CARES Act unemployment funds using falsified bank statements and tax forms while posing as fake small business owners (obtaining at least $87,663), and Guess sought at least $125,978 in pandemic unemployment benefits from Louisiana and Maine agencies with falsified employment and residency details (obtaining at least $15,859); sentences were 104, 96 and 24 months.
WaysToIdentify: At the pharmacy claim level the payer can validate the prescriber's DEA/NPI status and treating relationship: forged scripts show as prescribers with no prior claims for the member, out-of-area prescriber-pharmacy-member geography, and a spike of Promethazine-Codeine/hydrocodone attributed to a prescriber whose specialty and history never included them. PDMP linkage and prescriber-confirmation callbacks resolve it prepay; the PPP/EIDL and multistate PUA components have no payer-side claims control and belong to lender and workforce-agency identity/payroll verification.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a controlled-substance prescriber-authentication edit (live DEA registration/schedule authority check, licence-specialty plausibility, no-prior-relationship flag) that rejects prepay and notifies the prescriber of record for attestation. Add a pharmacy-level monitor of the share of controlled-substance fills written by prescribers outside the pharmacy's normal referral network and by prescribers with sudden volume breaks, escalating above-percentile pharmacies to prepay review and on-site audit; state the loan/UI counts are out of payer scope.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Dr. José Alzadon (medical director, Kentucky Addiction Centers); Michael Bregenzer (CEO); Barbie Vanhoose (billing manager); Kentucky Addiction Centers (KAC)
State_County: Kentucky - Winchester (Clark County); Paducah (McCracken County); Paintsville (Johnson County); London (Laurel County)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Upcoding; IdentityFraud; Drug_Prescriptions; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Operators of Kentucky Addiction Centers opioid treatment clinics billed Medicare and Kentucky Medicaid over $8 million for services never performed or billed at higher complexity than delivered, and billed services and Suboxone prescriptions under the identity and DEA registration of Alzadon's elderly father to bypass Alzadon's credentialing problems, even though the father never saw the patients. All three defendants were convicted at trial.
WaysToIdentify: Billing under a proxy prescriber is visible prepay: the elderly father's NPI/DEA suddenly appears as rendering provider on thousands of OTP/Suboxone claims at a clinic where his co-located, credentialing-barred relative works, with implausible daily service volumes and no travel/presence evidence, and the barred individual appears in ownership or payroll disclosures. Upcoding is detectable from the clinic's code-level distribution — near-universal high-complexity E/M and counseling codes versus same-specialty peers — and from time-unit totals per NPI-day exceeding a feasible schedule.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider plausibility check per NPI-day: total timed/E-M minutes, patient counts, and age/licence status of the NPI, plus a shared-address/shared-owner link to any excluded or credential-denied individual; a hit triggers prepay suspension and an in-person attestation/site visit. Add an OTP code-distribution outlier model (share of high-complexity codes, counseling units per patient-month, buprenorphine prescriptions per prescriber-day) that pushes above-percentile clinics to prepay documentation review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Rita Shaba; Samer Kammo; Christina Anasi
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Three defendants submitted fraudulent Paycheck Protection Program loan applications for several business entities, misrepresenting payroll data, falsely certifying permissible use of funds, and supporting the applications with fictitious payroll, health insurance, bank and tax records; they obtained over $3 million, of which over $2.1 million has been seized/recovered.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim in this case — it is pure PPP loan fraud, so no payer adjudication control would have caught it; detection sits with the lender/SBA, via matching the applicant's claimed payroll to IRS Form 941/W-2 filings and to state wage records, and validating submitted bank statements directly with the depository. Multiple entities sharing owners, addresses or bank accounts each claiming separate payroll is the strongest pre-disbursement signal.
FeaturesToCreate: The nearest applicable control is an enrolment/payment-integrity identity module: before disbursing any program funds, cross-verify applicant-reported payroll against authoritative tax and state wage data and cluster applications by owner SSN/EIN, address, phone and bank account, holding funds where a cluster claims duplicative payroll. For payer systems, apply the same clustering to provider enrolment applications so related shell entities are scored as one; otherwise no payer-side claims control applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Amy Winslow (former CEO, Magellan Diagnostics, Inc.); Hossein Maleknia (former COO); Reba Daoust (former Director of Quality Assurance and Regulatory Affairs); Magellan Diagnostics, Inc. (medical device company)
FraudTypeAll: Other - FDA Submission Fraud; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Three Magellan Diagnostics executives concealed and misled customers and the FDA about a malfunction in the company's LeadCare II and LeadCare Ultra blood lead testing devices that produced inaccurately low results for venous blood samples, keeping the misbranded devices in interstate commerce to protect sales; thousands of children and other patients received inaccurate lead test results before the FDA forced a recall. All three pleaded guilty (two to introducing misbranded devices, one to false statements); sentencing was pending.
WaysToIdentify: This is device-manufacturer/FDA misbranding, not claims fraud, so a payer would not catch it at adjudication; the detectable payer-side signal is post-payment analytic — an implausible shift in result distributions from labs using LeadCare devices, i.e. venous lead results clustering below the reference threshold versus capillary results and versus labs on other platforms. Complaint/recall feeds (FDA MedWatch, MAUDE, Class I recalls) and the manufacturer's own customer-complaint volume are the earliest external signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a device/assay-level result-distribution monitor where lab results are reported (state lead registries, HEDIS/lab-result feeds): per test platform and specimen type, compute mean and percent-elevated rates and alert when a platform diverges from all others, triggering payer notification and re-test coverage. Add an automated FDA recall/MAUDE ingestion that flags claims for tests or devices under active recall and suspends payment for the affected device/specimen-type combinations.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Amy Winslow (former CEO, Magellan Diagnostics, Inc.); Hossein Maleknia (former COO); Reba Daoust (former Director of Quality Assurance and Regulatory Affairs)
FraudTypeAll: Other - FDA Submission Fraud; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Three former Magellan Diagnostics executives concealed and misled customers and the FDA about a malfunction in the company's LeadCare II and LeadCare Ultra blood lead testing devices when used with venous samples, hiding when the defect was discovered and its nature, extent and risks, causing thousands of children and other patients to receive falsely low lead results; the devices were ultimately recalled for venous use. Winslow and Maleknia pleaded guilty to introducing misbranded medical devices into interstate commerce and Daoust to false statements; sentences were home detention/probation plus fines totaling $30,600 across the three defendants.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion case: concealment from FDA and customers about a venous-sample defect is outside claim adjudication, so a payer could only detect it post-payment by comparing lead-result distributions across testing platforms and specimen types, where the defective analyzer produces anomalously low venous results. Recall and adverse-event feeds plus state childhood-lead registry data provide the external trigger.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a platform-stratified result-distribution surveillance job over reported lead results (percent elevated by device model and specimen type, by lab, over time) that alerts on a single platform diverging from peers and triggers member re-test outreach and recovery from the manufacturer. Ingest FDA recall/MAUDE feeds nightly and auto-flag claim lines for recalled device/test combinations for payment hold and coverage-policy update.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
FraudEntity: Ciera Washington; Raven White; Bryan Otero
State_County: New York - Northern District of New York (including Albany); New York - Bronx County; New Jersey - Wood-Ridge (Bergen County)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges White and Otero supplied Washington with stolen names, dates of birth and Medicaid ID numbers, which Washington used to submit fraudulent prescriptions to pharmacies across the Northeast; rideshare drivers were dispatched to collect the Medicaid-funded medications, which were then delivered to Otero and other buyers who paid Washington. HHS-OIG states false claims were submitted for both transportation and medications.
WaysToIdentify: The prescriptions are forged against real member IDs, so adjudication-time signals are strong: fills for members with no prior relationship to the prescriber, fills at pharmacies far outside the member's home region and scattered across multiple states, high-value drug fills clustered on the same prescriber or same courier pickup, and pickups not by the member. Non-emergency transport claims billed for the same dates and members with no accompanying medical visit at the destination is a second, independent prepay flag.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a member-level geographic-plausibility edit for pharmacy claims: compute distance from member address to dispensing pharmacy and to prescriber, count distinct states of fill in a rolling window, and prepay-reject or hold fills exceeding the calibrated dispersion with a member-contact verification requirement. Build a transport-to-service linkage edit that denies NEMT/rideshare claims lacking a matching same-day covered service claim at the destination provider, and cluster pharmacy fills by pickup-agent/delivery pattern for investigation referral.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Drew Pierce (former CEO of Primary Health Network); Jack Laeng (former CEO of Primary Health Network); Mark Marriott (former facilities manager); TopCoat (company owned by the defendants)
State_County: Pennsylvania - Mercer County (Sharon); Pennsylvania - Mercer County (West Middlesex); Pennsylvania - Mercer County (Sharpsville)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Two former CEOs and a facilities manager of Primary Health Network, a non-profit community medical provider in Sharon, PA, inserted their own company TopCoat between PHN and its vendors, paying the vendor and billing PHN a marked-up amount (on one 2017 deal, over $200,000 more than the true vendor cost), and issued invoices for work TopCoat never performed, splitting the spread via checks from TopCoat's account. In a separate scheme, Pierce, Laeng and a co-conspirator caused PHN to contract with a third party that kicked back 50% of its fees—more than $1.7 million between 2013 and 2020—to an entity they controlled. Amounts and pleas span three defendants; sentencings are set for March 2026.
WaysToIdentify: This is vendor-procurement self-dealing and kickbacks inside a grantee organization, not claim submission, so payer claim edits would not see it; detection sits with grant/cost-report oversight and vendor-payment auditing — comparing the intermediary's invoices to underlying vendor invoices for markup, and matching officer/manager names and home addresses against vendor corporate filings and bank signatories. Payments to a vendor with no employees, no other customers, and an owner who is also an executive of the payer organization are the auditable signal, plus a contract returning 50% of fees to an executive-controlled entity.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a related-party procurement check for organizations submitting cost reports or receiving grant/FQHC funds: match vendor EINs, registered agents, officers and addresses against employee/officer rosters and disclosed ownership, and flag any vendor payment stream to a matched entity for mandatory conflict-of-interest documentation before cost reimbursement. Add an invoice-markup test comparing intermediary invoices to third-party vendor invoices for the same work and a no-substance vendor test (no payroll filings, single customer), each triggering payment hold and audit referral.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: 1st Adult N Pediatric Healthcare Service (Medicaid-enrolled home health agency); Carolyn Bryant-Taylor (owner/operator); Kafomdi "Josephine" Okocha (owner/operator); Samuel Okocha (owner/operator); Shekita Gore, a.k.a. Shekita Steele (director of nursing); Eno Utuk (personal care/nursing employee); Elizabeth Ilome (personal care/nursing employee)
State_County: Virginia - Lynchburg (Western District of Virginia); statewide Commonwealth of Virginia
SchemeSummary: Owners and staff of a Medicaid-enrolled home health agency billed Virginia Medicaid for private duty nursing, personal care and respite services that were never provided or were billed in excess of what was provided; parents/guardians of patients were paid cash for pre-signed blank nursing notes that employees (including the director of nursing) filled out to document the fictitious visits. Seven individuals/entities are named; six co-defendants have pled guilty (two to conspiracy on this date, one to misprision, three in prior weeks).
WaysToIdentify: Phantom private-duty nursing and personal care hours are catchable prepay through EVV: claims with no matching electronic visit verification record, visits with identical start/stop times, hours exceeding the authorized plan of care, and caregiver-day totals exceeding feasible working hours across overlapping members. Pre-signed blank notes surface when requested documentation shows identical handwriting/signature blocks, notes completed by staff who have no EVV check-in, and guardians receiving cash — the latter only via post-payment interview, but the hour arithmetic is prepay.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an EVV-to-claim reconciliation edit that denies or holds any PDN/personal-care/respite line without a matching verified visit at the member's address, and a caregiver-day aggregator that flags overlapping or over-24-hour totals per employee across members. Add an authorization-versus-billed-hours edit per member-month and a documentation request/prepay review for agencies whose share of unverified or authorization-exceeding units is above the calibrated peer percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jeremie Vargas Ramirez (de facto owner of NOVA DME); Jordana Lee Arpa (nominal President and CEO); Dennis William Karnes (health care consultant/lead broker); Kynetic Medical Group d/b/a NOVA DME (DME supplier)
State_County: Virginia - Fairfax County (Vienna); California - Riverside County (Lake Elsinore)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Ramirez secretly owned DME supplier NOVA DME while Arpa was falsely named President/CEO and made false statements to obtain Medicare enrollment; Karnes supplied unvetted 'leads' from Mexican- and Russian-based coconspirators, and NOVA DME billed Medicare approximately $13.5 million (paid $7.6 million) for unnecessary and unwanted DME shipped to beneficiaries who did not request it, with Karnes altering and resubmitting denied claims and laundering at least $4.06 million to a Russian-based owner through shell company Sharp Ventures, LLC. All three were sentenced (24 months for Ramirez and Karnes, 6 months for Arpa) and each ordered to pay $2,256,787 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Enrolment screening should have caught the straw officer: verify the disclosed President/CEO against tax filings, bank signatories, lease and corporate records, and interview/site-visit new high-risk DME suppliers, while linking the hidden true owner through shared addresses, phone numbers and payment flows. At adjudication the scheme shows as a new supplier billing braces/DME nationwide to beneficiaries with no prior treating relationship to the ordering prescriber, high denial-then-resubmission rates on the same claims, and money movement to an unrelated shell (Sharp Ventures) visible in payment-address changes.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment verification module that cross-matches disclosed owners/officers to IRS, banking and corporate-filing data and requires in-person verification for new DME suppliers, auto-holding billing privileges on mismatch. Build a claim-behavior monitor per supplier: beneficiary geographic dispersion, share of orders from prescribers with no prior same-item history or no prior member encounter, and resubmission-after-denial ratio; above-percentile suppliers go to 100% prepay review requiring signed physician orders, proof of delivery and beneficiary confirmation, and any payment-address/EFT change triggers re-verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Kossie Lamon Simmons (beneficial owner); Katina Marzie Simmons (listed 70% owner and manager); Tritia Margalizita Townsend (pharmacist in charge); SarJo Pharmacy, Inc.
SchemeSummary: SarJo Pharmacy billed the Federal Employees' Compensation Fund approximately $28.7 million (paid ~$16.3 million) for prescription medications supposedly dispensed to injured U.S. Postal Service claimants, when the drugs were not based on valid prescriptions, were not stocked by the pharmacy, and were never dispensed. Three defendants - the beneficial owner, the 70% owner/manager, and the pharmacist in charge - were charged by indictment.
WaysToIdentify: Billing for drugs never stocked is provable prepay by reconciling billed NDC units against the pharmacy's wholesaler purchase data — a pharmacy cannot dispense what it never bought. Additional adjudication signals: nearly all claims tied to one claimant population (FECA/USPS injured workers) via a small set of prescribers, high-cost compounds and topicals per claimant, and no valid prescription on file when records are requested.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an NDC-level purchase-to-dispense reconciliation per pharmacy per month using wholesaler/ARCOS or 340B purchase feeds; when billed units exceed purchases beyond a calibrated tolerance, suspend payment for those NDCs and require invoices. Add a concentration edit (share of revenue from a single payer/claimant cohort and single prescriber, average cost per claimant versus peer pharmacies) that routes outlier pharmacies to prepay review with mandatory prescription-image submission.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: William Stephan (medical doctor, family practice); Erik Berg; Scott Trapp; Michael Luehrsen
PayerName: Express Scripts, Inc.; unspecified health care benefit programs
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: A family practice doctor signed pre-filled compounded medication prescriptions presented to him by Erik Berg for 19 patients who were not his own, without a doctor-patient relationship or review of authorized refills; the prescriptions, averaging over $16,000 each and refilled more than 500 times, generated $8,750,315 in reimbursements from health care benefit programs, and Stephan later falsely told an Express Scripts audit that he had written the prescriptions himself. Stephan received one year probation and 100 hours community service; co-defendants Berg, Luehrsen and Trapp were separately convicted.
WaysToIdentify: The prescriber-patient relationship gap is visible at adjudication: high-cost compounded prescriptions written by a family-practice physician for members who have no prior or subsequent office-visit claims with him, all originating from one marketer, with per-prescription cost and refill counts far above peer norms. Concentration of one prescriber's compound scripts at a single compounding pharmacy, plus long automatic refill chains without any interval visit, are prepay flags; the physician's false audit attestation is caught by comparing his claim history to the scripts and by requesting chart notes.
