FeaturesToCreate: Build a compounded-drug prior-authorization edit requiring an office-visit claim between the prescriber and member within the lookback period and denying refills beyond the calibrated count without a documented re-evaluation. Add a prescriber-pharmacy concentration model (share of a prescriber's high-cost compound scripts flowing to one pharmacy, average allowed per script versus specialty peers, share of members outside the prescriber's normal panel) that triggers prepay hold, chart-note requests and direct prescriber attestation rather than a pharmacy-mediated audit response.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Health First Urgent Care (urgent care clinic, Richland and Pasco, Washington)
State_County: Washington - Benton County (Richland); Washington - Franklin County (Pasco)
SchemeSummary: Health First Urgent Care billed Medicare and Washington Medicaid for PCR respiratory and urinary tract infection panel tests by 'unbundling' the predetermined panel and billing each individual component test separately, collecting more than the bundled panel rate; Washington also alleged the clinic billed for more expensive panel tests that were not medically necessary, such as for patients presenting with Covid-19 symptoms.
WaysToIdentify: Unbundling is a pure adjudication-time catch: the component CPT codes of a defined respiratory or UTI PCR panel billed on the same date for the same member should be recoded to the panel code, and providers whose component-to-panel billing ratio diverges from same-specialty peers are identifiable in claim history. Medical necessity is testable prepay from diagnosis linkage — large multiplex panels ordered on members whose only documented presentation is COVID-19 symptoms, or reflex panels ordered on nearly every urgent-care visit.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a panel-rebundling edit that groups component molecular CPT codes by member-date-provider and, when the count of components meets the panel definition, reprices to the single panel code and denies the excess lines. Add a utilization/necessity edit limiting large multiplex respiratory or UTI panels to claims with qualifying diagnoses and no prior same-panel test within the calibrated interval, plus a provider-level monitor of panel-per-visit rate versus urgent-care peers that triggers prepay documentation review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Health First Urgent Care (urgent care clinic, Richland and Pasco, Washington)
State_County: Washington - Richland (Benton County); Washington - Pasco (Franklin County)
SchemeSummary: The urgent care clinic billed Medicare and Washington Medicaid for each individual component test of PCR respiratory and urinary tract infection panels rather than billing the single bundled panel code, inflating reimbursement; Washington also alleged the clinic billed for more expensive panel tests that were not medically necessary, such as for patients presenting with Covid-19 symptoms. Resolved by a $2,807,729 False Claims Act settlement.
WaysToIdentify: Panel unbundling is visible at adjudication: the same claim or same-day claims for one patient carry the individual PCR component CPT codes whose combination equals a defined respiratory or UTI panel code, and the aggregate allowed amount exceeds the panel rate. Reimbursement-per-encounter for respiratory/UTI testing at this urgent care would sit far above same-specialty peers, and diagnosis linkage (COVID-19 symptoms only) fails to support a multi-pathogen or comprehensive UTI panel.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a claim-family rebundling edit: group all molecular pathogen component codes for the same beneficiary, DOS and TIN, and if the count of components meets the panel-definition threshold, deny/reprice the components to the single panel code prepay. Add a medical-necessity edit that flags panel-tier codes where the only supporting diagnosis is a single-pathogen or generic symptom code, and a provider-level outlier report on components-per-specimen versus urgent care peers triggering documentation request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Troy Health, Inc. (Medicare Advantage, Part D, and Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan provider)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Troy admitted that its territory managers used proprietary software to unlawfully access pharmacy records and customer lists containing beneficiaries' names, dates of birth, Medicare ID numbers and insurance information, then used that stolen data to make deceptive sales calls and to enroll beneficiaries into Troy's Medicare Advantage plans without consent, including batch/automatic enrollments (over 300 in one day, over 2,700 during the Jan-Mar 2022 open enrollment) and manual fraudulent entries on the CMS website; Troy also paid kickbacks to pharmacies for enrollment referrals submitted through its Troy.ai platform. Resolved via non-prosecution agreement with a $1,430,008 criminal penalty adjusted for ability to pay.
WaysToIdentify: This is a Medicare Advantage enrolment-integrity and data-misuse scheme, detectable in CMS enrolment transaction data rather than claims: bursts of enrolment submissions from one plan/agent ID in a single day, enrolments with no recorded scope-of-appointment or call recording, and beneficiaries whose applications originate from pharmacy-sourced data rather than beneficiary contact. Rapid disenrolment/complaint (CTM) rates and enrolments clustered by the same pharmacy referral source are the strongest pre-payment signals; kickbacks per referral show as per-enrolment payments in the plan's vendor ledgers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment-velocity monitor at agent/plan/upstream-referral-source level: count applications per submitting user per day and per pharmacy referral code, and suspend batch submissions above the calibrated percentile pending beneficiary verification callbacks. Add an audit control matching every enrolment to an authenticated beneficiary consent artifact and flag enrolments whose beneficiary demographic data trace to pharmacy dispensing records; screen plan marketing vendor contracts for per-enrolment compensation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Alice F. Martin (owner/operator of Martin Logistics, TSA Transportation, A.F. Martin, Martin Global)
SchemeSummary: Trucking company owner phased out a tax-indebted company (Martin Logistics) while continuing operations through new entities, directing roughly $18 million in gross receipts from TSA Transportation into the bank account of another company she controlled (A.F. Martin) and moving trucks and trailers into Martin Global, thereby failing to report $3.6 million in taxable income and evading approximately $1.2 million in federal taxes.
WaysToIdentify: No payer-side claims component: this is corporate income tax evasion via successor entities and diverted gross receipts, detected through IRS collection and bank-records analysis, not claim adjudication. The transferable signal is a tax-delinquent entity ceasing operations while new entities with common ownership, addresses, and assets continue the same business.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control is enrolment/vendor screening: link entities by owner SSN/EIN, officers, address, phone and bank account, and flag new applicants that are successors to an entity with outstanding federal debt or revoked billing privileges, holding the application for verification. Otherwise no payer-side claims control applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Ladd Clayton Atkins (Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine)
SchemeSummary: Atkins, an osteopathic physician in Tulsa, was charged by information with conspiring with others to unlawfully prescribe Adderall, a Schedule II controlled substance, and with conspiracy to commit health care fraud, defrauding Medicare and Medicaid; the charge was announced as part of DOJ's 2025 National Health Care Fraud Takedown.
WaysToIdentify: Stimulant pill-mill prescribing is visible in Part D/Medicaid pharmacy data before payment: one prescriber's share of Schedule II amphetamine claims, patients per day, adult new-start ADHD volume, and average daily MME-equivalent dosing all far above same-specialty peers. Corroborating signals are patients traveling long distances, cash-pay office visits with no supporting E/M claim, and clustering of the prescriber's patients at a few pharmacies.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-level controlled-substance profile computing Schedule II stimulant claim counts, distinct beneficiaries, beneficiary travel distance and share of patients with no corresponding evaluation claim; fire when multiple metrics exceed the calibrated peer percentile. Action: prepay prior authorization on that prescriber's stimulant claims plus a records request, and pharmacy-side edit denying stimulant fills with no billed office encounter in the lookback window.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Jacqueline Espino (Arizona Department of Economic Security claims adjudicator); Brandilyn Lorenzen (Arizona Department of Economic Security claims adjudicator)
PayerName: Arizona Department of Economic Security (unemployment insurance and Pandemic Unemployment Assistance programs)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
SchemeSummary: Two Arizona DES adjudicators accepted bribes to approve unemployment insurance and Pandemic Unemployment Assistance claims for individuals who were not eligible (Espino: 9 claims causing $140,298 in payments; Lorenzen: 24 claims causing $532,964), and each also embezzled DES funds for themselves and others (Espino $600,672; Lorenzen $2,461,520). Lorenzen was sentenced to 30 months and ordered to pay $2,994,484 restitution; Espino pleaded guilty and awaits sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: This is unemployment-benefit adjudicator corruption and embezzlement, not medical claims, but it is a classic insider-override pattern detectable in the benefit system's audit logs before disbursement: a small set of adjudicator IDs approving claims that failed wage-verification or identity checks, approvals concentrated in a few claimant clusters, and payments routed to repeated bank accounts or addresses. Embezzlement shows as payments the adjudicator created and approved without a claimant of record.
FeaturesToCreate: Build adjudicator-level override analytics: for each examiner compute approval rate on claims lacking employer wage records, count of approvals sharing a bank account/address/IP, and self-created-plus-self-approved payment counts; fire above the calibrated percentile and suspend disbursement pending supervisory review. Enforce maker-checker separation so no single user can both create and approve a payment, and match every payment bank account against employee banking data.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Avanish Kumar Jha; Rajnish Kumar Jha; Dhrishti Pharma International (company)
SchemeSummary: The Jha brothers, through their company Dhrishti Pharma International, advertised prescription drugs online and shipped counterfeit and adulterated medications from India to U.S. buyers, including fake 'Keytruda' containing none of the active cancer-fighting ingredient; payment was taken by wire transfer, direct money exchange, and cash picked up by U.S. intermediaries, with packaging designed to evade customs detection.
WaysToIdentify: Direct-to-consumer sale of counterfeit imported drugs is largely outside the claims stream, so payer detection is indirect: no NDC-level dispensing claims exist for these units, and the tell is patients with high-cost oncology drug claim histories showing therapy gaps while clinically progressing, plus specialty-drug claims for product acquired outside the legitimate supply chain. Post-payment routes are FDA/CBP import interdiction, pedigree/DSCSA verification and manufacturer serial-number checks.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a supply-chain provenance edit for high-cost specialty and biologic products: require the dispensing NDC plus serialized lot/pedigree data from an authorized distributor on the claim, and deny or pend claims where the product cannot be matched to an authorized trading-partner transaction record. Add member-level alerting where an oncology or specialty drug is administered with no corresponding paid dispensing claim, prompting product-source investigation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Zachary J. Lipman MD (physician); Michael Woo-Ming MD (physician, co-owner of Revive Medical of San Diego and Medical Wellness Group); Kevin Brown (Riverside County chiropractor, scheme orchestrator)
State_County: California - Butte County (Chico); California - Riverside County (Murrieta); California - San Diego County (San Diego)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Upcoding; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Chiropractor Kevin Brown used companies he owned to bill Medicare for surgically implanted neurostimulators when in fact staff merely taped disposable 'Stivax' electroacupuncture devices to patients' ears, a non-reimbursable item; Dr. Lipman received kickbacks from Brown for referring patients for Stivax devices ($290,000 settlement) and Dr. Woo-Ming's companies submitted the false neurostimulator implant claims ($85,000 settlement), for a combined $375,000 across the two defendants announced here.
WaysToIdentify: The core signal is a coding impossibility: surgically implanted neurostimulator codes billed by chiropractor-owned entities and physician offices with no operating-room facility claim, no anesthesia, no surgical implant supply, and no NPI with surgical privileges. Auricular electroacupuncture devices are non-covered, so the volume of implant claims per patient and repeat 'implants' at short intervals for the same beneficiary are further prepay flags.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a site-of-service and specialty edit that denies implantable neurostimulator procedure/device codes when the billing/rendering provider taxonomy is not surgical, place of service is office, and no facility or anesthesia claim exists for the same beneficiary and date. Add a per-beneficiary lifetime frequency edit on implant codes and a referral-concentration report flagging physicians whose Stivax/neurostimulator referrals concentrate in one supplier, triggering documentation request and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; USAO - Central District of California
FraudEntity: Karpis Srapyan; Susanna Harutyunyan; Petros Fichidzhyan; Juan Carlos Esparza (sham hospice owner); Mihran Panosyan
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Winnetka, greater Los Angeles area)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Defendants used four sham hospice companies - one owned by a co-defendant and three nominally owned by foreign nationals but controlled by the defendants - to bill Medicare nearly $16 million for hospice services that were never provided and not medically necessary, using foreign nationals' identities to open bank accounts, enroll with Medicare and sign leases, and misappropriating the identities of doctors (two deceased) to submit claims. Proceeds of roughly $3.2 million were laundered through accounts in the sham companies' and foreign nationals' names and spent on personal expenses including a BMW; figures span multiple co-defendants, with Fichidzhyan already sentenced to 12 years.
WaysToIdentify: Enrolment screening would have caught it: newly enrolled hospices with nominee foreign-national owners, shared addresses/leases, sequential bank accounts, and attending/certifying physician NPIs belonging to deceased or non-consenting doctors. At adjudication, hospice election periods with no visit records, certifying physician NPIs flagged deceased in the death master file, and beneficiaries simultaneously receiving full curative Part A/B services are all pre-payment signals.
FeaturesToCreate: Build enrolment-time controls: validate owner identity documents, cross-link new hospice applicants by address, phone, bank account and IP to other enrollees, and place newly enrolled hospices under prepay review with a 100% claim hold for an initial period. Add adjudication edits rejecting any claim whose certifying/attending NPI is deceased, inactive, or has never billed for that beneficiary, and flag hospice election overlapping curative treatment claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Syed Murtuza Kablazada (owner/operator of purported medical laboratories); Syed Mehdi Hussain (owner/operator of purported medical laboratories)
State_County: Illinois - Cook County (Arlington Heights); Illinois - DuPage County (Carol Stream)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Defendants operated purported medical laboratories that billed Medicare approximately $227 million (about $136 million paid) for over-the-counter COVID-19 test kits that were rarely provided, submitting claims for beneficiaries who never requested kits, including deceased individuals, using beneficiary names purchased from a marketing company. They installed foreign nationals as nominee/straw owners of the labs who were expected to flee the U.S. once investigations began.
WaysToIdentify: OTC COVID test-kit claims were mass-submitted for beneficiaries with no relationship to the lab, so prepay signals are stark: claim volume per lab spiking from zero to national scale within weeks, beneficiaries spread across all states with no local ordering provider, duplicate kit claims exceeding the per-beneficiary monthly benefit cap, and claims for beneficiaries with dates of death before service. Nominee foreign-national owners and shared addresses/bank accounts across labs are visible at enrolment.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a hard prepay edit rejecting OTC test-kit claims that exceed the per-beneficiary period quantity cap, that post-date the beneficiary's date of death, or that duplicate another supplier's kit claim for the same period. Add new-supplier ramp-rate monitoring (billed dollars per week versus enrolment age and peer labs) with automatic payment suspension above the calibrated percentile, plus enrolment link analysis on owners, addresses, bank accounts and IPs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Ramon Apellaniz (a/k/a "Kristopher Rockefeller," de facto operator, unlicensed); Suhail Aponte (manager and registered agent of Minds Cornerstone LLC, unlicensed); Minds Cornerstone LLC dba Minds Cornerstone Behavior Therapy Services
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Apellaniz, an unlicensed provider previously convicted in state court for Medicaid fraud through The Gemini Project, allegedly ran Minds Cornerstone LLC under a pseudonym (including while incarcerated) with nominal manager Aponte, and the two billed Connecticut Medicaid over $1.8 million for applied behavior analysis services to autistic children that were never rendered - including services on dates payroll showed no employee was paid, BCBA supervision billed without any corresponding behavioral technician service, and services for patients who were actually hospitalized inpatient. Some of the proceeds were allegedly used to pay restitution Apellaniz owed from his earlier state Medicaid fraud conviction.
WaysToIdentify: Multiple prepay-checkable contradictions exist: the beneficial owner was an excluded/previously convicted individual operating under a pseudonym, so OIG/state exclusion and criminal-history screening against owners and managers at enrolment should have blocked participation. In claims, BCBA supervision codes billed with no same-day technician direct-service line, ABA services billed on dates the member has an inpatient hospital claim, and service hours exceeding paid staff hours in payroll are all detectable at adjudication or via targeted audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment control that screens all owners, officers and managers against exclusion lists, state fraud convictions and alias/SSN matching, and denies or revokes on match. Add prepay edits: deny supervision/direction codes lacking a paired technician service line for the same member and date; deny outpatient ABA on dates overlapping an inpatient stay; and run a rendering-staff capacity check comparing billed service hours per NPI/technician per day against a feasible maximum, pending claims above it for documentation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Christopher Kyle Johnston (general counsel, Central Rexall Drugs); Trent Brockmeier (chief operating officer, Central Rexall Drugs); Central Rexall Drugs (compounding pharmacy)
PayerName: TRICARE; New Jersey State Health Benefits Program (state and local government and education employee health plans)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Two executives took over a Louisiana compounding pharmacy and designed pain, scar, antifungal and vitamin compound formulas based solely on which ingredient combinations yielded the highest insurance reimbursement, testing formulas by submitting false claims using identifying and insurance information taken without consent from pre-existing pharmacy prescriptions. An outside sales force obtained prescriptions signed without patient visits or knowledge and paid patients and doctors, generating roughly $100 million in medically unnecessary claims to TRICARE and New Jersey public employee health plans; Johnston received about $34 million and Brockmeier about $5 million in profits, and 50 people have been convicted in the overarching conspiracy.
WaysToIdentify: Reimbursement-driven compounding leaves a distinctive fingerprint at adjudication: a single pharmacy's compound claims cluster on a handful of high-cost ingredient NDCs, average paid per claim far above peers, refills auto-generated without patient contact, and prescriber NPIs writing high volumes with no corresponding office-visit claims and no geographic proximity to the patients. Test claims submitted under patients' data with no prescription of record, and TRICARE/plan member complaints about unrequested creams, are further prepay flags.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a compound-claim edit set: flag claims whose ingredient mix matches high-margin formulas, require prior authorization for compounded topical/vitamin claims above the calibrated cost percentile, and deny where no evaluation encounter by the prescriber exists in the lookback or where prescriber-patient distance exceeds a calibrated bound. Add pharmacy-level monitoring of average paid per claim and refill-without-contact rate with payment suspension, plus beneficiary verification calls before paying first fills.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Kenneth Charles Kessler III (owner/operator of DME supply companies); Michael Andrew Gomez (owner/operator of DME supply companies)
State_County: Florida - Miami-Dade County; Florida - Broward County
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Two men who owned seven Florida DME supply companies allegedly paid kickbacks to marketing companies that used deceptive telemarketing to obtain Medicare beneficiaries' personal information, then had purported telemedicine companies generate doctors' orders for medically unnecessary orthotic braces and continuous glucose monitors, which the defendants used to bill Medicare approximately $34.8 million.
WaysToIdentify: Telemarketing-plus-telehealth DME schemes are visible prepay: a small set of telehealth NPIs ordering braces and CGMs for thousands of beneficiaries nationwide, no prior treating relationship or associated E/M claim, orders for multiple braces per beneficiary across body regions in a short window, and CGM claims without diabetes diagnosis or insulin history. Common ownership across seven supplier NPIs sharing address, bank account and marketing vendor is detectable at enrolment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-provider concentration edit: for each ordering NPI compute distinct DME beneficiaries, states, and share of orders with no prior encounter with that provider; when above calibrated peer percentiles, pend all downstream supplier claims for documentation. Add beneficiary-level edits denying multiple-brace combinations within a short window and CGM claims lacking diabetes diagnosis/insulin evidence, and link suppliers by owner/address/bank for coordinated suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Stephen Kash (laboratory sales executive, True Health Diagnostics); Courtney Love (laboratory sales executive, True Health Diagnostics); Christopher Grottenthaler; Blake Whitaker; Chrissy Alfaro; Charles Dickens; Marty Flores; Frederick Brown; Little River Healthcare (rural hospital); Stamford Memorial Hospital; True Health Diagnostics (clinical laboratory)
State_County: Texas - Milam County (Rockdale); Texas - Jones County (Stamford); Texas - Collin County (Frisco)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; Upcoding
SchemeSummary: Two rural Texas hospitals partnered with clinical lab True Health Diagnostics so that THD processed advanced cardiovascular lipid blood tests for a fee while the hospitals billed insurers for them as higher-paying hospital outpatient services; the hospitals paid a share of lab revenues to marketers who ran sham management services organizations offering 'investment returns' that were in fact disguised kickbacks to referring physicians, and THD sales executives leveraged those MSO kickbacks to boost referrals, revenues and commissions. Sentences and forfeitures span two defendants: Kash 18 months and $779,773.70 forfeiture, Love 12 months and one day and $217,268.75 forfeiture; Kash was also indicted for conspiring to launder the kickback proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: Pass-through lab billing shows as a small rural hospital's outpatient lab volume for advanced lipid/cardiovascular panels exploding beyond its inpatient census, service area population and on-site capability, with specimens originating from physicians hundreds of miles away and no corresponding hospital encounter. Referring physicians participating in the MSO 'investment returns' appear as a tight set of high-volume orderers whose lab referrals concentrate almost entirely in these two hospitals; ownership/compensation disclosures at credentialing would show the MSO interests.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a facility-based lab edit: for each hospital outpatient lab claim require an associated hospital encounter and a referring provider within a calibrated service radius, and pend claims where the specimen-collection site or referring provider is remote or the test is not on the facility's CLIA/capability profile. Add hospital-level ratio monitoring of outpatient advanced-lab dollars to total facility volume versus rural peers, and a referral-concentration/Stark-AKS screen flagging orderers whose volume concentrates in one facility for financial-relationship disclosure review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Cori Lempiainen (nurse practitioner); Paul Baumert, M.D. (physician)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Device, DME; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Two practitioners billed Medicare for office visits and medical discussions they never provided (over 650 claims by Lempiainen, over 200 by Baumert) and signed thousands of orders for medically unnecessary orthotic braces based only on listening to recorded cold calls to beneficiaries, with whom they had no contact; they agreed to pay $150,000 and $14,325.96 respectively under the False Claims Act.
WaysToIdentify: Both parts are prepay-detectable: E/M and telephonic discussion claims from practitioners whose daily claim counts and per-beneficiary contact records are implausible and unmatched by any other claim for those beneficiaries, and thousands of brace orders signed by a practitioner with no billed encounter and no geographic relationship to the beneficiaries. High volume of orders per signing day is a direct capacity impossibility.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a signer-capacity check: count DME orders attributed per ordering NPI per day and the share lacking any billed encounter with that NPI in the lookback window; above the calibrated threshold, suspend downstream supplier claims and demand records. Add a prepay edit denying telehealth/telephonic E/M claims where the practitioner's same-day claim count exceeds a feasible-minutes-per-day model, and cross-check that ordering practitioners are licensed in the beneficiary's state.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee; U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee at Greeneville
FraudEntity: Monika D. Schorer (VA Medical Center employee); Teresa D. Schorer (VA Medical Center employee); Eric S. Smith (surgical sales representative); Landon Chester (surgical sales representative); Four Corners Medical Supply and Equipment LLC (VA vendor)
State_County: Tennessee - Mountain Home VA Medical Center (Washington County area, Jonesborough); Virginia - Bristol
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; Upcoding; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Two twin-sister VA Medical Center employees took cash-stuffed envelopes and a promised ownership stake in vendor Four Corners Medical Supply and Equipment LLC from surgical sales reps Eric Smith and Landon Chester, in exchange for allowing the reps to overbill the VA for surgical supplies, often medically unnecessary items; the employees set the vendor up in the VA payment system, filed false ethics disclosures, and tipped off the reps about supervisor scrutiny. Each sister received 8 months and a $10,000 fine plus $213,154.50 restitution; Smith received a year and a day and paid $120,433.45 restitution, and Smith and Chester forfeited $185,422.10, with total government recovery across all participants of $852,598 (Chester not yet sentenced).
WaysToIdentify: This is procurement/insider bribery inside a VA facility, catchable in vendor-master and purchasing controls before payment: a newly created supplier onboarded by the same employee who approves its invoices, prices above federal supply schedule benchmarks, quantities exceeding surgical case volume, and employee financial-disclosure filings that omit an ownership interest in a vendor. Overbilling shows as unit-price and quantity variance against contract catalogs.
FeaturesToCreate: Build vendor-onboarding segregation-of-duties controls: flag any vendor whose master-file creator, requisitioner and invoice approver overlap, and require independent verification before first payment. Add invoice-line price/quantity variance edits against FSS/contract catalogs and against facility surgical case counts, and run automated matching of employee disclosure and payroll/HR identity data (names, addresses, bank accounts) against vendor ownership and payment records, holding payment on match.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Josue Torres; Anthony Guerra
State_County: New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Bronx County
PayerName: Private health insurance (unnamed commercial insurers); pharmaceutical manufacturer copay assistance programs
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants allegedly accessed e-prescribing platforms using stolen identities of 18 physicians to issue approximately 693 fraudulent prescriptions (about 55,626 units, ~$2.64 million in value) for high-cost HIV and other medications in the names of 'sham patients' who did not need them, then used copay assistance cards in the sham patients' names (with private insurers paying part of the cost) to obtain the drugs cheaply at pharmacies and resell them on the black market.
WaysToIdentify: Prescriber-credential takeover is visible prepay: e-prescribing traffic from a physician's NPI originating from new IPs/EPCS accounts, sudden appearance of high-cost HIV regimens outside the prescriber's historical drug mix and specialty, and patients with no prior claim history for that prescriber or condition. Copay-card usage patterns cluster the sham patients into a few pharmacies with abnormal HIV-drug volume, and quantities/units far exceed one-patient needs.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-behavior-shift detector: per NPI, compare new claims against the prescriber's historical therapeutic-class profile, specialty, and geography, and pend claims for high-cost specialty drugs that are out-of-profile or come from a newly registered e-prescribing credential pending prescriber confirmation. Add member-level edits for first-fill high-cost HIV/oncology drugs with no supporting diagnosis or lab claim history, plus pharmacy-level monitoring of copay-card-assisted specialty volume for suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Daniel Motha (co-owner and CEO of JDM Supply LLC); Jeffrey Motha (co-owner and head of sales of JDM Supply LLC); JDM Supply LLC; Jason Colantuoni (co-conspirator, pleaded guilty)
State_County: Massachusetts - Suffolk County (Boston); Florida - Miami-Dade County (Miami)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Two brothers who co-owned JDM Supply LLC sold approximately 850,000 facemasks, manufactured by Advoque Safeguard, to a hospital for about $2.6 million by misrepresenting them as NIOSH-approved N95 respirators and supplying NIOSH-passing test results and approval documents belonging to a different mask; lab testing showed filtration efficiency of 83.94%-93.24%, below the 95% N95 requirement. They also sold scarce N95 masks to Massachusetts hospitals above prevailing market price in violation of the Defense Production Act. Both defendants received one year probation and a $9,500 fine each (totaling $19,000); a third conspirator awaited sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: No claim-adjudication component; this is PPE procurement fraud and price gouging, catchable in supplier vetting: the NIOSH approval number and test report submitted did not correspond to the model shipped, and the certificate could have been verified against the NIOSH Certified Equipment List before payment. Price benchmarking against prevailing market rates and the absence of any prior respirator-manufacturing history for the vendor are further pre-payment flags.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a procurement document-verification control: for respirator and PPE purchases, programmatically match the claimed NIOSH approval number, manufacturer and model on the certificate to the official certified-equipment database and reject mismatches before payment release. Add unit-price screening against a rolling market benchmark with escalation above the calibrated percentile, plus mandatory sample lot testing and vendor-history checks for new PPE suppliers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Boris Arencibia (procured and sold diverted drugs); Jose Armando Rivera Garcia (owner of LDD Distributors); LDD Distributors
SchemeSummary: The two defendants bought high-priced prescription drugs (including HIV and cancer medications) from illicit street sources, including patients who sold their prescriptions and people who obtained prescriptions by fraud, then repackaged them without proper storage safeguards and falsified paperwork to make them appear to come from manufacturers or legitimate wholesalers. Through sham distribution companies (including Rivera Garcia's LDD Distributors) they sold roughly $28 million of diverted, misbranded drugs to pharmacies nationwide - some bottles containing wrong medications, vitamins or pebbles - and laundered the proceeds; figures and the 57-month sentence span both defendants across two related cases.
WaysToIdentify: Drug diversion into the pharmacy supply chain is detectable via pedigree and inventory reconciliation before payment: pharmacies acquiring high-cost HIV/oncology product from unregistered or newly formed 'wholesalers' whose DSCSA transaction histories cannot be traced to a manufacturer, and dispensing volumes exceeding documented purchases. On the beneficiary side, patients with repeated early fills and no corresponding lab/visit evidence indicate prescription-selling upstream.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an acquisition-source control: require dispensing pharmacies to report supplier DEA/wholesaler license and match every high-cost NDC dispensed against verified purchase records from licensed distributors; pend or deny claims where dispensed units exceed verified purchases or the supplier is unlicensed. Add pharmacy-level inventory reconciliation analytics and a beneficiary early-refill/no-clinical-evidence flag routing to investigation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Yousef Ennab (licensed pharmacist, supervising pharmacist at Forest Care); Mohamed Hassan (licensed pharmacist, owner of more than a dozen pharmacies); Dr. Somsri Ratanaprasatporn (physician); Leticia Smith (medical receptionist); Bassam Amin (pharmacist); Omar Elsayed (pharmacist); Michael Kent (drug dealer); Anthony Mathis; Raymond Walker
State_County: New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Queens County; New York - Richmond County (Staten Island)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Prescriptions for 30-day supplies of oxycodone 30 mg were written out of a Brooklyn pill-mill medical practice (some by the doctor's receptionist, often for patients never examined and in some cases for stolen identities), then filled at pharmacies owned or supervised by the defendant pharmacists; the pills were handed to street drug dealers for cash payments, and the pharmacists also billed insurance companies for the medically unnecessary pills. Over 1.2 million pills worth more than $36 million in street value were distributed; two pharmacists were convicted at trial while seven co-defendants pleaded guilty (co-defendant Michael Kent received 9 years, and Hassan was later sentenced to 18 years).
WaysToIdentify: Classic pill-mill signals sit in claims and PDMP data prepay: one practice writing near-uniform oxycodone 30 mg 30-day-supply prescriptions at extreme volume, prescriptions signed on days the physician did not bill any encounter or was absent, patients traveling far and clustering at a handful of commonly owned pharmacies, and cash-plus-insurance dual billing for the same fills. Members with no chronic-pain diagnosis history and stolen-identity members with no other utilization are further flags.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a prescriber-pharmacy dyad monitor: compute share of a prescriber's claims that are high-dose Schedule II with identical day-supply, beneficiary travel distance, and the concentration of fills into pharmacies with common ownership; fire above the calibrated percentile and impose prepay prior authorization plus payment suspension. Add edits denying opioid fills with no billed encounter by that prescriber in the lookback window or no supporting pain diagnosis, and duplicate-fill detection across commonly owned pharmacy NPIs.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Mohamed Hassan (pharmacist, owner of approximately 20 pharmacies); Yousef Ennab (supervising pharmacist, Forest Care); Anthony Mathis (street narcotics dealer/patient recruiter); Michael Kent (co-defendant); Dr. Somsri Ratanaprasatporn (physician, pill mill); Leticia Smith (receptionist who forged prescriptions); Bassam Amin (pharmacist); Omar Elsayed (pharmacist); Raymond Walker (street dealer)
State_County: New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Queens County; New York - Richmond County (Staten Island)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Prescriptions for 30-day supplies of oxycodone 30 mg were forged/illegally issued out of a Brooklyn pill-mill medical practice - often in the names of recruited nominal patients or people whose identities were stolen and who were never examined - then filled at roughly 20 pharmacies controlled by pharmacist Mohamed Hassan; the pills were handed to street dealers for cash while the pharmacists also billed insurers for the medically unnecessary pills, distributing more than 1.6 million oxycodone pills worth over $48 million in street value. Figures span multiple co-defendants: Hassan received 18 years, Kent 108 months, Walker 84 months, Mathis 36 months and Ennab 30 months, with forfeitures of $535,989.12 (Mathis) and $13,472.76 (Ennab) plus an undetermined amount for Hassan.
WaysToIdentify: The same dyad pattern, plus a pharmacy-ownership network signal: roughly twenty pharmacies controlled by one pharmacist all filling identical oxycodone 30 mg 30-day scripts from a single Brooklyn practice, with beneficiaries who have no other utilization or whose identities were stolen, and prescriptions issued on dates with no billed physician encounter. Uniform quantity/day-supply, distance between prescriber and pharmacies, and purchase-versus-dispense reconciliation at the wholesaler level are all checkable before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build pharmacy-network link analysis (shared owners, pharmacist-in-charge, addresses, bank accounts, DEA order data) and aggregate controlled-substance volume across the network versus peers, suspending payment and referring for site visits above the calibrated percentile. Add prepay edits denying Schedule II opioid claims lacking a corresponding billed encounter or supporting diagnosis, flagging identical-quantity/day-supply prescribing concentration by prescriber, and requiring beneficiary verification for members with no other claims history.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Dr. Asim Muhammad Ali (physician, owner of Central Diagnostic Laboratory and Institute for Pain Management LLC); Dr. Mohd Azfar Malik (psychiatrist, owner of Psych Care Consultants LLC)
PayerName: Medicare; Missouri Medicaid; private health insurers
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Drug_Prescriptions; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Dr. Ali performed telephone-only 'annual wellness visits' for Medicare patients of Dr. Malik's Psych Care Consultants and billed them under Malik's name and Medicare billing number (Medicare paid $3,902), while Malik submitted claims to Medicare, Missouri Medicaid and private insurers for in-person services (including an inpatient hospital visit and a ketamine infusion) performed when he was out of state or out of the country, causing $19,442 in losses; Ali separately admitted paying kickbacks for urine specimens referred to his lab and pre-signing controlled-substance prescriptions without seeing patients. Figures span two defendants.}
WaysToIdentify: Both mechanics are visible at adjudication: claims billed under Malik's NPI for face-to-face services (inpatient visit, ketamine infusion, in-person AWV) on dates when Malik was demonstrably absent — cross-check against travel/border data only post-pay, but prepay you can test place-of-service and modality consistency (telephone-only encounters billed as in-person E/M, no telehealth modifier/POS 02), and rendering-vs-supervising provider mismatch where a second physician's schedule shows the same time slots. Kickbacks for urine specimens show as a lab whose UDS referral volume is concentrated in a few ordering NPIs with payments disclosed nowhere, and pre-signed controlled-substance scripts appear as PDMP prescriptions issued on dates with no corresponding encounter claim for that patient.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a provider-day activity edit: per billing NPI per date of service, count in-person-only codes and flag when the same NPI has concurrent telehealth-origin encounters, impossible same-day multi-site activity, or a rendering provider whose claims all originate from another practice's patient panel; suspend and request appointment logs/attestation. Add a prescriber-encounter reconciliation job matching PDMP controlled-substance fills to an E/M or telehealth claim for the same patient within a window, and a lab UDS concentration monitor (share of specimens from top ordering NPIs, plus payment relationships) that triggers prepay review of that lab's UDS claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Jared Wheat (founder, owner and CEO of Hi-Tech Pharmaceuticals, Inc.); Hi-Tech Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (dietary supplement manufacturer)
SchemeSummary: After a legitimate third-party audit found 75 GMP deficiencies at Hi-Tech's supplement plant, Wheat and Hi-Tech fabricated a GMP compliance certificate from 'PharmaTech Consulting' (secretly owned by Wheat), forged a Belize attorney's signature, altered the audit report's 'Not Acceptable' entries to 'Acceptable,' and also faked FDA Certificates of Free Sale; these documents were sent to customers (some of whom passed them to foreign regulators), and customers paid at least $4,763,292 to Hi-Tech, with the company also convicted of laundering the proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: No payer claims component — this is commercial wire fraud on supplement customers using forged GMP and FDA Certificate of Free Sale documents, so no claim edit would have caught it. The applicable control is credentialing/vendor due-diligence: verify certification documents directly with the issuing auditor or FDA rather than accepting supplier-provided PDFs, and check whether the 'certifying' consultancy is beneficially owned by the audited party. Detection is otherwise post-hoc via customer or regulator complaint.
FeaturesToCreate: For any payer or PBM that contracts with manufacturers/suppliers, build a certificate-provenance check: every GMP/FDA certificate uploaded during vendor onboarding is validated against the issuer's registry or by direct issuer callback, and the certifying entity's ownership is screened against the vendor's own beneficial-owner list for overlap. Fire on unverifiable issuer, ownership overlap, or a document version differing from the issuer's copy, and hold contracting until resolved.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Normita Sierra (owner/operator of Golden Meadows Hospice Inc. and D'Alexandria Hospice Inc.); Rowena Elegado; Carl Bernardo (marketer); Relyndo Salcedo (nurse practitioner); Golden Meadows Hospice Inc.; D'Alexandria Hospice Inc.
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Sierra's two hospices billed Medicare over $4.8 million (paid ~$3.8M) for hospice services for patients who were not terminally ill; marketers were paid kickbacks of up to $1,300 per patient per month (code-named 'girl scout cookies') to recruit patients, and a nurse practitioner falsified assessments exaggerating patient conditions so hospice physicians would certify them as terminally ill. Patients were typically discharged around six months, sometimes to Sierra's home health company or other hospice. Two co-participants (Bernardo and Salcedo) have pleaded guilty and await sentencing; Sierra and Elegado were arrested on indictment.
WaysToIdentify: Hospice enrolment of non-terminal patients shows prepay as a benefit-period pattern: high share of live discharges clustered near the end of the second benefit period, patients with no hospice-appropriate diagnosis, low medication/symptom burden in prior claims history, and re-admission to a commonly-owned home health agency after discharge. Certification integrity is testable by concentration — a single nurse practitioner or two attending physicians certifying nearly all admissions, with assessment content boilerplate. Kickbacks to marketers are visible on payroll/1099 and per-patient-per-month payment structure, usually only on audit or via ownership-linkage analysis of the hospice, HHA, and marketing entities.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a hospice admission-integrity score at the agency level: live-discharge rate, share of discharges in months 5-7, share of discharges to a commonly-owned HHA/hospice (via ownership graph from enrolment records), and certifier concentration; agencies above the calibrated percentile go on prepay documentation review requiring the full certification and face-to-face assessment. Add a beneficiary-level edit that flags admissions where the preceding 12 months of claims show no terminal-trajectory indicators and requires the physician narrative before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida; Justice Department Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Marek Rex Vernon Harrison (true beneficial owner and manager of CTD Network LLC); CTD Network LLC (purported telemedicine company)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Harrison allegedly ran telemedicine company CTD Network, whose providers conducted sham telehealth consultations to approve medically unnecessary genetic (cancer-risk) testing orders for Medicare beneficiaries referred by marketing companies and labs, with no treatment relationship or use of results; CTD billed Medicare over $2.7 million for the telehealth services and was paid over $600,000. CTD also allegedly filed false Medicare enrollment forms naming other people as owners/managers to hide Harrison's control and his 2019 bank fraud conviction.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment: the ownership/managing-employee disclosures can be validated against corporate registries, bank signatories, and exclusion/criminal-history screening — a straw-owner filing plus an undisclosed prior bank fraud conviction is a prepay denial of enrolment. At adjudication: telehealth E/M claims that are systematically followed within days by high-cost hereditary cancer panels from a small set of labs, with no treating relationship (no prior or subsequent claims from that provider for the patient) and no use of results, are the signature; marketer-driven referral funnels show as beneficiaries geographically dispersed far from the telehealth entity.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment integrity check that resolves each applicant's disclosed owners/managers against secretary-of-state filings, bank account signatories, shared addresses/phones with previously revoked entities, and criminal/exclusion databases, and refers mismatches for revalidation before billing privileges issue. Add a prepay link edit: for each telehealth encounter that precedes a genetic test order, compute the ordering provider's rate of order-only encounters (no follow-up care) and lab concentration; above the calibrated percentile, deny or pend both the telehealth claim and the linked lab claim pending records showing a treatment relationship.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Insys Therapeutics, Inc.; John N. Kapoor (founder and former Executive Chairman); Richard M. Simon (former National Director of Sales); Sunrise Lee (former Regional Sales Director); Joseph A. Rowan (former Regional Sales Director); Michael J. Gurry (former VP of Managed Markets); Michael Babich (former CEO and President); Alec Burlakoff (former VP of Sales)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Drug_Prescriptions; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Insys founder and executives used pharmacy data to identify high-volume rapid-onset opioid prescribers and paid them bribes/kickbacks (via sham speaker programs and similar inducements) to write more and higher-dose prescriptions of Subsys, a fentanyl spray approved only for breakthrough cancer pain, and then misled Medicare and private insurers about patients' diagnoses to obtain prior authorization and payment for medically unnecessary prescriptions. The $48,344,036 restitution figure is the total ordered across the seven convicted/pleading executives, now collected in full.
WaysToIdentify: The prior-authorization file itself carries the fraud: PA requests asserting a cancer/breakthrough-cancer-pain diagnosis can be reconciled prepay against the beneficiary's claims history for any oncology encounter, chemotherapy, or cancer diagnosis — TIRF claims with no cancer footprint should never have paid. Prescriber-level signals: sudden step-change in Subsys volume and dose escalation after a date, non-oncologist specialty, and payments received from the manufacturer visible in Open Payments/speaker-program disclosures. Cross-referencing top-decile TIRF prescribers with manufacturer speaker-fee recipients is a prepay-actionable overlay.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a TIRF eligibility edit that requires an on-file cancer diagnosis and an opioid-tolerance regimen in the member's own claims/pharmacy history before paying, and auto-rejects PA assertions contradicted by claims history, routing the call center's stated diagnosis to audit. Add a prescriber monitor joining Open Payments/speaker honoraria to the prescriber's TIRF volume, dose trajectory, and specialty; prescribers in the top calibrated percentile on both payments and volume go to prepay review of all their branded-opioid claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Raytheon Company; Teva Pharmaceuticals; Kabbage, Inc.
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Other - Unknown
SchemeSummary: Annual collections announcement rather than a single scheme: the office collected $60.17 million in FY2024 ($19.56 million criminal, $40.6 million civil) plus $14.87 million jointly, and over $1 billion in calendar year 2024, including a $575 million Raytheon procurement fraud resolution ($147 million criminal/$428 million civil), a $425 million Teva Pharmaceuticals settlement for paying kickbacks through two co-pay assistance foundations in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute and False Claims Act, and a $120 million settlement with lender Kabbage, Inc. for submitting false PPP loan forgiveness, guarantee and processing-fee claims to the SBA.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual collections round-up, not one scheme, and the components (defense procurement fraud, PPP forgiveness fees) are largely outside claims adjudication. The one payer-relevant mechanic is the Teva co-pay foundation kickback: manufacturer funding of a 'charity' that covers copays only for that manufacturer's drug is detectable by correlating foundation grant flows with a drug's Part D volume and by seeing beneficiaries whose cost-sharing is always covered by a single disease-specific fund tied to one product. Loan-forgiveness fee fraud is a lender-side, post-payment audit matter.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a copay-support linkage analysis: per manufacturer and per drug, track the share of federal-program claims where third-party cost-sharing comes from a foundation the manufacturer funds, and flag single-drug or single-manufacturer disease funds for AKS review and potential claim recoupment. No prepay claim edit applies to the procurement or PPP components.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Dakota
FraudEntity: Dunes Surgical Hospital; two unnamed physician groups
SchemeSummary: Annual debt-collection release noting that, in addition to $3,496,288.47 collected in FY2024, the office obtained a $12.7 million settlement resolving alleged False Claims Act violations arising from improper financial relationships between Dunes Surgical Hospital and two physician groups, plus $1.4 million in restitution in a separate pandemic fraud prosecution.
WaysToIdentify: Stark/AKS financial-relationship cases are detectable prepay only through disclosure and referral-pattern data: the hospital's physician-compensation arrangements (directorships, service-line management, leases) can be tested for fair market value and for whether the arrangement is in writing and current, and DHS claims from physicians with a financial relationship can be flagged when the arrangement is expired or undocumented. Referral concentration — a share of the hospital's surgical volume coming from the two paid groups far above peers — is visible in claims. Otherwise the route is post-payment FCA/qui tam.
FeaturesToCreate: Require hospitals to submit a physician financial-arrangement register (party NPI, term dates, compensation basis, time-record requirement) and build an edit that denies or pends DHS claims referred by a physician whose arrangement is expired, missing, or lacks required time documentation. Add a referral-concentration monitor per facility-specialty pair flagging groups whose referred volume and paid compensation both exceed the calibrated peer percentile for FMV/Stark audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
SchemeSummary: Annual collections announcement rather than a single fraud case: the office reported collecting $104.8 million in Fiscal Year 2024, comprising $9,239,721.20 in criminal restitution, $95,604,774.97 in civil actions (mostly False Claims Act recoveries), and $2,441,761 in asset forfeiture, with recoveries stemming from matters including crop insurance fraud, employee-related theft, and health care fraud.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual collections announcement covering unrelated crop insurance, employee theft, and health care matters; there is no single scheme with an identifiable claim signature, so nothing here is catchable by a specific prepay edit. The generic payer-side route is post-payment FCA recovery and qui tam intake, which is what produced these numbers.
FeaturesToCreate: No case-specific control applies. Nearest applicable payer control is a recovery-pipeline capability: route qui tam allegations and OIG referrals into a case-management system that automatically pulls the named provider's claim history and places new claims on prepay review while the allegation is open.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
SchemeSummary: No specific fraud scheme described; the release announces the annual meeting of the Western District of North Carolina's Health Care Fraud Working Group, a multi-agency partnership (FBI, HHS-OIG, IRS-CI, VA-OIG, DCIS, NC and SC Medicaid units) focused on detecting health care fraud, and provides fraud reporting contacts.
WaysToIdentify: No scheme is described — this is a working-group meeting and fraud-reporting announcement, so there are no claims to adjudicate and no signal to detect.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side detection control applies. The nearest useful build is an intake/triage feature: normalize hotline and multi-agency referral tips into provider identifiers and auto-attach them to the provider's risk score so future claims from tipped providers can be pended for review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nevada
FraudEntity: Paulino Gonzalez (registered nurse); Mary Huntly (nurse practitioner)
SchemeSummary: Two Las Vegas nurses were charged by information for applying amniotic wound allografts—some medically unnecessary—to Medicare beneficiaries in exchange for illegal kickbacks from an allograft distributor; Gonzalez received about $7,391,584 in kickbacks while a wound care company billed Medicare over $94 million (paid over $54 million) for allografts he and others applied (Oct 2021–Apr 2024), and Huntly's wound care company billed Medicare about $14,333,550 (paid about $9,105,563) from Sept 2022 through Apr 2024. Figures span both defendants; part of the 2025 national takedown involving 324 defendants and $14.6 billion in intended loss.
WaysToIdentify: Amniotic/skin-substitute allograft billing is highly visible prepay: per-square-centimeter units far above wound size, application counts per beneficiary and per applying clinician per day exceeding what is clinically feasible, extreme dollar concentration in a handful of nurse practitioners, and product/HCPCS billed at a price point where a single distributor dominates. Kickbacks from the distributor to appliers appear as 1099/consulting payments, generally only post-pay, but the volume anomaly alone justifies prepay suspension. Also check whether wounds have any prior wound-care history or debridement claims supporting a graft.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a skin-substitute utilization edit: per rendering NPI per day, compute applications and total cm² billed, and per beneficiary compute cumulative graft cm² and application count versus documented wound size/diagnosis; pend claims above the calibrated peer percentile and require wound measurements, photographs, and the treatment plan. Add a distributor-linkage monitor tying HCPCS/product to supplier and to appliers' outside payments, and place high-velocity appliers on payment suspension pending review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Gilead Sciences, Inc. (pharmaceutical manufacturer)
State_County: New York - New York County (Manhattan); nationwide
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (New York Medicaid among state programs); TRICARE
SchemeSummary: Gilead used 'HIV Speaker Programs' to funnel kickbacks - over $20 million in honoraria plus lavish meals at high-end restaurants (e.g., 157 events at the James Beard House) and travel to destinations like Hawaii and Miami - to high-volume prescribers of its HIV drugs (Stribild, Genvoya, Complera, Odefsey, Descovy, Biktarvy), inducing prescriptions that resulted in tainted claims paid by Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE; one speaker paid over $300,000 generated over $6 million in federal program payments. Resolved by a $202 million False Claims Act settlement ($176,927,889.28 to the U.S.) arising from an intervened whistleblower suit.
WaysToIdentify: Speaker-program kickbacks are detectable by joining Open Payments honoraria, meal, and travel records to the same prescriber's Part D/Medicaid/TRICARE volume for the sponsor's drug: prescribers with repeat honoraria at the same venue, implausible attendee patterns, and step-change increases in branded HIV prescribing after payments are the signature. Brand-share skew — a prescriber whose HIV regimen mix is almost entirely one manufacturer's products versus same-specialty peers — is visible in pharmacy claims prepay. Full proof of intent comes post-payment via FCA/qui tam.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a payment-to-prescribing correlation job at prescriber-drug-quarter granularity that merges Open Payments (speaker fees, meals, travel) with claim volume and computes post-payment volume lift and manufacturer brand-share versus peers; prescribers above the calibrated percentile on both are flagged for prepay review and referral. Add a program-level test on sponsors: repeat-attendee and repeat-speaker concentration across events, triggering AKS review and potential claim taint analysis.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: CVS Pharmacy, Inc. (national retail pharmacy chain)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; TRICARE; Federal Employees Health Benefits Program
SchemeSummary: CVS dispensed full five-pen insulin cartons that exceeded plan days-of-supply limits and, instead of obtaining overrides and reporting the true days-of-supply, instructed staff to report only the maximum days-of-supply allowed; because its dispensing/auto-refill software calculated refill dates from that understated data, CVS repeatedly refilled prescriptions prematurely and billed Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE and FEHBP for refills ineligible for reimbursement. Resolved by a $37.76 million False Claims Act settlement ($24,446,240 to the United States, remainder to states) after the Government joined five whistleblower suits.
WaysToIdentify: This is fully visible in the pharmacy claim: reported days-of-supply that equals the plan maximum while the metric quantity dispensed (five insulin pens) implies a longer supply is an internal inconsistency the adjudicator can compute from quantity, NDC package size, and directions. The downstream symptom is refill-too-soon: cumulative dispensed quantity per member per drug exceeding elapsed days at the prescribed daily dose. Chain-level patterns — one chain's insulin claims clustering exactly at the plan day cap — make it detectable prepay.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a days-supply plausibility edit: recompute expected days-of-supply from NDC unit strength, metric quantity, and sig-derived daily dose, and reject or pend any claim where reported days-of-supply is materially below the computed value or sits exactly at the plan cap while quantity implies more. Layer a cumulative-supply refill edit per member-drug (total dispensed units versus elapsed days at prescribed dose) that denies premature refills regardless of the reported days-supply field, and report chain-level clustering at the cap for audit.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: New York-Presbyterian Hudson Valley Hospital (hospital, formerly Hudson Valley Hospital Center)
SchemeSummary: The hospital entered three 2011-2012 agreements (melanoma center medical directorship, breast center medical directorship, and IORT service line management) paying a Westchester oncology practice hundreds of thousands of dollars per year; over $4 million was paid between 2011 and 2019 for work that was not performed, not performed as required, or undocumented by time records, continuing even after the agreements expired in 2016, in order to induce oncology patient referrals that the hospital then billed to Medicare and Medicaid in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute, Stark Law and False Claims Act. Resolved by a $6,836,764.30 settlement ($6,469,410.32 to the United States, remainder to New York State), arising from a whistleblower qui tam suit the Government joined.
WaysToIdentify: The tell is administrative rather than clinical: medical-directorship and service-line management payments continuing after the written agreements expired in 2016, with no time records supporting the hours paid — verifiable at contract/credentialing review of the hospital's Stark arrangement register. On the claims side, oncology referral volume from that single practice as a share of the hospital's oncology admissions, and IORT/melanoma-center service volume, can be compared to peers; DHS claims referred by a physician with an expired or undocumented compensation arrangement should be blockable. Full detection here came post-payment via qui tam.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a Stark arrangement register with mandatory term dates and time-attestation requirements, and an edit that pends or denies designated health service claims where the referring physician's arrangement with the billing facility is expired, unsigned, or missing time records for the paid period. Add an annual FMV/commercial-reasonableness review trigger when compensation per arrangement plus referred DHS revenue from that physician group both exceed the calibrated peer percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Walgreens (retail pharmacy chain)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Drug_Prescriptions; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: In a departure announcement summarizing office accomplishments, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Texas described a $97 million False Claims Act settlement with Walgreens for billing government health care payors for prescriptions that were never actually dispensed to patients. The same release also references separate resolutions not part of this settlement: $21.75 million with Medisca, Inc. for submitting false and inflated average wholesale prices for compounding ingredients, and $5.3 million paid by a Texas hospital CEO over illegal payments to physicians for laboratory referrals.
WaysToIdentify: Never-dispensed prescriptions are detectable prepay/near-pay by reconciling adjudicated claims to actual pickup: claims with no corresponding dispense-completion or return-to-stock event, and members with paid fills but no refill continuity or no encounter history for the drug. Inflated AWP for compounding ingredients is detectable by benchmarking submitted ingredient prices against independent pricing sources and against other compounders' submissions for the same NDC. Lab-referral payments from a hospital CEO to physicians appear as referral concentration plus undisclosed financial arrangements.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a dispense-reconciliation control requiring pharmacies to transmit pickup/return-to-stock status and auto-reversing or recouping claims lacking a pickup event within the plan window, with chains above the calibrated non-pickup percentile placed on prepay review. JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jawad Bhatti (pain management physician); Keri Ayres (owner, Ability Unlimited); Lori Adcock (operations manager, Ability Unlimited); Kevin White (owner, Ithiel Group residential group homes); Yvoune Kara Petrie (president/COO, Virginia Integrative Health); Cristina Schasse (Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetist)
State_County: Virginia - Richmond; Virginia - Fauquier County (Warrenton); Virginia - Loudoun County (Leesburg); Virginia - Henrico County (Glen Allen); North Carolina - Pender County (Hampstead)
PayerName: Medicare; Virginia Medicaid; CareFirst BlueCross BlueShield
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Upcoding; Device, DME; IdentityFraud; Drug_Prescriptions; FakeEncounter; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Six defendants charged in separate EDVA schemes: Bhatti allegedly used FDA-unapproved ozone gas devices and billed Medicare/Medicaid for the injections as nerve blocks and for ultrasound guidance not actually used (over $5.2M claimed); Ayres and Adcock of Ability Unlimited allegedly hid arbitrary profit margins in subcontractor costs for Medicaid home/vehicle environmental modifications (approx. $245,000 and $213,210 respectively); White billed Medicaid over $1,000,000 (paid $461,704) for group home residents who were hospitalized, incarcerated or away; Petrie billed CareFirst about $1.9M for hyperbaric oxygen therapy never provided or prescribed, using recruited family/friends as patients and four physicians' NPIs without permission; Schasse allegedly diverted fentanyl and Versed from a Pyxis machine and substituted mislabeled saline/Precedex syringes given to patients.
WaysToIdentify: Each sub-scheme has a distinct prepay signal: nerve-block plus ultrasound-guidance pairs billed at near-100% frequency by one practice using an unapproved drug/device (no valid J-code/NDC for ozone) versus peers; Medicaid environmental-modification claims priced above subcontractor invoices, testable by requiring the underlying invoice; group-home/residential per-diem or service claims overlapping inpatient hospital, incarceration, or absence dates — a direct date-overlap edit against institutional claims and correctional/eligibility files; HBOT claims where the rendering NPI did not authorize use and patients cluster as family members sharing addresses/phones; drug diversion detectable via Pyxis dispense-versus-administration reconciliation and patient pain-response anomalies rather than claims.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-day conflict edit that denies residential/day-service and outpatient therapy claims overlapping inpatient stays, incarceration, or out-of-state periods using institutional claims and eligibility feeds. Add an NDC/device validity edit rejecting injection claims lacking an approved drug code, a fixed-pair frequency monitor (e.g., guidance always billed with the procedure) for prepay review, an NPI-consent check flagging rendering NPIs whose claims originate from an unaffiliated biller with shared-address patient clusters, and require subcontractor invoices before paying home/vehicle modification claims. For diversion, require facilities to submit automated-dispensing-cabinet-to-MAR reconciliation exception reports.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Charles Adams, M.D. (physician); Adams' medical practice
SchemeSummary: A federal jury found that Dr. Charles Adams and his medical practice violated the False Claims Act by submitting false claims to Medicare for chelation therapy (drugs to remove heavy metals) that was not medically necessary; Medicare reimbursed more than $1.1 million, and post-trial penalties brought total liability to over $27 million.
WaysToIdentify: Chelation is covered only for documented heavy-metal toxicity, so the prepay signal is a claim for chelation infusion codes with no supporting toxicity diagnosis and, critically, no confirmatory heavy-metal laboratory result in the member's claims history. Practice-level concentration — one physician accounting for an outsized share of a payer's chelation volume, with repeated long infusion series per patient — is visible in claims and far above same-specialty peers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a medical-necessity edit that pends chelation drug/infusion claims unless the member has a coded heavy-metal toxicity diagnosis and a prior qualifying lab result on file, and requires the lab report as documentation. Add a provider-volume monitor for chelation series length and patients-per-provider versus peers; providers above the calibrated percentile go on prepay documentation review of all chelation claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Michael L. Riggins
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Riggins paid for doctors' orders for medically unnecessary durable medical equipment and tricked physicians into signing DME orders and certificates of medical necessity, then submitted over $3.8 million in fraudulent claims to Medicare (reimbursed over $1.8 million) despite hundreds of victim complaints about fraudulent orders; he was sentenced to 57 months and roughly $1.8 million restitution. (The press release also lists unrelated non-health-care prosecutions.)
WaysToIdentify: Purchased/duped physician orders leave fingerprints in claims: a supplier whose orders come from a small number of distant physicians who have no other treating relationship with the beneficiary, identical CMN language across patients, and braces/equipment shipped in standardized bundles. The strongest available signal here was ignored — hundreds of beneficiary complaints about orders they never requested; complaint volume per supplier NPI is a directly actionable prepay trigger. New/recently enrolled suppliers with rapid claim ramp-up add to the risk profile.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a supplier risk engine keyed on beneficiary complaint counts, ordering-physician concentration and geographic distance, absence of any prior encounter between ordering physician and beneficiary, and claim-velocity ramp since enrolment; crossing calibrated thresholds triggers prepay review or payment suspension. Add a per-claim edit requiring a verifiable treating-relationship encounter for the ordering NPI within the lookback window and beneficiary contact verification before paying high-value DME.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Mexico
FraudEntity: William Monford Wood (former Los Alamos National Laboratory employee)
State_County: New Mexico - Los Alamos County; California - Alameda County (Oakland, Livermore); California - Santa Barbara County (Santa Barbara)
SchemeSummary: A former Los Alamos National Laboratory employee submitted 23 false claims for payment between July 2016 and December 2017 relating to business trips to California, claiming time he did not actually work and expenses he did not incur or that lacked a legitimate business purpose; he agreed to pay $67,500 (including $38,549.83 restitution) and to never again work on federally funded contracts.
WaysToIdentify: No health care payer is involved — this is employee travel/time reimbursement fraud against a federal contractor, so no claims edit applies. The detectable signal is internal: expense claims lacking receipts or business purpose, and claimed labor hours conflicting with travel dates, badge/access records, and project charge codes.
FeaturesToCreate: Not a payer control; the nearest analogue is an internal expense-and-timecard reconciliation rule that cross-checks claimed hours against travel itineraries, badge/system access logs, and receipt presence, auto-holding reimbursements with missing documentation or hour/location conflicts for supervisor and audit review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: Ashley Barnett (doctor of veterinary medicine); Laura Webb (doctor of veterinary medicine); Rachel Goldstein; Kristina Coomer (retail pharmacy employee); Matthew Ryan Elkins (advanced practice registered nurse-certified registered nurse anesthetist)
State_County: Kentucky - Jefferson County (Louisville); Kentucky - Washington County (Springfield); Kentucky - Oldham County (Crestwood); Indiana - Clark County (Jeffersonville)
SchemeSummary: Five defendants charged in Western Kentucky with controlled-substance diversion: two veterinarians allegedly used another's DEA registration number and, with a co-conspirator, issued prescriptions for over 25,000 Schedule II pills (oxycodone, hydrocodone) in the names of canines, including deceased and fictitious dogs, with the drugs actually going to the defendants; one defendant had a co-conspirator fill her own dextroamphetamine prescription and bill Medicaid, and other defendants stole oxycodone, buprenorphine and fentanyl from pharmacy/medical supply chains and tampered with a patient's fentanyl syringe.
WaysToIdentify: Veterinary-issued Schedule II prescriptions dispensed at retail pharmacies and billed to a human plan are visible at adjudication: prescriber DEA/taxonomy is veterinary, patient name is non-human or has no eligibility/claim history, and the prescription is for human-dosage oxycodone/hydrocodone. PDMP data would show a single DEA number writing high volumes of Schedule II with no corresponding animal-owner records, and the same DEA number used from locations/prescribers other than the registrant. The self-fill (a pharmacy employee filling her own dextroamphetamine and billing Medicaid) is caught by matching claim member ID to the dispensing pharmacy's employee/owner roster; diversion from inventory is caught post-payment by dispensed-versus-purchased reconciliation.
