FeaturesToCreate: Build a prepay edit at the pharmacy claim level that denies/pends any controlled-substance claim where the prescriber's DEA registrant business activity is veterinary, or where prescriber NPI taxonomy is absent from the human-provider registry, and a second edit where the billed member is not found in eligibility or the member's name matches an animal-name pattern or a deceased-file record. Add a prescriber-level PDMP monitor computing Schedule II MME volume and unique-patient counts per DEA number versus same-registration-type peers, firing a payment suspension and DEA referral above the calibrated percentile; add a claim-level conflict-of-interest edit when member ID appears on the billing pharmacy's employee/ownership file, and a monthly dispensed-versus-wholesaler-purchase reconciliation by NDC.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Terry Hill, Jr. (owner/operator of Recovery Street Central); Recovery Street Central (substance abuse treatment recovery facility)
SchemeSummary: Hill, excluded from Medicare and Medicaid in 2021 after a Medicaid fraud conviction, allegedly continued to secretly own and operate a Dayton substance abuse recovery facility that billed Medicaid more than $4 million for counseling services that were never provided or were provided in violation of Medicaid rules.
WaysToIdentify: Exclusion screening should be run not just on the billing NPI but on all owners, officers, managing employees and indirect/beneficial owners disclosed at enrolment and revalidation, and cross-checked against corporate registry filings, bank signatory records, lease and payroll data — Hill's continued control would surface as an undisclosed managing employee matching LEIE/state exclusion lists. Common addresses, phone numbers, prior NPIs and bank accounts shared with the previously convicted entity are a strong pre-enrolment linkage signal. The phantom counseling itself is testable at adjudication: billed counseling units per rendering clinician per day and licensure/credential status of the named counselors.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an enrolment/revalidation feature that fuzzy-matches every disclosed and inferred associate (owner, officer, managing employee, authorized official, bank signatory, address, phone, EIN) against LEIE, state exclusion and prior-adverse-action files, plus a linkage graph that flags a new provider sharing address/phone/bank/staff with a previously excluded or terminated entity; a hit triggers enrolment denial or a payment hold pending an ownership audit. Add a claim-level edit that requires a valid, currently licensed rendering-clinician NPI on every behavioral-health/SUD counseling line and a provider-level monitor of counseling units per clinician-day and per client-day against licensure hours, firing prepay documentation requests above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Penn State Health (multi-hospital health system)
SchemeSummary: Penn State Health self-disclosed in 2023 that between December 2015 and November 2022 it submitted Medicare claims for Annual Wellness Visits that were not supported by the wellness record; it entered a February 2024 settlement agreeing to pay $11,712,336. (The same collections release also noted an unrelated non-health-care SNAP benefit-for-cash scheme by Jimmy Tran of Asia Market, Harrisburg, PA, involving $1,843,534 in benefits and $299,174.60 in forfeiture/restoration.)
WaysToIdentify: Annual Wellness Visit claims (G0438/G0439) are highly rule-bound and testable at adjudication: prior AWV within the preceding 12 months, presence of an initial-versus-subsequent code mismatch, IPPE overlap, and same-day billing of a problem-oriented E/M without documented distinct service. A hospital/system billing AWVs at a rate far above same-specialty peers, or with AWVs clustered on days with implausible per-provider visit counts, indicates the wellness elements (HRA, personalized prevention plan) were not actually performed. Whether the record supports the required AWV elements is only verifiable through medical-record review, so use targeted prepay documentation requests plus post-payment probe sampling with extrapolation.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a claim-level AWV edit set: deny when a prior AWV exists inside the 12-month window or when G0438 is billed for a beneficiary with prior AWV/IPPE history, and pend same-day AWV+E/M pairs lacking modifier and distinct diagnosis. Add a provider/TIN-level monitor computing AWV share of all visits and AWVs per rendering NPI per day versus same-specialty peers, and auto-trigger a prepay documentation request for the wellness record (HRA, prevention plan, risk factors) on a rotating sample once a provider exceeds the calibrated percentile, escalating to prepay review of all AWV lines.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Total Access Urgent Care (TAUC); Dr. Nehal Modh (Festus pain management physician); two unnamed Jefferson County chiropractors; Dr. Amy Swegan (physician); Dr. Ashu Joshi (physician)
State_County: Missouri - St. Louis; Missouri - Jefferson County (Festus)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Annual collections announcement covering several health care matters: civil False Claims Act settlements for allegedly false claims for medical services by Total Access Urgent Care ($9.1 million) and pain management physician Dr. Nehal Modh ($1.2 million); nearly $1 million criminally collected in a continuing case where two Jefferson County chiropractors helped patients obtain disability payments fraudulently (27 patients pleaded guilty and were ordered to repay); and about $628,000 garnished from Dr. Amy Swegan, who admitted taking kickbacks from telemedicine companies in a nationwide fraud scheme. Figures span multiple defendants and cases; the listed SettlementAmt reflects the two civil false-claims settlements.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual collections round-up spanning several unrelated matters, so there is no single mechanic; the payer-relevant threads are urgent-care/pain-management billing for services not rendered, chiropractors manufacturing disability documentation, and a physician taking telemedicine-company kickbacks to sign orders. The catchable signals at adjudication are urgent-care/pain E/M and injection volumes per provider-day versus peers, and telehealth-sourced orders where the ordering physician has no prior or subsequent treating relationship with the beneficiary and signs orders across many distant states. Disability-certification fraud sits with the disability program rather than the claims system, and is detected by cross-matching a small set of certifying chiropractors to a disproportionate share of approved claimants.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-physician feature that, per NPI per month, computes the count of orders/prescriptions for beneficiaries with no other claim from that physician, the geographic spread of those beneficiaries, and the concentration of orders arriving from a single telehealth vendor's roster; above the calibrated percentile, prepay-suspend the downstream DME/lab/pharmacy claims tied to that orderer and request the encounter record. Add a provider-day service-intensity monitor for urgent care and pain management (units and procedures per rendering NPI per day) firing prepay review, and a certifier-concentration report for disability/attending-physician statements that flags certifiers whose share of approved claims exceeds peers for investigative referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Dr. Frank Li (physician, medical office owner)
SchemeSummary: In an annual collections announcement, the office reported obtaining $217,000 from the sale of Dr. Frank Li's Spokane medical office building, applied toward his $2.85 million civil settlement for health care fraud; no details of the underlying billing scheme are given.
WaysToIdentify: The release gives only an asset-sale collection against an existing settlement, so nothing is identifiable from the facts stated; the payer-side control is on the back end — tracking settled/convicted providers' assets and ownership interests so restitution is collectible, and ensuring the provider and any successor practices are flagged in enrolment. Prospectively, the practical prepay hook is that a provider under FCA settlement or corporate integrity obligations should be on a heightened-review list, and any new NPI sharing his address, staff or bank account should be linked to him.
FeaturesToCreate: Maintain a settled/sanctioned-provider registry that automatically places the provider's NPI/TIN on prepay review for the settlement term and links, via a shared-identifier graph (address, phone, bank account, billing agent, staff NPIs), any newly enrolling entity to that provider for enrolment scrutiny. Pair it with a debt-offset feature that withholds current-claim payments against outstanding FCA/restitution balances for the same TIN or successor entity.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Edward William Salko, D.O. (physician); Jackson & Coker LocumTenens, LLC (health care staffing company); Justin Leland (owner of Spokane Valley medical supply company)
State_County: Washington - Benton County (Richland); Washington - Spokane County (Spokane Valley)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: In an annual collections announcement, the office reported health care recoveries including $700,000 in civil collections from physician Edward William Salko and Jackson & Coker LocumTenens, LLC, and $224,620 from Justin Leland, based on allegations they took part in kickback schemes in which Medicare was billed for medically unnecessary durable medical equipment and diagnostic laboratory testing (figures span multiple defendants and separate settlements).
WaysToIdentify: Classic order-mill kickback pattern: a physician (here supplied through a locum-tenens staffing company) signs DME and diagnostic lab orders for beneficiaries he never treated, so the ordering NPI appears on DME/lab claims with no corresponding E/M claim, and orders cluster in remote geographies and arrive through one or two supplier/marketing entities. At adjudication the payer can see order-to-treating-relationship gaps, brace/orthosis and panel-test volume per orderer versus same-specialty peers, and identical code combinations across unrelated beneficiaries. Kickback payments themselves surface only post-payment through financial records or whistleblowers, but the billing footprint is prepay-visible.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-provider risk score at NPI-month level: share of ordered DME/lab claims for beneficiaries with no prior/subsequent E/M by that provider, count of distinct downstream suppliers and states, and order volume versus same-specialty peers; above the calibrated percentile, prepay-suspend affected DME/lab lines and issue documentation requests for medical necessity and the treating encounter. Add a supplier-side concentration edit that flags any DME supplier or lab whose orders concentrate on a small set of orderers or a single staffing/telehealth vendor, and route those claims to prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Unnamed network of healthcare companies (telehealth psychological care providers); Unnamed operators of Connecticut dental practices
SchemeSummary: Annual collections release noting two health care civil recoveries: approximately $4.5 million from a network of healthcare companies alleged to have submitted false claims to Medicare and Connecticut Medicaid for telehealth psychological care services, and more than $1 million from operators of Connecticut dental practices alleged to have paid patient recruiters to steer Connecticut Medicaid patients to their practice. Figures span multiple unnamed defendants.
WaysToIdentify: For the telehealth psychology network, the prepay signals are billed therapy units per rendering clinician per day (impossible session counts), identical session lengths/codes across members, unlicensed or non-credentialed staff behind a supervising NPI, and clusters of related corporate entities sharing addresses and billing agents. For the dental patient-recruiter scheme, the signals are Medicaid patients travelling implausible distances to one practice, sudden surges of new members from specific ZIP codes or group-home/recruiter addresses, and members sharing an address or phone with practice-affiliated recruiters. Actual kickback payments to recruiters are provable only post-payment via financial records and interviews.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-clinician-day capacity edit for psychotherapy codes (total timed units and distinct members per licensed NPI per day, cross-entity within the network graph) that denies or pends lines exceeding a feasible workday and validates licensure/credential status on every line. For dental, build a member-origination monitor per practice computing new-patient volume by ZIP, member-to-practice distance, and shared member address/phone clusters versus same-specialty peers, firing prepay review plus a marketing/transportation-arrangement disclosure request when concentration exceeds the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Keven Ellis Partin
PayerName: TRICARE; Medicare; Department of Veterans Affairs; Department of Labor
SchemeSummary: In a debt-collection recap press release, the office noted that Keven Ellis Partin pleaded guilty to offering or paying health care kickbacks and was ordered to pay $338,805 in restitution to the Department of Labor, TRICARE, the Department of Veterans Affairs and Medicare; the district recovered $287,521.53 of that in FY2024 through liens and other enforcement tools (other collections listed in the release involve non-health-care bank fraud and drug cases).
WaysToIdentify: The release is a collections recap and gives no billing detail, but the mechanic — paying kickbacks that induce claims to TRICARE, VA, DOL-OWCP and Medicare — leaves the standard cross-payer footprint: the same beneficiaries and the same small set of prescribers/marketers generating high-margin items across multiple federal programs simultaneously. Because DOL/VA/TRICARE adjudicate separately, the signal is best seen by cross-program matching of beneficiary+prescriber+product combinations. Kickback payments themselves require post-payment financial investigation.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a cross-program matching job keyed on beneficiary ID (SSN hash) and ordering NPI that flags beneficiaries with concurrent high-cost DME/compound/lab claims in two or more of Medicare, TRICARE, VA and DOL-OWCP within a short window, and prescribers appearing in that pattern above the calibrated percentile; fire prepay suspension and a medical-necessity documentation request. Add a marketer-entity linkage feature (shared phone, address, bank account, billing agent between suppliers and telemarketing firms) to place linked suppliers on prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Shephard Spruill
SchemeSummary: In an annual collections announcement, the office reported recovering over $800,000 that criminal defendant Shephard Spruill had transferred and concealed; Spruill had participated in fraudulent billings to Medicaid by abusing his access to patient information. (The release also notes an unrelated $500,000 recovery from Michael Robinson for USDA farm assistance program fraud.)
WaysToIdentify: Insider misuse of patient identifiers to generate billings shows up as claims for members whose only recent utilization comes from one provider or billing agent, with members who never appear at the location, plus a spike in new-member claims traceable to the employee's access account. Access-log analytics (which staff account viewed which member records, versus which members were subsequently billed) is the discriminating data, and it lives with the provider/plan rather than the claim, so combine it with beneficiary-verification mailings and EOB/explanation-of-benefits response rates. Concealment of proceeds is post-payment; asset-tracing follows conviction.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a beneficiary-verification loop: for provider-month cohorts of newly billed members with no prior relationship to the provider, sample and mail/IVR service-verification notices and treat non-response plus beneficiary denial as a trigger for prepay suspension of that provider's claims. Add an identity-integrity edit flagging claims where member demographics conflict with service location distance, where many members share a contact phone/address, or where a member's identifiers were recently accessed by a staff account under investigation, and require documentation before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
FraudEntity: Guidehouse, Inc. (federal contractor); Nan McKay and Associates (subcontractor); Richard J. Sherwood; Thomas K. Lagan; Derek R. Schwartz; Michael T. Mann (former ValueWise CEO)
State_County: New York - Northern District of New York
FraudTypeAll: Other - Unknown; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Annual collections announcement, not a single health care fraud case: the Northern District of New York's Asset Recovery Unit collected $39,262,324 in FY2024, including an $11.3 million False Claims Act settlement with Guidehouse and subcontractor Nan McKay for failing to perform required cybersecurity testing on a federally funded COVID-era rental-assistance application website, $4,950,440 restored to victims of Sherwood and Lagan's theft of approximately $11.8 million from three sisters' estates, and $1 million recovered from Derek Schwartz (sentenced to 72 months) for conspiring with ValueWise CEO Michael Mann to defraud lenders to ValueWise subsidiaries. Figures span multiple unrelated defendants and cases.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual district collections announcement with no health care claims component: the underlying matters are a cybersecurity-testing FCA settlement on a rental-assistance website, estate theft, and lender fraud. No claims-adjudication signal exists. The nearest applicable federal control is contract/grant oversight — verifying that contractually required deliverables (here, security testing artifacts) were actually performed before invoices are paid.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side claims control applies; instead build an invoice-to-deliverable verification gate for federally funded contracts that withholds payment on any invoice line tied to a required test/certification until the artifact (penetration-test report, attestation, scan output) is uploaded and validated. Add contractor-level flags for repeated missing-deliverable invoices to trigger audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon
FraudEntity: Riverpark Operations, LLC (operator of Avamere Riverpark of Eugene skilled nursing facility); Avamere Group, LLC (parent company)
SchemeSummary: Riverpark billed Medicare and Oregon Medicaid for skilled nursing facility services at its 119-bed Eugene facility that were allegedly grossly substandard because staffing fell below minimum requirements, leading to preventable urinary tract infections, pressure sores and falls; Riverpark and parent Avamere paid $2 million and entered a five-year Quality-of-Care Corporate Integrity Agreement with HHS-OIG.
WaysToIdentify: Grossly substandard SNF care is measurable pre-payment by joining payroll-based staffing data to daily census: nurse and aide hours per resident-day falling below required minimums on many days, in the same periods the facility bills full skilled per-diems. Corroborating claim-side signals include facility-acquired UTI, pressure-ulcer and fall-related diagnoses and transfers appearing on resident claims at rates above same-size peers, plus survey deficiency history and high staff turnover. The quality failure is detectable from the payer's own PBJ, MDS, survey and claims data before per-diem payment cycles close.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a facility-day feature joining payroll-based journal hours to census to compute HPRD by discipline, and a facility-month rate of resident harm indicators (UTI, stage 2+ pressure ulcer, fall with injury, weight loss, dehydration transfers) risk-adjusted against same-size peers; fire when HPRD is below the required minimum on a sustained share of days or harm rates exceed the calibrated percentile. Action: place the facility on prepay review with medical-record/MDS documentation requests for the affected stays, notify the survey agency, and condition continued payment on a quality-of-care corrective plan.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Amstrong Chapajong (personal care aide and community support worker); Michelle Shropshire (WMATA employee); Harlisha Jones (WMATA employee); Sharon Washington (WMATA employee); Selethia Blake (WMATA employee); Brady Turner (WMATA employee); Lushawn Foreman (WMATA employee); Margot Jackson (WMATA employee)
State_County: District of Columbia (Washington, DC); Maryland; Virginia
PayerName: Medicaid (District of Columbia Medicaid program); American Family Life Assurance Company of Columbus (AFLAC)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Two D.C. cases charged as part of the 2025 national takedown: Chapajong, working as both a personal care aide and community support worker, billed D.C. Medicaid for in-home personal care and behavioral health services to multiple clients in different places at the same time, with EVV data showing he was not near clients' homes (Medicaid paid $461,369); separately, WMATA employees Shropshire and Jones and other co-workers submitted fraudulent AFLAC health care and short-term disability claims using forged medical excuse notes and physician statements for injuries and treatments that never occurred, with Jones kicking back about 20% of the roughly $58,750 she received to Shropshire (AFLAC paid at least $362,035 on the other employees' false claims). Figures span multiple defendants; Shropshire was later sentenced to 24 months.
WaysToIdentify: For the D.C. Medicaid aide, the payer already holds the disproving data: EVV check-in/out GPS and timestamps show the aide away from the client's home and overlapping shifts with different clients, and the same person billing simultaneously as a personal care aide and community support worker creates same-time-different-place conflicts detectable at adjudication. For the AFLAC disability claims, the signals are forged physician statements — provider NPIs/signatures that don't match the licensing registry or that appear across many claimants from one employer — plus clusters of claimants sharing an employer, work unit and bank/address, and kickback-sized transfers between claimants.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an aide-level overlap edit that rejects any personal care or community-support claim line whose service interval overlaps another line by the same rendering caregiver, and a geofence edit that denies or pends lines where EVV GPS distance from the client's registered address exceeds tolerance or where EVV is missing/manually keyed above the calibrated percentile. For disability/supplemental claims, build a certifier-verification check against the state licensure and NPPES registries with automated flagging of duplicate or reused excuse-note templates, and an employer-cluster monitor that pends claims when claimants from one employer unit spike or share contact/bank identifiers pending document authentication with the treating provider.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Medisca, Inc.; Booz Allen Hamilton; Elara Caring and subsidiaries (hospice provider); Ma Acupuncture Center and Dr. Dongxin Ma; Five Point Enterprises LLC; Lafayette RE Management LLC and Thibault Adrien; Freedom Solar LLC; Oncology San Antonio and Dr. Jayasree Rao; Dr. Alfonso Luevano; Shrieve Chemical Company LLC; Sachnikumar Patel, RPh., Medical Arts Pharmacy, and Express Pharmacy
State_County: Texas - Western District of Texas (San Antonio; El Paso)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Upcoding; FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Annual roundup of over 25 civil enforcement recoveries totaling $55,969,678.60 by the Western District of Texas in 2024, spanning multiple defendants: Medisca allegedly reported false and inflated Average Wholesale Prices for compounding ingredients ($21.75M); Elara Caring allegedly billed hospice services for patients who were not terminally ill ($4.2M); Ma Acupuncture Center/Dr. Ma allegedly submitted inflated acupuncture bills to the VA ($2.3M judgment); Oncology San Antonio/Dr. Rao allegedly paid unlawful kickbacks and billed medically unnecessary tests and treatments ($1.3M); Dr. Luevano and pharmacy defendants allegedly issued/dispensed unlawful controlled-substance prescriptions; and PPP borrowers allegedly made false certifications to obtain or have loans forgiven. Figures span multiple unrelated defendants.
WaysToIdentify: Each thread has its own prepay signal: AWP-based compounding-ingredient pricing can be validated against independent acquisition-cost benchmarks and invoice audits before reimbursement; hospice claims for non-terminal patients show up as long lengths of stay, live discharges, absent decline in functional/diagnostic data and non-hospice-typical diagnoses; inflated acupuncture and oncology billing shows as units per patient-day and add-on test volumes above same-specialty peers with kickback-linked referral concentration; and controlled-substance prescribing is testable against MME/day, distance travelled and prescriber-pharmacy pair concentration. PPP false certifications are not a claims matter and are checked by matching applicant EINs against common-ownership and employee-count data.
FeaturesToCreate: Build (a) a drug-pricing validation feature comparing manufacturer-reported AWP/WAC for compounding ingredients to independently surveyed acquisition cost, pending claims priced above tolerance; (b) a hospice election-level monitor of length of stay, live-discharge rate, and absence of decline markers versus peers, firing a certification/medical-record request before continued-period payment; (c) provider-day unit-intensity edits for acupuncture and oncology add-ons with referral-concentration scoring; and (d) prescriber MME and prescriber-pharmacy concentration monitors triggering prepay suspension. For PPP-type programs, add an affiliation check joining applicant EINs by common ownership before disbursement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: David A. Parks (physician); James M. Bilderback (clinical manager and clinical research coordinator); Michelle J. Scheer (front desk assistant)
PayerName: Medicare; Missouri Medicaid; private health insurers
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a St. Louis clinic physician, clinical manager and front desk assistant conspired to prescribe controlled substances outside the usual course of professional practice to maximize patient volume and profit, and that Parks and Bilderback billed Medicare, Missouri Medicaid and private insurers for services falsely identifying Parks as the rendering provider, including while he was out of the country.
WaysToIdentify: Billing a physician as rendering provider while he was out of the country is directly testable: cross-check claim service dates against the provider's own absence markers — no other claims, no e-prescribing/PDMP activity, hospital privilege logs, and (post-payment) travel records — and against implausible daily volumes for one NPI when non-physician staff actually saw patients. Pill-mill prescribing shows in PDMP as high MME/day, uniform drug cocktails, short visit intervals, cash-heavy patient mix and patients travelling long distances to one clinic and a few pharmacies. Clinic-level signals include one physician's NPI attached to visits at multiple sites simultaneously.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a rendering-provider attribution edit that pends claims when the billed rendering NPI exceeds a feasible patient-count/units-per-day threshold, when the same NPI is billed at overlapping times across locations, or when the NPI shows a continuous multi-day service run with zero independent corroborating activity (no e-prescribe, no facility encounter) — requiring attestation and schedule/sign-in documentation before payment. Add a prescriber-level controlled-substance monitor (MME/day, same-cocktail share, patient travel distance, pharmacy concentration) that triggers prepay review of the clinic's E/M and drug claims and a PDMP/DEA referral above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Kentucky
SchemeSummary: Annual statistical press release rather than a single fraud case: the Eastern District of Kentucky reported collecting over $20 million for crime victims and taxpayers in FY2024 (including $14,299,361.43 through its Financial Litigation Program and asset forfeitures) and obtaining $20,078,263.98 in civil settlements and judgments, of which over $19.7 million came from False Claims Act enforcement and more than $300,000 from civil penalties paid by healthcare providers who violated the Controlled Substances Act. No individual defendant, payer, or scheme is identified.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual district statistics release with no identified defendant, payer or scheme, so there is nothing to detect pre-payment; the only substantive payer-relevant element is the recurring category of providers paying civil penalties for Controlled Substances Act recordkeeping/dispensing violations. Those are detectable from dispensing and inventory data rather than claims narratives.
FeaturesToCreate: No case-specific control applies; the nearest useful build is a registrant-level dispensing-integrity monitor that reconciles billed/dispensed controlled-substance quantities to wholesaler purchase (ARCOS-style) data by NDC per pharmacy per month and flags unexplained gaps or excess for audit. Feed CSA penalty and settlement outcomes back into the provider risk registry so affected NPIs are placed on prepay controlled-substance review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Graciela Venegas, aka "Graciela Salgado" (U.S. Postal Service employee)
PayerName: U.S. Department of Labor (federal workers' compensation program); U.S. Postal Service
SchemeSummary: Venegas, a USPS employee receiving federal workers' compensation benefits since 2012, allegedly continued to claim her spouse as a dependent after their 2013 divorce and his 2014 death, thereby collecting augmented monthly benefits equal to an extra 8 1/3 percent of her pre-injury pay and pocketing $51,776 in unentitled payments from 2013 to 2024. Charged with five counts of wire fraud and one false statement to the U.S. Department of Labor.
WaysToIdentify: Not a claims-payment scheme — this is benefit eligibility fraud against DOL workers' compensation, and it is catchable by automated periodic matching of the claimant's certified dependents against the Social Security Death Master File and state vital records (spouse died 2014) and against divorce/marital-status records or IRS filing status. The augmented-rate flag persisted for a decade because dependency was self-certified and never re-verified.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an annual dependency-recertification job that matches every augmented-rate claimant's listed dependents (SSN/name/DOB) against the Death Master File, state marriage/divorce indices and tax filing status, and automatically suspends the augmentation and issues a verification demand on any death or marital-status mismatch. Add a rule that the augmented percentage cannot be paid without a dated recertification inside the current cycle.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Unified Care Services LLC (skilled nursing facility chain); Emmanual David (owner); Casa Montana LLC; Geri-Care Inc.; Geri Care V LLC; Pacific Palms Healthcare LLC; Foothill Care Center Inc.; Mount Megiddo LLC; Canyon Properties III LLC; Cloverleaf Enterprises Inc.; Foothill Care Center LLC; Foothill Care Center II LLC; David Kleis III LLC; David Kleis II LLC; Miramonte Enterprises LLC; Washington Enterprises III LLC
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: A chain of skilled nursing facilities and its owner allegedly falsely certified on PPP loan and loan-forgiveness applications in 2020 that each applying entity was a small business with fewer than 500 employees, concealing that the entities were part of a larger commonly owned and controlled chain that made them ineligible for PPP loans; they agreed to pay $18 million to resolve the qui tam FCA suit, with $2,070,000 going to the whistleblower.
WaysToIdentify: Not a claims scheme but a loan-eligibility one, and it was detectable at application: the applying entities shared common ownership and control, and the payer/agency already holds the linkage data — Medicare/Medicaid enrolment ownership disclosures (PECOS), shared owners, officers, addresses, EINs and management companies — which aggregate to well over the employee cap. Aggregated payroll reported across affiliated entities in the same chain would also exceed the size standard.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pre-disbursement affiliation check that resolves each applicant EIN into an ownership graph using provider-enrolment ownership disclosures, state corporate filings and shared address/officer/bank identifiers, sums employees and payroll across the resolved group, and blocks or holds the application when the aggregate exceeds the program size standard. Retain the same graph for forgiveness review and for Medicare/Medicaid chain-level risk scoring.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: People's Rx, Inc., d/b/a The People's Pharmacy Shoppe (pharmacy)
PayerName: Medicare Part D; New Jersey Medicaid
SchemeSummary: The pharmacy submitted claims to Medicare Part D and New Jersey Medicaid for prescription drugs never dispensed to beneficiaries; wholesaler inventory records showed it had not purchased enough of the medications to fill the prescriptions it billed. It agreed to pay $995,420 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: The disproving data is inventory: billed dispensed quantities by NDC exceeded what the pharmacy ever purchased from wholesalers, a reconciliation the payer/PBM can run monthly against wholesaler and 340B/ARCOS-style purchase reporting. Supporting prepay signals include very high per-beneficiary drug costs, refills without patient contact, high-cost NDC concentration versus same-region pharmacy peers, and beneficiaries living far from the pharmacy. Beneficiary verification letters on high-dollar fills provide independent confirmation.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a pharmacy-NDC-month reconciliation feature computing billed dispensed units minus verified wholesaler purchase units (plus opening inventory), flagging any negative balance and immediately suspending payment on that NDC pending invoice production. Add a prepay edit requiring purchase-invoice documentation for high-cost NDCs when a pharmacy's cost-per-beneficiary or single-NDC share exceeds same-region peer percentiles, plus sampled beneficiary receipt verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Premier Medical, Inc. (clinical laboratory); Kevin S. Murdock (former CEO and owner of Premier Medical); Michael Conroy (former Vice President of Compliance, Premier Medical); Freedom Medical Labs, LLC (marketing/referral entity); Robert Alan Richardson (Freedom Medical); Edward Burch (Freedom Medical)
PayerName: Medicaid (Georgia Medicaid; Colorado Medicaid; South Carolina Medicaid)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Premier Medical and its owner paid kickbacks to Freedom Medical marketers who set up tables at bus stops, dollar stores and street corners in low-income areas of GA, CO and SC, paid Medicaid beneficiaries up to $20 for DNA swabs, and bought telemedicine physician orders from providers with no treating relationship; Premier then billed state Medicaid programs up to roughly $12,000 per cancer genetic (CGX) test. Judgments/settlements total over $114 million across all defendants (Premier default judgment $71,015,255.70; Murdock consent judgment $27,544,460; Richardson and Freedom Medical $8 million; Burch $8 million; Conroy $15,000), against actual program losses of about $13.77 million.
WaysToIdentify: Textbook CGX swab-mill footprint visible at adjudication: high-dollar cancer genetic panels ordered for beneficiaries with no cancer diagnosis or family-history documentation, orders signed by a handful of telemedicine physicians who have no other claims for those members, beneficiaries clustered by recruitment location and spread across multiple states, and near-identical panel code combinations per member. Beneficiary inducement (cash for swabs) surfaces through complaint lines and verification calls; the marketing contracts and kickback flows require post-payment financial investigation.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a claim-level CGX edit that denies or pends hereditary-cancer panel claims lacking a qualifying diagnosis/family-history indicator or where the ordering NPI has no prior treating-relationship claim with the member, and cap/pend duplicate panels for the same member across labs. Add a lab-month monitor of orders-per-ordering-physician concentration, member geographic dispersion, telehealth-sourced order share and average allowed amount per test versus peers, auto-suspending payment and triggering ordering-physician attestation plus beneficiary verification when the calibrated percentile is exceeded.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
SchemeSummary: Annual statistical announcement rather than a single case: the Middle District of Tennessee U.S. Attorney's Office reported collecting $137,054,515 in FY2024, including $135,738,858 in civil recoveries largely under the False Claims Act (including Medicare and TennCare fraud) and over $59 million in Controlled Substances Act civil penalties, about $4,130,000 in criminal money judgments, and $939,718 in forfeited assets.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual district collections statistic with no named defendant, payer or scheme, so nothing is detectable pre-payment from the release itself; the recurring components are FCA recoveries involving Medicare/TennCare and large Controlled Substances Act civil penalties. Detection would depend on the underlying individual matters, not on this announcement.
FeaturesToCreate: No case-specific control applies; the nearest applicable payer control is a feedback pipeline that ingests FCA settlements, CSA penalties and exclusions into the provider risk registry, automatically placing named NPIs/TINs and their ownership-linked affiliates on prepay review and offsetting outstanding debts against current payments. Pair with a controlled-substance dispensing reconciliation monitor for penalized registrants.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Lafayette Physical Rehabilitation Hospital; Acadiana Management Group (parent company); Dr. Carolyn Smith (physician)
SchemeSummary: In a False Claims Act settlement announced among the district's notable cases, Lafayette Physical Rehabilitation Hospital and its parent Acadiana Management Group paid $1.2 million and Dr. Carolyn Smith agreed to pay $575,000 to resolve allegations that they submitted claims to Medicare for inpatient rehabilitation services that were not medically necessary.
WaysToIdentify: Inpatient rehab facility (IRF) claims carry the signals needed prepay: the admission's pre-admission screening, post-admission physician evaluation, individualized overall plan of care, and the 3-hour therapy rule are all documentation-verifiable, and case-mix group/tier assignment plus the referring physician's NPI are on the claim. A payer could rank IRFs on share of admissions with low-acuity primary diagnoses (e.g. debility, joint replacement without complications), short pre-transfer acute stays, and discharge home without ongoing therapy, and rank the certifying physician on the concentration of IRF certifications they alone sign.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an IRF-level and certifying-physician-level profiling job: per quarter compute share of admissions in low-acuity CMGs, mean therapy minutes documented per day, share of admissions transferred internally from the same corporate acute hospital, and readmission/discharge disposition mix, all versus same-region IRF peers. Above the calibrated percentile, place the facility and the certifying physician on prepay medical-review with mandatory submission of the pre-admission screening, post-admission evaluation and therapy logs before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
SchemeSummary: Not a specific fraud case: this is a press release announcing the departure of U.S. Attorney Dena J. King, noting generally that her office's reconstituted Health Care Fraud Task Force secured settlements with hospitals, telemedicine companies, DME suppliers, physicians and therapists and recovered millions in restitution for Medicare and Medicaid. No individual defendant, conduct period, or dollar amount is identified.
WaysToIdentify: No payer-side control applies to this document: it is a press release about a U.S. Attorney's departure with no defendant, conduct period or billing mechanic. The mixture of provider types mentioned (hospitals, telemedicine, DME, physicians, therapists) reflects the office's caseload, not a single scheme.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control is generic: maintain a cross-payer referral-linkage monitor that joins telehealth ordering NPIs to DME and lab billing NPIs and flags order clusters concentrated on a handful of ordering providers, feeding prepay review. Otherwise no case-specific check can be derived.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Vermont
SchemeSummary: Not a fraud case document: this is a press release announcing the resignation of U.S. Attorney Nikolas Kerest for the District of Vermont, summarizing office accomplishments including a Controlled Substances Act settlement with eBay and recoveries from NextGen (electronic health records) and Vermont defense contractors, without describing any specific health care fraud scheme.
WaysToIdentify: Not a fraud case for claims purposes: this is a resignation announcement referencing a Controlled Substances Act settlement with eBay, an EHR vendor (NextGen) recovery and defense-contractor matters. No billing scheme or claim stream is described, so nothing was detectable at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable payer control is EHR-vendor exposure mapping: record the certified EHR product on attestation/claims metadata and, when a vendor is found to have induced coding behavior, run a retrospective cohort comparison of coding distributions among that vendor's users versus other vendors to target post-payment review. No prepay edit derives from this document.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
SchemeSummary: Not a specific fraud case: the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois announced the creation of a new Healthcare Fraud Section of six prosecutors to pursue upcoding, unbundling, fraudulent billing, and kickback schemes against Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers, noting the office has charged nearly $2 billion in healthcare fraud schemes.
WaysToIdentify: Not a specific case: this announces the creation of a prosecutorial section, with no defendant, dates or dollars, so there is no claim stream a payer could have screened.
FeaturesToCreate: Nearest applicable control is standing coding-integrity surveillance: monthly provider-level E&M level distribution, unbundling (NCCI pair) rates and modifier override rates versus same-specialty peers, with above-percentile outliers routed to prepay documentation requests. No case-specific check exists.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California; U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Barco Uniforms Inc. (apparel seller/importer); Kenny Chan (operator of supplier companies); David Chan (operator of supplier companies); Able Allied Limited; Nathan Global Direct Inc.; J&K Garment Inc.; Mega Goodwill Ltd.; JS Garment Co.; Superway Import & Export Inc.
SchemeSummary: The United States intervened in a qui tam False Claims Act suit alleging that Barco Uniforms and Chan-controlled supplier companies used a double-invoicing scheme, submitting false entry summaries to U.S. Customs and Border Protection that undervalued garments imported from China and elsewhere, thereby reducing and underpaying customs duties owed; the underpayment allegedly continued after a third-party auditor warned Barco about duty-calculation risks.
WaysToIdentify: This is customs duty evasion via double invoicing, not health care claims; no payer adjudication event exists. The detectable route is on the import side: comparing declared unit values on CBP entry summaries against the importer's own purchase ledgers and against industry unit-value benchmarks for the same garment HTS codes and country of origin, plus the existence of a third-party audit warning that went unremediated.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The analogous control for a purchasing agency is a supplier price-integrity job: for each vendor and item, compare invoiced/declared unit values against contract price files and peer-vendor unit-value distributions for the same commodity code, and hold payment on entries where the same shipment appears at two different values across document sets.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Aetna, Inc. and affiliates (Medicare Advantage insurer); Elevance Health, Inc. (formerly Anthem) (Medicare Advantage insurer); Humana Inc. (Medicare Advantage insurer); eHealth, Inc. and an affiliate (insurance broker); GoHealth, Inc. (insurance broker); SelectQuote, Inc. (insurance broker)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: The United States intervened in a qui tam False Claims Act suit alleging that Aetna, Elevance/Anthem and Humana paid hundreds of millions of dollars in kickbacks, disguised as marketing or other payments, to broker organizations eHealth, GoHealth and SelectQuote in exchange for steering Medicare beneficiaries into their Medicare Advantage plans regardless of suitability; Aetna and Humana also allegedly threatened to withhold these payments to pressure brokers to enroll fewer disabled beneficiaries perceived as less profitable.
WaysToIdentify: This is detectable in plan-side data rather than claim lines: enrollment records tie each beneficiary to a broker/agent ID, and the plan's own general-ledger payments to broker organizations can be compared against regulated commission and administrative-payment caps, with excess labeled 'marketing', 'co-op advertising' or 'technology fees'. Signals include broker organizations whose per-enrollee total compensation from a plan exceeds allowable commission structures, and enrollment mix by broker showing under-representation of disability-eligible or high-risk beneficiaries versus the plan's service-area demographics.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a broker-compensation reconciliation: per plan-year and per broker entity, sum all payments of any label divided by net new enrollments and flag where non-commission payments exceed allowable compensation, requiring documentation of bona fide services and fair market value. Second, a broker-level enrollment-mix check computing share of disability-eligible/ESRD/high-risk-score enrollees versus service-area eligible population, firing when a broker's mix is below the calibrated percentile across multiple plans; escalate to marketing-misconduct review and payment suspension of the broker arrangement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Delaware
FraudEntity: Dr. Shayasta S. Mufti (physician)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleges Dr. Mufti referred more than 100 Medicare beneficiaries for expensive, medically unnecessary genetic laboratory tests based on brief telemedicine consultations or no consultation at all, without any treating relationship, examination, or use of results to manage patients' conditions, causing Medicare to pay claims of thousands of dollars per patient.
WaysToIdentify: Every element is on the claims: the ordering NPI on high-cost molecular/CGx lab claims, whether that NPI has any prior or subsequent evaluative claim history with the beneficiary, and whether the telehealth visit was a brief low-level code billed the same day as the order. A payer can flag ordering physicians whose CGx orders vastly exceed their own patient panel, whose ordered tests concentrate at one or two labs, and where no result-driven follow-up service appears in the following months.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit at the lab claim level: deny or pend high-cost genetic panels where the ordering NPI has no evaluation/management or specialty claim for that beneficiary within a lookback window, or where the only linked encounter is a brief telehealth code billed on or within days of the order. Add an ordering-provider counter — distinct beneficiaries with CGx orders per month, share of orders routed to a single lab TIN, and share lacking downstream management — and suspend the ordering NPI's lab-order authority for documentation review above the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Georgia; U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Vohra Wound Physicians Management LLC; Dr. Ameet Vohra (founder and majority owner); VHS Holdings, PA
SchemeSummary: DOJ alleges Vohra, a nationwide bedside wound care provider serving nursing homes and skilled nursing facilities, programmed its proprietary EMR to bill nonsurgical debridements as higher-paying surgical debridements, hired physicians without wound care expertise and trained them with misleading Medicare rules, and set revenue-driven debridement targets, causing medically unnecessary and upcoded Medicare claims. The EMR also automatically appended Modifier 25 to E&M claims so exams already included in the global surgical debridement package were separately billed.
WaysToIdentify: The mechanic is visible in code distributions: surgical debridement CPTs versus non-surgical/active wound care codes, per rendering physician and per group, plus a near-universal Modifier 25 rate on same-day E&M with a global-period procedure. A payer can also compare the physician's specialty/credentialing record (no wound care training) with a practice consisting almost entirely of surgical debridement, and compute debridements per patient per month across nursing-home rosters, which shows scheduled targets rather than clinical need.
FeaturesToCreate: Provider- and group-level monthly profiling: ratio of surgical to non-surgical debridement codes, Modifier 25 append rate on E&M paired with global-period wound procedures, and debridements per resident per month, each versus same-specialty peers. Fire a prepay edit denying Modifier 25 E&M when append rate exceeds the calibrated percentile and requiring the operative note (depth, tissue removed, instrument) for surgical debridement claims; escalate group-wide when the pattern is uniform across many rendering NPIs sharing one EMR/TIN.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: AIMA Business and Medical Support, LLC (medical billing and compliance company); Aaron Liston (CEO); Excellent Laboratories Inc. d/b/a Selecta Laboratory (diagnostic laboratory)
SchemeSummary: The government alleges AIMA, a billing and compliance company with a UK-based CEO and India-based staff, submitted approximately $15.18 million in Medicare Part B claims for genetic tests on behalf of Miami lab Excellent Laboratories (d/b/a Selecta Laboratory) despite knowing the tests were not medically necessary and were not ordered by beneficiaries' treating physicians; Selecta collected Medicare funds and paid AIMA for its billing services.
WaysToIdentify: Two prepay signals: the billing agent's identity and the ordering-physician linkage. Claims from many unrelated labs sharing one billing agent's submitter ID, IP geography outside the U.S., and identical claim templates are visible at the clearinghouse layer; separately, the ordering NPIs on Selecta's genetic claims had no treating relationship with the beneficiaries, checkable against the beneficiary's own claim history and geography (patient state versus ordering physician state versus lab state).
FeaturesToCreate: Build a submitter/billing-agent risk profile: cluster claims by EDI submitter ID and originating IP/geolocation, compute total billed genetic-test dollars and number of distinct billing TINs per submitter, and flag submitters with concentrated high-cost CGx volume for prepay review of all downstream labs. Pair with an ordering-relationship edit that pends genetic panels where the ordering NPI has no prior claim for the beneficiary or is more than a calibrated distance from the beneficiary's residence, and suspend payments to a new-ish lab whose CGx billing ramps above the calibrated percentile within months of enrollment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Local Initiative Health Authority for Inland Empire Health Plan d/b/a Inland Empire Health Plan (IEHP) (California Local Initiative Medi-Cal managed care health plan)
State_County: California - San Bernardino County (Rancho Cucamonga); California - Riverside County
SchemeSummary: The United States alleges IEHP, which received Medi-Cal Expansion funding required to be spent at least 85% on allowed medical expenses, avoided repaying surplus funds by creating sham provider 'incentive programs' and an extra-contractual retroactive rate increase - funneling payments for consultants, technology services, administrative costs and other patient populations through providers and backdating spending - and made false statements to DHCS (relayed to the federal government) about the nature, timing and purpose of those payments so it could retain the overpayment rather than return it.
WaysToIdentify: This is a managed-care MLR/medical-loss reporting issue, detectable at settlement rather than at claim adjudication: the state can reconcile the plan's reported 'allowed medical expense' line items back to encounter data and to provider contracts. Red flags are large lump-sum 'incentive' payments to providers with no encounter-level basis, retroactive rate increases outside the contract, payments booked in the reporting period but dated or approved after period close, and pass-through payments whose ultimate recipients are consultants or IT vendors.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an MLR attestation audit engine: for each plan-year, require line-item mapping of every claimed medical expense to either an encounter record or a contractually documented value-based arrangement, and flag any incentive/withhold pool whose dollars per attributed member exceed the calibrated percentile or that lacks pre-period written quality metrics. Add a backdating detector comparing general-ledger entry/approval timestamps and contract amendment execution dates to period end, and withhold surplus-refund settlement pending documentation for flagged pools.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California
FraudEntity: Local Initiative Health Authority for Inland Empire Health Plan d/b/a Inland Empire Health Plan (IEHP) (California Local Initiative Medi-Cal managed care health plan)
State_County: California - Riverside County and San Bernardino County (Rancho Cucamonga)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleges IEHP, which received Medi-Cal Expansion funding requiring at least 85% be spent on allowed medical expenses or refunded, misspent surplus funds through sham provider 'incentive' programs and an extra-contractual retroactive rate increase, disguising administrative, consultant and technology spending as incentive payments funneled through providers and backdating spending, while making false statements to DHCS (relayed to the federal government) to avoid repaying the difference.
WaysToIdentify: Same mechanic as the companion matter: retention of Medicaid expansion surplus by relabeling administrative, consultant and technology spending as provider incentive payments. Detectable at the state's 85% minimum-spend reconciliation by tracing reported medical expenses to encounter data and to executed contracts, and by testing whether provider payments were passed through to non-provider vendors or dated after the close of the measurement period.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement a surplus-reconciliation control that requires encounter-level or contract-level substantiation for every dollar counted toward the minimum medical-expense floor, rejecting lump sums with no member attribution, no pre-established metric, or an amendment executed after period end. Compute per-provider incentive dollars per attributed member versus peer plans and flag above the calibrated percentile; hold the refund determination and issue a documentation request before accepting the plan's certification.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania; DOJ Civil Division
FraudEntity: ProMedica Health System, Inc. (owner/operator); HCR ManorCare Inc. (affiliate); ProMedica Skilled Nursing and Rehabilitation - Pottstown; ProMedica Skilled Nursing and Rehabilitation - Riverview; ProMedica Skilled Nursing, Rehabilitation - Greenville East; ProMedica Skilled Nursing and Rehabilitation - Imperial
State_County: Pennsylvania - Pottstown; Ohio; South Carolina - Greenville; Virginia
SchemeSummary: The United States intervened in a qui tam FCA suit alleging four ProMedica/HCR ManorCare skilled nursing facilities billed federal health care programs for non-existent or grossly substandard nursing care from 2017-2023, failing to develop or follow individualized care plans (inadequate wound care, hygiene/showers, and feeding assistance causing severe weight loss), and falsely documented in resident medical records that services had been provided when they had not.
WaysToIdentify: Staffing and assessment data expose this before per-diem claims are paid: payroll-based staffing hours per resident-day versus reported acuity, MDS-reported care needs (pressure ulcers, weight loss, feeding assistance) versus care-plan and treatment documentation, and survey/complaint history. Claims that bill full skilled nursing per-diems while nurse-hours-per-resident-day sit below the calibrated percentile and MDS shows worsening weight loss and new-onset facility-acquired wounds are the observable signal; charting-time metadata showing block-entry documentation is a second signal available on audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Facility-level monthly job joining payroll staffing data, MDS assessments and claims: compute nursing hours per resident-day adjusted for case mix, incidence of facility-acquired pressure ulcers and significant unplanned weight loss, and MDS-versus-claim acuity mismatch. When multiple indicators fall/rise past calibrated percentiles, place the facility on prepay review requiring individualized care plans and treatment records for a sampled census, and escalate to payment suspension where documentation contradicts staffing capacity.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland; U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Dr. Richard Akoto, M.D. (family medical doctor); Richard O. Akoto, M.D. PC (his medical practice)
SchemeSummary: Akoto treated patients' pain with non-invasive auricular electro-acupuncture (P-Stim) devices taped behind the ear, a service Medicare does not cover, but billed Medicare using the code for surgical implantation of an implantable neurostimulator, a complex neurosurgical procedure, resulting in a $1,407,493.23 False Claims Act judgment against him and his practice.
WaysToIdentify: placeholder
FeaturesToCreate: placeholder

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Dr. Mohd Azfar Malik (psychiatrist, part-owner of Behavioral Health Services, LLC, which owned and operated Psych Care Consultants)
PayerName: Medicare; Missouri Medicaid; private health insurers
SchemeSummary: Psychiatrist billed Medicare, Missouri Medicaid and private insurers for face-to-face psychotherapy sessions he did not personally provide, including claims submitted while he was out of state or out of the country and for services actually rendered by other practitioners; resolved by a $501,556 FCA settlement (double the $250,778 restitution) alongside an April 2025 guilty plea to making false statements in health care matters.
WaysToIdentify: Two adjudication-time signals: impossible-day/volume tests on time-based psychotherapy codes (summed service minutes per rendering NPI per day exceeding a plausible workday) and provider-absence evidence, which appears as claims dated when the physician has no other footprint or as service locations far from the beneficiary. Rendering-versus-supervising NPI mismatch is also checkable, since services actually delivered by other practitioners were billed under his NPI without incident-to/supervision requirements met.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a time-based-service accumulator: per rendering NPI per date of service, sum required minutes for all timed psychotherapy/E&M codes and fire a prepay edit when the total exceeds a plausible-day threshold or when the same NPI bills at two locations that are geographically incompatible. Add a cross-check against the practice's licensed staff roster and scheduling data via documentation request when one NPI's rendered volume exceeds the peer percentile while other practitioners at the same TIN bill almost nothing.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: RegalCare Management Group, LLC; RegalCare Management 2.0, LLC (management companies); 19 skilled nursing facilities in Massachusetts and Connecticut; Eliyahu Mirlis (owner); Hector Caraballo (executive); Stern Therapy Consultants (therapy consultant)
State_County: Massachusetts - Amesbury; Massachusetts - Danvers; Massachusetts - Greenfield; Massachusetts - Harwich; Massachusetts - Holyoke; Massachusetts - Lowell; Massachusetts - Quincy; Massachusetts - Saugus; Massachusetts - Taunton; Massachusetts - Worcester; Connecticut
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (MassHealth and its managed care organizations)
SchemeSummary: Civil False Claims Act complaint (government intervention in a qui tam suit) alleging that RegalCare's skilled nursing facilities systematically billed Medicare for the highest level of skilled rehabilitation therapy and MassHealth for inflated long-term care services that patients did not clinically need, with an executive altering patient records beyond his licensing level to support the billing and the therapy consultant scheduling unnecessary therapy and pressuring therapists to deliver it; claims were also submitted before supporting clinical documentation was complete.
WaysToIdentify: The signature is a therapy-intensity distribution piled at the highest payment tier: share of stays at the top RUG/PDPM therapy or high-acuity case-mix category, therapy minutes clustering just above tier boundaries, and uniform intensity regardless of resident diagnosis or age. Record-integrity signals are also available: EHR audit trails showing assessment fields edited by a non-clinical or out-of-scope executive, and claims submitted with service dates preceding the completion timestamp of the supporting assessment/therapy note.
FeaturesToCreate: Facility-level monthly profiling of top-tier therapy share, minute clustering at tier thresholds, and therapy minutes per resident-day versus same-state SNF peers; above the calibrated percentile, apply prepay review requiring therapy logs and MDS support. Add a claim-level sequencing edit that pends any SNF or MassHealth long-term-care claim whose submission predates the finalization timestamp of the required assessment, and an authorship edit flagging assessment fields signed or altered by a user whose license scope does not permit that entry.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Idaho
FraudEntity: Bloom Care LLC (urgent care operator); its owners
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Department of Veterans Affairs
SchemeSummary: Bloom Care allegedly used the COVID-19 pandemic as a pretext to bill federal health care programs for medically unnecessary strep and influenza tests on asymptomatic patients at its Idaho and New Mexico urgent care centers, and billed high-level evaluation and management codes for COVID-19 patients by exaggerating time spent and complexity when lower-paying codes were warranted; settled for $3,000,000 with no admission of liability.
WaysToIdentify: Both prongs are visible in claim mix: rapid strep and influenza test volume per urgent-care visit approaching one-to-one with no supporting symptom diagnosis codes (pharyngitis, fever, ILI) on the same claim, and an E&M distribution skewed to the highest levels for a COVID-era visit population. Comparing each site's test-per-visit ratio and high-level E&M share against same-type urgent-care peers in the same period would have surfaced this before payment.
FeaturesToCreate: Claim-level edit: pend or deny strep/influenza rapid tests billed without a companion symptom diagnosis on the same encounter, and compute per-site test-per-encounter ratios monthly versus urgent-care peers. Separately profile each site's and clinician's high-level E&M share and time-based code use for respiratory encounters; above the calibrated percentile, route to prepay documentation request for the visit note substantiating time and complexity.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Matthew Maluchnik
FraudTypeAll: Other - Unknown; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: In an annual collections announcement, the USAO noted that Matthew Maluchnik was sentenced in October 2023 for health care fraud and making false statements on his tax returns, and was ordered to pay $941,068.50 in restitution; in April 2024 the office transferred $715,979.50 in forfeited funds to the court for payment to his victims. The release does not describe the billing mechanics or payer. (The same release also listed a separate $7.6 million False Claims Act settlement with the Cleveland Clinic Foundation over federal grant applications and progress reports.)
WaysToIdentify: The release is an annual collections round-up and does not describe the billing mechanic or even the payer for the health care fraud count, and the accompanying Cleveland Clinic matter concerns federal grant applications rather than claims; there is nothing specific a payer could have screened prepay. The grant prong is detectable only through grant-office review of progress reports against effort reporting and payroll.
FeaturesToCreate: No case-specific payer control derives. Nearest applicable: for grant-funded entities, reconcile reported personnel effort and progress-report milestones against payroll and subaward ledgers before drawdown approval; for the health care count, standard provider-level billing-outlier profiling versus same-specialty peers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Richard Hyland (Department of Veterans Affairs firefighter)
State_County: New Jersey - Lyons (Lyons VA Medical Center)
PayerName: U.S. Department of Labor (federal workers' compensation program)
SchemeSummary: Hyland, a VA firefighter who began receiving federal workers' compensation benefits after a 2014 back injury, falsely certified annually to the U.S. Department of Labor that he was not working or volunteering elsewhere while in fact working as a tow truck and long-haul truck driver and volunteering at his local fire department, collecting $479,341.26 in benefits from March 2017 through December 2024.
WaysToIdentify: No claims adjudication is involved; this is benefit eligibility fraud on annual workers' compensation self-certifications. It is catchable before each benefit continuation by matching the claimant's SSN against state wage/new-hire records, commercial-driver licensing and DOT/CDL medical certification files, and employer quarterly wage filings, all of which would show earnings and a CDL while he certified no employment.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a recertification cross-match: before approving each annual EN-1032 certification, run the claimant's identifiers against the National Directory of New Hires, state UI wage files, and CDL/DOT registries, and flag any earnings record or occupational license inconsistent with the certified non-work status. Firing suspends further benefit payments pending an eligibility interview and documentation request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Vault Medical Services, P.A.; Vault Medical Services of New Jersey, P.C.
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Vault provided COVID-19 specimen collection and vaccine administration via telehealth and in-person sites and billed the HRSA COVID-19 Uninsured Program for patients who actually had active health insurance, allegedly ignoring verified insurance information on file and failing to correct known patient data-integrity gaps; resolved for $8 million with no determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: The Uninsured Program was payer-of-last-resort, so every claim should have failed an insurance check first; the fraud is visible by re-running eligibility (Medicare/Medicaid/commercial via clearinghouse 270/271 and state Medicaid eligibility files) against the beneficiary identifiers on the submitted claims. Additional signals: the provider's own intake records already contained verified insurance for many of these patients, and per-provider rates of paid-uninsured claims that later match an active coverage record are far above peers.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit on every uninsured-program claim: automated 270/271 eligibility ping plus Medicare/Medicaid enrollment match on name, DOB and identifiers; deny if any active coverage exists on the date of service and require documented denial or non-coverage otherwise. Add a submitter-level monthly rate of retroactively-matched insured claims and, above the calibrated percentile, suspend further uninsured-program payment and require the provider's intake insurance fields to accompany each claim.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Omnicell (Delaware-based VA contractor selling/leasing medical device hardware and software)
SchemeSummary: Omnicell held a federal contract to sell and lease medical device hardware and software to the VA at set or negotiated discounted prices but did not always charge the correct contract prices; although it issued credits when specific customers raised pricing concerns, it failed to systemically correct known pricing-system errors or identify and refund other federal customers it had overcharged. Resolved under the False Claims Act following a qui tam complaint by a former employee, with $4,366,660 paid ($2,183,330 as restitution to VA; $785,998.80 to the relator).
WaysToIdentify: This is a contract-pricing overcharge, detectable at invoice adjudication by comparing each line's charged price against the awarded contract/schedule price file and any negotiated discount terms for that ordering agency. Signals include the same catalog item invoiced at different prices across federal customers, credits issued to complaining customers but no corresponding correction for identical overcharges elsewhere, and price variances that persist after a known system defect is identified.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a contract price-compliance edit in accounts payable: for each invoice line, join item/SKU to the active contract price file and reject or hold lines priced above the contract ceiling, including lease-schedule equivalents. Add a variance-recidivism monitor that, whenever a vendor issues a pricing credit, automatically re-prices all other federal invoices for the same SKU in the lookback window and generates a refund demand; escalate to contract review when overcharge rate exceeds the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Gregory Schreck (vice president of the company that operated DMERx); DMERx (internet-based platform)
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care benefit programs; other insurers
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Schreck and co-conspirators used misleading mailers, TV ads and offshore call centers to harvest Medicare beneficiaries' personal information and consent to unnecessary orthotic braces and pain creams, then used the DMERx platform to generate signed doctors' orders from telemedicine companies that paid doctors to sign without examining patients; DME suppliers and pharmacies paid kickbacks for the orders and billed Medicare and other insurers over $1 billion, of which more than $360 million was paid.
WaysToIdentify: The signal is order-origin concentration: thousands of braces and compounded pain cream claims across many unrelated suppliers all trace to a small set of telemedicine prescribers who have no prior treating relationship with the beneficiary, no other claims for that patient, and impossible cross-state ordering volume in a single day. At adjudication this is visible by joining the DME/pharmacy claim's ordering NPI to that NPI's own E/M claim history, beneficiary geography, and per-day order counts. Marketing origin is also visible in beneficiary complaint logs and in bilateral-brace-set combinations ordered for the same patient across multiple suppliers.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-prescriber surveillance job: per NPI per day, count distinct beneficiaries with DME/compound orders, share with no prior or subsequent E/M encounter by that NPI, and number of distinct states and distinct billing suppliers; fire when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers and route all downstream claims from that NPI to prepay documentation review for the face-to-face encounter. Add a beneficiary-level edit rejecting multi-joint brace sets and topical compound kits ordered by a telehealth-only prescriber within a short window, and an enrolment-side link analysis flagging suppliers sharing addresses, bank accounts or ordering platforms.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Mississippi
FraudEntity: Laron Evans (organizer, purported owner/manager of fake companies); Travious Quinshad Jackson (co-defendant)
State_County: Mississippi - Warren County (Vicksburg); Mississippi - Forrest County; Maryland; Minnesota; Florida - Orlando
PayerName: Third-party Health Savings Account administrator companies (Maryland and Minnesota)
FraudTypeAll: IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Evans sent stolen personal identifying information for 57 real people to a Maryland third-party benefits administrator, falsely claiming they were employees of a fictitious company, so the administrator created and pre-funded Health Savings Account debit cards mailed to Vicksburg addresses; Evans and Jackson drained the cards on gift cards and goods, and Evans used proceeds to buy a $44,335 Suburban, then repeated the scheme with a Minnesota administrator (seeking $91,000 in HSA funding) while on bond in violation of court order. Restitution figures span both defendants ($1,917,231.26 for Evans and $302,099.34 for Jackson); Jackson received 2 years.
WaysToIdentify: This is HSA/benefits-administrator account funding fraud rather than claim adjudication, but the payer-side signal is at enrolment: a newly registered employer group with no verifiable EIN wage history, 57 enrollees whose SSNs and addresses do not match the employer's state, and dozens of pre-funded debit cards mailed to a handful of common Vicksburg addresses. Card spend at gift-card and retail merchants rather than health merchant category codes is a second, near-real-time signal. Repetition with a second administrator in another state would be caught by an industry shared-fraud registry.
FeaturesToCreate: At group onboarding, verify the employer against state wage/UI filings and EIN registration and score the census for identity anomalies (address clustering, mismatch between enrollee state and employer state, SSN-name mismatch on eCBSV/consumer-data match); hold card issuance and funding pending verification when the score exceeds the calibrated threshold. Post-issuance, monitor MCC codes and block/suspend cards with non-qualified-merchant spend, and add cross-administrator negative-file sharing keyed to mailing address, device and bank account.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Dr. Scott Saffold (physician); Chesapeake Bay, ENT, P.C. (his medical practice)
State_County: Virginia - Virginia Beach; Virginia - Belle Haven (Accomack County)
SchemeSummary: Government alleged the doctor and his ENT practice billed federal and state health programs for medically unnecessary balloon sinus dilations - performing the procedure on six sinuses even absent medical indication - and staged the procedures side-by-side at separate times to increase reimbursement, while also billing CPT 31235 (endoscopy with sphenoid sinusoscopy) for services not actually performed. Resolved for $625,000 following a qui tam whistleblower suit.
WaysToIdentify: Balloon sinus dilation billed on the maximum number of sinuses per patient, and repeatedly staged on separate dates for the same beneficiary, stands out in claim-line counts of sinus-dilation codes per patient per year versus same-specialty ENT peers.
