Absence of supporting diagnosis history (documented chronic sinusitis, failed medical management) and absence of prior imaging claims in the beneficiary history is checkable at adjudication. Billing CPT 31235 alongside dilation codes at near-100% frequency is an unbundling/never-performed pattern visible in code-pair ratios.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: for each beneficiary, sum sinus-dilation units across all dates within a rolling year; when units reach the anatomic maximum or the same sinus is billed twice, or when there is no antecedent chronic sinusitis diagnosis plus CT/imaging claim, pend the claim for operative note and medical-management documentation. Add a provider-level ratio monitor for 31235 billed with dilation and for staged same-patient sessions, flagging outliers versus ENT peers for prepay review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: NEXT Bio-Research Services LLC, d/b/a NEXT Molecular Analytics (clinical laboratory)
SchemeSummary: NEXT allegedly paid doctors in Texas and Arkansas thousands of dollars disguised as consulting and medical director fees to induce them to order NEXT laboratory tests, and paid independent contractor marketers commissions based on the volume and value of referrals, then billed Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE for the resulting lab tests. Resolved for $758,000 under the False Claims Act following a qui tam suit; relators receive $113,700.
WaysToIdentify: The kickback shows up as extreme referral concentration: a handful of ordering physicians in two states account for the bulk of one lab's volume, with per-physician test ordering far above same-specialty peers and panels ordered uniformly regardless of diagnosis. Cross-referencing CMS Open Payments and the lab's disclosed medical-director/consulting arrangements against those same physicians' referral volume exposes payments tracking referrals. Marketer commissions are visible only in the lab's books, so post-payment audit or CID is the route for that element.
FeaturesToCreate: Build an ordering-physician/lab dyad monitor computing each lab's share of a physician's total lab orders, the physician's rank in that lab's revenue, and growth after the first Open Payments transfer from that lab; fire when concentration and payment coincidence exceed calibrated thresholds and place the lab's claims from those NPIs on prepay medical-necessity review. At enrolment/revalidation, require attestation and disclosure of all medical-director and consulting agreements with ordering providers and reconcile against actual referral volume.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Dr. Ameet Vohra (owner); Vohra Wound Physicians Management LLC
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Vohra, a nationwide bedside wound-care provider for nursing home and skilled nursing facility patients, allegedly pressured, trained and financially incentivized its physicians to perform debridements at as many visits as possible regardless of medical need, and programmed its EHR/billing software so Medicare was always billed for the higher-reimbursed surgical excisional debridement (even when only routine non-surgical wound management or no procedure occurred) with false supporting documentation, plus non-billable evaluation and management services; resolved for $45 million plus a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement.
WaysToIdentify: The mechanic is a near-invariant coding profile: excisional debridement billed at essentially every visit for every nursing-home patient, with the surgical-debridement code chosen at a rate approaching 100% of wound encounters, far above same-specialty peers, and repeated debridements on the same wound without documented improvement or wound-measurement change. Facility-level clustering (one group billing debridement for most residents of a SNF) and E/M billed with the procedure add signals. All of this is visible in claim-line code mixes and per-beneficiary longitudinal series at adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: Provider-level edit: compute the excisional-versus-non-excisional debridement ratio and debridements per beneficiary per 90 days per rendering NPI and per group TIN; when both exceed the calibrated percentile versus wound-care peers, apply prepay documentation requests requiring operative note with tissue level, instrument, and wound measurements. Add a same-wound repeat-debridement counter that pends after the calibrated number of sessions absent documented size change, and a bundling edit denying E/M billed with the debridement on the same visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: VRA Enterprises, LLC dba Precision Rx (pharmacy)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Retention of Overpayment; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Under the CMS OTC COVID-19 Test Demonstration Project (which reimbursed $12 per test, up to eight tests per beneficiary per month), the Tampa pharmacy billed Medicare Part B for over-the-counter COVID-19 tests it never shipped to beneficiaries, including roughly 136,491 January 2023 claims for tests not shipped until April 2023, and despite internally acknowledging it should refund Medicare for unshipped tests, it retained the payments.
WaysToIdentify: Because the demonstration paid a fixed amount per test, the only real evidence of delivery is shipment; claims can be matched against carrier tracking/proof-of-delivery data, and here 136,491 January claims had ship dates months later. A prepay signal is a single pharmacy billing the per-beneficiary monthly maximum for enormous numbers of beneficiaries, many out of its service area or with no other dispensing history at that pharmacy. Retention after internal acknowledgment is a 60-day overpayment issue reachable post-payment via self-disclosure and audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Require submission of a shipment tracking identifier on each OTC test claim and hold payment until a delivery-confirmation feed validates a ship date on or before the date of service; auto-deny when ship date postdates service date. Add pharmacy-level monitors for share of beneficiaries at the monthly cap, beneficiary-to-pharmacy distance, and share of beneficiaries with no other claims at that pharmacy, with payment suspension and full prepay review above calibrated thresholds.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Sonya Lenise Davis (owner of Sonya's Braiding)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Davis submitted a PPP loan application to the SBA for her business, Sonya's Braiding, inflating employee count and income, and helped co-conspirators submit fake IRS wage forms and fake bank statements to support their own PPP applications, obtaining more than $85,000 in COVID relief loan funds.
WaysToIdentify: This is SBA loan fraud with no health care claim component, so no claim-adjudication control applies. The lender-side signals were verifiable at underwriting: employee counts and payroll on the application versus IRS transcripts (Form 941/W-2/W-3) obtained by consent, and bank statements validated through direct account-data feeds rather than uploaded PDFs. Clusters of applications sharing a preparer, IP address, or identically formatted wage forms are the network signal.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side claims control applies; nearest control is an underwriting verification service that requires IRS transcript matching of reported payroll and API-based bank-account verification before disbursement, auto-declining or pending when reported payroll exceeds transcript payroll beyond tolerance. Add document-forensics and application-clustering checks (same preparer, device, IP, template metadata) that route grouped applications to manual review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Walgreen Co. (national pharmacy chain)
SchemeSummary: Walgreens pharmacies allegedly reported inflated 'usual and customary' prices for certain generic medications to MassHealth and Georgia Medicaid, which reimburse at the lowest of four price points, causing the programs to pay more than they should have for those generics; resolved for over $2.8 million following a qui tam whistleblower suit.
WaysToIdentify: Usual-and-customary reporting fraud is detectable by comparing the U&C submitted on Medicaid claims for a given generic/NDC/quantity against the chain's own cash and discount-generic program prices for the same drug in the same store and period, which payers can obtain via price-list submission or secret-shopper price surveys. A prepay signal is a store's Medicaid U&C sitting well above the discount-program price and above other pharmacies' U&C for the same NDC. Full quantification typically needs post-payment audit of the pharmacy's cash transaction file.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a U&C reasonableness edit: for each pharmacy/NDC/quantity, compare submitted U&C to the pharmacy's registered discount-program price and to the same-chain and market median; pend or reprice to the lower amount when the submitted value exceeds the calibrated deviation. Require periodic attestation and upload of discount-program price schedules at contracting and audit-sample cash claims to validate, with recoupment of the differential.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York; U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Walgreens Boots Alliance; Walgreen Co. and subsidiaries (national pharmacy chain)
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care programs
SchemeSummary: Walgreens pharmacists allegedly filled millions of invalid controlled substance prescriptions - excessive opioid quantities, early refills, and 'trinity' drug combinations - despite clear red flags, and then billed Medicare and other federal health programs for those unlawful prescriptions. Walgreens agreed to pay $300 million (plus an additional $50 million if sold/merged before FY2032) and entered DEA and HHS-OIG compliance agreements; relators receive 17.25% of the FCA recovery.
WaysToIdentify: Invalid-prescription red flags are computable from the payer's own pharmacy claim stream and PDMP data: early refills before the calculated days-supply exhaustion, cumulative MME above thresholds, and 'trinity' co-dispensing of an opioid, benzodiazepine and muscle relaxant, often across multiple prescribers and pharmacies. Prescriber-level concentration (one prescriber generating most of a store's controlled dispensings, long patient travel distances, cash-alongside patterns) is visible at adjudication. Store- and chain-level rates of these flags versus peers identify where volume pressure overrode review.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits at the pharmacy claim: reject or pend refills submitted before the calibrated percentage of days supply has elapsed, pend claims that push cumulative daily MME above the calibrated level, and pend trinity combinations pending prescriber consultation documentation. Add store- and prescriber-level dashboards of flag rates and multi-prescriber/multi-pharmacy patient counts, with prepay review, PDMP cross-check requirements and referral where rates exceed peers.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs; U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois; U.S. Attorney's Offices for the Northern District of Illinois, Middle District of Florida, District of Maryland, Eastern District of New York, and Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Walgreens Boots Alliance; Walgreen Co. and various subsidiaries (national retail pharmacy chain)
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care programs (TRICARE/Defense Health Agency; OPM FEHB; Department of Veterans Affairs; Department of Labor programs)
SchemeSummary: DOJ alleged Walgreens pharmacists knowingly filled millions of invalid controlled substance prescriptions (excessive opioid quantities, early refills, 'trinity' drug combinations) despite red flags, while the company pressured pharmacists to fill quickly and withheld prescriber data from them, then billed Medicare and other federal health programs for those unlawful prescriptions. Walgreens agreed to pay $300 million (based on ability to pay) plus an additional $50 million if sold, merged or transferred before fiscal year 2032, with whistleblower relators receiving 17.25% of the FCA recovery, and entered into a DEA memorandum of agreement and a five-year HHS-OIG Corporate Integrity Agreement.
WaysToIdentify: Identical mechanic to the companion case: the payer's own claim history supports detection of early refills, high cumulative MME, and trinity combinations, and PDMP linkage shows multi-prescriber/multi-pharmacy shopping before the fill is paid. Withholding prescriber red-flag data from pharmacists is an internal control failure, but the payer can supply the missing view by feeding prescriber-level risk scores back into adjudication. Chain-level comparison of red-flag rates and fill-speed metrics per store versus peers highlights the pressure effect.
FeaturesToCreate: Implement controlled-substance prepay edits (early refill against calculated days supply, cumulative MME ceiling, trinity concurrency, duplicate-therapy across prescribers) that pend for documented prescriber verification rather than auto-pay. Publish a prescriber risk indicator to pharmacies at point of sale and monitor store-level red-flag override rates, escalating outlier stores to prepay review, targeted audit and corporate-integrity reporting.
FeatureCategory: Controlled Substance Point Of Sale Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Marlenin Vito (Medicaid Coordinator at assisted living facility; later bookkeeper)
State_County: Connecticut - Stamford (Fairfield County); Connecticut - Hartford; New York - White Plains (Westchester County)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: As Medicaid Coordinator at a Stamford assisted living facility, Vito generated roughly 500 checks from the facility's system, forged a coworker's signature, cashed them as if disbursing cash to residents, kept about $310,820, and falsified ledger entries debiting residents' patient trust accounts; she also pocketed residents' COVID-19 Economic Impact Payments and continued deducting for cancelled supplemental insurance. After termination she stole about $23,558 from an alarm company (false overtime and personal orders) and about $27,179 from a Hartford law firm via forged 'Petty Cash' checks.
WaysToIdentify: This is embezzlement from resident patient-trust funds and stolen stimulus checks, not claim submission, so it is not detectable at claim adjudication; the payer/regulator route is patient-trust-fund audit. Observable signals include ~500 checks with a single signature pattern, cash-disbursement volume per resident far above facility norms, ledger debits without resident signature receipts, and continued insurance deductions for a cancelled policy. Bank data plus trust ledger reconciliation surfaces it.
FeaturesToCreate: Require facilities to submit periodic resident trust-fund reconciliations and build an audit analytic on the ledger extract: per-resident cash disbursement frequency and amount versus facility and statewide norms, checks lacking dual signature or resident acknowledgment, and deductions for terminated coverage; fire for on-site audit and license action. Enforce segregation of duties and dual authorization as a survey/condition-of-participation check at the facility level.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report And Related Party Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Michele Devine (executive director of Southeastern Regional Action Council on Substance Abuse, Inc. (SERAC))
FraudType: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
FraudTypeAll: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: As executive director of SERAC, a Connecticut nonprofit funded by state DMHAS and federal HHS/SAMHSA grants for substance abuse, gambling and mental health services, Devine used organization funds beginning around 2008 for personal expenses including home appliances, travel, timeshare fees, spa stays and private school donations; she pleaded guilty to wire fraud and was ordered to pay $397,064.93 restitution and a $2,000 fine plus 24 months in prison.
WaysToIdentify: No claims were billed; this is grant-fund embezzlement, so the control sits with the grantor's financial monitoring rather than claim adjudication. Signals available pre-disbursement include cost reports and drawdown requests containing unallowable categories (appliances, travel, timeshare fees, spa charges, donations), vendor payments to consumer retailers and resorts, and expenditures authorized solely by the executive director. Single-audit findings and bank/credit-card level transaction review would surface these.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a grant expenditure screening rule over the grantee's general-ledger/drawdown detail: classify vendors by merchant category and flag any spend in personal-consumption categories, any single-approver transaction above the calibrated amount, and any card spend outside approved cost categories; hold the next drawdown pending documentation. Require annual independent audit submission and dual-approval attestation as a condition of continued funding.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Ashley Jackson (sole owner of Roc City Transport); Roc City Transport
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Upcoding; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Jackson, sole owner of Roc City Transport, billed Medicaid for non-emergency medical transportation trips that were never performed, billed individual rides as higher-paying group rides, and paid kickbacks to Medicaid recipients (mostly traveling to Rochester methadone clinics) to drive themselves instead of using Roc City; approximately $40,123.29 in fraudulent billing.
WaysToIdentify: Phantom NEMT trips are testable against the member's own service claims: a paid trip on a date with no corresponding methadone-clinic or medical encounter, or trips for members whose clinic dosing records show self-transport. Group-ride upcoding is detectable when a claimed group trip has only one member billed for that vehicle/time slot, or when the same vehicle is billed as group for overlapping single passengers. Kickbacks to recipients typically require post-payment interviews, though gaps between paid trips and any provider encounter give the lead.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: for each NEMT claim, require a matching same-day medical encounter claim or authorized standing order for the member; deny or pend when absent. Add a group-ride validator that requires two or more distinct member trip legs sharing vehicle, driver and time window before the group modifier/rate pays, plus GPS/trip-log submission and provider-level monitoring of group-ride share and trips-per-vehicle-hour feasibility.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Suhail Aponte (sole principal and registered agent of Minds Cornerstone LLC dba Minds Cornerstone Behavior Therapy Services); Minds Cornerstone LLC
PayerName: Medicaid (Connecticut Medical Assistance Program / HUSKY, Connecticut Department of Social Services)
SchemeSummary: Aponte, an unlicensed owner of an autism services company, and a co-conspirator billed Connecticut Medicaid roughly $1.88 million for applied behavior analysis services to children with autism that were never rendered - including services on dates when payroll records show employees were not paid, BCBA supervision billed without the corresponding technician code, services for patients who were hospitalized inpatient, and visits parents and former employees confirmed never occurred. She agreed to forfeit about $459,000 in seized funds plus additional accounts and two Hartford land parcels.
WaysToIdentify: Multiple independent cross-checks were available before payment: ABA claims on dates when no staff were on payroll, BCBA supervision codes billed without the paired technician session code, and service dates overlapping inpatient hospital stays visible in the same Medicaid claim history. Owner/agency licensure and rendering-staff credential status are checkable at enrolment. Provider-level billed hours per rendering staff member exceeding feasible working hours is a further adjudication-time signal.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits: deny ABA supervision codes with no matching technician direct-service claim for the same member/date; deny any outpatient ABA claim overlapping an inpatient facility claim; require rendering-provider NPI with active credential on every line and reject unlicensed/uncredentialed renderers. Add an agency-level capacity check comparing billed service hours per rendering staff to reported payroll/roster hours, suspending payment and requesting payroll and session notes when billed hours exceed reported hours.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Michelle Shropshire (WMATA train operator, scheme organizer); Harlisha Jones (WMATA train operator); Sharon Washington (WMATA employee); Selethia Blake (WMATA employee); Brady Turner (WMATA employee); Lushawn Foreman (WMATA employee); Margot Jackson (WMATA employee)
PayerName: American Family Life Assurance Company of Columbus (AFLAC)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: WMATA train operators submitted fraudulent health care and short-term disability insurance claims to AFLAC under Jones's policies for injuries, treatments and disability periods that never occurred, supporting them with forged medical excuse notes and physician's statements bearing real doctors' identities and forged signatures; after AFLAC paid, claimants kicked back about 20% of the proceeds to Shropshire, who also helped numerous other WMATA employees file similar false claims (AFLAC paid ~$58,750 to Jones and at least $362,035.14 across all participants). Five co-participants pleaded guilty and Shropshire was later sentenced to 24 months.
WaysToIdentify: This is disability/supplemental insurance claim fraud detectable at the carrier's claim intake: multiple claimants from a single employer and single agent-of-record, doctors' statements and excuse notes with matching template text and signatures that do not match the physician's file signature or come from practices with no corresponding treatment claim. Direct provider verification (calling the NPI's office) and checking for any medical claim history for the alleged treatment would have failed. Kickbacks to the organizer are only visible post-payment through banking records among claimants.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a claim-cluster detector keyed to employer, policy writer/agent, and attesting physician: fire when claimant counts per employer-agent-physician triple exceed calibrated norms, and require independent verification of the physician statement (direct-to-office callback or portal attestation) before benefit payment. Add document forensics on submitted notes (signature match against verified physician signature, template/metadata duplication, sequential note numbering) and pend payment on any positive hit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Western New York Medical P.C. (WNY Medical) (health care provider)
State_County: New York - Erie County; New York - Niagara County
SchemeSummary: WNY Medical billed Medicare for Chronic Care Management encounters under CPT codes requiring at least 20 minutes of clinical staff time per month, but for a portion of those encounters clinical staff did not actually provide the required 20 minutes during the billed month; the provider agreed to pay $251,477 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: CCM codes are time-based, so the payer can require the reported cumulative clinical-staff minutes and compare them against the practice's own time-logged EHR data; a practice billing the code for nearly all enrolled patients every month, with total implied staff minutes exceeding available staff hours, is an adjudication-time outlier. Absence of any documented care-plan or interim contact claim/encounter in the month is a second signal. Precise per-encounter minute shortfalls generally require post-payment record review.
FeaturesToCreate: Build a CCM capacity edit: per TIN per month, multiply billed CCM units by the code's minimum minutes and compare with reported clinical-staff FTE minutes; fire and pend when implied minutes exceed available capacity or when the share of enrolled patients billed each month exceeds the calibrated percentile versus peers. Also require beneficiary consent and care-plan attestation on file and sample-request time logs for flagged practices.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Jessica Stuart (unlicensed provider impersonating a Board Certified Behavior Analyst); Helping Hands Academy, LLC (ABA services provider)
SchemeSummary: Stuart, who had no degree, license, or BCBA certification, stole the professional identity of a legitimate Board Certified Behavior Analyst so that Helping Hands Academy could bill Medicaid for applied behavior analysis services she performed but was not qualified to provide; over 1,900 fraudulent claims for 12 autistic children caused about $369,439 in Medicaid losses while Stuart was paid at least $146,000. She was originally sentenced to 27 months, and on Feb 26, 2025 received an additional 10 months for supervised release violations involving misuse of a SNAP card and false unemployment benefit certifications.
WaysToIdentify: The core signal is credential impersonation, catchable at enrolment and at adjudication: the rendering BCBA's certification number can be verified live against the BACB registry, and the real certificant's other billing footprint, address, and taxpayer identity would conflict with the agency's roster. Impossible service volume attributed to a single BCBA across 12 children, and a rendering NPI whose demographics do not match the agency's employment records, are visible before payment. Identity-theft confirmation comes from contacting the certificant of record.
FeaturesToCreate: At enrolment/revalidation and on every claim line, validate rendering-provider certification number, name, DOB and NPI against the certifying-board registry and NPPES, rejecting mismatches and pending claims where the same certificant is billed by multiple unrelated agencies. Add a per-certificant capacity monitor (billed service hours per day/week versus feasible maximum) with payment suspension and identity verification outreach to the certificant when exceeded.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Lourdes Navarro (co-owner of Matias Clinical Laboratory d/b/a Health Care Providers Laboratory); Imran Shams (co-owner); Matias Clinical Laboratory d/b/a Health Care Providers Laboratory (HCPL)
PayerName: Medicare; HRSA COVID-19 Uninsured Program; private health insurance company (unnamed)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Owners of a clinical lab obtained nasal swab specimens and COVID-19 test orders from nursing homes, assisted living/rehab facilities and schools, then ran expensive respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests on most specimens although only COVID-19 screening had been ordered and RPP tests were not medically justified for asymptomatic individuals; approximately $369 million was billed to Medicare, the HRSA COVID-19 Uninsured Program and a private insurer, yielding about $46.7 million in reimbursements. Figures span both co-owners: Navarro received 9 years and forfeited $11,662,939 (total seized/forfeited from both defendants $14,518,485) plus $46,735,400 restitution, while Shams was sentenced to 10 years (and a separate 5-year sentence in EDNY).
WaysToIdentify: The mechanic is add-on panel testing beyond the order: a lab where nearly every COVID-19 screening specimen also generates a high-cost respiratory pathogen panel, with panels billed for asymptomatic congregate-setting and school populations and no symptomatic diagnosis on the claim, is a clear adjudication-time outlier versus lab peers. Requisition/order documentation would not support the RPP. Duplicate billing across Medicare, the HRSA Uninsured Program and a commercial payer for the same specimen is detectable by cross-program matching on beneficiary, date and specimen.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edit: pend or deny multiplex RPP codes billed with a COVID-19 test on the same specimen/date absent a symptomatic diagnosis, and require submission of the signed requisition showing the panel was ordered. Add lab-level ratio monitors (RPP-to-COVID-test ratio, share of claims from congregate/school settings, panel rate versus lab peers) triggering payment suspension, plus a cross-payer/HRSA duplicate-claim match on beneficiary-date-specimen.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section (National Rapid Response Strike Force) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Alexandra Gehrke (owner of wound graft companies, incl. Apex Medical LLC); Jeffrey King (co-owner of wound graft company, Gehrke's husband)
PayerName: Medicare; TRICARE; CHAMPVA; commercial health insurers
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Gehrke and King used medically untrained 'sales representatives' to canvass elderly Arizona Medicare beneficiaries (many in hospice) for wounds of any kind and to order the largest available amniotic membrane skin-substitute allografts, then had contracted nurse practitioners apply whatever was ordered regardless of medical necessity - including large grafts on small wounds, multiple grafts per wound, grafts on non-existent wounds and on dying palliative patients - and billed roughly $1.21 billion to Medicare, TRICARE, CHAMPVA and commercial insurers (paid $614.9 million). Gehrke's companies took over $279 million and King's company $130 million in kickbacks from the wholesale graft distributor for ordering its grafts, and she paid kickbacks onward to the sales reps; figures and payments span both defendants (restitution, forfeiture and separate False Claims Act settlements of $279.9 million and $30 million).</thinking>
WaysToIdentify: Skin-substitute graft claims carry size units, so the payer can compare billed graft square centimeters against the documented wound surface area and flag grafts far exceeding wound size, multiple grafts per wound, and repeat applications without wound closure progress. Overlap with an active hospice election or a terminal-diagnosis palliative population is directly visible in the same beneficiary's Medicare history and is clinically incompatible with aggressive grafting. Extreme cost concentration in one product/wholesaler across a few NP rendering NPIs, and rendering volume per NP exceeding feasible visits per day, are adjudication-time outliers; the distributor kickbacks require post-payment financial audit.
FeaturesToCreate: Prepay edits: deny or pend skin-substitute claims where billed graft area exceeds documented wound area beyond tolerance, where units per wound per session exceed the calibrated maximum, or where the beneficiary has an active hospice election; require photographs, wound measurements and prior conservative-care documentation. Add provider/product monitors for grafts per rendering NPI per day, applications per wound, single-manufacturer concentration and per-beneficiary allowed amounts versus wound-care peers, with prepay review and payment suspension above calibrated thresholds.
